units.la: Reuc vixit artes sed an rationem qui enim non ignorant sed sunt sine ratione seu ratione deficiuntur. Qui sunt sine ratione seu qui rationem tollunt, athei sunt [?] exceptio. Gabrat Caput vestum tuum. Rationem nesciunt. Quotlibet arii sunt, Ius omne tollunt.
units.tr: Reuc lived by the arts, but by reason; for those who do not ignore it but are without reason, or fall short of reason. Those who are without reason, or who remove reason, are atheists [?] with an exception. ... They do not know reason. However many they are, they remove all right.

units.la: Ius natio est ut nisi. Iuspositivum est et ars sed determinatio [?] applicatio. Obedire est executare vn ordinem. Modificatio iuris naturalis. Iusibile nititur fixio.
units.tr: Right is nature, as unless. Positive right is art, but determination [?] application. To obey is to carry out an order. Modification of natural right. Right rests on fixed ground.

units.la: on ne fait point de compte d'une visite en passant, d'une visite qui n'est exprey, de dessein, d'on n'en a obligation qu'au [?] visité, qu'on n'en merue pas une tout exprey.
units.tr: One makes no account of a visit in passing, of a visit that is not expressed or intended; one owes it only to the visited, and one does not deserve a wholly expressed one.

units.la: non est Reductio ad quarto Inter honestum et non honestum Sed Ratio ngm abire pt In nāam non rationis Scientia non pt deiici ad opinionem, nedu ad errorem nec Iure potest Opinio gaudere priuilegijs Scientiæ.
units.tr: There is no reduction to the fourth between the honest and the not honest; but reason ... science cannot be cast down to opinion, much less to error, nor can opinion by right enjoy the privileges of science.

units.tr: Virtue cannot be brought down to vice ... [obscure], it is not false, not itself but abiding ... deceives.

units.la: NEque rem insolentem facimus, Amplissime Præsul, qui librum hunc, jam alterius Illustrissimi Herois nomini à nobis inscriptum, tuo quoq; dicamus; siquidem in promtu sunt exempla multorum ac sapientum virorum, qui idem factitarunt: & justissimam habuimus causam, quare ita nobis faciundum existimaremus. Quum enim plurima maximaq; in nos beneficia contuleris, & quidem alterum quoq; nostrûm ante aliquot annos honorificis conditionibus in Hiberniam evocatum (longè aliud iter tunc, atq; in Patriam reditum meditantem) prolixè admodum habueris, atq; propensissimo animo, omnibusq; veræ ac summæ benevolentiæ indiciis exinde jugiter prosecutus sis: committere non potuimus, quin hoc saltem gratitudinis nostræ monimentum extare vellemus, atq; publicè, quantum tibi deberemus, testatum facere. Neq; verò alienum à te videri potest hoc opus, qui tantus es in Philosophia quoque, atq; in omni humaniorum literarum parte, acsi tota vitâ hoc tantùm egisses, atq; ijs studijs totum te dedidisses: quum tamen is sis Theologus ac Episcopus, qui non gradu ac dignatione magis, quàm operibus ac meritis, principem in isto ordine locum obtineas. Namq; ut nihil dicamus de rara admodum, & hostibus quoq; depraedicata vitae morumq; sanctimonia; ac de egregijs & nervosissimis scriptis, propugnandae contra adversarios divinae Veritati publicatis: quis satis celebraverit sedulam tuam ac laboriosissimam in docendo Christi populo, inq; annunciando Dei verbo assiduitatem: cui muneri ita semper (nullis honoribus mutatus, contra quàm in alijs plerisq; videmus) incubuisti, ut nullo unquam praetextu, ne adversae quidem valetudinis, quamdiu ea non prorsus prostrata esset, & ubicunq; locorum agens, vacationem ab eo tibi esse volueris, neq; committere, quominus singulis diebus Dominicis sacrum suggestum conscendens, Fidelium Gregem cum cura de rebus ad salutem aeternam pertinentibus instrueres, atq; efficacissime cohortareris. ad quod exemplum si se composuissent permulti de isto ordine, qui nunc haud contenti neglexisse penitus ista ad functionem suam praecipue pertinentia, omnem insuper operam suam in adulteranda atq; destruenda vera Religione collocarunt; haud tantum odij atq; invidiae tum sibimetipsis, tum & universo Episcoporum ordini in Anglia conflavissent, neq; tanta unquam in eum tempestas ibi coorta fuisset: quae nunc nisi eo de medio sublato, atq; penitus extincto, videtur finem non habitura. Nos Dominum Iesum comprecamur, ut & ista, quâ optimum, componat; & tibi, qui adeo fideliter ipsi inseruis, omnia vera bona abunde largiatur. Londini 3o. Iulij. Dublin 12o. Iulij: Anno Christi MDXLI.
units.tr: Most distinguished prelate, we are not doing anything unusual in dedicating this book to you as well, though it already bears the name of another most illustrious hero. Many learned men have done the same, and we had a most just reason for thinking we ought to do so. You have bestowed very many and very great kindnesses upon us. When another of us was summoned to Ireland some years ago with honourable terms, he was then intending quite a different journey, namely a return to his homeland, and you treated him most generously. Since then you have continually shown him every sign of true and great goodwill, with a most willing mind. We could not refrain from wishing that this book at least should stand as a monument of our gratitude, and from declaring publicly how much we owe you. Nor can this work seem out of place to you. You are so great in philosophy too, and in every part of polite literature, as if you had spent your whole life on these alone and devoted yourself entirely to such studies. Yet you are a theologian and bishop who holds the leading place in that order not so much by rank and dignity as by your works and merits. To say nothing of your rare holiness of life and manners, praised even by your enemies, or of your excellent and vigorous writings, published to defend divine truth against adversaries: who could sufficiently celebrate your diligent and most laborious devotion to teaching Christ's people and proclaiming the word of God? You have always applied yourself to this duty, unchanged by any honours, unlike what we see in most others. Under no pretext, not even of poor health, so long as it did not utterly lay you low, and wherever you were acting, have you wished to be excused from it. You have never failed, mounting the sacred pulpit on every Lord's Day, to instruct the flock of the faithful carefully and to exhort them most effectively in matters pertaining to eternal salvation. If many of that order had conformed themselves to this example, rather than, not content with having wholly neglected the things chiefly belonging to their office, devoting all their effort to corrupting and destroying true religion, they would not have kindled such hatred and envy against themselves and against the whole order of bishops in England. Nor would such a storm have arisen there, which now seems likely to have no end unless that order is removed from the midst and utterly extinguished. We pray the Lord Jesus to set these things in order in the best way, and to bestow abundantly every true good upon you, who serve him so faithfully. London, 3 July. Dublin, 12 July, in the year of Christ 1641.

Quod ingens beneficium sicuti certa cum spe à te, cum bono Deo expectant omnes probi, atq; ab eximia ista pietate, integritate, prudentia, aliisq; raris ac maximis dotibus, quibus summam tibi domi forisq; celebritatem comparasti: ita avidissimis animis eum exoptant diem, atq; admoveri anxie desiderant, in quo præsentem te intueri liceat, atq; pedem ponere in possessionem beatæ istius conditionis, quam à te atq; sub tua gubernatione sibi pollicentur. Quanquam autem Viro Principi, & tot tantisq; negotiis distracto, minus aptum videri posset scholasticum hoc munus: summa tamen tua humanitas, & eruditio quoq; haud vulgaris, ac quæ vel inter homines nihil aliud quàm literatos emineret, quam ore plurimorum in te prædicari audivimus, animum nobis addiderunt, ut auderemus hoc qualecunq; scriptum, sed Veritati tamen (quacunq; in re haud contemnendæ, & tibi unicè charæ) eruendæ atq; illustrandæ dicatum, tuo amplissimo nomini inscribere, atq; sub tanti tituli umbra in hominum manus emittere: in quo siquid temeritate peccatum est, ejus rei culpam sedulo deprecamur, ac nos nostraq; omnia tuo benigno favori supplicitèr commendamus. Londini, 3º. Iulij: Dublini, 12º. Iulij: Anno Christi 1641.
units.tr: reformed and restored for the better, or shaken, you are to renew and establish for them their former happiness, indeed greater than their former, and altogether new. This great benefit all good men expect from you, with God's blessing, in sure hope, and from that outstanding piety, integrity, prudence, and other rare and great gifts by which you have won the highest renown at home and abroad. So with the most eager minds they desire that day, and anxiously long for it to come, on which they may be permitted to see you present and set foot in possession of that blessed condition which they promise themselves from you and under your government. Although this scholarly gift may seem less suited to a prince burdened with so many and such great affairs, yet your great kindness, and your learning, which is not common and which, even among men, stands out as nothing other than that of scholars, as we have heard many praise you, have encouraged us to dare to inscribe to your most illustrious name this writing, of whatever sort it is, but dedicated to the bringing forth and clarifying of Truth (which in any matter is not to be despised and is uniquely dear to you), and to send it into men's hands under the shadow of so great a title. If anything has been sinned in rashness in it, we earnestly beg pardon for that fault, and commend ourselves and all our affairs humbly to your gracious favour. London, 3 July; Dublin, 12 July; in the year of Christ 1641.

units.la: VUm in illustri Gymnasio Ultrajectino, ubi non tantùm utriusq; Lingua, sed & Artium Liberalium cognitio diligenter traditur, & in quo nos studiorum tyrocinium posuimus; post perceptam Linguam Latinam atq; Græcam, & Rhetorico quoq; ac Logico stadio decurso, ordine ad Rerum Naturalium disciplinam pervenissemus: una cum eâ magna quoq; Aristotelis admiratio nobis instillata fuit, tanquam Naturæ summi adeoq; unici Mystæ, nihilq; prælectum aut expositum, quàm quod ex ipso haustum esset; neq; quicquam æque inculcatum, quàm despere quicunq; ob eo in Naturæ investigatione discordarent: quorum propterea vix nomina nobis tunc cognoscenda putavimus, nedum ut scripta eorum nobis tractanda aut vel inspicienda existimaremus. Hoc in Aristotelem studium, atq; reliquorum, qui ab eo dissentirent, aversatio, duravit nobis etiam, postquam in tuum, Alma Mater, sinum nos recepimus, atq; ibi Hippocrati ac Galeno nos in Medicinæ disciplinam tradidimus. units.tr: When we were at the famous Gymnasium of Utrecht, where knowledge of both languages and of the liberal arts is diligently taught, and where we made our first beginnings in study, we came, after learning Latin and Greek and completing the course in rhetoric and logic, in due order to the study of natural things. Along with it, a great admiration for Aristotle was instilled in us, as the highest and indeed the only master of nature. Nothing was lectured on or expounded except what had been drawn from him, and nothing was impressed on us more than that anyone who disagreed with him about the investigation of nature was to be despised. For this reason we then thought the names of such men hardly worth knowing, let alone that their writings should be handled by us or even looked at. This devotion to Aristotle, and aversion to all who dissented from him, continued with us even after we had taken ourselves into your bosom, dear Alma Mater, and there had given ourselves over to the discipline of medicine under Hippocrates and Galen. In the beginning, while we devoted effort to physiology (with which all who treat medicine methodically

units.la: A stant, auspicantur) operam damus, & postea quoq;, quando jam ad ulteriora in studio Iatrico provecti, sic quoq; Physicis multum diligentia multumq; succisivi temporis impendebamus; nihil vel publice ex cathedris, vel in privatis prælectionibus audivimus, unde pristina nobis opinio minueretur: nisi quòd mirati interdum sumus, tam altum esse apud Galenum de Forma substantiali silentium. qui tamen scrupulus haud magnopere nos vexabat, neq; ut altius ea de re cogitaremus permovebat, cum videremus Galenicos omnes tanto consensu pro confessa sumere Aristotelicam de Formis doctrinam.
units.tr: begin), and afterwards too, when we had advanced further in medical study, we also gave much diligence and much of our spare time to natural philosophy. Yet we heard nothing, either publicly from the chairs or in private lectures, that would diminish our earlier opinion, except that we sometimes wondered that Galen was so silent about substantial form. This doubt did not trouble us greatly, nor move us to think more deeply about the matter, since we saw all the Galenists accept the Aristotelian doctrine of forms so unanimously as established.

units.la: Sicuti autem omni isto tempore nihil ex Præceptoribus audivimus, quo de pristina super Aristotele atq; Aristotelicis dogmatis sententia deduceremur: ita neq; in jis Autoribus, quos ipsi per nosmet evolvebamus, quicquam offendimus, quod eam labefactaret. Namq; ut reliquos, Aristoteli penitus mancipatos, omittamus; Fernelius & Sennertus (quorum scriptis inter Recentiores, sicuti Galeno inter Priscos, unice delectabamur, diurnâ nocturnâq; manu ea terentes, & legentes ac relegentes; sicuti hodieq; ea merito plurimi facimus) exhibebant quidem nonnulla, imò posterior satis multa, ab Aristotele nunquam prodita, & ipsius philosophiæ superaddita; sic tamen ut fundamenta ipsius relinquerent inconcussa; nullumq; ex præcipuis ejus decretis subverterent aut convellerent, sed ea passim pro veris ac certis usurparent; eaq; velut talia sermonibus suis, etiam quando longius progrediebantur, & res ipsi intentatas incognitasq; explicare adoriebantur, substernerent.
units.tr: Yet during all that time we heard nothing from our teachers that would lead us away from our earlier view of Aristotle and the Aristotelian doctrines, and in the authors we read ourselves we found nothing that would shake it. To omit the rest, who were wholly devoted to Aristotle: Fernel and Sennert, whose writings we alone delighted in among the moderns, as Galen among the ancients, handling them day and night, reading and rereading them, and whom we rightly still hold in high esteem today, did indeed present some things, and indeed rather many, never handed down by Aristotle, which they added to his philosophy. Yet they did so in such a way that they left its foundations unshaken, and overturned or undermined none of its principal decrees, but everywhere used them as true and certain. They laid these down as such in their discourses, even when they went further and undertook to explain matters untried and unknown to him.

units.la: Interea quoq; cum ipsa Aristotele interiorem, ut sic dicamus, notitiam contraximus; neq; contenti amplius, uti in gymnasio prius, ac postea inter Medicinæ initia quoq; feceramus, per Interpretes eum intelligere, ac placita ipsius cognoscere: ipsum loquentem audire volumus, ipsiusq; scripta penitus atq; accuratissime perlustrare, & in plerisq; ne simplici quidem aut iterata lectione defungi. unde, atq; ex assidua lectione Scaligeri, quem summum Aristotelis admiratorem, atq; acerrimum propugnatorem, præ cæteris omnibus Peripateticis unice charum ac tantumnon in delicijs habebamus, atq; jugiter versabamus; tantopere nobis crevit ille in Aristotelem inq; ipsius
units.tr: Meanwhile we also acquired a more inward acquaintance with Aristotle himself, so to speak. No longer content, as we had been before in the gymnasium and afterwards at the beginning of medicine, to understand him through interpreters and learn his opinions, we wanted to hear him speaking himself, to go thoroughly and most carefully through his writings, and in many places not to be satisfied with a single or even a repeated reading. From this, and from the constant reading of Scaliger, whom we held above all other Peripatetics as the greatest admirer and fiercest defender of Aristotle, dear to us beyond all others and almost a delight, and whom we constantly consulted, our admiration grew so greatly towards Aristotle, and into his...
PREFACE.

units.la: ipsius physiologiam affectus, ut absq; ulla haesitatione omnia ab ipso tradita (nisi quae directe cum Religione nostra ac Divina Veritate pugnarent) pro verissimis amplecteremur atq; adamaremus; ideoq; operam duntaxat nos lusuros arbitraremur, si ad lacessitandos ipsius adversarios diverteremus, ullumve ipsorum scriptis tempus insumeremus. Itaq; toto eo aliquot annorum spatio, quos apud te, Charissima Mater, morati sumus, ne unum quidem eorum, qui contra Aristotelem in Physicis sentirent, evolvimus, aut vel leviter delibavimus, aliter ve quàm solo nomine omnes istos cognitos habuimus.
units.tr: His physiology so affected us that, without any hesitation, we would have embraced and loved all the things handed down by him as most true (except those which directly clashed with our Religion and Divine Truth). We would therefore have thought we were wasting our effort if we turned aside to attack his opponents or spent any time on their writings. So throughout that whole span of some years, which we spent with you, most dear Mother, we did not read through a single one of those who held views against Aristotle on natural philosophy, nor even touched them lightly; we knew all of them only by name.

units.la: Ita educati atq; instituti, si miraris quomodo quare-ve postea adeo mutaverimus, atq; ab Aristotele, in quem tanto affectu tantaq; veneratione nos imbueras, tantopere diversi abierimus, ac liber iste, quem tuo sapienti justoq; judicio debita cum observantia sistimus, manifestum facit: audi nunc aquis, quaesumus, auribus, omnem rem breviter, quantum ipsius magnitudo permittit, narrantes, idq; eadem cum simplicitate, qua alteram partem prius, & quas colendi potius atque defendendi Aristotelis quàm insectandi aut lacessendi causas habeamus, ingenue exposuimus.
units.tr: Brought up and trained in this way, you may wonder how or why we later changed, and departed so far from Aristotle, into whom you had imbued us with such affection and such veneration. This book, which we place before your wise and just judgment with due respect, makes it plain. Now listen, we beg you, with willing ears, while we briefly set out the whole matter, as far as its magnitude allows, and explain with the same simplicity as before the reasons we have for honouring and defending Aristotle rather than attacking or assailing him.

units.la: Quum peracto Medicinae studio, ejus facultatem ac docendi autoritatem & insignia, post debitum examen, ac solennia in isto casu specimina exhibita, è manibus tuis accepissemus; & relictâ patriâ in Angliam, ac Regiam ibi urbem Londinum, nos contulissemus, ibiq; exercendae Arti statim nos applicuissemus: per unum alterumq; annum, dum Praxeos initia totos nos occupatos tenent, omnemq; animi nostri intentionem in se vocant; atq; à studijs istis merè theoricis penitus abductli, Physicas disputationes perraro, nec fere nisi oblectandi animi gratia, in congressibus atq; inter deambulandum, tractamus: deferbuit sensim ardor ille, juvenum animis in medio studiorum cursu adeo familiaris in Praeceptores suos, quo Aristoteli atq; Aristotelicis placitis prius nos addixeramus. & temporis decursu Chymicis quoque, à quibus prius instar pestis abhorreveramus, aquiores nos praebere, ac commentarios ipsorum introspicere cœpimus. Ab istorum nonnullis cum Aristotelis dogmata mire exagitari videremus; et quotidianâ experientiâ, dum exorientes subinde difficultates haudquaquam liquido ex Aristotelis Principijs expedire quimus, illos haud prorsus vana afferre deprehenderemus: primò quidem hoc tantùm à nobis impetravimus, ut crederemus non omnia adeo sana certaq; esse in Peripato, ac hactenus senseramus. Paulatim autem ulterius progressi, & veras rerum causas indies solicitius rimantes, quum magis ac magis nullum in Aristotelica Physiologia difficultatum exitum inveniremus; omnesq; solutiones, principijs ipsius superstructas, labare, & vix ad tenuissimam probabilitatem, siquis penitus excuteret, procedere animadverteremus: oculos tandem attollere ausi sumus contra istam tantopere nobis prius dilectam, ac tot seculorum consensu approbatam Philosophiam, & in quam tantum studij ac laboris sumseramus. & discussâ veluti caligine, quam longa consuetudo, & imbibita ἀντεξεταςως per tot annorum seriem doctrina, aciei nostræ obduxerat; omniq; affectu, quo antea cæcati fueramus, seposito: non modo probationes ac collectiones ex Aristotelicis principijs ductas, sed ipsa quoq; illa principia in dubium revocare, & tot de causis suspectam jam ipsorum soliditatem propius explorare, atq; severo Veritatis examini subjicere aggressi sumus: id quod non paucorum dierum aut mensium, sed longiplane temporis opus fuit; nobis omnes vacuas horas, & quidquid otij nancisci potuimus, in eam rem conferentibus.
units.tr: When we had finished the study of medicine, and had received from your hands its licence, the authority to teach and its insignia, after due examination and the customary specimens of our ability, and when we had left our homeland for England and betaken ourselves to the royal city of London, and there had at once applied ourselves to practising the art: for a year or so, while the beginnings of practice kept us wholly occupied and drew all the attention of our mind to themselves, and, withdrawn entirely from those purely theoretical studies, we discussed natural philosophy very rarely, and almost only for the pleasure of the mind, in conversation and while walking about, that ardour gradually cooled, that ardour which had been so familiar to young minds in the middle of their studies towards their teachers, and by which we had previously bound ourselves to Aristotle and his doctrines. And as time went on, we began to show ourselves more open even to the Chemists, from whom we had earlier shrunk back as from a plague, and to look into their commentaries. When we saw that some of them were attacking Aristotle's doctrines with remarkable vigour, and when, through daily experience, as difficulties kept arising that we could by no means clearly resolve from Aristotle's principles, we found that they were not bringing forward wholly baseless points, at first we granted only this much: that we believed not all things in the Peripatetic school were as sound and certain as we had until then thought. Gradually, however, advancing further and examining the true causes of things more anxiously day by day, when we found more and more that no way out of the difficulties in Aristotelian physiology could be discovered, and noticed that all the solutions, built upon his principles, were tottering and could scarcely stand even on the slightest probability if someone examined them thoroughly, we at last dared to raise our eyes against that philosophy which we had so long loved and which the agreement of so many centuries had approved, and on which we had expended so much study and labour. And, the mist which long habit and doctrine drunk in through a long series of years had cast over our sight having been, as it were, dispelled, and every bias by which we had previously been blinded having been set aside, we began not only to call into doubt the proofs and inferences drawn from Aristotelian principles, but also those very principles themselves, and to examine more closely their soundness, now suspect for many reasons, and to subject them to the strict test of Truth. This was a task requiring not a few days or months, but a very long time, as we devoted to it all our empty hours and whatever leisure we could gain.

units.la: Quanquam autem ita hic nos gessimus, ut Aristoteli quantum pote faveremus, atq; in omni disquisitione decreta ipsius pro viribus tueri conaremur, abyjq; nunquam nos nisi inviti, atq; aperta Veritate convicti, divelli pateremur: itatamen usu venit, ut pleraq; omnia pro infirmis, omniq; Veritatis atq; idoneorum argumentorum fulcimento destitutis, condemnare atq; deserere coacti fuerimus.
units.tr: Although we conducted ourselves in this way, so as to favour Aristotle as much as possible and to try, in every inquiry, to defend his decisions to the utmost of our powers, and never to suffer ourselves to be torn away from him except reluctantly and when convicted by manifest Truth, nevertheless it so happened that we were compelled to condemn and abandon almost everything as weak, and lacking all support of Truth and of suitable arguments.

units.la: Et quum apud Chymicos quoque, qui primi Aristotelem nobis suspectum reddiderant, & a quibus propterea omnia meliora expectanda jure videbantur, pleraq; nihilo praestantiora aut firmiora, cunctaq; valde incerta, & multa summè futilia aut monstrosa comperissemus, & vix quicquam in ipsorum libris occurreret, quod animum expleret: desperatio
units.tr: And since among the Chemists also, who first made Aristotle suspect to us, and from whom therefore all better things were rightly expected, we found most things no better or firmer, all things very uncertain, and many things extremely trifling or monstrous, and hardly anything in their books occurred that could satisfy the mind, despair
PREFACE.

units.la: Desperatio nos cepit Veritatis hac Philosophia in parte unquam inveniendi; adeo quidem ut omni de manibus physiologiæ studio depositio, diu de eo ne cogitaremus quidem, aut inter nos loqueremur. Sed quum veterum Amorum, & quidem in negotio tantam tamque arctam cum Medicina cognationem habente, non possemus penitus oblivisci; animusque recurrentibus ac subinde ultro ingerentibus se de eo imaginationibus inquietatus aliquoties, coepisset seipsum languoris coarguere atque ignavię, si rerum naturalium originem atque causas adeo in obscuro demersas putaremus, ut nulla ingenii indagine, nulloque animi nisu vestigari possent: spem nonnullam tandem cepimus, aliquid efficiendi, si toto pectore in hanc curam incumberemus.
units.tr: Despair seized us that the truth of this part of philosophy could ever be discovered; so much so that, laying aside all work on natural philosophy, we for a long time did not even think about it, nor speak of it among ourselves. But since we could not wholly forget the studies of the ancients, especially in a matter having so great and so close a kinship with medicine, and since our mind, troubled at intervals by images that returned and forced themselves upon us unbidden, had begun to accuse itself of sloth and cowardice if we judged the origin and causes of natural things to be so buried in obscurity that they could not be traced by any keenness of wit or any effort of mind, at last we took some hope that we might accomplish something, if we applied ourselves to this task with our whole heart.

units.la: Itaque quantum succisivi à Medicinæ praxi temporis nancisci potuimus, huic negotio impendentes, quum intra tempus haud itaque multum, & post primas statim dissertationes, veluti per nebulam nonnihil tamen lucis conspicati essemus; hoc successu animati, ad alia, & inde rursus ad alia perrexîmus; donec tandem toto hoc veluti saltu Naturalis scientia peragrato, justum ac magnum doctrinæ physicæ corpus efficeremus. id quod sane aliquot annorum labore nobis constitit: quippe quibus statutum erat, non rudem ac informem fœtum, & qui postea in multis retrahendus nobis veniret, foras præcipitare; sed omnia prius quantum ejus fieri poterat, limare atque expolire. Hoc autem ut consequeremur, istam fere consuetudinem observabamus. Singulis congressibus (qui post peracta Artis opera plerumque quotidiani, interdum duos pluresve dies habebant interjectos) unum aliquod caput, unamve quæstionem pertractare solebamus, omnibusque diligenter pensitatis, tum quæ ab Aristotele & Aristotelicorum præstantissimis (è quibus excepta proprio labore omnia fere, quæ alicujus momenti essent, atque in certas classes distributa, ut unumquidque quærentibus præsto esset, in promptu semper habebamus) affirmarentur, tum quæ Veritas ipsa dictare videbatur, id seligere ac arripere, quod maxime nobis probabile appareret. Quod autem prima velitatione sic constitueramus, non id ita linquendum existimabamus; sed proximis colloquiis quidcunque contra objici posset excogitabamus, atque in medium afferebamus: quæ omnia si solide, atque ita ut nobismetipsis (qui minime favorabiles propriis conceptibus) valde difficiles ac pro veritate quodammodo morosos nos prabebamus) plene satisfaceremus, diluere valebamus; rem ita, uti primitus eam decreveramus, sinebamus. Sin vero, & siquid non solubile se offerret: mutabamus, aliudq; magis probabile circumspiciebamus. neq; unquam dogmata nostra, & contrariorum dogmatum confutationem, fingere ac refingere cessabamus, donec invenissemus id, in quo animus tuto acquiesceret & contra quod nulla occurreret difficultas, quae non repelli ac redargui posse nobis videretur. Hoc pacto, & labore ac tedio incredibili, concinnavimus tandem, atq; ad umbilicum, priusquam invicem discederemus, perduximus hoc Philosophiae Naturalis Reformatae opus; cujus tituli atq; appellationis causam non est ut verbose exponamus, quum ipsa sese satis clare manifestet.
units.tr: Accordingly, devoting to this business as much of the spare time from the practice of medicine as we could obtain, within a not very long period, and after the first discussions, having glimpsed as it were through a mist some light nonetheless, encouraged by this success we went on to other matters, and from there again to others; until at last, having traversed the whole of natural science in this manner as it were by a leap, we produced a sound and substantial body of physical doctrine. This indeed cost us the labour of some years, since we had resolved not to hurl forth a rude and shapeless offspring, one which would afterwards have to be called back by us in many respects, but first to file and polish everything as far as it could be done. To achieve this we kept to the following custom. At each meeting (which, after the work of our art was finished, were usually held daily, though sometimes with an interval of two or more days) we were accustomed to treat one chapter or one question; and, having weighed everything carefully, we always kept ready at hand, so that each could be consulted at once, both what was affirmed by Aristotle and the most distinguished Aristotelians (from whom we had chosen almost everything of any importance, apart from our own labour, and distributed it into definite classes), and what Truth itself seemed to dictate; and we selected and seized upon whatever appeared most probable to us. But what we had thus settled in the first trial we did not think should be left as it stood; at our later conferences we devised whatever objection could be brought against it and set it before the company. If we could answer all of these solidly, and so fully satisfy ourselves (we who were very unfavourable to our own conceptions, and in a manner rather hard to please and somewhat stubborn for the sake of truth), we allowed the matter to stand as we had first decided it. But if any objection could not be resolved, or something presented itself, we changed our view and looked about for something more probable. Nor did we ever cease to frame and reframe our doctrines and the refutation of opposing doctrines, until we found that in which the mind could rest securely, and against which no difficulty arose that did not seem to us capable of being repelled and refuted. In this way, with incredible labour and weariness, we at last put together, and brought to completion before we parted from one another, this work of Reformed Natural Philosophy; there is no need for us to explain at length the reason for its title and name, since it makes itself sufficiently clear.

units.la: Es primo quidem libro, quem nunc publico damus, ea tractantur, in quorum nonnullis jam ante nos quidam glaciem fregerunt, eandemq; nobiscum sententiam tutati sunt: a quibus tamen haud ita multum nos adjutos, nihilq; prorsus exijs huc esse transcriptum, comperiet quisquis nostra cum ipsorum scriptis contulerit. & sane nulli ipsorum ante inchoatum hoc opus, primiq; haud prius quam magna ipsius parte jam perfecta, reliqui non nisi in fine, aut eo jam prorsus consummato, in manus nostras venerunt, aut a nobis inspecti fuerunt. In reliquis autem libris (quos isti submittemus, prout opportunitas dabitur) soli fere incedimus; & non modo diversum ab Aristotelico, sed & plane novum Philosophiae genus introducimus: tam in secundo ac tertio, ubi de Materia Elementisque, & de Natura ac Proprietatibus Rerum; quam in quarto, ubi de Generatione ac Causis Generantibus, omniq; Efficientium varietate; & in quinto quoq;, ubi de Anima ejusq; Facultatibus agitur.
units.tr: In the first book, which we now publish, are treated those matters in some of which certain men before us had already broken the ice and defended the same opinion as ours; yet whoever compares our writings with theirs will find that we were not much helped by them, and that nothing whatever has been copied from them here. Indeed, none of them came into our hands before this work was begun, and the first part of it had been largely completed, and the rest only at the end or once it had been entirely finished, or they were not examined by us at all. In the remaining books (which we shall submit to them as opportunity offers) we proceed almost alone, and we introduce a kind of philosophy not only different from the Aristotelian but plainly new: in the second and third, where we treat of matter and the elements, and of the nature and properties of things; in the fourth, where we treat of generation and generating causes, and the whole variety of efficient causes; and also in the fifth, where we discuss the soul and its faculties.
PREFACE.

units.la: Quid nos moverit, Charissima Mater, ut ab Aristotele discessionem facientes, Novam hanc Physicam condueremus, quemq; ea in re modum ac ordinem custodierimus, succinctè simul ac vere narravimus: cui orationi nostra, ab omni fuco ac falsitate aliena, fidem te adhibituram speramus; ac proinde etiam aequo animo laturam, quod relictâ eâ, ad quam nos instituerās, Physices disciplinâ, Novam ac propriam excogitaveri-
units.tr: What moved us, dearest Mother, to depart from Aristotle and to set about this New Physics, and what method and order we have followed in doing so, we have related briefly and truthfully at the same time; we hope you will give credence to this account, which is free from all varnish and falsehood, and that you will therefore also bear with an even mind that, having set aside the discipline of Physics in which you had trained us, we have devised a new and our own.
PREFACE.

units.la: verimus: quum planum fiat ex supradictis, quàm non leviter ac temere, & quàm deliberato consilio viam hanc instituerimus.
units.tr: ...so that it becomes clear from what has been said above how far from light or rash this path was, and with how deliberate a purpose we chose it.

units.la: Quod si quis credere malit, ambitione aut novitatis pruritu nos ad hoc scribendi genus accessisse, is nihil aliud nisi propriam sçævitatem ac κακοήθειαν prodet; qui postulet homines toto vitæ ac morum genere à cunctis fallacijs procul remotos, mendacij reos agere in eo, quod sincere à se dictum profitentur, haud alijs ductus argumentis, quàm quæ prava suspicacitas ipsi suggesserit. Namque etiamsi omnia nostra & quæ contra Peripateticam Philosophiam afferimus, & quæ pro propriis invehimus, everti atque expugnari possent; non plus tamen inde sequeretur, nisi deceptos nos fuisse, ac dum alios erroris arguimus, ipsos in errore versari: quare quum nihil sit inter homines vulgatius, veniam id sane apud omnes æquos Judices meretur. Neque aliud in omni hoc disputationum atque disquirenda Veritatis studio culpandum venit, quàm si qui aut sponte ac libenter errant (si modo tales ulli inveniuntur) aut stultissimis nugis adhærentes, Veritati inepte vel malitiose adversantur; eis etiam, ubi planissime convicti sunt, neque solidi quicquam habent quod reponant, pertinaciter tamen reclamant: à quibus vitijs mores nostri quàm longissime abhorrent. Quippe sicuti ingens hoc opus, immensumque laborem, optimo animo, solóque Veritatis propagandæ studio suscepimus: ita promtissime quandocunque meliora edocti fuerimus, manus dabimus; omnesque errores, quorum coargui potuerimus, relinquemus ac ejurabimus: neque unquam inhonesto noxioque pudore à corrigendis nobis ac nostris absterrebimur.
units.tr: But if anyone prefers to believe that we came to this kind of writing out of ambition or an itch for novelty, he will only reveal his own savagery and malice [κακοήθειαν]. He would have us, whose whole manner of life and conduct is far removed from every deceit, stand accused of lying in what we declare we have said sincerely, and he is moved by no other grounds than those that a perverse suspicion has suggested to him. For even if everything we say against Peripatetic philosophy, and everything we advance as our own, could be overturned and refuted, it would still follow only that we had been deceived, and that while we charge others with error, we ourselves are in error. Since nothing is more common among men, this deserves pardon from all fair judges. Nor is there anything to blame in all this discussion and inquiry after truth, except when some men either err willingly and gladly (if any such men are to be found at all), or, clinging to the most foolish trifles, stubbornly oppose the truth, whether through folly or malice. Even when such men have been plainly refuted, and have nothing solid to put forward in reply, they still obstinately protest. Our way of life stands as far as possible from these vices. Just as we have undertaken this huge work and immense labour with the best intentions, and with the sole aim of spreading the truth, so we will most readily yield whenever we are taught something better. We will leave behind and renounce every error that we can be shown to have, and we will never be kept from correcting ourselves and our own by any dishonourable or harmful shame.

units.la: Qui autem primo statim aspectu, & ob idipsum quod Nova sunt, hæc condemnabunt; & ne audienda quidem, quia à Vetustis & tanto ævo receptis placitis desciscunt, pronuntiabunt (quales non defuturos certi sumus) eos nos commiseratione potius quàm responso dignos existimamus: quum omnium ingeniorum infelicissima sint, quæ Verum à Falso haud aliâ quàm longævitatis aut novitatis notâ secernere valent; ullam-ve Vetustatem Veritati præscribere posse autumant, aut opinionem quamcunque ob id tantùm, quia recens est, repudiandam. Quippe nihil in rebus humanis est valde vetustum: & quæ inijs sunt vetustissima, aliquando recentia fuerunt.
units.tr: But those who, at first sight, and for the very reason that these things are new, will condemn them, and will pronounce that they should not even be heard because they depart from ancient opinions accepted over so long an age (and we are certain that such men will not be lacking), we consider worthy of pity rather than of an answer. They are the most unfortunate of all minds, those who cannot distinguish truth from falsehood by any mark other than age or novelty, and who claim that antiquity can prescribe anything to truth, or that any opinion should be rejected merely because it is recent. Indeed, nothing in human affairs is very ancient, and what is most ancient among them was once recent.
SUMMARY OF THE BOOK.
