units.tr: I. Natural substance, the subject of physics. II. Physics is to be taught from the treatment of principles. III. Aristotle's confused treatment of principles and causes. IV. The wondrous and very frigid excuses offered by the Aristotelians to defend this error of their Master. V. Others do not excuse this error but cunningly conceal it. VI. Some have already noted this error of Aristotle, and Piccolomini in no way objects to their just censures.

units.la: PHysicam disciplinam esse scientiam, quippe quæ in contemplatione tota occupatur, cum & per de manifestum sit, & à multis fusè disputatum, non est utinos huic disputationi immorari, quippe quibus nihil minus propositum est, quam aliorum dicta otiosè repetere. Quum autem in omni scientia nihil prius cognoscere debemus, quam proprium cujusque subjectum, quod nam
units.tr: That physics is a science, since it is wholly occupied with contemplation, is both plain and has been discussed at length by many. It is not our purpose to linger over this dispute, since nothing is further from our intention than to repeat idly what others have said. Yet since in every science we must know nothing before we know its proper subject, what the subject of physics is must first be settled.

units.la: B nam sit Physicæ subjectum ante omnia constituendum est: quâ quidem de re multum superioribus temporibus digladiati inter se sunt Peripatetici. nunc autem omnes in illam fere convenerunt sententiam, corpus naturale esse hujus scientiæ subjectum: Id quod & nobis non improbatur, dummodo rite sumatur corporis vocabulum, neque ita angustè, quomodo à Peripateticis sumi solet. Revera enim & Angeli sub eo comprehendi debent, & Mentes quoque humanæ, quæ proinde duplici jure cadunt sub considerationem Philosophi naturalis, quum & partes sint ac principia corporum naturalium, quatenus hominem integrum unà cum corpore peculiariter dicto constituunt; & ipsæ quoque sunt corpora naturalia, in quantum suam seorsim habent consistentiam, ac per se considerantur. Certè & Angelos naturain habere, & Mentes (ac tanto magis Cœlum & sidera, de quibus multi inter Aristotelicos id negant) ex ijs, quæ de natura dicturi postea sumus, manifestum fiet. Corpora autem dicimus & Angelos & Mentes, quia nullam extra solùm Deum credimus esse substantiam, quæ non suo modo sit corporea, suamq; habeat quantitatem, sive, quod idem est, dimensiones. Quodsi igitur ita ampla tribuatur corpori acceptio, tunc & ipsi assentimur, Corpus naturale esse hujus scientiæ subjectum. Sin verò ex more Peripati corporis vocabulum ad solas substantias sensibiles astringatur; tunc non possumus ijs accedere, qui corpus naturale assignant pro Physicæ subjecto; sed aliud generalius pro eo substituendum est, dicendumq; Scientiam hanc non Corpus naturale, sed Substantiam naturalem pro subjecto habere.
units.tr: This matter the Peripatetics disputed fiercely among themselves in earlier times, but now nearly all have come to agree that the natural body is the subject of this science. We do not reject this either, provided the word body is taken properly and not as narrowly as the Peripatetics usually take it. For indeed angels must be included under it, and human minds as well. These fall under the consideration of the natural philosopher on two grounds: they are parts and principles of natural bodies, insofar as they constitute the whole man together with the body so called in the proper sense, and they are themselves natural bodies, insofar as they have their own separate existence and are considered in themselves. That angels have a nature, and minds too (and all the more the heavens and the stars, which many Aristotelians deny), will become plain from the things we shall say later about nature. We call angels and minds bodies because we believe that there is no substance outside God alone which is not corporeal in its own way and has its own quantity, or, what is the same, its dimensions. If, then, so wide a meaning is given to the word body, we also agree that the natural body is the subject of this science. But if, following the custom of the Peripatetics, the word body is restricted to sensible substances alone, then we cannot join those who assign the natural body as the subject of physics. Instead another, more general term must be substituted, and we must say that this science has as its subject not the natural body but natural substance.

units.la: II. Quia autem, Naturale quid sit, nosci nequit, nisi cognoverimus, quid sit Natura; inde fit, ut Aristotelici pleriq; statim à Naturæ explicatione ordiendam esse Physicam tractationem censuerint. Contra autem Aristoteles à principiorum explanatione eam inchoavit, idq; ob eam rationem, quam in ipso operis principio propositi, Quod ut in alijs scientijs contemplativis, ita in Physiologia etiam ab omnium primis & maximè communibus incipiendum sit. Et hoc nobis probatur magis: quùm principia sint universaliora & communiora quàm natura, quippè quæ sub principiorum ambitu comprehenditur, atq; ad illa se habet, uti species ad genus. Namq; & Natura est principium ejus rei, cujus natura est, sicuti postea monstrabimus; ac proinde Principium est Naturæ genus. Planè igitur perversum, ac contra omnem bonæ methodi ordinem foret, à speciei alicujus, ac non abipsius generis tractatione ordiri. Quod autem ad vulgatam illorum rationem pertinet, qui à Natura auspicandum esse contendunt, ea certè nulla est. Quanquam enim concedamus, cognosci perfectè non posse quid sit Naturale, nisi cognito priùs, quid sit Natura: sufficit tamen Physicæ studioso, rudis illa sui subjecti cognitio omnium animis insita, qua Naturale artificioso opponitur, quaq; omnia creata vel generata, quatenus talia, Naturalia dicuntur. Longè sanè alia hic est contemplativarum disciplinarum, quàm factivarum ratio. Hæ enim in ipso statim limine pernoscere suum subjectum debent, quod nisi fecerint, postea ubi id faciant, opportunitatem non habebunt: veluti in medicina nisi ante omnia doceatur corporis humani structura, postea neq; in progressu Physiologiæ tradi illa opportunè poterit, nec in pathologia, neq; in methodo medendi. Ast disciplinæ speculativæ cum non alium habeant scopum, quàm cognitionem sui subjecti (quòd factivæ propterea tantum cognoscunt, ut illo uti, vel in ipsum agere rectè noverint) non opus est ut in ipso statim vestibulo tradatur accurata de ipso doctrina, quod procedente institutione fieri commodiùs potest. Nos igitur à Principijs incipiemus, idq; eo ordine, ut priùs Aristotelis super ijs opinionem examinemus, postea quid nobis ipsis videatur, proponamus; quem ordinem ipse etiam secutus est Aristoteles, quippè qui priùs veterum super hoc negotio sententias expenderit, quàm propriam aperiret; quos tamen nimis calumniosè tractasse, non sine causa plerisq; videtur; quod suo loco plenius à nobis considerabitur: nunc ad ipsum veniamus.
units.tr: Since, however, what is natural cannot be known unless we have first learned what nature is, most Aristotelians have judged that the treatment of physics must begin with an explanation of nature. Aristotle, on the other hand, began it with an explanation of principles, for the reason he gives at the very beginning of his work: that in physiology, as in the other contemplative sciences, one must begin with the very first and most common things. We approve this more: principles are more universal and more common than nature, since nature is comprehended under the scope of principles and stands to them as species to genus. For nature is the principle of that thing whose nature it is, as we shall show later, and therefore principle is the genus of nature. It would clearly be perverse and contrary to all good order of method to begin from the treatment of some species and not from the genus itself. As for the common argument of those who insist that we must begin with nature, it is in fact no argument. Although we grant that what is natural cannot be perfectly known unless what nature is has first been known, yet for a student of physics that rough knowledge of his subject, implanted in all minds, is enough: it is the knowledge by which the natural is opposed to the artificial, and by which all created or generated things, as such, are called natural. The case of the contemplative sciences is quite different from that of the productive ones. The productive sciences must know their subject thoroughly right at the threshold, for if they do not, they will have no opportunity to do so later. For example, in medicine, unless the structure of the human body is taught first of all, it can neither be taught conveniently later in the course of physiology, nor in pathology, nor in the method of healing. But since speculative sciences have no other aim than knowledge of their subject (the productive ones know it only so that they may use it or know how to act rightly upon it), there is no need for an exact teaching about the subject to be given at the very outset; this can be done more conveniently as the instruction proceeds. We shall therefore begin with principles, and in this order: first we shall examine Aristotle's opinion about them, and afterwards set forth what seems right to us. Aristotle himself followed this same order, since he weighed the opinions of the ancients on this matter before he set out his own. Yet many think he handled them too calumniously, and not without reason; this we shall consider more fully in its proper place. Now let us come to the matter itself.

units.la: III. Priùs autem de ipso Principij vocabulo videndum, quod
units.tr: III. But first we must consider the word "principle" itself, which
Chapter I.

units.la: quod cùm valdè sit ambiguum, & ad plurimas satis diversas adhibeatur significationes, quas & in exordio quinti Metaphysicorum ex professo, sed non omnes, enumerat, & in suis scriptis passim ac promiscuè usurpat longè plures; (qua de re dicetur à nobis inferius) oportuerat ante omnia positam hic distinctionem, quo potissimum modo in Physiologia illud intelligendum sit, & quid à causa ac elemento differat: quod minimè fecit. Si tamen mens ipsius cognoscenda est è libris physicæ acroaseōs, dicendum; quod causa illi fuerit generalior quam principium, itaut hoc sub illa contineretur. Præcipua enim illa duo principia, Materiam & Formam, Causarum speciēs facit; reliquas autem causas ab arctiore illa principij notione amovet; quā de re nemo dubitabit, qui primum Physicorum legerit, in cujus epilogo cùm posuerit hæc verba, Οὐ μὲν οὖν ἐισὶν ἀρχαί, καὶ τίνες, καὶ πόσαι τὸν ἀριθμόν, διορίζω ἡμῖν οὕτως. Quod igitur sint principia, & quæ, ac quot numero, ad hunc modum à nobis definitum esto, satis declaravit; Efficientem & Finem, de quibus in sequenti libro agit, in isto autem verbum facit nullum, à principij notione se amovere, & iis tantum, quæ illo libro posita ac pertractata sunt, Materiæ, Formæ & Privationi, appellationem hanc donare; quod & in clausula capitis septimi apertè profitetur, ubi hactenus disputata in summam contrahens, concludit tria numero esse principia, ΑΛΛ' ὅλ' αἱ ἀρχαὶ τρεῖς, καὶ πῶς τρεῖς, καὶ τίς ὁ τρόπος αὐτῶν. Sed quod principia sint tria, ac quomodo tria, & quis modus ipsorum, &c. Itaq; suus eum destituit conatus, qui cùm propositullet à maximè universalibus incipiens, ad minùs universalia progredi, id nequaquam præstitit: quippè exorsus Physiologiam à Principijs, quam à Causis ordiri debuerat, cùm in Causarum complexu etiam Principia contineantur, ex ipsius doctrinâ. Non enim obest quod Privationem, quam facit unam è Principijs, inter Causas nunquam reposuerit; cùm sub Materia eam quodammodo comprehendant cùm Aristotele omnes Peripatetici. itaq; in illud incidit vitium, quod fugiendum esse alibi ipse monuit, ut nisi maximè universalia prius dicantur,
units.tr: Since this word is very ambiguous and is applied to many quite different meanings, which he lists deliberately at the beginning of the fifth book of the Metaphysics, though not all of them, and which he uses everywhere in his writings, and far more often, indiscriminately (we will say more about this below), it was necessary above all to set out here a distinction: in what chief sense the word is to be understood in Physics, and how it differs from cause and element. This he did not do at all. Still, if his mind is to be learned from the books of the Physics lectures, it must be said that for him cause was the more general notion, so that principle was contained under it. For he makes those two chief principles, Matter and Form, into kinds of cause, and he removes the remaining causes from the narrower notion of principle. No one who has read the first book of the Physics will doubt this, for in its epilogue he writes these words: "Now, what the principles are, and which, and how many in number, I have defined for us in this way. Let it therefore be settled by us, as defined in this way, what the principles are, which they are, and how many. That they are sufficiently declared. As to the efficient and the final cause, of which he treats in the following book, he says nothing in this one; he removes them from the notion of principle, and gives this name only to Matter, Form and Privation, which were posited and treated in that book." He openly professes this also at the end of the seventh chapter, where, summing up what has been argued so far, he concludes that there are three principles in number: "But the principles are three, and how three, and what their mode is" [ΑΛΛ' ὅλ' αἱ ἀρχαὶ τρεῖς, καὶ πῶς τρεῖς, καὶ τίς ὁ τρόπος αὐτῶν]. But that the principles are three, and how three, and what their mode is, etc. And so his own attempt failed him. He proposed to proceed from the most universal things to the less universal, and he did not manage it at all. For he began his Physics from the Principles, when he ought to have begun from the Causes, since, by his own doctrine, the Principles are contained within the complex of Causes. Nor does it count against this that he never placed Privation, which he makes one of the Principles, among the Causes, since all the Peripatetics, following Aristotle, comprehend it in some way under Matter. Thus he fell into the fault which he himself warned elsewhere should be avoided, namely that, unless the most universal things are discussed first, the same things must often be said again. For he who in the first book had said so many great things about Matter and Form was forced to treat them again among the Causes in the second book, since he makes them the kinds of Cause everywhere. This needless repetition has caused great perplexity to most interpreters. He would by no means have fallen into it if he had begun from Causes and divided them so that the notion of principle applied to some and not to others. Having done this, he would have been free to treat first whichever kind of Cause he wished: either the one to which he would leave only the generic name of Cause, or the one to which he would give the specific name of Principles.

units.la: {¶} De Part. ca. I. & 4. tur, sæpius idem dicendum sit. nam qui primo hoc libro tot tantaq; de Materia & Forma dixisset ; de ijs in secundo libro inter Causas agere de novo coactus fuit, cum illas faciat ubiq; Causarum species ; in quam repetitionem otiosam, & plerisq; interpretibus magnæ perplexitatis. autorem, nequaquam incidisset, si a Causis incœpisset, easq; ita divisisset, ut alijs principij ratio competeret, alijs minime : quo facto integrum illi fuisset de utra vellet Causarum specie prius tractare, vel de illa, cui genericam tantum Causæ appellationem relinqueret, vel de ea, cui specificum Principiorum nomen imponeret.
units.tr: IV. Since he did not do this, he gave his followers the greatest occasion for perplexity. They cannot grasp why he treated as principles, and discussed under that name, the things he had first set down as such, and then repeated them among the Causes. To extricate themselves from this difficulty, they took one of two routes: some took a short and easy one, simply passing over the matter altogether; others took a longer and rougher one, searching out excuses and reasons why Aristotle thought he ought to do it so. (De Part. ca. I. & 4.) ... it must often be said the same thing again. [Note: the remainder of this unit is garbled in the transcription; the sense is that the author, had he begun from Causes, would not have fallen into this repetition, and that the Causes would have been divided so that the notion of principle suited some and not others.]

units.la: IV. Hoc cum non fecerit, maximam æstuationis occasionem sectatoribus suis objecit, qui animo non capiunt, cur quæ fecerat prius principia, ac sub isto nomine pertractaverat, postea inter Causas repetiverit; è qua difficultate ut se explicarent, geminum iter ingressi sunt, alij compendiosum & expeditum, ex toto illam dissimulando : alij longius & salebrosius, excusationes ac rationes investigando, cur ita sibi faciendum putaverit Aristoteles.
units.tr: IV. Since he did not do this, he gave his followers the greatest occasion for perplexity. They cannot grasp why he should have treated as principles, and discussed under that name, the things he had first called principles, and then repeated them among the Causes. To extricate themselves from this difficulty, they took one of two routes: some took a short and easy one, passing the matter over entirely; others took a longer and rougher one, searching out excuses and reasons why Aristotle thought he ought to have done so.

units.la: De posterioribus est Zabarella, qui scribit, Materiam & Formam ab Aristotele in primo Physicorum considerari, ut principia generationis corporis naturalis, in secundo ut principia motus & quietis, secundum quam considerationem competit eis nomen naturæ. Non enim omnibus corporibus naturalibus competere considerationem istorum principiorum, quatenus corpus naturale ex ijs generetur & constet, quia cælum Aristoteli ex his principijs genitum non sit, neq; ex ijs constet : ipsi tamen aptari illa posse, quatenus in secundo libro considerantur ; quia in ipso sit aliquod motus principium, formæ inferiorum analogum. itaq; totius naturalis philosophiæ verum initium sumendum esse à secundo libro physicorum : primum vero fuisse antepositum propter nostram faciliorem cognitionem, non quod re vera ad eos libros pertinuerit : & similia repetit capite nono. Sed hæc excusatio, præterquam quod alia multa continet non parum absurda, in eo etiam vana deprehenditur, quòd presupponit supponit Aristotelem id de Cœlo sensisse, quod de eo sensit Averroes, nimirum illud non ut nostratia hæc compositum esse ex Materiæ & Formæ, sed esse corpus simplex, in quo nulla talis compositio reperiatur. Hoc autem Aristoteles nusquam in scriptis suis dixit, neq; hoc inter cœlestia ac nostratia corpora discrimen, quòd hæc composita sint è Materia & Forma, illa vero secus, ullibi proposuit; sed multis in locis planè contrarium dixit. Namq; primi de Cœlo, cap. 8. ex professo hac de re agens, demonstrare conatur, cœlum esse individuum, ac proinde ex materia & forma compositum, Επεὶ οὖν ἐσὶν ὁ οὐρανὸς ἀιδηλὸς, τῶν ναδένασον ἂν εἴη· τὸ γὰρ αἰδηλὸν ἅπαν, ἐν τῇ ὕλῃ ὑπῆρχεν· ἕτερον ἀρα ὁδὲ ὁ οὐρανὸς, καὶ οὐρανὸς ἀπωλῶς. καὶ τὸ μὲν, ὡς εἶδος καὶ μορφὴ, τὸ δ' ὡς τῇ ὕλῃ μεμιγμένον. Quandoquidem igitur cælum est sensibile, sequitur ut sit de numero individuorum. omnia enim sensibilia in materia existunt. aliud igitur est hoc cœlum, quam cœlum simpliciter: & hoc quidem [est] tanquàm Species & forma; illud autem tanquàm Materia mixtum. Verum quidem est, hic voce Οὐρανοῦ non Cœlum tantum, sed totum mundum intelligi (quod plerique interpretes non animadvertunt) Attamen hæc ratio si ullum de toto mundo momentum habet; ejusdem quoq; roboris esse respectu ipsius cœli, apertum est. Quodsi Aristoteles aliter censuisset, alio quovis vocabulo potiùs, quam οὐρανῦ, usus hic ad significandum mundum fuisset. Quod sicui hæc non satisfaciunt, is inspiciat secundi de Generatione & Corruptione nonum, ubi de solo cœlo agens, multo adhuc expressiùs eandem hanc ex materia & forma compositionem, quæ in nostratibus inveniatur, in ipso statuit, λεκτέον περὶ πάσης γενέσεως ὁμοίως, πόσα τε, καὶ τίνες αὐτῆς αἱ ἀρχαί. εἰσὶν οὖν ηὰ τὴν ἀιδιὸν ἴσαι, καὶ τῷ γένει αἱ αὐταὶ ὥσπερ ἐν τοῖς ἀϊδίοις καὶ πρῶτοις· ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἔστιν, ὡς ὕλη, ἡ δὲ ὡς μορφή. Dicendum pariter de omni generatione, quot ac quæ sint ipsius principia. sunt igitur & numero æquales, & genere eædem, ac eæ quæ sunt in æternis & primis. una enim est, est, ut Materia; altera autem, ut Forma. Qui locus adeò clarè continet Aristotelis super hac re sententiam, ut rectè Toletus in Commentarijs dicat, Insigniter hunc locum facere contra Averroem, atq; Aristotelem hîc adeò manifestè materiam & formam eodem modo ponere in corporibus inferioribus & cœlestibus, ut nullam aliam expositionem patiatur, neq; ullo modo effugere possint Averroistæ, quin Aristoteles hoc loco ponat in cœlo intrinsecam compositionem ex materia & forma. Quùm autem hisce in locis ex professo rem hanc tractet, magis inde mens ipsius petenda est, quam ex octavo Metaphysicorum, capite quarto, ubi aliud agens, & perfunctorie rem hanc attingens, non tamen asserit, cœlum carere materia, sed leviter de eo dubitat. Ἐπεὶ δὲ τῶν φυσικῶν μὲν, ἀιδίων δὲ οὐσιῶν, ἄλλος λόγος· ἴσως γὰρ ἔνια ὅν ἔχει ὕλην, ἢ ὁ τοιαύτην, ἀλλὰ μόνον καὶ τὸ τὸπω κινητῶν. Substantiarum autem quæ Naturales quidem sunt, sed æterna, alia est ratio. fortassis enim quedam non habent materiam, aut non talem, sed duntaxat loco mobilem. quibus verbis non tam materiam aufert à cœlo, quam ab ejus materia corruptibilitatem. neq; eum aliud sibi voluisse istis verbis, apertum est ex ejusdem libri capite primo, ubi cùm dixisset, omnes sensibiles substantias habere materiam, quæ materia sit subjectum omnium mutationum; & quæcunq; patiuntur substantialem illam mutationem generationis & corruptionis, etiam reliquas mutationes pati, nimirùm accretionem & imminutionem, alterationem & motum localem: subjungit, non tamen sequi, ut quæcunq; una duabusve istarum mutationum afficiuntur, obnoxia etiam sint mutationi substantiali. Καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσι δὲ ταύτῃ αἱ ἄλλαι μεταβολαί. τῶν δ' ἄλλων ἡ μίαν ἢ δύο αὐτῇ ἀκολουθεῖ. ὃ γὰρ ἀνάγκη, εἴπερ ἔχει ὕλην τοπικὴν, τοῦτο καὶ γεννητὴν, καὶ φθαρτὴν ἔχειν. Et hanc quidem comitantur cætera mutationes. ast cæterarum vel unam vel duas hæc non [semper] comitatur. non enim necesse est, ut quod materiam habet localem, idem habeat etiam generabilem & corruptibilem. quibus similia iterum scribit
units.tr: Of the latter kind is Zabarella, who writes that Aristotle considers Matter and Form in the first book of the Physics as the principles of the generation of a natural body; in the second book as the principles of motion and rest, and according to this consideration the name of nature belongs to them. For the consideration of these principles does not apply to all natural bodies insofar as a natural body is generated from them and consists of them, since in Aristotle's view the heaven was not generated from these principles and does not consist of them. Yet these can be applied to it insofar as they are considered in the second book, because in it there is some principle of motion, analogous to the form of lower things. Therefore the true beginning of the whole of natural philosophy is to be taken from the second book of the Physics; the first book was placed before it for our easier understanding, and not because it truly belonged to those books. He repeats similar things in the ninth chapter. But this excuse, apart from containing many other things that are not a little absurd, is also shown to be vain in this respect: it presupposes that Aristotle thought about the heavens what Averroes thought, namely that they are not composed of matter and form as our bodies are, but are a simple body in which no such composition is found. Yet Aristotle never said this in his writings, nor did he anywhere propose the distinction between heavenly and earthly bodies that the latter are composed of matter and form and the former are not. On the contrary, in many places he said quite the opposite. For in the first book On the Heavens, chapter 8, treating this matter deliberately, he tries to demonstrate that the heaven is individual, and therefore composed of matter and form: "Since, therefore, the heaven is sensible, it follows that it is one of the individuals, for all sensible things exist in matter. The heaven here is therefore different from the heaven in the general sense; and the one is as form and shape, but the other is mixed with matter" [Επεὶ οὖν ἐσὶν ὁ οὐρανὸς ἀιδηλὸς ... ἕτερον ἀρα ὁδὲ ὁ οὐρανὸς ... τὸ μὲν, ὡς εἶδος καὶ μορφὴ, τὸ δ' ὡς τῇ ὕλῃ μεμιγμένον]. It is true that here by the word Heaven [Οὐρανοῦ] is understood not only the heaven but the whole world, which most interpreters do not notice. Yet if this argument has any weight concerning the whole world, it is plainly of the same force with respect to the heaven itself. If Aristotle had thought otherwise, he would have used some other word rather than Οὐρανός to signify the world. If anyone is not satisfied with this, let him look at the ninth chapter of the second book On Generation and Corruption, where, treating of the heaven alone, he establishes in it, even more explicitly, the same composition of matter and form as is found in our bodies: "One must speak in the same way of all generation, how many and what its principles are. They are therefore equal in number and the same in kind as those in eternal and primary things; for the one is as Matter, and the other as Form" [λεκτέον περὶ πάσης γενέσεως ὁμοίως, πόσα τε, καὶ τίνες αὐτῆς αἱ ἀρχαί. εἰσὶν οὖν ηὰ τὴν ἀιδιὸν ἴσαι, καὶ τῷ γένει αἱ αὐταὶ ... ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἔστιν, ὡς ὕλη, ἡ δὲ ὡς μορφή]. This passage so clearly contains Aristotle's opinion on this matter that Toletus rightly says in his Commentaries: "This passage notably goes against Averroes, and Aristotle here so plainly posits matter and form in the same way in lower and in heavenly bodies that it admits of no other exposition, and the Averroists cannot in any way escape the conclusion that Aristotle in this place posits an intrinsic composition of matter and form in the heaven." But since he treats this matter deliberately in these places, his mind must be sought from them rather than from the fourth chapter of the eighth book of the Metaphysics, where, dealing with another subject and touching on this matter only in passing, he does not assert that the heaven lacks matter, but merely doubts it lightly: "But the substances that are natural yet eternal have another account; for perhaps some do not have matter, or not such matter, but only matter that is mobile in place" [Ἐπεὶ δὲ τῶν φυσικῶν μὲν, ἀιδίων δὲ οὐσιῶν, ἄλλος λόγος· ἴσως γὰρ ἔνια ... τὸπω κινητῶν]. By these words he does not so much remove matter from the heaven as remove corruptibility from its matter. And that he did not mean anything else by these words is plain from the first chapter of the same book, where, having said that all sensible substances have matter, which is the subject of all change, and that whatever undergoes that substantial change of generation and corruption also undergoes the other changes, namely increase and decrease, alteration and local motion, he adds that it does not follow that whatever is affected by one or two of these changes is therefore also subject to substantial change: "And the other changes accompany this one; but of the others, one or two accompany it. For what must have local matter must also have generable and corruptible matter" [Καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσι δὲ ταύτῃ αἱ ἄλλαι μεταβολαί. τῶν δ' ἄλλων ἡ μίαν ἢ δύο αὐτῇ ἀκολουθεῖ. ὃ γὰρ ἀνάγκη, εἴπερ ἔχει ὕλην τοπικὴν, τοῦτο καὶ γεννητὴν, καὶ φθαρτὴν ἔχειν]. "Indeed, the other changes accompany this one; but of the others, one or two follow it. It is not necessary that what has local matter also has generable and corruptible matter." In similar terms he writes again
Chapter I.

units.la: 12. Metaphys. 2. πάντα δ' ὅλως ἔχει, ὅσα μεταβάλλει, ἀλλ' εἴ ὅ τι ἀ ἐξ ἐρών, καὶ τῶν ἀιδίων ὅσα μὴ γεννητὰ, ... ἀλλ' ὅ γεννητῶν, ἀλλὰ πόθεν πῇ. Materiam omnia habent, quæcunq; mutantur, licet diversam, etiam æterna illa, quæ non sunt generabilia, sed loco mobilia; non tamen generabilem, sed [mutabilem] de loco in locum. planè igitur Aristoteli compositum esse cœlum ex Materia & forma isti quoq; loci, æquè ac illi priores, convincunt, cùm illi diserte materiam attribuat; materia autem absq; forma subsistens, maximum sit in ipsius schola monstrum. Scimus quidem quomodo hæc Aristotelis testimonia eludant Averroes ac Averroistæ; dicentes ipsum cœli corpus vocari materiam, respectu Intelligentiæ motricis; aliaq; ad eundem modum. Sed hæc & planè fatua sunt, & ab Aristotelis mente prorsùs aliena; sicuti unusquisque, sine prejudicio istos aliosq; similes locos legens, fateri cogetur. ac proinde stare nullo modo potest excusatio illa à Zabarella allata; quippè quæ Aristoteli affingit ejusmodi sententiam, à qua ipse, quantùm ex ipsius scriptis apparet, fuit alienissimus. Multa autem adhuc alia ab aliis dicuntur, ad excusandum hunc Aristotelis errorem, cur de eadem re bis in duobus diversis unius operis libris docuerit, semel sub Principiorum, & rursus sub Causarum appellatione: cujus rei cùm veram originem, antea à nobis traditam, ignoraverint, aut non perpenderint, mirum non est, si futilia admodum omnes pariter protulerunt: quod sanè fecerunt alij non minus quàm Zabarella, quamvis alio atq; alio modo. Etenim Thomas dicit, agi in primo libro de principiis rerum naturalium, quæ essendi principia vocari solent; in secundo autem agi de principiis scientiæ naturalis, hoc est, de principiis cognoscendi, ut ex eo refert Zabarella capite 11. ejusdem libri, ubi admodum verbosè etiam tractat, cur tractatio de causis in secundum Physicorum librum collata sit. Alia est ratio eorum, qui & Materiam & Formam alium esse dicunt primam, aliam secundam; de illis agi ut de principiis, de hisce ut de causis; fis ; ut latius videre est apud Velcurionem, qui istam opionem amplectitur, & prolixius exequitur. Portius, referente Vicomercato, in priori rerum Principia, ut fiunt, in secundo, ut sunt, considerari existimat. Simplicius in secundo tradi propria substantialis mutationis ; in primo de universali mutatione, tam substantiae quam accidentis, dictum esse. Philoponus, in primo praecipue de Materia, parum de Forma ; in secundo praecipue de Forma, parcius de Materia agi.
units.tr: 12. Metaph. 2. "All things that change have matter of some kind, though not the same kind; and even among the eternal things, those that are not generable but are movable in place [have matter]" [the Greek is garbled in the scan]. All things that change have matter, though of different kinds, including those eternal things which are not generable but move in place; yet they have not generable matter but matter that is changeable from place to place. Clearly, then, these passages also show that for Aristotle the heavens are composed of matter and form, just as the earlier passages show. He explicitly attributes matter to them, and matter subsisting without form would be the greatest monstrosity in his own school. We know how Averroes and the Averroists try to escape these testimonies of Aristotle, saying that the body of the heavens is called matter in relation to the moving Intelligence, and other things of the same sort. But these are utterly foolish and wholly alien to Aristotle's mind, as anyone who reads these and similar passages without prejudice will be compelled to admit. Consequently, that excuse brought forward by Zabarella cannot stand in any way, since it ascribes to Aristotle an opinion from which he, as far as appears from his own writings, was most remote. Many other explanations are offered by others to excuse this error of Aristotle, namely why he taught about the same matter twice in two different books of one work, once under the heading of Principles and again under the heading of Causes. Since they did not know, or did not weigh, the true origin of this, which we have set out earlier, it is no wonder that they all alike put forward quite trivial things; which indeed others did no less than Zabarella, though in a different way. For Thomas says that the first book treats of the principles of natural things, which are usually called the principles of being, while the second treats of the principles of natural science, that is, of the principles of knowing; Zabarella reports this from him in chapter 11 of the same book, where he also treats at great length why the discussion of causes was placed in the second book of the Physics. Another explanation is given by those who say that matter and form are one thing as first and another as second; that the former are treated as principles and the latter as causes. This can be seen more fully in Velcurio, who embraces that opinion and works it out at greater length. Portius, as reported by Vicomercatus, thinks that in the first book the principles are considered as they come into being, and in the second as they are. Simplicius holds that the proper nature of substantial change is taught in the second book, and that the universal change, of substance and of accident alike, is discussed in the first. Philoponus holds that the first book deals chiefly with matter and little with form, and the second chiefly with form and more sparingly with matter.

units.la: V. Plura afferri poterant. sed nos taedet infructuosae operae ; itaq; ad alios nos convertimus, qui difficultatem hanc prorsus dissimularunt, inter quos sufficiat nominasse Conimbricenses & Vicomercatum. Illi enim proponentes Synopsim librorum Physicorum, dicunt in primo agi de tribus rerum Physicorum Principijs, Materia, Forma, & Privatione ; in secundo de Natura, & naturalium rerum Causis : ac postea deprædicant continuatam in Aristotelis Physiologia seriem, atq; omnium partium sese mutuo ac decenter excipientium, quasi in structuram unius corporis, conspirationem. Vicomercatus autem ait illum duobus istis libris totam de Principijs & Causis naturalibus tractationem esse persecutum, ita ut in priore de ijs egerit, quae in re insunt, in altero etiam amplexus sit, quae extra sunt posita, alia quaedam de priore genere adjiciens, quae libro primo fuerant praeterita ; & hunc sequitur Magirus, qui Principia dividens in intrinseca & extrinseca, postquam ad Causas pervenit, quas extrinsecorum Principiorum nomine designat, altum agit de Materia & Forma silentium.
units.tr: V. More could be brought forward, but we are weary of fruitless labour, and so we turn to others who have altogether passed over this difficulty. Among them it is enough to name the Conimbricenses and Vicomercatus. For they, in proposing a synopsis of the books of the Physics, say that the first book treats of the three principles of natural things, matter, form and privation, and the second of nature and the causes of natural things. They then proclaim that in Aristotle's natural philosophy there is a continuous sequence, and a harmony of all the parts succeeding one another mutually and fittingly, like the structure of a single body. Vicomercatus, however, says that in those two books he pursued the whole treatment of natural principles and causes, so that in the first he dealt with those things which are within the thing, and in the second he embraced also those which are placed outside it, adding some further things of the first kind which had been passed over in the first book. Magirus follows him, and he, dividing principles into intrinsic and extrinsic, after he reaches the causes, which he designates by the name of extrinsic principles, maintains a deep silence about matter and form.

units.la: VI. Nihil igitur hi omnes viderunt ; quod eo magis mirum, cum non defuerint ante nos, qui commissum ab Aristotele errorem detegentes, asserrerent Aristotelem pervertisse ordinem, quia communiora prius sunt declaranda, Causae autem declaratae in secundo Physicorum, sint communiores Principijs declaratis in primo ; sicuti refertur à Picco-
units.tr: VI. None of all these men therefore saw anything, which is all the more remarkable since there were before us some who, detecting the error committed by Aristotle, asserted that Aristotle had reversed the order, because the more common things must be explained first, while the causes explained in the second book of the Physics are more common than the principles explained in the first; as is reported from Piccolomini.
Chapter I.

units.la: Piccolomineo: qui justissimæ huic censuræ putat se occurrere posse levissimis ratiunculis, quia in primo libro declarentur rerum Principia, ut fiunt; in secundo, ut sunt & cognoscuntur: præterea q; Causam non esse simpliciter communius Principio, sed solum de pluribus dici. hæc autem nihili sunt, cum vana sit utraq; illa distinctio. absurdum enim dictu est, eadem principia aliter debere tradi, quatenus per ea fit res, quam quatenus per ea est ac cognoscitur, cum hæc tria cohæreant indivulsè. Et Causam non esse priorem Principio, quomodo animal est prius homine (hoc enim exemplum ponit Piccolomineus) nimis confidenter asseritur, cum æquè ac animal est genus hominis, ita Causa sit genus Principij, ex doctrina Aristotelis: quanquam revera aliter se res habet, ut postea dicetur. Caeterum non alium in finem de Principijs, alium de Causis institutam esse ab Aristotele tractationem, manifestò apparet ex ipsius verbis; quippè quam in primo libro, acturus de Principijs, consilij sui rationem reddiderat; naturalem scientiam à Principijs inchoandam esse, quia τὸ εἰδέναι καὶ τὸ ἐπίσασθαι συμβαίνει περὶ πάσας τὰς μεθόδους, ἓν εἰσὶν ἀρχαὶ, ἢ αἰτίαι, ἢ στοιχεῖα, ἐν τοῦ ταῦτα γνωρίζειν. Τότε γὰρ οἰόμεθα γινώσκειν ἕκαστον, ὅταν τὰ αἰτία γνωρίσωμεν τὰ πρῶτα, καὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς τὰς πρώτας, μέχρι τῶν στοιχείων. Cognitio & Scientia in omnibus Doctrinis, quæ habent Principia aut Causas, aut Elementa, provenit ex horum notitia. tunc enim nos unum quodq; nosse putamus, ubi noverimus primas causas, & prima principia, & usq; ad elementa: eandem consimilibus verbis repetit in secundo, atq; tractationi de Causis præfationis vice præmittit: Ἐπισκεπτέον περὶ τῶν αἰτίων, ποῖα γε καὶ τόσα ἐστὶν ἀριθμόν, ἐπεὶ γὰρ πού εἰδέναι χάριν τὸ φυσικὸν ἢ πραγματεία, εἰδέναι δὲ πρότερον οἰόμεθα ἕκαστον, περὶ ἂν λάβωμεν ἀπλῶς περὶ ἕκαστον, τοῦτο δὲ δεῖ λαβεῖν τὴν πρώτην αἰτίαν, ἀναλόγως καὶ ἡμῖν τοῦτο ποιητέον, καὶ περὶ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς, καὶ περὶ πάσης φυσικῆς μεταβολῆς, ὅπως εἰδῶμεν αὐτῶν τὰς ἀρχὰς, ἀνάγειν. γεν εἰς αὐτὰς πειρώμεθα τῶν ζητουμένων ἕκαστον. Consi- derandum de Causis, quales ac quot numero sint, quum enim hac tractatio [instituta sit] gratia noscendi naturalia, ac non prius nos aliquid novisse arbitremur, quàm perceperimus propter quid illud sit, hoc autem est percipere primam Causam; videlicet nobis quoq; hoc faciendum est, tùm circa Generationem & Corruptionem, tùm circa omnem naturalem Mutationem: ut noscentes ipsarum Principia, namquam quæstionem ad ea reducere conemur. in quibus verbis fatali inconstantia vocabulum ἀρχὰς æquè generale facit ac ἀιτία, & pro eodem sumit, quod & in primis illis primi libri verbis fecit, consensu plerorumq; interpretum; parvo errore, aut fortè nullo, nisi ipse magnum fecisset, duabus illis Causarum speciebus, Materiæ & Formæ, Principij nomen peculiariter ut proprium attribuendo. sed hoc passim in ipso animadvertere licet, quod de Platone observavit Laërtius, ὁ πολλάκις διαφέρουσιν ὀνομασιν ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ σημαινομένου χρῆνται: quod sæpè diversis vocabulis ad eandem rem significandam utatur: pro exemplo afferens Ideam, quam & εἶδος appellat, & γένος & πόρα-δειγμα, & ἀρχὴν & αἴτιον. Hoc morbo, elegantiæ sermonis majorem curam gerendi, quam exactæ rerum traditionis, nihil concessit præceptori suo Aristoteles: quippè qui variare sermonem malit, ac copiam ostentare, varia in eandem notionem vocabula usurpando, quàm idem sæpiùs repetendo, accuratiùs quidem sed incomptiùs res docere: quod interpretibus, minùs hoc perpendentibus, miros certè lusus creat; dum nescio quæ non mysteria inde sibi exsculpunt. sed hoc mittentes, ipsa ab Aristotele tradita Principia cujusmodi sint, sigillatim videamus.
units.tr: Piccolomini, who thinks he can meet this most just criticism with the lightest of little arguments: namely, that in the first book the principles of things are explained as they come to be, and in the second as they are and are known; and further, that a cause is not simply more common than a principle, but is said of more things only. These, however, are worth nothing, since that distinction is empty. For it is absurd to say that the same principles ought to be taught differently insofar as through them a thing comes to be, and insofar as through them it is and is known, since these three things cohere inseparably. And to say that a cause is not prior to a principle, as an animal is prior to a man (for Piccolomini gives this example), is asserted too confidently; for, just as an animal is the genus of man, so by the teaching of Aristotle a cause is the genus of a principle; although in truth the matter stands otherwise, as will be said later. Moreover, that Aristotle did not set out the treatment of principles and that of causes for different ends is clearly apparent from his own words. For in the first book, about to treat of principles, he had given the reason for his plan: that natural science must begin from principles, because knowing and understanding occur in all methods which have principles, or causes, or elements, from the knowledge of these. For then we think we know each thing when we have known its first causes, and its first principles, down to the elements [Greek]. Knowledge and science in all doctrines which have principles or causes or elements arise from the knowledge of these. For then we think each thing is known when we have known its first causes and first principles, and as far as the elements. He repeats the same thing in similar words in the second book, and places it before the treatment of causes as a kind of preface: "We must consider the causes, what and how many they are in number. For since this natural inquiry aims at knowing, and we think we know each thing only when we have grasped its reason why, and this is to grasp the first cause, we must do the same also in regard to generation and corruption and every natural change, so that, knowing their principles, we may try to reduce each of the things sought to them" [Greek]. In these words, with a fatal inconsistency, he makes the term ἀρχὰς (principles) as general as αἰτία (causes), and takes them for the same thing, as he also did in the first words of the first book, with the agreement of most interpreters. This would have been a small error, or perhaps none at all, had he not himself made a great one by attributing the name of principle peculiarly and as its own to those two kinds of cause, matter and form. But it can be noticed everywhere in him what Laertius observed of Plato: that he often uses different words for the same meaning, that is, he uses various terms to signify the same thing, giving as an example the Idea, which he calls εἶδος, and γένος, and παράδειγμα, and ἀρχὴ, and αἴτιον. To this habit Aristotle, who cared more for elegance of style than for exact transmission of things, gave way from his teacher. For he preferred to vary his language and show off his richness by using various words for the same notion, rather than to repeat the same word more often, teaching things more accurately but less elegantly. This certainly produces strange games for interpreters who weigh this less carefully, while they carve out for themselves I know not what mysteries from it. But setting this aside, let us look one by one at what kinds of principles are handed down by Aristotle himself.
SECTION II. ON PRIME MATTER.

units.la: Materiam præexistentem requiri in omni generatione, cum veteres cuncti, quorum ipse super hac Aristotele dixerunt, [illegible, ~10 letters]
units.tr: That a pre-existing matter is required in every generation, since all the ancients, of whom Aristotle himself speaks on this subject, [illegible]

units.la: praeuiaria, praeuisio, praeparatio, praeuisio, de Boëtiò, de puro, praestio. prouisionum.
units.tr: forethought, foresight, preparation, foresight, of Boethius, of the pure, provision of provisions.
Chapter I.

units.la: hac re sententiam nimis calumniose detorquet. II. De Materia prima Aristotelis opinio breviter exponitur. III. Materiam primam nullo argumento probat Aristoteles; Aristotelici tantum uno, petito à mutatione substantiali; quod nullius est roboris, nisi positis Formis substantialibus. IV. Idem argumentum amplius refellitur: contra eos, qui Formas in uno composito ponunt. V. Contra eos, qui duntaxat unam; quia hoc posito, Nulla erit mixtio: & proinde, Non opus erit quatuor Elementis ad generationes, & consequenter, Peperam ab Aristotele reprehensi veteres, qui unum modo Elementum ponebant: ac, Vana omnia, quae de Materia secunda dicuntur: & verum, Quidvis fieri à quovis. VI. Quidvis fieri è quovis, posita Materia prima, & singularitate Formarum; amplius adhuc probatur. VII. Repetitur, & concluditur, Materiam primam non demonstrari per substantialem mutationem; si Forma Elementorum in mixto maneant. VIII. Ἀμεταςοιχειώσις nequicquam probatur Materia, cum illa non fiat: quae si fieret, omnino Materiam primam astrueret: contra Valesium. IX. Rami duo argumenta contra Materiam primam. X. Commentitiam esse Materiam primam, clamant innumerabiles de ea celeberrimorum Peripateticorum dissentientes, atque ex diametro sibi oppositae, opiniones.
units.tr: He twists the sense of this statement too maliciously. II. The opinion of Aristotle concerning prime matter is briefly set out. III. Aristotle proves prime matter by no argument; the Aristotelians use only one, drawn from substantial change, which has no force unless substantial forms are posited. IV. The same argument is refuted further, against those who place forms in a single compound. V. Against those who posit only one element; for if this is granted, there will be no mixture, and consequently there will be no need of four elements for generations. It follows that the ancients whom Aristotle reprehends for positing only one element were right, and that everything said about secondary matter is empty, and that anything at all can come from anything. VI. That anything can come from anything, once prime matter and the singularity of forms are posited, is proved still further. VII. It is repeated and concluded that prime matter is not demonstrated through substantial change, if the forms of the elements remain in the mixed body. VIII. The transmutation of elements [Ἀμεταςοιχειώσις] is in vain adduced to prove matter, since it does not happen; and if it did happen, it would establish prime matter altogether: against Valesius. IX. Two arguments against prime matter are given. X. Innumerable opinions of very famous Peripatetics, who disagree with one another and are diametrically opposed to one another, cry out that prime matter is a fiction.

units.la: Materiam aliquam praexistentem requiri in omni generatione, quae apud nos fit (de Creatione enim alia res est, neque de ea quicquam Aristoteles) quod ipse oppido quam laboriose astruit in primo physicorum, libenter concedimus, & nemo sanus negaverit, ut non fuerit ipsi tantum operae ponendum in re omnium rerum certissima, ac quam nemo unquam in controversiam vocavit. certe Veteres ad unum omnes pro indubitato supposuerunt Physiologi, nihil ex nihilo fieri, aut in nihilum perire, neque aliud sibi voluerunt, diecndo οὐδὲ γίνεσθαι τῶν ὄντων οὐδὲν, οὐδὲ φθείρεσθαι, nihil eorum, quae sunt, generari, aut interire,
units.tr: That some pre-existing matter is required in every generation that takes place among us (for creation is another matter, and Aristotle says nothing about it) is something we readily concede, and no sane person would deny it. Aristotle labours excessively to establish this in the first book of the Physics, and he need not have spent so much effort on a matter that is the most certain of all things and that no one has ever called into question. Certainly all the ancient natural philosophers without exception took it as indubitable that nothing comes from nothing or passes into nothing. They meant nothing else when they said that nothing of those things which are is generated or perishes [οὐδὲ γίνεσθαι τῶν ὄντων οὐδὲν, οὐδὲ φθείρεσθαι].

units.la: I Physic. 8. rire, quod nimis maligne in alium sensum detorquet Aristoteles, ac si simpliciter nihil nec oriri nec occidere putassent, omnémque generationem sustulissent; quod nemo tam amens ut afferat, nedum ut id fecerint illi viri; oi πρῶτοι ζητήσαντες καὶ φιλοσοφίαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν, καὶ τὴν φύσιν τῶν ὄντων. qui primi in philosophia quaesiverint veritatem & naturam entium, quo encomio ipse eos afficit. Imò vel ex ipsius scriptis apparet, quid isto axiomate sibi voluerint. ita enim de eadem re scribit, 1 Metaphysic. 3. Ἐξ οὗ γὰρ ἔστιν ἅπαντα τὰ ὄντα, καὶ ἐξ οὗ γίνεται πρῶτον, καὶ εἰς ὃ φθείρεται τελευταῖον, τὸ μὲν οὐσίας ὑπομένον, τοῖς δὲ πάθεσι μεταβαλλόμενον, τοῦτο στοιχεῖον καὶ ταύτην τὴν ἀρχὴν φασὶν εἶναι τῶν ὄντων. Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο οὔτε γίνεσθαι ἁπλῶς οἴονται, οὔτε ἀπόλλυσθαι, ὡς τῆς τοιαύτης φύσεως ἀεὶ σωζομένης. Ex quo omnia entia sunt, & ex quo primo fiunt, ac in quod ultimum intereunt, ita ut substantia quidem permaneat, sed affectionum mutationem subeat; hoc dicunt esse Elementum atque Principium entium. ac proinde neque generari quicquam arbitrantur, neque corrumpi, quum ista natura semper servetur. Et quomodo illi negarent absolutè, quicquam aut fieri aut interire, quorum constat omnem disquisitionem de ortu rerum ac interitu fuisse, déque eorum modis ac causis investigandis; (ὤσπερ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς ὁ λόγος πᾶσιν αὐτοῖς, omnium ipsorum pertractatio de generatione & interitu; inquit ipse, in principio octavi physicorum) quod ipsum fecerunt non sine erroribus, sed non ita puerilibus, ac ijs affingit Aristoteles, & plerumq; minus magnis, quam quos ipse commisit.
units.tr: Aristotle, Physics 1, interprets this too maliciously in a different sense, as if they had supposed that nothing simply arises or perishes, and had abolished all generation. No one is so foolish as to assert this, much less that those men did so, the first who sought in philosophy the truth and the nature of beings [οἱ πρῶτοι ζητήσαντες καὶ φιλοσοφίαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν, καὶ τὴν φύσιν τῶν ὄντων], which is the praise he himself bestows on them. Indeed, it appears from his own writings what they meant by this axiom. For he writes thus about the same matter in Metaphysics 1, chapter 3: "For from that from which all beings are, and from which they first come to be, and into which they finally perish, the substance remaining while the affections change, this they say is the element and principle of beings" [Ἐξ οὗ γὰρ ἔστιν ἅπαντα τὰ ὄντα, καὶ ἐξ οὗ γίνεται πρῶτον, καὶ εἰς ὃ φθείρεται τελευταῖον, τὸ μὲν οὐσίας ὑπομένον, τοῖς δὲ πάθεσι μεταβαλλόμενον, τοῦτο στοιχεῖον καὶ ταύτην τὴν ἀρχὴν φασὶν εἶναι τῶν ὄντων]. And therefore they think that nothing is generated or corrupted absolutely, since such a nature is always preserved [Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο οὔτε γίνεσθαι ἁπλῶς οἴονται, οὔτε ἀπόλλυσθαι, ὡς τῆς τοιαύτης φύσεως ἀεὶ σωζομένης]. And how could they absolutely deny that anything comes to be or perishes, when it is agreed that their whole inquiry concerned the origin and destruction of things, and the investigation of their modes and causes? (As Aristotle himself says at the beginning of Physics 8, "for the discussion of generation and corruption was common to all of them" [ὤσπερ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς ὁ λόγος πᾶσιν αὐτοῖς].) They did this not without errors, but not such childish ones as Aristotle attributes to them, and for the most part less grave than those he himself commits.

units.la: II. Certè de Materia plerosq; ipsorum sequaris minoribus periculo, quam Aristotelem cum sua illa Materia prima (quam tamen non ipse primus excogitavit, sed à Platone accepit, qui eadem fere omnia de ipsa opinatus est, ut è Timæo apparet) sentit autem, Esse unam quandam atq; eandem omnium rerum Materiam, e quâ primâ omnia fiant, & in quam ultimam omnia resolvantur, cùm ipsa sit ortus expers & interitus; nullâ aliâ praedita differentiâ, nisi quam à Formis habet: per se enim esse omnis Formae expertem, sed omnibus Formis recipiendis pariter habilem, earumq; appetentem; nunquam autem in ulla sui parte vel ad temporis momentum per se solam subsistere, sed necessario semper sub aliqua Forma manere: esse enim ens potentiâ tantùm, non actu: imò esse puram potentiam, ita ut non possit à Deo produci (verba sunt Conimbricensium) aliqua substantia despicatior, quàm ipsa; propterea√ cognitu difficillimam esse, ut què tota fugiat mentis nostrae captum: ipsam pati tantùm posse, omni agendi vi destitutam. Hæc breviter est apud omnes Peripateticos recepta Aristotelis de Materia prima sententia, quam totidem ferè verbis ex ipsius scriptis excipias, praecipuè ex octavo Metaphysicorum, & primo Physicorum.
units.tr: II. Certainly, concerning matter, you would follow most of them with less risk than Aristotle with that prime matter of his. (Yet he was not the first to devise it; he took it from Plato, who held almost the same opinions about it, as is clear from the Timaeus.) He holds that there is one and the same matter of all things, from which all things first come to be and into which all things are finally resolved, since it is free from origin and destruction. It is endowed with no difference other than that which it has from forms. For by itself it is devoid of every form, but equally fitted to receive all forms and desirous of them. It never subsists by itself, even for a moment, in any part of itself, but necessarily always remains under some form, for it is a being only in potency, not in act. Indeed, it is pure potency, so that (in the words of the Conimbricenses) no substance can be more despised than it, and therefore it is most difficult to know and escapes the grasp of our mind altogether; it can only be acted upon, being destitute of all power of acting. This is briefly the opinion of Aristotle concerning prime matter, which is accepted among all the Peripatetics, and which you may extract almost word for word from his writings, especially from Metaphysics 8 and Physics 1.
III.

units.la: Talem nos Materiam nullam agnoscimus; eámque esse inane commentum, facile probare possumus; quanquam poteramus simplici negatione defungi, contra Aristotelem certè; qui esse aliquam in omni generatione ac mutatione Materiam praeexistentem, in primo Physicorum probavit, rem nullius probationis indigentem, utpotè omnibus confessam: sed eam Materiam esse in omnibus eandem, per se omnis Formae expertem, atq; omnibus Formis suscipiendis idoneam, neque ibi probavit, aut probare aggressus est, neque alibi usquam. Interpretes autem ejus probare illam satagunt, sed unico tantùm argumento, ducto à mutatione substantiali, quam solam esse medium, quo prima Materia ignota probetur existere, ex Averroe scribit Zabarella; idq; exemplo declarat Magirus: Cibum converti in chylum, chylum in sanguinem, sanguinem in carnem, ossa, arterias, venas; eas rursus partes, intereunte homine, redire in sua principia, è quibus rursus herba oriantur, quibus bos pascatur; carne bovis vesci hominem, in cujus substantiam illa rursus mutetur. in hisce tot mutationibus cùm semper eadem maneat materia, subjectum illarum
units.tr: We acknowledge no such matter, and we can easily prove that it is an empty fiction. We could have dismissed it with a bare denial, at least against Aristotle, who in the first book of the Physics proved that there is some pre-existing matter in every generation and change. That is a point needing no proof, since everyone grants it. But he did not prove, nor did he attempt to prove, either there or anywhere else, that this matter is the same in all things, altogether without any Form of its own, and fit to receive all Forms. Its interpreters, however, labour to prove it, but with a single argument only, drawn from substantial change. Zabarella writes, following Averroes, that this alone is the means by which prime matter, unknown in itself, is shown to exist. Magirus illustrates it with an example: Food is converted into chyle, chyle into blood, blood into flesh, bones, arteries, and veins; and these parts, when the man dies, return to their principles, from which grass again arises, on which the ox feeds; and a man eats the flesh of the ox, and that flesh is changed again into his substance. In all these changes, since the same matter always remains, the subject of those vicissitudes must necessarily lack any proper substantial Form, because two substantial Forms cannot concur in one thing.

units.la: 1 De Materia prima. 5. rum vicissitudinum; necessario illam earere Forma propria substantiali, quia impossibile sit, duas Formas substantiales in una re concurrere. Sed haec argumentatio statim corruet, nulliusq; esse momenti deprehendetur, si negaverimus id, quod in ea sibi sumunt, dari Formam substantialem. Hanc enim Hypothesin esse basin ac fundamentum istius ratiocinationis, praeterquam quod per se apparet, fatetur Suarez, qui prae ceteris Peripateticis diligenter hanc pro Materia primo probationem, a substantiali mutatione petitam, excolere aggressus est. totum autem super ista re sermonem ita claudit: In his inferioribus substantiis, quoniam mutuo transmutabilia sint, recte concluditur aliquod commune & primum subjectum. Ut autem concludatur, hoc subjectum esse vere materialem causam ipsiusmet substantiae talium rerum, necesse est addere, illam mutuam transmutationem earum inter se esse secundum substantiam, & non tantum secundum accidentia; quia si in solis accidentibus transmutarentur, satis esset in eis dari primum subjectum talium accidentium, sive illud esset substantia simplex, sive composita, & sive esset unius rationis in omnibus, sive diverse. additq; ad concludendum, quod detur materia prima, qualem Aristoteles posuit, probandum esse, quod corporum transmutatio substantialis sit, non accidentalis; quae probatio in eo consistat, ut demonstretur dari Formas substantiales. Hae enim si dentur, necessario dari materiam primam, quae sit subjectum earum, & cum eis componat unam substantiam integram, quod est esse causam materialem substantiae. idemque repetit & in sequenti Sectione, §. 3. inquiens; Si corpora generabilia non transmutantur substantialiter, nec differunt per substantiales Formas, sed per accidentia, aut diversos modos se habendi; revera nulla datur materialis causa substantiae, sed datur tantum substantia simplex, quae non est alia & alia essentialiter, sed una aliter & aliter se habens sub diversis accidentibus. Nequaquam igitur, confitente Suarezio, Materiam primam inferre licet ex mutationibus illis, quas cernimus in generationibus & corruptionibus rerum, nisi si dentur
units.tr: 1 On Prime Matter. 5. But this argument collapses at once and will be found to be of no weight at all, if we deny what they assume in it, namely that a substantial Form is given. Suarez confesses that this hypothesis is the base and foundation of the reasoning, which is evident in itself. He, more diligently than the other Peripatetics, undertook to elaborate this proof of prime matter drawn from substantial change, and he closes his whole discussion of the matter thus: In these lower substances, since they are mutually transmutable, it is rightly concluded that there is some common and primary subject. But in order to conclude that this subject is truly the material cause of the substance of such things, it is necessary to add that their mutual transmutation is according to substance and not merely according to accidents. For if they were changed only in accidents, it would be enough that there be a primary subject of such accidents, whether that subject were a simple or a composite substance, and whether it were of one kind in all things or of different kinds. He adds, to conclude, that to prove that there is prime matter such as Aristotle posited, it must be shown that the transmutation of bodies is substantial and not accidental; and this proof consists in demonstrating that substantial Forms are given. For if they are given, prime matter, which is their subject and composes with them one complete substance, must necessarily be given too, and this is what it is to be the material cause of a substance. He repeats the same thing in the following Section, §3, saying: If generable bodies are not changed substantially, nor differ by substantial Forms but by accidents or different modes of being; then in truth no material cause of substance is given, but only a simple substance, which is not essentially one thing and then another, but one thing that is variously disposed under different accidents. Therefore, by Suarez's own admission, one may by no means infer prime matter from those changes which we see in the generations and corruptions of things, unless

units.la: dentur Formæ substantiales: quod etiam Fonseca non obscurè innuit, aiens, inventionem primæ Materiæ sine inventione Formæ substantialis nequaquam posse absolvi. Quùm autem nullas dari Formas nos in proxima sectione ostensuri simus, poteramus hac sola responsione esse contenti, ad diluendum hoc argumentum, quod unicum habent Aristotelici ad probandam Materiam primam.
units.tr: substantial Forms are given. Fonseca also hints at this clearly, saying that the discovery of prime matter can by no means be accomplished without the discovery of a substantial Form. Since we shall show in the next section that there are no such Forms, we could be content with this single answer to refute this argument, which is the only one the Aristotelians have for proving prime matter.

units.la: IV. Verùm futilitas istius probationis tanta est, ut mente etiam illa de Formis substantialibus Hypothesi, everti tamen facillimè posset, & liquidò confici, aliarum quidem rerum mutationes nequaquam id inferre quod ipsi volunt, & omnia tandem eo recidere, ut probetur Elementa inter se transmutari: quo non probato, reliquæ mutationes nihil planè eos juvent. Id ita se habere, quomodo nos dicimus, frustraq; aliarum substantiarum mutationes allegari, ad probandam ijs Materiam primam, patet ex ipsis Peripateticis, quorum magna pars & Elementorum Formas in similaribus, & ipsorum similarium Formas in magis compositis corporibus, ut stirpibus & animalibus, retinent. Et hæc planissimè est sententia Averrois, tradita tum alijs in locis, tùm 3. Phys. 31. quam non Fernelius modò approbat, sed & Aristotelici multi sequuntur. Imò hæc fuit ipsius Aristotelis sententia, partibus similaribus esse suas peculiares quibusque Formas, à totius Forma diversas; quod tùm aliunde excipere licet, tùm è 1. Metaph. in fine, propter Rationem sive Formam & carnem esse, & os, & reliquorum unumquodq;, non autem propter Materiam. Itaq; mutatio substantialis non probat Materiam primam, si licet in uno subjecto plures simul esse Formas; sicut isti volunt. namq; partes similares præter peculiares Formas, (ut tantisper ponamus Formas, & cum Peripateticis loquamur) quibus sibi est unaquæq; quod est, alteram insuper Formam habent, ipsam nimirùm Animam, per quam sunt partes viventis, & unum totum constituunt: & quomodo similaria milaria in toto, ita Elementa in similaribus suas Formas retinent. Dicunt quidem illas Formas inferiores, quae superiori aliqua Forma continentur, esse in potentia, non actu. sed haec distinctio vana est; quia si dantur ullae Formae substantiales, non possunt illae esse in subjecto aliter quam actu, sicuti infra hoc ipso in capite ostensuri sumus. namq; illud, esse in potentia, re vera nihil est aliud quam non esse: quare cum dicant elementorum Formas in similaribus, & similarium in toto, manere; omnino dicunt, plures Formas esse in uno subjecto.
units.tr: IV. Yet the futility of this proof is so great that, even granting the hypothesis of substantial Forms, it could very easily be overturned and it could be made clear that changes in other things by no means imply what they want, and that all of it finally comes down to proving that the elements transmute into one another. If that is not proved, the remaining changes do them no good at all. That this is so, as we say, and that other substances' changes are cited in vain to prove prime matter, is plain from the Peripatetics themselves, many of whom hold that the Forms of the elements remain in mixed bodies, and the Forms of mixed bodies remain in more compound bodies such as plants and animals. This is quite clearly the opinion of Averroes, set out in other places and in the third book of the Physics, comment 31, which not only Fernelius approves, but many Aristotelians also follow. Indeed it was the opinion of Aristotle himself that similar parts have their own particular Forms, different from the Form of the whole. This may be gathered from elsewhere, and from the first book of the Metaphysics at the end: the flesh and the bone and each of the other things exist on account of the Reason or Form, and not on account of the Matter. Therefore substantial change does not prove prime matter, if it is allowed that several Forms can be in one subject at once, as these men want. For similar parts, besides their particular Forms (let us for the moment posit Forms, and speak with the Peripatetics), by which each is what it is, also have another Form, namely the Soul itself, through which they are parts of a living thing and constitute one whole. And just as similar parts are in the whole, so the elements retain their Forms in the similar parts. They indeed say that those lower Forms, which are contained in some higher Form, are in potency and not in act. But this distinction is empty, because if any substantial Forms are given, they cannot be in the subject otherwise than in act, as we shall show later in this same chapter. For that "being in potency" is really nothing other than "not being." Therefore, when they say that the Forms of the elements remain in similar parts, and those of similar parts in the whole, they are altogether saying that there are several Forms in one subject.
V.

units.la: V. Et ne reliqui excipiant Peripatetici, sibi non eandem esse mentem, propterea-que apud se non valere illud argumentum a pluralitate Formarum in uno subjecto; dabimus rationes, ob quas & illis ita sentiendum sit, quomodo priores illi sentiunt. namq; nisi id statuatur, nihil erunt Mixta, nisi ipsa Materia prima cum peculiari istius Mixti Forma; & sic ne Mixta quidem appellare illa licebit, non magis quam Elementa. nihil enim refert plura Elementa assumta fuisse ad tale aliquod corpus constituendum. desierunt enim esse plura, postquam exutis proprijs Formis, unam communem subierunt; propterea-q; vanissima erunt, quaecunq; de mixtione & temperamento a Peripateticis non minus quam a Medicis disputantur. si enim propterea dicendum est corpus esse mixtum, quia ex diversis confiatum est, & respiciendum est non ad unionem ipsius, licet vel maxime unum sit una Materia sub una Forma, sed ad multitudinem partium ejus, quae olim, antequam ad ipsum constituendum concurrerent, inter se differebant, & in communi Materia diversas Formas obtinebant; nihil obest, quin ipsa quoque Elementa dicantur composita: quod exemplo Aëris facile declarari potest. Dicit Aristoteles, & cum eo omnes dicunt Peripatetici, Elementa invicem transmutari, non tamen proxime omnia. terram enim non abire in ignem, nisi prius in aquam mutata fuerit, ex aqua in aërem, ut sic ex aëre demum transeat in ignem. proxime enim inter se immutari ultro citroq;
units.tr: V. And lest the rest of the Peripatetics object that they do not hold the same view, and so that the argument from the plurality of Forms in one subject does not hold for them, I will give reasons why they too must think as the former ones do. Unless this is established, Mixed bodies will be nothing but the first Matter together with the particular Form of that mixed body; and so they could not even be called mixed bodies, any more than elements could. For it makes no difference whether several elements were taken up to constitute some such body. They cease to be many once, having put off their own Forms, they undergo one common Form. Therefore all the discussions of mixture and temperament that the Peripatetics, no less than the physicians, conduct will be utterly vain. For if a body is to be called mixed because it is made up of diverse things, and we look not to the union of its parts (even though it is most truly one, one Matter under one Form), but to the multitude of those parts, which before they came together to constitute it differed from one another and held diverse Forms in a common Matter, then nothing prevents the elements themselves from also being called compounds. This can easily be shown by the example of air. Aristotle says, and all the Peripatetics with him, that the elements change into one another, though not all of them directly. For earth does not turn into fire unless it has first been changed into water, and from water into air, so that only from air does it finally pass into fire. For the immediate changes are back and forth

Hunc aërem oportebit appellare corpus mixtum, cùm ex diversis Elementis conflatus sit; aut si hoc falsum (quale profecto illud esse dicent omnes Peripatetici) falsum etiam corpora illa, quæ vulgo Mixta dicuntur, esse revera talia, cùm æquè atq; Elementa sint simplicia, & in una Materia unicam tantùm Formam obtineant, quam omnia pariter Elementa susceperint, suis pristinis Formis depositis; æquè ac aqua & ignis in aërem mutata, suam Formam cum aëris Forma commutarunt. nihil enim refert, Forma totius, in aliqua parte præexistiterit, an omnibus simul partibus de novo ingeneretur. Ex his porrò sequitur, nihil necesse esse, ut ponantur quatuor Elementa, ob rerum generationes, cùm illæ, ex consequentia hujus opinionis, quæ unicam tantùm in uno subjecto Formam ponit, peragi æquè feliciter possint, si unum tantum sit Elementum, quam si quatuor; & fortasse felicius. non apparet enim, cur Principio generanti putemus esse difficilius, Formam illam, quam rei generandæ impertiri debet, introducere in massam ex unico Elemento desumtam, quam ex quatuor Elementis corrogatam: & si aliquid difficultatis habet veteris Formæ expulsio, promptius sit unicam, quam quatuor diversas eodem tempore expellere. propterèaque caulam nullam habuit Aristoteles, cur quaternarium Elementorum numerum tanto conatu assereret. Imò nullum omninò poni Elementum, saltem ob generationes, necesse esset, si Materia illa prima aut Formam aliquam propriam haberet, aut sine Formâ subsistere posset. melius enim ac facilius esset ipsam immediate assumi, quam per Elementorum ambages quæri. sed quia negant alterutrum ipsorum fieri posse, ac contendunt. Materiam tùm ex sese caret omni Formæ, tùm non nisi sub aliqua Forma subsistere posse; hoc quidem non urgebimus. Nihil tamen impedit, quominùs vera esse possit Veterum Physicorum, Thaletis, Anaximenis, Heracliti opinio, quorum quisque unum tantum Elementum, sed alius aliud, pro universa rerum Materia teria statuebant; non quod negarent plura uno esse Elementa, sed quod & reliqua tria, & omnia illa, quae vulgo composita vocantur, ex uno illo, quod pro Basi habebat quisque, fieri existimarent. quos insectari, aut erroris insimulare non debuit Aristoteles (si vera est eadem haec de uno subjecto singularitate opinio) cum revera idem dicant atq; ipse,& illorum Elementum, sit ipsius Materia prima, non interest enim, habeat rerum Materia aliquam Formam propriam necnè, si novas semper ascisci Formas potest; quod utrique de sua Materia pariter affirmant. neque enim Thales dixisset, terram & aerem idem esse quod aquam, sed Materiam illorum esse ab aqua sumtam, quae pristinam faciem nova specie commutasset, quomodo & Aristoteles diceret terram, aquam, aerem esse Materiam primam sub terrae, aquae, aeris Forma. Et sic diserte testatur de Anaximene Cicero, quod cum Aerem statueret Universalem rerum materiam, ex eo gigni dixerit Terram, Aquam, Ignem, è quibus porro omnia orirentur. taliaque de ijs & ipse Aristoteles testatur: de qua re alibi agetur. non pertinet autem ad rem, quod Veteres illi Formam nullam agnoverunt nisi accidentalem, quae Aristoteli est substantialis. Hoc enim an illud statuas, nihilo seciius procedit quod hic volebamus, cum unico Elemento aeque faciliter expediri posse generationes rerum, quam cum quatuor, si illa suas in mixtis Formas amittunt, atque sub nova Forma in unum coalescunt. Inutile quoq; erit hoc pacto effugium, quo eludere solent eos, qui contra Materiam primam ita argumentantur, ut dicant, ea posita quidvis fieri è quovis. Hoc enim ita solvunt, ut dicant, res non fieri immediatè ex Materia prima, sed ex Materia secunda, quae rei certae ac determinatae est accommodata, quapropter nequeat quodvis è quovis produci. Haec responsio ex ipso petita est Aristotele, cujus haec sunt verba, Περὶ δὲ τῆς ὕλης οὐσίας δεῖ μὴ λανθάνειν, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ πάντα πεφύκασι ... ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων. De Materiali causa sciendum est, quod etiamsi omnia
units.tr: and forth between earth and water, water and air, air and fire. Now let some part of air be taken, one third of which has been made from water, one third from fire, and one third has pre-existed. This air must be called a mixed body, since it is made up of different elements. Or, if this is false (as all the Peripatetics will surely say it is), then those bodies too which are commonly called mixed are in truth not such, since they are just as simple as the elements, and in one Matter they hold only a single Form, which all the elements alike have taken up after putting off their earlier Forms; just as water and fire, changed into air, have exchanged their Form for the Form of air. For it makes no difference whether the Form of the whole pre-existed in some part, or whether it is generated anew in all the parts at once. From this it further follows that there is no need to posit four elements for the sake of the generations of things. On the consequence of this opinion, which posits only a single Form in one subject, generations can be carried out just as successfully if there is only one element as if there are four, and perhaps more successfully. For it does not appear why we should think it harder for the Principle that generates to introduce into a mass taken from a single element that Form which it must impart to the thing to be generated, than to introduce it into a mass gathered from four elements. And if the expulsion of the old Form has some difficulty, it is easier to expel one Form than four diverse ones at the same time. Therefore Aristotle had no cause to assert with such effort the number four of the elements. Indeed, if the first Matter either had some Form of its own or could subsist without a Form, it would be necessary to posit no element at all, at least for the sake of generations. For it would be better and easier for it to be taken up immediately than to be sought by the roundabout way of the elements. But because they deny that either of these can happen, and they contend that Matter by itself lacks all Form and can subsist only under some Form, I shall not press this point. Nevertheless, it does not prevent the opinion of the ancient natural philosophers, Thales, Anaximenes and Heraclitus, from being true, each of whom posited a single element as the Matter of the whole universe, though each posited a different one. They did not deny that there are more elements than one, but they thought that the other three, and all those things which are commonly called compounds, were generated from that one which each held as the Base. Aristotle ought not to have attacked them or accused them of error (if this same opinion of a single subject is true), since they really say the same thing he does, and their element is his first Matter. For it does not matter whether the Matter of things has some Form of its own or not, if it can always take on new Forms; both sides affirm this alike of their Matter. For Thales would not have said that earth and air are the same as water, but that their Matter was taken from water, which had changed its earlier appearance into a new species; just as Aristotle would say that earth, water and air are the first Matter under the Form of earth, of water, of air. And Cicero clearly bears witness to this about Anaximenes: that, while he held air to be the universal matter of things, he said that earth, water and fire were generated from it, and from these all things arose. Aristotle himself bears witness to such things about them; this matter will be treated elsewhere. Nor does it matter that those ancients recognised no Form except an accidental one, whereas for Aristotle it is substantial. For whether you hold this or that, what we are arguing here still follows: the generations of things can be explained just as easily with a single element as with four, if the things they become lose their Forms in the mixed bodies and coalesce into one under a new Form. This escape, by which they are wont to elude those who argue against the first Matter in this way, that given such a Matter anything can come from anything, will also be useless. For they resolve it by saying that things are not generated immediately from the first Matter, but from the second Matter, which is adapted to a certain and determinate thing, and therefore cannot allow anything to be produced from anything. This answer is taken from Aristotle himself, whose words are these: Περὶ δὲ τῆς ὕλης οὐσίας δεῖ μὴ λανθάνειν, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ πάντα πεφύκασι ... ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων [Concerning the material substance it must not escape notice that all things naturally arise from the same ... from opposites].
