units.la: omnia ex eodem primo, aut ijsdem ut primis, aut eadem Materia [ sit ] ut principium ijs quae generantur; cujusq; tamen est quaedam [ Materia ] propria. additq; exempla pituitae & bilis, quarum illi pinguia & dulcia, huic amara aut alia quaedam sint pro Materia proxima. itaque fieri ut multae sint ejusdem rei materiae, si proxima ejus Materia & ipsa habeat proximam Materiam, ut ita se habeat pingue ad dulce, quomodo dulce se habet ad pituitam; priores enim illas materias esse Materias πρὸ ὁδοῦ illi rei, in cujus proximam materiam successive a prima Materia per illas pervenitur. idcirco quando de alicujus compositi Materia quaeritur, non modo Materiam primam excludit, sed & Elementa quoque, jubens proximam cujusq; rei Materiam assignari. Δεῖ δὲ ηρῶτα τὰ ἐγγύτατα αἰτία λέγειν, τίς ἡ ὕλη, μὴ πῦρ, ἢ γῆν, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἰδίαν. Oportet autem & proximas causas afferre, [ ubi quaeritur ] qua sit materia; non ignem, aut terram, sed propriam [ Materiam assignando. ] Haec omnia sint verissima, quae de secunda Materia hic tradit Aristoteles, sed quae defendi ex ipsius decretis nullo modo possunt, nisi statuatur Elementorum Formas in Mistis manere. tunc enim, cum varia admodum esse possit ipsorum mixtio, & varia inde exurgere Materia secunda, apertum est quomodo res non nisi ex determinata Materia fieri possint: unde tamen sequitur id, quod nequaquam admissuri sint Peripatetici, neq; salvis sui praeceptoris dogmatis admittere possint, Unumquidq; esse tale quid non a Forma sola, sed & a Materia; quum tamen contrarium statuerit Aristoteles, Δεῖ ἐν λόγῳ ηρῶτα σαρξ καὶ ὁσοῦν ὅτι, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἕκαστον, καὶ ὁ ἁ τὴν ὕλην. in quam sententiam alibi quoque dixit, Materiam non facere differentiam, Ἡ δὲ ὕλη ὁ ποιεῖ διαφορὰν. & sic Scaliger commentario ad quarti de Causis Plant. cap. 16. Materia non variat Formam, sed a Forma variatur Materia. Ast si Elementa in Mistis Formam suam sub potioris Formae imperio deponunt, nihili sunt quae de Materia secunda dicuntur, neque ulla talis inveniri potest, in qua plus hujus aut illius Elementi sit; quam Materiae secundae
units.tr: Everything comes from the same first thing, either from things that are themselves primary, or from one and the same matter as a principle for the things that are generated; yet each thing also has a matter peculiar to itself. He adds the examples of phlegm and bile, of which the former are for phlegm rich and sweet matter, and for bile bitter or some other matter, as the proximate matter. So it happens that there are many matters of the same thing: if the proximate matter itself has a proximate matter, so that fat stands to sweet as sweet stands to phlegm. For those earlier matters are matters "on the way to" (πρὸ ὁδοῦ) that thing, into whose proximate matter one passes successively from prime matter through them. Therefore, when the matter of some compound is asked about, he excludes not only prime matter but the Elements as well, requiring that the proximate matter of each thing be assigned. One must state the nearest causes, what the matter is: not fire or earth, but its own proper matter. One must also give the proximate causes when the matter is asked; not fire or earth, but assigning the proper matter. All these things that Aristotle here delivers about secondary matter are most true; but they cannot be defended from his own doctrines, unless it is held that the forms of the Elements remain in mixed bodies. For then, since their mixture can be quite varied, and from it a varied secondary matter arises, it is plain how things can be made only from a determinate matter. From this, however, there follows what the Peripatetics will by no means admit, and cannot admit without overthrowing their master's teaching: that each thing is such a thing not by its Form alone but also by its matter. Yet Aristotle has asserted the contrary: In the definition one must first state flesh and bone, and each of the other things, and the matter. To this same opinion he also said elsewhere that matter does not make the difference: Matter does not make the difference [Ἡ δὲ ὕλη ὁ ποιεῖ διαφορὰν]. And so Scaliger, in his commentary on the fourth book of the Causes of Plants, chapter 16: Matter does not vary the Form, but the matter is varied by the Form. But if the Elements in mixed bodies lay aside their own form under the rule of the more powerful Form, then what is said about secondary matter is nothing, and no such matter can be found in which there is more of this or that Element; of secondary matter, as Scaliger hands it down, as a specific difference. For since the whole business depends on the Form, and each thing is such not from its matter, which is the same and common to all, but because it has obtained such a Form in common matter, it makes no difference what kind of secondary matter is taken, since it cannot receive a new Form unless the former one is abolished; once that is abolished, nothing remains but prime matter. And so it does not appear why phlegm cannot be produced from the bitter as well as from the sweet. For bitterness, as well as sweetness, like all other qualities, follows the Form (as they themselves wish) with an inseparable bond, and therefore once that is expelled they cannot remain. But if from something sweet some new substance, likewise sweet, arises, this does not happen because the earlier sweetness remained, but because the new Form brought that quality with it, by their own teaching. Therefore there is no necessary secondary matter in the generation of any thing, since it ought to be equally easy for the agent cause, the giver of Form, to do its work, whatever matter is given to it. It is possible (he says in the eighth book of the Metaphysics, chapter 4) [Ἐνδέχεται] that, when the matter is one, different things come to be through the moving cause, as from wood a chest and a bed. It can happen that from the same matter different things are made, because of the moving cause, as from wood an ark, and a bed. For it is witty what he adds in the same place as if to the contrary: Of some things, which are different from one another, the matter is different of necessity; for example, a saw cannot come to be from wood, because of the moving cause. Of some things the matter is different of necessity, since they differ, as a saw cannot be made from wood. [Ἐνίων δ᾽ ἑτέρα ἡ ὕλη ἐξ ἀνάγκης, ἑτέρων ὄντων, οἷον πρίων ἂν γένοιτο ἐν ξύλῳ]. Of things that are different among themselves the matter is necessarily different. For example, a saw cannot be made from wood, and this is not within the power of the Efficient Cause. For no one can make a saw from wool or wood. This comparison, we say, is too witty, like the other countless ones in those books of Divine Philosophy. For an artificer cannot make a saw from wood or wool (why he did not add mud and snow as well is a marvel), because he cannot change their natural qualities; but he must be content with such matter as he has received, since he brings nothing new except an accidental figure, which by no means changes the essence of the thing. units.la: Metaph. 9. cundæ velut specificam differentiam tradit Scaliger. cum enim totum negotium dependeat à Forma, & unumquódque tale sit non à Materia, quæ omnibus eadem & communis, sed quia talem Formam in communi Materia nactum est; nihil refert qualiscunq; Materia secunda assumatur, cum novam Formam suscipere non possit, nisi pristina aboleatur; qua abolita, nihil manet nisi Materia prima. & sic non apparet, cur pituita nequeat ex amaro æquè ac ex dulci procreari. tum amaritudo enim, tùm dulcedo, ut omnes aliæ qualitates, Formam sequuntur ( ut ipsi volunt ) individuo nexu, propterèaque illa expulsa, manere ipsæ non valent. quod si ex dulci fit aliqua substantia nova itidem dulcis, non hoc fit, quia prior dulcedo remansit, sed quia nova Forma illam secum qualitatem adduxit, ex ipsorum doctrina. Itaq; nulla est necessaria Materia secunda in ullius rei generatione, cùm Agenti Causæ, Formæ datori, æquè facile esse debeat, opus suum facere, quæcunq; illi Materia detur. Εναέχεται ὅτι (inquit ipse 8. Metaphysic. 4.) μιᾶς τ᾽ ὕλης οὔσης, ἕτερα γίνεσθαι διὰ τὴν κινοῦσαν αἰτίαν, οἷον ἐκ ξύλου καὶ πιθωοῦ καὶ κλίνη. Fieri potest, ut ex eadem materia fiant res diversæ, propter Causam movent em: uti ex ligno & arca, & lectus. nam facetum est quod velut in contrarium ibidem subjungit. Ενίων δ᾽ ἑτέρα ἡ ὕλη ἐξ ἀνάγκης, ἑτέρων ὄντων, οἷον πρίων ἂν ἂν γένοιο ἐν ξύλῳ, διὰ τὴν κινοῦσαν αἰτίαν τοῦτο· ὁ δὲ πιθ... πρίονα ἐξ ἑτέρας ἡ ξύλα. Quorundam, quæ inter se diversa sunt, necessario diversa est Materia. exempli gratia, è ligno serra fieri nequit, neq; hoc est in Causæ Efficientis potestate. nemo enim serram è lana aut ligno facere potest: nimis, inquimus, faceta est hæc comparatio, ut aliæ in iis Divinæ Philosophiæ libris innumeræ. artifex enim serram facere nequit è ligno aut lana (mirùm cur non lutum quoque & nivem appositurit) quia naturales ipsorum qualitates immutare non potest, sed quales in materia accepit, talibus contentus esse debet, cùm nihil ipse afferat novi, nisi accidentalem duntaxat figuram, quæ essentiam rei nequaquàm immutat. ast si ad
units.tr: Metaph. 9. of the second matter, as Scaliger hands down as its specific difference. For since the whole business depends on the Form, and each thing is such not from its matter, which is the same and common to all, but because it has obtained such a Form in common matter, it makes no difference what kind of secondary matter is taken, since it cannot receive a new Form unless the former one is abolished; once that is abolished, nothing remains but prime matter. And so it does not appear why phlegm cannot be produced from the bitter as well as from the sweet. For bitterness, as well as sweetness, like all other qualities, follows the Form (as they themselves hold) with an inseparable bond, and therefore once that is expelled they cannot remain. But if from something sweet some new substance, likewise sweet, arises, this does not happen because the earlier sweetness remained, but because the new Form brought that quality with it, by their own teaching. Therefore there is no necessary secondary matter in the generation of anything, since it ought to be equally easy for the agent cause, the giver of Form, to do its work, whatever matter is given to it.
Chapter I.

units.la: si ad figurae illius introductionem, necessario sequerentur omnes conditiones ferrae requisitae, posset artifex vel ex ligno serram fabricari, & ex lana quoque, modo prius compacta esset in unum corpus, sive textura ut in pannis, sive multa subactione, ut in pileis fieri solet. (ad has ineptias nos pertrahit θαυμασιωλὰτητ illa Princeps Philosophia) & ita demum aptè cum Generante Artifex comparetur. Causa enim Generans (ut tritissimo inter ipsos axiomate vulgatum est) Formam conferens, omnia confert simul, quae Formam consequuntur; quod decretum suum si perpendisset Aristoteles, non inficiatus esset, Quidvis posse generari ex Materia prima, exemplo à lanea ferra petito. Manet igitur objectio, Posita Materia prima cum singularitate Formarum in uno composito, quidvis fieri è quovis; & nihili est illa responsio de Materia secunda: quod amplius adhuc probamus.
units.tr: If the introduction of that form were necessarily followed by all the conditions required for iron, then a craftsman could make a saw from wood, and also from wool, provided the wool had first been compacted into one body, either by weaving, as in cloth, or by heavy pressing, as is usually done with felt hats. (It is to these absurdities that that famous Prince of Philosophy drives us, [θαυμασιολατρεία].) Only then is the craftsman fairly compared with the generating cause. For a generating cause, as is commonly held in the most hackneyed axiom among them, when it confers the form, confers at once everything that follows the form. Had Aristotle weighed this decree, he would not have denied that anything at all can be generated from prime matter, using the example of a woollen saw. The objection therefore remains: if prime matter is posited, with the individuality of forms in one composite, anything can be made from anything. That answer about secondary matter is worthless, and we prove this further still.

units.la: VI. Néque enim negant Materiae adversarij, res fieri ex alijs rebus jam sua Forma praeditis, hoc est ex Materia secunda; sed hoc dicunt, cum Materia omnibus Formis admittendis ex aequo apta sit, neque ulla Forma Materiae adhaereat inseparabiliter, generatio autem nihil sit aliud, nisi novae Formae introductio; necessario sequitur quidvis fieri posse è quovis. nam illa Materiae secundae aptitudo, merum est figmentum. si enim ulla est, illa est à Forma. Materiam enim dicunt ad omnes pariter Formas propensionem habere, neque magis ad unam, quam ad aliam. erit igitur illa aptitudo à Forma; quod sanè fatetur Zabarella, qui ex vulgata opinione cum Materiae geminam potentiam assignasset, alteram universalem, eamq; inseparabilem, quae sit propensio Materiae ad omnes Formas indistincte; alteram particularem, qua magis hanc Formam respiciat quam illas; addit, eam fieri partim ab agente ita Materiam praeparante ad hanc Formam recipiendam, ut non sit apta recipere alias (quod omninò vanum est) partim à Forma praesente, seu à qualitatibus eam insequentibus; idque confirmat (valdè quidem futiliter) exemplo
units.tr: VI. For the opponents of matter do not deny that things are made from other things already endowed with their form, that is, from secondary matter. But they say this: since matter is equally suited to receive all forms, and no form adheres inseparably to matter, and generation is nothing but the introduction of a new form, it necessarily follows that anything can be made from anything. For that aptitude of secondary matter is a mere fiction. If there is any such aptitude, it comes from the form. For they say that matter has an equal inclination toward all forms, and no more toward one than another. That aptitude, then, comes from the form. Zabarella certainly admits this. Following the common opinion, he assigned matter a twofold power: one universal and inseparable, which is matter's indistinct inclination toward all forms; the other particular, by which matter regards this form more than those. He adds that this particular power arises partly from the agent, which so prepares matter to receive this form that it is not apt to receive others (which is utterly vain), and partly from the form present, or from the qualities that follow it. He confirms this (quite feebly) by the example

units.la: {x} Potentia Materiae secundae ... (marginal note) emplo humani seminis, cum cujus Forma conjunctæ sint quædam qualitates, quæ Materiam reddunt magis aptam recipere Formam hominis, quàm Formam lapidis. ast hoc stare non potest cum ipsorum decretis, qui statuant omnia appetere sui conservationem. illæ enim Formæ appeterent sui interitum, siquidem substantiam, cui insunt, facerent aptam ad hostem suum, novam Formam, intromittendum; qua suscepta, ipsam aboleri sit necesse. & hæc absurditas, prolixè etiam & nervosè à magno viro Bassono disputata, major est quàm ut dilui à Peripateticis possit: Præterea cum in omni mutatione substantiali aboleatur prior Forma, in cujus locum nova succedat; necesse est illam prioris Formæ abolitionem aut cum aliqua ipsius resistentia conjunctam esse, aut cum nulla. si hoc dicant, omnino manet quod dicebamus; quodvis fieri è quovis. sin illud, necesse esset contrarium evenire, ac nunc evenire videmus. vix enim ullum est animal, cui ipsa elementa sint pro cibo, sed herbis, frugibus, fructibus, lacte, melle, atq; aliorum animantium carnibus vescuntur, & magnam inde utilitatem percipiunt, ea nimirum concoquendo, & in corporis sui substantiam convertendo; quod de elementis non fecerint. at debebant hæc citiùs & minore negotio posse concoquere, & in chylum ac sanguinem vertere; cùm par sit, vilissimas illas Formas, néque Materiæ firmiùs hærere, néque majori resistendi vi præditas esse, quam alias nobilissimas, quas Materia ægriùs ac valdè invita è complexu suo amittit, de priorum amissione non multum curans, ut consentaneum est trito inter illos ac cato axiomati, Appetitum Materiæ respectu Formæ, quam nondum possidet, Appetitum desiderij; respectu ejus, qua fruitur, Appetitum complacentiæ nunc utpari. probabile enim est, majorem esse illam complacentiam (ut barbaræ ac ridiculæ phrasi nos tantisper accommodemus) quam percipit ex dignioris ac patriciæ Formæ præsentia, ac illa, quæ proveniat ex humilis atq; plebeiæ Formæ fruitione; nisi si, ut dicunt alibi, prorsus barda ac stupida res est illa Materia.
units.tr: {x} The potency of secondary matter ... (marginal note) by the example of human seed, with which certain qualities are joined, which make the matter more apt to receive the form of a man than the form of a stone. But this cannot stand with their own decrees, who hold that all things seek their own preservation. For those forms would then seek their own destruction, since they would make the substance in which they inhere apt to admit a new form, their enemy; and once that form is received, the former must necessarily be abolished. This absurdity, which the great man Basso has argued at length and vigorously, is too great for the Peripatetics to dilute. Furthermore, since in every substantial change the prior form is abolished to make way for a new one, that abolition must either be joined with some resistance from the prior form or with none. If they say the latter, then what we said stands entirely: anything can be made from anything. If the former, then the contrary would have to happen to what we now see happening. Hardly any animal has the elements themselves for food. Instead they feed on herbs, grains, fruits, milk, honey, and the flesh of other animals, and they gain great benefit from these by digesting them and converting them into the substance of their own body. They would not do this with the elements. Yet these ought to be digested more quickly and with less effort, and turned into chyle and blood. For it is only fitting that those basest forms should neither cling to matter more firmly, nor be endowed with greater power of resistance, than the most noble forms, which matter parts with only slowly and very reluctantly from its embrace, caring little for the loss of the former. This accords with the hackneyed and cat-like axiom of those men: The appetite of matter toward a form it does not yet possess is an appetite of desire; toward the form it now enjoys, it is an appetite of complacency. It is probable that this complacency (to accommodate ourselves for a moment to their barbarous and ridiculous phrasing) is greater, which matter perceives from the presence of a nobler and more patrician form, than that which arises from enjoying a humble and plebeian form. Unless, as they say elsewhere, that matter is a utterly dull and stupid thing.
VII. But if

units.la: VII. Sin verò & hanc difficultatem devitantes, & priores, suam cuiq; elemento in mixtis Formam relinquere malunt, cadit illud pro Materia prima Argumentum, à substantiali rerum mutatione petitum; etiamsi verum esset, quod in ipso supponitur, dari Formas substantiales. utut enim novas subinde Formas acquirunt illa atq; amittunt, nunquam tamen ad Materiam primam deveniunt, cum sub novis illis Formis, eadem semper elementa permaneant, suasq; proprias Formas retineant. nullum igitur ex mixtis, & substantiali ipsorum mutatione, potest pro Materia Aristotelica argumentum desumi.
units.tr: VII. But if, avoiding both this difficulty and the earlier ones, they prefer to leave each element its own form within mixed bodies, then the argument for prime matter drawn from the substantial change of things falls away. Even if what is assumed in it were true, namely that substantial forms exist, still, although they acquire and lose these forms from time to time, they never arrive at prime matter, since under those new forms the same elements always remain and keep their own proper forms. Therefore no argument for Aristotelian matter can be drawn from mixed bodies and their substantial change.

units.la: VIII. Omnis igitur ipsorum spes in eo sita est, si decantatam illam inter ipsos μεταστοιχείωσιν [?] demonstrare valeant. illâ enim posità, ultrò fatemur sequi, ut detur Materia prima Aristotelica. néque enim probare possumus Valesium, qui cum statuat & elementa non manere in mistis actu, sed potentia, & ipsa quoque inter se Elementa transmutari, Materiam tamen primam rejicit, utpotè quæ nihil omninò sit, nisi Hypothesis ob rudiores conficta. namq; verè & exactè simplicium nullam esse Materiam, sed factum esse illorum quodcunq; ex Materia, ut ignem ex aëre, non in Materia, ut sigillum in cera. itaq; fieri res singulas, etiam simplicissimas, ex Materia aliqua, unam verò eandemq; omnium nullam esse; néque necesse esse, ut quod ex alio fit, immanentem habeat Materiam. artificialibus quidem proprium esse, ut nihil nisi in quadam Materia fiat, ut lectus ex immanente ligno, sigillum ex cera; naturalibus non item. has enim ex se mutuo fieri, non ut immanentibus, velut lectulus è Nuce, sed ut desinentibus, velut mensa ex arca. propterea non opus esse, ponere primam Materiam rerum naturalium, sed fieri alias ex aliis. & plurima adhuc addit in eandem sententiam, quæ nimis tædiosum foret huc omnia transcribere. est autem hæc opinio admodum mirabilis, & adeò subtilis, ut animo comprehendi non possit, nedum refutari, quomodò aliqua res fiat ex alia, néque tamen habeat in se illam Materiam, teriam,
units.tr: VIII. Their whole hope therefore rests on whether they can demonstrate that much-vaunted mutual transmutation of the elements [μεταστοιχείωσιν]. For once that is granted, we freely admit that prime matter in Aristotle's sense must follow. Nor can we approve of Valesius. Although he holds that the elements do not remain in mixed bodies actually but only potentially, and that the elements themselves are transmuted into one another, he nevertheless rejects prime matter, as something that is nothing at all but a hypothesis devised for the cruder sort. For strictly and exactly speaking, simple things have no matter. Rather, whatever they are, they are made out of matter, as fire is made out of air, not in matter, as a seal is in wax. So individual things, even the most simple, are made from some matter, but there is no one matter common to all of them. Nor is it necessary that what is made from another should have an inherent matter. It is indeed proper to artificial things that nothing is made except in some matter, as a bed from inherent wood or a seal from wax. Natural things are not so. For these are made from one another not as inherent, like a little bed from a nut, but as ceasing to be, like a table from a chest. Therefore there is no need to posit a prime matter of natural things; rather, some are made from others. He adds very many more points to the same effect, which would be too tedious to transcribe here. This opinion is indeed most remarkable, and so subtle that it cannot be grasped by the mind, let alone refuted: how one thing can be made from another and yet not have in itself that Matter

units.la: De sacra Phil. c.69. teriam, quæ erat in priore, ex qua ipsa facta est. Valesio igitur omisso, dicimus, posita elementorum transmutatione, necessario etiam poni Materiam primam.
units.tr: On Sacred Philosophy, ch. 69: that matter which was in the prior thing, from which it itself was made. Setting Valesius aside, then, we say that once the transmutation of the elements is posited, prime matter is necessarily posited too.

units.la: IX. Sed cum nugatoria tota sit & ad libitum conficta Elementorum mutua transmutatio (quod hic supponentes, posteà, in loco magis proprio, probatum dabimus) relinquitur ut explodenda sit, quæ hoc solo argumento probari poterat, Materia prima : ut nihil necesse sit nos contra illam uti argumentis Rami, qui illam impugnat ex eo, quod Aristoteles dixerat, finem Physicæ esse, τὸ φαινόμενον ἀεὶ κυρίως καὶ κατὰ τὴν αἴσθησιν, id quod semper sensibus evidenter percipitur. & physico propositum esse σῶμα ἁπλοῦν, corpus tactile, quæ conditiones Materiæ primæ, cujusmodi ab ipso describitur, haudquaquam competunt. Hæc quidem ratio firma est adversus eos, qui mordicus tenent ac tuentur, quidquid semel dixit Aristoteles; sed non urget eos, qui hisce authoritatibus insuper habitis, velint de ipsa Materiæ Natura disputationem instituere. firmius est illud alterum, allatum è primo Phys. 4. Elementa corporum sensibilium esse corpora; unde sequeretur Materiam primam, utpotè sensibilium corporum Elementum, esse sensibilem & corpoream, quorum tamen prius ab omnibus, alterum à plerisq; Aristotelicis ipsi denegatur.
units.tr: IX. But since the mutual transmutation of the elements is entirely trifling and fabricated at will (which we, supposing it here, will prove later in a more proper place), it follows that prime matter, which could be proved by this argument alone, must be discarded. So there is no need for us to use against it the arguments of Ramus, who attacks it on the ground that Aristotle had said the end of physics is what always appears properly and according to sense [τὸ φαινόμενον ἀεὶ κυρίως καὶ κατὰ τὴν αἴσθησιν], that which is always evidently perceived by the senses, and that the subject of physics is simple body [σῶμα ἁπλοῦν], tangible body, conditions which by no means fit prime matter as he describes it. This argument is indeed firm against those who stubbornly hold and defend whatever Aristotle once said. But it does not press those who, setting these authorities aside, wish to conduct a discussion about the very nature of matter. That other argument, brought from Phys. 4 in the first book, is firmer: the elements of sensible bodies are bodies. From this it would follow that prime matter, being the element of sensible bodies, is sensible and corporeal. Yet the former is denied to it by all Aristotelians, and the latter by most of them.

units.la: X. Sed etiamsi nulla essent contra Materiam primam argumenta, poterat tamen ad detegendam istius commenti futilitatem abundè sufficere, illas maximarum & inutilissimarum rixarum, quæ indè pullularunt, & circa ejus essentiam atq; naturam agitatæ inter Peripateticos semper fuerunt, ac hodièq; agitantur; quas omnes comportare, Herculeus labor esset. satis erit, velut in gustum & specimen, paucas de plurimis in medium afferre; & oppositas sibi ex diametro assertiones exhibere. Aiunt enim alij, alij negant, Materiam primam corpus esse, & corpoream Formam de substantiæ genere sibi congenitam obtinere; Absolutè eam corpus non esse, nec esse posse, nisi generatio
units.tr: X. But even if there were no arguments against prime matter, the sheer futility of this fiction could be exposed well enough by those quarrels, the greatest and most useless, which have sprung from it and have always been stirred up among the Peripatetics concerning its essence and nature, and are still stirred up today. To gather them all together would be a labour of Hercules. It will be enough, by way of a taste and a sample, to bring forward a few out of very many and to set out the assertions that are diametrically opposed to one another. For some say, and others deny, that prime matter is a body and holds a corporeal form as something congenital to its kind of substance. They hold that it is not, and cannot be, a body absolutely, unless generation
Chapter I.

units.la: ratio prorsus tollatur. Materiam, tametsi corpus non est, nec corporis Formam obtinet, secundum se tamen, & ante receptionem Formæ, esse quantam, & habere trés dimensiones, longitudinem, latitudinem, & profunditatem, sed nullis certis terminis, nisi quos à Forma accipiat; Nullam esse in ea quantitatem coævam, sed omnes naturalium corporum quantitates insequi Formas, & à Formis tribui. Materiam esse secundum se puram potentiam non actum, neque aliquid ex actu & potentia compositum; Esse rem actu existentem, neque existentiam suam à Forma mutuari, sed per essentiam sibi propriam esse id quod est, & ab aliis differre. Ingenitum esse. Materiæ appetitum Formæ: Hunc appetitum nequaquam illi competere. Materiam semper moliri maleficium, atque novas Formas appetere; Eam præsentibus Formis jucundè perfrui atq; acquiescere. Materiam posse per se intelligi; Nequaquam aptam esse per se intelligi. Materiam ad compositi naturalis essentiam pertinere: Non esse partem quidditatis seu essentiæ compositi naturalis. Posse Materiam divinitus absq; omni Forma existere: Non posse absq; Forma existere. Potentiam Materiæ esse absolutam, ab ejus essentia non distinctam, & de genere substantiæ; Esse relativam & de genere qualitatis, ac proinde accidens. Hæ aliæque ejusdem Farinæ circa Materiam primam quæstiones quamplurimæ Peripateticos exercent nullo fine, neq; vulgum modo, sed eminentissimos quoq; inter ipsos qui & cum aliis & inter se quam acerrimè de ijs digladiantur, ut nescias miserèri malis an ridere, tantum fluctuum in Simpulo excitari videns, tantúmq; turbarum ac bellorum cieri pro re nihili ac commentitia; cum hi tanti animorum motus, ac tanta prælia, possint comprimi jactu exigui pulveris, Nullam esse Materiam primam; quod si quis nobis, & nostris argumentis, credere non vult, censemus certamina ista prius componat, quam ad ipsius defensionem se accingat. ijs enim manentibus, valdè erit difficile, cuiquam sani cerebri persuadere, existere revera illam rem, in cujus natura tantopere excutierunt atq; hallucinati sint consul-
units.tr: unless the reasoning for generation is altogether removed. Matter, although it is not a body and does not have the form of a body, nevertheless in itself and before it receives form is quantified and has three dimensions, length, breadth and depth, yet with no fixed limits except those it receives from form. There is no quantity in it coeval with it; rather, the quantities of all natural bodies follow the forms and are assigned by the forms. Matter in itself is pure potency, not act, nor something composed of act and potency. It is a thing existing in act, and it does not borrow its existence from form, but through its own essence it is what it is and differs from other things. It is unbegotten. Matter has an appetite for form, but this appetite does not belong to it at all. Matter always strives for mischief and desires new forms; it delights in and is content with the forms it has at present. Matter can be understood through itself; it is by no means fit to be understood through itself. Matter belongs to the essence of a natural compound; it is not a part of the quiddity or essence of a natural compound. Matter can exist by divine power without any form; it cannot exist without form. The potency of matter is absolute, not distinct from its essence, and of the genus of substance; it is relative and of the genus of quality, and therefore an accident. These and many other questions of this sort about first matter keep the Peripatetics busy with no end, and not only the common run of them but also their most eminent men, who fight among themselves and with others as fiercely as they can. One does not know whether to pity their troubles or laugh at them, seeing such waves stirred up in a teacup, and so much turmoil and war raised over a thing of nothing and invented. Yet these great movements of minds and these great battles could be quelled by casting a little dust: there is no first matter. But if anyone does not wish to believe us and our arguments, we advise him to settle these disputes first before he sets himself to defend it. For while they remain, it will be very difficult to persuade any sound mind that that thing actually exists, in whose nature the most learned interpreters of the discipline have so greatly searched and been deceived.

units.la: × Nulle. Nulle. Vn beau Nulle. Lerio. Je dis de la matiere Vn beau Nulle.
units.tr: × None. None. A fine None. Lerio. I say of matter, a fine None.

units.la: × Re Vera consultissimi quiq; Peripateticae disciplinae interpretes. Quippe qua in re tam pugnantia statuerunt, necesse est alteram saltem partem à Veritate toto coelo aberrasse; probabile utramq; pari, quanquam dissimili, erroris indagine implicatam fuisse.
units.tr: × Indeed, the most learned interpreters of the Peripatetic discipline. For since they have laid down such contradictory things on this point, it is necessary that at least one side has strayed far from the truth; it is probable that both sides, though in different ways, were entangled in the search for error.
SECTION THREE.
CONCERNING FORM.

units.la: I. Aristotelis Sententia de Forma; cujus ignorationem Veteribus exprobrat. II. Nullo argumento eam probat, sed similitudinibus tantùm, petitis à Formis accidentalibus. III. Error hic est magnus, ipsiq; multorum errorum Causa. IV. Imprudens passim sequitur Democriti à se damnatam opinionem, Formam esse accidens. V. Indè natum, quod Formam dicit esse extremitatem rei. VI. Locus Aristotelis è secundo de Generatione & Corruptione, ubi nonnulli interpretes aiunt eum probare Formam, excutitur. VII. Primum Peripateticorum argumentum, ad probandam Formam, ex ipsa rerum naturalium constitutione petitum. Materia prima ineptè adhibetur ad probandam Formam. VIII. Ex eo, quod in rebus detur aliquid plus quam Materia (in quo ipso probando, nonnulla falsa admiscet Peripatus) non sequitur dari Formam substantialem. IX. Forma nequicquam asseritur ex specificis rerum proprietatibus. Formam inesse rebus, nec sensu nec intellectu deprehenditur. X. Nullum officium assignari potest, ob quod Formę in rebus requirantur: specifica differentia non opus habent Formâ. nullius ponderis illa objectio, Sic fore ut omnia accidentaliter tantùm differrent. XI. Formam non requirit ad constituendam aut continendam rerum unitatem. XII. Sublatâ Formâ non tollitur generatio substantiarum. XIII. Facultates & operationes non probant Formam; præsertim cum ipsi Peripatetici fateantur, omnem actionem ab accidentibus peragi. XIV. Figmentum illud, Qualitates actívas esse Formarum instrumenta, excutitur. XV. Idem amplius impugnatur. XVI. Multa actiones, in quibus ne fingi quidem potest (etiamsi darentur Forma) Formam cum qualitatibus concurrere ad agendum. Peripateticorum vani conatus, in solvenda hac difficultate, introducendo Instrumenta separata. XVII. Multi de ipsis Peripateticis fatentur, Accidentia principaliter operari. Pererij levitas hac in re. XVIII. Argumentum pro Forma, ab essentiali rerum unitate petitum, excutitur. quatenus verum sit, ex pluribus entibus completis non posse ens verè unum constitui. XIX. Peripateticorum argumenta ad probandum, quod substantia naturales nequeant ex sola Materia & accidentibus constitui. XX. Ipsorum inanitas ostenditur: ac monstratur, unde fiat, ut cuiq; substantia sua certa accidentia insint. XXI. Falsum, ex subjecto, & accidentibus separabilibus, non posse fieri unum per se. Essentia variabilitas incassum hic obicitur. XXII. Vanitas istius objectionis, Quod suppositá, ex Materia & accidentibus constata, neq; substantia sint, neq; accidens. XXIII. Argumenum pro Forma, ductum a temperamenti conservatione, inane. XXIV. Ejusdem momenti illud, à statu rerum secundum aut præter naturam. XXV. Argumentum pro Forma ex eo, quod per intensiorem unius facultatis operationem, alterius facultatis operatio imminuitur aut impeditur. XXVI. Respondetur illi. XXVII. Argumentum petitum à reductione rerum ad naturalem statum, perpenditur. Suarezij objectiones contra Qualitates Virtuales, profligantur. XXVIII. Alind pro Forma argumentum, ab alterationibus desumtum, evertitur. unde nonnullorum accidentium inseparabilitas pendeat. XXIX. Ratiocinatio Aristotelicorum, Omnes res naturales esse ex Materia & Forma compositas, quia homo ex anima & corpore constat. brutorum & stirpium exemplum magis hic quadraret, quàm homi-nis. Consequentia hac nulla est, quum dissimillima sit animarum conditio, quam que Formis assignatur: quare anima perperam Formarum nomine donantur. XXX. Corpora viventium non ita se habent ad animas, quemodo Materiam se habere ad Formas dicitur, ac proinde Materiæ nomine perperàm censentur. XXXI. Falsa assertio, Partes cadaveris non esse id, quod erant in corpore vivente, nisi æquivocè. XXXII. Rationes pro ea allata redarguuntur. XXXIII. Ɛ præcedentibus concluditur, frustrà inferri Formam substantialem ex eo, quod viventia ex anima & corpore constant. Suarezij super hoc negotio dicta sigillatim examinantur. XXXIV. Rationes contra Formam. prima, sumta à Formarum inhæsione; quòd docent Formam esse in subjecto, & tamen negent substantiæ convenire, ut subjecto insit. XXXV. Futilitas subterfugiorum, quibus utuntur Peripatetici, ut ex hac difficultate evadant. XXXVI. Aliud contra Formas argumentum ex eo, quod unam tantùm in quibusdam substantiis Formam specificam posse inesse statuitur; quam sententiam multa premunt absurda, unde non pauci Peripatetici plures uni rei Formas attribuerunt, quanquam cum hac evasione, quod una tantùm Forma inest actu, reliquæ verò in potentia. XXXVII. Absurditas istius evasionis. XXXVIII. Altera ratio contra illam. XXIX. Eadem evasio amplius premitur ex generali ipsius Peripati de Formis doctrina. XL. Tertia contra Formas difficultas, indè emergens, quod eas statuunt simplices, indivisibiles & quantitatis expertes. contra primum pugnat experientia de pluribus seminibus in unam stirpem coalescentibus. XLI. Quantitatem Formis absurdè adimunt Peripatetici, cum statuant, singulis Materia partibus singulas materialium Formarum partes respondere. inepta stropha, Formas esse quantas per accidens. XLII. Formas cunctas materiales esse divisibiles, fatetur universa Peripatus, sed cum hac cavillatione, quod dividantur per accidens: cujus cavillationis vanitas ostenditur. XLIII. Simplicitas essentialis, quam Formis attribuunt buunt Peripatetici, redarguitur ex eo, quod tùm in stirpibus, tùm in animalibus, species miscentur. Nonnulli de ipsis Peripateticis concedunt in Formis compositionem è partibus heterogeneis. XLIV. Aliud de Formis axioma, Eas non intendi nec remitti; convellitur, per multiplicem in multis speciebus varietatem. XLV. De stirpium degeneratione, atq; in aliam speciem mutatione. XLVI. Inextricabiles difficultates ex Peripateticorum de Formarum ortu doctrinâ orientes. XLVII. Formas ex nihilo fieri, necessario dicendum Peripateticis, ut sibi ipsis consentanea loquantur. Hinc autem porro sequitur, eas non esse substantias. XLVIII. Difficultas ista, quomodo Formæ & sint substantiæ, & tamen è nihilo fiant, solvitur, si dicantur à Deo creari; quod & dixerunt nonnulli. sed & veritas illis repugnat, & à maxima Peripateticorum parte rejiciuntur. XLIX. Alij Peripatetici hunc nodum, quod Formæ sint substantiæ, quanquam è nihilo fiant, mirabiliter solvunt, sibi ipsis apertissimè contradicendo, atq; aiendo, quod Formæ non fiant è nihilo, quia è Materia potentia educantur. L. Absurditas earum phrasium, qua Forma dicitur fieri è subjecto, & è Materia potentia educi. LI. Ipse Scaliger hanc phrasin condemnat, quanquam non universim ad omnes generationes hoc extendit, sed ad æquivocas tantùm. LII. Impossibile ut aliquid & fiat ex nihilo, & tamen non ex nihilo fiat; quod de Forma hîc impudentissimè afferunt Peripatetici. Vanitas subterfugiorum, quod creatio non sit nisi per se subsistentium, eorumq; quæ independenter fiunt. LIII. Formæ cœlestes eandem Peripateticis habent à Materia dependentiam, ac aliæ Formæ; & tamen fatentur eas creatas, non è Materia potentia eductas. LIV. Immanis absurditas istius assertionis, qua simul Formas & fieri è nihilo, & non è nihilo fieri asseritur. LV. Alia monstruosior istius nodi, Quomodo Formæ substantiales ex nihilo fiant ab Agentibus naturalibus; solutio: quod non fiant omninò, aut non proprie fiant, sed confiant composito. LVI. Aristotelis axioma, Solum compositum generari; super quo extructa est precedens solutio. LVII. Falsum hoc est in compositis accidentalibus (ut vocant) & si vel maxime verum in iis esset, ad Formas tamen substantiales transferri nullo modo posset. LVIII. Mirifica Aristotelis in hoc negotio vertigo. LIX. Amplius exagitatur stultitia istius effati, quo sola composita fieri, ac propterea Formas non fieri, dicitur. Aristotelus incogitantia in usurpando aliena dogmata pro suis. LX. Quale sit, quod dicunt, Composita proprie fieri, & consequenter Formas improprie fieri. LXI. Veritati magis consentaneum est, ut composita confieri, sive non primo fieri dicantur. LXII. Respondetur rationibus, quibus probare conantur, quod Composita primario generentur. LXIII. Conclusio eorum, qua de difficultatibus, Formarum ortum comitantibus, disputata hactenus sunt. LXIV. Alexandri & Cardani opiniones de Forma. LXV. Forma in nihilum intereunt: quod ipsum est aliud contra eas argumentum. LXVI. Ineptissima tergiversatio, Composita primario interire, ac proinde Formas non interire nisi per accidens. LXVII. Ridicula Pereriy assertio, Formas penitus interire, & tamen in nihilum non redigi. LXVIII. Galenus Formam substantialem plane repudiavit. quid sit Galeno tota rei Substantia. LXIX. Veritatis, non carpendi studio, ab Aristotele in multis Galenus dissensit. LXX. Aristoteles ipse sua de Formis placita evertit, statuens eas extrinsecus advenire: quam rem & Scaliger interdum fatetur. LXXI. Forma separabiles multo probabilius potuissent defendi, quam quales Aristoteles confinxit.
units.tr: I. Aristotle's opinion concerning Form, and his reproach to the ancients for being ignorant of it. II. He proves it by no argument, but only by similitudes drawn from accidental forms. III. This error is great, and is the cause of many errors. IV. Heedlessly he everywhere follows the opinion of Democritus, which he himself condemned, that form is an accident. V. Hence it arises that he says form is the extremity of a thing. VI. The passage of Aristotle from the second book On Generation and Corruption, where some interpreters say he proves form, is examined. VII. The first argument of the Peripatetics for proving form, taken from the very constitution of natural things. Prime matter is absurdly employed to prove form. VIII. From the fact that something more than matter is found in things (in proving which, the Peripatetics mix in several falsehoods), it does not follow that a substantial form exists. IX. Form is asserted in vain from the specific properties of things. That form is present in things is not detected either by sense or by intellect. X. No office can be assigned for which forms are required in things: specific differences have no need of form. That objection is of no weight, "so that all things would differ only accidentally." XI. Form is not required to constitute or to maintain the unity of things. XII. With form removed, the generation of substances is not removed. XIII. Faculties and operations do not prove form, especially since the Peripatetics themselves admit that every action is performed by accidents. XIV. That fiction, that active qualities are the instruments of forms, is examined. XV. The same is attacked further. XVI. Many actions, in which (even supposing forms existed) it cannot even be imagined that form concurs with qualities in acting. The vain efforts of the Peripatetics in solving this difficulty by introducing separate instruments. XVII. Many of the Peripatetics themselves confess that accidents act principally. The levity of Pereira in this matter. XVIII. The argument for form, taken from the essential unity of things, is examined: how far it is true that a true one being cannot be constituted from several complete beings. XIX. The arguments of the Peripatetics for proving that natural substances cannot be constituted from matter and accidents alone. XX. Their emptiness is shown, and it is demonstrated whence it comes that each substance has its own certain accidents. XXI. The falsehood that from a subject and separable accidents one thing per se cannot arise. The objection from variability of essence is here vainly raised. XXII. The vanity of that objection, that supposita made from matter and accidents are neither substances nor accidents. XXIII. The argument for form drawn from the conservation of temperament is empty. XXIV. Of the same weight is that from the state of things according to or beyond nature. XXV. The argument for form from the fact that by the more intense operation of one faculty, the operation of another faculty is diminished or hindered. XXVI. A reply to it. XXVII. The argument taken from the restoration of things to their natural state is weighed. Suárez's objections against virtual qualities are overthrown. XXVIII. Another argument for form, derived from alterations, is overturned: on what the inseparability of certain accidents depends. XXIX. The reasoning of the Aristotelians, that all natural things are composed of matter and form because man consists of soul and body. The example of brutes and plants would fit here better than that of man. This consequence is no good, since the condition of souls is most unlike that which is assigned to forms; hence souls are wrongly given the name of forms. XXX. The bodies of living things do not stand to souls in the way that matter is said to stand to forms, and therefore they are wrongly judged to be called by the name of matter. XXXI. The false assertion that the parts of a corpse are not what they were in a living body, except equivocally. XXXII. The reasons brought forward for it are refuted. XXXIII. From what precedes it is concluded that a substantial form is inferred in vain from the fact that living things consist of soul and body. What Suárez has said on this matter is examined point by point. XXXIV. Arguments against form. The first, taken from the inherence of forms: they teach that form is in a subject, and yet deny that it belongs to substance to be in a subject. XXXV. The futility of the evasions by which the Peripatetics try to escape this difficulty. XXXVI. Another argument against forms, from the fact that it is held that only one specific form can be present in certain substances; a view which many absurdities press upon, whence not a few Peripatetics have attributed several forms to one thing, though with this evasion, that only one form is present actually, while the others are present only potentially. XXXVII. The absurdity of that evasion. XXXVIII. A second reason against it. XXXIX. The same evasion is pressed further from the general doctrine of the Peripatetics themselves concerning forms. XL. A third difficulty against forms, arising from this, that they posit them as simple, indivisible and without quantity. Experience, concerning several seeds coalescing into one plant, fights against the first point. XLI. The Peripatetics absurdly deny quantity to forms, since they hold that to the individual parts of matter there correspond individual parts of material forms. The silly quibble that forms are quantified only accidentally. XLII. The whole Peripatetic school admits that all material forms are divisible, but with this sophism, that they are divided accidentally: the vanity of this sophism is shown. XLIII. The essential simplicity which the Peripatetics attribute to forms is refuted by the fact that species are mixed both in plants and in animals. Some of the Peripatetics themselves concede that forms are composed of heterogeneous parts. XLIV. Another axiom about forms, that they are neither intensified nor remitted, is overturned by the manifold variety in many species. XLV. Concerning the degeneration of plants and their change into another species. XLVI. Inextricable difficulties arising from the Peripatetic doctrine of the origin of forms. XLVII. The Peripatetics must necessarily say that forms are made out of nothing, if they are to speak consistently with themselves. From this, moreover, it further follows that they are not substances. XLVIII. The difficulty, how forms can be both substances and yet be made out of nothing, is solved if they are said to be created by God; which some have said. But truth also opposes them, and they are rejected by the greater part of the Peripatetics. XLIX. Other Peripatetics wonderfully untie this knot, that forms are substances although they are made out of nothing, by most plainly contradicting themselves and saying that forms are not made out of nothing, because they are educed out of matter in potency. L. The absurdity of those phrases by which form is said to be made from a subject and to be educed out of matter in potency. LI. Scaliger himself condemns this phrase, though he does not extend it universally to all generations, but only to the equivocal ones. LII. It is impossible that something should both be made out of nothing and yet not be made out of nothing; which the Peripatetics most shamelessly assert about form here. The vanity of the evasions, that creation is only of things that subsist of themselves and of those things which come to be independently. LIII. The heavenly forms have the same dependence on matter as other forms for the Peripatetics; and yet they confess that these were created, not educed out of matter in potency. LIV. The monstrous absurdity of that assertion, by which it is said at once that forms are made out of nothing and are not made out of nothing. LV. Another more monstrous knot: how substantial forms are made out of nothing by natural agents; the solution: that they are not made at all, or not properly made, but are compounded with the composite. LVI. Aristotle's axiom, that only the composite is generated, upon which the preceding solution is built. LVII. This is false of so-called accidental compounds; and even if it were most true of them, it could in no way be transferred to substantial forms. LVIII. Aristotle's marvellous vertigo in this matter. LIX. The folly of that saying, by which only composites are said to be made, and therefore forms are not made, is further exposed. Aristotle's thoughtlessness in taking up foreign doctrines as his own. LX. What it means, what they say: that composites are properly made, and consequently forms are improperly made. LXI. It agrees more with the truth that composites are said to be compounded, or not to be made primarily. LXII. A reply to the reasons by which they try to prove that composites are generated primarily. LXIII. The conclusion of what has been disputed so far concerning the difficulties accompanying the origin of forms. LXIV. The opinions of Alexander and Cardano concerning form. LXV. Forms perish into nothing: which itself is another argument against them. LXVI. The most inept evasion: that composites perish primarily, and therefore forms perish only accidentally. LXVII. The ridiculous assertion of Pereira, that forms perish completely, and yet are not reduced to nothing. LXVIII. Galen utterly rejected the substantial form. What the whole substance of a thing is to Galen. LXIX. Galen dissented from Aristotle in many points, from a desire for truth and not for carping. LXX. Aristotle himself overturns his own opinions about forms, by positing that they come in from outside: a thing which Scaliger too sometimes confesses. LXXI. Separable forms could have been defended far more probably than those which Aristotle invented.

units.la: 1Sed nos jam missa Materia prima, ad Formam, alterum Aristotelis Principium, progrediamur. De ea quid dicatur ab Aristotele & Aristotelicis, non potest cuiquam esse ignotum, Illam esse digniorem compositi substantialis
units.tr: 1But now that prime matter has been set aside, let us proceed to form, Aristotle's other principle. What Aristotle and the Aristotelians say about it cannot be unknown to anyone: that it is the more worthy part of the substantial compound

units.la: {y} aliud medico sed medicatus. aliud physico sed physiologo. stantialis partem, quæ naturam rei sive ipsam rem principaliter constituit, per quam unumquodq; est id quod est, & à qua omnis actio fluit. separari à Materia & per se subsistere nequaquam posse: nec generari, nec corrumpi ipsam, sed compositum: esse simplicissimam, propterea que non paulatim nec per partes, sed in momento simul totam introduci. Hæc aliaq; plura de Forma Aristoteles, qui non uno in loco gloriatur, illam à se præcipuè in Philosophiam naturalem fuisse introductam, cum prisci illam, ut & finalem causam, attigissent nunquam, præter solum Empedoclem & Democritum, qui duo tamen non nisi parcissimè illam delibassent. ejus itaq; ignorationem Veteribus illis multorum magnorúmque errorum causam fuisse, qui non alia rerum Principia nisi materiale & essectivum considerabant. Locus, ubi hæc dicat, præ cæteris insignis est I. de Part. anim. cap. I. ubi cum multa dixisset de duobus Causæ generibus, τὸ οὖ ἕνεκα, καὶ τὸ ἐξ ἀνάγκης, illo cujus gratia, & necessario, hæc subjungit: ὅλ μὲν οὖν δύο τρόποι τὰ αἰτίας. καὶ δεῖ λέγοντας τυγχάνειν μάλιστα μὲν ἀμφοῖν, εἰ δὲ μὴ, δῆλόν γε πειρᾶσθαι ποιεῖν (lege πειρᾶσθαι γε ποιεῖν, δῆλον) καὶ οἱ πάντες τοὺς μὴ λέγοντας, ἐδὲν ὡς εἰπεῖν περὶ φύσεως λέγουσι· ἀρχὴ γὰρ ἡ φύσις μᾶλλον τῆς ὕλης. ἔνιαχοῦ δὲ αὐτὴ καὶ ἐμπεδοκλῆς περιπίπτει, ἀγόμενος ὑπ' αὐτῆς τῆς ἀληθείας, καὶ τὴν φύσιν καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἀναγκάζεται φάναι τὸν λόγον εἶν. & paulo post, ἄτοπον δὲ τοῦ μὴ ἐλθεῖν εἰς προγενεστέρας ἐπὶ τὸν πρότερον τοῦτον, οὗ τ' ἦν τί ἦν εἶναι καὶ τὸ ὁρίζεσθαι τὴν οὐσίαν ἐκ ἦν. ἀλλ' ἥψατο μὲν Δημόκριτος πρῶτος, ὡς ἐν ἀναγκαίας δὲ τῇ φύσιν ἐπιστήμη. Quod igitur duo sint causarum modi, & quod in differendo oporteat utramq; assequi, aut saltem conari id facere; manifestum est: uti &, quod omnes hoc non exponentes, nihil, ut sic dicamus, de Natura exponunt. Natura enim magis est Principium quam Materia. Alicubi autem & Empedocles in ipsam incurrit, ductus ab ipsa veritate, cogiturq; dicere, quod Ratio sit Natura & Essentia. Causa autem cur Antiquiores
units.tr: another thing to the physician but to the one treated; another to the natural philosopher but to the physiologist. The part of the substantial composite which principally constitutes the nature of the thing, or the thing itself, through which each thing is what it is and from which all action flows. It cannot be separated from matter and subsist on its own; it is not generated or corrupted itself, but the composite is. It is most simple, and therefore it is introduced not gradually or by parts, but wholly and at once in an instant. Aristotle says these and many other things about Form, and he boasts in more than one place that he was the first to introduce it into natural philosophy, since the ancients never touched on it, as they did not touch on the final cause, except Empedocles and Democritus, who yet only barely tasted it. Therefore their ignorance of it was the cause of many great errors for those ancients, who considered no principles of things other than the material and the efficient. The passage where he says this is especially notable in book I of On the Parts of Animals, chapter 1, where, after saying much about the two kinds of cause, τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα [that for the sake of which] and τὸ ἐξ ἀνάγκης [the necessary], he adds: "Now, to speak generally, there are two modes of cause; and in discussing them one ought to hit upon both, or at least, if not, clearly try to do so [ὅλως μὲν οὖν δύο τρόποι τῶν αἰτίων. καὶ δεῖ λέγοντας τυγχάνειν μάλιστα μὲν ἀμφοῖν, εἰ δὲ μή, δῆλόν γε πειρᾶσθαι ποιεῖν]; and all those who do not state them, say, so to speak, nothing about nature; for nature is more a principle than matter [καὶ οἱ πάντες τοὺς μὴ λέγοντας, ἐδὲν ὡς εἰπεῖν περὶ φύσεως λέγουσι· ἀρχὴ γὰρ ἡ φύσις μᾶλλον τῆς ὕλης]. Somewhere Empedocles too falls into it, led by the truth itself, and is compelled to say that nature and essence is the account [ἔνιαχοῦ δὲ αὐτὴ καὶ ἐμπεδοκλῆς περιπίπτει, ἀγόμενος ὑπ' αὐτῆς τῆς ἀληθείας, καὶ τὴν φύσιν καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἀναγκάζεται φάναι τὸν λόγον εἶν]." And a little later: "It is absurd not to have gone back to the earlier ones, who first, for the reason that what it is to be a thing, and the defining of substance, is the account, [ἄτοπον δὲ τοῦ μὴ ἐλθεῖν εἰς προγενεστέρας ἐπὶ τὸν πρότερον τοῦτον, οὗ τ' ἦν τί ἦν εἶναι καὶ τὸ ὁρίζεσθαι τὴν οὐσίαν ἐκ ἦν]. But Democritus first touched on it, though as if it were not necessary for the knowledge of nature [ἀλλ' ἥψατο μὲν Δημόκριτος πρῶτος, ὡς ἐν ἀναγκαίας δὲ τῇ φύσιν ἐπιστήμη]." That there are two modes of cause, and that in discussing them one ought to grasp both, or at least try to do so, is clear; and likewise that all who do not explain both say, so to speak, nothing about nature. For nature is more a principle than matter. Empedocles too sometimes stumbles upon it, driven by the truth itself, and is forced to say that the account is nature and essence. The reason why the more ancient writers did not come to this mode is that the quiddities and definitions of substances were not in use.

units.la: Quod igitur duo sint causarum modi, de Natura exponunt. tiquiores non venerint ad hunc modum, ea est, quod Quid-ditates & Definitiones substantiarum non erant [in usu]. Sed Democritus quidem primus hoc attigit, ita tamen ac si non esset necessarium ad physicam contemplationem. consimilia etiam legere est in principio quinti de Generatione Animalium. & 2. Physic. 2. quoque ait, 'Ἐπὶ μηδέν ἃ μέρος ἐμπεδοκλέην καὶ Δημόκριτον τοῦ εἶδος καὶ τοῦ-τ' ἢν εἶναι ἀφαθαι. Empedoclem & Democritum ex parva quadam parte attigisse Formam & Quidditatem.
units.tr: That there are two modes of cause, and that all who do not explain nature in this way say almost nothing about it. The reason the earlier thinkers did not come to this mode is that the quiddities and definitions of substances were not in use. Democritus indeed first touched on this, but as if it were not necessary for physical contemplation. One may read similar things at the beginning of the fifth book of On the Generation of Animals. And in Physics 2 he also says: Empedocles and Democritus touched on Form and quiddity only from a small part. [Ἐμπεδοκλέα καὶ Δημόκριτον ἐκ μικρᾶς τινος μερίδος ἅψασθαι τοῦ εἴδους καὶ τοῦ τί ἦν εἶναι.]
II.

units.la: Cum igitur ipse si non inventor, primus tamen excultor fuerit Formæ, oportuerat rem tanti momenti, quæ utramque faceret paginam in Naturali scientia, non positam simpliciter, sicut ipse posuit, sed demonstratam, quod neque fecit, neque facere usquam aggressus est; quod & de Materia prima ab ipso commissum esse, supra notabamus. Certè & in primo Physicor. qui sub Principiorum nomine de Materia, Forma & Privatione totus agit, & in secundo, ubi inter Causas Forma repetitur, & in Metaphysicis, quorum magna pars in speculationibus ad Formam pertinentibus occupata est, nè unicum quidem extat argumentum, quo Forma ista, qualis ab ipso introducta est, demonstretur, imo adeò confusè versatur in hoc negotio, ut passim, ubi de Forma agit substantiali, delabatur in mentionem illius Formæ, quæ est quarta species qualitatis, ac Formæ artificialis (quæ & ipsa ad figuram plerumq; pertinet, interdum alio, ut Forma domus, & Forma syllabæ) & quidem ita perverso modo, ut de his duabus Formis accidentalibus agat tanquàm de proprio disputationis suæ subjecto; de altera verò illa, qua de præcipuè, imo unicè agendum illi erat, vix pauca verba hic illic cursim inserat. ítaque passim deludit lectorem suum, ea afferens exempla, quæ ad propositum nequaquàm faciunt. Néque modo Formas illas accidentales, sed quævis etiam qualitates affert loco verææ Formæ, ut demonstret nimirùm, Substantias ex Materia & Forma compositas esse, sic 1. Physic. cùm dixisset, ἐκάστου ὁ λέγεται
units.tr: Since Aristotle, if not the discoverer of Form, was at least its first cultivator, it was necessary that a matter of such importance, which fills both pages of natural science, be not simply posited as he posited it, but demonstrated. This he neither did nor ever attempted anywhere, as I noted above concerning prime matter. Certainly neither in the first book of the Physics, which treats entirely of matter, form and privation under the name of principles, nor in the second, where form is repeated among the causes, nor in the Metaphysics, much of which is occupied with speculations concerning form, is there even one argument by which that form, as he introduced it, is demonstrated. Indeed he handles the business so confusedly that, wherever he treats of substantial form, he slips into talk of that form which is the fourth species of quality, and of artificial form (which also mostly pertains to shape, sometimes to other things, such as the form of a house or the form of a syllable). And he does so in such a perverse way that he treats these two accidental forms as if they were the proper subject of his discussion, while of the other form, about which he ought chiefly, indeed solely, to treat, he inserts only a few words here and there in passing. Thus he repeatedly deceives his reader, offering examples that do not in the least bear on the question. Nor does he offer only those accidental forms, but even any qualities at all, in place of the true form, in order to show that substances are composed of matter and form. So in the first book of the Physics, after saying that whatever is called a thing according to its essence comes to be simply out of the subject and the form, [ἐκάστου ὁ λέγεται κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν γίγνεται ἁπλῶς ἐκ τοῦ ὑποκειμένου καὶ τῆς μορφῆς], he confirms this with a fine example: [συγγένεια γὰρ ὁ μουσικὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐξ ἀνθρώπου καὶ μουσικῆς τρόπον τινά] "for a musical man is, in a sense, composed of a man and of music." And many more things of the same kind are found in that book, and the Metaphysics is full of such things.

units.la: {x} Cap.I. x timitis assignatio γεται κατὰ τὴν ουσίαν, γίγνεται ἁπλῶς ἐκ τοῦ ὑποκειμένου καὶ τῆς μορφῆς, Id quod singula dicuntur secundum essentiam, fiunt omnia ex subjecto atque Forma, id porro declarat bello hoc exemplo. Συγγενεῖαι γὰρ ὁ μουσικὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐξ ἀνθρώπου καὶ μουσικῆς τρόπου ἵνα. namque homo musicus compositus quodamodo est ex homine & musico. & plura ibidem ejusdem farinæ. Metaphysica autem talibus scatet.
units.tr: Chapter 1. The assignment of limits. [Whatever is called a thing according to its essence comes to be simply out of the subject and the form.] He declares this by a fine example: [for the musical man is composed in a way out of man and music]. Namely, a musical man is composed in some manner of a man and of music. And many similar things occur in the same passage, and the Metaphysics abounds in such things.

units.la: Scimus quidem quomodo Peripatetici excusent præceptorem suum, Ista exempla eo tantùm sine adduci, ut similitudine quadam declaretur, quomodo se habeat Forma ad Materiam; quo animo illa à se poni, ipse indicet Aristoteles 1. Phys. 7. ὥς γὰρ πρὸς ἀναλγίαν χαλκὸς, ἢ πρὸς κλίνην ξύλον, ἢ πρὸς ἄλλο ἃ τῶν ἐχόντων μορφὴν ἡ ὕλη, οὕτως αὕτη πρὸς οὐσίαν ἔχει καὶ ζῷδέ ἕ. quomodo enim as ad statuam, aut lignum ad lectum, aut [quævis] Materia ad aliud quid eorum, quæ Formâ predita sunt, se habet, ita hæc se habet ad essentiam, & ad esse hoc aliquid. & in eandem fere sententiam 8. Metaph. 2. Οὐσία μὲν ἓν ὧλέν τούτων, ὧλὲ σωλυαζόμενον, ὅμως δέ ἡ ἀνάλογον ἐν ἐνέργειᾳ ἡμῖν ὡς ἐν ταῖς οὐσίαις, ἡ ἡ ὕλης καταγορεύμενον, αὐτὴ ἡ ἐνέργεια, ἡμῖν ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις ὁσμοῖς μάλισα. Nihil quidem horum, neque id quod ex iis componitur, essentia est. proportio tamen in unoquoque [clucet.] & quomodo in substantiis Materiæ prædicatum est ipse Actus, in fere & in aliis definitionibus. Sed absurdum est, in docenda ulla re, præsertim nova ac tanti momenti, præter nudas positiones afferre nihil pro omni demonstratione, nisi sola exempla ostendere et proponere.
units.tr: We know how the Peripatetics excuse their master: these examples were brought in only so that by some likeness it might be made clear how form stands to matter, and Aristotle himself indicates in the first book of the Physics, chapter 7, with what intention he set them down: [ὥς γὰρ πρὸς ἀνδριάντα χαλκὸς ... οὕτως ἡ ὕλη πρὸς τὴν οὐσίαν ἔχει], "for as bronze stands to a statue, or wood to a bed, or matter to any other of those things that have a form, so matter stands to essence and to this particular being." And to much the same effect in the eighth book of the Metaphysics, chapter 2: [οὐσία μὲν οὖν οὔτε τούτων οὐδὲν ... ἀναλογία ...] "Nothing of these things, nor that which is composed of them, is essence; yet a proportion is found in each, as in substances, where matter is said of actuality itself, and so forth." Nothing of these, neither the matter nor the compound, is essence, but there is a proportion, as in substances, in which matter is predicated of actuality. But it is absurd, in teaching any subject, especially a new one of such importance, to offer nothing as proof beyond bare assertions and mere examples set forth to show the point.

units.la: III. Néque tamen hoc omne peccatum est hac in re Aristotelis. Aliud est longè gravius, quod similitudines usurpaverit adeò dissimiles, ut nihil ab ijs ad ipsam rem, cui illustrandæ adhibentur, transferri possit. nam néque quomodo illæ sunt in Materia, nec quomodo unum cum Materia constituunt, ita substantialem Formam inesse Materiæ, aut unum cum illa efficere, unquam admiserit Aristoteles, aut Aristotelicorum quispiam, ut postea latius disseretur. & tamen ac si par esset utrarumq; Formarum ratio, accidentalium ac substantialium, ita quaedam illis solis propria, ad haec quoque transtulit, nullo alio argumento, quam à comparatione sumpto. Huic enim fundamento superstruxit magna illa axiomatum mysteria, Formas non esse separabiles, & neq; generari neq; interire aut ipsas aut Materiam, sed compositum duntaxat; quia nimirum ita se res habeat de Formis accidentalibus neq; enim aut globositatem posse à globo separari, ut per se existat, neque simitatem à naso, neque Formam domus, nimirum, esse ἀγγεῖον σκεπαστικὸν χεγμάτων καὶ σωμάτων, receptaculum obtegens res & corpora, à domo; & consequenter neque fieri ista accidentia, sed Materiam cum ipsis, hoc est compositum, ut globum aeneum, nasum simum. Ast nihil facilius, quam vanitatem istarum similitudinum redarguere. etenim globositas & simitas accidentia sunt, & accidentium natura haec est, non posse subsistere nisi in subjecto. ast Formam vult esse substantiam & quidem longe digniorem Materia, ita ut haec ad illam comparata, sit paulo plus quam nihil. substantiae vero hoc proprium facit ubique, non esse in subjecto: quae prerogativa si competit Materiae, quatenus substantia est, multo magis competet Formae, quae substantia est longe nobilior. propterea; nullâ prorsus consequentiâ concluditur, Formas substantiales non posse separari à Materia ac seorsim existere, neque fieri aut interire, quia neutrum cadat in Formas accidentales; Et tamen posterius illud nè de ijs quidem verum est, si rem exactè ponderemus. qui enim globum facit ex aere, omnino facit globositatem, & nihilo verius dixeris, aes factum esse globosum, quam globositatem factam esse in aere. & si rursus confletur globus in quadratam aut alterius figurae massam, non globus tantùm perierit, sed & globositas; imo si proprie loquendum sit, soli globositati, non item globo competit, ut perijsse dicatur. neq; enim credimus Averroi, dicenti Formas artificiosas non habere generationem, nec corruptionem, quia sint accidentia. Namq; propter hoc ipsum, quod
units.tr: III. Yet this is not the whole of Aristotle's fault in this matter. There is a far graver one: he used such dissimilar likenesses that nothing from them can be transferred to the thing they are meant to illustrate. For neither in the way in which those accidental forms are in matter, nor in the way in which they form one thing with matter, did Aristotle, or any of the Aristotelians, ever admit that a substantial form is in matter or makes one thing with it, as will be discussed more fully later. Yet, as if the reasoning about accidental and substantial forms were the same, he transferred to the substantial forms certain things that belong to the accidental forms alone, using no other argument than a comparison. On this foundation he built those great mysteries of axioms: that forms are not separable, that neither they nor matter are generated or perish, but only the compound; because, of course, this is how things stand with accidental forms. For the sphericity cannot be separated from the sphere so as to exist by itself, nor snubness from the nose, nor, to be sure, the form of a house, that is, a covering receptacle for goods and bodies, from the house; and consequently these accidents do not come to be, but matter together with them, that is, the compound, as a bronze sphere or a snub nose. But nothing is easier than to refute the emptiness of these likenesses. For sphericity and snubness are accidents, and it is the nature of accidents that they cannot subsist except in a subject. But Form is meant to be a substance, and indeed one far more worthy than matter, so that matter compared with it is little more than nothing. Now substance has this as its own mark everywhere, that it is not in a subject; and if this privilege belongs to matter, insofar as it is substance, it will belong much more to form, which is a far nobler substance. Therefore it is in no way a valid inference that substantial forms cannot be separated from matter and exist apart, or be generated or perish, because neither of these applies to accidental forms. And yet even that latter claim is not true of accidental forms, if we weigh the matter exactly. For whoever makes a sphere out of bronze certainly makes the sphericity, and you could no more truly say that the bronze has been made spherical than that the sphericity has been made in the bronze. And if the sphere is again melted into a square or some other shaped mass, not only the sphere but also the sphericity has perished; indeed, if one must speak strictly, it is the sphericity alone, not the sphere, that can be said to have perished. For we do not believe Averroes, who says that artificial forms have neither generation nor corruption because they are accidents. For on account of this very thing, that
Chapter I.

units.la: quod sunt Accidentia, utrunq; hoc in eas cadit; cum revera solis substantijs proprium sit, nec generari absolutè, (in hisce quidem ordinarijs generationibus) nec corrumpi. & falsa igitur ex parte est illa similitudo, & si vera esset cum maximè, haudquaquàm tamen quadrat, cum ex ipsius placitis longè alia sit substantiarum quam accidentium ratio. Itaq; magnus error, quidcunq; accidentali Formæ competit, id statim, absq; ulla alia demonstratione, substantiali accommodare: quem errorem suum alicubi, velut è profundo somno evigilans, ipse quoque agnovit: sic enim scribit 8. Metaph. 3. εἰ δ' εἰσὶ τῶν φθαρτῶν αἱ οὐσίαι χωρισταί, ὀὐδέν πω δῆλον· ἀλλὰ γε εἰσίων ὃν ἐνδέχεται, δῆλον, ὅτι μὴ οἷόν τε πᾶσα ἰδέα εἶναι, οἷον οἰκίαν ἢ σωεύσης. ἴσως μὲν οὖν οὐσίαι εἰσὶν ἐνίαι ἀὐτὰ ταῦτα, οὔτε τι τῶν ἄλλων, ὅσα μὴ φύσει συνέστηκε. τὴν δὲ φύσιν μόνην ἂν τις ἕτερ, τὴν ἐν τοῖς φθαρτοῖς, οὐσίαν. An corruptibilium essentiæ separabiles sint, nondum liquet. ast quod nonnullorum [essentiæ] nequeant [esse separabiles] manifestum est, videlicet eorum, quæ non possunt esse præter ipsa individua, ut vas aut ædificium. fortassis autem neq; hæc ipsa sunt essentiæ, neq; quisquam aliorum, quæ non effecta sunt per naturam. forsitan enim sola natura, quæ est in corruptibilibus, essentia censenda est.
units.tr: Because they are accidents, both of these apply to them. In truth, however, it belongs only to substances neither to be absolutely generated (in these ordinary generations) nor corrupted. So that comparison is false in part, and even if it were entirely true, it would by no means fit, since on his own principles the nature of substances is quite different from that of accidents. Hence it is a great error to assign at once to a substantial form whatever belongs to an accidental form, without any further demonstration. Aristotle himself, waking as if from a deep sleep, somewhere acknowledged this error. For thus he writes in Metaphysics 8.3: [εἰ δ' εἰσὶ τῶν φθαρτῶν αἱ οὐσίαι χωρισταί, οὐδέν πω δῆλον· ἀλλὰ γε εἰσὶ τῶν ὄντων ἃ ἐνδέχεται, δῆλον ὅτι μὴ οἷόν τε πᾶσαν ἰδέαν εἶναι, οἷον οἰκίαν ἢ σκεύους. ἴσως μὲν οὖν οὐσίαι εἰσὶν ἔνιαι αὐταὶ ταῦτα, οὔτε τι τῶν ἄλλων, ὅσα μὴ φύσει συνέστηκε· τὴν δὲ φύσιν μόνην ἂν τις ἕτερ(ον) οὐσίαν.] Whether the substances of perishable things can exist apart is not yet clear. But it is plain that of some things it is impossible, namely those which cannot exist apart from the individual things themselves, such as a vessel or a house. Perhaps, however, these too are not substances, nor is anything else that has not come into being through nature. For perhaps only the nature which is in perishable things should be counted as substance.

units.la: IV. Sed Aristoteli hic usu venit, quod & de modo visionis, & de aliis plerisque, ut alienis & à se damnatis opinionibus sermonem magis accommodet quam suis. passim enim de Forma disserens, videtur non id spectasse, quod ipse de ea statuisset, sed quod Democritus, qui non aliam agnovit quam accidentalem; quippè qui omnium eandem esse Materiam dicebat, sola figura aut situ differentem, quod de eo testatur ipse 1. Phys. 2. Καὶ ἐι ἀτειγους [ἰάς ἀρχὰς ἴσθεον] ἢ οὔτως, ὡς ἀμφονεῖς, τ' γένος ἐν, σχήματι δὲ ἢ εἴδει διαφέρειν, ἢ ἐναντίας. Quod si Principia infinita ponenda sunt, id vel ita faciendum est, quomodo Democritus fecit, qui ea ponebat genera una, figurâ vero aut specie differentia vel contraria, &c. & 8. Metaph. 2. Λοιπὸν τὴν ὡς ἐνέργειαν οὐσίαν τῶν αἰσθητῶν εἶναι, τίς ἐστι. Δημόκριτος μὲν οὖν τρεῖς διαφορὰς ἔοικεν οἰομένῳ εἶναι. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ ὑποκείμενον σῶμα, τὴν ὕλην, ἓν καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ, διαφέρειν δὲ ἢ ῥυσμῷ, ὅ ἐστι σχῆμα, ἢ τροπῇ, ὅ ἐστι θέσις, ἢ διαθιγῇ, ὅ ἐστι τάξις. Reliquum est, eam sensibilium essentiam, quæ est tanquam Actus, exponere, quænam sit. Democritus certè videtur opinari tres [ipsius] differentias esse. namq; [censet] subjectum corpus, hoc est Materiam, unum atq; idem esse; differre autem vel Rusmo, hoc est figurâ, aut Trope, hoc est situ, aut Diathige, hoc est ordine. Neque de aliis modo rebus, sed de ipsis quoque animalibus illum ita sensisse, ut non aliam in ijs Formam agnosceret, nisi figuram, ipsi objicit 1. Part. anim. 1. Εἰ μὲν οὖν τῶν σχημάτων καὶ τῶν χρωμάτων ἕκαστον ὅτι τῶν τε ζῴων καὶ τῶν μορίων, οἷον ἂν Δημόκριτος λέγοι. Φάνεται δὲ οὕτως ὑπολαβεῖν, φησὶ δὲ παντὶ δῆλον εἶναι οἷον [f. οἷος] τὴν μόρφην ἔστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὡς ὄντος αὐτοῦ τῶν τε σχημάτων καὶ χρωμάτων. Si igitur unumquodq; animal atq; membrorum est [id quod est] figura atq; colore; Democritus rectè dicit. Apparet enim, eum sic existimare. quippè inquit, cuivis manifestum esse, qualis Forma sit homo; tanquam [homo] sit [homo] figurâ atq; colore. idq; reprehendit ibidem, quia cadaver habet eandem figuram, quàm homo vivus, neq; tamen est homo, non magis quàm manus lignea est manus, aut pictura medici est medicus. hanc tamen Democriteam ab ipso repudiatam opinionem multò magis sapit tota illa in Physicis ac Metaphysicis de Forma tractatio, quam ipsius propriam. alioqui non ita prompte ad Formas substantiarum transferret illa, quæ Formis artificialibus ac figuris propria sunt.
units.tr: IV. But here it happens to Aristotle, as it does in many other places concerning the manner of vision and similar matters, that he adapts his discourse to opinions that are foreign to him and that he himself has condemned, rather than to his own. For when he discusses Form in many places, he seems to have had in view not what he himself had established about it, but what Democritus had said, since Democritus recognised no form other than the accidental one. Democritus held that all things have the same matter, differing only in shape or position, as Aristotle himself attests in Physics 1.2: [καὶ εἰ ἄπειρους τὰς ἀρχὰς ποιεῖσθαι, ἢ οὕτως, ὥσπερ Δημόκριτος, ἕν μὲν γένος, σχήματι δὲ ἢ εἴδει διαφέροντα ἢ ἐναντία.] And if the principles are to be posited as infinite, this must be done either as Democritus did, who posited them as one genus differing in shape or in species or in contrariety, and so on. And in Metaphysics 8.2: [λοιπὸν τὴν ὡς ἐνέργειαν οὐσίαν τῶν αἰσθητῶν εἶναι τίς ἐστι. Δημόκριτος μὲν οὖν τρεῖς διαφορὰς ἔοικεν οἴεσθαι εἶναι· τὸ μὲν γὰρ ὑποκείμενον σῶμα, τὴν ὕλην, ἓν καὶ τὸ αὐτό, διαφέρειν δὲ ἢ ῥυσμῷ, ὅ ἐστι σχῆμα, ἢ τροπῇ, ὅ ἐστι θέσις, ἢ διαθιγῇ, ὅ ἐστι τάξις.] It remains to say what the substance of sensible things is, which is as actuality. Democritus seems to suppose there are three differences. For the underlying body, namely the matter, is one and the same, but it differs either in rhythm, which is shape, or in turning, which is position, or in contact, which is order. Aristotle objects that Democritus held this not only of other things but also of the animals themselves, so that he recognised in them no form other than shape. In De partibus animalium 1.1 he says: [εἰ μὲν οὖν τῶν σχημάτων καὶ τῶν χρωμάτων ἕκαστον ἐστι τῶν τε ζῴων καὶ τῶν μορίων, οἷον ἂν Δημόκριτος λέγοι.] If, then, each of the animals and of their parts is shape and colour, as Democritus would say, he seems to have thought so; and he says it is plain to everyone what sort of form man has, as though man were his shape and colour. And there he rebukes him because a corpse has the same shape as a living man, yet is not a man, any more than a wooden hand is a hand or a painted physician is a physician. Yet the whole treatment of Form in the Physics and Metaphysics savours far more of this Democritean opinion, which Aristotle himself rejected, than of his own view. Otherwise he would not so readily transfer to the forms of substances what belongs to artificial forms and figures.
V.

units.la: Quale etiam illud, Formam esse extremitatem rei. de figura enim hoc dicere liceat quodammodo, quanquam proprie loquendo nè illa quidem est extremitas rei, sed duntaxat (quod ipsum tamen non nimis accuratum dictu est) in extremitate, quo respectu dicebat Themistius, Artem
units.tr: Similar is that saying that Form is the extremity of a thing. For this may be said in some sense of shape, though strictly speaking shape is not even the extremity of a thing, but only (though this is not very exact to say) in the extremity; and in this respect Themistius said that Art
Chapter I, Section III.

units.la: tem nihil agere in corpore, nisi in extremitatibus tantùm; nimirùm non de cunctis loquens artibus (falsum enim sic foret hoc ejus dictum) sed de ijs tantùm, quorum opus est, certo modo subjectum suum figurare. Ast de Forma substantiali dicere, quod sit rei extremitas, absurdissimum certè est, ab ijs prolatum, qui toti Materiæ totam immistam esse prædicant. & tamen hoc non semel dixit Aristoteles. Insignis præ cæteris est hic locus è 4. Phys. 2. 'Ει δὲ ἔσιν ὁ τόπος ὁ πρῶτον περιέχον ἕκαστον τῶν σωμάτων, πέρας ἂν εἴη· ὥσε δόξειεν ἂν τὸ εἶδος, καὶ ἡ μορφὴ ἑκάστου, ὁ τόπος εἶναι, ᾧ ὁρίζεται δ' μέγεθος, καὶ ἡ ὕλη τὸ μεγέθους. τοῦτο δ' ἑκάστῳ πέρας. Quod si locus est id, quod primum continet quævis corpora; extremitas est. itaq; videri potest, quod cujusq; speciei atq; forma sit locus, quo terminatur magnitudo, & Materia magnitudinis. hæc enim est cujusq; extremitas. Hæc non de figura dici, sed de Forma Aristotelica, docet consimilis locus 3. Phys. 7. περιέχεταί δ' ὡς ἡ ὕλη ἐντὸς, ἡ δ' ἄπειρον. περιέχει δὲ τὸ εἶδος. Namq; infinitum, itidem atq; Materia, intùs continetur. Forma autem continet. & consentiunt interpretes; quorum tamen nonnulli concoquere hoc non possunt, inter quos est Themistius, qui commentario ad hunc locum, velut succensens præceptori, notat Formam, proprie loquendo, non esse terminum rei, nec superficiem, sed ejusdem rationem, & τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι; & excusat tamen, id aliquatenus posse dici, inquantum Forma Materiam fusam diffluentemq; quasi coercet finibus, & intra certos limites revocat: quæ excusatio satis frigida est, etsi meliorem illâ dari nullam posse libenter concedimus.
