units.tr: ...that art does nothing in a body except at its extremities only. He meant, of course, not all arts (for in that sense his statement would be false), but only those whose task is to shape their subject in a certain way. But to say that the substantial Form is the extremity of a thing is most absurd, coming from those who maintain that the whole Form is wholly mingled with the whole Matter. And yet Aristotle said this more than once. Outstanding above the rest is this passage from Physics 4, ch. 2: 'Ει δὲ ἔσιν ὁ τόπος ὁ πρῶτον περιέχον ἕκαστον τῶν σωμάτων, πέρας ἂν εἴη· ὥσε δόξειεν ἂν τὸ εἶδος, καὶ ἡ μορφὴ ἑκάστου, ὁ τόπος εἶναι, ᾧ ὁρίζεται δ' μέγεθος, καὶ ἡ ὕλη τὸ μεγέθους. τοῦτο δ' ἑκάστῳ πέρας.' If place is that which first contains each of bodies, it is an extremity. So it may seem that the species and form of each thing is place, by which the magnitude is bounded, and the matter of the magnitude. For this is the extremity of each. That these words are said not of figure but of the Aristotelian Form is shown by a similar passage in Physics 3, ch. 7: 'περιέχεταί δ' ὡς ἡ ὕλη ἐντὸς, ἡ δ' ἄπειρον. περιέχει δὲ τὸ εἶδος.' For the infinite, like matter, is contained within. But Form contains. The interpreters agree, though some of them cannot stomach this, among whom is Themistius. In his commentary on this passage, as if vexed with his teacher, he notes that the Form, properly speaking, is not the boundary or surface of a thing, but its essence, 'τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι'. Yet he excuses the saying, allowing that it can be said to some extent, insofar as the Form, as it were, restrains the matter that flows and spreads out, and calls it back within certain limits. This excuse is quite feeble, though we gladly concede that no better one can be given.
VI.

units.la: Et comparationes igitur ac similitudines, quibus pro Forma sua utitur Aristoteles, ejusmodi sunt, ut Substantialem esse Formam, nullo pacto ex ijs sequatur, sed potiùs contrarium omninò; & aliam tamen præter hasce demonstrationem nullam pro ea attulit. Nam quod Commentatores mentatores nonnulli 2. de Generatione & Corruptione ad textus 39. 40. & 41. scribunt, Aristotelem ibi demonstrare Formam à Generatione Naturali ; in eo falluntur. Versatur enim illic duntaxat in reprehendendo Empedocle qui quum omnem Substantiarum compositarum varietatem ex certa Elementorum inter se mixtione consurgere assereret, neque aliud praeterea, quam Elementa sub certa proportione commista, in compositis poneret ; ait, ex eius doctrina rationem generationis naturalis, & cur unumquodq; generet sibi simile, reddi non posse : quandoquidem neque ipsa elementa, neque haec ipsorum mixtio atq; proportio, causa esse possint talis generationis: imo nec Philia ac Neicos (Empedocléa principia effectiva) quippe quae generalem duntaxat congregandi ac segregandi vim habeant. Interim suam hac in re doctrinam Empedoclea obiter opponens, innuit, se isto incommodo non teneri, meliusq; causam generationis naturalis assignare posse ; quoniam non, ut ille, in certa Elementorum proportione, sed in Forma substantiali collocaret uniuscujusq; compositi essentiam atq; naturam ; quae Forma habeat etiam vim effectivam, sefeq; propagare, atq; aliam sibi similem producere valeat : quo supposito, locum non habeat illa objectio, qua ipse hic utitur contra Empedoclem, qui fiat nimirum, ut frumentum gignat frumentum, non oleam aut ossa. Quum igitur hic nuda utatur assertione Aristoteles, ac simpliciter affirmet, à Forma substantiali pendere generationem naturalem ; nimis perfunctorie hunc locum inspexerunt, qui argumentum demonstrativum, à generatione naturali desumtum, pro Forma afferri hic putant.
units.tr: So the comparisons and similitudes by which Aristotle illustrates his Form are of such a kind that from them it does not follow in any way that the Form is substantial; rather the contrary altogether. And yet he brought forward no proof for it apart from this one. For what some commentators write on On Generation and Corruption 2, at texts 39, 40 and 41, namely that Aristotle there demonstrates the Form from natural generation, they are mistaken about. For there he is concerned only with refuting Empedocles, who, while asserting that all the variety of compound substances arises from a certain mixture of the Elements among themselves, and positing nothing in compounds beyond the Elements mixed in a fixed proportion, says that on his doctrine no account can be given of natural generation, or of why each thing produces something like itself. For neither the Elements themselves nor their mixture and proportion can be the cause of such generation; nor can Love and Strife (Empedocles' efficient principles), since they have only a general power of uniting and separating. Meanwhile, while incidentally setting his own doctrine against the Empedoclean one, he hints that he is not troubled by this difficulty and can assign a better cause of natural generation, because he places the essence and nature of each compound not in a fixed proportion of Elements but in a substantial Form. This Form has also an efficient power, and can propagate itself and produce another like itself. On this supposition that objection, which he himself uses here against Empedocles, namely that wheat would then produce wheat and not an olive or bones, does not apply. Since therefore Aristotle here uses a bare assertion, and simply affirms that natural generation depends on the substantial Form, those who think that a demonstrative argument drawn from natural generation is brought forward here for the Form have looked at this passage too carelessly.

units.la: Et quomodo verum est, Aristotelem hic non adhibuisse Generationem Naturalem ad demonstrandam Formam ; ita certum quoque est, cum, si id fecisset, operam lusurum fuisse, non modo ex rei veritate, sed vel ex confessione ipsorum Peripateticorum ; quorum multi quum strenuè laboraverint in conquirendis pro Forma argumentis, vix tamen invenias, qui hoc argumentum attingat, aut Formam ex eo probari dicat, quod res naturales sibi similia gignant.
units.tr: And just as it is true that Aristotle did not here use natural generation to demonstrate the Form, so it is also certain that, had he done so, he would have labored in vain, not only by the truth of the matter but even by the admission of the Peripatetics themselves. Many of them have strenuously toiled to find arguments for the Form, yet you will scarcely find one who touches on this argument, or says that the Form is proved from the fact that natural things beget things like themselves.
Chapter I.

units.la: gnant : & ipse Fonseca, diligentissimus Formarum propugnator, dicit eos, qui ex generatione Substantiarum probant Formas, quia scilicet accidentia non possint substantiam generare, nisi ut instrumenta substantiæ ; sumere id, quod probandum erat, nempè equum, ignem & cæteras, quæ ab agentibus naturalibus gignuntur, habere aliquid substantiæ præter Materiam. Nisi enim hoc ponatur (inquit) nihil concluditur.
units.tr: ...beget. And Fonseca himself, the most diligent champion of Forms, says that those who prove Forms from the generation of substances, because accidents cannot generate a substance except as instruments of a substance, are assuming what was to be proved, namely that a horse, fire, and the other things produced by natural agents have something of substance over and above matter. For unless this is posited (he says) nothing is concluded.

units.la: VII. Aristotelici autem hac in parte diligentiores præceptore suo fuerunt, & quod ab eo omissum viderunt, ipsi supplere conati sunt, non affirmando tantùm, dari Formas substantiales, sed & conquirendo argumenta, quibus eæ astruerentur. quanquàm sanè operam luserunt, uti in processu apparebit. Et quum multi in hoc laboraverint, reliquos diligentia facile superant Fonseca & Suarez, quorum ille omnia pro Forma argumenta ad quatuor summa capita redigit. Primum caput continere dicit rationes ex ipsa rerum naturalium constitutione ductas. Res naturales (inquit) non sunt ipsa Materia prima duntaxat, sed aliquid aliud includunt : alioquin omnes essent ejusdem rationis & essentiæ, nullumq; esset earum internum Principium, nulla generatio & corruptio, nulla proprietatum distinctio, quæ essentialem distinctionem sequitur : proinde quælibet aut omnes omninò proprietates haberet, aut nullam. at illud, quod prætereà includunt, nobilius est quàm Materia prima, quum ab eo proveniat non modo ipsarum distinctio, & Generationis absolutio, sed etiam omnis agendi facultas, proprietatum varietas, & perfectionis ordo. ergo si Materia prima est substantia, quod omnes tanquam notissimum supponunt ; multò magis id quod additur ad complendam rerum naturalium constitutionem, substantia erit. completur autem per Formam. datur ergo Forma substantialis. Hisce verbis duo agit Fonseca. partim enim probare nititur, esse aliquid in substantijs, præter Materiam primam, partim, id quod Materiæ primæ superadditur, quoque ipsa completur, substantiam esse, non accidens. Sed multò paucioribus verbis hæc probatio poterat absolvi. Si enim datur Materia prima, qualis in Peripato statuitur, quæ videlicet nuda sit potentia, ac substantia partialis, adeò imperfecta, ut per se ipsa subsistere nullo modo possit, ac proindè alterius substantiæ partialis societate indigeat, quâ actuetur, atq; existentiam accipiat; omnino perspicuum est, dari Formam substantialem: quum hæc inter se convertantur. Quum igitur ejusmodi Materia prima, qualis supponitur, adeò sufficiat ad Formæ substantialis probationem, ut vel solo ejus nomine audito, necessario Forma substantialis unà concipiatur; supervacua hic est mentio differentiarum specificarum, proprietatum, functionum, generationis & corruptionis. quippè satis est dictu, Quandoquidem Materia existere non potest, nisi per alteram substantiam partialem compleatur & actuetur; inevitabiliter sequi, quod detur Forma substantialis. namq; & nos libenter concedemus hanc consequentiam; & nemo, qui sanus sit ratiocinator, ipsi refragabitur. Verum quidem est, & Priscorum Philosophorum non paucos, & Galenum quoque, posuisse Materiam primam, seu unam omnibus rebus communem Materiam, neq; tamen Formas substantiales agnovisse: sed alia ipsorum erat ratio, quippè quorum Materia erat vera ac suopte marte subsistens substantia, non ejusmodi potentia (ut loquuntur Aristotelici) quæ nullam ex sese existentiam habeat, adeóque paulò plus sit quam nihil. Quum autem Materia communis, de qua hic Fonseca alijq; Peripatetici loquuntur, non sit talis, ac illa Galeni & Priscorum, sed genuina ac pura puta ipsorum Materia prima; omnino, ipsâ positâ, etiam poni Formam substantialem, ut diximus, necesse est, ac proindè Suarez, hoc argumentum tractans, consequenter loquitur, dicens, Quum Materia sit potentia, id quod ei additur ad complendam essentiam rei, fore actum, quia potentia dicat essentialem ordinem ad actum. non posse autem illum actum, qui ad complendam rei essentiam Materia adjungitur, esse accidentalem, quia cum Materia sit substantialis potentia, non expleatur per actum accidentalem. Sed enimvero
units.tr: VII. The Aristotelians, however, have been more diligent in this matter than their master. What he left out they have tried to supply themselves, not only by asserting that substantial Forms are given, but also by seeking arguments by which they might be established. Yet they labour in vain, as will appear as we proceed. Although many have worked at this, Fonseca and Suarez easily surpass the rest. Fonseca reduces all his arguments for Form to four main heads. He says the first head contains the arguments drawn from the very constitution of natural things. Natural things (he says) are not merely prime matter, but include something else. Otherwise they would all be of the same kind and essence, there would be no internal principle in them, no generation and corruption, and no distinction of properties, which follows essential distinction. Thus each thing would have either all properties or none. But what they include in addition is nobler than prime matter, since from it comes not only their distinction and the completion of their generation, but also every power of acting, the variety of properties and the order of perfection. Therefore, if prime matter is a substance, which everyone assumes as most well known, then much more so is that which is added to complete the constitution of natural things a substance. It is completed, however, by Form. Therefore a substantial Form is given. In these words Fonseca does two things. He tries partly to prove that there is something in substances besides prime matter, and partly that what is superadded to prime matter and completes it is also a substance, not an accident. But this proof could have been completed in far fewer words. For if prime matter is given, as the Peripatetics posit it, namely a mere potency and a partial substance so imperfect that it can in no way subsist by itself, and so needs the association of another partial substance by which it may be actuated and receive existence, then it is entirely evident that a substantial Form is given, since these are convertible. Since such prime matter, as it is supposed to be, is so sufficient for proving a substantial Form that, merely on hearing its name, a substantial Form is necessarily conceived along with it, the mention of specific differences, properties, functions, generation and corruption is superfluous here. It is enough to say: since matter cannot exist unless it is completed and actuated by another partial substance, it inevitably follows that a substantial Form is given. We too will gladly grant this consequence, and no one who is a sound reasoner will dispute it. It is true that not a few of the ancient philosophers, and Galen also, posited prime matter, or one matter common to all things, and yet did not acknowledge substantial Forms. But their reasoning was different, since for them matter was a true substance subsisting in its own right, not that kind of potency (as the Aristotelians call it) which has no existence of its own and is therefore little more than nothing. But since the common matter of which Fonseca and the other Peripatetics speak here is not like that of Galen and the ancients, but is their own genuine and pure prime matter, it is entirely necessary, once it is posited, that a substantial Form also be posited, as we have said. Accordingly Suarez, treating this argument, speaks consistently when he says: Since matter is potency, whatever is added to it to complete the essence of the thing will be act, because potency implies an essential order to act. But that act which is joined to matter to complete the essence of a thing cannot be accidental, because since matter is substantial potency, it is not completed by an accidental act. But indeed

units.la: Materia prima ejusmodi, est hypothesis, & quidem talis, cujus probatio à Forma praecipuè, imò in totum pendeat. quum enim dixerunt, quicquid dicere possunt Peripatetici, ad demonstrandam Materiam primam; tandem ultro fateri coguntur, omnia alia argumenta pro Materia prima esse invalida, nisi constet prius, dari Formas fubftantiales, neque aliunde quam per Formas substantiales eam idoneè probari posse: sicuti ipsorum super hac re consessionem supra exposuimus. Quae igitur haec est argumentandi ratio, rei incertae atq; ignotae fidem ex aequè incerta atq; ignota quaerere? & Formas substantiales probare ex eo, quod ipsum probari haud aliter queat, nisi Formis ejusmodi praesuppositis? Sanè ludere hoc est potius, quam serio agere; meraq; ac nimis absurda est principij petitio, Formas extruere super Materia prima, quum ipsa Materia prima stare haud aliter possit, nisi ut à Formis sustentetur. Quum nos igitur nullam agnoscamus Materiam primam, ac multò minus talem, quae nuda sit potentia substantialis (quod ipsi de sua Materia prima somniant) merito pro inani ac frivola repudiamus hanc pro Forma probationem, à Materia prima petitam: nihilq; minus admittimus, quam illud Suarezij, qui cùm dixisset, Praecipuam rationem probandae Formae substantialis sumendam esse ex ipsius fine, qui sit, constituere ac complere essentiam entis naturalis, subjungit, hunc finem seu effectum esse absolutè necessarium in rerum natura, quia alioqui in rebus corporeis nihil esset in sua substantiali natura completum & perfectum. Haec enim necessitas non urget, nisi eos, quibus Materia est valdè imperfectum ens (uti ipse loquitur ibidem) & qui pro vero recipiunt, quicquid de Materia prima Peripatus sibi somniavit, apud eos autem, qui aliter statuunt, fumo evanidius est, quicquid in hanc sententiam dicitur. & haec argumentatio, à rerum naturalium constitutione ducta, ad probandam Formam, prout ab ipsis instituitur, haud aliam vim habet aut sensum, quam si simpliciter dicerent, Res naturales constant ex Materia prima & Forma substantiali; ali ; ergo datur Forma substantialis : qui argumentandi modus ridiculus est, ac planè nullus. & tamen totidem ferè verbis hoc loquitur Pererius, inquiens Formam sic ostendi ex Compositione : Res naturales substantiæ sunt compositæ : oportet igitur præter Materiam esse aliam partem componentem, quæ sit Substantia : hæc autem est Forma.
units.tr: Prime matter of this kind is a hypothesis, and one on which its proof depends mainly, indeed wholly, on Form. For when the Peripatetics have said all they can to demonstrate prime matter, they are at last compelled to admit freely that all their other arguments for prime matter are invalid unless it is first established that substantial Forms are given, and that prime matter can be properly proved in no other way than through substantial Forms. We have set out their own confession on this point above. What kind of reasoning is this, to seek credence for an uncertain and unknown thing from something equally uncertain and unknown? And to prove substantial Forms from the fact that matter cannot be proved except by presupposing such Forms? Surely this is trifling rather than serious argument. It is a pure and quite absurd begging of the question, to build Forms upon prime matter when prime matter itself can stand in no other way than by being sustained by Forms. Since we therefore acknowledge no prime matter, and much less one that is a mere substantial potency (which is what they dream of their prime matter), we rightly reject as empty and frivolous this proof for Form taken from prime matter. Nor do we admit less of Suarez's claim, who, having said that the principal reason for proving a substantial Form is to be taken from its end, which is to constitute and complete the essence of a natural being, adds that this end or effect is absolutely necessary in the nature of things, since otherwise nothing in corporeal things would be complete and perfect in its substantial nature. This necessity presses only on those for whom matter is a very imperfect being (as he himself says there), and who accept as true whatever the Peripatetics dreamed about prime matter. For those who think otherwise, whatever is said in this opinion vanishes like smoke. This argument, drawn from the constitution of natural things and used to prove Form as they put it forward, has no force or sense other than if they had simply said: Natural things consist of prime matter and substantial Form; therefore a substantial Form is given. This mode of arguing is ridiculous and altogether no argument at all. Yet Pererius says almost the same words, saying that Form is thus shown from composition: Natural substances are composite; therefore there must be, besides matter, another component part which is substance: and this is Form.

units.la: VIII. Quod si verò omissâ Materiâ primâ, solum Materiæ nomen adhibeatur, nihil planè pro Forma facit, quicquid hic à Fonseca congeritur de ijs, quæ Rebus naturalibus includantur præter Materiam. ad summum enim nihil aliud probat, nisi dari in rebus non Materiam tantum, seu substantiam, sed & Accidentia Materiæ inhærentia ; quod nullius probationis eget, utpote per se clarum, ac proinde à nemine sano inficiandum. Sed ex eo, quod dantur in rebus accidentia, argumentari, quod dentur Formæ substantiales ; nulla est consequentia : de quo mox plura. Interim observandum, in ostendendo hoc ipso, quod in rebus naturalibus detur aliquid aliud quam Materiæ, haud pauca parum solida, aut etiam falsa à Fonseca admisceri, dum videlicet dicit, Alioquin omnes futuras ejusdem rationis & essentiæ, nullum fore earum internum Principium, nullam proprietatum distinctionem, & proinde quamlibet aut omnes omninò proprietates habituram, aut nullas. Etenim Elementa omnia non tam accidentibus inter se differunt, quam ipso substantiæ modo. etiamsi igitur accidentia diversa sortita sint, ac proinde accidentibus quoque inter se differunt ; non tamen, si cunctis accidentibus nudari possent, ac nudarentur, propterea omnia ejusdem rationis & essentiæ futura essent ; cum suus cuiq; Elemento sit peculiaris substantiæ modus, ab omni alia substantia diversus. & composita quoque, licet in eorum constitutione multò plus sibi vendicent accidentia, quam in Elementis ; non tamen solis accidentibus invicem distinguuntur, quum Materialiter quoque inter se differant, utpotè ex diversa Materiæ seu Elementorum proportione conflata. Ac quum proprietates aliæ sint substantiales, sive ipsi
units.tr: VIII. But if, leaving aside prime matter, only the name of matter is retained, what Fonseca heaps up here about the things included in natural bodies besides matter does nothing at all for Form. At most it proves only that there are in things not only matter or substance but also accidents inhering in matter. This needs no proof, being evident in itself, and therefore to be denied by no sane person. But to argue from the fact that accidents exist in things that substantial Forms exist is no consequence, of which more shortly. Meanwhile it should be observed that in showing this very point, that something other than matter is found in natural things, Fonseca mixes in not a few things that are weakly grounded or even false. For example he says: Otherwise all things would be of the same kind and essence, there would be no internal principle in them, no distinction of properties, and therefore each thing would have either all properties or none. For indeed all the elements differ from one another not so much in accidents as in the very mode of substance. So even if they have different accidents, and therefore differ also in accidents, it does not follow that, if they could be stripped of all accidents, and were so stripped, all would be of the same kind and essence, since each element has its own peculiar mode of substance, different from every other substance. And compounds too, although they claim far more for accidents in their constitution than the elements do, are not distinguished from one another by accidents alone, since they also differ materially, being formed from a different proportion of matter or elements. And since some properties are substantial, that is the essential modes of substances themselves, and others are accidental, even if nothing were in things except matter or substance itself, the distinction of properties would not be abolished, nor would any thing have either all properties or none; but...

units.la: {a} Pererius, Physic. 6. Phys. 2. ipsi substantiarum essentiales modi, aliæ verò accidentales: etiamsi nihil in rebus esset, præter ipsam Materiam seu Substantiam, non tamen tolleretur omnis proprietatum distinctio, neque quævis res aut omnes omnino proprietates haberet, aut nullam; sed nihilo seciùs essentialibus proprietatibus substantiæ inter se differrent. quarè errat iterùm, quum mox dicit, Ab eo, quod res includunt præter Materiam, provenire ipsarum distinctionem, & proprietatum varietatem: quum id nequaquàm universim, sed ex parte tantùm verum sit. Quod verò ait, in isto casu nullum fore rerum internum Principium; mirabilis admodùm est sententia. etenim Principia interna ipsis Peripateticis sunt, e quibus res constant, sicuti ipse Fonseca in comm. ad 1. Metaph. 7. Principium internum rei naturalis idem facit cum Elemento. quum ítaque ipsa Materia sit internum Principium, quo pacto dici potest, Nullum fore rerum naturalium Principium internum, si è sola Materia constent?
units.tr: {a} Pererius, Physic. 6. Phys. 2. The essential modes of substances are the substances' own; the others are accidental. Even if there were nothing in things besides matter itself, or substance, not every distinction of properties would be removed, nor would every thing have all its properties or none at all. Substances would still differ from one another in their essential properties. So he is wrong again when he says soon after, The distinction of things and the variety of their properties arise from what things contain besides matter, since that is by no means true universally, but only in part. And what he says, that in that case there would be no internal principle of things, is a very strange opinion. For the Peripatetics themselves hold that the internal principles are those from which things are composed, as Fonseca himself says in his commentary on Metaphysics 1, 7: an internal principle of a natural thing is the same as its element. Since matter itself is therefore an internal principle, how can it be said that there would be no internal principle of natural things if they consisted of matter alone?

units.la: IX. Sed ut hæc, aliaq; in hanc sententiam inconsultius à Fonseca prolata omittamus, atq; rem ipsam videamus; neq; proprietates rerum, atq; specifica ipsarum distinctio, neq; generatio atque corruptio, néque facultates agendi (quæ tria capita hic à Fonseca adhibentur ad probandam Formam substantialem) quicquam omninò conducunt ad Formæ assertionem. Quantum ad primum; Pererius quidem id tanti facit, ut tria inde extruat argumenta. Forma enim ostenditur, inquit, ex existentiâ rerum naturalium: quia res naturales existunt per se determinata ad aliquam speciem, quæ quidem existentia à substantia profisciscitur: at non ab Materia, quippè quæ aut nullam ex se habet existentiam, aut ea certè est indefinita: proficiscitur ergo à Forma. Deinde ex distinctione: si enim non esset Forma substantialis, quum Materia prima sit una & communis omnium rerum, omnes res naturales eadem essent secundum substantiam & quiddiatem, nec differrent aut genere aut specie. Præterea ex propria cujusq; rei natura. si enim nulla actuositas à Substantiâ, quæ non sit substantialis. Substantia natalis ... [illegible, ~20 letters] nulla est Forma substantialis, quaero, unde spectanda sit natura atque esse cuiusque rei, &c. Sanè apparet magna argumentorum inopia Pererium laborasse, qui unam eandemque rem in tres diversas rationes diducat. esse enim determinatum ad unam aliquam speciem, revera idem est, quod genere & specie ab aliis rebus differre: & eo ipso, quod aliquid determinatum est ad certam quandam speciem, ab omnibus aliarum specierum rebus, specie; ab iis vero, quae etiam diversi sunt generis, genere quoque differt. Est porrò quaevis res certae speciei, & ab aliis rebus specificè distincta, non per aliud, quam per naturam suam atque essentiam. quare, ut diximus, non tres sunt hae rationes, sed unica duntaxat. Sed specificae rerum proprietates frustrà allegantur ad probandam Formam, quandoquidem sola Materia cum accidentibus sufficit ad specificas rerum differentias constituendas. & Elementa quidem ipso substantiae modo praecipuè inter se differunt, (uti paulò ante quoq; diximus) ac diversarum inter se specierum sunt, non tam ob qualitates (quum & paucissimae iis insint, & nonnullae earum sint diversis Elementis communes; ac iis quoque amissis, ut quum aër aut aqua exuto nativo frigore calefacta sunt, nihilominus in specie sua perseverent) quam essentiali ipsarum substantiarum differentiâ. Eorum verò quae ex Elementis fiunt, alia solâ certorum accidentium in Materiam introductione constituuntur (uti illae substantiae, quae ex unico tantùm Elemento fiunt) alia verò partim certâ diversorum Elementorum, debitâ proportione inter se conjunctorum, Mixtione, partim certarum qualitatum in materiam illam, ex diversis substantiis conflatam, impositione. & praeterea in aliis etiam certa Materiae dispositio ac figuratio, non tantùm commistio, requiritur; & diversarum quoq; substantiarum conjunctio atque unio, non qualis illa est diversorum Elementorum, ad unius corporis constitutionem conflatorum, sed alterius generis; quomodo, verbi gratia, anima & corpus ad constituendam unam stirpem aut animantem conciantur: de quibus omnibus accuratius & latius alibi dicetur.
units.tr: IX. But let us set aside these and other points that Fonseca has put forward too carelessly in this direction, and look at the matter itself. Neither the properties of things nor their specific distinction, nor generation and corruption, nor the powers of acting (the three heads which Fonseca here uses to prove the substantial form) contribute anything at all to the assertion of a form. As to the first, Pererius indeed sets so much store by it that he builds three arguments from it. A form is shown, he says, from the existence of natural things, because natural things exist as determined to some species by themselves, and this existence comes from substance; but it does not come from matter, which either has no existence of its own or at least has an indefinite one; therefore it comes from the form. Next, from distinction: if there were no substantial form, since prime matter is one and common to all things, all natural things would be the same in substance and quiddity, and would differ neither in genus nor in species. Moreover, from the proper nature of each thing: if there is no activity from a substance that is not substantial... [illegible, about twenty letters] there is no substantial form, I ask, from what is the nature and being of each thing to be judged, and so on. Clearly Pererius laboured under a great lack of arguments, since he draws one and the same point out into three different reasons. For to be determined to one particular species is really the same as differing from other things in genus and species; and by the very fact that something is determined to a certain species, it differs in species from all things of other species, and from those of a different genus it also differs in genus. Moreover, any thing of a certain species, and specifically distinct from other things, is so through nothing other than its own nature and essence. Therefore, as we have said, these are not three reasons but only one. But the specific properties of things are cited in vain to prove the form, since matter alone with accidents suffices to constitute the specific differences of things. The elements indeed differ among themselves chiefly by the very mode of their substance (as we also said a little earlier), and they belong to different species not so much because of their qualities (since very few of these are in them, and some of these are common to different elements, and even when these are lost, as when air or water is heated after losing its native cold, they nevertheless remain in their own species), but because of the essential difference of their substances. Of the things that are made from the elements, some are constituted solely by the introduction of certain accidents into matter (such as those substances which are made from only one element), while others are constituted partly by the mixture of different elements, joined together in due proportion, and partly by the imposition of certain qualities upon that matter, compounded from different substances. Moreover, in other cases a certain arrangement and shaping of matter is required, not merely a blending; and also a conjunction and union of different substances, not of the kind that exists among the different elements combined to make up one body, but of another kind, as for example soul and body come together to constitute one plant or animal. All of these matters will be discussed more accurately and fully elsewhere.

units.la: Cap. I. dicetur. Hæc sunt vera rerum Elementa seu Principia interna, omnem specierum varietatem constituentia, quæ tùm in ipsos sensus incurrunt, tùm per firmissimas rationes, ex sensibus atq; manifestis experimentis ductas, demonstrantur: & ipsorum usus ac necessitas, & quid quæque in rerum constitutione faciant, indaganti perquàm clarè apparet. Forma autem substantialis (exceptis animabus, quas in Formarum classem referunt, quum nihil habeant cum illis , ut posteà conficiemus) néque alterutrò istorum κειμηλίων inesse rebus deprehenditur; neq; ullum ipsi officium assignari potest, ob quod ad rerum constitutionem requiratur. Sensibus non percipi certum est, & Peripatetici fatentur; ut Averröes. comm. ad 12. Metaph. §. 14. Thomas tractatu de sens. & sensib. alijq; passim. Et quum neq; ipsa, neq; ullus ejus effectus in sensus cadat, intellectui nihil de ea constare potest; quandoquidem de nulla re (extra ea, quæ Fidei sunt, & divinâ nituntur auctoritate) affirmare quippiam Ratiocinatio debet, nisi in quantum rebus sensu perceptis subnititur. In sensibus enim (uti rectè alicubi Scaliger dixit) omne est omnium artium atq; scientiarum fundamentum. Quanquam igitur largiamur Peripateticis, verum esse illud tantopere apud ipsos tritum, Formas comprehendi intellectu (intellectu enim comprehendi valent non vera tantùm entia, sed monstruosissima etiam figmenta, ut poetarum Chimærę & Harpyæ; & sic non difficile est assequi, quales sibi Formas substantiales finxerit Aristoteles, quomodò item Platonicas ideas, rem æquè fictitiam, nullo negotio imaginamur) non tamen largimur, intellectum ulla evidente ratione duci, ad Formas ejusdmodi in rebus agnoscendas. Et sanè non aliter ab Aristotelicis intelligi Formas, quam à nobis intelligantur, hoc est, eos duntaxat imaginari sibi illud, quod de Formis acceperunt ab Aristotele, planum est ex ipsorum doctrina, qui passim tradunt, ignotas sibi esse Formarum essentias, ac proindè vix posse à se assignari essentialem ullius rei definitionem, quum omnis talis definitio debeat constare nominibus propriis Materiæ ac Formæ.
units.tr: Chap. I. will be said. These are the true elements or internal principles of things, constituting all the variety of species, which both fall under the senses themselves and are demonstrated by most firm reasons drawn from the senses and from manifest experiments; and their use and necessity, and what each does in the constitution of things, is quite clearly apparent to anyone who investigates. But a substantial form (excepting souls, which they count in the class of forms, though they have nothing in common with those, as we shall show later) is found in neither of these treasures of things, nor can any office be assigned to it for which it is required in the constitution of things. It is certain that it is not perceived by the senses, and the Peripatetics confess this, as Averroes in his commentary on Metaphysics 12, §14, Thomas in his treatise on sense and the sensible, and others everywhere. And since neither it nor any of its effects falls under the senses, nothing about it can be known by the intellect; for reasoning ought to affirm nothing about any thing (apart from those things that belong to faith and rest on divine authority) unless it rests upon things perceived by the senses. For in the senses (as Scaliger rightly said somewhere) is the foundation of all the arts and sciences. Although, therefore, we grant to the Peripatetics what is so commonly repeated among them, that forms are comprehended by the intellect (for the intellect is able to comprehend not only real beings but also the most monstrous fictions, such as the Chimaera and the Harpies of the poets; and so it is not difficult to grasp what kind of substantial forms Aristotle invented, and in the same way we easily imagine the Platonic ideas, an equally fictitious thing), we nevertheless do not grant that the intellect is led by any evident reason to recognise forms of this sort in things. And indeed that the Aristotelians understand forms in no other way than we do, that is, that they merely imagine for themselves what they have received about forms from Aristotle, is plain from their own teaching, for they everywhere declare that the essences of forms are unknown to them, and so they can hardly assign the essential definition of any thing, since every such definition ought to consist of the proper names of Matter and Form.

units.la: Fonf. 5. Dial. 5. Minutifimi-ni̇s ... (marginal handwritten annotation, illegible in parts) ma rei, quae definitur. Apertam habemus super hac re Scaligeri confessionem, qui disputans contra Alexandrum, assignantem gravitatem pro Forma terrae, Tuto gravitatem, inquit, esse terrae proprium accidens: Forma autem essentiam latere nos, quemadmodum & alias multas, ac fortasse omnes. In magno enim periculo versamur ne ullam veram teneamus definitionem: ne nostra scientia repat humi per tenebras, circa sola accidentia. quibus etiam concordat illud Exerc. 307. §. 12. Nulla est Forma nobis nota plenè & planè. Formarum enim cognitio est rudis, confusa, nec nisi per effectus. Et in eundem sensum Thomas, Formae substantiales sunt incognitae nobis, quia insensibiles. ideo per qualitates, quae sunt principia immediata transmutationis, exprimuntur. Itaque Albertus, dicens, Formam omnem esse intelligibilem per se, & principium intelligendi aliud, quod est formatum per ipsam (quod non abludit ab illo Simplicij, Eum, qui cognoverit Formam naturalem, cognoscere quoq; Materiam tali Forme subjectam, com. ad 2. Phys. 26.) non ad res ipsas respexit, sed ad conceptus illos imaginarios, ex Aristotelis de Materia prima ac Forma traditionibus ortos; quarum haec quoq; una est, Formam esse Principium non essendi tantum, sed & cognoscendi, quod si verum est, fateantur Peripatetici, se nihil cognoscere, quum ipsas Formarum essentias non cognoscant (uti fatentur ipsi, quando verum loqui audent) ac per res sibi ignotas ad aliarum rerum ignotarum intellectionem pervenire non possint.
units.tr: Fonseca, 5. Dial. 5. Most minute... (marginal handwritten annotation, illegible in parts) ...of the thing that is defined. We have an open confession on this matter from Scaliger, who, disputing against Alexander, who assigned gravity as the form of earth, said: Gravity is safely a proper accident of earth; but the form, we say, is hidden from us, as are many others, and perhaps all. For we are in great danger of holding no true definition at all, lest our science crawl on the ground through darkness, concerned with accidents alone. With this agrees what he says in Exercise 307, §12: No form is fully and plainly known to us. For our knowledge of forms is rough and confused, and comes only through effects. And Thomas to the same effect: Substantial forms are unknown to us because they are insensible; therefore they are expressed through qualities, which are the immediate principles of change. So Albertus, saying that every form is intelligible through itself, and is the principle of understanding something else, which is formed through it (which does not differ from that saying of Simplicius, He who has known the natural form also knows the matter subject to such a form, commentary on Physics 2, 26), did not look to the things themselves, but to those imaginary concepts arising from Aristotle's teachings on prime matter and form. One of these is also this: that form is the principle not only of being but also of knowing. If this is true, the Peripatetics must admit that they know nothing, since they do not know the essences of forms themselves (as they confess when they dare to speak the truth), and cannot reach the understanding of other unknown things through things unknown to them.

units.la: X. Sed neq; ullum apparet Formarum officium, ob quod requirantur ad res constituendas; si inanissimum illud somnium de Materia prima, ejusq; potentialitate (ut sic dicamus) seponatur.
units.tr: X. But no office of the Forms appears for which they are required in constituting things, if that most empty dream about prime matter and its potentiality (so to speak) is set aside.

units.la: Nam quod Suarez ait, nisi datis Formas, non futuram multitudinem & varietatem specierum substantialium (in qua maxime consistit hujus universi corporei mirabilis dispositio & pulchritudo) quia omnia essent unius essentiae, solumq; accidentaliter differrent: vanissimum est, subtracto illo de Materia prima com-
units.tr: For what Suarez says, unless Forms were given, there would not be the multitude and variety of substantial species (in which the admirable arrangement and beauty of this corporeal universe chiefly consists), because all things would be of one essence and would differ only accidentally, is most vain: once that notion of prime matter is subtracted com-
{x} Exerc. 101. sect. 14.

units.la: Comm. ad 1. de Gener. & Corr. text. 6.
units.tr: Comm. ad 1. de Gener. & Corr. text. 6.
1 Coeli, tract. 3. cap. 4.

units.la: Disp. 15. sect. 1. §. 18. commento, cui soli hæc verba innituntur. Sed etiamsi omnia ex una eademq; constarent Materia, non tamen propterea tolleretur specierum varietas; quum alia atq; alia accidentia in Materiam imposita, possint alias atq; alias species constituere: sicuti nunc quoq; videmus multa, quæ eandem habent Materiam, plurimum inter se differre, ac diversissimarum esse specierum (exempli gratia, animas leonis & quercus) ob diversa, quæ in eadem Materia sortita sunt, accidentia. Sanè illa objectio, Sic fore, ut substantia non essentialiter, sed accidentaliter inter se differant, præterquàm quod in se inanis est, quum illa membra non sint ita inter se opposita, ut invicem excludant, quandoquidem ipsa quoque accidentia, etiamsi non omnia, ad rerum essentiam pertinent; non efficit illud quod intenditur. Etiamsi enim daretur postulatum illud, Sic fore ut res non essentialiter, sed tantùm accidentaliter differant: non plus hinc sequitur, nisi omnem specierum distinctionem fore accidentalem; quod longè aliud est, quàm omnem specierum varietatem tolli. substantia enim non desinit esse substantia, etsi accidentibus tantùm ab alia substantia differat: ac propterea species substantiales non desinent esse substantiales, etiamsi accidentibus duntaxat inter se distinguatur. itaq; prava utitur ratiocinatione Suarez, qui non contentus dicere, quod sublatis Formis substantialibus, tollatur essentiale substantiarum discrimen (quod tamen ipsum non uno modo falsum est, uti vel ex iis, quæ paulò ante diximus, apparet) præterea infert, omnem hoc pacto tolli specierum varietatem; id quod nullis machinamentis effici potest, ut inde consequatur. Quare hoc quidem officium, quod Formas Substantiales propterea requirit, ut detur varietas ac multitudo specierum substantialium, utq; illæ non accidentaliter tantùm, sed & essentialiter distinguantur; inane est.
units.tr: Disp. 15. sect. 1. §. 18, the commentary on which alone these words rest. But even if all things were made of one and the same matter, the variety of species would not for that reason be removed, since different and differing accidents imposed on matter can constitute different species. Thus we see now too that many things which have the same matter differ greatly from one another, and belong to most diverse species (for example, the soul of a lion and of an oak) because of the different accidents that have fallen to them in the same matter. Certainly that objection, that it would follow that substances would differ from one another not essentially but accidentally, apart from being empty in itself (since those members are not so opposed to one another that they exclude each other, seeing that accidents themselves, though not all of them, pertain to the essence of things), does not achieve what it intends. For even if that postulate were granted, that things would differ not essentially but only accidentally, nothing more would follow from it than that every distinction of species would be accidental; and this is far different from saying that every variety of species is abolished. For a substance does not cease to be a substance, even though it differs from another substance only by accidents; and therefore substantial species do not cease to be substantial, even if they are distinguished from one another merely by accidents. So Suarez reasons badly: not content to say that, with substantial Forms removed, the essential difference of substances is removed (which itself is false in more than one way, as appears even from what we said a little earlier), he further infers that in this way every variety of species is removed; and no machinery can bring it about that this follows. Therefore this office, by which substantial Forms are required so that there may be a variety and multitude of substantial species, and so that these are distinguished not only accidentally but also essentially, is empty.

units.la: XI. Aliud præterea in rerum constitutione officium Formarum commenti sunt nonnulli Peripatetici, ipsam scilicet Substantiarum unitatem, quæ à Forma pendeat.
units.tr: XI. Some Peripatetics have invented another office of Forms in the constitution of things, namely the very unity of substances, which depends on the Form.
Everything
Chapter I.

units.la: Omne quod est (inquit Scaliger) unum est non solum propter continuationem, ac privationem purae contiguitatis, sed propter actum quoque, cujus vi sit, ut illa partes unum fiant. Actum voco Formam, per quam sit, ut partes, quae natura suâ atque aptitudine coire poterant ad unionem, unum actu sint. & similiter alibi, Sunt invenustissimi studiosorum, qui putant, ex multiplici Materia (hoc enim sunt Elementa) & ejus Formis coagmentatis, posse per se fieri Formam unam, quae totius molis autor sit existendi, sine adventu externo Formae unius, qua totum illud in fide atque officio continuitatis atque unitatis contineatur. homo enim nihil aliud quam mistum esset, unumque fortuitum, quod per accidens vocant philosophi. Itidem & Fernelius, Necesse est, totius compositi unam esse Formam simplicem, quae à simplicium partium Formis diversa, illas in toto contineat.
units.tr: Everything that is (says Scaliger) is one not only on account of continuity and the mere privation of contiguity, but also on account of the act, by whose power those parts become one. I call the act the Form, through which it comes about that the parts, which by their nature and aptitude could come together into unity, are actually one. And similarly elsewhere: There are most unlovely students who think that from a manifold matter (for these are the Elements) and its Forms joined together, there can of itself arise one Form, which is the author of the whole mass of existence, without the external arrival of one Form by which that whole is held together in the bond and office of continuity and unity. For a man would be nothing other than a mixture, and a chance unity, which philosophers call accidental. Likewise Fernelius: It is necessary that there be one simple Form of the whole compound, which, different from the Forms of the simple parts, contains them within the whole.

units.la: Et putaverit aliquis, Aristotelem quoque hoc dixisse 8. Metaph. cap. ultimo, ubi haec habentur: πάντων ὅσα πολλὰ μέρη ἔχει, καὶ μή ἐστιν οἷον σωρὸς ἢ πᾶν, ἀλλ' ἔστι ἡ τὸ ὅλον παρὰ τὰ μόρια, ἔστι ἡ ἄξιον. Omnium, quae plures partes habent, ita ut universum non sit tanquam acervus, sed ut totum sit aliquid praeter partes; est aliqua causa. Revera tamen de Formis suis ibi non agit Aristoteles, neque hoc ijs officium ascribit, ut res in unitate contineant; sed duntaxat quaerit (quaestionem sane admodum otiosam) de Definitionibus, quid nimirum efficiat, ut illae sint unum, quum ex diversis partibus constent; id quod liquet tum ex universo sermone, tum ex ejus exordio, quod ita se habet. Περὶ δὲ τῶν ἀπορίας τῶν εἰρημένων περὶ τε τὸ ὁρισμὸς, καὶ περὶ τὸ ἀριθμὸς, τί ἐστι τὸ ἄξιον τῷ ἓν εἶναι: de quaestione autem dicta, circa definitiones ac numeros, quae sit causa ut unum sint, &c. neque aliorsum haec in commentariis accepit Averroes. Sed neque in ullo eorum locorum, quos pro se allegat Fernelius, quicquam tale ab Aristotele expresse dicitur, ac eum dicentem ipse facit: quanquam sane primi de Anima quinto ejusmodi quid innuere videtur, aiens animam non habere partes, quia si haberet, necesse foret aliquid esse τὸ συνέχον ἡ μία.
units.tr: And someone might think that Aristotle also said this in the last chapter of the eighth book of the Metaphysics, where these words occur: πάντων ὅσα πολλὰ μέρη ἔχει, καὶ μή ἐστιν οἷον σωρὸς ἢ πᾶν, ἀλλ' ἔστι ἡ τὸ ὅλον παρὰ τὰ μόρια, ἔστι ἡ ἄξιον [Of all things that have many parts, and that are not like a heap or a mere whole, but the whole is something besides the parts, there is some cause]. In truth, however, Aristotle does not there treat of his Forms, nor does he ascribe to them the office of holding things in unity; he merely inquires (a quite idle question) about definitions, namely what it is that makes them one, since they consist of different parts. This is clear both from the whole discussion and from its opening, which runs thus: Περὶ δὲ τῶν ἀπορίας τῶν εἰρημένων περὶ τε τὸ ὁρισμὸς, καὶ περὶ τὸ ἀριθμὸς, τί ἐστι τὸ ἄξιον τῷ ἓν εἶναι [Concerning the difficulties stated about definitions and numbers, what is the cause of their being one, etc.]. Nor did Averroes understand these words otherwise in his commentaries. But neither in any of the passages which Fernelius cites in his own favour is anything of this kind expressly said by Aristotle, and in the one where he speaks, Aristotle himself makes it so; although in the fifth chapter of the first book On the Soul he does seem to hint at something of the sort, saying that the soul has no parts, because if it had, there would have to be something τὸ συνέχον ἡ μία [that holds them together as one].

units.la: {x} Ratio communicandi, ratio distinctio, Nov. Institutio. Sed ratio unitatis: Vnum esse fuit ratio ex partibus constans sed Unitatem.
units.tr: {x} Reason of communicating, reason of distinction, New Institution. But the reason of unity: to be one was a reason consisting of parts, but unity.
Chapter I.

units.la: μίαν ποιῶν τὴν ψυχήν, quod animam contineret, ac unam faceret. Verum hoc quidem parum refert (nostri saltem respectu, & omnium eorum, qui similiter affecti sunt) dixerit hoc idem, quod Scaliger & Fernelius dicunt, an non dixerit Aristoteles. Quantum vero ad rem ipsam attinet; probatio hæc neque generalis est, quippe quæ ad Elementa non attinet (uti per se manifestum est) & præterea infirmitatem suam eo prodit, quod nihil valeat, nisi prius supponatur, dari Formas substantiales, nimirum Formas illas partiales, quæ Formæ superioris moderamine in officio contineantur. Et tamen ne illis quidem, qui ponunt Formas illas partiales, & unicuiq; parti similari in animalibus ac plantis suam assignant peculiarem Formam, necesse est Formam illis superinducere superiorem, quæ illas velut invicem colliget. possunt enim dicere, quod diciṫ Suarez, Esse Formas illas partiales, & aptas, ut inter se uniantur ac continuentur, & ideo componere unam integram Formam totius, scilicet animam, quæ constet ex partibus heterogeneis, & ex earum inseparabili unione tota consurgat. quo posito, sequitur id, quod ipse porro infert, Absurdum esse, fingere aliam Formam totalem, superadditam his Formis partialibus, & omnes illas partes iterùm informantem. Afferunt quidem & aliam rationem, quare compositis hoc vinculo opus fit; Quia nimirùm non possint simplicia, maximè autem contraria, in unum coire & contineri, nisi arcto velut vinculo, fortius quid atq; valentius ipsa stringat & coerceat, ne divulsa dissipataq; mox distrahantur, & eò redeant, unde singula professa sunt. Nisi enim quatuor illa (inquit Scaliger) rectorem habeant, temere ac sine modo metâq; ullâ jactabunt, & jactabuntur. Sed cum hæc innitantur vulgato illo sommnio, quo Elementa finguntur æternum inter se bellum gerere, semperq; mutuo agere & pati (cujus fictionis vanitatem in tractatu de Generatione & Corruptione, ubi de mixtione ac temperamentis prolixè agendum, evidenter confutabimus) non est ut verbosè ijs contradicamus. sicuti enim illi ultro sibi sumunt illam hypothesin, quanquàm quàm nullis argumentis unquam confirmatam; ita nos eandem pari facilitate negamus, asserentes (id quod res est) nullas tales Elementis inter sese inimicitias ac discordias intercedere; neq; ita malè ijs inter se convenire, ut pacem omnem oderint, ac omni conatu, ubi ad corporis alicujus constitutionem in unum conducta sunt, iterum nitantur sejungi, nisi alicujus superioris imperio ac praesentia in officio contineantur. Nequaquam enim ita screm habere, satis clarè apparet ex multarum stirpium cadaveribus, quæ egressâ animâ (quam ipsi volunt esse Formam) minimè vel statim, vel mox dilabuntur, sed per aliquot annos, imò per aliquot secula, eandem servant unitatem, quam habebant, dum vita fruerentur: id quod fieri non posset, si tam infida est Elementorum societas, ut nisi vi coacta durare unà non queant.
units.tr: Making the soul one [μίαν ποιῶν τὴν ψυχήν], because it would contain it and make it one. But it matters little (at least for our purposes, and for all who are similarly affected) whether he said this, as Scaliger and Fernelius say, or whether Aristotle did not say it. As far as the matter itself is concerned, however, this proof is neither general, since it does not apply to the elements (as is evident in itself), nor is it sound, since it has no force unless it is first assumed that substantial forms exist, namely those partial forms which are kept in their duty by the governance of a superior form. Yet even those who posit these partial forms, and assign to each similar part in animals and plants its own peculiar form, are not obliged to superimpose a higher form that would gather them together, as it were. For they can say what Suárez says: that those partial forms exist and are fit to unite and be joined with one another, and so compose one whole form for the whole, namely the soul, which consists of heterogeneous parts and arises entirely from their inseparable union. Granted this, there follows what he goes on to infer himself: that it is absurd to feign another total form, superadded to these partial forms and informing all those parts again. They do indeed bring another reason why compounds need this bond: simples, and especially contraries, cannot come together and be held in one unless they are bound as with a tight chain, which something stronger and more powerful grips and restrains, lest, once torn apart and scattered, they soon be pulled asunder and return to where each came from. For unless those four (says Scaliger) have a ruler, they will toss about rashly and without measure or limit, and will be tossed about. But since these arguments rest on that common dream, by which the elements are imagined to wage eternal war among themselves and always to act and be acted upon in turn (the vanity of which fiction we will clearly refute in the treatise on Generation and Corruption, where mixture and temperaments are to be discussed at length), there is no need to contradict them at length. For just as they readily assume that hypothesis, though it has never been confirmed by any arguments, so we deny it with equal ease, asserting (as is the case) that no such enmities and discords exist between the elements, nor do they agree so badly that they hate all peace and, whenever they have been brought together into the constitution of some body, strive with every effort to separate again, unless they are held in their duty by the command and presence of some superior. That things are not so is quite clear from the corpses of many plants, which, once the soul (which they want to be the form) has departed, by no means fall apart at once or soon, but for some years, indeed for some centuries, keep the same unity they had while they enjoyed life. This could not happen if the society of the elements were so faithless that they could not last together unless forcibly constrained.
XII.

units.la: Secundum hujus loci argumentum, quo ad probandum Formam Substantialem Fonseca utitur, est Generatio atq; Corruptio, quas nullas futuras ait, nisi dentur Formæ substantiales. Conimbricenses autem hoc explicatius sic proponunt: Si Forma esset accidens, nulla esset generatio substantialis; siquidem Materia signi non potest, inductio autem accidentium, non substantialis; sed accidentaria generatio est. & totidem ferè verbis Pererius: Si nulla est Forma substantialis, nulla item est generatio: etenim nec generatur Materia, nec productio accidentium est generatio, sed alteratio. Ad quod nos respondemus, nullam (ordinariâ viâ, creatione sepositâ) dari Substantialem Mutationem seu Generationem, ita accipiendo hanc vocem, quomodo ipsi accipiunt, ut nimirùm Substantialis Mutatio seu Generatio sit illa, qua ipsius substantiæ, quæ generatur, aliqua pars substantialis de novo fit, quum non existeret prius. in quo sanè nulla est absurditas; neq; afferri quicquam potest, cur ad substantiæ generationem magis necessarium sit, ut aliqua ipsius pars, quam ut tota ex nihilo fiat. Hoc autem posterius, fatentibus Peripateticis, adeò non est necessarium, ut ne fieri quidem possit.
units.tr: The second argument of this place, which Fonseca uses to prove substantial form, is generation and corruption, which he says would not exist unless substantial forms were given. The Conimbricenses set this out more explicitly thus: "If form were an accident, there would be no substantial generation; for matter cannot be generated, and the induction of accidents is not substantial but accidental generation." And Pererius, in almost the same words: "If there is no substantial form, there is likewise no generation: for matter is not generated, nor is the production of accidents generation, but alteration." To this we reply that no substantial change or generation is given in the ordinary way (creation set aside), taking this word as they themselves take it, namely that substantial generation is that by which some substantial part of the substance being generated comes newly into being, when it did not exist before. In this there is certainly no absurdity; nor can anything be brought forward to show why it should be more necessary for the generation of a substance that some part of it be made, than that the whole be made from nothing. The latter, as the Peripatetics themselves admit, is so far from necessary that it cannot even come about
1. Physic. 9. quæst. 9. art. 2.
6. Phys. 2.
Chapter I.

units.la: fit nisi divina virtute, ac propterea in generationibus ordinariis locum habere non queat. Et quum ipsi Peripatetici sint monstri instar exibilaturi, si quis affirmet substantiales generationes ordinario modo fieri ita, ut Materia ipsarum non assumatur praexistens, sed tum demum de novo fiat; nimis certè audaces sunt, qui ut substantiarum, generatio non accidentalis sit, sed substantialis, necessarium esse dicunt, ut altera ipsarum pars, longè illa ac longè nobilior quam Materia (ut quidem ipsi praedicant) tunc demum fiat, atq; initium sui accipiat. Quanquam autem substantialis generatio, hoc quidem sensu, nulla datur, omnésque substantiae, ordinariâ viâ, novorum accidentium introductione fiant, propterea tamen non sequitur (id quod temere inde conantur inferre Peripatetici) substantiarum generationem tolli. Aliud enim est, substantias generari; aliud, generari ita, ut aliqua ipsarum pars substantialis non praeexstiterit. Sanè ejusmodi substantia, quae maximè essentialiter & sui ipsius ratione ab omni alia substantia differat (quomodo nimirum Elementa, seu corpora simplicia, differunt inter se) ex alia substantia fieri nequit; ac proinde aliter generari non potest, nisi generatione substantiali, qua videlicet substantiae è nihilo producuntur. Ad generationem autem earum substantiarum, quae solis accidentibus differunt ab aliis substantijs, sufficit, ut ea accidentia, in quibus ipsorum natura consistit, in Materiam praexistentem introducantur: quae accidentium introductio sicuti est accidentalis mutatio, respectu substantiae, in qua fit; ita est Generatio, respectu substantiae, quae ex praeexistente substantia sic immutata consurgit. Quod igitur illi aiunt, Sublatis Formis substantialibus, generationem nullam fore, quia accidentium introductio non fit Generatio, sed accidentalis mutatio; in eo nihil aliud quam suam ipsorum insciitiam produnt: quum ipsa Mutatio accidentaria, fit substantiae generatio, quia nova substantia, seu novum individuum substantiale, per eam constituitur.
units.tr: except by divine power, and therefore cannot take place in ordinary generations. And since the Peripatetics themselves would hiss as monsters anyone who affirmed that substantial generations occur in the ordinary way, so that their matter is not taken as pre-existing but only then first comes into being, they are very bold who say that for the generation of substances to be substantial rather than accidental, another part of them, far more noble than matter (as they themselves claim), must then first come to be and receive its beginning. Although, in this sense, no substantial generation is given, and all substances in the ordinary way come about through the introduction of new accidents, it does not follow (as the Peripatetics rashly try to infer) that the generation of substances is abolished. For it is one thing for substances to be generated; it is another to be generated in such a way that some substantial part of them did not pre-exist. Certainly a substance which differs from every other substance most essentially and by its own nature (as the elements, or simple bodies, differ from one another) cannot be made from another substance; and therefore it cannot be generated otherwise than by substantial generation, by which substances are produced from nothing. For the generation of those substances which differ from other substances only in accidents, it is enough that those accidents, in which their nature consists, be introduced into pre-existing matter. This introduction of accidents, as it is an accidental change with respect to the substance in which it occurs, so it is generation with respect to the substance which arises from the pre-existing substance thus changed. Therefore, when they say that with substantial forms removed there will be no generation, because the introduction of accidents is not generation but accidental change, in this they betray nothing but their own ignorance, since accidental change itself becomes the generation of a substance, because a new substance, or a new substantial individual, is constituted through it.

units.la: XIII. Tertium hujus loci argumentum ab operationibus
units.tr: XIII. The third argument of this place, from operations

units.la: bus & facultatibus agendi Fonseca depromit. & à Conimbricensibus idem hoc sic proponitur : Singulis rebus naturalibus aliqua propria & peculiares functiones conveniunt, ut homini ratiocinari, equo hinnire, igni calefacere: atq; ita cateris. sed ejusmodi functiones oriri nequeunt ab esse Materia, quae nullam effectricem vim habet: oriuntur ergo à substantiali Forma. & ita Averroes quoque multis in locis scribit, Formae indicium ab operationibus desumi. Animadvertendum autem hic est, receptum illud axioma, quod Materiae omnem denegat activitatem (hausum ab ipso Aristotele, qui 1. de Gener. & Corr. 7. ait, ἡ μὲν ὕλη ἡ ὕλη, πάσχειν: Materia, quatenus Materia, passibilis est, & 2. de Gener. & Corr. 9. τῆς ὕλης τὸ πάσχειν ἐστὶ καὶ τὸ κινεῖσθαι: Materia est, pati, & moveri: qualia etiam alibi habet) non esse universim verum; quum ipsa etiam Materia qualdam per se operationes edat: qua de re alias dicetur. Ut vero nunc hoc omittamus, & quod illi de omni actione dicunt, de ijs tantum actionibus, quae non à Materia fiunt (quarum sane numerus est longè maximus) intelligamus: gratis asseritur, quia operationes non proficiscantur ab ipsa Materia, propterea dandam esse Formam substantialem. non enim istuc inde sequitur, sed hoc duntaxat, Dari igitur in rebus aliquid praeter ipsam Materiam, quod sit Principium effectivum istarum operationum. Haec sane consequentia evidens est. Sed quod illud agendi Principium debeat esse substantia, non accidens; haudquaquam apparet. Et sane mirum est, quomodo per operationes Formam demonstrare instituant Peripatetici, quum ipsi omnes actiones acceptas referant Qualitatibus, videlicet facultatibus agendi; quod acceperunt à praeceptore suo, cujus sententia est, monente Julio Scaligero, Nullam esse actionem Substantiarum sine qualitatibus: id quod aperte ipse tradidit in tractatu de sensu & sensilibus, aiens, Nec aquam, nec ignem, nec ullam aliam rem agere quicquam, nisi quatenus certas obtinent qualitates. ἢ μὲν οὖν πῦρ, ὁμοί ἢ γῆ, ὅλλεν πέφυκε ποιεῖν, ἢ πάσχειν, ὅλ' ἄλ-λο ὅλλην ἢ δ' ὑπάρχει ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐναντιότης, ταύτῃ πάντα ποισι
units.tr: Fonseca draws out a third argument from the operations and powers of acting, and the Conimbricenses propose the same point in this way: To each natural thing belong some proper and peculiar functions: to man to reason, to a horse to neigh, to fire to heat, and so on for the rest. But such functions cannot arise from matter, which has no effective power; they therefore arise from the substantial form. Averroes too writes in many places that the form is inferred from operations. Here, however, it must be noted that the accepted axiom which denies all activity to matter is not universally true. It is taken from Aristotle himself, who says in On Generation and Corruption 1.7, "matter, as matter, is passive" [ἡ μὲν ὕλη ἡ ὕλη, πάσχειν], and in On Generation and Corruption 2.9, "it belongs to matter to be acted upon and to be moved" [τῆς ὕλης τὸ πάσχειν ἐστὶ καὶ τὸ κινεῖσθαι], and he has similar statements elsewhere. Matter itself produces certain operations of its own, and I shall speak of this elsewhere. But let us set that aside for now, and let us understand what they say about every action only of those actions which do not come from matter (and these are certainly by far the greater number). It is groundless to assert that, because operations do not proceed from matter itself, a substantial form must therefore be posited. For this does not follow; what follows is only this: there is therefore something in things besides matter itself which is the effective principle of these operations. This consequence is certainly evident. But that this principle of acting must be a substance and not an accident does not appear at all. And indeed it is strange how the Peripatetics undertake to prove the form through operations, when they all refer actions to qualities, that is, to powers of acting. They received this from their teacher, whose view, as Julius Scaliger warns, is that there is no action of substances without qualities. He plainly taught this in his treatise on sense and sensibles, saying that neither water, nor fire, nor any other thing does anything except insofar as it possesses certain qualities. [ἢ μὲν οὖν πῦρ, ὁμοίως ἢ γῆ, ὅλλεν πέφυκε ποιεῖν, ἢ πάσχειν, ὅλ' ἄλλο ὅλλην· ἢ δ' ὑπάρχει ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐναντιότης, ταύτῃ πάντα ποιεῖ]
Chapter I.

units.la: πoιεῖσι κ.τ.λ. : Ignis quatenus est ignis, & terra quatenus est terra, nihil valet efficere, aut pati; uti neq; alia res ulla. quatenus autem inest iis contrarietas [id est, quatenus iis insunt contrariae qualitates] eatenus omnia agunt & patiuntur. Et in eandem sententiam Conimbricenses aiunt, Nullam Substantiam creatam esse immediatum agendi Principium, aut sine instrumentaria accidentium ope operari. ac Fonseca quoque, Nullam substantiam esse activam, nisi per aliquam potentiam activam; quae potentia activa in creaturis sint qualitates accidentariae. & rursus ibidem, Omnem substantiam creatam, & activam, per qualitatem accidentariam agere, quicquid agit. Estque recepta haec inter Peripateticos opinio, cui nemo ipsorum contradicit, nisi quantum ad ipsam Formarum productionem, in qua Scotus, cum suis sectatoribus, nullum Accidentibus locum relinquit, volens eam ab ipsis Formis peragi: in qua tamen re dissentit ab ipso maxima pars Peripateticorum, qui hic quoque Accidentium operam adhibent. Sed hoc quidem ipsis inter se decidendum relinquimus, neque de hoc actionum genere quicquam praeterea dicere volumus, quum nullas censeamus dari Formas, ac propterea neque Formarum productionem. Quum autem in iis actionibus, quae non fictitiae (ut ista productio Formarum) sed verae sunt actiones, omnes in universum consentiant Peripatetici, eas ab accidentibus seu qualitatibus fieri; mirari profecto licet, ut dicebamus, quomodo ab operationibus petant Formarum substantialium confirmationem. Fateri enim, operationem omnem ab Accidentibus edi, ac qualitates activas esse omnium functionum effectrices; & tamen arguere, quod actiones indicent esse in compositis Formam quandam substantialem, a qua ipsae edantur; hominum est valde sutiliter ratiocinantium. nullo enim modo haec cohaerent, Actiones fiunt a qualitatibus; ergo propter actiones opus est in compositis ponere Formam substantialem. imo prior positio potius destruit secundam, ut quoniam operationes ab activis qualitatibus peraguntur, superfluum sit, aliud effectivum earum
units.tr: Poiousi [ποιεῖσι] and so on: Fire, insofar as it is fire, and earth, insofar as it is earth, can effect or undergo nothing, and neither can any other thing. But insofar as contrariety inheres in them, that is, insofar as contrary qualities inhere in them, they act and are acted upon in all respects. To the same effect the Conimbricenses say: No created substance is an immediate principle of action, nor does it operate without the instrumental aid of accidents. Fonseca too says: No substance is active except through some active power, and in creatures this active power is accidental qualities. And again in the same place: Every created substance that is active acts through an accidental quality, whatever it does. This is the opinion received among the Peripatetics, and none of them contradicts it, except as regards the production of forms themselves. Here Scotus and his followers leave no place for accidents, wishing that production to be carried out by the forms alone. Yet on this point the greater part of the Peripatetics dissent from him, since they here too call in the help of accidents. But we leave this question for them to settle among themselves, and we do not wish to say anything further about this kind of action, since we hold that no forms exist, and therefore neither is there any production of forms. Since, however, all the Peripatetics agree in general that in those actions which are not fictitious (such as this production of forms) but are true actions, these are performed by accidents or qualities, one may indeed well wonder, as we said, how they seek from operations the confirmation of substantial forms. For to admit that every operation is performed by accidents, and that active qualities are the effecters of all functions, and yet to argue that the actions show that a certain substantial form is in composites, from which the actions themselves proceed, is the mark of men who reason very subtly. For these claims do not hang together: actions are performed by qualities; therefore, on account of actions, it is necessary to posit a substantial form in composites. Indeed the former assertion rather destroys the latter: since operations are carried out by active qualities, it is superfluous to seek or to posit another principle of them, an effective one, in substances.

units.la: 2 Phys. 7. qu. 18. art. 2. — Metaph. 2. qu. 6. sect. 3. — 5. Metaph. 2. qu. 6. sect. 3. carum Principium in substantijs quærere, aut ponere: quare etiam Alexander ad illa Aristotelis verba, paulo ante allata, diserte notat, eo, quod actio tribuitur Qualitatibus, Formam ab agendo excludi, dicens, ignem non edere actionem, quatenus ignis, sed quatenus calidus est, id est, non per Formam ignis, sed per calorem.
units.tr: 2 Phys. 7. qu. 18. art. 2. — Metaph. 2. qu. 6. sect. 3. — 5. Metaph. 2. qu. 6. sect. 3. Hence Alexander, on those words of Aristotle quoted a little earlier, expressly notes that because the action is attributed to the qualities, the form is excluded from acting, saying: fire does not produce the action insofar as it is fire, but insofar as it is hot, that is, not through the form of fire but through heat.
XIV.

units.la: Non ignoramus quidem, quo hic effugio utantur, dicentes nimirum, quanquam actiones fiant à qualitatibus, qualitates tamen in operando non esse agentia primaria, sed instrumenta Formarum, quæ Formæ ipsæ sint Principales Actrices, quum Accidentia in ipsarum virtute (ita loqui solent) operentur. Sed hoc figmentum est inane, uti planissimè apparebit, sive rationes spectes, quibus illud confirmare tendunt, sive rem ipsam consideres. Rationes à Fonseca duæ afferuntur. prima est, Accidentia habent esse suum à substantijs, ergo & agendi vim, quæ eorum entitatem sequitur. non sunt igitur prima activa, sed ipsæ Formæ substantiales. altera, Actiones sunt singularium subsistentium: singularia autem subsistentia sunt substantiæ: proficiscuntur ergo actiones effectivè à substantijs: at non ratione Materiæ, quæ nullo modo activa, sed receptiva est: igitur ratione Formæ: est igitur Forma substantialis Principium, quo res naturales agunt. Eædem rationes verbis paulo alijs sic à Conimbricensibus proponuntur: Agere, una de præcipuis est rerum naturalium affectionibus, adeo ut communi Philosophorum assensu dixerit Aristoteles, Unum quodq; suæ operationis causam esse. Par est igitur, ac naturæ ordini consentaneum, ut actio in ipsa rerum substantia causam habeat, à qua dimanet: hæc autem substantia non potest esse Materia, quæ nullam effectricem vim possidet: est igitur Forma 2. Actio sequitur esse: ergo idem erit primarium essendi & agendi Principium. Sed Forma substantialis est primarium ac principale Principium essendi, unde ab Aristotele dicitur ratio ipsa quiddicitatis. erit igitur prima origo, & quasi fons, è quo rei naturalis actio proficiscatur. His utriq; adjungunt testimonia
units.tr: We are not unaware of the escape to which they resort here, namely that although actions are performed by qualities, the qualities are not the primary agents in operating, but the instruments of the forms, and that the forms themselves are the principal agents, since the accidents operate by the power of these forms (so they are wont to speak). But this fiction is empty, as will plainly appear, whether you look at the arguments by which they try to confirm it or at the thing itself. Fonseca offers two arguments. The first is: Accidents have their being from substances, therefore also their power of acting, which follows their entity. They are therefore not the first active things, but the substantial forms themselves. The second: Actions belong to individual subsistent things, and individual subsistent things are substances. Actions therefore proceed effectively from substances; but not by reason of matter, which is in no way active but receptive; therefore by reason of form. Therefore the substantial form is the principle by which natural things act. The Conimbricenses set out the same arguments in slightly different words: Acting is one of the chief affections of natural things, so much so that by the common assent of philosophers Aristotle said that each thing is the cause of its own operation. It is fitting, and consonant with the order of nature, that the action should have its cause in the very substance of the thing, from which it flows; but this substance cannot be matter, which possesses no effective power; therefore it is form. Action follows being; therefore the primary principle of being and of acting will be the same. But the substantial form is the primary and principal principle of being, whence Aristotle calls it the very reason of what a thing is. It will therefore be the first origin, and as it were the fountain, from which the action of a natural thing proceeds. Both sides add to these the testimonies
5. Metaph. 2. quæst. 6. sect. 2.

units.la: 2. Phys.7. quæ. 18. art.2. nia Aristotelis, qui varijs in locis Formæ substantiali difertis verbis efficientiam attribuerit. Sed quid ille dixerit, nos quidem non moramur; néque in ulla re controversa curamus ipsius autoritatem. Ipsæ autem rationes sunt perquàm futiles. quod enim dicitur, actiones debere esse à Forma, quia actiones sint singularium subsistentium; eo nihil vanius cogitari potest. quippe ex eo, quòd unaquæq; substantia est causa suarum actionum (quod sanè verum est, & apertissimum) non sequitur, quòd aut se totâ, aut substantiali sui parte debeat eam causalitatem (ut sic dicamus) exercere. namq; etiam illa est substantiæ, seu singularis subsistentis actio, quam per aliquod accidens sibi na-turaliter inhærens exercet: & quum omnis substantia sit ex Materia & accidentibus composita, accidentia non minus ad ipsius integritatem pertinent (præsertim in corpo-ribus non primis, sed quæ ex primis sive Elementis conflata sunt) quam ipsa pars Materialis. & etiamsi non pertinerent, nihilominus tamen rectè dicatur efficere, quod à qualicunque ipsius accidente efficitur; quanquam non eo modo, quo ipsum accidens. Etenim actionum, quæ ab accidentibus eduntur, ipsa Accidentia sunt Causa per se: substantiæ autem, quibus ipsa inhærent, sunt earundem Causa secundum quid. quod & in actionibus, quæ à Materia fiunt, locum obtinet. namq; & harum actionum ipsa Materia est Causa per se; totum verò compositum, non aliter quam secundum quid: sicuti hæc libro quarto, ubi de Divisionibus Efficientium, latius explicabuntur. Ita igitur patet, quomodo Substantiæ sint Causæ earum actionum, quæ per qualitates ipsis inhærentes eduntur. quod si quis his non contentus, pertendat substantias debere esse suarum actionum Causas ea ipsa sui parte, quæ est substantialis; rationes dictæ sui afferat prius, quàm expectet, ut fidem ipsi adhibeamus. Altera verò ratio, mera est Principij petitio, adversus eos, qui ipsas Formas negant, uti nos facimus, ac propterea nullius prorsus momenti, aut pluribus verbis impugnanda. eo ipso enim, quod Formam negamus, negamus etiam, quidquid de Forma prædicant aut fingunt Peripatetici. Sed præterea hæc ratio, quomodo à Fonseca proponitur, adeo est ficulnea, ut nullam omnino vim habeat, etiamsi supponatur dari Formas. Etenim nemo Peripateticus unquam dixit, Formam esse accidentium ipsam comitantium efficientem aliter, nisi per emanationem; quam nequaquam esse veram ac propriam efficientiam, sed remotam ac radicalem, (uti loqui amant) confitentur. & hoc ipsum multo adhuc clarius explicat ipse Fonseca. Iis enim, qui ad confirmationem certæ opinionis, inter Peripateticos controversæ, proponunt ut rem notam ac confessam, Formam substantialem cujusvis rei, esse Principium immediatè productivum illius passionum: respondet, Passionem propriam non effici à subjecto, sed ab eo agente, a quo subjectum efficitur; & qua actione ponitur subjectum in rerum natura, eadem consecutivè poni propriam ejus passionem. quare sibi ipsi contradicit Fonseca, asserens accidentia habere esse suum à substantijs sive Formis. ab eo enim res habet esse suum, à quo effecta est. accidentia autem à suorum suppositorum Formis effecta esse, Fonseca inficiatur.
