Imo si hoc quoque supponeretur, non modo dari Formas, sed & esse eas accidentium ipsas comitantium effectrices, & quidem veras & proprias; ne sic quidem sequeretur, Formas esse principalia agentia earum actionum, quę per qualitates ab ipsis productas efficiantur: nisi si omnes efficientes sunt Causæ principales operationum, quas edunt res ab ipsis effectæ; aut nisi (quod idem est) omnes res in omnibus suis actionibus non sunt aliud quam instrumenta earum rerum, à quibus ipsæ productæ fuerunt: id quod nemo dixerit, neq; ipse Fonseca concesserit: qua de re mox iterum dicetur.
units.tr: 2. Phys. 7. quæ. 18. art. 2. of Aristotle, who in various places expressly attributes efficiency to the substantial form. But what he said we do not dwell on, nor in any controverted matter do we regard his authority. The arguments themselves, however, are exceedingly flimsy. For as to what is said, that actions must be from the form because actions belong to individual subsistent things, nothing more vain can be thought. Indeed, from the fact that each substance is the cause of its own actions (which is certainly true and most obvious) it does not follow that it must exercise that causality (as we may call it) either with its whole self or with its substantial part. For that action also belongs to the substance, or individual subsistent thing, which it exercises through some accident naturally inhering in it. And since every substance is composed of matter and accidents, accidents pertain no less to its integrity (especially in bodies that are not primary but compounded out of the primary or elements) than the material part itself. And even if they did not pertain to it, it would nonetheless be rightly said to effect whatever is effected by any of its accidents, though not in the same way as the accident itself. For of the actions that are performed by accidents, the accidents themselves are the cause per se, while the substances in which they inhere are their cause secundum quid. This also holds in the actions that are performed by matter: for of these actions matter itself is the cause per se, while the whole compound is only secundum quid, as will be explained more fully in the fourth book, where the divisions of efficient causes are treated. Thus it is clear how substances are causes of those actions which are performed through the qualities inhering in them. But if anyone, not content with this, insists that substances must be the causes of their actions by that very part of themselves which is substantial, let him first set out his arguments, before he expects us to give him credence. The other argument, however, is a mere begging of the question, against those who deny the forms themselves, as we do; and therefore it is of no weight at all and need not be attacked at length. For by the very fact that we deny the form, we also deny whatever the Peripatetics assert or imagine about the form. Moreover, this argument, as Fonseca puts it, is so fig-leaf-thin that it has no force at all, even if it be supposed that forms exist. For no Peripatetic has ever said that the form is the efficient of the accompanying accidents in any way other than by emanation; and they confess that this is by no means a true and proper efficiency, but a remote and radical one, as they like to put it. Fonseca himself explains this much more clearly still. To those who, to confirm a certain opinion disputed among the Peripatetics, propose as a known and admitted fact that the substantial form of any thing is the immediate productive principle of its passions, he replies: A proper passion is not effected by the subject, but by that agent by which the subject is effected; and by the same action by which the subject is placed in the nature of things, its proper passion is consecutively placed too. Therefore Fonseca contradicts himself, asserting that accidents have their being from substances or forms. For a thing has its being from that by which it has been effected. But Fonseca denies that accidents have been effected by the forms of their subjects. Indeed, even if this too were supposed, namely that forms exist and that they are true and proper effecters of the accompanying accidents, not even so would it follow that forms are the principal agents of those actions which are effected through the qualities produced by them; unless indeed all efficients are the principal causes of the operations which the things effected by them perform, or unless (which is the same thing) all things in all their actions are nothing other than the instruments of those things by which they were produced. Nobody would say this, and Fonseca himself would not have conceded it; on this point we shall speak again shortly.
XV.

units.la: Et ita quidem apparet, nihili esse eas rationes, quæ adhibentur ad probandum, quod Formę debeant esse Principalia agentia earum actionum, quæ à qualitatibus activis eduntur. Sed rem quoque ipsam, per se consideratam, esse valde absurdam, adeo quidem, ut repudianda sit, etiamsi darentur Formæ substantiales; facilè monstrari potest. Notandum verò prius est, phrasin illam, qua accidentia dicunt operari in virtute substantiæ, duplicem habere apud ipsos explicationem; vel quod à substantijs sive Formis ad accidentia derivetur virtus quædam, per quam ipsa operentur: vel duntaxat, quod accidentia sint virtus instrumentaria Formarum principaliter operantium. Prius quidem, licet à multis Thomistis dicatur, non tamen ab ijs dicitur respectu omnium actionum, sed tantummodo respectu generationis substantiæ, seu productionis Formæ; in qua tamen productione multi de ipsis Thomistis hunc agendi modum rejiciunt; & hic quoque, accidentia operari in virtute substantia, non aliud esse dicunt, nisi quod substantijs inserviant pro instrumentis. Quum igitur prior modus neq; pertineat, ad eas actiones, de quibus nos hic agimus, scilicet productiones accidentium, & non modo ab alijs Peripateticis, sed à plurimis ipsorum Thomistarum (in qua tamen secta natum ac educatum est hoc figmentum) pro improbo ac ridiculo explodatur: isto omisso, de altero tantum modo tractabimus, quo per illa verba, quod nimirum Accidentia agant in virtute substantiæ, intelligitur, quod sint Formarum principaliter operantium instrumenta. Nolumus nunc verbosè explicare, quid sit Agens Principale, aut Instrumentarium; aut in quo ipsorum ratio consistat: quia alius & oportunior dabitur prolixius de hoc agendi locus. Breviter tantum dicimus; nullum Agens subire instrumenti rationem, nisi quatenus ab alio ad agendum cietur: id quod tribus modis fieri potest, imperio vel hortatu, tacito instinctu, applicatione. primus modus locum non habet, nisi respectu agentium proæreticorum, idq; inter diversa supposita. quod enim aliquem imperare sibi ipsi, & cohortari seipsum dicimus, in eo vulgari magis loquendi usui, quam philosophicæ accurationi nos accommodamus. & si vel maxime concederemus, unam animæ facultatem in alteram habere aliquod imperandi aut hortandi jus; nemo tamen ausit asserere, ipsam animæ substantiam in facultates suas exercere aliquam. quam jussionis aut exhortationis speciem. In ijs autem Agentibus, quæ non sunt Agentia libera, sed Necessaria (ut vocari solent) nullus locus est huic modo, uti per se liquet; neque eorum qualitates activæ possunt dici Formarum instrumenta ea ratione, quod ipsarum jussu aut hortatu operentur. Sed neq; secundus modus, nimirum instinctus, horum respectu admitti potest: quandoquidem instinctus, ille saltem, de quo nos loquimur (qui est latens quædam impulsio ad agendum) spectat solummodo ad viventia, neq; viventia omnia, sed animalia duntaxat. in ijs autem, sicuti intellectu facile est, quomodo & ipsa ab aliqua vi superiore, ut Deo vel Angelis; & nonnullæ ipsorum facultates animales una ab altera hoc modo cieantur; sita imaginari difficile est, quomodo ipsa animæ substantia facultates suas ad istum modum impellere possit. De tertio autem modo, qui est applicatio, quiq; fit duobus modis (vel admovendo agens ad patiens, vel patiens ad agens) evidentissimum est, quod per eum Formæ nequeant esse Agens primarium respectu qualitatum activarum; quippe quę neq; patiens qualitatibus, neq; qualitates patienti admovere valent. Quum igitur neq; Anima (quam illi pro Forma habent) neq; aliæ Formæ (si darentur) fingi queant ullo istorum trium modorum facultates suas ciere ad agendum, neq; ullus alius ciendi modus detur, & omnino sit de Ratione Causæ primariæ, ut Causam eam, quæ ipsius instrumentum dicitur, ad agendum cieat; apparet vanum esse illud commentum (etiam suppositis Formis substantialibus) quod Qualitates activas dicit esse Formarum instrumenta in actionibus suis obeundis.
units.tr: And so it appears that the arguments used to prove that forms must be the principal agents of the actions produced by active qualities are worthless. But the matter itself, considered in its own right, is also very absurd, so much so that it must be rejected even if substantial forms were granted. This can easily be shown. First, it must be noted that the phrase by which they say that accidents act in virtue of the substance has two explanations among them: either a certain power is derived from substances or forms to the accidents, by which the accidents act, or merely that the accidents are instruments of the forms that act principally. The first explanation, although many Thomists give it, is not given with respect to all actions, but only with respect to the generation of a substance, or the production of a form. Yet even in this production many of the Thomists themselves reject this mode of acting, and here too they say that accidents act in virtue of the substance means nothing other than that they serve the substances as instruments. Since the first mode does not pertain to those actions with which we are dealing here, namely the productions of accidents, and since it is rejected as improper and ridiculous not only by other Peripatetics but by most of the Thomists themselves (although this fiction was born and bred in their school), we will set it aside and treat only the other mode, by which those words, that accidents act in virtue of the substance, are understood to mean that they are the instruments of the forms that act principally. We do not wish to explain at length now what a principal agent is, or an instrumental one, or what their nature consists in, because a fuller opportunity for this will be given elsewhere. We say only briefly that no agent takes on the character of an instrument unless it is moved to act by another. This can happen in three ways: by command or exhortation, by tacit impulse, or by application. The first mode has no place except with respect to voluntary agents, and even then between different subjects. For when we say that someone commands himself or exhorts himself, we are accommodating ourselves to the more common usage of speech rather than to philosophical precision. And even if we granted that one faculty of the soul has some right to command or exhort another, no one would dare to assert that the substance of the soul itself exercises its faculties by any kind of command or exhortation. In those agents which are not free but necessary (as they are usually called), there is no place for this mode, as is plain in itself; nor can their active qualities be called instruments of the forms on the ground that they act at their command or exhortation. But neither can the second mode, namely impulse, be admitted with respect to these agents, since impulse, at least that of which we speak (a hidden urging to act), pertains only to living things, and not to all living things but to animals alone. In animals, as can easily be understood, both are moved by some higher power, such as God or the angels, and some of their animal faculties are moved in this way by one another; but it is hard to imagine how the substance of the soul itself could drive its faculties in this manner. As for the third mode, which is application, and which happens in two ways (either by bringing the agent to the patient or the patient to the agent), it is most evident that through it forms could not be the primary agent with respect to active qualities, since they can bring neither the patient to the qualities nor the qualities to the patient. Since, therefore, neither the soul (which they hold to be a form) nor other forms (if there were any) can be imagined to move their faculties to act by any of these three modes, and no other mode of moving is given, and since it is altogether of the nature of a primary cause to move to action the cause which is said to be its instrument, it appears that this fiction (even granting substantial forms) that active qualities are the instruments of forms in performing their actions is empty.

units.la: XVI. Et hoc ipsum amplius etiamnum demonstratur ijs exemplis, in quibus ita agunt Qualitates, ut fingi non possit, Formam cum ijs ad agendum concurrere.
units.tr: XVI. This very point is demonstrated still further by those examples in which qualities act in such a way that it cannot be imagined that a form concurs with them in acting.

units.la: Etenim ipsi illi, qui dicunt Qualitates esse instrumenta Formarum, fatentur, non omnia accidentia a Forma subjecti, cui insunt, dirigi ad agendum, sed naturalia tantum, seu quæ rei secundum naturam suam habenti insunt. ast calor in aqua
units.tr: For indeed those very people who say that qualities are the instruments of forms admit that not all accidents are directed to acting by the form of the subject in which they inhere, but only the natural ones, that is, those which inhere in a thing according to its nature. But heat in water

units.la: fervida, ferro candenti, & similibus, non calefacit tantum, sed & urit, nequaquam à Forma ferri aut aquæ adjutus. Formæ enim illæ sunt quam maximè alienæ à calore, istarum actionum auctore, utpote contrariæ qualitatis, nimirum frigoris, conciliatrices subjectis suis, ex recepto inter omnes Peripateticos axiomate, quo propria cujusq; rei accidentia Formam sequi, atq; ab ea fluere dicuntur. Non possunt igitur Formæ, quæ naturaliter frigus trahunt comitem, & proinde calori sunt inimicæ, concurrere cum calore, ad actionem ullam edendam. Et cum in hujusmodi subjectis calor suo marte ac proprijs viribus agat quodcunq; agit; non est cur dubitetur, quin & in proprio subjecto existens, totus suæ spontis sit in agendo, neq; Formæ concursu indigeat, merito autem ad alias quoque omnes Qualitates activas id transferatur, quod de calore est manifestum.
units.tr: that is boiling, in red-hot iron, and in similar things, not only warms but also burns, by no means aided by the form of the iron or of the water. For those forms are most opposed to heat, the author of these actions, being as they are of a contrary quality, namely cold, and conciliators of their subjects, according to the axiom accepted by all Peripatetics, by which the proper accidents of each thing are said to follow and flow from its form. Therefore forms which naturally bring cold as their companion, and so are hostile to heat, cannot concur with heat in performing any action. And since in such subjects heat acts by its own force and its own powers in whatever it does, there is no reason to doubt that heat, even when existing in its own subject, is wholly self-moving in acting and needs no concurrence of the form. And this rightly applies to all the other active qualities as well, as is clear in the case of heat.

units.la: Reluctantur quidem illi, qui hanc de instrumentaria Qualitatum operatione sententiam fovent: & quanquam negare non audent, quod illa Accidentia, quæ insunt in tali subjecto, cujus Forma ijs penitus adversetur, nequaquam dici possint per concursum istius Formæ operari; aliquid tamen comminiscuntur, quo se extricent ex hisce angustijs. Sed incassum se fatigant, magnisq; se induunt absurditatibus, dum nituntur istam objectionem solvere. Mirabili enim audacia, quam opem invenire non possunt in Forma ejus subjecti, cui calor inest, eum petunt à Forma istius suppositi, à quo calor ille in aquam est introductus. quippe aiunt Conimbricenses, calorem aquæ calida ita calefacere, ut non propriâ, sed ignis virtute agat. Formam enim substantialem ignis esse principale Principium activum, à quo in aquam calor defluxit, quodq; in eo calore, ut in sua virtute operatur. deniq; ipsum ignem esse præcipuum agens, qui mediate mediatione suppositi, sed immediatione virtutis, eam calefactionem exhibet. Et non Conimbricenses tantum, sed multi quoque alij Peripatetici hanc fovent absurditatem, unde etiam nata inter illos est illa instrumenti divisio in conjunctum & separatum, quam ita inter alios explicat Toletus, ut dicat, Instrumentum conjunctum esse, quod moveri non potest, nisi altu moveatur à principali agente, ut calamus ad scribendum, calor ignis ad calefaciendum. Separatum verò, quod quamvis alterius operatur virtute, tamen potest absq; illius præsentia operari, ut virtus seminis productiva, ut calor in aquâ ab igne productus, qui & ab igne separatus calefacit, & hujusmodi alia. Ad hunc autem de instrumento separato errorem (uti ad alios plerosque) præivit ijs ipse Aristoteles, cujus hoc est commentum, semen animalium & plantarum, esse parentum instrumentum, uti apparet è secundi de Generatione animalium primo; idq; adeò receptum est in Peripato, ut vix invenias in ea, qui dubitet, quin semen sit ac rite dicatur Instrumentum generantis. Si autem hoc verum est, omnino statuenda sunt instrumenta separata, quomodo ipsi ea statuunt; neq; pejori jure calor in aqua productus dicatur instrumentum ignis, qui eum produxit, quam virtus seminis, instrumentum genitoris. Sed nos totum hoc de instrumento separato negotium, quomodo ab ipsis explicatur, pro figmento mero habemus.
units.tr: Indeed those who cherish this opinion, that qualities operate as instruments, resist; and although they do not dare to deny that those accidents which inhere in a subject whose form is wholly opposed to them cannot be said to act through the concurrence of that form, they devise something by which to extricate themselves from these straits. But they wear themselves out in vain, and they embrace great absurdities while they strive to resolve this objection. For with remarkable boldness, having failed to find help in the form of the subject in which the heat inheres, they seek it from the form of that compound from which the heat was introduced into the water. For the Conimbricenses say, that the heat of hot water warms not by its own power but by the power of fire. For the substantial form of fire is the principal active principle, from which heat flows into the water, and it acts in that heat as in its own power. Finally, the fire itself is the chief agent, which exhibits that warming mediately through the compound, but immediately through its power. And not only the Conimbricenses but many other Peripatetics also cherish this absurdity, and from it arose among them that division of instrument into conjoined and separated, which Toletus explains as follows, saying: A conjoined instrument is one which cannot be moved unless it is moved at the same time by the principal agent, as a pen for writing, or the heat of fire for warming. A separated instrument, on the other hand, is one which, although it operates by the power of another, can nevertheless act without that other's presence, such as the productive power of seed, or heat produced in water by fire, which, when separated from the fire, still warms, and others of this kind. But Aristotle himself, whose invention this is, led the way into this error about the separated instrument (as into many others), by asserting that the seed of animals and plants is the instrument of the parents, as appears from the first chapter of the second book of the work On the Generation of Animals. And this has been so widely received among the Peripatetics that you will scarcely find anyone among them who doubts that seed is rightly called the instrument of the one who generates. But if this is true, then separated instruments must be posited altogether, just as they posit them; and heat produced in water is no less justly called an instrument of the fire that produced it than the power of seed is called an instrument of the parent. But we hold this whole matter of the separated instrument, as they explain it, to be a pure fiction.

units.la: Nolumus de nomine ipso pugnare, neq; cum eo litigabimus, qui voluerit instrumenta quædam appellare separata. Quum enim instrumentorum alia sint proæretica, alia alterius naturæ; proæretica, quæ jussu, aliove consimili modo diriguntur, possunt separatorum appellatione donari, ad distinctionem eorum, quæ per appellationem diriguntur. quanquam sanè neq; omnia non proæretica instrumenta ita applicantur à primario agente, ut ipsa moveantur; sed sæpe contingit, ut ipsis manentibus quietis, ipsa res, in quam agere debent, ipsis applicetur ab agente principali; quæ res infra accuratius explicabitur. Quando autem aliqua istorum instrumentorum ita operantur, ut non ipsa ad patiens, sed patiens ad ipsa moveatur; tunc & ipsa poterunt quodammodo instrumentorum separatorum nomen sustinere, quippe quæ ab agente principali abjuncta sunt, neq; ullam habent cum eo connexionem. Hoc igitur modo explicata ista Instrumentorum divisio in conjuncta & separata, poterit tolerari;
units.tr: We do not wish to quarrel about the word itself, nor will we dispute with anyone who chooses to call certain instruments "separate." Since some instruments act by choice (proaeretic) and others by a different kind of nature, those that are directed by command or some similar manner may be given the name of separate instruments, to distinguish them from those that are directed by appointment. Yet in truth not all non-proaeretic instruments are so applied by the primary agent that they are themselves moved. Often it happens that, while they remain at rest, the thing on which they ought to act is applied to them by the principal agent; this will be explained more precisely below. When some of these instruments operate in such a way that they are not themselves moved toward the patient, but the patient is moved toward them, then they too may in some sense bear the name of separate instruments, since they are cut off from the principal agent and have no connection with it. Thus explained, this division of instruments into conjoined and separate may be tolerated.
Chapter I.

units.la: tolerari; quanquam sanè utilitatem sic quoque aut perexiguam habet, aut nullam. Quæ vero ipsi invehunt instrumenta separata, omnino sunt repudianda. Instrumento enim (quod nemo negaverit, nisi qui omnem loquendi legem velit pervertere) aliquod saltem debet cum eo, cujus instrumentum dicitur, intercedere commercium. ast hisce instrumentis separatis, quæ vocant, adeo nihil est negotij cum Causis illis primarijs, quas indigetant; ut nihil ipsorum interfit, etiamsi plane abolitæ sint, ac de rerum natura sublatæ; néque propterea quicquam in suo agendi modo sint mutaturæ: uti in exemplis supra allatis manifestum est. aqua enim fervens & ferrum candens nihilo secius calefacient, etiamsi ignis, à quo ipsa calorem acceperunt, sit exstinctus. Quodsi igitur aliquid dicere volunt, nihil ijs in promtu est, ob quod instrumenta separata à se vocata afficiant instrumentorum nomine, nisi quia ab ijs Causis, quibus ea dicunt inservire pro instrumentis, producta sunt. Sed hoc dicendo, in aliam rursus non parvam absurditatem devolvuntur. Namque si calor aquæ, verbi gratia, dicendus est instrumentum ignis, qui cum produxit, ob hoc ipsum quòd eum produxit; nihil obstat, quin eodem jure omnes qualitates activæ dicantur instrumenta eorum Efficientium, à quibus ipsæ productæ sunt. & sic ipsius quoque ignis calor non erit instrumentum istius ignis, à quo aqua calefacta est, sed alterius ignis, ejus nimirum, qui hunc ignem generavit. Par est enim utrobique ratio. Namq; etiamsi verum foret, calorem esse naturalem illi substantiæ, quæ cum accensa est, ignis dicitur; aquæ autem præter aut contra naturam (quod tamen dubitatione non caret, sicuti ex ijs, quæ de igne disputabuntur libro sequenti, apparebit) attamen ne sic quidem possent cùm ulla probabilitate invehere hoc discrimen, ut alias qualitates dicerent esse virtutes ipsarum substantiarum, in quibus insunt, alias verò substantiarum, à quibus productæ sunt: sed ad minimum eo redigentur, ut fateantur, in illis substantijs, ubi qualitates sunt præter naturam, illas esse instrumentum Efficientium duntaxat; in ijs verò
units.tr: …be tolerated, although indeed such a use has either very little value or none. The separate instruments they put forward are altogether to be rejected. For an instrument (which no one will deny, unless he wishes to overturn every rule of speech) must have some real connection with that of which it is called the instrument. But with these so-called separate instruments there is so little to do with those primary causes for which they are said to stand in, that it makes no difference to them whether those causes are wholly abolished and removed from nature; nor will they therefore change anything in their manner of acting. This is clear from the examples cited above: hot water and red-hot iron will heat just as well even if the fire from which they received their heat has been extinguished. If, then, they wish to say something, they have no ready answer as to why they should call separate instruments by the name of instruments, except that they were produced by those causes which they say they serve as instruments. But in saying this they fall back into another no small absurdity. For if the heat of water, for example, is to be called an instrument of the fire which produced it, simply because it produced it, nothing prevents the same reasoning from calling all active qualities instruments of the efficient causes by which they themselves were produced. And so the heat of the fire itself will not be an instrument of that fire by which the water was heated, but of another fire, namely of the one which generated this fire. For the reasoning is equal on both sides. Indeed, even if it were true that heat is natural to that substance which is said to be set on fire, and is contrary to or beyond the nature of water (which yet is not free from doubt, as will appear from what is discussed about fire in the following book), still they could not, even so, introduce this distinction with any probability, so as to say that some qualities are the virtues of the substances in which they inhere, and others of the substances by which they are produced. At the least they will be driven to confess that in those substances where qualities are beyond nature, these are merely the instrument of the efficient causes; but in those [substances]

units.la: { } Ignis minor secundo ... (marginal manuscript annotation, partly illegible) vero, ubi naturaliter insunt, eas quidem suarum Forma-rum, quas comitantur, instrumentum esse; sed tamen & illarum, à quibus procreatæ sunt. Si enim adversaria aquæ Forma, non potest arcere Formam ignis, quominus imperium exerceat in calorem ipsi introductum, multo minus id faciet illa Forma, quæ sociabiliter atq; amice cum Forma productrice conspirat. Ast hoc, quod omnes Qualitates activæ sint Instrumentum eorum Efficientium, à quibus in sua subjecta introductæ sunt, adeo est absurdum, ut neminem inter Peripateticos inventurus sis, qui id afferere audeat; etiamsi nonnulli eorum de Gravitate & Levitate (quæ non sunt quidem Qualitates Activæ, sed ab ijs pro talibus habentur) permiserunt sibi in tantum delirare, ut auderent statuere, gravitatem & levitatem, qua corpora naturaliter ferri dicunt in sua loca, esse quidem Efficiens proximum illius motus; principaliter tamen hunc motum generanti, qui Formam, & mediante illa gravitatem, à qua motus resultat, indidit, tribuendum esse; ita ut non moveant nisi ut instrumentum generantis, & vice ejus: sicuti hac de re scribit Suarezius, qui & ipse fovet hanc sententiam: sicuti neq; alienus est ab eo figmento, quod calor aquæ calefactæ sit instrumentum ignis qui eam calefecit, ut è sequente Paragrapho constat. Quod ipsi ac sociis ipsius tunc credemus, cum nobis ostenderint, qua ratione potius hæc qualitas activa debeat dici Instrumentum generantis, quam aliæ pleræq;, quarum actionem ipse negat, in eodem Paragrapho 27. posse generanti ascribi.
units.tr: Lesser fire, secondly ... (marginal manuscript annotation, partly illegible) ...where they naturally inhere, they are indeed the instrument of their forms, which they accompany; but nonetheless also of those things by which they were brought into being. For if the contrary form of water cannot restrain the form of fire from exercising its rule over the heat introduced into it, much less will that form do so which agrees sociably and amicably with the producing form. But that all active qualities should be the instrument of their efficient causes, by which they have been introduced into their subjects, is so absurd that you will find no one among the Peripatetics who would dare to assert it. Yet some of them, concerning heaviness and lightness (which are not indeed active qualities, but are held to be such by them), have permitted themselves to rave so far that they dared to maintain that heaviness and lightness, by which bodies are said naturally to be carried to their places, are indeed the proximate efficient of that motion; yet that this motion must chiefly be attributed to the one generating it, who imposed the form and, through it, the heaviness from which the motion results; so that they move only as the instrument of the generator and in his place. Suarez writes thus on this matter, and he himself favours this opinion; nor is he a stranger to that fiction that the heat of heated water is an instrument of the fire which heated it, as is clear from the following paragraph. We shall believe this him and his fellows when they have shown us by what reasoning this active quality ought rather to be called an instrument of the generator than the many others, the action of which he himself denies can be ascribed to the generator in the same paragraph, number 27.
XVII.

units.la: Atq; ex his omnibus satis apparet, positis etiam Formis, nihili esse ea, quæ dicuntur ad ostendendum, quod Qualitates non sint Primaria seu Principalia Agentia suarum operationum, sed instrumentaria. Et hoc adeo clarum est, ut propterea multi de ipsis Peripateticis figmentum illud de instrumentaria Qualitatum actione repudiarint. namq; ut vetustiores (quorum multi hoc fecerunt) omittam, Suarezius existimat, Multa accidentia sine concursu Formarum
units.tr: And from all these things it sufficiently appears, even granting the Forms, that what is said to show that the Qualities are not the primary or principal agents of their operations, but instrumental ones, is worth nothing. And this is so clear that, for this very reason, many of the Peripatetics themselves have rejected that fiction about the instrumental action of the Qualities. For, to pass over the older ones (of whom many did this), Suarez thinks that many accidents [act] without the concurrence of the Forms,
Disp. 18. sect. 7. §. 26.
Chapter I.

units.la: rum operari, & propria virtute; ac proinde esse principales suarum actionum Causas; uti ex Disputationis decimaoctavæ sectione quinta ac sexta apparet: & Pererius quoq; defendit, Formas nec mediate nec immediate operari, sed quicquid agant Accidentia, id ab ijs tanquam à Primarijs agentibus proficisci. Quandoquidem igitur omnium consensione Actiones eduntur ab Accidentibus; & illud quod de Formarum cum Accidentibus concursu ad operandum dicitur, figmentum merum esse deprehenditur, adeo quidem, ut à magna ipsorum Aristotelicorum parte repudietur: valde futilis est argumentatio, quæ adhibetur ad probandam ex Actionibus Formam Substantialem, quare etiam Suarezius, dum hunc pro Forma locum, qui à rerum constitutione petitur, tractat, nullam facit Actionum sive Functionum mentionem. Namq; Pererium sane mirari licet, qui cum nullas Formæ (ut diximus) in operando partes relinquat, totumq; negotium Accidentibus vendicet: nihilominus tamen huic argumento, quod à functionibus ducitur, locum fecit inter reliqua, quæ affert ad probandam Formam substantialem. ita enim scribit: Postea ex operationibus [ostenditur Forma.] singulæ enim res proprium habent motum & operationem, ut magnes vim trahendi ferrum, quæ vis manat à substantia rei: non quidem à Materia, siquidem ea vim tantùm patiendi; & hujusmodi vis ac facultas esset in cunctis rebus naturalibus, in quibus est Materia, nec ab accidentibus. nam quod ipsa agant prasfinito & accommodate ad suam cujusq; rei speciem, non habent ex se, sed à substantia specifica, cujus sunt instrumenta. atq; eadem levitate in proœmio libri sexti ait, Formam esse fontem omnium actionum, ac motuum naturalium, & admirabilium operum architectricem: accidentia autem esse velut instrumenta quædam ad actiones Formæ obeundas. & rursus ejusdem libri toto capite decimo septimo ita de Forma loquitur, acsi ipsa sola esset omnium rerum principalis effectrix, ac disertis verbis dicit, Omnem actionem esse à Forma. quæ sanè incogitantia summa est, & intolerabilis, ut eo in loco, ubi hanc quæstiquaestionem, an accidentia sint primaria agentia, vel instrumentaria, ex professo tractat, negativam partem amplectatur, formasq; prorsus ab agendo excludat; alibi vero ita loquatur, ac si certum esset ac confessum, Formam principales in agendo partes tenere, atq; accidentibus uti pro instrumentis; & argumentum quoq; hinc petat, ad Formarum confirmationem. Quum enim haec inter se directo pugnent; tuendo utrumq; simul, apertissima seipsum involvit contradictione: id quod sicuti in se est absurdissimum, & viris doctis planè indignum, ita saepius ijs evenire cernimus, qui Peripati somnijs sese addixerunt; quippe quibus ita male cum veritate convenit, ut melior ac firma ipsorum defendendorum ratio iniri vix possit.
units.tr: ...operate, and by their own power; and therefore that they are the principal causes of their own actions, as appears from the fifth and sixth sections of the eighteenth disputation. Pererius also maintains that forms neither operate mediately nor immediately, but whatever the accidents do, it proceeds from them as from the primary agents. Since, then, by the agreement of all, actions are produced by accidents, and what is said of the concurrence of forms with accidents in acting is found to be pure fiction, to such an extent that it is rejected by a large part of the Aristotelians themselves, the argument that is brought forward to prove a substantial form from actions is quite weak. This is why Suarez too, when he treats this argument for form, which is drawn from the constitution of things, makes no mention of actions or functions. Indeed one may well wonder at Pererius, who, while leaving forms no part at all in operating (as we have said) and claiming the whole business for accidents, nevertheless gives a place among the other arguments he brings to prove a substantial form to this one, which is drawn from functions. He writes as follows: Afterwards, from operations [the form is shown]. For each thing has its own motion and operation, as a magnet has the power of drawing iron, which power flows from the substance of the thing, not indeed from the matter, since that has only the power of being acted upon; and such a power and faculty would be in all natural things in which there is matter, and not from the accidents. For that they act in a fixed and suitable way toward the species of each thing, they do not have from themselves, but from the specific substance, of which they are the instruments. And with the same lightness, in the preface to the sixth book, he says: The form is the source of all actions and natural motions, and the architect of admirable works; but accidents are as it were certain instruments for the form to carry out its actions. And again, throughout the whole seventeenth chapter of the same book, he speaks of the form as if it alone were the principal author of all things, and he says in plain words: Every action is from the form. This inconsistency is extreme and intolerable: that in the place where he treats this question expressly, whether accidents are primary agents or instrumental ones, he embraces the negative part and excludes forms altogether from acting, yet elsewhere speaks as if it were certain and agreed that forms hold the principal parts in acting and that accidents are used as instruments, and he also draws from this an argument for confirming forms. For since these views directly contradict one another, by defending both at once he entangles himself in the plainest contradiction. This, as it is in itself most absurd and wholly unworthy of learned men, so we see it happen more often to those who have given themselves over to the dreams of the Peripatetics; for these agree so badly with the truth that a better and firmer rationale for defending them can scarcely be devised.
XVIII.

units.la: Secundum pro Formarum assertione locum derivat Fonseca ab unitate rerum naturalium, alio nimirum modo, quam de qua supra paragrapho undecimo egimus. Ait enim, Quum unaquaeq; res naturalis sit unius essentiae, & unum ens simpliciter; non posse eas constare ex Materia & accidentibus: quia & Materia, si non perficitur in genere substantiae per Formam Substantialem, sit ens completum; & accidentia itidem entia completa, cum proprie & directo ad certa praedicamenta pertineant. at ex pluribus entibus completis non constitui ullam veram essentiam & naturam, quantumcunq; illa in ordinem redigantur & coaptentur. Ad quae nos respondemus: sicuti verum est, unamquamq; rem naturalem esse simpliciter unam atq; unius essentiae; ita falsum esse, quod ejusmodi entia non possint ex pluribus entibus completis constitui: nisi si vocem Completi in arcta admodum significatione accipias, intelligendo nimirum per Entia completa ejusmodi Individua, quae ad nullam ulteriorem compositionem destinata, sibi ipsis sunt hoc quicquid sunt, ac superioris substantiae partes fieri respuunt: cujusmodi Individua sunt Animalia, & stirpes: etiamsi enim multarum stirpium partes in unum corpus cum alia stirpe coalescere apta nata sunt; non putamus tamen dari ullam stirpem, quae integra cum alia
units.tr: Fonseca derives the second argument for the assertion of Forms from the unity of natural things, though in a different way from the one we discussed above in paragraph eleven. He says: since each natural thing is of one essence and is simply one being, they cannot consist of matter and accidents. For matter, unless it is perfected in the genus of substance by a substantial form, is itself a complete being, and accidents are likewise complete beings, since they properly and directly belong to certain categories. But no true essence or nature is constituted from several complete beings, however much they are arranged and fitted together. To this we reply: just as it is true that each natural thing is simply one and of one essence, so it is false that such beings cannot be constituted from several complete beings, unless you take the word "complete" in a very narrow sense, understanding by "complete beings" those individuals which, destined for no further composition, are whatever they are in themselves and refuse to become parts of a higher substance. Such individuals are animals and plants. For although the parts of many plants are naturally apt to grow together into one body with another plant, we do not think there is any plant which can be joined whole with another
{x} otherwise there would be a contradiction.

units.la: {x} quomodo ut accidens reuoque veniat cum substrata ad estimatem substrata? alia integra coagmentari possit ad tertiam stirpem, cujus ipsæ non nisi partes sint, constituendam. certe Viscum & Polypodium arboribus, quibus innascuntur, pro solo tantum utuntur, neque magis unum cum ijs faciunt, quam Hedera cum ijs arboribus, ac muris, quos scandit, quibusq; se per immissas subinde novas radices illigat. & si quà ex pluribus seminibus unica planta nascitur (quod multi asserunt) non illic integræ stirpes uniuntur, sed stirpium duntaxat rudimenta. De hisce igitur Entibus Completis, animalium scilicet ac stirpium individuis, verum est, ex pluribus eorum non constitui unam essentiam. Quodsi autem in latiori significatione sumatur vox Completi (quomodo nimirum à Fonseca hic sumitur) omnino falsum est, e pluribus entibus completis non posse constitui ens verè unum. namq; & essentiales animalium aliorumq; animatorum partes, corpus, & anima, sunt sibi quæq; ens completum (quippe quæ suam sibi habent essentiam, neq; eam inter se in totum, vel ex parte commodant, aut mutuantur) ac tamen individua verissimè una constituunt: & ipsa rursus animatorum corpora, uti & aliæ substantiæ inanimes, quamquam eorum unumquodq; sint ens verè unum, constituuntur è concursu variorum Elementorum; quæ Elementa per sese considerata, omnino sunt entia completa. Quodsi jam ex diversis substantijs completis una atq; unius essentiæ substantia constitui potest: multo magis id fieri poterit ex subjecto & accidentibus, quum præsertim accidentia subsistere per se nullo modo queant, sed in hoc ordinata sint, ut subjectis inhæreant, & vel ijs insint, vel ne sint quidem omnino: ut mirum non sit, si cum substantijs concurrant ad unam rem constituendam, cum quibus tam arcto nexu hærent, ut pereundum ijs sit, cum quibus tam arcto nexu hærent, ut pereundum ijs sit, si quando earum consortium relinquere coguntur. & sicuti hæc ratio valida est pro ijs Accidentibus, quæ vera sunt entia per se, (cujusmodi sunt solæ Qualitates) ita multo magis obtinet pro ijs, quæ nullam separatam habent essentiam, sed totum hoc, quod sunt, sunt substantiarum, utpote earum non sunt nisi modi. Si autem vel
units.tr: {x} how, as an accident, can it come back together with the substrate into the substrate? Another whole thing could be joined to a third plant, which would be constituted of them as mere parts. Certainly mistletoe and polypody use trees on which they grow only as ground, and they make no more one with them than ivy does with the trees and walls it climbs and binds itself to by sending in new roots from time to time. And if a single plant springs from several seeds (as many assert), the whole plants are not united there, but only their rudiments. Concerning these complete beings, then, the individuals of animals and plants, it is true that one essence is not constituted from several of them. But if the word Complete is taken in the wider sense (as Fonseca takes it here), it is wholly false that a truly one being cannot be constituted from several complete beings. For the essential parts of animals and other living things, body and soul, are each a complete being in itself (since each has its own essence and does not share or lend it to the other, wholly or in part), and yet they most truly constitute one individual. And again, the bodies of living things themselves, as also other lifeless substances, although each of them is a truly one being, are constituted by the concurrence of various elements, which elements, considered in themselves, are wholly complete beings. But if one substance of one and the same essence can be constituted from diverse complete substances, much more will this be possible from a subject and accidents, especially since accidents cannot subsist through themselves in any way, but are so ordained that they inhere in subjects, and either are in them or are not at all. So it is no wonder if they concur with substances to constitute one thing, with which they cling by so close a bond that they must perish when they are compelled to leave that partnership. And just as this reasoning is strong for those accidents which are true beings through themselves (such as qualities alone), so it holds much more for those which have no separate essence, but whatever they are, they are of substances, since they are nothing but modes of them. But if indeed it were most true, as Fonseca urges here, that one essence is not constituted from a subject and accidents,

units.la: Non pluviquo vibus vel maxime verum esset, id quod hic urget Fonseca, ex subjecto & Accidentibus non constitui essentiam unam, non nos magis, qui Formam tollimus, premeret hoc incommodum, quam ipsum aliosque, qui eam ponunt: quandoquidem ex hac doctrina neque calor ignis unum ens per se constituet cum suo subjecto, neq; facultates animæ cum ipsa anima. Quodsi vero ipsi absurdum non putant, ut unum per accidens constituatur ex subjecto, & ijs accidentibus, quæ adeo sunt essentialia, ut substantię, ad quas pertinent, non modo consistere sine ijs ac nomen suum sustinere non possint, sed ne animo quidem aut imaginatione concipi: non est cur nobis vitio vertant, quod ea tradimus, è quibus sequatur, quod res naturales non sint unum per se, sed unum per accidens. ipsi enim æque huic criminationi sunt obnoxij cum suis Formis, à quibus non plus lucrantur, nisi ut res naturales faciant unas per se ex altera duntaxat parte, nimirum substantiali (quod & nobis æque contingit, tum in Elementis, tum in ijs substantijs, quæ ex unico duntaxat Elemento, introductione certarum qualitatum, factæ sunt) non vero totas, quippe qui ab illa unitate excludunt omnia accidentia, quorum tamen plurima ad ipsam rerum integritatem atq; essentiam pertinent. quomodo enim, ad rei essentiam non pertineat ea pars, sine qua existere ipsa nequaquam potest? Sane ipsis velint nolint fatendum hoc est, ac proinde vel inviti condemnare coguntur tritum illud inter ipsos axioma, qua totam rei essentiam atq; naturam ita soli Formæ transcribunt, ut nullam plane accidentium videantur rationem habere: qua re insulsius nihil fieri potest, etiamsi verum foret, dari Formas substantiales; nisi forte dicere audeant, ignem posse esse ignem absq; calore, & mentem humanam posse esse rationalem absq; intellectu & ratione.
units.tr: It would not press us who remove the form any more than it presses Fonseca himself and the others who posit it, if this were most true. For by this doctrine neither the heat of fire will constitute one being through itself with its subject, nor the faculties of the soul with the soul itself. But if they do not think it absurd that one thing through accident should be constituted from a subject and those accidents which are so essential that the substances to which they belong cannot not only subsist without them and sustain their name, but cannot even be conceived in mind or imagination, then there is no reason for them to find fault with us for teaching things from which it follows that natural things are not one through themselves, but one through accident. For they themselves are equally liable to this accusation with their forms, from which they gain nothing except that they make natural things one through themselves from one part only, namely the substantial part (which happens to us equally, both in the elements and in those substances which were made from a single element by the introduction of certain qualities), and not wholly one, since they exclude from that unity all accidents, many of which nevertheless pertain to the very integrity and essence of things. For how could the part without which a thing cannot exist at all not pertain to its essence? Certainly they must admit this, whether they wish or not, and so, unwillingly, they are compelled to condemn that commonplace axiom among themselves, by which they so assign the whole essence and nature of a thing to the form alone that they seem to have no regard for accidents at all. Nothing can be more foolish than this, even if it were true that substantial forms exist; unless perhaps they dare to say that fire can be fire without heat, and that the human mind can be rational without understanding and reason.

units.la: Ut autem hæc concludamus, sciendum errorem ejus effati, quod ex pluribus entibus completis negat posse conflari unam veram essentiam, atque unum ens per se, in eo consistere, quod unitas atq; essentia vera sumatur pro unitate & essentia simplici; ac cum ea
units.tr: To conclude these points, we should note the error of that saying, which denies that one true essence can be formed out of several complete beings, and that a single being through itself consists in this: that unity and true essence are taken to mean simple unity and essence; and together with it

units.la: × Nog. Iunitas pro unitate generis quæ sunt dinos ig vig & sunt unitas generis.
units.tr: × Nog. Unity taken for the unity of a genus, which are [garbled in the scan] and are the unity of a genus.
Chapter I.

units.la: ea confundatur, acsi hæc plane eadem essent, neq; quicquam inter se differrent; quum tamen plurimum inter ea interfit. Sane istius axiomatis fabricatores decepit unitas numeralis, non in rebus considerata, sed in sese, ut est numerus duntaxat, atq; ens intentionale, ut vocant. talis enim unitas omnem respuit compositionem, ac ne esse quidem potest, nisi ut sit simplex. ast unitatis naturalis longe alia est ratio: quippe hac unitate esse aliquid unum potest, quod ex partibus diversis, & ijs quidem valde inter se differentibus, coagmentatum est. quanquam autem talis res non sit simpliciter una, ac proinde neque simplicis essentiæ, suam tamen habet veram essentiam, estq; verissime una, non minus quam illæ res, quæ cum omnis sint compositionis expertes, unitatem atque essentiam habent simpliciter unam; cujusmodi non modo sunt qualitates pleræq;, sed & Elementa absq; qualitatibus suis considerata. & sicuti de unitate atq; essentia simplici certum est, eam non posse inveniri in rebus, quæ ex diversis entibus completis sint conflatæ, ita alteri unitati atq; essentiæ adeo non officit, ex pluribus entibus constitui, ut potius necessarium ipsi sit, atq; ad eam efficiendam planissime requiratur. neq; ulterius verum est, ex diversis entibus non posse unam veram essentiam constitui, nisi ubi illa ita inter se conjunguntur, ut nulla reali ac physica unione inter se devinciantur: id quod nequaquam locum habet in illa copulatione, qua anima & corpus ad constituendam animantem vel stirpem, aut diversa Elementa, ad constituendum corpus aliquod naturale, inter se ac cum suis accidentibus conlociantur. Et sic cadit illa Fonfecx argumentatio, Si semel admittatur constitutio verarum essentiarum ex entibus completis, fore ut cuiq; liceat nullo negotio quamplurimas rerum essentias conficere, multitis eorum conjunctis, & ordine collocatis: non enim quævis variorum entium collocatio & conjunctio sufficit, ut novum inde ens naturale exurgat; sed conjunctionem eam esse physicam ac realem, ut diximus, necesse est. qualis conjunctio quum non contineat milites in exercitu, multoq; minus omnia quæ sunt in mundo (quæ exempla illic à Fonseca afferuntur) propterea non sunt partes unius physicæ entitatis, neq; unam veram essentiam constituunt.
units.tr: they are confused, as if these were altogether the same and differed in no way from one another, whereas in fact there is a very great difference between them. Indeed, the makers of this axiom were deceived by numerical unity, considered not in things but in itself, as it is merely a number, and as an intentional being, as they call it. For such unity rejects all composition and cannot even exist unless it is simple. But the case of natural unity is quite different: by this unity something can be one which is put together from diverse parts, and indeed from parts that differ greatly from one another. Although such a thing is not simply one, and therefore does not have a simple essence, it nevertheless has its own true essence, and is most truly one, no less than those things which, being free of all composition, have a unity and essence that is simply one. Of this kind are not only most qualities, but also the Elements considered apart from their qualities. And just as it is certain that simple unity and essence cannot be found in things compounded from diverse complete beings, so the other kind of unity and essence is not hindered at all by being constituted from several beings; rather, this is necessary for it and is plainly required to bring it about. Nor is it further true that one true essence cannot be constituted from diverse beings unless they are so joined together that they are not bound to one another by any real and physical union. This by no means holds in that coupling by which soul and body are combined to constitute an animal or a plant, or by which diverse Elements are arranged with one another and with their accidents to constitute some natural body. And so that argument of Fonseca falls: "If once the constitution of true essences from complete beings is admitted, it will follow that anyone may with no trouble make very many essences of things, by joining many things together and arranging them in order." For not every arrangement and conjunction of various beings is enough for a new natural being to arise from it; but, as we have said, the conjunction must be physical and real. Since such a conjunction does not hold soldiers in an army, much less all the things that are in the world (which examples Fonseca brings forward there), they are therefore not parts of one physical entity, nor do they constitute one true essence.

units.la: XIX. Porro multa adhuc alia in hujus loci tractatione congerit Fonseca, quibus putat probari, quod res naturales nequeant ex Materia tantum & accidentibus, absque Forma substantiali constare. Si essentia rerum naturalium (inquit) constant Materia & accidentibus, aut quælibet accidentia sunt satis ad earum constitutionem, aut requiruntur certa & determinata. Quod quælibet sint satis, nemo unquam ita deliravit qui diceret: quare vanum sumit laborem Fonseca, contra hoc disputando. Alteram autem & veriorem sententiam, quæ Res naturales conficit ex Materia & determinatis accidentibus, ita impugnat, ut arguatur, accidentia illa aut inseparabilia statuenda, aut separabilia, non posse statui inseparabilia, inde arguit, quia Materia sit indifferens ad omnia, excepta duntaxat quantitate interminata, ex qua cum Materia non possit ulla rerum naturalium varietas confici. Sed neq; licere accidentia illa facere separabilia, concludit ob duo incommoda. prius est; quia essentia, quæ ex eis cum Materia constabit, non erit una, nisi per accidens, & ratione subjecti, quæ unitas non sit satis; ut ex ea colligas unam essentiam, ex subjecto & Forma constatam. alterum est; quia cum hæc conjunctio variabilis sit, variabilis quoq; futura sit essentia, quæ ex ea constituetur, neq; habitura ullum fixum perfectionis gradum. verbi causa, si ignis constet ex Materia & calore actuali, aut siccitate, aut deniq; raritate; quum hæc magis & minus accipiant, fore quoque ignem modo magis ignem, modo minus: quod dici non possit. Hisce demum adjungit, quod si ex Materia & accidentibus, sive uno sive pluribus, constet aliqua vera essentia; quum omnis vera essentia sit vel substantia, vel accidens; ejusmodi quoq; essentiam fore substantiam, vel accidens. atqui non fore accidens, quippe quæ & in subjecto non inerit, & ex substantia constabit; neque item substan-
units.tr: XIX. Moreover, Fonseca heaps up many other things in his treatment of this point, by which he thinks it is proved that natural things cannot consist of matter and accidents alone, without a substantial form. "If the essences of natural things," he says, "consist of matter and accidents, then either any accidents whatever are sufficient for their constitution, or certain and determinate ones are required." That any accidents whatever suffice, no one has ever been so mad as to say; so Fonseca takes up a pointless labour in arguing against this. But the other and truer opinion, which constitutes natural things from matter and determinate accidents, he attacks in this way: he argues that those accidents must be posited either as inseparable or as separable, and that they cannot be posited as inseparable. He argues this because matter is indifferent to all things except indeterminate quantity, and from matter together with that no variety of natural things can be made. Nor, he concludes, may those accidents be made separable, on account of two inconveniences: (1) the essence that would consist of them together with matter would not be one except accidentally and by reason of the subject, and that unity is not sufficient for one to infer a single essence composed of subject and form; (2) since this conjunction is variable, the essence constituted from it would also be variable, and would not have any fixed degree of perfection. For example, if fire consists of matter and actual heat, or dryness, or finally rarity, then since these admit of more and less, fire too would now be more fire and now less fire, which cannot be said. Finally, he adds that if some true essence consists of matter and accidents, whether one or several, then, since every true essence is either a substance or an accident, such an essence would also be a substance or an accident. But it would not be an accident, since it would not inhere in a subject and would consist of substance; nor likewise a substan-

units.la: × accidentalē unimus ips constitutionē ... (marginal handwritten note, partly illegible)
units.tr: accidental union itself ... constitution ...
Chapter I.

units.la: substantiam, ut quæ constabit ex accidente, atq; ab eo spe- ciem accipiet, tanquam à propria Forma. nullam igitur essentiam ex Materia & accidente, aut accidentibus constare posse; quia alioquin oporteret, contra communem omnium sententiam, & ipsam quoque rationem, ponere medium quoddam genus inter substantiam & accidens, quod nec substantia sit, nec accidens, sed quippiam ex utroq; constitutum. id quod si verum sit; hoc solum genus rerum naturalium poni debere, quippe ad quod Materiam & accidentia reducere oporteat, tanquam partes ad totum, nullamq; jam materialem substantiam, aut accidens, sore ens completum: quæ omnia sint absurdissima.
units.tr: substance, since it would consist of an accident and receive its species from that accident as from its proper form. Therefore no essence can consist of matter and accident, or of accidents; for otherwise one would have to posit, contrary to the common opinion of all and to reason itself, some intermediate genus between substance and accident, which is neither substance nor accident but something made up of both. If that were true, this would have to be the only genus of natural things, since matter and accidents would have to be reduced to it as parts to a whole, and no material substance or accident would be a complete being. All of these consequences are most absurd.

units.la: Præter hæc aliam adhuc rationem huc spectantem habent Conimbricenses, à Fonseca omissam, vel non satis declaratam. Quæro, aiunt, cur isthæc potius accidentia in hac Materia, quam illa conspiciantur? cur igni potius calor quam frigus competat? cur aërem levitas, non gravitas sequatur? Cum igitur hujus rei Causa ad Materiam referri non possit, plane sequitur talium accidentium originem ad Formam substantialem, uti ad ipsorum fontem, referendam esse. & similiter Pererius, Si tollas Formam substantialem, nulla potest reddi Causa, cur aliqua accidentia sint reliquorum propria, neq; cur certa accidentia in certis rebus uniantur & copulentur. nam Materia ipsa una est atq; indifferens ad omnia accidentia. horum quodlibet per se non requirit talem unionem. quid ergo est, quod eam hoc vel alio modo & gradu requirat, si tollatur Forma substantialis? Etiam Suarez proponit hanc rationem, sed ita ut eam permisceat cum illa Fonsecæ, qua dicit, Substantias non posse constare ex Materia & accidentibus separabilibus. quia essentia talis non esset una, nisi per accidens, & ratione subjecti. sic enim scribit: Quum in uno ente naturali multæ proprietates conjungantur, hæc multitudo & varietas proprietatum requirit unam Formam, in qua omnes uniantur: alioqui essent mere accidentaliter congregatæ in eodem subjecto, & unâ omnino sublatâ, non propterea recederet alia. at oppositum constat experientia. ergo
units.tr: Besides these arguments, the Coimbra commentators have another argument bearing on this point, which Fonseca omitted or did not explain sufficiently. They ask: why do these accidents appear in this matter rather than those? Why does heat belong to fire rather than cold? Why does lightness, not heaviness, follow air? Since the cause of this cannot be referred to matter, it plainly follows that the origin of such accidents must be referred to the substantial form, as to their source. Pererius similarly: If you take away the substantial form, no cause can be given why some accidents are the proper accidents of certain things, nor why certain accidents are united and joined in certain things. For matter itself is one and indifferent to all accidents. None of them by itself requires such a union. What then is it that requires it in this or that way and degree, if the substantial form is removed? Suárez also proposes this argument, but mixes it with Fonseca's, where he says: Substances cannot consist of matter and separable accidents, because such an essence would not be one except accidentally and by reason of the subject. For he writes: since many properties are joined in one natural being, this multiplicity and variety of properties requires one form in which they are all united; otherwise they would be merely accidentally gathered together in the same subject, and when one was removed, the others would not thereby cease. But experience shows the opposite. Therefore
Phys. 9. qu. 10. art. 2.
Phys. 2.

units.la: Disp. 15. sect. 1. §. 14. ergo signum est, talia accidentia in tali numero, pondere, & mensura, in tali subjecto & ente requisita, non habere illam connexionem respectu solius primi subjecti, seu Materiae primae, sed respectu alicujus compositi, quod ratione Formae illum accidentium inter se ordinem requirit.
units.tr: Disp. 15. sect. 1. §. 14. Therefore it is a sign that such accidents, in such number, weight and measure, required in such a subject and being, do not have that connection with the first subject alone, or prime matter, but with some compound, which by reason of its form requires that order of the accidents among themselves.

units.la: XX. Hæ objectiones quam nullius sint momenti, planum fiet ex verae sententiae declaratione, quam postea in libro de Natura ampliter executuri, hic paucis breviter comprehendemus. Principio rerum, quum Universum hoc Deus fabricaret, ac decrevisset apud se, quot ac quales Rerum species aut ipse tunc facere, aut ab alijs postea fieri vellet, unicuiq; speciei suas certas attribuit conditiones, in quibus ipsius integritas ac perfectio consisteret. & quum aliae quidem species mensurae semper essent, absq; ulla individuorum vicissitudine, aliae vero perpetuas oriendi atq; intereundi vices in suis individuis experturae; utriusq; quidem generis substantias omnibus conditionibus, à se ipso pro unaquaq; specie destinatis, ornavit; pro alteris vero curam quoq; gessit, ut Agentia illa, quae novas ejusmodi substantias postea generatura essent, cunctos eosdem characteres (nisi alicunde impedirentur) ijs imprimerent: sicuti & pro illis speciebus, quarum nulla individua istis sex dierum operibus ipse molitus est, ita providit, ut Effectores illi, à quibus suo tempore essent producendae, omnibus eas debitis notis, à sese unicuiq; ipsarum assignatis, insignirent. Hæc igitur specifica perfectio, ab ipso Deo constituta, in Causa est, cur talia atq; talia Accidentia in quaque specie reperiantur; ut proinde supervacuum sit, fingere Formas substantiales, ad quas eorum origo tanquam ad fontem referenda sit, & quarum ratione composita illam accidentium congregationem atq; connexionem requirant. Imo si vel maxime darentur Formae, nihilosecius tamen maneret illa Conimbricensium quaestio, Cur isthaec potius accidentia quam illa in hac Materia conspiciantur? cur igni calor potius quam frigus competat? namq; si respondeant, tales Formas tanlium lium accidentium comitatum sibi deposcere; quæremus porro, qui fiat, ut hæc aut illa Forma hujusmodi sibi accidentia postulet, & non alia. neq; aliquid habebunt quod respondeant (si modo non velint insanire) nisi quia Deus hæc ita ordinavit, ac certis Formis certa accidentia attribuit: quo pacto in idem nobiscum recident, atq; certum in quaq; specie accidentium numerum haud alij rei, quam Divinæ institutioni primitus ferent acceptum; cui institutioni obtemperantes genitores (in hisce nimirum rebus, quæ generari solent) tali Formæ à se productæ talia accidentia adjungant. Ita sane, quanquam somniare solent, proprietates rerum à Formis emanare, non tamen docent, ipsam primam accidentium productionem à Forma fieri, sed ab eodem Effectore, à quo Forma producatur; unde pervulgatum illud, Dant Formam, omnia quæ Formam consequuntur. Sicuti igitur illi dicunt, unicuiq; generanti præfinitum esse, ut cum tali Forma producat talia accidentia; ita nos simpliciter dicimus, præstitutum esse generantibus, quibus accidentibus fœtus suos debeant adornare: in quo nulla absurditas ostendi potest, neq; verbum dici, cur Generanti difficilius esse debeat, præscriptas sibi à Deo leges servare, in subjecto suo debitis notis excolendo, si hoc tantum agat, quam si Formam quoque substantialem præterea producat. à Forma enim (etiamsi darentur Formæ) potius gravaretur ipsius pensum, quam ut ullum ipsi effectionis suæ adjumentum inde accederet, quum neq; parentem suum admonere Forma posset officij sui in productione fratrum suorum seu pedissequorum, videlicet accidentium sibi (ut loquuntur) connaturalium; neq; laborem ipsi suum commodare, atq; operas cum ipso partiri. quippe ipsi docent, Formas accidentibus esse natu posteriores, & priusquam Forma introducatur, apparari Materiam ad ipsius susceptionem, introductione scilicet accidentium secuturæ Formæ congruentium: quam præviam alterationem interdum quoq; Generationis nomine afficiunt (quum proprie per generationem non soleant intelligere nisi ipsam Formæ introductionem, quæ momento fiat) eaq; à Scaligero Generatio præparatoria nuncupatur, in comment. ad Theophrasti secundum de Causis, Est in generatione (non illa momentanea, quæ est introductio Formæ, sed præparatoria) nihil aliud quam conflictus pugnantium Qualitatum, quoad unum fiant. & quanquam nonnulli ipsorum ita delirant, ut dicant omnes illas qualitates, quibus Materia ad Formæ susceptionem fuerit disposita, ipso momento, quo Forma accedit, vanescere, aliasq; novas, prioribus consimiles, subito oriri; tamen hi absurditatis à multis suorum sociorum damnantur, & receptissimo inter ipsos Aristotelis scito manifeste repugnant, quo statuitur, nullam alterationem fieri in momento, sive in instanti (ut vocant) sed aliquod temporis spatium requiri ad eam perficiendam: quo posito, fieri non potest ut eodem momento, quo Forma producitur, accidentia Formæ consectaria producantur; sicuti neq; post Formæ introductionem locum esse ulli tali alterationi ipsi fatentur, utpote qui doceant, quod sicuti ante generationem, id est momentum illud, quo introductâ Formâ res est id quod est, multi fiunt motus; ita Formâ introductâ fiat quies sive status. Formæ itaq; (ut ad rem redeamus) nihil conferrent Causæ generanti, ad productionem accidentium specificorum, etiamsi essent aliquæ Formæ: neq; Causa, cur in hoc vel illo subjecto hæc vel illa accidentia naturaliter reperiantur, ad ipsas Formas, sed ad Genitores, convenienter Divinæ injunctioni, ac facultatibus ab ipso acceptis, operantes, esset referenda; æquæ ac nunc à nobis, qui Formam tollimus, refertur.
units.tr: XX. How utterly without weight these objections are will become plain from a declaration of the true view, which I will later set out more fully in my book on Nature; here I will briefly summarise it. At the beginning of things, when God was fashioning this universe and had decided within himself how many and what kinds of species of things he himself wished to make, or wished to be made later by others, he assigned to each species its own fixed conditions, in which its integrity and perfection would consist. Some species were always to remain the same, without any change of individuals, while others were to experience perpetual cycles of coming into being and passing away in their individuals. For both kinds of substances he furnished every condition that he had destined for each species. As for the latter, he also took care that those agents which were later to generate new substances of this sort should imprint on them all the same characters (unless they were hindered in some way). Likewise, for those species of which he himself made no individuals in the works of those six days, he provided that the producers by whom they were to be produced in their time should mark them with all the due signs that he had assigned to each of them. This specific perfection, then, established by God himself, is the cause why such and such accidents are found in each species. Hence it is superfluous to imagine substantial forms, to which their origin would have to be referred as to a source, and by reason of which the compound would require that gathering and connection of accidents. Indeed, even if forms were granted, the question of the Coimbra men would still remain: Why do these accidents appear in this matter rather than those? Why does heat belong to fire rather than cold? For if they answer that such forms demand such a company of accidents for themselves, we will go on to ask how it comes about that this or that form demands these accidents and not others. Nor will they have anything to answer (unless they wish to be mad) except that God so ordained these things and assigned fixed accidents to fixed forms. In this way they fall back into the same position as ours, and must attribute the fixed number of accidents in each species to nothing other than the divine institution from the beginning. Obeying this institution, the parents (in those things, of course, which are usually generated) join to the form they produce such accidents as belong to it. Thus, although they are wont to dream that the properties of things emanate from forms, they do not teach that the very first production of accidents comes from the form, but from the same agent by which the form is produced. Hence the well-known saying: those who give the form, give everything that follows the form. Just as they say that it is predetermined for each begetter that with such a form he produces such accidents, so we simply say that it has been prescribed for those who beget what accidents they ought to adorn their offspring with. In this there can be shown no absurdity, nor can any reason be given why it should be harder for the begetter to keep the laws prescribed to him by God, adorning his subject with the due marks, if he does only this, than if he also produces a substantial form besides. For the begetter's task would be burdened rather than helped by a form (even if forms existed), since the form could neither remind its parent of his duty in producing his brothers or attendants, that is, the accidents (as they say) connatural to it, nor lend him its labour and share its work with him. Indeed, they themselves teach that forms are posterior in nature to accidents, and that before a form is introduced the matter is prepared to receive it, by the introduction of accidents which will be congruent with the form to follow. They sometimes call this preparatory change by the name of generation, though strictly speaking they usually understand by generation only the introduction of the form itself, which happens in an instant. Scaliger calls this preparatory generation, in his commentary on the second book of Theophrastus's On Causes: In generation (not that instantaneous generation which is the introduction of the form, but the preparatory kind) there is nothing other than a conflict of opposing qualities, until they become one. And although some of them rave so far as to say that all those qualities by which the matter was disposed to receive the form vanish at the very moment the form arrives, and that other new qualities, similar to the former, suddenly arise, yet these are condemned by many of their own fellows as absurd, and they plainly contradict the most accepted maxim of Aristotle, by which it is established that no change takes place in a moment, or in an instant (as they call it), but some span of time is required to bring it to completion. Given this, it is impossible that the accidents consequent upon the form should be produced in the same moment in which the form is produced. Likewise, they themselves admit that after the introduction of the form there is no room for any such change, since they teach that just as before generation, that is, in that moment in which, with the form introduced, the thing is what it is, many motions occur, so when the form has been introduced there occurs rest or stasis. Therefore forms (to return to the matter) would contribute nothing to the generating cause for the production of specific accidents, even if there were some forms. Nor would the cause why these or those accidents are naturally found in this or that subject have to be referred to the forms, but to the begetters, who act in accordance with the divine injunction and the faculties received from him; just as it is now referred by us, who remove the form.

units.la: XXI. Quod verò Fonseca ait, Si accidentia statuantur separabilia (ut revera sunt, & statui debent) non posse ex ijs & subjecto fieri unam essentiam per se; in eo de- cipitur.
units.tr: XXI. As for Fonseca's claim that if accidents are held to be separable (as they indeed are, and must be held to be), they cannot together with the subject make one essence per se, he is mistaken in this.

units.la: Partium enim inseparabilitas nequaquam requiritur ad rei veram unitatem, sed duntaxat ad ipsius perpetuitatem atq; æternitatem. homo enim, cujus anima ac corpus essent inseparabiles, seu qui à morte esset immunis (quomodo Elias & Enochus ab ea fuerunt immunes) non esset
units.tr: For the inseparability of parts is by no means required for the true unity of a thing, but only for its perpetuity and eternity. A man whose soul and body were inseparable, or who was exempt from death (as Elijah and Enoch were exempt from it), would not be
Chapter I.

units.la: esset magis unus ac verus homo quam nos qui morti succumbimus. & ipsi Peripatetici statuunt ex Materia & Forma fieri essentiam verissime unam, quum tamen ista esse separarabilia fateantur. Quantum vero attinet ad essentiae variabilitatem (quod alterum à separabilitate accidentium derivat incommodum Fonseca) eam nos ultra fatemur, quippe qui pro inani condemnemus illud Peripateticorum axioma, Substantiam non recipere magis & minus, nimirum ita late sumtum, quomodo ab ipsis sumi solet. quippe eodem redit, ac si dicerent, omnes substantias in summo perfectionis gradu semper esse constitutas, nec posse unquam aut seipsis, aut aliis ejusdem generis esse imperfectiores: id quod aperte falsum est. Pleraque enim aut omnes substantiae partibus constant, alijs quidem adeo essentialibus, ut aliquâ ipsarum sublatâ, & ipsas perire sit necesse; alijs vero ad integritatem quidem ipsarum & specificae naturae perfectionem requisitis, non tamen adeo necessarijs, quin ipsis sublatis ipsae manere nihilominus queant. Iam sicuti priorum partium respectu Substantiae non possunt esse magis aut minus substantiae, hoc est perfectiores aut imperfectiores (quum earum partium nullum dispendium patiantur; atq; aut habere illas debeant, aut necesse quidem omnino) ita quoad posteriores certissimo patiuntur illam majoris aut minoris perfectionis vicissitudinem: & si quis ignis est alio igne calidior, est etiam magis ignis, sive perfectior ignis, quam ille minus calidus. Quodsi negare haec velint Aristotelici, atq; axioma suum, quo substantias non suscipere magis & minus statuunt, tueri; necesse est omnes de mundo morbos, mutilationes, atque debilitates tollant. Neq; tamen ex hoc, quod substantiae obnoxiae sunt imperfectioni, essentiamq; habere possunt magis aut minus integram, sequitur, (quod inde infert Fonseca) nullum futurum fixum gradum perfectionis essentiarum. certus enim ac fixus est quaq; speciei gradus perfectionis, isq; semper idem manet ac invariabilis, etiamsi vel aliqua vel omnia individua, alia quidem magis, alia vero minus, abea declinent. illa enim in individuis, perfectionis atq; imperfectionis gradus.
units.tr: more one and a truer man than we who succumb to death. The Peripatetics themselves hold that an essence composed of matter and form is most truly one, although they admit that these are separable. As far as concerns the variability of essence (the second inconvenience Fonseca derives from the separability of accidents), we grant this too, since we condemn as empty that Peripatetic axiom, Substance does not admit of more and less, at least when it is taken as broadly as they usually take it. For this comes to the same thing as saying that all substances are always established at the highest degree of perfection, and can never be more imperfect than themselves or than others of their kind, which is plainly false. Most, or indeed all, substances consist of parts: some of these are so essential that if any one of them is removed the substance must necessarily perish; others are required for the integrity of the substance and the perfection of its specific nature, yet are not so necessary that the substance cannot remain when they are removed. Now, just as with the former parts substances cannot be more or less substances, that is, more or less perfect (since they suffer no loss of those parts, and must either have them or altogether lack the substance), so with respect to the latter they certainly undergo a variation of greater or lesser perfection; and if a fire is hotter than another fire, it is also more of a fire, or a more perfect fire, than the less hot one. But if the Aristotelians wish to deny this and defend their axiom that substances do not admit of more and less, they must remove all diseases, mutilations and debilities from the world. Nor does it follow from the fact that substances are subject to imperfection, and can have a more or less complete essence, that (as Fonseca infers) there will be no fixed degree of perfection of essences. For the degree of perfection of each species is certain and fixed, and remains always the same and unchanging, even if some or all individuals decline from it, some more and some less. For the degrees of perfection and imperfection are in the individuals.

units.la: {x} Decessus, decessiones, aut tolli, annullari. perfectionis variabilitas non tollit certitudinem perfectionis ipsi speceiei præstitutæ. Et hic latet origo erroris Aristotelicorum atq; Aristotelis, qui id, quod ipsi speceiei debetur, ab eo, quod in ipsis speciei individuis invenitur, nescierunt distinguere; & quia illic nihil aut addi aut detrahi potest, hic quoque nihil posse addi detrahive existimarunt: in quo non minus imperite faciunt, quam si quis in quovis Oratore inesse diceret omnes illas conditiones, quas in perfecto oratore vel Cicero vel Quintilianus desideravit.
