Multæ sane Causæ dantur, quæ Causas generantes impedire valent ac solent, quominus in efformando partu suo omnia ad specificæ perfectionis normam exigere ac perficere queant: & si vel maxime genitores suum officium fecerint, omniaq; fœtui suo, quæ conferri poterant ac debebant, contulerint; incurrentes tamen postmodum injuriæ de nativa perfectione non parum detrahere, eamq; multum imminuere solent: quibus rebus fit, ut, quę speciei debetur perfectio, non semper in ipsis individuis deprehendatur; quæ individua proinde dicenda sunt minus perfecta, quam illa, quæ omnia ad specificam perfectionem pertinentia plene sortita sunt.
units.tr: {x} Decrease, decreases, or be taken away, be annulled. The variability of perfection does not remove the certainty of the perfection prescribed for the species itself. And here lies the origin of the error of the Aristotelians and of Aristotle himself, who did not know how to distinguish what is owed to the species itself from what is found in the individuals of the species; and because nothing can be added or taken away there, they thought that nothing can be added or taken away here either. In this they act no less foolishly than if someone said that every one of those qualities which Cicero or Quintilian required in a perfect orator is present in any orator whatever. Indeed there are many causes which can and often do hinder the generating causes from bringing everything in the forming of their offspring up to the standard of specific perfection; and even if the parents have done their duty to the utmost and have contributed to their offspring everything that could and should be contributed, nevertheless injuries incurred afterwards often take away not a little from its native perfection and greatly diminish it. From these circumstances it comes about that the perfection owed to the species is not always found in the individuals themselves; and those individuals must accordingly be called less perfect than those which have fully received everything pertaining to specific perfection.

units.la: XXII. Porro illud, quod postremo loco addit Fonseca.
units.tr: XXII. Furthermore, as to what Fonseca adds last.

units.la: Suppositia illa, ex Materia & accidentibus conflata, neque substantiam meram futuram, neq; accidens, sed aliquid inter utrumq; medium, & ex utroq; constitutum: hoc totum ipsi concedimus, neq; ullum inde absurdum (uti ipse putat, ac declamat) sequitur: & si sequeretur, non nobis magis hæreret, quam Peripateticis, inter quos nemo adhuc inventus fuit, qui substantiam meram (hoc est, quæ ex sola Materia & Forma constaret, omnium accidentium expers) inveniri diceret. & præterea fateri coguntur, pleraq; accidentia adeo esse ad constitutionem substantiarum necessaria, ut sine ijs consistere substantiæ nullo modo queant (sicuti paulo ante quoq; dicebamus) quare effugere non possunt, quin concedant (nisi in animum induxerunt plane fatuari) tales res esse ex substantia & accidentibus
units.tr: Those composites, made up of matter and accidents, which will be neither pure substance nor accident, but something intermediate between the two and constituted from both: we concede all of this, and no absurdity follows from it (as he himself thinks and declaims); and even if it did follow, it would cling to us no more than to the Peripatetics, among whom no one has yet been found who would say that pure substance (that is, substance consisting of matter and form alone, free of all accidents) can be found. Moreover, they are compelled to admit that most accidents are so necessary to the constitution of substances that substances cannot in any way subsist without them (as we also said a little earlier). Therefore they cannot escape conceding (unless they have resolved to play the fool entirely) that such things are composed of substance and accidents.
Chapter I.

units.la: bus compositas, non compositione per accidens (uti cavillari solent) sed verâ ac perse: & sic locum contra eos habebunt omnia illa, quae ijs, apud quos ex Materia & accidentibus, absq; Forma substantiali, componuntur res naturales, hic à Fonseca objiciuntur. Et quanquam adeo stomachetur adversus eos, qui Materiam & accidentia reducant ad res naturales, tanquam partes ad totum, idq; pro absurdissimo rejiciat: nihil tamen dicit, unde tam severae ipsius censurae fides ac autoritas concilietur, ac proinde non videmus, quidni nobis liceat contrariam ipsius opinionem, ac totam hanc declamationem, æque severiter repudiare, ac pro absurda condemnare. Namq; quod videtur vereri, ne hoc pacto tollatur recepta illa divisio, qua Entia in Substantiam & Accidentia distinguuntur; itemq; ne Substantia & Accidens sint entia completa: in eo fallitur. Etenim & divisio illa nihilosecius manet, recte intelligendo vocem Entis, non pro re seorsim ac per se existente (quippe sic nullum ens creatum vel substantia mera est, vel accidens, omniaq; entia sunt ex substantia & accidentibus constata) sed quae existentiam suam habeat in natura rerum, etiamsi nunquam sola, sed alteri semper conjuncta reperiatur. Et quanquam substantia nusquam sine accidente, neq; accidentia extra substantiam inveniantur; hoc tamen non impedit, quominus & substantia, & accidentia (quae quidem accidentia sint absoluta) possint entia completa suo modo appellari; quandoquidem non dubitant Peripatetici, quin compositum ex potentia & actu substantiali, sive ex Materia & Forma constatum, sit ens completum, etiamsi fateantur tale ens nudum ac per se, & nullis accidentibus conjugatum, nullibi reperiri. Quod si per Entia completa intelligantur non ea, quae sint aliquid reale, suamque veram essentiam habeant; sed quae per se subsistant, neq; alterius rei partes, sed sibimet tota sint: tunc ultro fatemur, neq; substantiam Materialem (ut ipse vocat) néq; Accidentia entium completorum nomine donanda. Quanquam autem res naturales, ex substantia materiali & accidentibus compositas, soleamus simpliciter Substantias indigetare; hoc non facimus, quia illarum rerum essentiam in sola substantia putemus constare; sed quia & substantia pars rei est præcipua, quantum quidem ad existentiam; & quia alio commodo nomine, ad designandam rem ex substantia materiali & accidentibus compositam, carèmus; neq; ullum, ex tali hujus nominis usurpatione, erroris periculum provenire potest, nisi apud eos, qui ultro decipi desiderent.
units.tr: compounded of them, not by a compounding through accident (as they are wont to quibble), but truly and in themselves. And so all those objections which Fonseca raises here will have force against those who hold that natural things are composed of matter and accidents without a substantial form. Although he rages so fiercely against those who reduce matter and accidents to natural things as parts to a whole, and rejects this as most absurd, he says nothing by which the credibility and authority of his so severe censure could be secured. Therefore we do not see why we may not with equal severity reject his opposite opinion and this whole declamation, and condemn it as absurd. For as to his fear that by this means the accepted division, by which beings are distinguished into substance and accidents, would be destroyed, and that substance and accident would not be complete beings, he is mistaken. For that division remains nonetheless, if the word "being" is rightly understood not as a thing existing separately and by itself (for in that sense no created being is either pure substance or accident, and all beings are made up of substance and accidents), but as that which has its existence in the nature of things, even though it is never found alone but always joined to something else. And although substance is nowhere found without accident, nor accidents outside substance, this nonetheless does not prevent substance and accidents (which indeed are absolute accidents) from being called complete beings in their own way. For the Peripatetics do not doubt that the compound of potency and substantial act, that is, made up of matter and form, is a complete being, even though they admit that such a being is found nowhere in a bare and independent state, unjoined to any accidents. But if by complete beings are meant not those which are something real and have their own true essence, but those which subsist by themselves, and are not parts of another thing but whole in themselves, then we readily grant that neither material substance (as he calls it) nor accidents should be given the name of complete beings. Although we are accustomed to call natural things, compounded of material substance and accidents, simply "substances," we do not do this because we think their essence consists in substance alone, but because substance is the chief part of the thing, at least as regards existence, and because we lack another convenient name for designating a thing compounded of material substance and accidents. Nor can any danger of error arise from such use of this name, except among those who are willing to be deceived.

units.la: XXIII. Tertius Fonsecæ locus, ad demonstrandam Formam, fundatur in rerum naturalium conservatione.
units.tr: XXIII. The third argument of Fonseca, for demonstrating the Form, is founded on the conservation of natural things.

units.la: Cernimus (inquit) qualitates contrarias, ad certam quandam temperiem redactas, naturaliter in Mixtis conservari. ejus autem stabilitatis ac naturalitatis Causa non sunt ipsæ Qualitates, quippe quum natura sua repugnent mutuo; non item Materia prima, quum sit indifferens ad quemlibet earum statum; nec denique Causa externa duntaxat, quia is status non esset à natura rei. igitur aliqua Causa interna danda est, cujus ratione illæ naturaliter unitæ sint, & stabili consensione connexæ, quod aliud esse nequit, quàm Forma substantialis, aut natura aliqua ex ea constans. & hoc multo magis evinci putat ex iis Mixtis, in quibus una aliqua Qualitas, aut duæ Qualitates, reliquas magno intensionis excessu superent, quæ inæqualitas quum brevioris durationis Causa esse debuerit, plurimæ tamen harum rerum multo diutius conservantur, quam in quibus major temperies cernitur. Ab unâ igitur aliqua natura id provenire, quæ primis qualitatibus prior sit, & consequenter ab aliqua substantiali Forma, cui ejusmodi qualitatum status congruat. Hæc argumentatio quantum polleat (etiam suppositâ vulgari de Temperamentis doctrina) monstrabit pro nobis Suarez, qui eo in loco, ubi Formæ defensionem tractat, omnesq; rationes eo facientes diligentissime conquirit, fatetur hanc confirmationem (quæ nimirum Formam asserit ex eo, quod accidentia contraria in mistis ad certos gradus redacta, ita conservantur) nullam iam omnino vim habere: quia quatuor prima qualitates ad eam temperiem redacta, in qua possint simul esse in eodem subjecto, non indigeant alia interna causa vel Principio, ut in eo perpetuò conserventur in eodem statu, sed sola remotione extrinseci agentis corrumpentis; quia illæ qualitates in eodem gradu constitutæ, nec sint proprie contrariæ, nec possint habere inter se actionem: & si habere eam possent, non posset Forma substantialis eam impedire, aut conciliare. Itaque concludit, Ex hac conservatione temperamenti, ex contrarijs qualitatibus constantis, præcisè sumta, non inferri Formam substantialem; sed eatenus tantum id valere, quatenus aliqua qualitas, quæ extrinsecus vel aucta vel imminuta fuerat, redit ad priorem proportionem, remoto externo agente: quod tamen nullum novum sit argumentum, sed coincidat cum illo de reductione rei ad naturalem statum: quod argumentum ab ipso Fonseca seorsum proponitur, & à nobis mox examinabitur. Præter autem hanc Suarezij responsionem, aliam meliorem nobis suppeditat ipsa veritas quæ plane abdicat, ac pro inani figmento condemnat, quicquid Hippocrates prius & Aristoteles, ac deinde Galenus (longe hac in re magistros suos supergressus) de temperamentis, ex quatuor Primarum, ut vocant, Qualitatum certa proportione exurgentibus, imaginati fuerunt: sicuti alio magis opportuno huius operis loco prolixè, favente Divinâ gratia, docebimus.
units.tr: "We see," he says, "that contrary qualities, reduced to a certain fixed temperament, are naturally conserved in mixed bodies. But the cause of this stability and naturalness is not the qualities themselves, since by their nature they are mutually opposed; nor is it prime matter, since it is indifferent to any state of these; nor finally is it merely an external cause, because that state would not be from the nature of the thing. Therefore some internal cause must be granted, by reason of which those qualities are naturally united and joined in stable harmony; and this can be nothing other than a substantial form, or some nature consisting of it." He thinks this is proved even more strongly from those mixed bodies in which one quality, or two qualities, surpass the rest by a great excess of intensity. Since this inequality ought to be the cause of a shorter duration, yet very many of these things are conserved much longer than those in which a greater temperament is seen. Therefore this comes from one nature, which is prior to the primary qualities, and consequently from some substantial form, with which such a state of the qualities agrees. How strong this argument is (even granting the common doctrine about temperaments) Suárez will show on our side, who, in the place where he treats the defence of the Form, and diligently collects all the reasons tending to it, admits that this confirmation (namely, that which asserts the Form from the fact that contrary accidents in mixed bodies, reduced to certain degrees, are thus conserved) now has no force at all: "because the four first qualities, reduced to that temperament in which they can be together in the same subject, do not need another internal cause or principle in order to be perpetually conserved in the same state in it, but only the removal of the external corrupting agent; because those qualities, established in the same degree, are neither properly contrary, nor can they have action upon one another; and if they could have it, a substantial form could not prevent or reconcile it." Therefore he concludes: "From this conservation of a temperament, made up of contrary qualities, taken precisely, a substantial form is not inferred; but this holds only so far as some quality, which had been increased or diminished from outside, returns to its former proportion when the external agent is removed. Yet this is no new argument, but coincides with that about the restoration of a thing to its natural state," which argument Fonseca himself proposes separately, and which we shall presently examine. Besides this answer of Suárez, truth itself supplies us with another and better one, which utterly renounces and condemns as an empty fiction whatever Hippocrates first, and Aristotle, and then Galen (who in this matter far surpassed his masters) imagined about temperaments arising from a certain proportion of the four so-called primary qualities. As we shall teach at length, with divine grace, in another more suitable place of this work.

units.la: XXIV. Prædictis de Temperamento subjungit Fonseca,
units.tr: XXIV. After the foregoing on temperament, Fonseca adds,

units.la: Quod quum morbus adversetur naturali statui animalium, sanitas vero eidem conveniens sit, (quibus affectionibus aliæ quoque in cæteris rebus, quæ dignantur & intereunt, proportione respondeant) & hæ contrariæ affectiones ex varietate primarum quatuor qualitatum nascantur; igitur natura aliqua lateat sub primis quatuor qualitatibus, cui affectio altera consentanea sit, altera dissentanea, præsertim quum sint admodum variæ in diversis rebus, & quæ uni congruit, alteri adversa sit. Cum igitur ea natura nec sola
units.tr: Since disease is opposed to the natural state of animals, and health is suited to it (and other things that are worthy and perish correspond in proportion to these affections), and since these contrary affections arise from the variety of the four primary qualities, therefore some nature lies hidden beneath the four primary qualities, to which one affection is consonant and another dissonant, especially since they are very varied in different things, and what agrees with one is adverse to another. Since then that nature is neither

units.la: {x} Sit vnde ætiam ... consentaneitas ... dissentaneitas. sola Materia sit, nec Materia cum quantitate, aut qualitate aliqua priori primis quatuor, non dubium esse quin constet ex Materia & Forma substantiali. Sed profecto ne tenuissimum quidem consequentiae vestigium est in hac argumentatione, neque ullo modo ex eo, quod morbus adversatur naturali statui, & sanitas eidem congruit, inferri potest Forma substantialis, neque eam fingere opus est, ut sit cui status ille naturalis, aut praeter naturam, congruat aut adversetur. Hoc enim est ipsa res, seu totum illud, quod ex Materia & accidentibus constat. quae accidentia si debito modo se habeant, tunc illa res recte valere dicitur, atque naturaliter se habere, quippe constituta in eo statu, qui isti speciei, ac proinde singulis speciei individuis, debetur. sin vero accidentia abeant a praescripto, necesse est illam rem male habere, quippe quae non fruitur eo statu, qui ipsi naturaliter competit, quomodo etiam in substantiis artificiosis, quae ex Materia certis accidentibus affecta constant, non quaerendum est aliquid aliud, cui conveniat aut adversetur recte vel secus se habere, praeter rem ipsam, quae ex subjecto ejusq; accidentibus consurgat. Et hoc quidem planius est, quam ut plura verba de eo fieri debeant: quare etiam Suarez silentio plane praeterijt hoc argumentum, utpote in quo non modo vim ullam probationis, sed neq; speciem quidem videret.
units.tr: {x} Let it be whence also ... agreeableness ... disagreeableness. Is it only matter, or matter together with some quantity or quality prior to the four primary ones? If not, there can be no doubt that it consists of matter and substantial form. But there is not even the faintest trace of consequence in this argument, and from the fact that disease is opposed to the natural state and health agrees with it, a substantial form cannot be inferred in any way, nor is it necessary to feign one, so that there may be something to which that natural, or against nature, state agrees or is opposed. For this is the thing itself, or that whole, which consists of matter and accidents. If these accidents are in due condition, then that thing is said to be well and to be in a natural condition, being established in that state which is owed to this species and therefore to each individual of the species. But if the accidents depart from the prescribed order, the thing must be ill, since it does not enjoy the state which naturally belongs to it. So also in artificial substances, which consist of matter affected by certain accidents, nothing else need be sought, besides the thing itself which arises from the subject and its accidents, to which it may agree or be opposed by being well or ill disposed. This is plainer than that many words need be spent on it. Therefore Suarez also passed over this argument in silence, since in it he saw not only no force of proof but not even the appearance of one.

units.la: XXV. Quartus & ultimus probationum locus Fonsecae desumitur ab Actionibus, non quidem omnibus simpliciter (quippe id jam prius in primo capite fecerat, & nos ibi id excussimus) sed peculiaribus quibusdam, ijsq; duorum tantum generum. Prioris generis facit actiones Potentiarum sive Facultatum, de quibus sic infit, Experimur res naturales ita saepe occupatus esse in operatione unius facultatis, ut simul exercere nequeant operationes aliarum, praesentibus etiam objectis, veluti quum quis ita intentus est in rem, quam oculis cernit, aut animo volvit, ut alta etiam voce clamantem non audiat, interdum ita sit totus in ea re occupatus, ut nec calor ipse stomachi quicquam pane operis faciat. In actione etiam & passione corporum inanimatorum sæpe fit, ut agens in superando externo contrario ita occupetur, ut interim non possit eam sui partem, quæ à contrario vincitur, simul tueri, donec externum contrarium itä superet, ut suis jam partibus in pristinum statum redeundi operam dare possit. Hoc autem quid aliud est, quam dari in unaquaque re naturali Materiam, atque Formam aliquam omnibus facultatibus priorem, isqué omnibus mirâ quadam ratione præsidentem, perqué eas operantem, cujus vires & applicatio cum sinite sint, si per unam facultatem alicui operi valde se applicet, sæpè neqneat per eandem, aut etiam per alias, in aliud opus incumbere. Deinde addit, Id quod in viventibus fieri dixit, non posse concursui spirituum principaliter tribui; quia etiamsi necesse est, ut quum illi frequentes confluunt ad unum membrum, alia deserant, tamen, nisi una Forma detur omnibus facultatibus natura prior, & quæ in suo ordine prima concurrat ad omnes rei actiones, ratio sæpe reddi non queat, cur ejusmodi spiritus, & quasi actionum ministri, non æque subserviant omnibus potentijs, sed alia membra deserant, ut alijs accurrant.
units.tr: XXV. The fourth and last ground of proof that Fonseca takes is from actions: not from all actions simply (for he had already done that in the first chapter, and we examined it there), but from certain peculiar ones, and only of two kinds. Of the first kind he makes the actions of powers or faculties, and he begins thus: We experience that natural things are often so occupied in the operation of one faculty that they cannot at the same time exercise the operations of others, even when objects are present; just as someone so intent on a thing he sees with his eyes or turns over in his mind that he does not hear another shouting in a loud voice; sometimes he is so wholly occupied with that thing that not even the heat of the stomach does any work at all. In the action and passion of inanimate bodies too it often happens that the agent, in overcoming an external contrary, is so occupied that meanwhile it cannot defend that part of itself which is overcome by the contrary, until it overcomes the external contrary, so that it can now set about restoring its parts to their former state. But what is this other than to say that in every natural thing there is a matter and some form prior to all the faculties, presiding over them all in a wondrous way and operating through them; whose powers and application, since they are finite, if it applies itself very much to some work through one faculty, can often not apply itself, through the same or even through others, to another work? Then he adds that what he said happens in living things cannot be attributed principally to the concourse of spirits. For even if it is necessary that, when these flow in frequently to one member, they desert the others, nevertheless, unless one Form is given which is prior by nature to all the faculties and which in its own order concurs first to all the actions of the thing, the reason often cannot be given why such spirits, and as it were ministers of actions, do not serve all the powers equally, but leave other members to run to others.

units.la: Hoc argumentum magni facit etiam Suarez. Experimur, inquit, rem aliquam habentem plures operandi facultates, dum intense per unam operatur, impediri ne per aliam operari possit, aut ne cum tanto conatu. ergo signum est, illas facultates esse subordinatas eidem Formæ, quæ per eas principaliter operetur. nam si nullam subordinationem inter se haberent, neq; cum aliquo communi Principio, qualibet earum haberet suam operationem independenter ab alia, neq; esset ulla ratio, cur conatus unius impediret conatum alterius, magis quam si essent in diversis subjectis. At vero ex subordinatione ad eandem Formam reddittur optima ratio, quia illa cum sit finita virtutis, dum intense applicatur ad unam operationem, distrahitur ab altera, & tanto conatu potest uni incumbere, ut ibi exhauriatur ejus virtus. Attamen quod Fonseca non solùm potentijs tantum animæ, sed & in inanimatis quærit hujus rei probationem, in eo ab ipso dissentit, ac ostendit ; dit, istam ab inanimatis confirmationem nullius esse roboris, ac proinde rejiciendam. Antecedens, inquit, ab aliquibus declaratur in rebus seu Agentibus naturalibus, que dum intense agunt ad vincendum contrarium, sese non possunt omnino tueri, quin aliqua ex parte vincantur, vel patiantur à contrario. Veruntamen hac experientia de repassione agentium naturalium non provenit ex subordinatione plurium facultatum ad unam Formam, sed ex eo quod res non est semper æque potens ad resistendum, ac est ad agendum. Unde etiam ferrum calidissimum, dum calefacit aquam, ab ea repatitur, quamvis Forma ferri nihil prorsus ad illam actionem conferat: imo ibi non intercedunt operationes diversarum facultatum, sed actio unius qualitatis, scilicet caloris, & actio eidem aliqua ex parte contraria, que ex eo provenit, quòd calor non est tam potens ad resistendum, quam ad agendum. Quocirca in rebus inanimatis vix credo inveniri posse experimentum aliquod, quo illud antecedens probetur; quia in actionibus accidentalibus, que à vitâ non procedunt, non videtur proxime intercedere aliquis concursus Forma substantialis, ratione cujus remittatur actio unius facultatis ex conatu alterius. Ita Suarez contra alteram hujus à Fonseca allati argumenti partem; quæ cum sufficienter hisce profligetur, nos aliud ad eam responsum non quæremus aut dabimus, hoc Suareziano contenti. Porro quod ad facultates animæ pertinet, in ijs rem esse planissimam putat Suarez, non minus quam ipse Fonseca. itaq; sic pergit: In viventibus autem, præsertim in nobis, experimur manifeste hujusmodi effectum, interdum enim interior cogitatio attenta impedit, ne res etiam præsentes videamus, imo & actionem nutritiva partis impedire solet diuturna meditatio. & hisce subjungit de concursu spirituum similia fere ac Fonseca, interq; alia dicit, Ipsum concursum spirituum ad unam facultatem magis quam ad aliam, esse signum unius Formæ utentis ipsis spiritibus & facultatibus ad duas actiones: quia aliàs nulla esset ratio, cur spiritus magis ad unam facultatem confluerét quam ad aliam. Et eandem hanc quæstionem etiam alibi, nimirum disp. 18. sect. 5. (quanquam alium in finem) tractat Suarez. summa autem eorum, quae ibi ad ab ipso dicuntur, haec est: Quod actiones vitales tam intimo modo fiant, ut ab ipso primo Principio vitae, quod est Anima, procedere videantur, hinc probari, quia ex nimia intentione ad opus unius facultatis, impeditur opus alterius (sicuti si nimis attente homo aliquid inspiciat, non audit loquentem) & attentio intellectus impedit operationem sensus (sicuti oculus, licet praesentem habeat imaginem, non videt, si anima ad illam non attendat) imo etiam opera nutritiva partis impedit, vel suspendit; cujus rei nulla foret ratio, si unaquaeque facultas sola per se ipsam haberet suam operationem. nam multiplicatis virtutibus, si una ab altera non pendet, neque amba ab uno tertio (cujus virtus, dum utrique applicatur, minuatur in singulis) nihil esse cur earum operationes non possint simul exerceri aeque perfecte. Posse etiam desumi argumentum a connexione operationum: nam dum intellectus intelligit, voluntatem exercitari ad amandum. hoc autem ideo esse, quia eadem anima per utramque potentiam actu operetur: nam solam veluti habitualem radicationem, sive remotam dimanationem ab eadem anima, non satis futaram ad hanc actualem causalitatem, seu motionem & exercitationem, si unaquaeque operatio a sua sola potentia actualiter prodiret, sine connexione in aliquo communi Principio.
units.tr: Suarez also makes much of this argument. We experience, he says, that a thing having several faculties of operating, while it operates intensely through one, is prevented from operating through another, or not with such effort. Therefore it is a sign that those faculties are subordinated to the same Form, which operates principally through them. For if they had no subordination among themselves, nor to any common principle, each would have its own operation independently of the other, and there would be no reason why the effort of one should hinder the effort of another, any more than if they were in different subjects. But from subordination to the same Form the best reason is given: because that Form, being finite in power, when intensely applied to one operation, is drawn away from another, and can lean upon one with such effort that its power is exhausted there. Yet in this Fonseca differs from him, in that he seeks proof of this not only in the powers of the soul but also in inanimate things, and shows that this confirmation from inanimate things is of no strength and therefore to be rejected. The antecedent, he says, is explained by some in natural agents, which, when they act intensely to overcome the contrary, cannot wholly defend themselves without being overcome in some part or suffering from the contrary. But this experience of natural agents being acted upon does not arise from the subordination of several faculties to one Form, but from the fact that a thing is not always as strong at resisting as it is at acting. Hence also red-hot iron, while it heats water, is itself acted upon by the water, although the form of the iron contributes nothing at all to that action. Nay, there no operations of diverse faculties intervene, but the action of one quality, namely heat, and an action partly contrary to it, which arises from the fact that heat is not as strong to resist as to act. Wherefore in inanimate things I scarcely think any experiment can be found by which that antecedent is proved; because in accidental actions, which do not proceed from life, no concourse of a substantial Form seems to intervene proximately, by reason of which the action of one faculty is relaxed through the effort of another. Thus Suarez against the other part of the argument brought forward by Fonseca. Since this is sufficiently overthrown by these words, we shall seek and give no other answer to it, content with this of Suarez. Further, as far as the faculties of the soul are concerned, Suarez thinks the matter as plain as Fonseca himself does. So he goes on: In living things, however, especially in ourselves, we clearly experience this kind of effect: for sometimes an attentive inner thought prevents us from seeing even present things; nay, lengthy meditation is wont to hinder even the nutritive action of a part. To these he adds, about the concourse of spirits, things much like Fonseca, and among other things he says: That the very concourse of spirits to one faculty rather than to another is a sign of one Form using the spirits and faculties for two actions, because otherwise there would be no reason why the spirits should flow more to one faculty than to another. Suarez treats this same question also elsewhere, namely disp. 18, sect. 5, though for another purpose. The sum of what he says there is this: That vital actions are done in so intimate a way that they seem to proceed from the very first principle of life, which is the soul, is proved thus: because by excessive intention to the work of one faculty, the work of another is impeded (as when a man attends too closely to something he does not hear one speaking to him), and the attention of the intellect impedes the operation of the sense (as the eye, though it has the image present, does not see if the soul does not attend to it); nay, the nutritive work of a part also impedes or suspends it. There would be no reason for this if each faculty by itself had its own operation. For when powers are multiplied, if one does not depend on another, nor both on some third (whose power, when applied to each, is diminished in each), there is no reason why their operations could not be exercised together, equally perfectly. An argument can also be drawn from the connection of operations: for while the intellect understands, the will is exercised in loving. This is so because the same soul operates actually through each power. For a mere habitual rooting, or remote emanation from the same soul, would not suffice for this actual causality, or motion and exercise, if each operation proceeded actually from its own power alone, without connection in some common principle.
XXVI.

units.la: Hae Fonsecae & Suarezij rationes, allatae ad probandum, quod ipsa animae substantia facultatibus suis cooperetur, quam non sint validae, apparebit ex nostra responsione, quam praecipue dirigemus ad posteriorem Suarezij locum e Disputatione decima octava, quandoquidem ibi rem hanc plenius tractat quam Fonseca, vel ipse in altero loco. Principio autem libenter concedimus, quod de spiritibus contendunt. tantum enim ab eo abfumus, ut eorum discursum faciamus principalem praesentis negotij Causam, ut ipsi nullum plane hic locum relinquamus. quippe vulgatam Aristotelicorum ac Galenicorum rum doctrinam de spiritibus, qui velut animæ vehiculum sint, eamq; suo interventu corpori connectant, omnino repudiamus, neq; ullos tales spiritus agnoscimus: cujus nostræ sententiæ suo loco idoneas rationes reddemus. De cætero autem sic respondemus. si substantia animæ, dum intense applicatur ad unam facultatem atq; operationem, distrahitur ab altera, hoc aliter fieri non potest, nisi ut plus de substantia animæ præsto sit illi potentiæ, cujus attentior operatio alterius potentiæ operationem obscurat. Ast istius assertionis absurditas tanta est, ut seipsam, vel nobis tacentibus, abunde refutet. Non enim potentiæ sunt res per se subsistentes, atq; aliquo loci spatio invicem disparatæ, ad quas anima modo accedat, modo ab ijs recedat, ita ut quanto magis uni appropinquat, tanto longinquius ab altero abeat. Sed neq; concesserint Peripatetici, ita distincte in anima inhærere potentias, ut suum cuiq; certum spatium sit attributum, quod ordinarie occupent, sed ita ut idem vel dilatetur, vel contrahatur, siquando vel hujus potentiæ, vel illius operationem anima attentius exercet; ita ut tot animæ partes, quot alicui potentiæ, cujus actio contentius editur, accedunt, totidem alteri subtrahantur ac decrescant. Ast præter hos duos modos ne fingi quidem alius potest, quo anima modo plus, modo minus de sua substantia huic aut illi potentiæ accommodet. Quodsi non hoc voluerunt, neq; hujusmodi animæ applicationem intelligunt, sed Metaphoricam; necesse est alterum duorum dicant, aut virtutem aliquam ab anima emanare in facultates, cujus virtutis ratione facultates ad agendum excitantur, atq; in agendo juventur; aut ipsam per se animam edere peculiarem actionem, quæ actio jungatur actioni facultatis, eiq; cooperetur, ita ut omnes actiones vitales è duabus quasi partibus constent, èq; duabus actionibus sint conflatæ, quarum altera sit actio facultatis, altera vero ipsius substantiæ animæ. Ast utrumvis horum dicant, summa seipsos absurditate involvent. Namq; & illa virtus emanans ab ipsis Peripateticis rejicitur pro ridiculo commento; & ne Thomistæ quidem (quorum nonnulli eam soli fovent) alibi locum ipsi faciunt, quam in substantiae generatione, sive Formae productione: uti supra quoque dicebamus. & actiones facultatum per se mancas esse ac mutilas, quare supplemento indigeant, quo hic earum defectus expleatur, nimirum ipsius animae cooperatione, non minus manifestariae est futilitatis. Sin vero per animae applicationem ad facultates & influxum ac cooperationem, intelligunt tantummodo, Facultates ab animae substantia moveri & excitari ad agendum (quod potius sensisse videtur Suarez, ut colligi potest ex his ejus verbis, Disp. 18. sect. 7. §. 3. Potentiae animae ad actiones vitales, merito dici possunt instrumenta conjuncta Animae, quatenus illi subordinantur sicut principali Formae, ut sine actuali influxu, & quasi motione illius, suas operationes efficere non possint) monstrandum illis superest, quo pacto animae substantia facultates sibi inhaerentes ciere ad agendum valeat. Id quod si facere nequeunt, veniam nobis dabunt, ut quomodo ipsi opinantur, facultates ab anima instingui ad agendum, indeq; fieri, ut plures operationes simul exerceri attente non possint, quia anima nequeat plures eodem tempore facultates aeque potenter ad munera sua obeunda concitare; ita nos opinemur, potius proficisci a tacita quadam inter ipsas facultates conspiratione, atq; conjunctione, quod unius facultatis intentior operatio alterius operationem praepediat; quia nimirum Deus ita istas facultates instituerit, atq; inter se coordinaverit, ut non possint plures simul summa cum attentione exerceri, a quo etiam naturali consensu, vel connexione, aut quomodocunq; appellare libet, pendeat, quod una facultas ab alia excitetur ad agendum. solam enim habitualem in eadem anima radicationem (ut Suarez loquitur) non esse satis ut una facultas ab altera excitetur ad agendum, ultro concedimus. Et quanquam exemplum a Suarezio positum non probamus (intellectum enim & voluntatem non putamus esse duas distinctas facultates, sed unam sub diversis respectibus consideratam; qua de re alibi plura) pro certo tamen habemus, dari illam facultatum cultatum connexionem, qua una ab altera ad agendum impellatur. Sane tacita hæc impulsio miro quodam fit & ine-narabili modo, cujus tamen vestigia sparsa sunt per totam rerum naturam: in qua cum videamus plurimas actiones, quæ in eo consistunt, ut virtutes dissitorum corporum inter se agant (quarum actionum, etiamsi ipsæ sint certissimæ, rationem tamen nemo satis explicaverit) quid mirum est, si unius ejusdemq; corporis virtutes eam fortitæ sunt conditionem, ut invicem ciere queant? Quanquam autem explicare non possumus, quomodo facultas altera alteram impellat, & quare duæ simul facultates intente operari non valeant; non tamen propterea potior est adversariorum opinio, quandoquidem neq; ipsi declarare valeunt, quomodo animæ substantia facultates moveat ad agendum, & quare duas simul facultates æque perfecte movere nequeat: quamobrem hoc quidem respectu nihilo probabiliora illi dicunt, quam nos dicimus. Aliunde tamen potiorem esse nostram sententiam, ex iis apparebit, quæ postea de Anima docebimus, videlicet duas distinctas esse in homine animas, unam mortalem, corpori addictam, ejusq; commodis inservientem, & sensuum ac motuum autorem; alteram vero immortalem, intellectu ac ratione præditam. ast hoc posito (quod ponendum esse, firmis argumentis evincemus) omnino necessarium est, rem ita se habere, ac nos dicimus. Non modo enim animæ mortalis facultates inter sese, sed & Mentis facultates cum nonnullis alterius animæ facultatibus habent hanc, quam dicebamus, connexionem, easq; ad agendum ciere valent: ubi non potest ille instinctus, quo facultas ad operandum excitatur, ad animæ substantiam referri (quum ne imaginari quidem possimus, quomodo substantia unius animæ in alterius animæ potentias hoc jus exerceat) sed omnino inter ipsas facultates est collocandus. Porro etiamsi totum hoc, quod hic intendunt Fonseca ac Suarez de animæ cooperatione cum suis potentijs, ipsis concederetur, nihil tamen inde lucrarentur ad Formæ demonstrationem. Siquid enim utilitatis ijs hic ab animabus provenire
units.tr: These arguments of Fonseca and Suárez, brought forward to prove that the substance of the soul itself cooperates with its faculties, will be shown to be weak by our reply, which we shall direct chiefly at the later passage of Suárez, from Disputation eighteen, since there he treats this matter more fully than Fonseca, or than he himself in the other passage. At the outset we gladly concede what they contend about spirits. We are so far from making their discussion of spirits the principal cause of the present business that we leave them no place here at all. Indeed we utterly reject the common doctrine of the Aristotelians and Galenists about spirits, which are as it were the vehicle of the soul and by their intervention join it to the body, and we acknowledge no such spirits. We will give suitable reasons for this opinion of ours in its own place. But as to the rest, we reply thus. If the substance of the soul, while it is intensely applied to one faculty and operation, is drawn away from another, this cannot happen otherwise than that more of the substance of the soul is present to that faculty whose more attentive operation obscures the operation of another faculty. But the absurdity of this assertion is so great that it refutes itself abundantly, even if we keep silent. For faculties are not things subsisting in themselves and separated from one another by some interval of place, to which the soul now draws near and now withdraws, so that the more it approaches one, the further it departs from another. Nor would the Peripatetics concede that the faculties inhere in the soul so distinctly that each has its own certain space assigned to it, which it ordinarily occupies. Rather, the same space is either expanded or contracted whenever the soul exercises more attentively the operation of this or that faculty, so that as many parts of the soul as come to some faculty whose action is more intensely put forth, so many are withdrawn from another and diminish. But beyond these two ways no other can even be imagined by which the soul would apportion more or less of its substance to this or that faculty. If they did not mean this, and do not understand such an application of the soul but a metaphorical one, then they must say one of two things: either some power emanates from the soul into the faculties, by virtue of which the faculties are roused to act and are aided in acting; or the soul itself produces a peculiar action of its own, which is joined to the action of the faculty and cooperates with it, so that all vital actions consist, as it were, of two parts and are compounded of two actions, one being the action of the faculty and the other the action of the substance of the soul itself. But whichever of these they say, they will entangle themselves in the greatest absurdity. For that emanating power is rejected by the Peripatetics themselves as a ridiculous invention, and the Thomists too (some of whom alone cherish it) assign it a place nowhere except in the generation of a substance, or the production of a form, as we also said above. And that the actions of the faculties are in themselves maimed and mutilated, so that they need a supplement by which their defect is made good here, namely the cooperation of the soul itself, is no less manifestly futile. But if by the application of the soul to the faculties, and by influx and cooperation, they mean only this, that the faculties are moved and roused by the substance of the soul to act (which Suárez seems rather to have thought, as may be gathered from these his words, Disp. 18, sect. 7, §3: The powers of the soul for vital actions can rightly be called instruments conjoined to the soul, insofar as they are subordinated to it as to its principal Form, so that they cannot produce their operations without its actual influx, and as it were its motion), it remains for them to show by what means the substance of the soul is able to rouse the faculties inhering in it to act. If they cannot do this, they will pardon us if, while they think the faculties are stirred by the soul to act, and hence that several operations cannot be exercised attentively at the same time because the soul cannot rouse several faculties equally powerfully to discharge their offices at once, we on our part think rather that this arises from a certain tacit conspiracy and conjunction among the faculties themselves, so that the more intent operation of one faculty hinders the operation of another. This is because God has evidently so instituted these faculties and coordinated them among themselves that several cannot be exercised together with the greatest attention; and on this natural consent or connection (or whatever one likes to call it) depends the fact that one faculty is roused by another to act. For we readily concede that a merely habitual rooting in the same soul (as Suárez puts it) is not enough for one faculty to be roused by another to act. And although we do not approve the example Suárez gives (for we do not think the intellect and the will are two distinct faculties, but one considered under different aspects, a matter on which we say more elsewhere), we nevertheless hold for certain that there is that connection of faculties by which one is impelled by another to act. Indeed this tacit impulse happens in a certain wonderful and inexplicable manner, yet its traces are scattered throughout the whole of nature. For since we see very many actions which consist in the powers of distant bodies acting upon one another (and no one has yet sufficiently explained the reason for these actions, though the actions themselves are most certain), what wonder is it if the powers of one and the same body have this condition, that they can rouse one another? Although we cannot explain how one faculty impels another, and why two faculties cannot operate intently at the same time, the opinion of our opponents is not for that reason the stronger, since they too cannot declare how the substance of the soul moves the faculties to act, and why it cannot move two faculties equally perfectly at the same time. Wherefore in this respect they say nothing more probable than we do. Yet on other grounds our opinion will appear the stronger, from what we shall teach later about the soul: namely, that there are in man two distinct souls, one mortal, bound to the body and serving its advantages, and the author of the senses and motions; the other immortal, endowed with intellect and reason. But granted this (which we shall prove by firm arguments must be granted), it is wholly necessary that the matter stands as we say. For not only the faculties of the mortal soul among themselves, but also the faculties of the Mind with some faculties of the other soul, have this connection of which we spoke and can rouse one another to act. Here that impulse by which a faculty is excited to operate cannot be referred to the substance of the soul (since we cannot even imagine how the substance of one soul could exercise this right over the powers of another soul), but must be placed wholly among the faculties themselves. Moreover, even if all that Fonseca and Suárez maintain here about the cooperation of the soul with its powers were granted them, they would gain nothing thereby for the demonstration of Form. For if any advantage were to come to them here from the souls
{x} It is established, I know not how.

units.la: {x} Forte habuerunt quia sunt in arbitrio meo, sortes mea. venire potest, id non ab ipsarum cum facultatibus suis cooperatione, sed ab ipsis directo sumere debebant; ut quandoquidem animas in Formarum numerum redigere solent, & nos fatemur animas (ac proinde aliquas Formas, ex eorum loquendi more) dari, inde porro inferant, reliquas quoq; dari Formas substantiales. Quodsi autem haec argumentatio nihil ipsos juvat, atq; inanis deprehenditur (uti sane facit: quod infra contra Suarezium demonstrabimus) multo minus ipsos juvabit, quicquid de animae operationibus atq; cooperationibus dicere valent. Namq; si vel maxime verum esset, facultates animae non esse sui martis in agendo, sed indigere concursu ipsius substantiae animae ad operationes suas obeundas, non tamen inde sequeretur, dari Formas substantiales (quae enim haec est ratiocinationis species, Anima cooperatur facultatibus suis; ergo dantur Formae substantiales) sed hoc duntaxat, Quod cum aliae qualitates activae verissime sint Principia principalia suarum actionum, quia ex vi illius perfectionis solius, quam habent ex sua specie vel entitate, eliciunt tales actiones (sicuti hac de re loquitur Suarez) potentiae animae non sint nisi Principia instrumentaria suarum operationum, quum ab ipsa anima substantia, tanquam a primario agente, ad operandum cieantur: id quod nihil plane facit ad propositum, atq; ad probandas Formas substantiales.
units.tr: {x} Perhaps they had it because they are at my disposal, my lot. might come to them, it should not come from the cooperation of the souls with their faculties, but they ought to draw it directly from the souls themselves. For since they are accustomed to reduce souls to the number of Forms, and we admit that souls (and therefore, in their manner of speaking, some Forms) are given, they could then infer that the remaining substantial Forms are given too. But if this argument does nothing to help them, and is shown to be empty (as indeed it is, as we shall demonstrate against Suárez below), it will help them far less whatever they can say about the operations and cooperations of the soul. For even if it were most true that the faculties of the soul are not sufficient of themselves in acting, and need the concurrence of the substance of the soul to discharge their operations, it would not follow from this that substantial Forms are given. (For what kind of reasoning is this: the soul cooperates with its faculties; therefore substantial Forms are given?) It would follow only this: that since other active qualities are most truly the principal principles of their own actions, because they elicit such actions by the force of that perfection alone which they have from their species or entity (as Suárez speaks on this matter), the powers of the soul are only the instrumental principles of their operations, since they are roused to act by the substance of the soul itself as by the primary agent. This contributes nothing whatever to the purpose, or to proving substantial Forms.

units.la: XXVII. Aliud Actionum genus, quibus ad asserendam Formam substantialem hic utitur Fonseca, est reductio rerum ad naturalem statum, ut cum aqua calefacta recuperat nativum frigus, remoto calefaciente: id quod non nisi a Forma substantiali fieri posse asseverat. Et hoc argumentum Suarez quoq; multis prosequitur.
units.tr: XXVII. Another kind of action, by which Fonseca here tries to establish a substantial form, is the return of things to their natural state: when heated water recovers its native coldness once the heating agent is removed. He asserts that this can be done only by a substantial form. Suarez also pursues this argument at length.

units.la: Quod autem hoc debeat ascribi, inde inferunt, quia neq; Principium externum ejus rei Causa esse potest, neq; aliud Principium internum. Non defuerunt quidem, qui Principio externo hoc referrent acceptum; sed eos errare & ipsi monstrare conantur, & nos libenter concedimus. Quod autem haud aliud Principium internum, quam Formaman
units.tr: They infer that this must be ascribed to the form because no external principle can be the cause of the thing, and no other internal principle can be either. Some have indeed attributed this to an external principle, but we try to show that they are wrong, and we gladly grant the point. However, we do not agree with them that no internal principle other than the Form (or matter) can be the cause of this effect.

units.la: × emancipatas seu ubnoxias mam, hujus rei Causam statui posse dicunt; in eo haud quaquam ipsis accedimus. Sane reliquas omnes de Principijs internis opiniones (varij enim varia hic dixerunt, uti apud ipsos videre est, & nos infra alia occasione paulo latius exponemus) unaniniter cum ipsis rejicimus: sed Qualitatem Virtualem irrito conatu ab ipsis impugnari dicimus, proptereaq; nihil impedire, quominus ipsi hujus reductionis Causa attribuatur. Per Qualitatem autem Virtualem (ut recepto hic, quanquam minus probo, vocabulo utamur) intelligitur Qualitas ejusmodi, quę alteram diversi ordinis Qualitatem in suo subjecto producere valeat. Contra hanc Qualitatem quatuor à Suarezio argumenta proferuntur. Primum est, Quia repugnet, dari in Elementis Qualitates aliquas priores primis; quum teste Ariftotele primæ Elementorum Qualitates, sint formalis calor, frigiditas, &c. Alterum, Quia illa Qualitas immediate & per se non sentitur, sed ex hoc effectu naturalis emanationis dignoscitur; quare nullo fundamento dicatur, illud internum Principium esse Qualitatem accidentalem, & non Formam substantialem. Tertium, Illud Principium esse primum actum Materiæ, complentem cum illa hoc ens naturale, quod aquam appellamus: ergo esse actum substantialem, & non accidentalem. Quartum, Quodsi frigori in aqua respondeat Qualitas virtualis, seu frigus virtuale; debere etiam humiditati, densitati, & aliis proprietatibus, respondere totidem Qualitates Virtuales (quia etiam in hisce aqua immutata à naturali statu, statim ad eum redit, simul ac contrarium agens recesserit) quod natura abhorreat, ac omnino superfluum sit: ac proinde ponendam esse unam Formam substantialem, in qua omnes illæ proprietates radicentur ac colligentur. His objectionibus satisfacere, perquam est proclive. Sane adeo sunt infirmæ, ut duas aut tres primas indignas duxerit Fonseca, quarum mentionem faceret: Quantum enim ad primum, id nuda innititur Ariftotelis aliorúmque, qui in hac re cum ipso senserunt, autoritate, quæ contra veritatem valere nihil quicquam debet. Non enim ex eo, quod Ariftoteles stoteles alijq; Calorem, Frigus, Humiditatem, & Siccitatem, appellaverunt Qualitates Primas, sequitur, alias qualitates hisce priores non dari, sed ab ijs agnitas non fuisse, id quod duntaxat ipsorum ignorantiam arguit: quam ne nimium miremur, faciunt alia multa ac gravissima peccata, in negotio Qualitatum ab ijs commissa, inter quae haud postremum est, quod in decantatissimo illo Quaternario duo reposuerunt, quae neq; Qualitates Primae sint dicendae, neq; secundae, neq; Qualitates omnino; humiditatem inquimus & siccitatem, quas in Qualitatum censum perperam referri, alibi ostendemus. & ipsum quoque illud Primarum nomen hisce qualitatibus (etiam ijs, quae re vera sunt Qualitates, Calori & Frigori) temere admodum impositum fuisse, suo loco planum faciemus. Quamobrem frivola prorsus haec est ratio, quae Qualitates virtuales ideo rejicit, quia Aristoteles alijq; Calorem, Frigus, &c. dixerunt Qualitates primas. Secundum argumentum aeque contra Formam retorqueri potest, ac contra Qualitatem Virtualem intenditur. Namq; & illa immediate ac per se non sentitur (uti clarum est, atq; omnes Peripatetici unanimiter fatentur) & ex hoc tantum effectu conjectura ejus capitur. namq; caetera omnia, unde ea astruitur, plane nihili sunt, uti ex supra dictis apparuit, & ex postea dicendis amplius apparebit. quare nobis liceat, contrario modo, quam ipse facit, concludere, Quod nullo fundamento dicatur, illud internum Principium esse Formam substantialem, & non Qualitatem accidentalem. Tertium vero argumentum respicit Peripateticum somnium de potentialitate (ut vocant) Materiae, quae nullam a se existentiam habeat, neq; subsistere omnino valeat, nisi aliunde actuetur. quod si quis hoc de Materia somnium fovens, dicit Virtuale frigus esse id, quo Materia prima actuetur ad hoc substantiae genus, quod aquam vocamus, constituendum; contra eam fortasse valeat haec argumentatio, negans ejusmodi Materiam posse ab accidente actuari. Sed nos & totum hoc de Materia prima ejusq; actuatione commentum rejicimus; & nullo modo dicimus, aquam ab ista qualiqualitate habere ut aqua sit; quum essentialis Elementorum differentia, qua & ipsa in certo substantiæ genere collocantur, & ab omnibus alijs Elementis atq; substantijs distinguntur, non tam in ullis accidentibus, quam in substantiali ipsorum parte sita sit: uti supra quoque monuimus. quare nullam planè vim habet hoc quoque argumentum. Sed neq; majoris ponderis est quartum: quippe & absurdum magnopere non foret, plures qualitates Virtuales in uno Elemento statuere, si res id ita requireret; neq; tamen id facere necessarium est. vix enim plures quàm duæ aut tres in universum sunt Qualitates, quæ in suis subjectis respondentes sibi habeant Qualitates Virtuales; & harum non nisi una in ullo Elemento reperitur, videlicet frigus. calor enim nulli Elemento naturaliter competit, sicuti alias docebimus. Multa autem eorum, quæ vulgo pro Qualitatibus Elementorum habentur, non sunt Qualitates, aut accidentia omnino, sed modi substantiales, unde neque amitti possunt, ac proinde non indigent Principio, à quo restituantur. Siqua autem alia accidentia Elementis naturaliter insunt, aut ne recuperare quidem ea sua sponte possunt semel amissa; aut si queunt, nullo ad id peculiari Principio indigent: quæ omnia ex particulari Elementorum historiâ, suis locis in hoc opere pertractandâ, fient manifesta. Et sic quartum quoq; Suarezij argumentum enervavimus, quum virtualium qualitatum ea in uno subjecto multitudo (quam ipse criminatur) nulla sit metuenda, etiamsi aquæ reductionem ad naturale frigus, aliasq; consimiles reductiones, Qualitatibus Virtualibus referamus acceptas. Quum itaq; appareat, ea quæ contra Qualitates Virtuales dicuntur, ne minimi quidem esse momenti, concidit hoc quoq; pro Forma argumentum, à reductione rerum ad naturalem statum petitum, quippe quum liceat illam reductionem alteri Causæ referre acceptam, ut proinde nulla necessitas urgeat, aut probabilitas suadeat, ob eam ponere Formas substantiales.
units.tr: Certainly we reject with them all the other opinions about internal principles. (Different men have said different things here, as one can see in their works, and we shall set them out more fully elsewhere.) But we say that the virtual quality is attacked by them in vain, and so nothing prevents this return from being attributed to it. By virtual quality (using the term as it is received here, though I approve it less) we mean a quality of such a kind that it can produce another quality of a different order in its subject. Suarez brings four arguments against this quality. The first is that it is impossible for the elements to have any qualities prior to the first ones, since, according to Aristotle, the first qualities of the elements are formal heat, cold, and so on. The second is that this quality is not perceived immediately and of itself, but is recognised only from the effect of its natural emanation; so it is said, with no foundation, that this internal principle is an accidental quality and not a substantial form. The third is that this principle is the first act of matter, which completes with it the natural being that we call water; therefore it is a substantial act and not an accidental one. The fourth is that if a virtual quality corresponds to the coldness in water, then equally many virtual qualities must correspond to its wetness, density and other properties (since water, changed in these respects too, returns to its natural state as soon as the contrary agent withdraws). Nature abhors this, and it is wholly superfluous; therefore one substantial form must be posited, in which all those properties are rooted and gathered together. It is quite easy to answer these objections. Indeed they are so weak that Fonseca thought the first two or three unworthy of mention. As to the first, it rests bare on the authority of Aristotle and the others who agreed with him in this matter, and such authority ought to count for nothing against the truth. For it does not follow, from the fact that Aristotle and the others called heat, cold, moisture and dryness first qualities, that no other qualities prior to these exist, or that they were not known to them. That only shows their ignorance; and we should not be too surprised at it, since they made many other very serious errors about qualities. Among these, not the least is that in their much-celebrated quaternary they included two things which should be called neither first qualities, nor second qualities, nor qualities at all: I mean moisture and dryness, which we shall show elsewhere are wrongly counted among the qualities. And we shall make plain in its place that the very name first was rashly applied to these qualities (even to those which really are qualities, heat and cold). Therefore this reason, which rejects virtual qualities on the ground that Aristotle and others called heat, cold, and so on first qualities, is utterly frivolous. The second argument can be turned against the form just as much as it is aimed against the virtual quality. For the form too is not perceived immediately and of itself (as is clear, and all the Peripatetics unanimously admit), and its existence is conjectured only from this effect. All the other things from which it is supported are plainly worthless, as has appeared from what was said above and will appear more fully from what follows. So we may, in the opposite way to his, conclude that since it is said, with no foundation, that this internal principle is a substantial form and not an accidental quality, the argument is inconclusive. The third argument concerns the Peripatetic dream of the so-called potentiality of matter, which has no existence of its own and cannot subsist at all unless it is actualised by something else. If someone who cherishes this fiction about matter says that the virtual cold is that by which prime matter is actualised so as to constitute this kind of substance which we call water, then perhaps this argument may hold against him, denying that such matter can be actualised by an accident. But we reject the whole fiction about prime matter and its actualisation, and we do not say at all that water has from that quality its being water. For the essential difference of the elements, by which they are placed in a definite kind of substance and distinguished from all other elements and substances, lies not so much in any accidents as in their substantial part, as we have also noted above. Therefore this argument too has no force whatever. Nor is the fourth of greater weight. Indeed it would not be greatly absurd to posit several virtual qualities in one element, if the thing required it; yet it is not necessary to do so. For there are hardly more than two or three qualities in general which have corresponding virtual qualities in their subjects, and of these only one is found in any element, namely cold. For heat belongs naturally to no element, as we shall teach elsewhere. Moreover, many of the things commonly held to be qualities of the elements are not qualities or accidents at all, but substantial modes; and so they cannot be lost, and consequently do not need a principle by which they are restored. If any other accidents are naturally inherent in the elements, either they cannot recover of their own accord once lost, or if they can, they need no special principle for it. All this will become clear from the particular history of the elements, to be treated in their proper places in this work. And so we have also weakened Suarez's fourth argument, since the multiplicity of virtual qualities in one subject, of which he accuses us, is nothing to fear, even if we attribute the return of water to its natural cold, and other similar returns, to virtual qualities. Since it therefore appears that what is said against virtual qualities is of no account at all, this argument for the form, drawn from the return of things to their natural state, also falls, since that return may be attributed to another cause; so no necessity presses, and no probability recommends, that substantial forms be posited on account of it.

units.la: XXVIII. Huic de Reductione argumento aliud velut N ipsius
units.tr: XXVIII. To this argument about reduction, another argument of his, as it were...
Chapter I.

units.la: Ipsius consectarium subjungit Suarez, unde itidem probet Formam substantialem: quia nimirum alteratio in rebus inanimatis (ac multo evidentius in animatis) alias fit pura, ac maneat intra latitudinem mutationis substantialis, ita ut res alteratae maneant integrae, vel fere integrae in substantia sua, & facile ad priorem statum revertantur, si actio contrarij cessaret; sicuti videmus in aqua & ferro calefactis: interdum vero ita procedat, ut omnimoda transmutatio rei fiat, ac passum illud, quamvis removeatur agens, nunquam possit ad pristinum statum redire. Hanc autem majorem mutationem non posse esse aliam, nisi quia ipsum subsistentiale compositum dissolvitur, recedente Forma substantiali. Ultimam subsumtionem (ut vocat) ita probare instituit: Quia si tota substantia rei semper aeque maneret integra, quantumcunq; procederet alteratio, ipsa de se semper haberet eandem habitudinem ad accidentia. ergo vel semper post quamcunq; alterationem maneret quieta sub quibuscunq; accidentibus, quantum esset ex se, & remoto contrario agente; vel certe remotis ijsdem agentibus semper rediret ad eadem accidentia. Hisce porro aliud adtexit, de inseparabilitate nonnullorum accidentium. Quædam enim accidentia a quibusdam subjectis adeo esse inseparabilia, ut si illa auferantur, vel nimium diminuantur, omnimoda transmutatio fiat in subjectis, ita ut non possint per intrinsecam vim ad pristinum statum redire. ergo illam inseparabilitatem provenire ex connexione talium accidentium cum aliquo Principio interno talium rerum. quod cum nequeat esse Materia prima (quia respectu illius nullum accidens est inseparabile, ex his quæ per alterationem possunt acquiri vel amitti) neq; aliquod accidens; sistendum necessario esse in aliqua Forma, quæ sit prima respectu accidentium inseparabilium, illam ergo esse Formam substantialem, non accidentalem, cum constituat proprium essentiam, cui proprietates accidentales connaturaliter & inseparabiliter insunt. Quantum ad posteriorem hujus argumentationis partem, illi de novo respondere non est necesse, quum sufficiat huc accommodare dare ea, quæ supra paragrapho vigesimo disputavimus, ostendendo, proprietates rerum non arguere aliquod internum Principium substantiale, quod eas hoc vel alio modo & gradu requirat, sed sufficere specificam naturam & perfectionem ab ipso Deo institutam, cujus ratione sua certa accidentia in certis subjectis requirantur. Sane ab eadem Causa, à qua proficiscitur, ut sua certa naturaliter cuiq; rei sint accidentia, fit etiam, ut alia Accidentia sint separabilia, alia vero secus. Quanquam enim omnia accidentia, quæ alteratione acquiri vel amitti possunt, sint separabilia ratione Materiæ; ipsa tamen specifica rei natura facit, ut nonnulla ipsorum sint inseparabilia; non ut omnino à subjecto suo separari non possint, sed ut nequeant separari à re, ipsâ salvâ manente. Quod enim præcipuum est ad essentiam rei constituendam, illud tolli absq; rei pernicie non potest. Quum igitur res manere nequeat, natura suâ amissâ; & natura ipsa subsistere nequeat, ac nomen suum tueri, si id, quod in ea præcipuum est, perierit; hinc fit, ut accidentia quædam sint inseparabilia, id est, ejusmodi, quæ auferri, nisi ut res ipsa, cujus pars sunt, pereat, non possunt: quum alia accidentia minus principalia abesse citra rei exitium queant. quod declarari quodammodo potest exemplo corporum organicorum, quæ nonnullarum quidem partium jacturam sustinent, ijsq; mutilata subsistere tamen valent; nonnullæ vero partes si auferantur, ipsius corporis ratio destruitur, neq; subsistere id amplius potest, aut officium suum implere: quod latius à nobis exponitur sequentis capitis sectione secunda, paragrapho decimo octavo. Quod igitur Accidentia nonnulla sunt inseparabilia, id non indicat, latere sub ijs Formam aliquam substantialem, cum qua connexionem habeant, sed ipsa esse præcipua in essentia talis naturæ constituenda, quæ natura proinde ijs ablatis subsistere nequeat; quare ipsorum amissione rem ipsam, cujus erant, destrui necesse sit. Et doceri hoc amplius potest exemplis animarum mortalium (quales sunt illæ brutorum & stirpium, & inferior hominum anima) quarum unaquæq; suis certis facultatibus est instructa, &
units.tr: Suarez adds a corollary of this argument, by which he likewise proves a substantial form. In inanimate things (and far more evidently in animate ones), he says, alteration sometimes remains pure and stays within the range of accidental change, so that the altered things remain whole, or nearly whole, in their substance and readily return to their former state once the action of the contrary agent ceases. We see this in water and iron that have been heated. At other times, however, the alteration proceeds so far that the thing is wholly transformed, and the patient cannot return to its earlier state even when the agent is removed. He argues that this greater change could only happen because the substantial composite itself is dissolved when the substantial form departs. He sets out to prove the final premise (as he calls it) in this way: if the whole substance of a thing always remained equally whole, however far the alteration went, it would of itself always have the same relation to its accidents. Therefore either, after any alteration whatever, it would always remain, of its own nature, at rest under whatever accidents, once the contrary agent was removed; or, with the same agents removed, it would always return to the same accidents. To these he adds another point, about the inseparability of certain accidents. For some accidents are so inseparable from certain subjects that, if they are taken away or greatly diminished, a complete transformation takes place in the subjects, so that they cannot return to their former state by any inner power. Therefore that inseparability must arise from the connection of such accidents with some internal principle of such things. Since this cannot be prime matter (because no accident is inseparable with respect to prime matter, among those that can be acquired or lost through alteration), nor any accident, we must necessarily stop at some form which is first with respect to the inseparable accidents. This, then, must be a substantial form, not an accidental one, since it constitutes the essence itself, in which the accidental properties inhere naturally and inseparably. As for the latter part of this argument, it is not necessary to reply to it afresh, since it suffices to apply here what we disputed above in paragraph twenty, showing that the properties of things do not indicate some internal substantial principle which requires them in this or that way and degree, but that the specific nature and perfection instituted by God himself is sufficient, by reason of which certain accidents are required in certain subjects. Indeed, from the same Cause from which it comes that each thing naturally has its own particular accidents, it also comes that some accidents are separable and others are not. For although all accidents that can be acquired or lost through alteration are separable with respect to matter, the specific nature of the thing itself makes some of them inseparable; not in the sense that they cannot be separated at all from their subject, but in the sense that they cannot be separated from the thing while the thing itself remains intact. For what is chief in constituting the essence of a thing cannot be removed without the thing's ruin. Since, then, a thing cannot remain once its nature is lost, and a nature cannot subsist or keep its name if what is chief in it has perished, it follows that some accidents are inseparable, that is, of such a kind that they cannot be taken away unless the thing of which they are parts perishes, whereas other, less principal accidents can be absent without the thing's destruction. This can be explained in some measure by the example of organic bodies, which sustain the loss of certain parts and can nonetheless subsist mutilated; but if certain other parts are removed, the very reason of the body is destroyed, and it can no longer subsist or perform its function. This is set out more fully by us in the second section of the following chapter, paragraph eighteen. Therefore, that some accidents are inseparable does not indicate that some substantial form lies hidden beneath them with which they have a connection, but that they themselves are chief in constituting the essence of such a nature, which therefore cannot subsist once they are taken away; so that, when they are lost, the thing to which they belonged must necessarily be destroyed. And this can be taught further by the examples of mortal souls (such as those of the brutes and of plants, and the lower soul of man), each of which is furnished with its own certain faculties, and
