units.la: & ijs amissis, pro anima censeri nequaquam potest. neq; tamen hic fingere licet Formam aliquam substantialem, cujus ratione illæ facultates suis subjectis insint (quum ipsas has animas plerique Peripatetici, & duas saltem ipsarum species, brutorum, ac stirpium, omnes unanimiter habeant pro Formis, in quibus proinde aliæ Formæ inesse minime queant) sed ipsa specifica ratio sufficit, quæ nimirum requirit, ad animæ alicujus constitutionem, ut hæc vel illa accidentia in proprio subjecto concurrant; sicuti ipsius animalis vel stirpis specifica ratio postulat, ut talis anima (nimirum è tali subjecto ac talibus accidentibus confiata) tali corpori jungatur. Sicuti autem in animabus res clara est, accidentia ipsarum, quanquam ratione subjecti sint separabilia, esse tamen inseparabilia, non ratione alicujus interni Principij substantialis, cui proxime connectantur, ac cujus ratione ipsi subjecto, cui inhærent, & cum quo juncta animam constituunt, committantur & colligentur, sed quia ipsa specifica ratio illud exigit; (sicuti ipsi Peripatetici hoc, velint nolint, fateri coguntur) ita de aliis quoq; rebus, accidentia inseparabilia sortitis, res sese habet; ut nimirum accidentium illa inseparabilitas provenit non ab ipsorum connexione cum aliqua Forma substantiali, sed a specifica ratione ipsius rei, quæ ex illis accidentibus suo subjecto unitis consurgit. Quantum vero ad alteram hujus argumenti partem, quæ Formas substantiales arguit ex eo, quod nonnullis alterationibus conjungitur ipsius rei corruptio; & ipsa nihilo melior est aut validior. Namq; quod nonnullæ Alterationes conjunctam habeant majorem rei mutationem, adeo ut ipsum substantiale compositum dissolvatur, facile probatu est, atq; adeo superfluum, quum id per se sit manifestum. Quod vero illa compositi dissolutio fiat recedente Forma substantiali, sive quod illa dissolutio nihil sit aliud quam ipsa Formæ recessio, neque hinc sequitur, neq; ab ipso Suarezio probatur. Quippe probatio subsumtionis non plus infert, nisi totam rei substantiam in hujusmodi mutationibus non manere integram, id quod libenter concedimus: sed hoc
units.tr: and once these are lost, it can by no means be counted as the soul. Yet here we may not invent some substantial form by whose agency those faculties inhere in their subjects. Most Peripatetics unanimously hold these souls, and at least two of their kinds, those of brutes and of plants, to be forms, and in forms no other forms can inhere. The specific nature of the thing is sufficient for this. It alone requires, for the constitution of a given soul, that these or those accidents concur in their proper subject, just as the specific nature of the animal or plant itself demands that such a soul (namely one made up of such a subject and such accidents) be joined to such a body. Now in souls the matter is clear: their accidents, although they are separable in respect of the subject, are nonetheless inseparable. This is not because of any internal substantial principle to which they are immediately connected, and by which they are bound and gathered into the subject in which they inhere and with which they together constitute the soul. Rather it is because the specific nature itself demands it (as the Peripatetics themselves are forced to admit, whether they like it or not). The same holds for other things that possess inseparable accidents. The inseparability of such accidents arises not from their connection with some substantial form, but from the specific nature of the thing itself, which arises from those accidents united to their subject. As for the other part of this argument, which infers substantial forms from the fact that the thing's destruction is joined to certain alterations, it is no better and no stronger. That certain alterations bring with them a greater change in the thing, so that the substantial composite itself is dissolved, is easy to prove, and therefore superfluous, since it is self-evident. But that this dissolution of the composite happens by the withdrawal of the substantial form, or that the dissolution is nothing other than the withdrawal of the form, does not follow from this, nor is it proved by Suarez himself. The proof of the minor premise infers no more than that the whole substance of the thing does not remain intact in such changes, which we gladly concede. But this

units.la: × quo jure requirit quo jure hæc vel illa quo jure?
units.tr: By what right does it require? By what right this or that? By what right?
Not by the nature of the thing.
But because it so pleased wisdom.
By the sorting and redistribution of accidents.
The ipseity of the change; the accidentality.

units.la: Formæ substantiali nihil prorsus suffragatur. Namque si certum esset, dari Formam substantialem, eamq; esse reductionis authorem; tunc recte concluderetur, in majoribus hisce mutationibus recedere Formam, idque non aliunde modo, sed & ex reductionis defectu probaretur. at apud eos, qui negant Formam, & proinde negant quoq; reductionem ab ea fieri, nullo modo procedit hæc argumentatio, quæ in majoribus hisce mutationibus vult recedere Formam, idq; probat ex eo, quòd post eas reductio non fiat. Namq; positis etiam ijs, quæ nos ponimus, tum de Substantiarum generatione & corruptione, tum de Reductionis Causis, abunde explicari potest, quomodo per ejusmodi mutationes & interea compositum, & pristina accidentia, per alterationem corruptivam amissa, recuperare non possit. Quòd enim non est amplius, alterari certe non potest vel ab alio, vel à semet ipso: estq; futilitati proximum, quærere Causam, quare res, quæ interijt, restituere sibi ipsi pristinum aliquod accidens non possit, quum clarum sit rem, quæ dissoluta est, atq; esse desijt, non modo non agere amplius, sed neq; pati posse, ac consequenter non tantum à seipsâ, sed ab alio quoq; non posse alterari, & vel amissa accidentia, vel alia ulla adipisci, nisi ut de novo prius ipsa generetur. Totam igitur rei substantiam in majoribus istis mutationibus non manere integram, Suarezio assentimur. quòd verò illa substantiæ dissolutio fiat per Formæ Substantialis ablationem, neq; nos credimus, & Suarezius haudquaquam probat, imò nec probare aggreditur, quum tamen hoc solum ipsi hic fuerit probandum; quandoquidem alterum illud non est controversum, propterea q; haud indiget probationis.
units.tr: offers nothing whatever in favour of a substantial form. For if it were certain that there is a substantial form, and that it is the author of reduction, then one could rightly conclude that the form withdraws in these greater changes, and this would be proved not only from other sources but also from the failure of reduction. But this argument, which holds that the form withdraws in these greater changes and proves it from the fact that reduction does not follow afterwards, does not work against those who deny the form, and so deny that reduction is effected by it. For even granting what we ourselves posit, both concerning the generation and corruption of substances and concerning the causes of reduction, it can be fully explained how, through such changes, the composite and its former accidents, lost through corruptive alteration, cannot be recovered. Once a thing is no longer, it certainly cannot be altered either by another or by itself. It is near to frivolity to ask why a thing that has perished cannot restore to itself some former accident, since it is clear that a thing which has been dissolved and has ceased to be does not act any more, nor can it even be acted upon. Consequently it cannot be altered, either by itself or by another, and it cannot recover lost accidents or acquire any others, unless it is first generated anew. Therefore we agree with Suarez that the whole substance of the thing does not remain intact in these greater changes. But that this dissolution of the substance comes about through the removal of the substantial form, we do not believe, and Suarez by no means proves it, nor does he even attempt to prove it, although this alone was the thing to be proved here, since the former point is not in dispute and so needs no proof.

units.la: XXIX. Enumeratis hactenus atq; examinatis argumentis unum adhuc auctarij loco superaddit Fonseca, quod agmen claudat, ex ipsa fidei doctrina, ut ait, petitum. Confirmat, inquit, assertionem hanc (scilicet, dari Formas substantiales) orthodoxa fides, cum docet; primum, animam humanam esse immortalem, existentem, post separationem a corpore, unde sequitur esse substantiam: deinde, esse veram ac essentialem hominis Formam. Quum igitur homo cum ceteris animalibus, & animalia cum viventibus, & viventia cum non viventibus genere conveniant; efficitur, ut quemadmodum species humana completur per Formam substantialem, ita compleantur cetera entia naturalia. Hoc argumentum apud Suarezium obtinet primum locum inter omnia, quæ pro Forma substantiali affert, & multo verbosius ab ipso explicatur. Ratiocinatio ipsius in summam contracta hæc est. Anima humana (inquit) substantia est, quia per se manet separata a corpore: & est vera Forma corporis. non enim potest esse substantia assistens, aut extrinsecè movens corpus. alias non vivificaret illud, nec ex præsentia & conjunctione ejus penderent opera vitæ; neque deniq; esset ipse homo qui intelligeret, sed quædam alia substantia illi assistens. Constat ergo homo corpore ut materia, & animi rationali ut Formæ. Hominis autem compositio ex Materia & Forma substantiali, ostendit esse in rebus naturalibus subjectum quoddam substantiale, naturâ suâ aptum ut informetur actu aliquo substantiali. Præterea, ex eadem hominis compositione colligitur, aggregationem plurium Formarum accidentalium in simplici subjecto substantiali non satis esse ad constitutionem rei naturalis. nam in homine sunt illæ facultates & Formæ accidentales, plures fortasse ac perfectiores quàm in aliis naturalibus rebus, & tamen non sufficiunt ad constitutionem alicujus naturalis entis completi, sed præterea requiritur Forma, quæ velut præsit omnibus illis facultatibus & accidentibus, & in qua illa velut radicem & unitatem habeant: quare eadem ratione in aliis quoque entibus naturalibus Forma est necessaria.
units.tr: XXIX. Having listed and examined the arguments so far, Fonseca adds one more by way of an appendix, to close the line, which he says is drawn from the doctrine of the faith itself. The orthodox faith, he says, confirms this assertion (namely that there are substantial forms) when it teaches, first, that the human soul is immortal and exists after separation from the body, whence it follows that it is a substance; and second, that it is the true and essential form of man. Since, therefore, man agrees with the other animals in genus, and animals with living things, and living things with non-living things, it follows that just as the human species is completed by a substantial form, so the other natural beings are completed too. Among all the arguments Suarez brings for a substantial form, this one holds first place for him, and he explains it at much greater length. His reasoning, reduced to a summary, is this. The human soul (he says) is a substance, because it remains by itself separated from the body; and it is the true form of the body. For it cannot be a substance that merely assists the body or moves it from outside. Otherwise it would not give it life, nor would the works of life depend on its presence and conjunction, and finally man himself would not be the one who understands, but some other substance assisting him. Man therefore consists of body as matter and of the rational soul as form. Now the composition of man from matter and substantial form shows that there is in natural things some substantial subject, by its nature apt to be informed by some substantial act. Moreover, from the same composition of man it is gathered that an aggregate of several accidental forms in a simple substantial subject is not enough for the constitution of a natural thing. For in man there are those faculties and accidental forms, perhaps more numerous and more perfect than in other natural things, and yet they do not suffice for the constitution of a complete natural being. Besides them there is required a form which, as it were, presides over all those faculties and accidents, and in which they have their root and unity. Therefore by the same reasoning a form is necessary in the other natural beings also.

units.la: Tertio, quum idem modus generationis & corruptionis sit in aliis rebus, qui est in homine (excepta differentia in perfectione & subsistentia Formæ humanæ) sequitur, ut quomodo generatio & corruptio hominis non consistit in acquisitione vel amissione aliquorum accidentium, sed in unione vel disjunctione animæ rationalis, substantialiter informantis corpus humanum; eodem modo fiat generatio & corruptio aliorum quoque entium naturalium. Deniq;
units.tr: Third, since the same mode of generation and corruption holds in other things as holds in man (except for the difference in the perfection and subsistence of the human form), it follows that just as the generation and corruption of man does not consist in the acquisition or loss of some accidents, but in the union or separation of the rational soul, which substantially informs the human body, so too the generation and corruption of the other natural beings take place in the same way. Finally,

units.la: omnia indicia & signa substantialis compositionis, quæ in homine cogitari possunt, sunt in aliis entibus naturalibus, & præsertim in animantibus. Hoc argumentum & falsa nititur hypothesi; & si ea vel maxime vera esset, nihilominus tamen ipsum haudquaquam procederet. Sane præter Mentem seu Intellectum aliam quoq; in homine animam reperiri, & sic hominem non ex anima & corpore, sed ex corpore & duabus animabus constare, firmis rationibus suo loco demonstrabimus. Sed ut concederetur, unicam duntaxat homini animam esse, cumq; ex Mente tantum & corpore constare; non tamen inde recte inferretur, similem quoque esse brutorum animantium è duabus diversis substantijs compositionem, earumq; animam itidem esse substantialem; quum longe diversa sit conditio Mentis, & reliquarum animarum, & præcipua ratio, qua probatur animam humanam esse substantiam, nimirum ipsius immortalitas atq; separabilitas à corpore, in reliquis animabus defit, ex ipsorum Peripateticorum confessione. Verum hoc quidem urgere nolumus, neq; hanc inconsequentiam pluribus coarguere, quandoquidem rem ipsam, quæ hic intenditur, quantum ad animalia bruta, fatemur; nimirum & constare ea ex anima & corpore, & animam ipsorum esse substantiam: neq; de brutis solummodo, sed & de stirpibus, atq; omnibus in universum viventibus tantundem concedimus. ac proinde, si quid pro Formarum assertione valet hominis ex anima & corpore compositio, multo magis valebit illa brutorum & stirpium, quum pervulgata illa de Formis somnia multo magis quadrent in hasce animas, quam in Mentem: quamobrem longe probabilius ex brutorum & stirpium compositione ex anima & corpore, quam ex illa hominis, inferretur, reliquas quoq; substantias vitæ expertes simili quodam modo duabus diversis substantijs constare, atq; ex Materia & Forma compositas esse. Verum enimvero illam ex anima & corpore compositionem dissimillimam esse illi, qua Materia potentialis informetur actu substantiali, & ex duabus substantijs incompletis (ut loqui solent) fiat substantia non una tantum
units.tr: all the marks and signs of substantial composition that can be conceived in man are found in other natural beings, and especially in animals. This argument rests on a false hypothesis, and even if that hypothesis were entirely true, the argument would still not hold. Indeed, we will demonstrate in its proper place, by firm reasons, that in man there is found, besides the Mind or Intellect, another soul too, and so man consists not of soul and body, but of body and two souls. But granting that man has only one soul, and that he consists of Mind and body alone, it still would not rightly follow that the composition of brute animals is similar, from two different substances, and that their soul is likewise substantial. For the condition of the Mind is far different from that of the other souls, and the principal reason by which the human soul is proved to be a substance, namely its immortality and its separability from the body, is lacking in the other souls, by the admission of the Peripatetics themselves. Yet we do not wish to press this point, nor to refute this inconsequence at length, since we concede the very thing that is here at issue, so far as brute animals are concerned: that they consist of soul and body, and that their soul is a substance. And we grant just as much not only of brutes but of plants, and of all living things in general. Accordingly, if the composition of man from soul and body counts for anything in favour of the assertion of forms, it will count far more for the composition of brutes and plants from soul and body, since those widely spread dreams about forms fit these souls far better than the Mind. Therefore it is far more probable to infer from the composition of brutes and plants from soul and body than from that of man, that the other lifeless substances too consist in a similar way of two different substances, and are composed of matter and form. But in truth that composition from soul and body is most unlike that by which potential matter is informed by substantial act, and by which one substance, not one only, is made from two incomplete substances (as they are accustomed to say).

units.la: seu non ipsam tum, sed & simplex, seu quibuscunq; alijs verbis illam protritam ex potentia & actu substantiali compositionem exprimere placet; facile ostendi potest. Etenim animæ, etiamsi vim suam in totum corpus spargunt, non tamen substantiâ suâ illud totum penetrant, ac quaquaversus pervadunt, sed certis in corpore spaciis circumscribuntur, certisq; receptaculis continentur. præterea crescente corpore & ipsæ crescunt; & corpore jam perfectam molem adepto, ipsæ tamen continuas incrementi ac decrementi vices experiuntur, quippe quibus & quotidie aliqua, & nonnullis occasionibus permagna pars decedit, & factum damnum convenienti alimento rursus resarcitur. Super hisce compositæ ita sunt è subjecto & accidentibus, ut Materiam omnes sortitæ sint communem, nullaq; alia re nisi solis qualitatibus inter se distinguantur: quare etiam ablatis per mortem aliove casu qualitatibus specificis, substantia tamen ipsa manet, aptaq; est è qua aliæ rursus animæ generentur, congruis accidentibus in ipsam introductis. Hæc omnia ita se habere, ut dicimus, planum faciemus, quando ad Animæ tractationem deventum erit. ast cum Formarum natura (qualem sibi fingunt Peripatetici) hæc è directo pugnant: quandoquidem statuunt Formas penitus Materiæ se insinuare, nullamq; vel minimam ejus particulam inveniri, cui Forma non insideat, ac sese circumfundat, vel potius infundat. non enim ita hæc duo coagmentant, ut contigua tantum sint ac cohæreant, sed ut plane indiscreta, uno eodemq; spatio includantur, ac penitus in unum coaluerint. Sed & Formas neq; augeri dicunt, neq; imminui, sed ab ortu rei usq; ad ejus interitum eandem line ulla variatione perdurare: simplicissimasq; esse ipsas prædicant, omnisq; compositionis expertes; quare etiam intereunte composito Formas penitus deleri neq; quicquam ipsarum manere asserunt, & accidentia Formæ consectaria non ipsis Formis, sed in Materia informata aut in compositio ratione Materiæ collocant. Ast hoc postremum Animabus non quadrat, non modo secundum nos & Veritatem, sed & secundum ipsos, qui fatentur animæ facultates ipsi animæ mæ inhærere; quare etiam fateantur necesse est, animam esse aliquid ex substantia & accidentibus compositum. Namq; Scotus, qui tum ad vitandum hoc incommodum, tum ob alias quasdam febriculosas ratiunculas, statuit, potentias non esse qualitates, neq; quid reale, distinctum essentialiter ab ipsa anima substantia, sed esse idem cum illa, seu ipsammet anima substantiam, quæ cum varias operationes respiciat, variis etiam nominibus appellari soleat, quæ dicantur potentiæ animæ, quum idem re sint, quod ipsa anima substantia: nugari judicatur à maxima ipsorum Peripateticorum parte. & non minus nova est in illa schola Zabarellæ opinio, perquam sane monstrosa, asserentis, potentias animæ provenire quidem ab anima, ut à Principio & origine, non tamen in ea recipi ut in subjecto, sed in corpore animato: quum pleriq; omnes Aristotelici statuant, id quod res est, facultates animæ in ipsa anima inhærere.
units.tr: or whatever other words one prefers to express that worn-out composition of potency and substantial act, this can easily be shown. For souls, although they spread their power through the whole body, do not penetrate and pervade that whole body in their substance on every side. They are confined within certain spaces in the body and held in certain receptacles. Moreover, as the body grows, they too grow; and when the body has already attained its full mass, they still undergo continual alternations of increase and decrease, since each day some part of them departs, on some occasions a very large part, and the loss is made good again by suitable nourishment. Furthermore, composites are made up of subject and accidents in such a way that they all share a common matter and are distinguished from one another by nothing but their qualities alone. Hence, even when the specific qualities are removed by death or some other accident, the substance itself remains and is fit for generating other souls again, once suitable accidents have been introduced into it. We shall make plain that all these things are as we say when we come to the treatment of the soul. But the nature of Forms (such as the Peripatetics feign for themselves) is directly at odds with these things. For they hold that Forms insinuate themselves wholly into matter, and that no particle of it, however small, can be found in which the Form does not sit and spread itself around, or rather pour itself in. For these two are not joined so as merely to be contiguous and cohere, but are enclosed in one and the same space, completely indistinct, and have fused entirely into one. They also say that Forms are neither increased nor diminished, but from the origin of the thing to its destruction endure the same without any variation, and they declare them to be most simple and free of all composition. Hence, even when the composite perishes, they assert that the Forms are wholly destroyed and nothing of them remains, and they place the accidents, the consequences of the Form, not in the Forms themselves but in the informed matter, or in the matter as part of the composite. But this last does not fit souls, not only according to us and the truth but also according to the Peripatetics themselves, who admit that the faculties of the soul inhere in the soul itself. So they too must admit that the soul is something composed of substance and accidents. For Scotus, who, both to avoid this inconvenience and for certain other feeble little arguments, held that the powers are not qualities, nor anything real distinct essentially from the substance of the soul itself, but are the same as it, that is, the substance of the soul itself, which, since it regards various operations, is commonly called by various names, which are said to be the powers of the soul, since in reality they are the same as the substance of the soul itself, is judged by the greatest part of the Peripatetics themselves to be trifling. Nor is the opinion in that school of Zabarella less novel, indeed quite monstrous, asserting that the powers of the soul indeed proceed from the soul as from a principle and origin, yet are not received in it as in a subject, but in the animated body. Yet almost all Aristotelians hold, as is the case, that the faculties of the soul inhere in the soul itself.

units.la: Quandoquidem igitur animabus tanta intercedit dissimilitudo cum Formis (quales quidem eas sibi effingunt Peripatetici) frustra omnino viventium ex anima & corpore compositio adhibetur ad probandum, quod reliquæ quoque res naturales debeant ex Materia & Forma constare: quum animabus perperam indatur Formarum nomen, ideoque etiam non recte dicatur, viventia ex Materia & Forma constare.
units.tr: Since, therefore, there is so great a dissimilarity between souls and Forms (such as the Peripatetics indeed fashion them), the composition of living things out of soul and body is quite vainly adduced to prove that the other natural things too must consist of matter and form. The name of Form is wrongly given to souls, and therefore it is also not rightly said that living things consist of matter and form.

units.la: XXX. Sicuti autem hoc jam declaravimus quantum ad animam, ita proclive est, idem quoq; respectu Materiæ planum facere: atque ostendere, quod sicuti anima prave in Formarum classem redigitur, quum Formæ conditiones ipsi haudquaquam competant; ita etiam corpora viventium futiliter comparantur cum Materia, siquidem hæc corpora nequaquam ita se habent ad animas suas, quemadmodum Materiam se habere ad Formam peripatus pronuntiat.
units.tr: XXX. Just as we have now declared this as regards the soul, so it is easy to make the same plain with respect to matter: and to show that just as the soul is wrongly reduced to the class of Forms, since the conditions of a Form do not in any way belong to it, so also the bodies of living things are futilely compared with matter, since these bodies are by no means related to their souls as the Peripatetics pronounce that matter is related to Form.

units.la: Etenim ut alia omittamus, Materiam non habere ullam per se exilentiam, temperq; necessario esse sub aliqua Forma, ac propterea, ... prior Forma excedit, alteram eodem momento debere ipsi succedere: itidemq; Materiam per se indefinitam, à Forma ad certam speciem astringi, ab eaq; accipere omnia sua accidentia, quippe quæ Formæ consectanea sint, atq; ab ea emanent, & idcirco cum adveniente illa adveniant, ac cum discedente discedant aut omnia, aut pleraq; saltem (an enim aliquæ affectiones, quæ erant in re corrupta, possint manere in genita, inter ipsos disputatur) constans est Lycei doctrina. Ast hæc omnia in corporibus viventium falsa deprehenduntur. Hæc enim ab animabus hoc tantum habent, ut à cujusvis generis injurijs melius defendantur, atq; diutius conserventur. ut vero sint & existant, nequaquam animarum præsentiâ habent, sed à seipsis; quare etiam sunt & existunt, postquam anima ab ijs emigravit: quum tamen nulla alia anima & Forma in ipsius locum successerit. Nam quod nonnulli commenti sunt Formam cadaveris, quæ in viventis interitu statim generetur, atq; in animæ defunctæ locum surrogetur, ejusq; defectum suppleat ad corpus informandum; est delirium merum, quum istius Formæ nullum ne tenuissimum quidem indicium afferri queat, sed solummodo extructa sit super hoc ipso commento, quod ut animam Formæ, ita corpus Materiæ nomine indigetat; quo posito sequatur, ut quomodo aliis Formis exeuntibus, novæ intrent in Materiam, quæ non nisi sub aliqua Forma esse possit; ita excessum animæ ex corpore, alterius si non animæ, saltem Formæ introitus, ne corpus maneat omni Forma destitutum. hæc sola ratio afferri potest, non quâ ista cadaverosa Forma probetur, sed ob quam commenti eam sint ij, qui eam introduxerunt; & rem ita se habere ac dicimus, Suarez (unus ex ijs, qui Formam cadaveris ponunt) claris verbis fatetur, sic inquiens: Nunquam manere Materiam sine substantiali Forma, dubito an satis demonstratum sit. nam substantialem Formam non experimur, nisi ex effectibus vel accidentibus. Sape autem nullus est effectus, qui evidenter ostendat introductionem novæ Formæ post recessum prioris, ut in morte hominis. & ideo Scotus & alij negant, ibi introduci novam Formam; quanquam, ne cogantur fateri, Materiam manere sine Formâ, ponant Formam
units.tr: For, to omit other things: matter has no existence of its own and must necessarily be under some Form, so that when the prior Form departs, another must at the same moment succeed it; likewise matter, indefinite in itself, is bound by a Form to a certain species and receives from it all its accidents, since these are consequent on the Form and emanate from it, and therefore come with its arrival and depart with its departure, all of them or at least most of them (for whether some affections which were in the corrupted thing can remain in the generated thing is disputed among them). This is the constant doctrine of the Lyceum. But all these things are found to be false in the bodies of living things. For these have from souls only this, that they are better defended against injuries of any kind and preserved longer. But that they are and exist, they have not from the presence of the souls but from themselves; hence they also are and exist after the soul has departed from them, although no other soul or Form has succeeded in its place. As for what some have invented, that a Form of the corpse is generated immediately at the death of a living thing and is substituted in the place of the departed soul, supplying its lack in order to inform the body, this is sheer delirium, since not even the slightest indication of such a Form can be brought forward. It is merely constructed upon this very invention, which calls the soul a Form as it calls the body matter. Given this, it follows that just as, when other Forms go out, new ones enter matter, which can exist only under some Form, so the departure of the soul from the body requires the entrance of another soul, or at least of a Form, lest the body remain destitute of all Form. This is the only reason that can be given, not one by which that cadaverous Form is proved, but one on account of which those who introduced it devised it. That the matter stands as we say, Suárez (one of those who posit a Form of the corpse) clearly confesses, saying thus: "I doubt whether it has been sufficiently demonstrated that matter never remains without a substantial Form. For we do not experience a substantial Form except from its effects or accidents. Often, however, there is no effect that clearly shows the introduction of a new Form after the departure of the prior one, as in the death of a man. And therefore Scotus and others deny that a new Form is introduced there; although, lest they be compelled to admit that matter remains without Form, they posit a Form..."
(fragment: mam)
Chapter I.

units.la: mam corporeitatis, vel mistionis: qua seclusa, nos non alia ratione convincimus, in omni morte vel corruptione introduci novam Formam, nisi quia aliàs Materia maneret sine Forma, & ita videmur in his probationibus circulum committere. Sed licet verum sit, ex effectibus id non evidenter detere. Sed licet verum sit, nihilominus adeo est illud axioma consentaneum monstrari, naturis rerum, & fini, & usui, ac imperfectioni Materiæ, ut unanimi omnium fere antiquorum ac recentiorum philosophorum consensu, tanquam certum & indubitatum sit resphorum consensu, quod satis est ad philosophicam rationem fundanceptum, quod satis est ad philosophicam rationem fundandam.
units.tr: of corporeity, or of mixture. Setting this aside, we have no other ground for holding that a new form is introduced in every death or corruption, except that otherwise the matter would remain without form. So in these proofs we seem to be arguing in a circle. Yet even if this is true, it cannot be clearly established from the effects. Nevertheless, this axiom is so consistent with the natures of things, with their end and use, and with the imperfection of matter, that by the almost unanimous agreement of all the ancient and modern philosophers it is taken as certain and undoubted. That is enough to found a philosophical argument.

units.la: Quum igitur nulluin detur hujusmodi Formæ indicium, inq; ea asserenda planissime circulus committatur (sicuti ingenue fatetur Suarez) non est ut de ea confutanda laboremus, quum stultitiæ affine sit, omnes stultas nugas velle argumentis redarguere. & sane inter Peripateticos non pauci Formam hanc pro fatua ac futili explocos non pauci Formam hanc pro fatua ac futili explodunt.
units.tr: Since, therefore, there is no sign of any such form, and since asserting it plainly involves a circle (as Suarez frankly admits), we need not labour to refute it. It is close to foolishness to try to overturn foolish trifles with arguments. Indeed, among the Peripatetics, not a few reject this form as idle and futile.

units.la: Sicuti autem existentiam ab anima non habet corpus, ita neq; naturam specificam: os enim in cadavere manet os, & caro manet caro, itidemque reliquæ omnes partes similares: & partes organicæ seu heterogeneæ eandem servent figuram (aliquo quidem usque. certe non refert quamdiu, quum vel minimum temporis spatium nostro proposito sufficiat) atq; compositionem, quam durante vita obtinebant. & quum totum nihil sit aliud, quam omnes partes omnes simul sumtæ, sequitur, ut cum omnes corporis partes servent in morte naturam suam, quam in vita habuerant, totum quoq; idem esse dicatur post animæ excessum, quod ea præsente fuerat, ac proinde verasint illa Lucretij, Quod simul ac hominem lethi secura quies est Indepta, atq; animi natura animaq; recessit; Nil ibi libatum de toto corpore cernas Ad speciem, nihil ad pondus: mors omnia præstat, Vitalem præter sensum, calidumq; vaporem.
units.tr: Just as the body does not have its specific existence from the soul, neither does it have its specific nature from the soul. A bone in a corpse remains bone, and flesh remains flesh, and so with all the other similar parts. The organic or heterogeneous parts keep the same shape and the same composition that they had while life lasted (to some extent, at least; it does not matter for how long, since even the smallest span of time is enough for our purpose). And since the whole is nothing other than all its parts taken together, it follows that, since all the parts of the body keep in death the nature they had in life, the whole too may be said to be after the departure of the soul what it was while the soul was present. Thus those lines of Lucretius are true: "As soon as the calm of death has seized a man, and the nature of the mind and the soul has departed, you can see nothing of the whole body changed in its appearance or in its weight. Death takes away everything except the vital sense and the warm breath."

units.la: XXXI. Haud ignoramus aliam fuisse Aristoteli sententiam, quippe qui diversis in locis prodiderit, cadaveris partes, tum instrumentarias, non esse idem partes, tum similares, tum instrumentarias, non esse idem cum
units.tr: XXXI. We are not unaware that Aristotle held another opinion, since in various places he has declared that the parts of a corpse, both instrumental and similar, are not the same as they were in the living body, except in a homonymous sense.

units.la: Lib. 3. non Demisat in situa. cum eo, quod erant in corpore vivente, nisi homonymice. hoc scribit primi de Part. Anim. primo, Ἀπελλθόσης δ᾽ ψυχῆς, ὁλὴν τῶν μορίων τ᾽ αὐτὸ λείπεται, ὥλην ζῷον σχήματι μόνον, καθάπερ τὰ μυθευόμενα λιθῶδαι. Ubi anima discesserit, nulla pars relinquitur eadem, nisi solà figurâ, sicuti ea quae in fabulis memorantur lapidescere. & primo politicorum, Ἀναιρεσμένης τοῦ ὅλου, σχεδὸν ἔσαι πᾶς, ὁλὲ χεὶρ, εἰ μὴ ὁμωνύμως, ὥσπερ ἂν λέγοι τὴν λιθίνην. Pereunte Toto, non amplius erit pes, neq; manus, nisi aequivoce, itidem ac lapidea. itemq; primi de Gener. Anim. 19. Οὐδὲ ἡ χεὶρ, ἡ ἄλλο τι τῶν μορίων οὐδὲν, ἄνευ ψυχῆς ἢ ἄλλης τινὸς ζωοκρίσεως ἐστι χεὶρ, ἀλλὰ μόνον ὁμώνυμον. neq; manus neq; aliarum partium ulla, absq; anima aut alia quadam facultate est manus, aut alia quavis pars, sed tantum aequivocè. ac rursus secundi de generatione animalium primo, Οὐ γὰρ ὅτι πρόσωπον, μὴ ἔχον ψυχὴν, ὁλὲ σάρξ· ἀλλὰ Φιλοσοφία, ὁμωνύμως λεχθήσετ᾽, τὸ μὲν, ἓν πρόσωπον, τὸ δὲ, σάρξ. ὥστε ἂν εἰ ἐγίνετο ξύλινα, ἢ λίθινα. non enim est facies, non habens animam, neq; caro. quippe ubi interierunt, aequivoce carnis & faciei appellatione afficiuntur, non minus quam si lignea aut lapidea essent facta. Et hoc sequitur etiam Scaliger; neq; sequitur tantum, sed quod ipsi familiare de vanissimis quibusq; ac maxime ridiculis commentis, de hoc etiam facit, ut id pro maximo & plane impenetrabili secreto venditet. sic enim scribit Exerc. 366. Hæc contra Sectum: quæ latent ingenia plebeia. sicut & illud, Membra cadaveris alia esse specie ab iis, quæ fuerant viventis. soli sapientes hæc hauriunt ex penitioribus naturæ fontibus. & similia etiam habet exercitationis sextæ sectione duodecima, ubi Fernelium reprehendens, qui Aristoteli assentiens de partibus instrumentariis, aliud sentit de similaribus, aitq; os cadaveris esse verum os; tam mirifice sibi placet de hoc delirio, ut id numeret inter ea, quæ spinosiora cum sint, ac minime popularia, faciant sapientes, minime populares, coelo propiores agitare. Operæ pretium est.
units.tr: Book 3, not "Demisat in situa." He writes this in the first book of On the Parts of Animals: "When the soul has departed, no part remains the same, except in shape alone, like the things in fables that are turned to stone" [ὅταν ἀπέλθῃ ἡ ψυχή, οὐδὲν μόριον μένει τὸ αὐτό, ἀλλὰ μόνον τῷ σχήματι]. And in the first book of the Politics: "When the whole is destroyed, there will be no foot or hand, except in name, just as one would speak of a stone hand" [ἀπολλυμένου τοῦ ὅλου, οὐκέτι ἔσται πούς οὐδὲ χείρ, εἰ μὴ ὁμωνύμως]. Likewise in the first book of On the Generation of Animals, chapter 19: "Neither the hand nor any other part is a hand without soul or some other vital faculty, but only in name" [οὐδὲ ἡ χεὶρ ἄνευ ψυχῆς ἐστι χείρ, ἀλλὰ μόνον ὁμώνυμον]. And again in the first book of the second work on the generation of animals: "A face that has no soul is not a face, nor is flesh flesh; but they will be called so only in name, just as if they had been made of wood or stone" [οὐ γὰρ ἔστι πρόσωπον μὴ ἔχον ψυχήν, οὐδὲ σάρξ]. For once they have perished, the words "flesh" and "face" apply to them only equivocally, no less than if they had been made of wood or stone. Scaliger also follows this, and not merely follows it: he does what is characteristic of him with the most empty and most ridiculous inventions, and he peddles this as a great and quite impenetrable secret. For he writes in Exercise 366: These things are against Sextus: they are the sort of thing that hides in plebeian minds. So too is that claim that the members of a corpse are of another kind from those of a living man. Only the wise draw these things from the deeper springs of nature. He has similar things in section twelve of the sixth exercise, where he rebukes Fernel. Fernel, while agreeing with Aristotle about the instrumental parts, thinks otherwise about the similar parts, and says that the bone of a corpse is a true bone. Scaliger is so pleased with this nonsense that he counts it among those things which, being thorny and not at all popular, wise men alone, not popular men, stir up and bring closer to heaven. It is worth the effort.

units.la: x lignea est autem examinare hujus sententiæ fundamenta, ut sic ejus infirmitas elucescat. Aristoteles quidem unam tantum, quod sciamus, hujus opinionis affert rationem, quia nimirum partes cadaveris non possint amplius edere eas actiones, quas edebant dum viverent. Πάντα τῷ ἔργῳ ὥρισαι, καὶ τῇ δυνάμει· ὥσε μηκέτι τοιαῦτα ὄντα, ὁ λεχθεὶς τὰ αὐτὰ, ἀλλὰ ὁμώνυμα. omnia definita sunt opere, & potentia. itaq; ubi non amplius sunt talia [ut operari possint] non dicenda sunt eadem, sed æquivoca. & latius primi de Part. animal. primo, Ἐὰν δὲ ἀδύνατον εἶν χεῖρα ὀπωσοῦν διαπεπλισμένην, οἷον χαλκῆν ἢ ξυλίνην, τὴν ὁμωνύμως, οἷον γεγεφαμμένον ἰατρόν· ὁ δὲ ἀνυπόσεται ποιεῖν τὸ ἔκυσης ἔργον, ὥσπερ δὲ ἀυλοὶ λίθινοι τὸ ἑαυτῶν ἔργον, ἀλλὰ ὁ γεγεφαμμένος ἰατρὸς. ὁμάως δὲ τούτοις, ἀλλὰ τῶν τῷ τεθνεῶτος μορίων ἀλλὰ ἐν τῶν τοιούτων ἐστί. λέγω δ' οἷον ὀφθαλμός, χείρ. Præterea autem impossibile est, ut manus sit quomodocunq; affecta, veluti ænea aut lignea, nisi æquivoce, sicuti pictus medicus. non enim poterit opus suum facere, sicuti neq; tibiæ saxeæ opus suum [facere queunt] neq; pictus medicus. consimiliter autem neq; partium mortui ulla (ut oculus, manus) est id quod fuerat. Hoc quoque Scaliger expressit, dicens, Cadaveris os carere fine. nullum enim ejus officium esse, ut prius. non esse igitur idem. & aliam præterea addit rationem hanc. Una est in vivente Forma, qua unum est. Os Cæsaris viventis vivens est. Ubi Cæsar erit cadaver, abierit Forma; tunc corpus illud non erit id, quod nunc hoc est, numero. ergo neq; partes ejus, qua unum erant per id, per quod illud unum erat, ens, & tale aliquid ens. Caret igitur cadaveris os ea Forma, quæ erat os vivens. XXXII. Quantum ad priorem harum rationum, si ea valet in partibus cadaveris, valeat etiam oportet in partibus immedicabili paralysi obsitis; quæ cum officium suum amiserint, eque ac partes cadaveris, sequetur ut & ipsæ non sint amplius quod fuerant, utq; pristina appellatio ijs non amplius
units.tr: It is worth examining the foundations of this opinion, so that its weakness may come to light. Aristotle, as far as we know, gives only one reason for this view: the parts of a corpse can no longer perform the actions they performed while alive. "All things are defined by their work and by their power; so when they are no longer such, they are not to be called the same, but only homonymous" [Πάντα τῷ ἔργῳ ὥρισται καὶ τῇ δυνάμει· ὥστε μηκέτι τοιαῦτα ὄντα οὐ λεκτέα τὰ αὐτά, ἀλλὰ ὁμώνυμα]. All things are defined by their work and their power. So when they are no longer such, they are not to be called the same, but equivocal. He argues more fully in the first book of On the Parts of Animals: "It is impossible for a hand to be a hand in any condition, such as one of bronze or wood, except in name, as with a painted physician. Such a hand cannot perform its proper work, just as a stone flute cannot perform the work of a flute, nor a painted physician the work of a physician. In the same way, no part of a dead body (such as an eye or a hand) is what it was, but belongs to the same class of things" [ὁμοίως δὲ τούτοις καὶ τῶν τοῦ τεθνεῶτος μορίων οὐδὲν ἔτι ἐστὶν ὃ ἦν]. Moreover, it is impossible for a hand to be in any condition whatever, such as one of bronze or wood, except equivocally, like a painted doctor. For it cannot do its own work, just as a stone pipe cannot do its work, nor a painted doctor. Likewise, no part of a dead man (such as an eye or a hand) is what it was. Scaliger also expresses this, saying: The bone of a corpse lacks its end. For it has no office as before. Therefore it is not the same. And he adds another reason. In the living thing there is one form, by which it is one. Caesar's living bone is living. When Caesar becomes a corpse and the form departs, that body will not be numerically what it now is. Therefore neither are its parts, which were one through that by which that one thing was a being and a being of such a kind. Therefore the bone of a corpse lacks that form which was the living bone. XXXII. As for the first of these reasons, if it holds for the parts of a corpse, it must also hold for the parts afflicted with incurable paralysis. Since these have lost their function, just like the parts of a corpse, it would follow that they too are no longer what they were, and that their former name no longer belongs to them.
Chapter I.

units.la: amplius competat, nisi æquivoce. quod sane Aristoteles non concesserit; qui propterea concedere debet, in partibus etiam cadaveris non valere hanc rationem. Ast non debilis modo est hæc ratio, sed & falsa. Etenim partibus cadaveris, recentis nimirum (de tali enim Aristoteles quoque & Scaliger loquuntur, non de eo, cujus partes jam sunt putredine, aut aliter, vitiatæ & destructæ) eadem manet aptitudo ad operandum, quæ ijs erat in vita, ita ut accedente superiore agente nunc quoque adhiberi possint ad eadem actiones, ad quas adhiberi naturaliter aptæ sunt animali adhuc vivente. si enim redeat anima, omnes easdem functiones per eas edere poterit, quas edere solebat prius. Hoc ita est manifestum, ut nemo possit negare: & siquis ita sit impudens, ut neget, facile revincetur exemplo eorum, qui cum jam essent mortui, in vitam denuo sunt revocati (cujusmodi historias habemus complures in sacris) in quibus sane partes corporis non sunt restitutæ in alium statum, quàm in cadavere habuerant, sed anima duntaxat, quæ excesserat, in corpus rursum fuit introducta. Sapientius igitur istis Galenus, qui partes cadaveris, quanquam jam nulla amplius per illas actio fit, non esse tamen quicquam passas dicit in seipsis, quum non ipsarum culpâ sit, quod otiantur, sed animæ absentiâ id fiat: sicuti ex ijs, quæ in tractatu De tremore ac palpitatione contra Herophilum & Praxagoram disputat, colligi potest. Quantum verò ad alteram rationem à Scaligero allatam, ea non plus probat, nisi cadaver non vivere, ac proinde neque partes cadaveris; in quo nemo ipsi repugnaverit. Ast aliud est dicere, quòd cadaver, & partes cadaveris, non amplius vivant; aliud, quod non amplius sint id quod erant, quoad propriam ipsorum naturam atq; essentiam. Sane ab animæ conjunctione habet corpus ut vivat, (quanquam propriè loquendo non corpus vivit, sed animal corpore & anima constans) ac propterea illâ abeunte necessario vita ipsum relinquit. ast ut sit unum, & hoc aliquid, nequaquam habet ab anima, non magis quam anima habet à corpore, ut sit unum & hoc aliquid. & tamen multo probabilius asseri posset, animam à corpore, quam corpus ab anima, hoc beneficium accipere. etenim anima (bruta nimirum, aut vegetativa, de qua toto hoc sermone loquimur) definit esse anima, simulatq; corporis consortium relinquit, omnibusq; illis notis sive accidentibus exuitur, quorum cum subjecto unione efficiebatur ut & anima esset, & ad certam hanc animarum speciem pertineret. Quodsi anima, quae ita à corpore pendet, ut eodem momento, quo à corpore sejungitur, dissolvatur & intereat, non tamen à corpore habet (sicuti revera non habet ab ipso) ut sit hoc quod est; longe est dictu ineptius, corporis essentiam atque specificam naturam ab anima derivare, quum ipsa maneat integra, qualis erat prius (nisi siquid aliunde passa est) etiam post animae discessum. Manere autem, adeo est manifestum, certissimoq; sensuum indicio exploratum, ut eorum, qui ad tuendas deliras quasdam nænias, in suomet ipsorum cerebro natas, illud negare sustinent, impudentiam potius mirari debeamus ac stoliditatem, quam in ijs coarguendis laborem ullum sumere; quum plane perversam ineant ratiocinandi viam, ἐξ ἀδήλων ὑπὲρ τῶν φαινομένων συλλογιζόμενοι, ex incertis concludentes super ijs quae evidentia sunt, ut Galeni verbis utamur è 1. Simpl. 34. ὡς ἐν τῷ καταψεύδεσθαι τ᾽ αἰσθήσεως αὐτοῖς τὸ νικᾶν ὑπάρχοντος, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν αὐτῷ δὴ τοῦτο μέγιστον δεῖγμα τ᾽ τῶν λόγων αὐτῶν μοχθηρίας ἐσόμενον; acsi victoria ipsis sita esset in mendacijs contra sensus confingendis, ac non potius hoc ipsum foret maximum indicium futilitatis disputationum ipsorum, sicuti idem paulo ante ait. Sed hoc sophistis est solenne (ut ibidem monemur) ὃν ὀλίγα καταψεύδεσθαι τ᾽ αἰσθήσεως, non pauca contra sensus mendacia effutire, quippe quibus curae non est, quam consentanea veritati loquantur, duntaxat loquantur fictitijs suis dogmatis consentanea; quod ut faciant, parati sunt seipsos in rebus etiam clarissimis, ac vel cuivis idiotae absq; ulla difficultate deprehendendis, excaecare, ac proinde verissimam facere illam Aristotelis confessionem in Principio secundi Metaphysicorum, Ὥσπερ τὰ τῶν νυκτερίδων ὄμματα πρὸς τὸ φῶς ...
units.tr: Applies to them, except equivocally. Aristotle would certainly not have conceded this. He must therefore concede that this argument does not hold for the parts of a corpse either. But the argument is not only weak; it is also false. For the parts of a corpse, I mean a fresh one (Aristotle and Scaliger are speaking of such, not of one whose parts are already rotten or otherwise spoiled and destroyed), keep the same aptitude for acting that they had in life. So, once a superior agent is added, they can still be used for the same actions for which they were naturally fitted while the animal was alive. For if the soul returned, it could perform through them all the same functions it used to perform before. This is so plain that no one can deny it. And if anyone is so shameless as to deny it, he is easily refuted by the example of those who, though already dead, have been called back to life (we have several such stories in the sacred books). In those cases the parts of the body are not restored to any other state than they had in the corpse; only the soul, which had departed, is introduced into the body again. Galen is therefore wiser than these men. He says that the parts of a corpse, although no action is performed through them any longer, nevertheless suffer nothing in themselves, since it is not their fault that they are idle, but this happens through the absence of the soul. This can be gathered from what he argues in his treatise On Trembling and Palpitation against Herophilus and Praxagoras. As for the second argument brought forward by Scaliger, it proves no more than that a corpse does not live, and so neither do its parts; no one would dispute this with him. But it is one thing to say that the corpse and its parts no longer live; it is another to say that they are no longer what they were, as regards their own nature and essence. Certainly the body has from its union with the soul that it lives (though strictly speaking it is not the body that lives, but the animal, which consists of body and soul). Therefore, when the soul departs, life necessarily leaves the body. But that it is one thing and this particular thing, it has not at all from the soul, any more than the soul has from the body that it is one and this particular thing. And yet it could be asserted much more probably that the soul receives this benefit from the body rather than the body from the soul. For the soul (namely the brute or vegetative soul, of which we speak throughout this discourse) ceases to be a soul as soon as it leaves the company of the body, and it is stripped of all those marks or accidents by whose union with the subject it was made to be a soul and to belong to this particular species of souls. But if the soul, which depends on the body in such a way that at the very moment it is separated from the body it is dissolved and perishes, nevertheless does not have from the body (as in fact it does not have from it) that it is what it is, then it is far more absurd to derive the essence and specific nature of the body from the soul, since the body itself remains whole, just as it was before (unless it has suffered something from elsewhere), even after the soul has departed. That it remains is so manifest, and so certain by the evidence of the senses, that towards those who dare to deny it, in defence of certain mad trifles born in their own brains, we ought to wonder at their impudence and stupidity rather than take any trouble in refuting them. They plainly enter upon a perverse way of reasoning, concluding from things unclear about things that are evident, as we may use Galen's words from the first book of the Simple Medicines, section 34: [ἐξ ἀδήλων ὑπὲρ τῶν φαινομένων συλλογιζόμενοι]. As if their victory lay in inventing lies against the senses; whereas this very thing would be the greatest proof of the wickedness of their arguments, as the same author says a little earlier: [ὡς ἐν τῷ καταψεύδεσθαι τ᾽ αἰσθήσεως αὐτοῖς τὸ νικᾶν ὑπάρχοντος, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν αὐτῷ δὴ τοῦτο μέγιστον δεῖγμα τ᾽ τῶν λόγων αὐτῶν μοχθηρίας ἐσόμενον]. But this is customary with the sophists (as we are warned in the same place): [ὃν ὀλίγα καταψεύδεσθαι τ᾽ αἰσθήσεως], to utter not a few lies against the senses. For they do not care whether they speak what agrees with the truth; they care only that they speak what agrees with their invented dogmas. To do this they are ready to blind themselves even in the clearest matters, which anyone, however untrained, could grasp without any difficulty. So they make true that most accurate confession of Aristotle at the beginning of the second book of the Metaphysics: [Ὥσπερ τὰ τῶν νυκτερίδων ὄμματα πρὸς τὸ φῶς ...]

units.la: Cap.32. in fine ὑνὶ ἐχέισι ἄμματα πρὸς τὸ φέγγος ἔχει τὸ μετὰ ἡμέραν, οὕτω καὶ τὸ ἡμετέρας ψυχῆς ὁ νοῦς πρὸς τὰ τῆ φύσει φανερώτατα πάντων: sicuti vespertilionum oculi se habent ad lucem diei, ita animæ nostræ intellectus ad ea, quæ naturâ sunt omnium manifestissima. Sane res hæc, de qua nunc agimus (nimirum unamquamq; partem in cadavere esse idem, ejusdemq; naturæ, ac erat durante vita) adeo est clara, ut multos ipsorum Peripateticorum, quibus saltem aliqua sensuum τῶν φαινομένων cura, eam negare puduerit, quantum quidem ad partes similares; quare dixerunt etiam in corpore vivente os esse os, & carnem esse carnem, non ratione animæ totum corpus informantis, sed peculiarium Formarum, quæ Formæ etiam post mortem maneant, quo fiat, ut etiam in cadavere hæ omnes partes integræ maneant, ac proprias singula naturas servent, ita ut os maneat os, & caro maneat caro, & sic reliquæ omnes; sicuti hac de re loquitur Zabarella. alij vero, ut Henricus & Scotus, quandam peculiarem Formam introduxerunt, quam appellaverunt Formam corporeitatis, quæ corpori det suum esse, ac anima excedente remaneat.
units.tr: ...at the end of chapter 32: [ὥσπερ τὰ τῶν νυκτερίδων ὄμματα πρὸς τὸ φέγγος ἔχει τὸ μεθ᾽ ἡμέραν, οὕτω καὶ τὸ ἡμετέρας ψυχῆς νοῦς πρὸς τὰ τῇ φύσει φανερώτατα πάντων]. As the eyes of bats are to the light of day, so is the intellect of our soul to the things that are by nature most manifest of all. Indeed the matter we are now discussing (namely that each part in a corpse is the same and of the same nature as it was while life lasted) is so clear that many of the Peripatetics themselves, who have at least some regard for the evident facts of the senses, have been ashamed to deny it, at least as far as similar parts are concerned. Hence they have said that even in a living body bone is bone and flesh is flesh, not by reason of the soul informing the whole body, but by reason of peculiar forms, which remain even after death. So it happens that in a corpse all these parts remain whole and each keeps its own nature, so that bone remains bone, flesh remains flesh, and so on for the rest; as Zabarella speaks on this matter. Others, however, such as Henry and Scotus, have introduced a certain peculiar form, which they called the form of corporeity, which gives the body its being and remains when the soul departs.
XXXIII.

units.la: Quum ergo partes corporis, & consequenter totum corpus, non sint hoc quod sunt, ratione animæ, unde ut sit etiam post discessum idem maneant quod erant prius (sicuti & per se apertum est; & multi Peripatetici, rei evidentia convicti, fatentur) male omnino, ut Formæ animam, ita corpus Materiæ locum obtinere dicunt Peripatetici; quum ex ipsorum doctrina absurdum sit, planéque impossibile, ut Materia aut subsistat sine aliqua Forma, aut Formâ aliquâ amissâ, retineat eadem omnia accidentia eandémque naturam, quam illâ præsente obtinebat. Unde porro sequitur, ut cum illa brutorum & stirpium compositio ex anima & corpore (& multo magis illa hominum ex corpore & mente) dissimillima sit isti compositioni quam sibi somniant Peripatetici, ex Materia potentiali, & Forma substantiali ipsam actuante; nulla omnino sit hæc consequentia, quæ ex eo, quod homo reliquaq; liquaq; viventia ex anima & corpore constant, infert, dari Formam substantialem, & reliquas etiam res non animatas ex duabus diversis substantijs in unam conflatis, Materiâ videlicet & Forma substantiali, constare. Quanquam autem supervacuum est plura de hoc argumento dicere (quum res adeo sit evidens ex supradictis) placet tamen Suarezij verba superius posita magis adhuc minutatim examinare. Animam humanam ait esse veram Formam corporis, quia non sit substantia assistens. Quod anima corpori non assistat ita, quomodo nauta assistit navi, aut quomodo intelligentias fingunt assistere orbibus quos movent (hoc enim intelligit per substantiam assistentem, sicuti liquet ex ijs, quae cum alij hac de re tradunt, tum Zabarella capite secundo libri de mente humana) concedimus. sed quod propterea debeat corpus informare eo informationis genere, quod peripatus somniat, nequaquam sequitur; quandoquidem alij dantur veriores modi, duas pluresve diversas substantias ad unius rei constitutionem connectendi, cujus rei innumera habemus in artibus exempla, aut potius imitamenta, quum ipsarum operâ substantiae diversae, & quandoq; plurimum inter se differentes, solent ad unius corporis constitutionem inter se coagmentari. naturalium autem agentium vis atq; industria omnem artificum industriam longe superat, atq; post se relinquit, in diversis substantijs inter se nectendis, atq; ad unius rei constitutionem apte copulandis, non ut una alteram actuet aut informet, sed ut unaquaeq; & sibi ac per se sit hoc quod est, & integram partis rationem toti exhibeat. Porro quum hominis corpus ab anima non informetur, & corpus hoc non sit tale subjectum imperfectum & incompletum, qualem faciunt Materiam primam Peripatetici (sicuti ex ijs, quae supra disputavimus, apparet) ex hominis compositione non poteit inferri Materia prima, ac proinde neq; Forma substantialis, ad actuandam ejusmodi Materiam necessaria. Quantum ad secundam Suarezij rationem; aggregationem plurium accidentium in simplici subjecto substantiali non sufficere ad constituendas res naturales, concedimus quidem de plerisq; (non
units.tr: Since therefore the parts of the body, and consequently the whole body, are not what they are by virtue of the soul, they would not remain the same as they were before after the soul departs. This is plain in itself, and many Peripatetics, convinced by the evidence of the matter, admit it. The Peripatetics wrongly say that the body holds the place of matter just as the soul holds the place of form. By their own doctrine it is absurd and quite impossible for matter either to subsist without some form, or, once one form is lost, to keep all the same accidents and the same nature it had while that form was present. It follows further that the composition of brutes and plants out of soul and body (and much more that of men out of body and mind) is wholly unlike the composition the Peripatetics dream of, of potential matter actuated by substantial form. So there is no valid inference from the fact that man and other living things consist of soul and body to the claim that there is a substantial form, and that other non-living things also consist of two different substances joined into one, namely matter and substantial form. Although it is superfluous to say more on this subject, since the matter is so evident from what has been said above, it pleases us to examine more closely the words of Suárez quoted earlier. He says the human soul is the true form of the body, because it is not an assisting substance. We grant that the soul does not assist the body as a sailor assists a ship, or as the intelligences are imagined to assist the spheres they move. For by an assisting substance he means this, as is clear from what others have taught on the subject, and from Zabarella in the second chapter of his book on the human mind. But it does not at all follow that for this reason the soul must inform the body in the way the Peripatetics dream of. There are other and truer ways of joining two or more different substances into the constitution of one thing, and we have countless examples of this, or rather imitations of it, in the arts, where different substances, and sometimes very different ones, are usually fitted together into the constitution of one body. The power and skill of natural agents far surpasses and leaves behind all the skill of craftsmen in binding different substances together and aptly coupling them into the constitution of one thing. They do this not so that one actuates or informs the other, but so that each is what it is both for itself and by itself, and yet each presents the whole part of the thing. Further, since the human body is not informed by the soul, and this body is not such an imperfect and incomplete subject as the Peripatetics make prime matter (as appears from what we argued above), no prime matter can be inferred from the composition of man, and therefore neither can a substantial form, which is needed to actuate such matter. As to Suárez's second reason, that the aggregation of several accidents in a simple substantial subject is not sufficient to constitute natural things, we grant this indeed for most things
