Chapter I.

units.la: (non de omnibus, quum inveniantur res, quæ ex simplici tantum subjecto & accidentibus constant) non tamen propterea concedimus (quod inde inferre vult Suarez) res illas ex Materia potentiali, & Forma eam actuante, atq; accidentia Materiæ colligante, consistere; neq; id docetur exemplo hominis, quippe in quo ipso nequaquam ita se res habet; quum neq; anima informet corpus, neq; accidentia corporis in anima radicentur atq; unitatem habeant (ut Suarez loquitur) Et quod axioma illud, quo Forma statuitur necessaria ad accidentia inter se ac cum subjecto suo colliganda, sit inane, ex ijs, quæ supra paragrapho vigesimo disputavimus, clarum est.
units.tr: (not for all, since there are found things that consist only of a simple subject and accidents). Yet we do not grant, as Suárez infers, that those things consist of potential matter, a form actuating it, and the form binding the accidents of the matter together. Nor is this taught by the example of man, for in man himself the case is by no means so; for the soul neither informs the body, nor do the accidents of the body take root in the soul and have unity (as Suárez puts it). And that the axiom by which a form is held necessary to bind accidents together and to their subject is empty, is clear from what we argued in paragraph twenty above.

units.la: Quod vero Suarez tertio loco ait, ex hominis generatione & corruptione ostendi Formam substantialem in cæteris quoque rebus; hoc innititur hypothesi illi, qua anima humana statuitur corpus informare: quæ cum falsa sit, consequentia quoque hæc inde ducta concidat necesse est. & præterea imprudentiæ aut ignorantiæ plena sunt illa verba, quibus ait, eundem esse modum generationis & corruptionis in aliis rebus, qui est in homine: qua re nihil à vero alienus dici potest, sicuti ex ijs, quæ de generatione alibi opportuniore loco dicemus, apparebit.
units.tr: As for Suárez's third point, that the generation and corruption of man show a substantial form in other things also, this rests on that hypothesis by which the human soul is held to inform the body. Since that is false, the consequence drawn from it must also fall. Moreover, those words in which he says that the mode of generation and corruption is the same in other things as in man are full of carelessness or ignorance. Nothing can be said that is further from the truth, as will appear from what we shall say about generation in a more suitable place.

units.la: Sane ipsa viventium corpora consimili quodam modo generantur, ac reliquæ res naturales; quanquam & hic multa intercedunt, quæ diversitatem faciant non parvam. Totius autem vel hominis, vel alterius viventis generatio, simul sumta, immensum quantum differt ab aliarum rerum naturalium generatione. quod idem de corruptione quoque dictum esto, quum modus intereundi debeat modo oriundi respondere.
units.tr: Indeed, the bodies of living things are generated in a certain similar manner to other natural things, although many differences intervene here that make no small difference. But the generation of a whole man, or of any other living thing, taken together, differs immensely from the generation of other natural things. The same is to be said of corruption, since the manner of perishing ought to correspond to the manner of arising.

units.la: Ultimo loco ait, Omnia indicia & signa substantialis compositionis, quæ in homine cogitari possunt, in aliis quoq; rebus naturalibus reperiri. quod planissime falsum est, quantum quidem ad res inanimas attinet. Alijs enim in rebus nulla est compositio substantialis, nisi illa diversarum substantiarum sive diversorum Elementorum ad unum corpus constituendum commistio. ast in homine, reliquisq; viventibus, præterquam quod hæc quoq; invenitur compositio substantialis, ratione corporis videlicet, alia etiamnum datur, plurimum ab hac diversa, qua in reliquis quidem duae, in homine autem plures substantiae (quarum quaeq; suam peculiarem naturam essentiam sortita est) ita ad unius individui conturam atq; constitutionem concurrunt, ut non misceantur inter se (sicuti in altera illa compositione substantiali) sed duntaxat desit in altera illa compositione, conjunctione atq; connexione coalescant: cujus substantialis compositionis neq; ullum in reliquis rebus naturalibus vestigium est deprehendere, ipsaq; a commentitia illa ex Materia & Forma compositione quamplurimum abhorret, sicuti proxime ostendimus. Et sic huic quoque Fonsecae atq; Suarez rationi, Formam substantialem ex eo, quod homo ex anima & corpore constat, asserenti, satisfecimus, eamq; inanem deprehendimus, uti reliquas omnes, in hunc finem allatas: de quibus in universum ingenue fatetur Pererius, eas non esse rationes omnino firmas & necessarias, evidenter concludentes, sed argumenta tantum verisimilia ac probabilia: quanquam sane ne verisimilitudinis quidem aut probabilitatis quicquam in ijs compadinis quidem aut probabilitatis quicquam in ijs compareret, nisi apud eos, qui meris hypothesibus, ex ipsâ Peripateticorum circa Formas doctrinâ ductis, ac proinde Principium petentibus, aut alijs aeque incertis, innituntur: sicuti hac nostra disputatione cuivis libere judicanti, neq; partibus nimium pertinaciter addicto, apertum fecimus.
units.tr: Last, he says that all the indications and signs of substantial composition that can be thought of in man are found also in other natural things. This is plainly false, as far as inanimate things are concerned. In other things there is no substantial composition except the mixture of different substances, or different elements, into one body. But in man, and in other living things, besides this substantial composition, which is found here too, namely on account of the body, there is another, very different from it. In the other things there are two substances, but in man there are several substances, each of which has its own peculiar nature and essence, and they come together to form and constitute one individual. They are not mixed together, as in that other substantial composition, but they are only joined and connected, without merging into one another. Of this substantial composition no trace can be found in other natural things, and it is far removed from that fictitious composition out of matter and form, as we have just shown. And so we have also answered this argument of Fonseca and Suárez, who assert a substantial form because man consists of soul and body, and we have found it empty, like all the other arguments brought forward for this end. Pereira frankly confesses of them all in general that they are not wholly firm and necessary reasons, clearly concluding, but only plausible and probable arguments. Yet there would be no plausibility or probability in them at all, except among those who rest on mere hypotheses drawn from the Peripatetic doctrine of forms itself, and so beg the question, or on other equally uncertain grounds. As our present discussion has made clear to anyone who judges freely, and is not too stubbornly committed to a party.

units.la: XXXIV. Quum igitur non probent Formam substantialem ea, quae pro ejus probatione à Peripateticis adducuntur, poteramus illam nostro jure rejicere, absq; ulteriore disputatione. neque enim aequum est, ut quis novum aliquod atq; inauditum dogma (quale illud de Forma est respectu omnium ante Aristotelem Philosophorum, solo forsitan Platone excepto, qui tamen ipse non videtur talem Formas, ac Aristoteles posuit, introducens, illud sibi credi postulet, quamdiu argumentis & rationibus, saltem verisimilibus, id confirmare non valet: neque Forma est de genere illarum communium notionum, quae Principia demonstrationum cum sint ipsa
units.tr: XXXIV. Since the arguments the Peripatetics bring forward to prove a substantial form do not prove it, we could reject it by our own right, without further discussion. For it is not fair that someone should demand that we believe a new and unheard-of dogma, such as that about form, which, with the possible exception of Plato (who himself does not seem to have posited such forms as Aristotle did), no philosopher before Aristotle held. It demands belief for as long as it cannot be confirmed by arguments and reasons, at least plausible ones. Nor is form of the kind of common notions that are the principles of demonstrations, since they are themselves
Chapter I.

units.la: ipsa non egent ulla demonstratione. Ad majorem tamen evidentiam, ac veritatis confirmationem, alia adhuc supraddictis addemus, ostendemusq; doctrinam de Formis substantialibus, qualis ab Aristotele & Aristotelicis traditur, ejusmodi esse, ut vel alijs ipsius Aristotelis decretis, vel Rationi, certissimis experimentis innixæ, quàm manifestissime repugnet; quare Aristotelici vel plurimis absurditatibus in ea defendenda se involvere, vel eam velint nolint deserere, ac sibi ipsis contradicere coguntur. Hoc quum in multis capitibus possemus demonstrare, non tamen omnia persequemur, sed pauca quædam ac præcipua eligere erimus contenti; nimirum de Formarum Inhæsione, Unitate in uno subjecto, Simplicitate, Intensionis ac Remissionis carentia, & Ortu ac Interitu: quæ rite examinata, præbebunt totidem firmissima contra Formam substantialem argumenta.
units.tr: they do not need any demonstration. Yet for greater clarity and confirmation of the truth, we shall add some further points to those already stated, and show that the doctrine of substantial forms, of what kind it is as handed down by Aristotle and the Aristotelians, is of such a nature that it most plainly conflicts either with other decrees of Aristotle himself or with Reason and with the most certain experiments. Hence the Aristotelians are compelled either to entangle themselves in many absurdities in defending it, or, whether they wish or not, to abandon it and contradict themselves. Although we could demonstrate this in many chapters, we will not pursue every point, but will be content to choose a few principal ones: namely, the inherence of forms, their unity in one subject, their simplicity, their lack of intension and remission, and their origin and destruction. When these are examined properly, they will provide as many very firm arguments against the substantial form.

units.la: Quantum ad primum, Omnes unanimiter docent, Formam inesse & inhærere Materiæ, quam informat, atque ab ea sustentari; quod sane non aliud est dicere, quàm quod Forma sit in subjecto. & hoc ipsum expressis quoque verbis ab Aristotele aliquando dicitur, quippe illa 2. Phys. 1. ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ ἐστὶν ἡ φύσις ἀεί, natura semper est in subjecto, unanimi omnium interpretum consensu de Forma sunt prolata. & in definitione quoque Materiæ primæ, posita in calce primi physicorum, vocat eam πρῶτον ὑποκείμενον, primum subjectum, non respectu accidentium, sed ipsius Formæ substantialis, sicuti clarum est ex Principijs istius doctrinæ, & à Fonseca diserte asseritur. Quid est aliud (inquit) esse primum subjectum, quam esse quoddam quasi sustentaculum primæ Formæ, hoc est substantialis. Quare futile est Piccolominei discrimen, quo distinguit inter esse in Materia, & esse in subjecto, Formamq; esse quidem in Materia, sed non esse in subjecto asserit; comment. ad 1. phys. text. 5. id quod & Mercenarius sequitur, Dilucid. 12 inquiens, Accidentia proprie in subjecto esse; Formam verò substantialem verùm esse in Materia, quam in subjecto. Etenim eo ipso, quod Forma dicitur inesse Materiæ, Materia statuitur Formæ subjectum. jectum, quandoquidem in ipsa ratione inhærendi includi-tur subjectum (sicuti Suarez alicubi ait) & Aristoteles ex-presse asserit (ut diximus) Materiam esse Formæ subje-ctum, ac Formam esse in subjecto: & sic pleriq; etiam Peripatetici loqui passim solent, inter quos Fonseca claris verbis dicit, Materiam primam esse subjectum Formæ substantialis. Ast Formam esse in subjecto, repugnat conditionibus Substantiæ ab Aristotele, in tractatu Categoriarum, assignatis; inter quas una est, Substantiam non esse in subjecto: quod cum in Principio capitis de prima tantum substantia pronuntiasset, postea universali enunciatione utens, omni facit Substantiæ commune, Κοινὸν δὲ καὶ πάσης οὐσίας, τὸ μὴ ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ εἶναι, commune autem est omni substantiæ, non esse subjecto. & postea rursus, Ὧσε οὐ ἂν εἴη ἐοίκα, τῶν ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ, itaq; substantia non est de numero eorum, quæ sunt in subjecto. Nec est ut quis dicat, Aristotelem toto eo capite de duobus tantum substantiarum generibus agere, substantijs primis, & substantijs secundis, nulla facta substantiarum incompletarum mentione; quare etiam conditiones ibi propositæ non ad has, sed ad illas duntaxat pertinent. Etiamsi enim prior hujus assertionis pars vera est, alteram tamen excludit generalis Peripateticorum consensio. omnes enim statuunt, incompletas etiam substantias, ut vocant, nimirum Materiam & Formam, hac lege teneri, ut non insint in subjecto. Aperte hoc docet Mercernarius Dilucid. 12. Dicimus, de ratione substantiæ in communi non esse, per se existere, quoniam omnibus substantiæ speciebus, ut Materiæ & Formæ, minime convenit, sed solum Substantiæ composita proprietas est. neq; , per eandem rationem, de ratione substantiæ in communi est, subjci; siquidem non competit Formæ. sed ratio substantiæ in universum est, non esse in subjecto; penes quod ab accidente distinguitur, cujus ratio est, in subjecto esse. Hæc igitur inter se pugnant, Formam esse in Subjecto, &, Substantiam in Subjecto non inesse; neq; simul stare possunt.
units.tr: As to the first, all teach unanimously that the form inheres in and is joined to the matter which it informs, and is sustained by it. This is certainly nothing other than saying that the form is in a subject. Aristotle himself sometimes says this in express words, for in Physics 2.1 the statement nature is always in a subject [ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ ἐστὶν ἡ φύσις ἀεί] is put forward about form, with the unanimous agreement of all the interpreters. Also in the definition of prime matter, given at the end of the first book of the Physics, he calls it the first subject [πρῶτον ὑποκείμενον], the first subject, not with respect to accidents but to the substantial form itself, as is clear from the principles of this doctrine, and is plainly asserted by Fonseca. What else (he says) is to be the first subject, than to be a kind of support of the first form, that is, of the substantial form? Therefore the distinction of Piccolomini is futile, by which he distinguishes between being in matter and being in a subject, and asserts that the form is indeed in matter but not in a subject (Commentary on Physics 1, text 5). Mercenarius follows this too, saying in Dilucidatio 12: Accidents are properly in a subject; but the substantial form is truly in matter rather than in a subject. Indeed, by the very fact that the form is said to be in matter, matter is established as the subject of the form, since subject is included in the very notion of inhering (as Suárez says somewhere). Aristotle also expressly asserts (as we have said) that matter is the subject of the form and that the form is in a subject; and so most Peripatetics commonly speak throughout, among whom Fonseca says in plain words that prime matter is the subject of the substantial form. But that the form is in a subject conflicts with the conditions of substance laid down by Aristotle in the treatise on the Categories. Among these is that substance is not in a subject. Having stated this at the beginning of the chapter only of the first substance, he afterwards, using a universal statement, makes it common to all substance: it is common to all substance not to be in a subject [Κοινὸν δὲ καὶ πάσης οὐσίας, τὸ μὴ ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ εἶναι]. And again afterwards: so substance is not of the number of those things which are in a subject [Ὧσε οὐ ἂν εἴη ἐοίκα, τῶν ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ]. Nor can anyone say that Aristotle in that whole chapter treats only of the two kinds of substance, first substances and second substances, making no mention of incomplete substances; so that the conditions proposed there pertain not to these but only to those. For even if the first part of this assertion is true, the general consensus of the Peripatetics excludes the other part. For all maintain that even incomplete substances, as they are called, namely matter and form, are bound by this law, that they are not in a subject. Mercenarius teaches this openly in Dilucidatio 12: We say that it does not belong to the notion of substance in general to exist through itself, since this does not befit all species of substance, such as matter and form, but is the property of composite substance alone. Nor, for the same reason, is it of the notion of substance in general to be subject to something, since this does not belong to form. But the notion of substance in universal is not to be in a subject, by which it is distinguished from accident, whose notion is to be in a subject. These things therefore fight among themselves: the form is in a subject, and substance is not in a subject; nor can they stand together at the same time.
Disp. 14. sect. 1. §. 1.
Cap.I.

units.la: XXXV. Huic incommodo ut mederentur Aristotelici, frigidam quandam distinctiunculam commenti sunt, dicentes, Formam non ita esse in subjecto, quomodo accidentia insunt. Forma (inquit Toletus) dicitur esse in subjecto, non sicut accidens, & Materia dicitur subjectum, non sicut accidentium subjectum. & similiter Averroës, Forma substantialis non est in subjecto per quod ipsa sustentetur sicut accidentia. & in quo haec differentia sita sit, ita alibi explicat, Forma substantialis & accidens aequivoce dicuntur esse in subjecto, quia subjectum accidentis est ens in actu, sed subjectum Forma substantialis est ens in potentia: & quia Forma substantialis est pars essentialis substantiae composita; accidens autem nullum est pars substantiae. & hoc ipsum pluribus verbis exponit Vicomercatus. Dicimus, si Materia, aut subjecto, quae accidentium natura est, Forma inhaeret, non idcirco a substantiae genere excludi. In Materia enim non ut accidens inhaeret, sed ut actus inest in eo, quod potentia est; e quibus duobus unum per se potest existere, quod a subjecto & accidente non potest. Accidentis autem subjectum, antequam id accipiat, actu sit oportet, nec ut sit, ei acceptum refert. & paulo post, Non igitur, ut in subjecto accidens, in Materia Forma inest, sed ut perfectio in perfectibili, & ut actus in potentia. Sed haec nodum non solvunt, neq; efficiunt (etiamsi omnia admitterentur) ut Formae non insint in subjecto; sed duntaxat explicant, Materiam, in quantum subjecti vicem gerit, aliter se habere erga Formas substantiales, quam erga accidentia, aliterq; ac majoribus beneficijs ab illis affici, quam ab istis afficiatur. Hinc autem non tollitur difficultas, neq; docetur, quomodo Formarum inhaesio in subjecto stare possit cum illo Aristotelis decreto, quo negat Substantias in subjecto inesse. neq; enim ait, substantias non ita esse in subjecto, quomodo accidentia in subjecto insunt, sed simpliciter iis convenire negat, ut in subjecto insint. Sunt quidem nonnulli, qui contrarium asserant, dicantque Aristotelem substantijs non omnem in subjecto inhaesionem ademisse in isto tractatu de categorijs, sed eam tantum, qua id, quod inhaeret, non est
units.tr: To remedy this difficulty, the Aristotelians have devised a rather feeble distinction, saying that form is not in its subject in the same way that accidents inhere. Form (says Toletus) is said to be in a subject, not as an accident is, and matter is called a subject, not as the subject of accidents is. Averroes likewise: A substantial form is not in a subject in the way that accidents are sustained by it. He explains where this difference lies, elsewhere, as follows: Substantial form and accident are said to be in a subject equivocally, because the subject of an accident is a being in act, but the subject of a substantial form is a being in potency; and because a substantial form is an essential composite part of a substance, whereas an accident is no part of a substance. Vicomercatus sets out the same point at greater length: We say that if form inheres in matter, or in the subject, which is the nature of accidents, it is not for that reason excluded from the genus of substance. For it inheres in matter not as an accident, but as an act is present in what is potential; of these two, one can exist through itself, which a subject and an accident cannot. But the subject of an accident must already be actual before it receives the accident, and it does not owe its being actual to what it receives. And a little later: Therefore form is in matter not as an accident is in a subject, but as a perfection in what can be perfected, and as an act in potency. But these things do not untie the knot, nor do they show (even if all were granted) that forms are not in a subject. They only explain that matter, insofar as it plays the role of a subject, is related to substantial forms differently from the way it is related to accidents, and is affected by the former with greater benefits than by the latter. Yet the difficulty is not thereby removed, nor is it taught how the inherence of forms in a subject can stand together with that decree of Aristotle by which he denies that substances inhere in a subject. For he does not say that substances are not in a subject in the way accidents are in a subject; he simply denies that substances belong to the class of things that are in a subject. There are indeed some who assert the contrary, and say that Aristotle, in that treatise on the categories, did not deny substances every kind of inherence in a subject, but only that by which what inheres is a part of another thing.

units.la: {a} Insaevus synonimidi tom o Infuavet sed Constabilit, consubstantiat, & coessentiat subjecto cum primat ad subjectum. est pars alterius. Ita Mercenarius, de præsente difficultate agens, quomodo Forma sit substantia, quum in subjecto sit de ratione substantiæ, non esse in subjecto; respondet: Nodus iste dissolvitur ex Aristotele, libro categoriarum, capite de substantia, ubi describens esse in subjecto, inquit, illud proprie esse in subjecto, quod est in alio, parsq; alterius non est. licet ergo Forma substantialis in Materia sit, non tamen ut in subjecto est, quoniam pars est ipsius substantia. Verba Aristotelis, ad quæ digitum intendit Mercenarius, hæc sunt: Μὴ ταῦτα ἀλλὰ τὰ μέρη τῶν ὄντων, ὡς ἐν ὑποκειμένοις ὄντα τοῖς ὅλοις, μήποτε ἀναγκασθῇ ἐν οὐσίας αὐτὰ φάσκειν εἶναι. οὐ γὰρ οὕτω τὰ ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ ὄντα ἐλέγετο, ὡς τὰ μέρη ὑπάρχουσα ἐν τινι. porro ne nos conturbent partes substantiarum, quasi sint in totis ut in subjectis, unde cogamur fateri eas non esse substantias, non enim ea, quæ in subjecto sunt, ita dicebantur inesse, ut partes in aliquo insunt. his verbis non aliud sibi vult Aristoteles, nisi hoc axiomate, quo substantiæ negantur esse in toto, non effici, ut partes substantiarum non sint substantiæ; quia aliud sit, esse in altero, ut in subjecto; aliud, ut partem in toto. ille autem sensus, quem hic invenit Mercenarius, haudquaquam hinc elici potest. Etiamsi enim daretur, per partes substantiarum hic intelligi Materiam & Formam (quod tamen minus est verisimile) inde non plus sequeretur, nisi Materiam & Formam non esse in substantia composita tanquam in subjecto, sed tanquam partes in toto: quod longe diversum est ab eo sensu, quem Mercenarius hinc excudit. neq; duo diversa inhæsionis in subjecto genera hic ab Aristotele (ut ipse fingit) assignantur; sed monet tantum, ne omne inesse capiamus pro, esse in subjecto; quia aliquid potest esse in substantia, quod tamen non insit in ea ut in subjecto; quomodo nimirum partes insunt in toto, quum tamen totum nequaquam possit dici suarum partium subjectum. Quodsi autem hoc quoque concederetur, Aristotelem, quando substantias negat esse in subjecto, non hoc de omni inhæsione intellexisse, sed de ea, qualis est accidentium;
units.tr: {a} The marginal note here is garbled in the scan; it seems to say that the form constitutes, makes consubstantial and co-essential with the subject, and stands in relation to the subject as first. Mercenarius, treating the present difficulty, namely how form can be a substance when it is of the nature of substance not to be in a subject, answers: This knot is resolved from Aristotle's book of the Categories, in the chapter on substance, where, describing being in a subject, he says that that is properly in a subject which is in another and is not a part of another. Therefore, although substantial form is in matter, it is not in matter as in a subject, since it is a part of the substance itself. The words of Aristotle to which Mercenarius points are these: "But lest the parts of beings, as being in wholes as in subjects, should force us to say that they are substances; for those things were not called 'in a subject' in the sense that parts are present in something" [Μὴ ταῦτα ἀλλὰ τὰ μέρη τῶν ὄντων, ὡς ἐν ὑποκειμένοις ὄντα τοῖς ὅλοις, μήποτε ἀναγκασθῇ ἐν οὐσίας αὐτὰ φάσκειν εἶναι. οὐ γὰρ οὕτω τὰ ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ ὄντα ἐλέγετο, ὡς τὰ μέρη ὑπάρχουσα ἐν τινι.] In these words Aristotle means nothing other than this axiom: that substances are denied to be in a whole does not bring it about that the parts of substances are not substances, since being in another as in a subject is one thing, and being a part in a whole is another. The sense that Mercenarius finds here can by no means be drawn from them. Even if it were granted that by the parts of substances are meant matter and form here (which is less probable), it would follow only that matter and form are not in the composite substance as in a subject, but as parts in a whole; and that is far different from the sense Mercenarius hammers out of it. Nor does Aristotle here assign two different kinds of inherence in a subject (as he himself imagines); he only warns that we should not take every kind of being-in as "being in a subject," since something can be in a substance without being in it as in a subject, just as parts are in a whole, though the whole can by no means be called the subject of its parts. But if this too were granted, that Aristotle, when he denies that substances are in a subject, did not mean this of every kind of inherence, but of that kind which accidents have,
Dilucid. 12.
Chapter I.

units.la: tium; ne sic quidem proficerent quicquam Peripatetici. differentiae enim paulo ante recitatae, quas inter Formarum atq; Accidentium inhaesionem constituunt, nequaquam sunt essentiales, sed diversam duntaxat subjecti erga res inhaerentes dispositionem, diversaq; rerum inhaerentium erga subjectum effecta attingunt. ast haec nihil obstant, quominus in ipsa maxime propria inhaesionis ratione utraque paria sint, atq; inter se conveniant; quod ipsa facere, sequitur ex ijs, quae ipsi Peripatetici super hac re docent. Etenim Suarez exponentus rationem inhaesionis accidentium, mutuamque inter ipsa, & subjectum habitudinem, sic inquit: Entitas accidentalis in se subsistere non potest, sed indiget subjecto, in quo sustentetur, & ideo indiget Causa materiali, tanquam necessaria ex natura rei, ut esse possit. quidquid autem hic de Accidentibus, quantum ad ipsorum in subjecto inhaesionem, praedicatur, idem in Formas quoq; substantiales competit, si vera sunt quae de ea praedicant. Aiunt enim, Formas (sola Mente exceptâ, quam tamen esse corporis humani Formam non omnes concedunt) aeque ac accidentia, non posse ullo modo per se subsistere, neq; a Materia separari, nisi solo intellectu; namq; Formae separationem a Materia, esse ejus corruptionem: sicut apud Themistium, Averroem, omnesq; alios Aristotelicos, qui aliquid de Forma scripserunt, passim legere est. unde etiam sequitur, ut Formae, non minus quam accidentia, indigeant subjecto seu Causa materiali (ut Suarez vocat) tanquam necessariâ ex natura rei, ut esse possint; utq; hae, non minus quam illa, insint ita, ut aliter esse non possint, nisi ut in subjecto insint. quare etiam Scaliger ait, Materiam quoq; esse ἐντελέχειαν, quae ita se substernat Formae, ut eam existere faciat. quo etiam spectant illa Alexandri, Formam minus posse per se subsistere, quam Materiam, licet Materia secundum se subsistere nequeat absq; Forma. neq; alium sensum habet, quod asseritur a Piccolomineo, Materiatas Formas pro suo esse pendere ex Materia, in genere Materiae. & a Conimbricensibus, Formam pendere a Materia, ut a recipiente: quomodo nimi-
units.tr: ...nor would the Peripatetics gain anything even so. For the differences just now recited, which they set up between the inherence of forms and that of accidents, are by no means essential. They touch only on the different disposition of the subject towards the things inhering, and on the different effects of the inhering things towards the subject. But these differences do not prevent the two from being alike, and agreeing with each other, in the very principal character of inherence. That follows from what the Peripatetics themselves teach on this matter. Suarez, explaining the nature of the inherence of accidents and their mutual relation to the subject, says: An accidental entity cannot subsist in itself, but needs a subject in which it is sustained, and therefore it needs a material cause, as necessary by the nature of the thing, in order to be able to exist. Whatever is asserted here about accidents, as regards their inherence in a subject, applies equally to substantial forms, if what they assert about them is true. For they say that forms (the mind alone excepted, which, however, not all admit to be the form of the human body) cannot in any way subsist through themselves, any more than accidents can, nor be separated from matter except by the intellect alone. For the separation of a form from matter is its corruption. This is found everywhere in Themistius, Averroes, and all the other Aristotelians who have written anything about form. Hence it also follows that forms, no less than accidents, need a subject or material cause (as Suarez calls it), as something necessary by the nature of the thing in order that they may exist, and that they inhere in the same way as accidents, so that they cannot be otherwise than by inhering in a subject. Therefore Scaliger also says: Matter too is an entelechy, which so underlies form that it makes it exist. To this also belong those words of Alexander: A form can less subsist through itself than matter can, although matter cannot subsist of itself without form. Nor does what Piccolomini asserts have any other sense: forms made material depend for their being on matter, in the genus of matter. Nor does the Conimbricenses' statement: a form depends on matter as on the recipient, in the way they are wont to say, of accidents, that they depend on their subject.
Difp. 14. sect. 1. §. 1.

units.la: Com. in 2. de Plant. In Princ. Epit. de Anima.
units.tr: Com. in 2. de Plant. In Princ. Epit. de Anima.

units.la: Lib. 2. de Mat. prim. c. 12. 2 Phys. 7. quaest. 8. art. 1. rum de Accidentibus dicere solent, ea à subjecto pendere. Unde satis perspicitur, inhæsionem Formarum & Accidentium, ex ipsorum doctrina, in ipsa inhærendi ratione convenire, quum utraq; pariter sint ἀχώρισα, neq; esse aliter aut subsistere quàm in subjecto possint. Et hoc magis adhuc confirmatur ex eo, quod sicuti accidentia subjectum suum undiq; ac penitus pervadunt, atq; ab eo, ut sic dicamus, tota perbibuntur; itidem circa Formas rem se habere docent. Conditio necessaria ad causandum in Materia (inquit Suarez) est propinquitas intima, seu indistantia à Forma. itaq; sicut in Causa efficiente applicatio ad passum dicitur conditio necessaria ad agendum, ita in Materiali Causa applicatio ad Formam. Hac autem applicatio est per intimam propinquitatem & indistantiam: quia non possunt Materia & Formæ uniri, nisi sint indistantes, & quasi penetrent intime per entitates suas. Quomodo igitur Formæ sint in subjecto, & tamen sint substantiæ (quum substantijs non conveniat, esse in subjecto) nequaquam à Peripateticis explicatur. dum enim id facere conantur, à proposito scopo aberrant, afferendo differentiam inter inhæsionem Formæ & accidentium. in quo licet omnia ijs, quæ dicunt, concederentur, nihil tamen ad rem dicerent; quia etiamsi Formæ non ita insint in subjecto, uti insunt accidentia, insunt tamen; in quo omnis difficultas sita est. Et præterea tamen differentiæ, quas hic assignant, sunt minus principales; quum alioquin in ijs, quæ præcipua sunt in ipsâ inhæsionis ratione, eadem sit Formarum & accidentium conditio, ex ipsorum doctrina; sicuti ostendimus. Quandoquidem ergo hæc difficultas manet insoluta, non parva hinc ministratur Peripateticis occasio, suspectam habendi suam de Formis doctrinam; quum præsertim illud Aristotelis axioma, Substantiam non esse in subjecto, omnino sit rationi ac veritati consentaneum. Neq; est ut cum Scaligero causentur angustias intellectus humani, quem lateat exquisita illa cognitio, quomodo ex duobus unum fiat; quomodo Forma sit in toto, & in quacunq; parte tota: quamlibet enim partem
units.tr: Lib. 2. de Mat. prim. c. 12. 2 Phys. 7. quaest. 8. art. 1. ...as they are wont to say of accidents, that they depend on their subject. Whence it is sufficiently clear that, by their own doctrine, the inherence of forms and of accidents agree in the very manner of inhering, since both are inseparable and can neither exist nor subsist otherwise than in a subject. This is confirmed even more by the fact that, just as accidents pervade their subject on every side and thoroughly, and are, so to speak, wholly soaked up by it, so they teach that the matter stands in the case of forms as well. Suarez says: The necessary condition for causing something in matter is intimate proximity, or non-distance, from the form. Therefore, just as in an efficient cause the application to the patient is called the necessary condition for acting, so in a material cause the application to the form is such a condition. This application, however, is through intimate proximity and non-distance, because matter and form cannot be united unless they are non-distant and, as it were, penetrate each other intimately through their entities. How forms are in a subject, and yet are substances (since being in a subject does not belong to substances), is in no way explained by the Peripatetics. For when they attempt to do so, they stray from their proposed aim, by asserting a difference between the inherence of form and that of accidents. Even if everything they say were granted in this, it would still say nothing to the point. For even if forms do not inhere in the subject as accidents do, they still inhere, and in this lies the whole difficulty. Moreover, the differences they assign here are of minor importance, since in the things that are chief in the very nature of inherence, the condition of forms and of accidents is, by their own doctrine, the same, as we have shown. Since therefore this difficulty remains unsolved, no small occasion is given to the Peripatetics for regarding their doctrine of forms with suspicion, especially since that axiom of Aristotle, that substance is not in a subject, is wholly consonant with reason and truth. Nor is it right, as with Scaliger, to plead the narrowness of the human intellect, which does not grasp that exquisite knowledge of how two become one, how form is in the whole and in every part of the whole, for every part

units.la: Exerc.307.29. tem ignis ignem esse. facillimum enim intellectu est, fieri hoc nullo pacto posse, ac propterea esse somnia, quæ de Forma substantiali dicuntur. & misera est manifestissimam absurditatem amoliendi ratio, exclamare, Adeo divinam rem esse Formam, ut cum sit substantia, aliam totâ sui impleat substantiâ ita, ut ex utraq; fiat unum: Neq; animos veritatis avidos à detegendis ac repudiandis ejusmodi commentis abstterreant imperiosa verba, Ulteriorem disquisitionem morosi atq; satagentis animi esse: cum humanæ sapientiæ pars sit, quædam æquo animo nescire. Certe nimiam curiositatem haud alias magis nobis damnaverit, & immodestum illa rimandi studium, quæ humanæ cognitioni Deus subtraxit: sed rursus illa, quæ ita sunt manifesta, ut ultro sese ingerant, velle sponte nescire, ne ipsorum scientia cogaris vetusta quidem, sed fictitia, dogmata deserere, stoliditatis potius quam æquanimitatis nomen mereatur.
units.tr: Exerc.307.29. ...of fire is fire. For it is very easy to understand that this cannot happen in any way, and therefore that what is said of substantial form is dreams. It is a wretched way of removing a most manifest absurdity to exclaim: so divine a thing is form, that, though it is a substance, it fills another wholly with its own substance, so that the two become one. Nor should imperious words frighten minds eager for truth from unmasking and rejecting such inventions, words such as: Further inquiry is the mark of a fretful and busy mind, since it is part of human wisdom to be content not to know certain things. Certainly God has forbidden us, more than in any other way, excessive curiosity and that immodest eagerness of searching which he has withheld from human knowledge. But to choose willingly not to know those things which are so manifest that they thrust themselves upon us, lest we be compelled by their knowledge to abandon old, yet fictitious, dogmas, deserves the name of stupidity rather than of equanimity.
XXXVI.

units.la: Absoluto primo capite, quod erat de Formarum inhæsione, transeamus ad secundum, de ipsarum unitate, quam necessario infert generalis Peripateticorum de Formis doctrina. Aiunt enim, quod unaquæq; Forma substantialis dat rei suum esse, constituitq; veram substantiam, atq; eam determinat ad certam aliquam speciem. unde sequeretur, si plures darentur Formæ in uno supposito, illud suppositum simul in pluribus speciebus constitui, efficeq; plura individua substantialia diversarum specierum: quod est absurdissimum. Propterea plurimi Peripatetici (de quibus est Suarez, qui & integrum texit eorum catalogum, qui idem senserint) absolute asseruerunt, unius substantiæ compositæ tantum esse unicam causam formalem, & in uno Composito naturali tantum unicam esse Formam substantialem. At alij rursus permulti plures posuerunt in unica re Formas substantiales; quanquam non omnes eodem modo. Commune quidem illis est, ut Elementa in omni Mixto manere, suasq; Formas retinere dicant. sed alij dicunt, Mixtorum inanimorum Formas non esse aliud, quam certam Formarum elementarium harmoniam, seu Formas elementares sub certa proportione atq; harmonia inter se junctas, unamq; pariter Formam, ex illis quatuor componitam, constituentes. Forma mixti est Forma ex congressu Formarum Elementorum oriens, ita ut quae erant quatuor Formae, in unam migraverint, quae est Forma mixti: inquit Zabarella lib. 2. de motu gravium & levium cap. 5. qualia etiam habet libro de Ortu & Interitu, cap. 2. Alij vero (de quorum numero sunt Zimarra & Fernelius) aiunt, Formam mixti esse Formam quandam re a Formis Elementorum diversam, illisq; superadditam. & consequenter in partibus viventium alteri quidem tres statuunt Formas, Elementorum, Mixti, & Totius; alteri vero duas, Mixti (quae nimirum e Formis Elementorum constet) & Totius.
units.tr: Having finished the first chapter, which concerned the inherence of forms, let us pass to the second, concerning their unity, which the general doctrine of the Peripatetics about forms necessarily implies. For they say that each substantial form gives a thing its being, constitutes a true substance, and determines it to some definite species. From this it would follow, if several forms were given in one supposit, that the same supposit would at once be constituted in several species, and would make several substantial individuals of different species, which is most absurd. For this reason very many Peripatetics (among whom is Suárez, who also woven together a complete catalogue of those who held the same view) have flatly asserted that a single composite substance has only one formal cause, and that in one natural composite there is only one substantial form. But others, again, have posited very many substantial forms in one thing, though not all in the same way. They agree at least in this, that they say the elements remain in every mixed body and retain their own forms. But some say that the forms of inanimate mixed bodies are nothing other than a certain harmony of elemental forms, that is, elemental forms joined together under a certain proportion and harmony, and constituting likewise one form composed of those four. The form of a mixed body is a form arising from the meeting of the forms of the elements, so that the things which were four forms have passed into one, which is the form of the mixed body: so says Zabarella, book 2, On the Motion of Heavy and Light Things, chapter 5, and he holds similar things in his book On Generation and Corruption, chapter 2. Others, however (of whose number are Zimara and Fernel), say that the form of a mixed body is a certain form really distinct from the forms of the elements and superadded to them. And consequently, in the parts of living things, some of these hold three forms, of the elements, of the mixed body, and of the whole; the others hold two, of the mixed body (which of course consists of the forms of the elements) and of the whole.

units.la: Praeter hosce autem modos, adhuc alios invexerunt nonnulli, quibus plures Formae substantiales dentur in uno supposito. quippe & Henricus in homine, & Scotus in omni vivente, statuunt Formam quandam substantialem, intermediam inter animam & Materiam; quam Formam corporeitatis appellant. & Philophonus, Jandunus, Paulus Venetus, statuerunt esse in homine tres animas realiter distinctas. Sane quantum ad illos attinet, qui & Elementa revera manere in Mixtis, & viventium partes similares sua quamq; peculiari Forma, quae ab anima esset diversa, insigniri docuerunt, validis argumentis ad ita sentiendum moti fuerunt, sicuti videre est apud Zabarellam, libro de Gener. & Interitu, cap. 2. argum. secundo, quarto, & quinto (namq; primum & tertium parvi sunt momenti) & ex iis, quae supra tum sectione secunda de Materia secunda, tum hac ipsa sectione de cadavere disputavimus, intelligi potest. Attamen hi quoque omnes, quotquot plures in uno composito Formas collocant, unanimiter fatentur, duas Formas specificas simul in eadem Materia inesse non posse. Absurditatem autem, Principio hujus paragraphi propositam (quum omnis Forma, ex Aristotelica doctrina, conferat rei esse & speciem, ac proinde sit specifica) ita eludunt, ut dicant, eas tantum Formas esse
units.tr: Besides these views, however, some have introduced still other ways in which several substantial forms are given in one supposit. Indeed Henry holds, in man, and Scotus, in every living thing, a certain substantial form intermediate between the soul and matter, which they call the form of corporeity. And Philoponus, Jandunus, and Paul of Venice have held that there are three souls really distinct in man. Certainly, as far as those are concerned who taught both that the elements truly remain in mixed bodies and that the similar parts of living things are marked by their own peculiar form, distinct from the soul, they were moved to think so by strong arguments, as may be seen in Zabarella, On Generation and Corruption, chapter 2, arguments second, fourth, and fifth (for the first and third are of little weight), and it can be understood from what we have discussed above, both in the second section on secondary matter and in this very section on the corpse. Yet all of these as well, as many as place several forms in one composite, unanimously admit that two specific forms cannot be present at the same time in the same matter. But they evade the absurdity proposed at the beginning of this paragraph (since, according to Aristotelian doctrine, every form confers being and species on a thing, and therefore is specific) by saying that these are only forms
{x} that they are unified.
Chapter I.

units.la: esse specificas, quæ actu existant; & in illis substantijs, quibus plures Formæ insunt, unam tantum ac supremam actu existere; reliquas autem omnes esse ibi in potentia. & sic, quanquam cum alteris illis, qui unam tantum in quacunq; re Formam statuunt, fateantur, non posse plures unâ Formâ actu esse in uno subjecto, aut multas actu Formas sub una Forma contineri, nihil tamen impedire dicunt, quominus modo hoc per ipsos assignato plures Formæ simul sint in uno subjecto, ita nimirum ut non sint simul actu, sed una tantum ipsarum, ac cæterarum princeps. Ita Fernelius primi Abditorum quarto, quum proposuisset hanc objectionem, Si partibus similaribus, quarum singula suis sint insignitæ Formis, alia insuper totius simplex indnatur Forma, fore ut rei, quæ actu quodam & suâ Formâ integre perficitur, alia (quod nullo modo fieri queat) accedat Forma, & uni eidemq; rei multa perfectiones insint; atq; simplicis unius ac similaris partis, ut ossis aut carnis, multa ac diversæ habeantur species, per quas & è diversis constaret essentiis, & in dissidentia genera referretur: ad hunc modum ipsi respondet; Etiamsi partibus similaribus, quæ jam suis Formis insignitæ sunt, nova totius accedat Forma, idcirco non confici, parti cuiq; duas actu inesse Formas. Formam enim non accedere ovi actu manenti, sed obscurari inferioris Forma illum actum & perfectionem, quoties clarior & nobilior immittitur. Quocirca, neq; quicquam unum diversorum generum fore, sed ab una posteriori nobiliori Forma res omnes essentiam, nomen, genus, mutuaturas. Quanquam ergo eidem rei duae perfectiones simul inesse non possunt; neminem tamen negare, quin complures Formæ in eadem re potentia simul possint esse, & præter has una actu. & consimilia quoq; tradit secundo Physiologiæ, capite octavo: taliaq; passim legere est apud alios, ejusdem sententiæ fautores.
units.tr: are specific and actually exist; and in those substances in which several Forms inhere, only one, the highest, actually exists, while all the others exist there only potentially. So although those others who hold that only one Form is in any thing admit that more than one Form cannot actually be in one subject, nor many Forms actually be contained under one Form, they nevertheless say that nothing prevents several Forms from being together in one subject in the way they propose, namely that they are not together actually, but only one of them, the prince of the rest, is actual. Thus Fernelius, in the fourth book of his Abditorum, when he had put forward this objection: If, to similar parts, each of which is marked by its own Forms, a further form of the whole is added, then it follows that to a thing which is perfected entire by a certain act and its own Form, another Form is added (which cannot happen in any way), and many perfections are present in one and the same thing; and of one simple and similar part, such as bone or flesh, many and different species would be had, by which it would consist of different essences and be referred to differing genera. To this he replies thus: Even if to similar parts, which are already marked by their Forms, a new form of the whole is added, it does not follow that two forms are actually present in each part. For the Form does not come to the egg while it remains actual; rather, that act and perfection of the inferior Form is obscured whenever a clearer and nobler one is introduced. Wherefore nothing will be one of the different kinds, but all things will borrow their essence, name and genus from the one later and nobler Form. Although therefore two perfections cannot be present together in the same thing, no one denies that several Forms can be potentially together in the same thing, and besides these one actually. He hands down similar things also in the second book of the Physiology, chapter eight; and such things are everywhere to be read among others who favour the same opinion.
XXXVII.

units.la: Sed hæc evasio inepta est ob duas rationes. Primo enim incidunt in parem, sed contrariam absurditatem, atq; illi, qui cadaver partesq; cadaveris specifice isferred differre aiunt à corpore viuente, partibusq; corporis viuentis. sicuti enim illi dicere coguntur, ut sibi constent, carnem aut os cadaveris non esse carnem aut os, nisi homonymice, quum durante vitâ essent verum os, ac vera caro: ita his è diverso dicendum est (si consequentia loqui velint) in cadavere quidam esse veram carnem, & verum os; in corpore autem viuente non nisi æquivoce. Ut enim res sit hoc aliquid, atq; ad certam speciem pertinet, non nisi à Formâ actuante, atq; ad certam speciem determinante, habere potest, ut ipsi docent. Ast hæ partes non possunt actuari à suis Formis, quum ipsas Formas dicant non actu existere, sed potentia. Quomodo autem illud, quod ipsum actu non existit, alterum actu existere faciet? Saue si Forma carnis & ossis in corpore viuente sunt in potentia, caro quoq; & os non erunt caro & os actu sed in potentia. Causæ enim in potentia, effectus actu esse non potest; sed ut hic actu sit, illum actu existere necesse est, tradente ipso Aristotele, 9. Metaph. cap. 8. Αεὶ ἐκ τῆς δυνάμει ὄντος γίνεται τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ ὂν ὑπὸ ἐνεργείας ὄντος. semper ex eo quod potentiâ est, fit actu existens, ab eo quod actu existit. Et cum illud, quod est in potentia, non existat (quippe existere, est esse actu, & desijsse esse in potentia) caro & os non existent in corpore viuente; sed tum demum existere incipient, quando id cadaver factum est, atq; anima ex eo excessit. Et hoc, quod dicimus, sicuti per se clarum est, ita magis etiamnum inde confirmatur, quod ijdem hi, qui hanc fouent opinionem, non tantum dicunt, Formas illas inferiores esse in potentia; sed & conceptis verbis pronuntiant, eas, quamdiu superior Forma adest, Formarum officio non fungi, atq; Materiæ instar ad illam se habere. Mercenarius, Licet Elementorum Forme integra maneant in Mixto, non tamen dant esse simpliciter, sed hoc proficiscitur ab ultima Forma, quia priores Forme sunt quasi Materia posterioris. Vicomercatus, Dicendum, corporum, quorum plures sunt Forme, que successione quadam altera post alteram aduenunt, priorem quidem posterioris semper veluti potentiam esse;
units.tr: But this evasion is foolish, for two reasons. First, they fall into an absurdity like that of those who say that a corpse and the parts of a corpse differ specifically from a living body and the parts of a living body, but in the opposite direction. For just as those men are compelled to say, if they are to be consistent, that the flesh or bone of a corpse is not flesh or bone except homonymously, whereas while life lasted they were true bone and true flesh, so these men must say, conversely (if they want to speak consistently), that in a corpse there is true flesh and true bone, but in a living body only equivocally. For a thing can be this particular thing and belong to a definite species only through the form which actuates it and determines it to that species, as they themselves teach. But these parts cannot be actuated by their own Forms, since they say the Forms themselves do not actually exist but only potentially. How then will what does not actually exist itself make the other exist actually? Indeed, if the Forms of flesh and bone are only potential in a living body, then the flesh and bone will not be actual flesh and bone but potential. For a cause that is only potential cannot have an actual effect; but for the effect to be actual, the cause must necessarily be actual, as Aristotle himself teaches in Metaphysics 9, chapter 8: [Αεὶ ἐκ τῆς δυνάμει ὄντος γίνεται τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ ὂν ὑπὸ ἐνεργείας ὄντος] always from that which is potentially, there comes to be what is actually existing, by what actually exists. And since that which is in potentiality does not exist (for to exist is to be actual, and to have ceased to be in potentiality), flesh and bone will not exist in a living body; they will begin to exist only when that body has become a corpse and the soul has departed from it. And what we say is clear in itself, and it is confirmed even more by this: the same men who foster this opinion not only say that those inferior Forms are in potentiality, but also expressly declare that, as long as the superior Form is present, they do not perform the office of Forms, and stand towards it in the manner of matter. Mercenarius: Although the Forms of the elements remain whole in the mixed body, they do not give being simply; this proceeds from the last Form, because the prior Forms are as it were the matter of the posterior. Vicomercatus: It must be said that in bodies of which there are several Forms, which arrive one after another in a certain succession, the prior is always as it were a potency of the posterior;
Dilucid. 68.
Lib.2.de Princip. rerum natur. c. 4.
Chapter 1.

units.la: esse: at dum id evenit, Materiæ cujusdam una cum subjecto, in quo insunt, obtinent rationem. nec absurdum est, rei minus perfectæ Formam tam Materia, cujus Formæ est, perfectiori Formæ ut Materiam subjici. Zabarella, Perdictum illud (Unius rei unum tantum est esse) excluduntur illæ Formæ solum, quæ non sunt subordinatæ, nec una est præparatio ad aliam recipiendam. at non excluduntur Formæ subordinatæ, quarum sola ultima fungitur officio Formæ, & perficit omnes alias, quæ cum prima Materia constituunt Materiam proximam, & propriam ipsi ultimæ Formæ. Ex his apertissime sequitur, quod dicebamus, Carnem non esse carnem in corpore vivente, quia ut sit caro, debet à Forma sua habere: ab ea autem habere nequit, quum ipsa actu non existat, & Formæ officio non fungatur. Imò hinc ulterius sequitur, nullam in vivente esse inter partes similares differentiam, omnesq; esse ejusdem inter se rationis & essentiæ, si esse rei pendet à Forma actuante & realiter informante; omnes autem hæ partes una eademq; simplici Forma actuantur & informantur. Et sane Fernelius, apertâ rei consequentiâ inductus, ipse tantundem asserit. Partes illæ, inquit, quas tu tum in stirpe tum in animali dissimillimas esse statuis, ejusdem rationis ac Formæ sunt omnes, dum eorum utrunq; est in vivis. at mortem obeuntibus illis, totiusq; evanescente Forma, quæ superant partes, neq; Forma neq; essentia sunt ejusdem, sed omnino diversa. nam singula partes ad suas quoq; tum naturas redeunt, quæ præsente totius Forma unum quid & simplex erant. itaq; totius interitu, similaris cujusq; partis species in suum actum & in suam perfectionem erumpit, quæ, dum vivebat animal, solum inesse potentiâ dicebatur. actu enim fit, quod erat potentiâ. & illa quidem tum nobilioris Formæ lumine obscurata, nec elucere ipsa poterat, nec parti suam essentiam aut nomen conferre. Credibile quidem est, non omnes, qui hanc sequuntur opinionem, ita plane, ac hic facit Fernelius, locuturos, cumq; reprehensuros, quasi nonnulla imprudentius ab eo prolata fuerint. sed certum tamen est, quidcunq; ab eo hic dicitur, tur, necessario fuere ex ea hypothesi, quae Formas inferiores statuit potentia tantum inesse, propterea ab omnibus, qui illam amplectuntur, tantundem esse dicendum (nisi velint suis ipsorum decretis repugnare) nimirum quod os non sit os, neq; caro caro, quamdiu animal vivit: quod profecto omnem superat absurditatem.
units.tr: being. But while this happens, the forms count as the matter of something, together with the subject in which they inhere. Nor is it absurd that the matter of a less perfect form, whose form it is, should be subjected to a more perfect form. Zabarella says: the axiom "one thing has only one being" excludes only those forms that are not subordinate, and of which one is not a preparation for receiving another. It does not exclude subordinate forms, of which only the last performs the office of a form and perfects all the others, which together with prime matter make up the proximate matter, proper to that last form. From this it follows most clearly what we were saying: flesh is not flesh in a living body, because in order to be flesh it must have its being from its form, and it cannot have that from a form which is not actually existing and does not perform a form's office. Indeed, it further follows from this that in a living thing there is no difference among the similar parts, and that they all have the same nature and essence, if the being of a thing depends on the form that actuates it and really informs it; but all these parts are actuated and informed by one and the same simple form. And certainly Fernelius, led by the clear consequence of the matter, asserts just as much himself. Those parts, he says, which you hold to be most unlike in a plant and in an animal, are all of the same nature and form while each of them is in living things. But when those things die, and the form of the whole vanishes, the parts that remain are neither of the same form nor of the same essence, but entirely different. For the individual parts return to their own natures, which while the form of the whole was present had been one thing and simple. So at the death of the whole, the species of each similar part breaks out into its own act and its own perfection, which while the animal was alive was said to be present only potentially. For what was potentially becomes actually. And indeed that species, obscured by the light of the nobler form, could then neither shine forth itself nor confer its own essence or name on the part. It is credible that not all who follow this opinion would speak in quite the way Fernelius does here, and that they would reprove him, as if he had put forward some things rather carelessly. But it is certain that whatever he says here necessarily follows from that hypothesis, which holds that the lower forms are present only potentially. Therefore everyone who embraces that hypothesis must say just as much (unless they wish to contradict their own decrees): namely, that bone is not bone, nor flesh flesh, as long as the animal lives. This certainly surpasses every absurdity.

units.la: XXXVIII. Altera ratio, obsistens huic opinioni, quae Formas nonnullas non actu, sed potentia, ac sub alterius potioris Formae imperio, inesse asserit, petitur ex ipsa huius phraseos explicatione.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The second reason opposing this opinion, which asserts that some forms are present not actually but potentially, and under the rule of another, more powerful form, is drawn from the very explanation of this phrase.

units.la: Etenim substantia dicitur esse in potentia duobus modis, vel simpliciter, vel respective seu denominative. Hoc posterius rursus dupliciter fit; quum substantia dicatur esse in potentia vel ad aliquod accidens, quod nondum quidem habet, sed apta est habere, quomodo aqua frigida dicitur calida in potentia; vel ad aliam substantiam, in quam ipsa abire nata est, quomodo ovum dicitur gallina in potentia, & sanguis, in potentia caro. Hic modus respectivae potentiae (de quo multa Galenus in Principio tertij de crasibus) ad praesens propositum non pertinet, quum Formae illae inferiores, de quibus nunc agimus, non ita dicantur esse in potentia, sed priori modo, sive simpliciter. Eorum autem, quae ita dicuntur esse in potentia, duae sunt classes. Partim enim nondum sunt in rerum natura, nondumque existunt, sed existere possunt, quum dentur Causae, quae ipsa producere valeant, ac suo tempore, nisi quid impediat, productURAE sint; quomodo media hyeme rosa dicitur esse in potentia. atque huic potentiae opponitur ille actus, quo res jam existit extra Causas suas, sive jam producta est, atq; extat in rerum natura; quem actum videtur descripsisse Scaliger comm. in 6. de Caus. plant. cap. 17. inquiens, Est autem actu, quod per se est, atq; sejunctum à suis Causis, ita ut non opus habeat aliquo adjumento ut hoc fit, quod esse debet: quanquam haec descriptio laxior est, ita ut non ille tantum actus, qui potentiae simplici sed & qui potentiae denominativae opponitur, ea comprehendi videatur. Partim vero jam quidem in mundum producta sunt, atq; existentiam suam habent; esse autem seu existere in potentia dicuntur, quia existentia ipsorum non est manifesta; quum aliarum rerum admixtione obscurata, veluti delitescant & abscondantur. ita caseus & butyrum lacti insunt in potentia, non quia non sint ibi vere ac realiter, sed quia esse non deprehenduntur, quamdiu lac servat debitam consistentiam ac Mixtionis modum. itaq; huic potentiae opponitur ille actus, non quo res existere incipit, quum non existeret prius, sed quo ita existit per se, ut ab alijs rebus, quarum admixtione abscondebatur, sit segregata. & ad hunc modum referendum est, quod Aristoteles omnes alicujus Compositi seu Totius partes dicit esse in potentia, quamdiu constituunt Compositum; quae tamen assertio minus accurata & valde dura est. Ad horum modorum alterutrum necessario redigi debet illa potentia, in qua dicunt esse Formas illas, quas superioris Formae praesentia actum amittere dicunt: ipsorumq; optioni relinquimus, utrum eorum eligere velint. Utrumvis autem elegerint, causa sua eos cadere necesse est, omnibusq; fieri manifestum, locutionem illam temere ab ipsis hic adhiberi, ac non nisi inane esse subterfugium, quum nullus commodus sensus ipsi assignari queat. Etenim si Formas dicant esse in potentia priori modo, quo ea esse in potentia dicuntur, quae nondum producta sunt; tunc idem dicunt, acsi dicerent, Formas illas nequaquam adhuc esse in partibus similaribus, sed postea in ijs futuras, & intereunte superiori Forma demum producendas: quod sane haud quaquam volunt, ac propterea non est ut contra hoc verba faciamus. Quodsi vero ad secundum modum se conferant, tunc praeterquam quod hic ad Formas accommodari vix potest (praeterquam illo Aristotelico modo, qui huc nequaquam facit, quum eo omnes omnino Formae dici possint esse in potentia, dum Compositum constituunt) in illud incommodum incident, cujus vitandi Causa hujus phraseos ambagem quaesiverunt, ut nimirum cogantur fateri, unam eandemq; rem duabus Formis specificis simul informari. Forma enim vere ac realiter existens, non potest quin rei, cujus Forma est, omnia conferat, quæ Compositis conferri à Formis suis Peripatus docet, & consequenter eam specifice determinet, atq; specificæ Formæ provincia erga ipsam fungatur. Quæ enim dicuntur esse in potentia hoc posteriori modo, vere & realiter, ac quidquam aliud, existunt; sed duntaxat existere non videntur: ideoq; nostri solummodo respectu dicuntur esse in potentia, cum in se ac sui ipsorum respectu nequaquam sint in potentia, sed verissimo actu existant: quam rem magnus vir Fracastorius sub exemplo quatuor humorum (è quibus concretum esse omnem sanguinem, vulgo medici ac philosophi, inde à temporibus Hippocratis, putant) perspicue declarat. Eâ in massâ sanguinis (inquit) quæ intra venas continetur, confusi commixtiq; sunt & reliqui vocati humores, cholera, phlegma, & melancholia, sed ita ut quodammodo actu, quodammodo potentiâ in ea massâ sint, potentiâ quidem, quia ad minimas & indivisibiles particulas redacti sunt, nec monstrari possunt, hoc quidem phlegma, illud cholera, illud melancholia, nisi particulæ uniantur: at actu sunt, quoniam tametsi ad particulas minimas deducti sunt, proprij tamen generis rationem habent.
units.tr: For a substance is said to be in potentiality in two ways: either simply, or relatively (respectively, or denominatively). The latter again happens in two ways, since a substance is said to be in potentiality either with respect to some accident which it does not yet have but is fit to have, as cold water is said to be hot in potentiality; or with respect to another substance into which it is naturally apt to change, as an egg is said to be a hen in potentiality, and blood to be flesh in potentiality. This mode of relative potentiality (on which Galen says much at the beginning of the third book On Mixtures) does not pertain to the present proposition, since those lower forms with which we are now dealing are not said to be in potentiality in that way, but in the first way, that is, simply. Of those things that are said to be in potentiality in this way, there are two classes. Some are not yet in the nature of things, and do not yet exist, but can exist, since there are causes which are able to produce them, and which will produce them at their proper time, unless something hinders; so in midwinter a rose is said to be in potentiality. Opposed to this potentiality is that act by which a thing already exists outside its causes, or has already been produced and stands in the nature of things. Scaliger seems to have described this act in his commentary on the sixth book of On the Causes of Plants, chapter 17, saying: That is in act which exists through itself and is separated from its causes, so that it has no need of any aid in order to be what it ought to be. Although this description is rather loose, so that it seems to comprehend not only that act which is opposed to simple potentiality but also that which is opposed to denominative potentiality. Others, indeed, have already been brought into the world and have their existence, yet they are said to be or exist in potentiality because their existence is not manifest, being obscured by the mixture of other things, as if they lay hidden and concealed. Thus cheese and butter are present in milk potentially, not because they are not there truly and really, but because they are not perceived to be there as long as the milk keeps its proper consistency and mode of mixture. Therefore opposed to this potentiality is that act by which a thing does not begin to exist, since it did not exist before, but by which it exists in itself, so that it is separated from those other things by whose mixture it was concealed. To this mode must also be referred what Aristotle says, that all the parts of any compound or whole are in potentiality as long as they constitute the compound; yet this assertion is less exact and quite harsh. That potentiality in which they say those forms exist, which they say lose their actuality through the presence of a higher form, must necessarily be reduced to one of these two modes. We leave it to them to choose which of the two they wish. But whichever they choose, they must fall into their own trap, and it will be clear to all that the expression is rashly employed here by them, and is nothing but an empty evasion, since no suitable sense can be assigned to it. For if they say that the forms are in potentiality in the first way, in which those things are said to be in potentiality that have not yet been produced, then they say the same as if they said that those forms are by no means yet in the similar parts, but will be in them later, to be produced only when the higher form perishes. This they certainly do not wish, and therefore there is no need for us to argue against it. But if they betake themselves to the second mode, then, besides the fact that this can hardly be applied to forms (except in that Aristotelian sense, which is by no means relevant here, since in that sense all forms whatever could be said to be in potentiality while they constitute the compound), they fall into that inconvenience which they sought to avoid by this circumlocution, namely that they are compelled to admit that one and the same thing is informed by two specific forms at once. For a form that exists truly and really cannot fail to confer on the thing of which it is the form all the things that the Peripatetics teach that forms confer on compounds, and consequently it specifically determines it, and the office of a specific form is performed in relation to it. For those things that are said to be in potentiality in this latter mode really and truly exist, and are no less than anything else; they only do not appear to exist. Therefore they are said to be in potentiality only with respect to us, and not at all in themselves or with respect to themselves, but they exist in the most true actuality. The great man Fracastorius clearly explains this by the example of the four humours, out of which the common physicians and philosophers, from the time of Hippocrates onward, think all blood is composed. In that mass of blood (he says) which is contained within the veins, the other so-called humours, choler, phlegm, and melancholy, are also mixed and confused together; yet in such a way that they are in that mass in some respects actually and in some respects potentially: potentially, because they have been reduced to the smallest and indivisible particles, and cannot be shown, this one as phlegm, that one as choler, that one as melancholy, unless the particles are united; but they are actual, since, although they have been reduced to the smallest particles, they still have the nature of their own kind.

units.la: XXXIX. Hisce duabus rationibus nostris contra illam doctrinam, qua plures Formæ ita dicuntur esse simul in uno subjecto, ut una tantum ipsarum sit in actu, reliquæ verò in potentia, adjungi potest alia Peripateticorum, contrariam opinionem sequentium, qui ex communibus Principijs docent, hoc fieri minime posse, quod alteri dicunt, ut Forma aliqua substantialis cum suo subjecto habeat rationem Materiæ ad superiorem Formam.
units.tr: XXXIX. These two arguments of ours against that doctrine, by which several Forms are said to be in one subject at the same time so that only one of them is actual while the rest are potential, can be joined by another argument from the Peripatetics, who follow the contrary opinion. From common principles they teach that what the others say cannot happen: that a substantial Form together with its subject should have the character of matter with respect to a higher Form.

units.la: Equidem ex generali de Formis Doctrina, apud omnes Peripateticos recepta, sequitur, fieri nullo modo posse, ut una Forma substantialis sit dispositio proxima ad aliam substantialem Formam, simul permanens cum illa; quia unaquæq; Forma substantialis dat esse simpliciter, & constituit essentiam completam in genere substantiæ. Hoc ipso autem, quod unaquæq; sub-
units.tr: Indeed, from the general doctrine of Forms accepted by all Peripatetics it follows that in no way can one substantial Form be the proximate disposition for another substantial Form, remaining together with it; because each substantial Form gives being absolutely and constitutes a complete essence in the genus of substance. But from this very fact that each sub-

units.la: Substantialis Forma constituit substantialem naturam completam, ita determinat sibi Materiam quam informat, & quasi trahit illam ad suum esse, ut non admittat in ea aliam Formam substantialem. Et quum Forma substantialis per se respiciat potentiam substantialem; substantia completa non est jam in potentia substantiali, sed accidentali tantum: sicuti haec, aliaq; ad eandem rem, declarantur à Suarezio, Disputationis decimae quintae sectione decima, paragraphis 34. & 64. Quod si hanc consequentiam agnoscere nolint ij, qui plures simul Formas collocant, ac proinde persistunt in sua illa assertione, nihil impedire quominus ita se res habeat, ut quod unus sit potentia, alterum sit actus, ut prior Forma sit posterioris potentia, & potentia rationem subeat cum ea Materia, in qua inest; quia etiam si hujusmodi rerum minus perfectarum Forma cum sua Materia, perfectiori Forma ut Materia subjiciantur, tamen actus sint seu entelechia, quum alteri Forma non subjiciantur, nisi ut ejus, quod subsequentem Formam excipit, pars sunt; sicuti haec aliaq; in eundem sensum scribuntur à Vicomercato lib. 2. capite quarto (unde & paulo superius aliqua huc spectantia allegavimus) nihil tamen hoc ipsos juvabit, quominus difficultatibus modo enumeratis teneantur irretiti. Non enim quaerimus, quomodo Formae similarium se habeant ad Formam totius, sed ad ipsas partes similares, ubi sine ambagibus alterum duorum dicendum est, vel esse eas in potentia, vel in actu. utrumq; enim simul verum esse non potest, ipso sic scribente Vicomercato, in eodem loco: Unius autem & ejusdem rei potentiam & actum aliquid esse non licet, quomodo nec unius ratione habita, actu simul & potentia aliquid esse conceditur. eligant igitur alterutrum necesse est. sed neutrum eligere possunt, quin causam suam jugulent. si enim dicant Formas similarium, respectu ipsarum partium similarium, esse in potentia, incident in difficultates a nobis propositas, quum Formae sit (ut ipsi aiunt) perficere id, cujus est Forma: perficere vero alterum non possit, quod ipsum non est perfecte, aut potius non est omnino. Actus, inquit Scaliger, non est tantum ἐντελέχεια, λέχεια, perfectio, sed & ἐντελέχεια, perfectionis. & in eundem sensum ibidem, Actum vocat Formam seminis, atq; ei dat actum informandi. nullus autem est actus in potentia: informat enim. semen non esset, nisi ejus Forma esset. Si vero dicant, Formas eas, licet dicantur esse in potentia, ratione superioris Formae; actûs tamen vicem implere erga ipsas partes similares: in illud incident incommodum, ut cogantur fateri, unamquamq; partem habere duas Formas actu, suam propriam, & illam totius; quod nequaquam fieri posse, ut una res duas actu Formas obtineat, omnes ad unum, nemine excepto, clamant Peripatetici, atq; hi ipsi non minus, quam adversarij ipsorum (qui nullam, nisi eam totius, Formam agnoscunt) sese abhorrere testantur. Quandoquidem ergo inter se consentiunt Peripatetici, non nisi unam Formam specificam in uno subjecto dari; validissimum hinc quoq; contra doctrinam de Formis substantialibus argumentum depromere licet; quum ista unitas nullo modo defendi probabiliter queat. Nam qui hoc ita explicant, ut uni Formae actu existenti alias Formas in potentia adjungant, vel potius subjungant; involvuntur absurditatibus nunc commemoratis. Qui vero, ad hasce defugiendas, alteram sequuntur partem, ac stricte tenent, non nisi unam in quocunq; suppositio Formam substantialem inesse posse, premuntur gravissimis rationibus, ob quas alteri plures in una substantia Formas statuere coacti fuerunt, quarumq; praecipuas nos superius, tum in hac ipsa sectione, tum in praecedenti, recitavimus.
units.tr: A substantial Form constitutes a complete substantial nature and so determines the matter it informs to itself, and as it were draws it to its own being, that it does not admit another substantial Form into it. And since a substantial Form in itself looks to substantial potency, a complete substance is no longer in substantial potency, but only in accidental potency: as these and other things on the same point are set out by Suarez, Disputation 15, section 10, paragraphs 34 and 64. But if those who posit several Forms together refuse to acknowledge this consequence, and so persist in their assertion, nothing prevents the matter from being such that one Form is in potency while another is in act, so that the prior Form is in potency to the posterior, and takes on the character of potency with respect to the matter in which it inheres; for even if the Forms of these less perfect things, together with their matter, are subjected to a more perfect Form as matter, nevertheless they are act or entelechy, since they are not subjected to another Form except as parts of that which receives the subsequent Form; as these and other things to the same effect are written by Vicomercato, book 2, chapter 4 (whence we also cited some things bearing on this a little earlier). Yet this will not help them at all, so that they are not held caught in the difficulties just listed. For we are not asking how the Forms of similar parts relate to the Form of the whole, but to the similar parts themselves, where without circumlocution one of two things must be said: either that they are in potency or that they are in act. For both cannot be true at once, Vicomercato himself writing in the same place: It is not permitted that something be both potency and act of one and the same thing, just as it is not granted that something be both actually and potentially in virtue of one and the same respect. They must therefore choose one of the two alternatives. But they cannot choose either without cutting their own throat. For if they say that the Forms of similar things, with respect to the similar parts themselves, are in potency, they will fall into the difficulties we have proposed, since the function of a Form is (as they themselves say) to perfect that of which it is the Form; but it cannot perfect what is not perfectly, or rather is not at all. "Act," says Scaliger, "is not only ἐντελέχεια, perfection, but also ἐντελέχεια of perfection [i.e. the perfecting of a perfection]." And to the same effect in the same place: He calls the Form of the seed act, and gives it the act of informing. But there is no act in potency: for it informs. There would be no seed unless its Form were there. But if they say that these Forms, although they are said to be in potency with respect to the higher Form, nevertheless fulfil the role of act toward the similar parts themselves, they fall into this inconvenience: that they are forced to confess that each part has two Forms in act, its own and that of the whole. That one thing cannot have two Forms in act is cried out by all Peripatetics, one and all, none excepted; and these themselves no less than their opponents (who acknowledge no Form but that of the whole) declare that they shrink from it. Since therefore the Peripatetics agree among themselves that only one specific Form can be in one subject, a most powerful argument against the doctrine of substantial Forms may also be drawn from this, since that unity cannot be defended in any probable way. For those who explain it so as to add, or rather subjoin, other Forms in potency to one Form existing in act, are involved in the absurdities just mentioned. And those who, to escape these, follow the other part and hold strictly that in any supposed thing only one substantial Form can be present, are pressed by the most serious reasons, on account of which the others were compelled to posit several Forms in one substance; the chief of these we have recited above, both in this section and in the preceding one.

units.la: XL. Tertium de Formis axioma, unde commode seipsos explicare nequeunt Peripatetici, est simplicitas earum: quam duplicem ipsis assignant. Non modo enim ijs adimunt omnem compositionem, quae è partibus fiat dissimilis naturae seu heterogeneis, sed & eam, quae è partibus fit (ut sic dicamus) quantitativis; quare & negant duas Formas, etiam quae ejusdem sint generis, in unam conflari posse. Ex duabus Formis, inquit Scaliger, tanquam partibus, non potest una Forma fieri. & rursus ibidem, Forma cum
units.tr: XL. The third axiom about Forms, by which the Peripatetics cannot conveniently explain themselves, is their simplicity, which they assign in a twofold way. For they deny Forms not only every composition made of parts of dissimilar or heterogeneous nature, but also that which is made of parts that are (so to speak) quantitative; hence they also deny that two Forms, even those of the same kind, can be fused into one. From two Forms, says Scaliger, as parts, one Form cannot be made. And again in the same place, Form with
Exerc. 268.

units.la: cum sit simplex & indivisibilis, ex duobus componi non potest. Et quum id, quod omnino simplex, non habet partes è quibus constet, dividi nequeat (quippe nihil aliud est divisio, quam partium sejunctio) etiam indivisibiles seu infecabiles facere Formas coguntur. Hoc ab Averöe scriptum multis in locis, à Scaligero etiam passim inculcatur, ut comment. 9. in lib. 4. de Caus. Plant. Principium formale nec continuum est, neq; dissitum, sed unum indivisibile. Et rursus Exerc. 80. sect. 3. Forma est unum, non connexione, sed essentia maxime indivisibili. & notat ibi locos, ubi idem ab Aristotele indicatum est: passimq; hoc resonant omnes Peripatetici.
