Huc quoq; pertinet, quod magnitudinem & parvitatem in Formas non cadere aiunt, idq; adeo certum putant, ut Scaliger pronuntiet, illum abuti patientiâ sapientum, qui Formam majorem & minorem dicat. Quod itaq; Aristoteles de Intelligentijs scribit, ὅτι μέγεθος οὐκ ἔχουσι, καὶ ἀμερεῖς καὶ ἀδιαίρετοί εἰσι, quod magnitudinem nullam habent, quadq; è partibus non constant, & indivisibiles sunt: jam non est ijs peculiare, sed commune id habent cum omnibus Formis. Sane ista adeo inter se cohærent, ut quibus unum tribuitur, ijs reliqua quoque tribui necesse sit. Sed tueri hæc Peripatetici nequaquam possunt, facileq; est ipsos eo adigere, ut vel inviti fateantur, & componi Formas è pluribus, & magnitudinem habere, ac divisibiles esse, & proinde imaginariam esse simplicissimam hanc simplicitatem, quam ijs tribuunt. Quantum ad primum; multorum viventium animas (quas ipsi pro Formis habent) è pluribus animis seu animabus posse componi, ac proinde habere partes (quum duæ illæ, aut plures animæ, quæ in unam coaluerunt, necessario dicendæ sint partes illius totius animæ, quæ ex ipsarum conjunctione exurgit) præterquam quod evidentissime doceri potest exemplo animalium à diversigeneribus animalibus procreatorum (de quibus mox commodius agetur) clare etiam apparet ex eo, quod diversi graves auctores pro certo produnt, ex ejusdem generis feminibus simul satis, unam plantam emergere, tenellis plantis (quarum sane
units.tr: Since it is simple and indivisible, it cannot be composed of two. And since what is wholly simple has no parts of which it consists, it cannot be divided (for division is nothing other than the separation of parts). So they are compelled to make Forms indivisible or without parts as well. Averroes wrote this in many places, and Scaliger repeatedly insists on it too, as in comment 9 on book 4 of De Causis Plantarum: The formal principle is neither continuous nor scattered, but one and indivisible. And again, Exercitation 80, section 3: A Form is one, not by connection but by a most indivisible essence. There he also notes the passages where Aristotle indicates the same thing, and all the Peripatetics echo this everywhere. To this belongs also their claim that magnitude and smallness do not apply to Forms, which they consider so certain that Scaliger declares: he abuses the patience of the wise who says that a Form is greater or smaller. So what Aristotle writes about the Intelligences, that they have no magnitude and are without parts and indivisible, is not peculiar to them; they share it with all Forms. Indeed these claims are so bound together that whatever is granted of one must be granted of the rest. But the Peripatetics can by no means defend these claims, and it is easy to drive them to the point where, even unwillingly, they must admit that Forms are composed of several things, that they have magnitude, that they are divisible, and therefore that the most simple simplicity they attribute to them is imaginary. As to the first point: the souls of many living things (which they themselves hold to be Forms) can be composed of several souls or animas, and so have parts, since the two or more souls that have coalesced into one must necessarily be called parts of that whole soul which arises from their union. Besides, this can be most clearly shown from the example of animals produced from different kinds of animals (of which more will be said conveniently below). It also clearly appears from the fact that various serious authors affirm for certain that from seeds of the same kind a single plant emerges, when tender plants (each of which surely has its own soul) grow together into one stock.

units.la: Scaliger, Exerc. 101. §. 15. (handwritten annotations in the margin are not printed text and are omitted) sane suam quaeq; sibi habet animam) in unam stirpem coalescentibus. Hoc in nonnullis oleribus fieri solere, tradit Theophrastus, ποιεῖ δὲ μεγάλας ποιῶν τὰς ῥίζας καὶ τὰς βλάστας, καὶ ἐὰν πολείω ὡς εἰς ταυτὸ σπέρματα ξυνάγῃς εἰς ἀθόνιον φυτεύσῃ. Διὸ ποιῶν ἐπὶ ζυγῶν ζῶντο ποιοῦσι, καθάπερ ἐπὶ πέδας, στέλλης, καὶ ἑτέρων· ἰσχύει δὲ τὰ πολεῖα ἁπλοῦ μάλιστα, καὶ ἐξ ἀπάντων γίνεται μία ἰσχὺς φυσικὴ. Magnas facit radices, uti & germina, siquis plura simul semina linteolo colligans serat. itaq; & in nonnullis hoc faciunt, ut porro, apio, alysq. videlicet plus virium est in pluribus, atq; ex omnibus fit una quedam natura. Theophrasto succinit Columella, sic de porro scribens: Incrementum ejus quo majus fiat, raris linteolis cumplura grana illigantur, atq; ita obruuntur. itemq; de Apio, Quod siquis id velit lati foliy facere, quantum seminis possint tres digiti comprehendere, raro linteolo illiget, & ita in areolas dispositum releget. Idem de Palmis memorat Plinius, Seritur autem pronum, & bina juxta composita semina, superq; totidem, quoniam infirma singulis planta est: quaterne colescunt. Et ante Plinium hoc ipsum tradidit Theophrastus: Τῶν δὲ φετίνων ἴδιος ἡ φυσεία πρὸς τὰ ἄλλα φυτεύοντι, πλείους εἰς ταυτὸ τιθέντες, δύο ἄνω, καὶ δύο κάτω, ἐπιδιδύσιες. Διὰ τοῦτο δὲ εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ πλείους αὔξεσιν, ὅτε ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀξενὸς ἡ φυσεία· τούτων δὲ αἱ τε ῥίζαι πρὸς ἀλλήλας συμπλέκονται, καὶ εὐθὺς αἱ πρῶται βλαστήσεις, ὥστε ἐν γίνεσθαι τὸ σέλεχος. Palmarum autem alia est, quam reliquorum, satio; serunt enim plures [nucleos] simul ponentes, duos supra, ac duos infra, colligantes. ob hoc autem plures in unum ponunt, quia ab uno infirma planta [provenit.] Horum autem & radices inter se complicantur, & statim prima germina, ita ut unus truncus fiat. Ait quidem Johannes Porta, non posse semina in unum coire, ac quae super hac re scripta sunt, falsa esse & impossibilia: sed quanquam ipsi periclitanti experientia non responderit, non statim sequitur, rem ipsam fieri non posse, aut nunquam fuisse factam; quum multa intervenire potuerint, quae
units.tr: Scaliger, Exerc. 101. §. 15. Theophrastus says this usually happens with some potherbs, which make large roots and shoots when one gathers several seeds together in a little linen cloth and sows them. Thus they do it with leeks and the like, as with the leek and the stalk; and the mixed seeds are strongest, and from them all comes one natural strength. [ποιεῖ δὲ μεγάλας ποιῶν τὰς ῥίζας καὶ τὰς βλάστας, καὶ ἐὰν πολείω ὡς εἰς ταυτὸ σπέρματα ξυνάγῃς εἰς ἀθόνιον φυτεύσῃ. Διὸ ποιῶν ἐπὶ ζυγῶν ζῶντο ποιοῦσι, καθάπερ ἐπὶ πέδας, στέλλης, καὶ ἑτέρων· ἰσχύει δὲ τὰ πολεῖα ἁπλοῦ μάλιστα, καὶ ἐξ ἀπάντων γίνεται μία ἰσχὺς φυσικὴ.] They make large roots, and shoots as well, if one gathers several seeds together into a linen cloth and sows them. And they do this in some cases, as with leek, parsnip and celery, for there is more strength in several seeds, and from all of them comes one natural power. Columella echoes Theophrastus, writing thus of leeks: To make it grow larger, several grains are tied together in a thin cloth and so buried. And of celery: If anyone wants it to have broad leaves, let him tie as much seed as three fingers can hold in a thin cloth, and so put it into small beds. Pliny records the same about palms: They are sown lying flat, two seeds placed side by side, and as many above, since a single seedling is weak; they grow up four together. And before Pliny, Theophrastus himself gave the same account: The planting of palms is peculiar compared with the others, since they put several seeds together, two above and two below, binding them. They put several together in one place because a single seedling is weak. Their roots become intertwined with one another, and the first shoots at once, so that one trunk comes to be. Palms, however, are sown differently from the rest; they plant several nuts together, two above and two below, binding them. They put several in one place because a single seedling is weak. Their roots become entangled with one another, and the first shoots come up at once, so that one trunk results. John Porta indeed says that seeds cannot come together into one, and that what has been written on this matter is false and impossible. But although experience did not answer him when he tried it, it does not follow at once that the thing cannot be done, or was never done, since many obstacles may have intervened
Lib. 11. cap. 3.
2. Hist. Plant. 8.

units.la: Lib.3. Magiae natural.cap.5. quæ successum impedirent. & præterea ex ipsius verbis excipere satis clare licet, cum non in congenerum, sed in differentium stirpium feminibus hoc tentasse. Imò ne in congeneribus quidem omnibus aut plerisq; hoc fieri, prædicti autores aiunt; sed arborem tantum unicam, herbam non nisi unam alteramq; nominant, in quibus hoc eveniat. quare in hisce præcipue aut solis tentatum oportuit, antequam res tam multis autoribus testata falsi condemnari posset. Sane Iulius Scaliger non dubitat, quin illud de Palmis verum sit. namq; Exercitatione centesima sexta pro certissimo id narrat. & quanquam Theophrastum autorem laudat, ita tamen narrat, ut ipse expertus videatur. quippe in nucleorum sive seminum numero à Theophrasto discrepat, atq; non è quaternis, ut ille, sed è ternis unam consurgere arborem memorat. Verba ejus hæc sunt:
units.tr: Book 3 of Magia Naturalis, ch. 5, which might hinder success. Moreover, from his own words one may clearly gather that he tried this not with seeds of the same kind, but of different plants. Indeed, the said authors say that this does not happen even with all or most seeds of the same kind; they name only one tree, and only one or two herbs, in which it occurs. Therefore it ought to have been tried chiefly or only on these, before a matter attested by so many authors could be condemned as false. Certainly Julius Scaliger does not doubt that what is said about palms is true, for in Exercitation 106 he recounts it as most certain. And although he cites Theophrastus as his authority, he tells it in such a way that he seems to have tested it himself. Indeed he differs from Theophrastus in the number of nuts or seeds, and he records that one tree rises not from four, as Theophrastus says, but from three. His words are these:

units.la: Palmularum tria ossa serito: totidem inde orientur palmæ, ita demum distincta, ut erant ossa ipsa. ỹ tres stipites, actu unum hoc, quod est, existens sibi quisq; in unum actu coibunt: unica deniq;, unico contenta stipite, palma fient. atq; ex ijs ita, non alio satu, exit arbor illa, quemadmodum prodit Theophrastus. Unus, inquam, stipes numero, ex ternis truncis, ortu, Materia, quantitate, loco separatis. Quomodo autem hoc stare possit cum decantata illa Formarum simplicitate, & cum axiomate illo (quod non alij tantum, sed & ipse Scaliger toties inculcat) Unam Formam è duabus componi non posse: ipsi viderint. nobis quidem constat, hæc directo inter se pugnare, propterea-q; utrumq; simul haudquaquam verum esse posse.
units.tr: Sow three stones of little palms; from them will grow as many palms, each kept distinct just as the stones themselves were. The three stalks, existing in act as one, will in act come together into one: at last a single palm will be made, contained in a single stalk. And from these, not from any other planting, that tree arises, just as Theophrastus relates. One stalk in number, I say, from three trunks separated in origin, matter, quantity and place. How this can stand together with that much-praised simplicity of Forms, and with that axiom (which not only others but Scaliger himself so often insists on), that one Form cannot be composed of two, let them see for themselves. For our part, it is clear to us that these contradict each other directly, and therefore both cannot be true at the same time.

units.la: XLI. Quantum ad Magnitudinem, possent eam Aristotelici Formis adimere ita, ut nulla seipsos contradictione involverent, si statuerent, quamvis Formam esse totam in toto, & totam in qualibet parte: quod tamen minime faciunt. Videtur quidem Scaliger contrarium afferere Exerc. 307. sect. 29. ubi cum dixisset, Formam esse totam in toto, & totam in qualibet parte; pro exemplo, ad axiomatis hujus confirmationem, subjungit, Quamlibet ignis partem, esse esse ignem. Et similiter alij Peripatetici, tractantes de origine Formarum, atq; disputantes contra eos, qui aliquid Formæ præexistere dicunt in Materia, ante rei generationem; id negare solent eo argumento, quod in quacunq; parte Materiæ non possit esse aliquid Formæ, quin tota sit, quum Forma sit indivisibilis. Sed hæc totalitas (ut sic dicamus) de qua isti loquuntur, non est ea, de qua nunc agitur; non quantitativa inquimus, sed essentialis: ita ut per Formam totam non aliud intelligant, nisi Formam essentialiter perfectam & completam: dicentesq; hoc pacto Formam esse totam in qualibet parte, dicant tantum, ubicunq; est, esse totam seu integram secundum essentiam, non vero secundum quantitatem. qua de re plura legi possunt apud Zabarellam libro de Partitione Animæ, cap. 1. 2. & 6. Ubi vero de totalitate quantitativa sermo est; ipsi disertim magno consensu docent, Formas plerasq; non esse totas in tota Materia seu toto subjecto, sed singulis Materiæ partibus singulas Formæ partes respondere. a Cuiq; parti Materiæ (inquit Scaliger) destinata est sua pars Formæ. b Suarez, Formæ materiales, quando uniuntur Materiæ, coextenduntur illi, ita ut uniantur uni parti Materiæ per unam partem suam, & alteri per aliam partem. Formæ enim inseparabiliter adhærent partibus Materiæ. & similia nemo non dicit. In hoc tantum est inter ipsos dissensio, quod Thomas cum suis inanimatorum quidem Formas, itemq; plantarum & imperfectiorum animalium animas, concessit esse extensas ad corporis extensionem, & ita esse totas in toto, sed partem in parte: omnium autem perfectiorum animalium animas negavit esse extensas & quantas; proinde in toto esse indivisibiliter, ita ut tota etiam sit in singulis partibus. Alij vero omnes omnino Formas atq; animas (sola Mente excepta) ejusdem faciunt hac in re conditionis, dicuntq; cum Zabarella, Quod omnis Forma informans Materiam, & constituens Compositum, est extensa ad extensionem Materiæ; quodq; proinde tota secundum extensionem suam in toto est, non tota autem in parte, sed pars in parte. partem enim quæ informat unam corporis corporis partem, non informare aliam. Iam ut omisso eo, de quo inter se contendunt, sumamus id, in quo consentiunt; sufficit hoc ad evertendum generale illud de Formarum simplicitate quantitativâ, & magnitudinis carentiâ, axioma. Positis enim hisce, quae ipsi hic docent, nequaquam id locum habere potest, nisi in ijs Formis, quae Materiae non coextenduntur. Reliquae autem omnes necessario & è partibus constant, sive compositae sunt, si partes habent Materiae partibus respondentes, & consequenter magnitudinem quandam, quae & imminui potest & augeri, demtis vel appositis Formae partibus cum Materiae ademtione vel appositione. Itaq; qui Formas hasce majores & minores dicet, non abutetur patientiâ sapientum (uti Scaliger suos Peripateticos vocat) sed ea dicet, quae ex ipsorum placitis inevitabiliter fluunt. Nam quod ad sanandam manifestissimam hanc contradictionem aiunt, Formas esse quantas per accidens, quia Materiae quantae coextendantur: hoc omnino vanum est. Ipsi enim concedent (siquis ipsos interroget) Formas ab extensione sua, seu à Materia cui coextenduntur, non accipere partes suas, sed habere illas partes per se, & illarum partium ratione esse extensiles. quodsi autem Formae habent suas partes quantitativas, etiam quantae sunt: quum monstri simile sit, dicere quod aliquid constet è partibus quantitativis, & tamen quantum non sit. Suarez quidem (& ipse de corum numero, qui Formas materiales dicunt esse quantas per accidens) ut hic se expediret, partes entitativas, è quibus Formae materiales constent, commentus est. Formae materiales (inquit) naturâ suâ habent constare è partibus entitativis, quod non habent à quantitate, sed à sua specifica & essentiali ratione. ex hac vero naturâ in eis consequitur, ut quando uniuntur Materiae, coextendantur illi extensione entitativa, id est, quod uniantur uni parti Materiae per unam partem suam, & alteri per aliam; quam extensionem non habent formaliter per quantitatem, sed per entitatem suam. Sed ut haec ita essent, nihilominus maneret, & constare Formas è partibus (uti apertum est) & habere suam per se magnitudinem, si non quantitativam, saltem entitativam. sed revera ista partium entitativarum à quantitativis distinctio ridicula est (sicuti quivis, sobrie ista considerans, fateri cogetur) & perpulsus ad eam comminiscendam fuit Suarez ob id, quòd cum maxima Peripateticorum parte crederet, quantitatem esse accidens, ac proinde, quæcunque quanta sunt, esse quanta ob hujus accidentis, quod quantitas dicitur, inhæsionem; quare Forma per se quanta esse nequeat, utpote quæ per se non sit capax istius accidentis. Ast quum revera quantitas non sit accidens, sed modus essentialis, resq; quantæ sint tales non per aliquod accidens ipsis inhærens, sed essentialiter (quod non nobis tantum, sed & multis Peripateticis videtur) omnino superflua est atq; inepta, illa partium entitativarum à quantitativis distinctio; ac proinde Peripatetici, dum concedunt, Formas per se constare è partibus entitativis, revera concedunt, eas constare è partibus quantitativis, ac consequenter esse per se quantas; eoq; effugio, quòd dicunt Formas esse quantas per accidens, nihil juvantur (quum id planissime vanum sit) quo minus de quantitate Formarum sibi ipsis apertissime contradicant, eamq; Formis & adimant simul, & attribuant.
units.tr: XLI. As to magnitude, the Aristotelians could strip it from the Forms without contradicting themselves, if they held that a Form is whole in the whole and whole in every part. But they do not do this. Scaliger seems to assert the opposite in Exercitation 307, section 29, where, after saying that a Form is whole in the whole and whole in every part, he adds, to confirm the principle, every part of fire is fire. Other Peripatetics likewise, when they treat the origin of Forms and dispute against those who say that some Form pre-exists in the matter before the thing is generated, usually deny it on the ground that a Form cannot be present in any part of matter without being wholly there, since a Form is indivisible. But this totality, as they call it, of which they speak is not the one now under discussion. I say it is not quantitative but essential: by a Form being whole they mean nothing other than a Form essentially perfect and complete. When they say that a Form is whole in every part, they mean only that wherever it is, it is whole or entire according to its essence, not according to its quantity. More on this can be read in Zabarella's book on the Partition of the Soul, chapters 1, 2 and 6. But where they speak of quantitative totality, they expressly and with great agreement teach that most Forms are not whole in the whole matter or whole subject, but that a separate part of the Form corresponds to each part of matter. To each part of matter (says Scaliger) is assigned its own part of the Form. Suárez: material Forms, when they are united to matter, are co-extended with it, so that they are united to one part of matter through one of their parts and to another part through another part. For Forms inseparably adhere to the parts of matter. And nearly everyone says similar things. The only disagreement among them is this: Thomas conceded that the Forms of inanimate things, and likewise the souls of plants and of the less perfect animals, are extended to the extension of the body, and so are whole in the whole but part in part; but he denied that the souls of all the more perfect animals are extended and quantified, and therefore that they are indivisibly in the whole, so that they are whole also in each part. Others, however, make all Forms and souls (except the Mind) alike in this respect, and say with Zabarella: every Form informing matter and constituting the composite is extended to the extension of the matter, and therefore is whole according to its extension in the whole, not whole in the part, but part in part. For the part that informs one part of the body does not inform another. Now, setting aside the point on which they contend among themselves and taking what they agree on, this is enough to overthrow that general principle about the quantitative simplicity of Forms and their lack of magnitude. For if we posit what they themselves teach here, the principle can by no means hold except for those Forms which are not co-extended with matter. All the others necessarily consist of parts and are composite, if they have parts corresponding to the parts of matter, and consequently some magnitude which can be both diminished and increased, by parts of the Form being taken away or added together with the removal or addition of matter. So whoever calls these Forms greater and lesser will not be abusing the patience of the wise (as Scaliger calls his Peripatetics), but will be saying what inevitably follows from their own opinions. As for their claim, to escape this most obvious contradiction, that Forms are quantified only accidentally because the matter they are co-extended with is quantified, this is altogether empty. For they will concede (if anyone questions them) that Forms do not receive their parts from their extension, or from the matter with which they are co-extended, but have those parts in themselves, and are extensible by reason of those parts. But if Forms have their own quantitative parts, then they are quantified in themselves too; for it is monstrous to say that something consists of quantitative parts and yet is not quantified. Suárez indeed (who is himself among those who say that material Forms are quantified only accidentally), in order to extricate himself here, devised entitative parts, of which material Forms are composed. Material Forms (he says) by their nature have to consist of entitative parts, which they do not have from quantity but from their specific and essential nature. From this nature it follows in them that when they are united to matter, they are co-extended with it by entitative extension, that is, they are united to one part of matter through one of their parts and to another through another part; an extension which they do not have formally through quantity but through their entity. But even if this were so, it would still remain that Forms consist of parts (as is clear), and have their own magnitude, if not quantitative then at least entitative. But in truth this distinction of entitative from quantitative parts is ridiculous (as anyone who considers these matters soberly will be forced to admit), and Suárez was driven to devise it because, with the greater part of the Peripatetics, he believed that quantity is an accident, and therefore that whatever is quantified is quantified by the inherence of this accident which is called quantity; hence a Form cannot be quantified in itself, since it is not capable of this accident in itself. But since in truth quantity is not an accident but an essential mode, and things are quantified not by some accident inhering in them but essentially (which seems so not only to us but to many Peripatetics), that distinction between entitative and quantitative parts is wholly superfluous and foolish. Accordingly the Peripatetics, while they concede that Forms consist of entitative parts in themselves, in fact concede that they consist of quantitative parts and consequently are quantified in themselves; and by their escape, saying that Forms are quantified only accidentally, they gain nothing (since this is plainly empty), so far as their most manifest self-contradiction about the quantity of Forms is concerned: they both take quantity away from Forms and attribute it to them at the same time.

units.la: XLII. Idem fere faciunt etiam de Divisibilitate, licet enim pronuntient, Formas esse indivisibiles, passim tamen, eas dividi, fatentur.
units.tr: XLII. They do much the same with divisibility. For although they pronounce that Forms are indivisible, they nonetheless admit everywhere that they are divided.

units.la: Unanimiter enim docent, omnes Formas Materiæ coextensas dividi ad divisionem subjecti; ita ut aliqui quidem dicant, omnes præter Mentem seu Animam rationalem Formas ita secari; alij verò, cum Mente excipiant etiam animas omnium animalium persectorum; prout nimirum hasce animas esse subjectis suis coextensas alij asserunt, alij negant: de qua ipsorum controversia paulo ante diximus. a Forma & anima (inquit Averroes.) dividuntur divisione subjectorum. & similiter b Scaliger, Cuiq; Materia parti materialis Forme pars designata est, ita ut cum illius sectione secetur ipsa quoque. & alibi, c Planta anima est materialis, & dividitur ad sectionem
units.tr: For they unanimously teach that all Forms coextensive with matter are divided when the subject is divided. Some hold that all Forms except the Mind or rational soul are cut in this way, while others, excepting the Mind, include the souls of all perfect animals. Indeed, some assert and others deny that these souls are coextensive with their subjects, and we spoke of this controversy among them a little earlier. "A form and a soul," says Averroes, "are divided by the division of their subjects." And likewise b Scaliger: "To each material part a part of the material form is assigned, so that when that part is cut, the form is cut too." And elsewhere, c "The vegetative soul is material and is divided by the cutting of quantity."

units.la: a Disp. r. in lut. dub. 8. b Comm. in 1. meta. Plant. c Comm. in 5. metaph. Caus. 2. Etionem quantitatis. ac rursus, Sane Forma quoq; sino modo infinitas in partes dividi potest. nulla enim Forme portiuncula quantulacunq; datur, qua non sit ad quantitatis sectionem partibilis, si materialis Forma est, ut anima canis. taliaq; passim in nullo non Aristotelico occurrunt. Sed cum haec duo inter se pugnent ex diametro, Esse indivisibilem, & divisionem tamen pati; jure aliquis miratur quid hic praesidij excogitent Peripatetici. ipsis autem res perquam facilis videtur, & familiari effugio utentes, verbo se expediunt, dicentes, Formas dividi non per se, sed per accidens; ut videre est apud Averroem 3. de Anima, com. 24. & Disp. 1. in solutione dubij octavi. item in paraph. Metaph. 2. tract. 2. ubi ita scriptum est, Divisio accidit rei, ex parte ea quod est materialis, non ex eâ quod habet Formam. Forma enim non est divisibilis nisi per accidens. & sequitur Pererius, Nulla Forma est per se divisibilis. nam divisibilitas & extensio sunt propria quantitatis affectiones, quae nequeunt ad alteras res pertinere, nisi per accidens, & propter ipsam quantitatem. omnes autem Formae materiales sunt extensa atq; divisibiles per accidens, nempe ratione subjecti in quo sunt. itidemq; Vicomercatus, Forma, quanquam materiales, ex se & sui naturâ individua sunt, omnemq; suam divisionem ex Materia accipiunt. Sed sicuti modo ostendimus, inane esse hoc subterfugium circa quantitatem Formarum; ita hic quoq; frustra adhiberi, facile monstrare possumus. Non exponemus nunc, quot modis aliquid per accidens vel Agere vel Pati dicatur. infra enim, libro hujus operis quarto, commodior dabitur istam rem pertractandi locus. Impraesentiarum sufficiet dixisse, quod neque divisio, neque alia passio quaecunque, cadere possit in ullam rem, quae non habeat potentiam patiendi istam passionem. exempli gratiâ, aurum non potest ustione in cineres redigi, quomodo cineres proprie dicuntur. hanc passionem, quae per se ipsi non competit, nullo ingenio effecerit, quispiam, ut per accidens ipsi inferat: sed etiamsi unicam auri unciam in tenuissimas bracteas deducti commiscet mille libris lignorum, eaq; ligna in cinerem tota redigat, nunquam tamen men efficiet; ut aurum, quod istis lignis admixtum erat, unà in cineres versum esse recte dicatur, sive per accidens, sive alio quocunq; modo. Et ut exemplo propiore utamur; Mentes, quæ vere sunt indivisibiles, integræ manent & illæsæ, etiamsi corpora, in quibus insunt, in mille partes subito discerperentur. Itaq; etiam aliæ Formæ, si per se essent indivisibiles, privilegium illud contagione corporum nequaquam amitterent, sed in quacunq; ipsius dissectione ac dilaceratione ipsæ incolumes persisterent. Aut fateantur ergo, Formas nullas dividi ad divisionem subjectorum; aut si hoc fateri neq; volunt neq; possunt, fateantur Formas esse verè per se divisibiles, quia alioqui verè dividi nequaquam possent. si autem verè non dividuntur, ne dividuntur quidem omnino, quum nihil inter hæc sit intermedium. Quanquam igitur certo aliquo respectu possent Formæ dici, per accidens dividi; hoc tamen non impediret, quominus respectu ipsius divisionis, quam sustinent, per se dividerentur: quomodo, verbi causa calefacta, quod ab aqua calida calefit, dici quidem potest calefieri per accidens, respectu suppositi calefacientis; quantum tamen ad ipsam passionem seu calefactionem attinet, verè ac per se calefieri dicendum est. Utitur quidem Averroes similitudine à qualitatibus materialibus petita, quo hoc de Formarum indivisibilium divisione paradoxon confirmet, dicens Formas ita dividi per accidens; quomodo dividitur albedo. sed hoc nihil ipsum juvat, quum & hic æque errent, qui ita loquuntur. Uti enim de Formis, ita & de hisce accidentibus interrogamus, dividanturne ea, quando subjectum earum dividitur, an non dividantur. Si dividuntur verè & realiter, vere etiam ac realiter sunt divisibilia; quia (ut dicebamus) nulla res potest per accidens pati eam passionem, quam per se pati inepta sit, ac proinde neq; dividi, nisi eam naturam sortita sit, ut dividi possit. si autem non dividuntur, non dividuntur omnino; quum tamen dividi apertum sit, & Peripatetici fateantur. Nequeunt quidem hæc per se dividi, hoc est seorsim, quia nimirum ita per se seorsim existere non valent: quam esse For-
units.tr: a Disp. 1 in lut. dub. 8. b Comm. in 1 Meta. Plant. c Comm. in 5 Metaph. Quaest. 2. Also, a form, if it is material, can indeed be divided into infinitely many parts. For there is no tiny portion of a form, however small, that is not divisible by the cutting of quantity, as with the soul of a dog. Statements of this kind occur everywhere in nearly every Aristotelian writer. But since these two claims are flatly opposed, namely that a form is indivisible and yet suffers division, one may fairly wonder what defence the Peripatetics devise here. For them the matter seems quite easy, and by using a familiar escape they dispose of it with a word, saying that Forms are divided not per se but per accidens. This can be seen in Averroes, On the Soul, book 3, comment 24, and Disputation 1, in the solution of the eighth doubt, and likewise in the Paraphrase on the Metaphysics, book 2, tract 2, where it is written: "Division happens to a thing on the side of what is material, not on the side of what has the form. For a form is divisible only per accidens." And Pererius follows: "No form is divisible per se. For divisibility and extension are proper affections of quantity, which cannot belong to other things except per accidens and on account of quantity itself. But all material forms are extended and divisible per accidens, namely by reason of the subject in which they are." Likewise Vicomercatus: "Forms, though material, are individual of themselves and by their own nature, and they receive all their division from matter." But just as we have shown that this subterfuge is empty with respect to the quantity of Forms, so we can easily show that it is vainly employed here too. We will not now set out in how many ways something is said to act or suffer per accidens; that matter will be treated more conveniently in the fourth book of this work. For the present it will suffice to say that neither division nor any other passion whatever can fall upon any thing that does not have the power of suffering that passion. For example, gold cannot be reduced to ashes by burning, in the way that ashes are properly so called. No cleverness can bring it about that someone inflicts upon gold, per accidens, a passion that does not belong to it of itself. Even if someone mixes a single ounce of gold, beaten into the thinnest leaves, with a thousand pounds of wood, and reduces all that wood to ash, it will never be rightly said that the gold mixed with that wood was turned into ash along with it, whether per accidens or in any other way. And to use a nearer example: Minds, which are truly indivisible, remain whole and unharmed even if the bodies in which they dwell are suddenly torn into a thousand pieces. So too other Forms, if they were indivisible per se, would by no means lose that privilege through contact with bodies, but would remain intact through whatever cutting and tearing of their subject. Therefore let them either confess that no Forms are divided by the division of their subjects, or, if they neither will nor can confess this, let them confess that Forms are truly divisible per se, since otherwise they could never truly be divided. And if they are not truly divided, then they are not divided at all, since there is no middle course between these. Although, then, in a certain respect Forms could be said to be divided per accidens, this would not prevent them from being divided per se with respect to the very division they undergo. Thus, for example, when something warm is warmed by hot water, it can indeed be said to be warmed per accidens with respect to the warming agent; yet so far as the passion itself, that is, the warming, is concerned, it must be said to be warmed truly and per se. Averroes indeed uses a comparison drawn from material qualities to confirm this paradox about the division of indivisible Forms, saying that Forms are divided per accidens in the way that whiteness is divided. But this does him no good, since those who speak in this way err equally here. For just as we ask about Forms, so we ask about these accidents too: are they divided when their subject is divided, or not? If they are divided truly and really, then they are truly and really divisible, because (as we were saying) no thing can suffer per accidens a passion that it is unfit to suffer per se, and so cannot be divided unless it has been given the nature by which it can be divided. But if they are not divided, then they are not divided at all, although it is plain that they are divided, and the Peripatetics themselves admit it. These things indeed cannot be divided per se, that is, separately, because they are not able to exist separately of themselves; which is what the Forms are...
Disp. 1 in solut. dub. 8.
Chapter I.

units.la: Formarum quoq; materialium conditionem Peripatus ait, sed si hoc sufficit, ut per accidens dividi ac per se esse indivisibilia dicantur, quia non nisi cum subjecto secari valent; tempus est Peripateticis, ut Materiam quoq; per se indivisibilem, ac non nisi per accidens dividi dicant; quippe quam ipsam quoq; per se ac seorsim subsistere posse negant, quare neq; per se ac seorsim secari potest. Sane ut hæc concludamus; quum Formas materiales & è partibus constare aiant, & eas partes invicem posse separari concedant, non est cur negent, quando ejusmodi partium separatio fit, Formas proprie ac per se dividi, quum divisio nihil sit aliud, quam partium sejunctio. uti rursus ex eo, quod Formas ad divisionem subjectorum dividi concedunt, sequitur Formas è partibus constare, quia necesse est rem, quæ dividitur, verè ac realiter dividi, aut non dividi omnino; quod autem verè dividitur, necessario est è partibus concretum; quum id quod partes non habet, dividi nullo modo possit. Tot igitur absurditatibus intricantur Peripatetici, dum illud suum axioma, quod Formas facit simplices simplicitate quantitativa, defendere conantur.
units.tr: The Peripatetics also say that material forms are of this kind. But if this is enough to make them divisible per accidens and indivisible per se, because they can be cut only together with their subject, then the Peripatetics must also say that matter is indivisible per se and divisible only per accidens. They deny that matter can subsist per se and separately, so it cannot be cut per se and separately either. To draw our conclusion: since they say material forms consist of parts and grant that these parts can be separated from one another, there is no reason for them to deny that when such a separation of parts occurs, the forms are properly and per se divided, since division is nothing other than the separating of parts. Conversely, from the fact that they concede forms are divided when their subjects are divided, it follows that forms consist of parts. For whatever is divided must be divided truly and really, or not divided at all; and what is truly divided is necessarily composed of parts, since that which has no parts cannot be divided in any way. So the Peripatetics are entangled in many absurdities while they try to defend that axiom of theirs, which makes forms simple with a quantitative simplicity.

units.la: XLIII: Sed neque meliori cum successu tueri valent alteram Formarum simplicitatem, eam nimirum, ut non constent Formæ ex heterogeneis seu diversæ naturæ partibus: quandoquidem contra hoc pugnant manifesta experimenta, non in animalibus modo, sed & in stirpibus. Theophrastus quinti Causarum quinto tradit modum, quo diversi diversarum arborum surculi in unum coalescant, Τὰ σφύρα μαλάξαντες τὰς ῥάβδους, ἵνα συμφύωσι διὰ τὴν ἀφέλωσιν, συνλήξαντες, ἐφύτευσαν· εἶτα γίνεται τὸ μὲν ἐκ τῆς συμφύσεως. Malleo mollientes virgas, ut coalescant propter excoriationem, colligant eas, atq; ita in terram deponunt: hinc arbor fit una per coalitionem. non fit quidem hic specierum Mixtio, quum revera non una sit ista arbor, sed plures arbores arte junctæ, atq; velut in unum corpus coagmentatæ, sua cuique specie servatâ, quod & testatur Theophrastus: Διατηρεῖ δ᾽ ἕκαστον τὸ γένος, ἕλμον χαῖρ[?] χαθ' αὐτὸ, καὶ πέτλον τὴν τροφὴν, ἐδλεν δ' ἄλλο ἢ τ' σύμ- φύσεως κοινωνικίσης, servat autem quisq; surculus suum genus, alimentum per se trahens atq; concoquens; ita ut nullâ re inter se communicent, nisi sola concretione. ast Columella modum docet, quo revera ex diversis surculis ita concretis unica arbor efficiatur, non unius ipsorum, sed omnium mixtam naturam referens, si nimirum juxta medium crus, ubi maxime videntur surculi coisse, codex serra præcidatur, ac deinde rite curetur. emissurum enim ramos, in quibus variarum naturarum in unum confusarum fructus nascantur. Ipse quidem hoc de Vitibus tantum tradit. sed quin in aliis quoq; fieri hoc possit, dubitare non licet, quum Franciscus Porta hoc de propria narret experientia, aiatq; se primi ac mali medicæ surculos hoc pacto redegisse in unam arborem, quæ postea fructus tulerit ex utroq; pomo compositos. Sed & insitionibus hujusmodi speciérum conmixtio fieri interdum solet. quanquam enim surculi insiti subjecta arbore ut plurimum pro terra tantum utuntur, naturamq; suam in ea integram servant; interdum tamen aliter fit, neq; modo fructus surculi insiti mutantur quoad odorem, saporem, magnitudinem, & similia; sed interdum compositio fit ejusmodi, ut duos diversorum generum fructus, tum illum qui surculi, tum illum qui arboris subjectæ proprius erat, in unum coisse, atq; tertium quendam fructum, ab utroq; diversum, hinc enatum, planissime appareat. Notum est quid Plinius tradat de Nuciprunis, & prunis amygdalinis. Peculiaris impudentia est (inquit) prunorum nucibus insitorum, quæ faciem parentis, succumq; adoptionis exhibent, appellata ab utroq; nucipruna. & mox, Nuper in Betica malina coeperunt appellari malis insita, & alia amygdalina amygdalis. His intus in ligno nucleus amygdalæ est: nec aliud pomum ingeniosius geminatum est. Alibi vero etiam cerasorum laureorum meminit idem autor, quæ itidem ipsius ævo prodierint, insitâ ceraso in lauro. Ne autem putemus fabulas hæc esse (quod tamen ne suspicari quidem sine temeritate licet, quum Plinius hæc non, ut multa alia, fide alienâ
units.tr: XLIII: But they fare no better in defending the other simplicity of forms, namely that forms do not consist of heterogeneous parts, that is, parts of different nature. For manifest experiments oppose this, not only in animals but also in plants. Theophrastus, in the fifth book of the Causes, sets out the method by which the shoots of different trees grow together into one: having softened the rods with a mallet, so that they grow together through the abrasion, they bind them together and plant them; then one tree arises from the growing together. [Τὰ σφύρα μαλάξαντες τὰς ῥάβδους, ἵνα συμφύωσι διὰ τὴν ἀφέλωσιν, συνλήξαντες, ἐφύτευσαν· εἶτα γίνεται τὸ μὲν ἐκ τῆς συμφύσεως.] Here, to be sure, there is no mixing of species, since that tree is not really one, but several trees joined by art and fitted together as if into one body, each keeping its own species. Theophrastus also attests this: each kind keeps its own nature, drawing and digesting its own nourishment, and they share nothing with one another except by mere concretion. [Διατηρεῖ δ᾽ ἕκαστον τὸ γένος, ἕλμον χαῖρ[?] χαθ' αὐτὸ, καὶ πέτλον τὴν τροφὴν, ἐδλεν δ' ἄλλο ἢ τ' σύμφύσεως κοινωνικίσης.] But Columella teaches a method by which truly a single tree is made from such diverse shoots so joined. It bears not the nature of one of them, but a mixed nature of all of them, if namely, near the middle of the trunk where the shoots seem most to have joined, the trunk is cut through with a saw and then properly tended; for it will send forth branches in which the fruits of natures of various kinds, confused into one, are born. Columella himself says this only of vines. But that this can also happen in other plants there is no room to doubt, since Franciscus Porta relates it from his own experience. He says that he reduced the shoots of a pear and of a citron-apple in this way into one tree, which afterwards bore fruit compounded of both. Indeed, mixing of species often happens also through grafting of this kind. For although grafted shoots, when set on a host tree, mostly use it only as soil and keep their own nature whole, yet sometimes it turns out otherwise. Not only do the fruits of the grafted shoot change in smell, taste, size and the like, but sometimes the composition is such that two fruits of different kinds, both that which was proper to the shoot and that which was proper to the host tree, clearly appear to have come together into one, and a third fruit, different from both, to have sprung from them. It is well known what Pliny relates of nut-plums and almond-peaches. It is a peculiar impudence (he says) of plums grafted on nuts, which show the face of the parent and the juice of the adopted stock, and are called nut-plums from both. And soon after: Lately in Baetica, apples began to be called plums grafted on apples, and others almonds grafted on almonds. Inside them, in the wood, is the kernel of an almond; nor is any other fruit more ingeniously doubled. Elsewhere the same author also mentions cherries on laurels, which likewise appeared in his own time: a cherry grafted on a laurel. But lest we think these are fables (which one may not even suspect without rashness, since Pliny relates these things not, as many others, on another's authority

units.la: Lib.13.ca.9. Lib.3.Mag. Nat.cap.5. Lib.15 cap.13. Lib.15.ca.25.
units.tr: Lib.13.ca.9. Lib.3.Mag. Nat.cap.5. Lib.15 cap.13. Lib.15.ca.25.
Chapter I.

units.la: aliená, sed ut comperta sibi, ac suo tempore notissima, narret) facit idem Porta (quanquam ipse verbis suis Plinio fidem detrahere laborat) memorans suo ævo procurata per insitionem nova ac inusitata pomorum genera, amygdalopersica, & nucipersica; ac eas quidem arbores, quæ amygdalopersica ferrent, multis annis in pomarijs suis viruisse. Hæc negari non possunt; & Scaliger ingenuè fatetur, In insitione (inquit) actu Principia duo arte conjunguntur, & miscentur species, contra Peripateticorum vulgata placita: qui etiam alibi narrat visum sibi esse caulorapum, ita ut brassicæ radix sub terra esset condita, rapum super terra in stipite turgescceret.
units.tr: but as things known to himself, and very well known in his own time, he relates). The same Porta does this too, though he labours in his own words to weaken Pliny's credibility, recording that in his own age new and unusual kinds of fruit were produced by grafting, the almond-peach and the nut-peach, and that the trees bearing these almond-peaches had flourished for many years in his orchards. These facts cannot be denied. Scaliger frankly admits: In grafting, two principles are joined together by art and their species are mixed, contrary to the commonly held doctrine of the Peripatetics. He also elsewhere reports that he saw a cabbage-turnip, in which the root of a cabbage was buried under the earth while the turnip swelled on a stalk above the ground.

units.la: In animalibus autem multo adhuc evidentior & frequentior est hæc speciérum mixtura. nam ut omittamus coitum canis cum fele, hyæna, lupo, vulpe, tigre; tauri cum asina, equa; cameli cum equa, aliosque rariores; notissimum omnibus est, asinos equas, & equos asinas inire, eque eo conceptu mulos nasci, neutri parentum ex toto similes, sed ab utroq; aliquid habentes. quare velint nolint fateri coguntur Peripatetici (nisi velint impudentissime obstinati esse) falsum esse illud suum axioma, quod miscéri species negat, & hujusmodi animalium, à diversigeneris parentibus procreatorum, Formas sive animas esse ex partibus heterogeneris compositas.
units.tr: In animals, this mixing of species is far more evident and frequent still. To pass over the mating of a dog with a cat, a hyena, a wolf, a fox, or a tiger, or of a bull with a she-ass or a mare, or of a camel with a mare, and other rarer cases, it is best known to everyone that asses mate with mares and horses with she-asses, and that from this union mules are born, wholly like neither parent but having something from both. Therefore, whether they wish to or not, the Peripatetics are compelled to admit (unless they wish to be most shamelessly obstinate) that their axiom, which denies that species can be mixed, is false, and that the forms or souls of animals produced from parents of different kinds are composed of heterogeneous parts.

units.la: Quare Scaliger Exercit. 101. multum fluctuatus, atq; sibi reluctatus, an Formas miscéri decerneret, quanquam negare mallet, ne violaretur illud axioma, rei tamen evidentiâ victus id fatetur, aitq; certum esse, quòd equi & asini Formæ misceantur. & similiter alibi, Non est verum illud Porphyrii, speciem non miscéri cum specie. non enim esset mulus ab equo & asinâ tertia substantia. Præterquam autem quod hisce illud de Formarum simplicitate decretum abunde profigatur, nonnulli etiam de ipsis Peripateticis tam parvi illud fecerunt, ut quo suum dogma (quo non nisi unicam in quocunq; Composito Formam admittunt) tuerentur, veriti non sint illud usque adeo violare, ut dicerent, partium similarium Formas totius Formæ partes esse. Hanc opinionem non obscure fovet Suarez, uti apparet
units.tr: Accordingly Scaliger, in Exercitation 101, wavering greatly and struggling with himself over whether he should decide that forms are mixed, though he would rather deny it lest that axiom be violated, nevertheless, overcome by the evidence of the thing, admits it and says it is certain that the forms of horses and asses are mixed. Similarly elsewhere: That saying of Porphyry, that species is not mixed with species, is not true; for the mule would not be a third substance from a horse and an ass. Besides this, the decision on the simplicity of forms is thoroughly overthrown by these remarks. Moreover, some of the Peripatetics themselves have held this doctrine in such low esteem, in order to defend their own dogma (by which they admit only a single form in any composite), that they have not hesitated to violate it so far as to say that the forms of similar parts are parts of the whole form. Suarez clearly favours this opinion, as appears in:
Lib. 3. Mag. natur. c. 6. & 7.
Comm. in 2. Cauf. 18.

units.la: Comm. in 1. de Plant. apparet è Disp. 15. in cujus sectione decima, §. 31. sic scribit: Facile concedi potest, in diversis partibus heterogeneis esse diversas Formæ partes heterogeneas, nam revera in arbore non est ejusdem rationis illa pars Formæ, quæ est in fronde, & quæ est in fructu. sunt tamen partiales illæ Formæ, & aptè ut inter se uniantur & continuentur: & ideo componunt unam integram Formam totius. & mox rursus, §. 32. Ipsamet anima constat ex partibus heterogeneis, & ex earum inseparabili unione tota consurgit, ut supervacuum sit alias partiales Formas in singulis partibus confingere. Et Scaliger quoq; interdum similia profitetur, ut Exerc. 104. 2. Radix nulla est à suo stipite neq; genere neq; specie diversa. earum namq; Formæ, totius Formæ partes sunt, sicuti sua utriusvis Materia, Materiæ universæ pars est. & adhuc clarius alibi, Nasum habere Formam peculiarem, aliam ab oculo, sua specie, ut partem à parte differentem. esse enim totius unius Formas partiales; sub ea, unum inter se, multa; & esse sub eadem Forma tanquam partes, non tanquam species. Sane vel hinc indicium haud parvum sumi potest, qualis sit illa de Formis doctrina, quæ non modo argumentorum pondere facillime obruitur, sed & à proprijs sectatoribus aperte convellitur in præcipuis suis capitibus, cujusmodi inter alia hoc, de ipsarum simplicitate, habetur à longe maxima Peripateticorum parte, quibus nihil magis aut firmius de Formis asseverandum videtur, quam eas esse simplicissimas, atque è nullis partibus, præsertim heterogeneis, componi.
units.tr: Comm. in 1. de Plant. appears from Disp. 15, in whose tenth section, §. 31, he writes thus: It can easily be conceded that in different heterogeneous parts there are different heterogeneous parts of the form; for in truth the part of the form that is in a leaf is not of the same kind as that which is in the fruit of a tree. Yet these partial forms are fitted to unite and be continuous with one another, and therefore they make up one whole form of the whole. And soon again, §. 32: The soul itself consists of heterogeneous parts, and from their inseparable union the whole arises, so that it is superfluous to devise other partial forms in the individual parts. Scaliger too sometimes professes similar things, as in Exercitation 104, section 2: No root is different from its stalk either in genus or in species. For their forms are parts of the whole form, just as each of their matters is a part of the whole matter. And even more clearly elsewhere: The nose has a peculiar form, different from that of the eye in its species, as one part differs from another part. For there are partial forms of one whole; under this one form, many are one among themselves; and under the same form they are parts, not species. Certainly from this alone no small indication may be drawn of what kind of doctrine of forms it is: one which is not only very easily overthrown by the weight of arguments, but is also openly undermined by its own adherents on its principal heads. Among other things, this is held by by far the greater part of the Peripatetics concerning the simplicity of forms, although nothing seems to them more firmly or more surely to be asserted about forms than that they are most simple and composed of no parts, especially no heterogeneous parts.

units.la: XLIV. Sequitur nunc ut dicamus de Intensione ac Remissione, quam non cadere in Formas substantiales, uno ore omnes inculcant Peripatetici, quippe quibus neq; addi quicquam possit, nec detrahi, quin ipsarum essentia atque species mutetur; quare neq; dentur ulli Formarum gradus in eadem specie, quum omnes ejusdem sint essentiæ, ac proinde inter se simillimæ.
units.tr: XLIV. Next we must now speak of intension and remission, which all the Peripatetics with one voice insist does not apply to substantial forms, since nothing can be added to them or taken from them without their essence and species being changed; therefore there are no degrees of forms within the same species, since all are of the same essence and consequently most alike among themselves.

units.la: Averroes quidem, cum suis, Elementorum Formas dixit instar Qualitatum esse intensibiles ac remissibiles. sed acerrime ei contradicunt reliqui
units.tr: Averroes, indeed, with his followers, said that the forms of the elements, like qualities, are capable of intension and remission. But the rest contradict him most fiercely.
Cap.I.

units.la: qui Peripatetici; & ipse de reliquis omnibus Formis eandem omnino cum ipsis fovet opinionem, ut eas intensionis ac remissionis capaces esse neget. Nihil autem nocebit nonnulla super hac Formarum conditione testimonia è Peripateticis apponere. Thomas, Esse substantiale cuiuscunque rei in indivisibili consistit, & omnis additio vel subtractio variat speciem. Mercenarius, Nulla Forma substantialis intenditur & remittitur, sed quelibet in indivisibili consistit, & in hoc distinguitur a natura accidentali, quae habet latitudinem graduum, secundum quos a subjecto secundum esse intensum & remissum participatur. Vicomercatus, Est Forma una altera quidem minus perfecta, sed tamen in suo genere perfecta, qua quatenus talis, perfectior esse non potest. Scaliger, Caeterum & illud quod ais, perridiculum est; per gradus hasce animas distingui. essent enim qualitates accidentales, si intenduntur & remittuntur. nos Formarum gradus ponimus, ex duodecimo divinae philosophiae, sed non in una Forma. Praevivit autem suis ad hoc decretum ipse Aristoteles, qui expressis verbis illud tradidit octavi Metaphysicorum tertio; Καὶ ὥσπερ οὐδὲ ἀπ' ἀριθμῶν ἀφαιρεθέντος ἢ προστεθέντος, ἐξ ὧν ὁ ἀριθμός ἐστιν, οὐκέτι ὁ αὐτὸς ἀριθμὸς ἔστιν, ἀλλ' ἕτερος, ἂν τὸ ἐλάχιστον ἀφαιρεθῇ ἢ προστεθῇ· οὕτως δὲ ὁ ἐρισμὸς, δὲ τί ἦν εἶναι ἔσται, ἀφαιρεθέντος ἢ προστεθέντος. & pauculis interpositis, Καὶ ἡ οὐσία ἐν οὕτως, ἀλλ' ὅν ὡς λέγουσί τινες, οἷον μονάς ἢ οὐσία ἡ σιγμὴ, ἀλλ' ἐντελέχεια καὶ φύσις τις ἑνάσῃ· καὶ ὥσπερ δὲ ὁ ἀριθμὸς ἔχει τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ τὸ ἧττον, δὲ ἡ καλὰ τὸ εἶδος οὐσία. Et sicuti numerus, siquid eorum, e quibus ipse constat, ab ipso auferatur, aut siquid ipsi addatur, non amplius est idem numerus, sed alius, etiamsi vel minimum auferatur aut addatur; ita neque definitio neque Essentia amplius sunt idem, siquid ijs auferatur aut addatur. Et essentia ita est unum, non uti dicunt quidam, tanquam si esset unitas quaedam aut punctum, sed actus & natura quaedam est unaquaeque. & sicuti numerus non recipit magis & minus, ita neque formalis Essentia. Sed hoc axioma plane subvertitur per Cap. I. maximam illam diversitatem, quæ in plurimis tum stirpium tum animalium speciebus deprehenditur. Malorum, pyrorum, prunorum innumeræ varietates omnibus quotidie ob oculos versantur. De vitibus æquè nota res est. Universæ regiones (inquit Columella) regionumq; singulæ pene partes, habent propria vitium genera. Et Plinius, Genera vitium numero comprehendi posse, unus existimavit Democritus, cuncta sibi Gracia cognita professus. ceteri innumera atq; infinita esse prodiderunt, quod verius apparebit ex vinis. nec omnia dicentur, sed maxime insignia: quippe quæ totidem pene sunt, quot agri. Itidemq; ante hos Theophrastus, Ἐν πολείσῃ δὲ, ὡς εἰπεῖν, διαφορᾶ τὰ τῶν ἀμπέλων ἐσίν· εἰς δ᾽ ὅλην ἀγρῶν εἰδη, πεύγυτα ἐνές φασι καὶ ἀμπέλων εἶναι. maximam autem, ut sic dicamus, varietatem sortita sunt vites. quot enim agrorum sunt genera, tot esse & vitium, nonnulli prodiderunt. Et in multis quoque animalibus idem est cernere. ne longius abeamus, sola species humana amplissimum hujusce rei testimonium præbet, quippe intra cujus ambitum innumerabiles non corporum tantummodo, sed & animorum discrepantiæ ac dissimilitudines reperiuntur. Idem de canina specie affirmare liceat; de qua loquentem pro nobis audiamus Scaligerum. In ipso canina specie ambitu multa diversissime idea comprehenduntur; tam diversæ inquam, ut plus distet à catello melitæo britannicus canis, quàm à cerastè vipera. Iam quum Materia nunquam mutet Formam (sicuti Scaliger Exerc. 101. 18. ait) quumq; actio, & ea omnia, quæ insunt rebus naturalibus, Formæ tribuantur, atq; ab ea fluant (sicuti de communi Peripateticorum sententia scribit Toletus. 1. Phys. Quæst. 19.) quomodo ipsæ diversarum specierum differentiæ Formis, secundum Peripateticos, sunt ascribendæ; ita necessario sequitur, ut hæ substantiarum ejusdem speciei varietates itidem Formis debeant referri acceptæ. aut hinc porro concluditur, omnino dari Formarum gradus in eadem specie, & nequaquam in indivisibili constitui Formarum essentias, neq; eas omnes inter se similimas esse posse; quia si hoc foret, oporteret omnia etiam cujuscunq; speciei individua esse inter se similima, omnibusq; ad amussim ijsdem proprietatibus prædita; quod nunc quam longissime abest.
units.tr: who are Peripatetics. He himself holds the same opinion about all the other Forms, denying that they are capable of intension and remission. Nor will it do any harm to set out some testimonies from the Peripatetics on this condition of Forms. Thomas: The substantial being of any thing consists in what is indivisible, and every addition or subtraction changes the species. Mercenarius: No substantial Form is intended or remitted, but each consists in what is indivisible, and in this it is distinguished from accidental nature, which has a range of degrees, according to which it is participated by the subject in an intense or remiss way of being. Vicomercatus: There is one Form, less perfect in one case, yet perfect in its own kind, and insofar as it is such, it cannot be more perfect. Scaliger: As for what you say, that is utterly absurd: that souls are distinguished by these degrees. For they would be accidental qualities, if they were intended and remitted. We posit degrees of Forms, from the twelfth book of the Divine Philosophy, but not within one Form. Aristotle himself went before his followers in this decree, who stated it in express words in the third chapter of the eighth book of the Metaphysics: [Καὶ ὥσπερ οὐδὲ ἀπ' ἀριθμῶν ἀφαιρεθέντος ἢ προστεθέντος, ἐξ ὧν ὁ ἀριθμός ἐστιν, οὐκέτι ὁ αὐτὸς ἀριθμὸς ἔστιν, ἀλλ' ἕτερος, ἂν τὸ ἐλάχιστον ἀφαιρεθῇ ἢ προστεθῇ· οὕτως δὲ ὁ ἐρισμὸς, δὲ τί ἦν εἶναι ἔσται, ἀφαιρεθέντος ἢ προστεθέντος.] And a few words later: [Καὶ ἡ οὐσία ἐν οὕτως, ἀλλ' ὅν ὡς λέγουσί τινες, οἷον μονάς ἢ οὐσία ἡ σιγμὴ, ἀλλ' ἐντελέχεια καὶ φύσις τις ἑνάσῃ· καὶ ὥσπερ δὲ ὁ ἀριθμὸς ἔχει τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ τὸ ἧττον, δὲ ἡ καλὰ τὸ εἶδος οὐσία.] And just as a number, if anything is taken away from those things of which it consists, or anything is added to it, is no longer the same number but another, even if the least thing is taken away or added; so neither the definition nor the Essence remain the same, if anything is taken from them or added to them. And the essence is one in this way, not as some say, as if it were some unity or point, but each thing is an act and a certain nature. And just as number does not admit more and less, so neither does the formal Essence. But this axiom is plainly overthrown by that greatest diversity which is found in very many species both of plants and of animals. The countless varieties of apples, pears and plums are daily before our eyes. The same is well known of vines. All regions (says Columella), and almost every single part of regions, have their own kinds of vines. And Pliny: Democritus alone thought that the kinds of vines could be counted, professing that he knew all of them in Greece. Others have reported them as countless and infinite, which will appear more truly from wines. Nor will all be mentioned, but only the most notable: since they are almost as many as the fields. Likewise before these, Theophrastus: [Ἐν πολείσῃ δὲ, ὡς εἰπεῖν, διαφορᾶ τὰ τῶν ἀμπέλων ἐσίν· εἰς δ᾽ ὅλην ἀγρῶν εἰδη, πεύγυτα ἐνές φασι καὶ ἀμπέλων εἶναι.] Vines have, so to speak, the greatest variety. Some have reported that there are as many kinds of vines as there are kinds of fields. And in many animals the same can be seen. To say nothing of more distant examples, the human species alone offers the fullest testimony to this matter, since within its range are found countless differences and dissimilarities not only of bodies but also of minds. The same may be affirmed of the dog species, on which we may hear Scaliger speaking for us. Within the dog species itself many very diverse forms are comprehended; so diverse, I say, that the British dog differs more from the Maltese lapdog than from the horned viper. Now since Matter never changes the Form (as Scaliger says, Exerc. 101, sec. 18), and since action, and all those things which are in natural things, are ascribed to the Form and flow from it (as Toletus writes, following the common opinion of the Peripatetics, in Physics 1, Question 19), by what means the very differences of diverse species are to be ascribed to Forms, according to the Peripatetics, it follows necessarily that these varieties of substances of the same species must likewise be referred to Forms. Or from this it is further concluded that there are altogether degrees of Forms within the same species, and that the essences of Forms are by no means constituted in what is indivisible, nor can they all be most alike to one another; for if this were so, it would be necessary that all individuals even of any one species be most alike to one another and endowed with exactly the same properties; which is now very far from being the case.

units.la: XLV. Huic contra prædictum axioma objectioni adjungi altera potest, desumta à specifica unius rei in alteram mutatione, quæ fieri non posset, si illud ratum esset, uti docet Scaliger in commentarijs ad secundi de Causis caput vigesimum secundum; ubi ad hæc Theophrasti verba, ἀσ̃λα̃ τῆς ἐνάσχ ἡ φύσις, simplex est uniuscujusq; [plantæ] natura, sic scribit (parum sane ad mentem authoris, quum illa quidem verba longe alium sensum habeant: sed hoc nunc non agitur.) Sane optimum axioma: simplex omnium entium natura; quare non possit alterari, ut paulatim degeneret, donec mutetur in aliam. Ast passim authores produnt, in multis plantis hoc accidere, ut una mutetur in aliam speciem differentem; idq; duobus modis, ita ut mutatio fiat vel in ipso semine, alia herbâ ex eo prodeunte, quàm quæ prodire debebat; vel in adultis plantis. Quantum ad prius; Theophrastus quarti de Causis capite primo tradit, triticum ac hordeum degenerare in lolium; & capite sexto, Triticum in lolium, loliumq; rursus in triticum, ac Zeam in bromon transfire affirmat. Et Plinius lib. 18. cap. 17. hordeum in avenam degenerare scribit, ac lib. 19. cap. 10. E semine brassicæ veteris rapa fieri, atq; invicem. Galenus item, in fine primi de facultat. aliment. memorat patrem suum, quum se agriculturæ studio totum dedidisset, magnamq; super hac re exploranda diligentiam adhibuisset, sæpius propriâ experientiâ deprehendisse triticum in lolium, & hordeum in ægilopa, & lentes in aracos, securidacas atq; aparinen abire; & alia quoq; cerealia semina in alias zizanias degenerare. Et Scaliger quoq; alicubi narrat, sibi ipsi accidisse, ut quum semen apij, seu petroselini vulgaris, terræ mandasset, non quæ expectabatur herba è terra prodierit, sed planta longe diversissima, scorodotis nimirum seu alliaria. Quantum ad posterius muta-
units.tr: XLV. To this objection against the aforesaid axiom another may be added, drawn from the specific change of one thing into another, which could not happen if that axiom were valid, as Scaliger teaches in his commentaries on the twenty-second chapter of the second book of the Causes. There, on these words of Theophrastus, [ἁπλῆ τῆς ἑνὸς ἑκάστου φύσις], the nature of each single [of the plant] is simple, he writes thus (certainly little in keeping with the author's mind, since those words have a quite different sense; but this is not the matter now under discussion). Certainly an excellent axiom: the nature of all beings is simple; therefore it cannot be altered, so that it gradually degenerates until it is changed into another. But authors everywhere report that in many plants this happens, that one is changed into a different species; and this in two ways: either the change takes place in the seed itself, with a different herb coming forth from it than the one which ought to have come forth; or in mature plants. As to the former: Theophrastus, in the first chapter of the fourth book of the Causes, relates that wheat and barley degenerate into darnel; and in the sixth chapter he affirms that wheat changes into darnel, and darnel again into wheat, and that maize passes over into bromus. And Pliny, book 18, chapter 17, writes that barley degenerates into oats; and in book 19, chapter 10, that from the seed of old cabbage turnips come forth, and vice versa. Galen likewise, at the end of the first book of On the Properties of Foods, records that his father, when he had devoted himself wholly to the study of agriculture and had applied great diligence to investigating this matter, had very often discovered by his own experience that wheat turns into darnel, barley into goat-grass, lentils into vetch, and that securidaca and cleavers also change; and that other cereal seeds degenerate into other tares. And Scaliger too somewhere tells that it happened to himself that, when he had committed to the earth the seed of celery, or of common parsley, there came forth from the ground not the herb that was expected, but a quite different plant, namely scordotis or garlic-wort. As to the latter, the change...
Chapter I.

units.la: mutationis genus; Theophrastus secundi historiarum quar-to varias commemorat arbores, in quibus hæc permutatio fiat. mutari enim punicam dulces fructus ferentem in eam quæ ferat acidos; ficum in caprificum, & caprificum in ficum, oleam in oleastrum, & oleastrum in oleam: eamq; mutationem fieri, ὅτε μὲν ἐπὶ τῶν καρπῶν, ὅτε δὲ ὅλως ἐπὶ αὐτῶν τῶν δένδρεων, aliquando circa fructum tantum, aliquando autem circa totas penitus arbores. & quinti de Causis octavo hisce addit mutationem populi albæ in nigram. Prætea * diversis in locis testatur, sisymbrium degenerare in mentham. At-tham, & 5. Caus. 8. asserit, ocymum abire in mentham. Attamen an ex hisce satis firmiter probetur, dari specificā rerum permutationem; jure quis dubitare possit. Etenim ut de ijs prius agamus, quæ jam adulta mutari dicuntur; fortasse quæ dam istorum nunquam fiunt aut facta sunt. Non enim veritatem habet, quicquid in litteras relatum est. & Theophrastus ipse de nonnullis eorum parum affirmate loquitur: vel si fiant, forte fiunt non naturaliter, sed miraculose; quomodo sane ipse Theophrastus dicit, istum arborum permutationem, quando eveniat, pro monstro seu ostento haberi. Sed uti & fiant ista, & naturaliter fiant; non est illa permutatio rerum totâ specie differentium, quum mutatio fiat in res propinquas atq; affines, atq; adeo ejusdem speciei ambitu comprehensas; quod & Theophrastus adnotavit 2. Caus. 22. ἡ μεταβολὴ πᾶσιν εἰς ὁμοιόν, καὶ ὁ πόρρω τελέως. mutatio omnibus hisce est in simile quid, ac non valde dissitum. & 5. Caus. 8. Τὸ δὲ ὅλον, ὥσπερ ἄγαν ἰσως τὸ συμβαῖνον θαυμαστόν, ὥς εἰς τὸ σύνεγγυς ἐν ἄγαν ἰσως τὸ ὅμοιόν πως μεταβάλλειν. in totum autem, forsan non valde mirum est quod in hisce evenit, eò quòd in propinqua ac quodammodo similia mutentur. Quod vero ad ea attinet, quorum mutatio in semine fieri dicitur: præterquam quod posterior præcedentis responsionis pars, in nonnullis quoq; ipsorum locum habere videtur; in ijs multo vehementius suspectam habere licet harum narrationum fidem. Difficilis enim ad resciscendum est illa mutatio, quippe quam oculis usurpare non licet, quum in terræ gremio
units.tr: In the fourth chapter of the second book of his *History*, Theophrastus mentions various trees in which this kind of change occurs. A red pomegranate, he says, changes into one bearing sour fruit; the fig into the wild fig, and the wild fig into the fig; the olive into the wild olive, and the wild olive into the olive. This change, he says, happens [ὅτε μὲν ἐπὶ τῶν καρπῶν, ὅτε δὲ ὅλως ἐπὶ αὐτῶν τῶν δένδρεων] sometimes only in the fruit, and sometimes in the whole tree. In the eighth chapter of the fifth book of *De Causis* he adds the change of the white poplar into the black. Elsewhere he also bears witness that sisymbrium degenerates into mint. In the same eighth chapter of the fifth book of *De Causis* he asserts that basil turns into mint. Yet whether these examples prove firmly enough that a specific change of things really occurs, one may well doubt. For, to take first those things said to change when they are already grown, some of these perhaps never change, or never have. Not everything that has been put in writing is true, and Theophrastus himself speaks rather hesitantly about some of them. Or if they do happen, they perhaps happen not naturally but by miracle. Indeed Theophrastus himself says that such a change of trees, when it occurs, is regarded as a monster or portent. But even granting that these things do happen and happen naturally, this is not a change of things differing in their whole species, since the change is into things that are near and related, and therefore included within the compass of the same species. Theophrastus also noted this in the twenty-second chapter of the second book of *De Causis*: [ἡ μεταβολὴ πᾶσιν εἰς ὁμοιόν, καὶ ὁ πόρρω τελέως] the change in all these cases is into something similar, and not far removed. And in the eighth chapter of the fifth book of *De Causis*: [Τὸ δὲ ὅλον, ὥσπερ ἄγαν ἰσως τὸ συμβαῖνον θαυμαστόν, ὥς εἰς τὸ σύνεγγυς ἐν ἄγαν ἰσως τὸ ὅμοιόν πως μεταβάλλειν] on the whole, what happens in these cases is perhaps not very surprising, since things change into what is near and in some way similar. As for those things whose change is said to occur in the seed, the latter part of the preceding answer seems to hold good for some of them as well; but in their case one may suspect the reliability of these accounts much more strongly. That change is difficult to ascertain, since it cannot be observed with the eyes, the whole business being carried on in the bosom of the earth.
2 Hist.5. & 2. Caus. 22. & 5. Caus. 8.

units.la: 2. Hist. 5. gremio totum hoc negotium geratur. & quod fato certo femine, alia herba prodeat, hoc non est sufficiens signum istius mutationis; quum & femen penitus perijsse, & hanc herbam spontaneo ortu, aut femine è congenere herba, quæ prius ibi nata fuerat, delapso, atq; intra terram aliquamdiu detento, productam, arbitrari liceat: quare nihil concludit argumentum Galeni, qui hanc mutationem ex eo probari putat, quod quum cerealia femina pura, atq; abomni zizaniarum femine diligenter mundata, terræ essent commissa, nihilominus zizaniæ copiosæ provenerint. Nam quod ulterioris confirmationis causâ addit, cuiq; frumenti generi sua certa zizania innasci; ne hoc quidem pro mutatione seu degeneratione multum facit; quia certissimum est, quod sicuti zizania sponte, seu æquivoca generatione (ut vocant) provenire solent, ita non omnia ubiq; promiscue proveniunt, sed certa soli genera, certarumq; stirpium societatem amant; unde fit, ut alia in campis, alia in montibus, alia in pratis, dumetis, sylvis, segetibus frequentius conspiciantur; & alia quidem in uno segetum genere, alia in alio. & notissima sunt multa herbarum genera, quarum aliæ frequentius ac copiosius cum tritico, aliæ cum secale, aliæ cum hordeo solent provenire, quas nemo ex istorum permutatione aut degeneratione oriri unquam somniavit; quum tamen & ipsæ provenire soleant, etiamsi cerealia ista, quibuscum nascuntur, essent omnino pura, quum terræ mandarentur, nullumque alienum semen admixtum habentia. Ea igitur certa demum foret probandæ hujusce mutationis ratio, si quum ager aliquis certo semine consitus esset, nihil plane ejus, quod expectabatur, proveniret, sed ejus loco succresceret par proportio herbæ, in quam alteram herbam solere degenerare dicitur; dummodo unà constaret, nullum intervenisse tale aut ipsius seminis, aut soli tempestatumve vitium, unde suspicari daretur, semen plane interijsse; & herbam illam degenerem nulla habuisse in illo solo semina, neq; solere ibi sponte provenire. Hæc omnia si concurrerent, tunc sane liceret concludere, semen degenerasse, alienamq; stirpem pem ex eo provenisse. Sed an tale experimentum extiterit uniquam, valde dubitamus, quum nemo id prodat: propterea q; licet receptam hanc de seminum herbarumq; degeneratione opinionem pro falsa condemnare non sustinemus, pro incerta tamen merito ipsam suspectamus, ac proinde eam advocare non libet ad praesentis de Forma dogmatis impugnationem, quod priori objectione affatim confutatur.
units.tr: 2. Hist. 5. in the bosom of the earth. And the fact that a different herb springs up from a seed sown for a certain plant is not a sufficient sign of this change, since one may suppose either that the seed has wholly perished and this herb has arisen by spontaneous generation, or that a seed of a kindred herb, which had grown there earlier, has fallen and, having lain hidden in the earth for some time, has produced it. Hence the argument of Galen does not conclude anything, for he thinks this change is proved by the fact that when pure grain seed, carefully cleansed of every seed of darnel, was committed to the earth, darnel nevertheless sprang up in abundance. For what he adds, to confirm the point further, that each kind of wheat has its own certain darnel growing with it, does not greatly help the claim of change or degeneration either; for it is most certain that, just as darnel usually arises spontaneously, or by equivocal generation (as they call it), so not all kinds appear everywhere indiscriminately. Rather, certain kinds of soil and certain societies of plants are favoured, so that some are seen more often in fields, others in mountains, others in meadows, thickets and woods, and others in one kind of crop and others in another. Many kinds of herbs are well known: some commonly and abundantly come up with wheat, others with rye, others with barley. No one has ever dreamed that these arise from the change or degeneration of those grains, although these weeds too are wont to appear even when the grains they grow among were entirely pure when committed to the earth, with no foreign seed mixed in. The sure proof of this change would therefore be this: if a field were sown with a certain seed and nothing at all of what was expected came up, but in its place there sprang up a similar quantity of the herb into which the other herb is said to degenerate, provided it was also clear that no such fault had intervened either in the seed itself or in the soil or weather, which might give ground for suspecting that the seed had wholly perished, and that the degenerate herb had no seed in that soil and was not wont to appear there spontaneously. If all these things concurred, one could then certainly conclude that the seed had degenerated and that an alien stock had come from it. But whether such an experiment has ever been made, we greatly doubt, since no one reports it. Therefore, although we do not presume to condemn this commonly received opinion of the degeneration of seeds and herbs as false, we rightly regard it as uncertain, and accordingly we do not wish to bring it forward against the present refutation of the doctrine of Forms, which is sufficiently overthrown by the earlier objection.

units.la: XLVI. Quatuor capita hactenus examinata, futilitatem hujus de Formis doctrinae abunde ostendunt, ac sufficere valent ad omnem ipsi fidem adimendam.
units.tr: XLVI. The four chapters examined so far abundantly show the futility of this doctrine of Forms, and are enough to strip it of all credibility.

units.la: Sed super omnia est caput quintum, quod adhuc restat, de Formarum ortu & interitu; ubi ita implicati tenentur Peripatetici, ut quando ad illud explicandum accesserunt, ne minimam quidem probabilitatis speciem servent, sed absurdissima multa atq; ex diametro inter se pugnantia proferre, ac sibi ipsis apertissime contradicere cogantur. Quum enim docent generationem rerum sola Formae introductione pergi, & quod novam substantiam generari, nihil aliud sit, quam novam Formam in Materiam praeexistentem induci, Formas autem non praeexistere, sed tum demum incipere esse, quando ipsum Compositum esse incipit; sequitur, ut quando substantia aliqua generatur, Forma quoq; fiat seu generetur: & quum non fiat ex praexistenti, ex nihilo eam fieri necesse est. Haec consequentiae quum sint evidentissimae, negari nullo modo possunt, nisi ut id, unde ipsae ducuntur, una negetur; & sane ipsi non negant. At tamen eo vertiginis abripiuntur (dum formas substantiales quo jure quave injuria defendere satagunt) ut ubi haec concesserunt, mox tamen audeant ea negare rursus, atq; asserere, quod Formae non fiant e nihilo, sed e subjecto, imo quod non fiant omnino: quae non modo cum praecedentibus, sed & inter se manifesto pugnant. Haec autem omnia, breviter hic comprehensa, nunc plenius exequi animus est, ut summa ipsorum absurditas tanto magis eluceat.
units.tr: But above all there is the fifth chapter, which still remains, on the origin and destruction of Forms. Here the Peripatetics are so entangled that, when they come to explain it, they keep not even the slightest appearance of probability. They are forced to put forward many absurdities that are diametrically opposed to one another and to contradict themselves most plainly. For when they teach that the generation of things takes place solely by the introduction of a Form, and that to generate a new substance is nothing other than to induce a new Form into pre-existing matter, while Forms do not pre-exist but only begin to be when the Composite itself begins to be, it follows that when any substance is generated, its Form too is made or generated. And since it is not made from something pre-existing, it must be made from nothing. These consequences are so evident that they cannot be denied in any way, unless the premise from which they are drawn is denied. And indeed they do not deny it. Yet they are swept into such a whirl of dizziness (while they labour to defend substantial Forms, by what right or wrong I do not inquire) that, having granted these points, they soon dare to deny them again and to assert that Forms are not made from nothing but from a subject, indeed that they are not made at all. These assertions contradict not only what precedes but also one another. I now intend to set out all these matters, briefly summarised here, more fully, so that their great absurdity may shine out all the more clearly.

units.la: Formas nequaquam esse compositio vetustiores, seu ipsi praexistere, sed tum demum fieri vel generari, quando ipsum
units.tr: That Forms are by no means older than the composite, or exist before it, but only then come into being or are generated when the composite itself
Chapter I.

units.la: ipsum Compositum fit generatur, clarìs verbis dicitur à Vicomercato, Quum Forma non sit rerum naturalium Principium eodem modo ut Materia, efficitur at neq; aeterna sit, quemadmodum illa, sed potius esse tum incipit, tum definit, quum res oriuntur, ac occidunt. Nec vero aliquo temporis spatio ante rerum generationem existunt, sed eodem temporis spatio & Forma, & res cujus Forma est, esse incipit, genitaq; dicitur. Quum enim tot sint Forma, quot res generabiles, nec absq; Materia esse queant, nec simul multa in Materie una portione; esse incipiant, atq; oriantur, nec aeterna sint, necesse est. Et mox, Perspicuum est Formas naturales, quum antea non fuissent, esse incipere. Et cum Vicomercato idem hic docent omnes Peripatetici, sicuti cunctis, qui ipsorum scripta triverunt, notum est; ut supervacuum sit, pluta in hanc rem testimonia adducere.
units.tr: comes into being, is stated in clear words by Vicomercato: Since the Form is not a principle of natural things in the same way as matter, it follows that it is not eternal as matter is, but rather it begins to be and ceases to be when things arise and perish.
