Nor indeed do Forms exist for any span of time before the generation of things, but in the same span of time both the Form and the thing of which it is the Form begin to be and are said to be generated. For since there are as many Forms as generable things, and they can neither exist without matter nor many of them at once in one portion of matter, they must begin to be and arise, and they must not be eternal. And shortly afterwards: It is plain that natural Forms, since they did not exist before, begin to be. And all the Peripatetics teach the same here along with Vicomercato, as is known to everyone who has worn out their writings. So it would be superfluous to bring forward more testimonies on this point.

units.la: Iam si non praefuerunt Formae, sed tum demum fiunt, quando fiunt Composita; alterutrum dicendum est, aut ex praexistente eas fieri, aut ex nihilo, quum nulla alia via detur, ac proinde alterum horum duorum sit eligendum. Quantum ad prius; non defuerunt inter Peripateticos, qui ita decernerent. Quippe cum reformidarent fateri (ob difficultates mox tangendas) quod Formae ex nihilo fiant; consultius esse putaverunt, ut Formarum praeexistentiam in Materia statuerent. & quia absolutas statuere verecundabantur (tum ob alias Causas repugnantibus hoc Peripati de Forma decretis; tum quia sic, ut Suarez ait, è medio tolleretur vera rerum generatio & corruptio) statuerunt inchoatas, quae à proximo agente perficerentur. Sed haec de Formis inchoatis in Materia praeexistentibus sententia a longe maxima Peripateticorum parte pro commento unanimiter repudiatur, ac multis argumentis impugnatur à Vicomercato, Picolomineo, Conimbricensibus, Toleto, ac imprimis Suarezio, qui caeteris plenius hanc rem tractat.
units.tr: Now, if the Forms did not exist beforehand, but only come into being when the composites come into being, then one of two things must be said: either they are produced from something pre-existing, or from nothing, since no other way is available. Hence one of these two must be chosen. As for the first, there were some Peripatetics who did decide this way. Since they shrank from admitting (because of the difficulties I am about to touch on) that Forms come from nothing, they thought it more prudent to posit the pre-existence of the Forms in matter. And because they were ashamed to posit complete Forms (partly for other reasons, since Peripatetic doctrine on Form resists this, and partly because, as Suárez says, in this way true generation and corruption would be removed), they posited incomplete Forms, which the proximate agent would bring to completion. But this opinion about incomplete Forms pre-existing in matter is unanimously rejected as a fiction by by far the greatest part of the Peripatetics, and it is refuted by many arguments from Vicomercato, Piccolomini, the Conimbricenses, Toletus, and above all Suárez, who treats this matter more fully than the rest.

units.la: XLVII. Ast si non praecessit quicquam in Materia, ex quo Formae fiant, neque fiunt ex Materia ipla, Materiâ in Formam conversâ (quod qui dicere auderet, nemo adhuc
units.tr: XLVII. But if nothing preceded in matter from which Forms might come to be, and they do not come to be from matter itself, with matter converted into Form (which no one has yet dared to say,

Phys. quaest. 19. e Disp. 15. sect. 2. huc inter Aristotelicos inventus fuit) sequitur, ut è nihilo fiant; quum nihil inter hæc medium sit, ut diximus, debeantq; Formæ vel ex nihilo fieri, vel ex præexistenti. Quod si è nihilo fiunt, substantiæ non erunt; quum nulla substantia (ab ordinaria quidem potestate, & in ordinariis generationibus,) fieri è nihilo queat: quod adeo est evidens, ut inter tot dissentientes philosophorum sectas nemo nuquam extiterit, qui non id asseveraret: quod vel ex Aristotele constat, qui id testatur multis in locis, ut 1. de Gener. & Corrupt. 3. Ο μάλισα φοβούμενοι διεξέλεγχοι πρῶτοι φιλοσοφήσαντες, τ' ἐκ μηδενὸς γίνεσθαι προϋπάρχοντος. quod maxime semper reformidarunt ij, qui primi philosophari aggressi sunt, ne aliquid fiat ex non præexistenti. ita & 1. Physi. 8. & 3. de Cœlo, 1. idem dicit, sed cum calumnia manifesta: quippe hanc eorum sententiam, Nihil fieri aut interire, ita detorquet, ac si prorsus denegassent, quicquam Generari aut Interire; quod non philosophorum esset, sed insanientium, si ista vocabula in vulgari significatione usurpentur. sin arctius astringantur, ut Generari sit oriri ex nihilo; Interire, in nihilum redigi; verissimum est illud axioma, quodq; calumniam pati non debuit ab Aristotele, qui ipse idem sentiret, & passim diceret, in omni generatione requiri τὸ ἐξ οὗ. ut 2. Gen. Anim. 1. Ἀνάγκη γὰρ τὸ γινόμενον καὶ ἐκ τινος γίνεσθαι, καὶ ὑπό τινος καὶ τι. Necesse est ut id quod fit & ex aliquo fiat, & ab aliquo, & aliquid. & 1. Cœli 3. Δεῖ γὰρ γίγνεσθαι ἅπαν τὸ γιγνόμενον ἐξ ἐναντίου τε καὶ ὑποκειμένου τινός, καὶ φθείρεσθαι ὡσαύτως ὑποκειμένου τε τινος, καὶ ὑπ' ἐναντίου, καὶ εἰς ἐναντίον. Quia omne id, quod fit, fit ex contrario atq; subjecto aliquo; & similiter corrumpitur è subjecto aliquo, & à contrario, atq; in contrarium. & similia quamplurima in ipsius scriptis occurrunt. Et 3. de Cœlo, 2. ponit etiam rationem, Cur absolute ex nihilo fieri nihil possit, quia nimirum sic daretur κενὸν νεχωρισμένον. ἐν ᾧ γὰρ ἔσαι τόπῳ τὸ γενόμενον, εἰ ἐγένετο, ἐν τούτῳ πρότερον ὁ κενὸν ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι, σώματος μηδενὸς ὄντος. ὄντος. vacuum separatum. in quo enim loco esset id quod factum est, si fieret, in eo necesse esset prius fuisse vacuum, quum corpus nullum ibi esset. sed haec ratio nulla est. Possent enim multa in hunc mundum nova corpora introduci, aut quae prius fuerant educi, ut tamen propterea necesse non esset, aut prius fuisse vacuum, aut postea fieri: quae de re in libro sequente, inter Aeris ac Spiritus proprietates, dicendum erit. Vera causa est, Quia substantiam ex nihilo facere, aut in nihilum redigere, infinitae est potestatis, ac proinde nemini concessae, nisi soli Deo, qui usurpare quidem utramque, si velit, singulis potest momentis; facere tamen id nequaquam ipse cupit, sed alteram, si ulla unquam futura est (scire enim non possumus, cum ipse, qui solus notificare nobis poterat, id a nobis absconderit) reservavit novissimo tempori; altera in principio ita usus est, ut postea nunquam uti rursus voluerit. Ethnici quidem philosophi pleriq; , ac praecipue Aristoteles, adeo obstinate hoc tenuerunt, Nullam substantiam e nihilo fieri, ut neipsi quidem Deo concederent potestatem aliquid ex nihilo faciendi. sed illos hac in re turpiter erravisse constat. Caeteroqui post mundi primordia, ac post primam illam septimanam, nihil amplius creare, seu nullam amplius substantiam e nihilo facere (non quia non possit, sed quia non velit) unanimi consensu non Christiani tantum Theologi, sed & Iudaei ac Muhammedani (praeter paucissimos quosdam ex omni hoc numero; de quibus statim) docent, solis mentibus humanis exceptis, quas quotidie ad cujuscunq; hominis generationem creari, pleriq; ipsorum affirmant. Ab ordinarijs quidem agentibus nullam prorsus substantiam e nihilo posse produci, summo ac generali consensu inter omnes omnium aetatum ac sectarum philosophos constat, neq; ab ethnicis modo, sed & ab aliis proxime nominatis concorditer asseveratur.
units.tr: a 2. Princ. natur. 9. b De Creat. cap. 5. & 2. de Mater. 14. c 1. Phys. cap. 9. quaest. 12. art. 6. d 1. Phys. quaest. 19. e Disp. 15. sect. 2. has been found among the Aristotelians), it follows that they come from nothing; since, as we have said, there is no middle course between these, and Forms must come either from nothing or from something pre-existing. But if they come from nothing, they will not be substances, since no substance can come from nothing by ordinary power and in ordinary generations. This is so evident that, among so many dissenting schools of philosophers, no one has ever arisen who did not affirm it. This is clear even from Aristotle, who testifies to it in many places, as in On Generation and Corruption 1: [Ὁ μάλιστα φοβούμενοι διεξέλεγχοι πρῶτοι φιλοσοφήσαντες, τὸ ἐκ μηδενὸς γίνεσθαι προϋπάρχοντος.] That is, those who first began to philosophize have always most dreaded that anything should come to be from what does not pre-exist. Likewise in Physics 1, chapter 8, and On the Heavens 1, chapter 3, he says the same, but with manifest distortion. For he twists their opinion, Nothing comes to be or perishes, as if they had altogether denied that anything is generated or perishes. That would be the view not of philosophers but of madmen, if these words were taken in their common meaning. But if they are restricted more narrowly, so that to be generated means to arise from nothing, and to perish means to be reduced to nothing, then that axiom is most true, and it ought not to have been slandered by Aristotle, who himself held the same view and repeatedly said that in every generation there must be a from which. As in On the Generation of Animals 2, chapter 1: [Ἀνάγκη γὰρ τὸ γινόμενον καὶ ἐκ τινος γίνεσθαι, καὶ ὑπό τινος καὶ τι.] That is, it is necessary that what comes to be comes from something, and by something, and be something. And in On the Heavens 1, chapter 3: [Δεῖ γὰρ γίγνεσθαι ἅπαν τὸ γιγνόμενον ἐξ ἐναντίου τε καὶ ὑποκειμένου τινός, καὶ φθείρεσθαι ὡσαύτως ὑποκειμένου τε τινος, καὶ ὑπ' ἐναντίου, καὶ εἰς ἐναντίον.] That is, everything that comes to be comes from a contrary and from some underlying subject, and likewise perishes from an underlying subject, and by a contrary, and into a contrary. Very many similar passages occur in his writings. In On the Heavens 3, chapter 2, he also gives the reason why absolutely nothing can come from nothing: namely, that otherwise there would be [κενὸν νεχωρισμένον, ἐν ᾧ γὰρ ἔσαι τόπῳ τὸ γενόμενον, εἰ ἐγένετο, ἐν τούτῳ πρότερον ὁ κενὸν ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι, σώματος μηδενὸς ὄντος.] a separate void. For in whatever place the thing that came to be would be, if it came to be, in that place there would necessarily have been a void beforehand, since no body would be there. But this reason is worthless. For many new bodies could be introduced into this world, or those that existed before could be led out, without it being necessary either that a void existed beforehand or that it comes to be afterwards. This will be discussed in the following book, among the properties of air and spirit. The true reason is this: to make a substance from nothing, or to reduce it to nothing, is of infinite power, and therefore granted to no one but God alone, who can indeed use either power, if he wills, at any moment. Yet he does not at all desire to make use of it in that way, but has reserved the second, if it is ever to be exercised (for we cannot know this, since he who alone could make it known to us has hidden it from us), for the last time. The first he used at the beginning, in such a way that he afterwards never willed to use it again. Indeed, most heathen philosophers, and especially Aristotle, held so stubbornly that no substance comes to be from nothing that they did not even grant God himself the power of making something from nothing. But it is clear that they erred shamefully in this matter. Otherwise, after the beginnings of the world, and after that first week, God created nothing further, or made no further substance from nothing (not because he could not, but because he did not will to). This is taught by unanimous consent, not only by Christian theologians but also by Jews and Muhammadans (apart from a very few of all this number, of whom more presently), with the exception of human minds, which most of them affirm are created daily at the generation of each man. That no substance whatever can be produced from nothing by ordinary agents is agreed by the highest and general consent among all the philosophers of every age and sect, and it is affirmed harmoniously not only by the heathens but also by the others just named.

units.la: XLVIII. Iam quum ob hanc rationem Formae nequeant esse substantiae, si ab ordinarijs Agentibus producantur; nihil aliud requiritur (ut nimirum utrumque simul tueri quis possit,
units.tr: XLVIII. Since, for this reason, forms cannot be substances if they are produced by ordinary agents, nothing else is required (so that one may defend both at once,

units.la: possit, quòd & è nihilo fiant Formæ, & substantiæ tamen sint) nisi ut confugiatur ad superiorem potestatem, cui quum concessum sit substantias è nihilo facere, etiam Formas è nihilo producat. Sane hoc adegit Avicennam, ut fingeret Numen quoddam sublunare, seu Intelligentiam fublunaris Mundi gubernatricem, quæ Formas crearet, atq; in Materiam prædispositam introduceret. hoc & alij quamplurimi testantur. & Scaliger commentarijs ad primum de Plantis, ubi sic de hac re loquitur. Adeo exagitati sunt sapientes [ videlicet in explicanda Formarum origine ] ut Deum quendam subalternum creaverit Avicenna, cujus tum officio facta, tum beneficio data reciperentur in Materiam. Avicennæ vestigia secutus haud dubie fuit Fernelius, qui in opere de Abditis rerum Causis, magno id agit apparatu, ut doceat omnem Formarum originem esse divinam atque à Cœlo. Etenim Formam cœli omnes caducarum rerum Formas potestate comprehendere. non tamen substantiæ suæ quicquam rebus genitis elargiri, aut feorsim gentilem absolutamq; Formam in corpora immittere, sed spiritu illo suo per omnia sulo illam in subjectis præparatis producere. Imò Scaliger quoq; illam secutus est sententiam, ut fateretur omnes Formas à Deo creari, sive ab ipso proximè, sive per ministerium Angelorum. ita enim scribit, comment. in 1. de plantis, Alias Formas dari ab intelligentijs, acceptas ab opifice primo; animas nostras immediate ab ipso Deo factas ex nihilo; quanquam mox hoc rursus in dubium revocans, testatur, non satis constare inter primos philosophos, quis sit Formarum dator, aut unde proficiscantur, vel ἐκ τίνος ἐμψύχου depromantur. non enim facilem patere ingenijs humanis aditum ad hujusce sacrarij penetralia. Mirum certe non est, inveteratos errores non potuisse è naturali philosophia tolli ab ijs, qui ut validum quodq; se offerebat ad eos extirpandos argumentum, ita convertebantur ad majorem ipsorum admirationem, & nescio quæ sibi mysteria fingebant, quorum profunditatem non caperet humanus intellectus. Porro valde inconstans fuit hac in re Scaliger. quippe non hic modo cum dubitatione; sed & alibi incunctanter de origine Formarum similia prodidit. quippe Exerc. 6. 2. ait: Coelestes potestates dare Formas, & quae Formam consequuntur; quare coeli sint omnia, potestate efficiendi, sicuti Materia prima omnia potestate receptionis; Idq; ex eo loco in Indicem quoq; retulit, Intelligentias esse Formarum datrices, & tamen paulo post in eadem exercitatione valde acriter invehitur in Fernelium, qui sentiat Formas ab externo agente introduci; Quia sic nulla generatio esset nisi aequivoca, parentibus solam Materiam conferentibus: ut ubi Scaligerum hic invenias, aut quomodo pedem cum eo conferas, rationem inire vix possis; neq; mirum sit, eum intellectu difficillimam judicasse Formarum originem, de qua adeo nihil certi constituere ipse potuerit. Quanquam autem ij, qui coelo aut intelligentiis acceptam tulerunt Formarum originem, eatenus laudandi sunt, quod aliquam saltem verisimilitudinis curam gesserint; neq; ausi sint eo impudentiae progredi, ut simul asserent, & fieri Formas e nihilo, & haudquaquam e nihilo fieri (quod paradoxon tuetur maxima Peripateticorum pars, uti mox videbimus) erravisse tamen eos, hinc patet, quod saniores Theologi concorditer statuunt, & verissimum est, Potestatem res ex nihilo creandi, soli Deo propriam esse, neq; ulli unquam Creaturae ab eo concessam, aut concedendam. quare à coelo aut ab intelligentijs produci Formae non possunt, si Formae sunt substantiae; quum istis nequaquam communicaverit Deus hanc virtutem, substantias e nihilo procreandi; ut neque ulli alij creaturae: sed sibi soli eam reservaverit.
units.tr: that forms both come from nothing and yet are substances) except to take refuge in a higher power, to which it has been granted to make substances from nothing, and which can therefore also produce forms from nothing. Indeed, this drove Avicenna to imagine a certain sublunary deity, or intelligence governing the world below the moon, which would create forms and introduce them into prepared matter. Many others also bear witness to this. Scaliger, in his commentary on the first book of the De plantis, speaks of the matter as follows: The wise men have been so harassed [namely in explaining the origin of forms] that Avicenna created a certain subordinate god, by whose office things are made and by whose benefit they are received into matter. Following in the footsteps of Avicenna, Fernelius undoubtedly did the same, who in his work on the hidden causes of things takes great pains to teach that the origin of all forms is divine and from heaven. For he holds that the form of heaven comprehends by its power the forms of all perishable things, yet does not bestow any of its own substance on the things generated, nor does it introduce a separate, noble and absolute form into bodies; rather, by that spirit of its own it produces the forms in the prepared subjects, penetrating all things. Indeed, Scaliger too followed this opinion, so far as to confess that all forms are created by God, either immediately by himself or through the ministry of angels. For thus he writes in his commentary on the first book of De plantis: That other forms are given by intelligences, received from the first maker; that our souls are made immediately by God himself out of nothing; although soon after, calling this again into doubt, he testifies that it is not sufficiently agreed among the first philosophers who is the giver of forms, or whence they come, or from what animate thing [ἐκ τίνος ἐμψύχου] they are drawn. For there is not an easy approach for human wits into the inner sanctuary of this mystery. Certainly it is no wonder that inveterate errors could not be removed from natural philosophy by those who, as each argument presented itself as strong enough to root them out, turned themselves instead to increase their own wonder, and feigned I know not what mysteries for themselves, whose depth the human intellect could not grasp. Moreover, Scaliger was very inconsistent in this matter. For he set forth similar views about the origin of forms not only here with hesitation, but also elsewhere without hesitation. For in the sixth exercise, section 2, he says: The heavenly powers give forms, and whatever follows form; hence the heavens are all things in the power of producing, just as prime matter is all things in the power of receiving; and he also recorded this in his index, that intelligences are the givers of forms. And yet a little later in the same exercise he attacks Fernelius very sharply, because he holds that forms are introduced by an external agent: For thus there would be no generation except equivocal, parents contributing only matter; so that you could scarcely find out Scaliger's reasoning here, or how you might square your step with his. Nor is it surprising that he judged the origin of forms most difficult to understand, since he himself could establish nothing certain about it. Although, however, those who attributed the origin of forms to heaven or to intelligences deserve praise in so far as they at least took some care for probability, and did not dare to go to such impudence as to assert at once both that forms are made from nothing and that they are by no means made from nothing (a paradox which the greatest part of the Peripatetics defends, as we shall soon see), nevertheless that they erred is clear from this: the wiser theologians agree and state, and it is most true, that the power of creating things from nothing belongs to God alone, and has never been granted, nor is to be granted, to any creature. Therefore forms cannot be produced by heaven or by intelligences, if forms are substances; since God has by no means communicated to these the power of producing substances from nothing, any more than to any other creature; but has reserved that power to himself alone.

units.la: Hoc perpendens Philoponus, quum & ipse rectissime sentiret, Formas, si substantiae sunt, & ex nihilo fiunt, debere per Creationem fieri; non ad coelum aut intelligentias recurrit, sed ad ipsum Deum, a quo Formas in omni substantiarum generatione creari diceret. Et hoc sane dicendum est, velint, nolint, omnibus Peripateticis, ut sese ex his angustijs eripiant, ac probabiliter declarent, quomodo Formae, quum substantiae sint, ex nihilo fiant. Ast hoc nequaquam faciunt, & non modo Avicennae atque FernelioFernelio non accedunt longe maxima ipsorum pars, sed ne Philopono quidem, & hujus sententiam pariter atque illorum rejiciunt, & pro falsa repudiant. Et sane justissimam habent ita faciendi causam, quum à ratione abhorreat, omni generationi adjungere creationem, imò de medio tollere omnes generationes, easq; in creationes permutare. Contra hunc Avicenæ errorem (inquiunt Conimbricenses, quorum verba nihilo secius in Fernelium & Philoponum quadrant) reclamant tum natura ipsa, indigne ferens adimi sibi nobilissimam suam operationem, generationem substantialem, tum schola Peripatetica communi consensu.
units.tr: Philoponus, weighing this carefully, since he himself judged most rightly that forms, if they are substances and come from nothing, must come about by creation, does not have recourse to heaven or to intelligences, but to God himself, from whom he said forms are created in every generation of substances. And this certainly must be said to all the Peripatetics, whether they wish it or not: that they should extricate themselves from these straits, and show in a plausible way how forms, since they are substances, come from nothing. But they do not do this at all. Not only does by far the greatest part of them not agree with Avicenna and Fernelius, but neither do they agree with Philoponus, and they reject his opinion just as they reject theirs, and repudiate it as false. And indeed they have a very just reason for doing so, since it is contrary to reason to join creation to every generation, or rather to remove all generations altogether and change them into creations. Against this error of Avicenna (say the Conimbricenses, whose words fit Fernelius and Philoponus no less) nature itself protests, taking it ill that its most noble operation, substantial generation, should be taken away from it, and the Peripatetic school protests with common consensus.
XLIX.

units.la: Quodsi è nihilo fiunt Formæ, & tamen neq; ab alio superiore Agente, neq; ab ipso Deo fiunt; nihil aliud restare videtur, nisi ut ipsis agentibus ordinarijs (siquidem ab ijs Formæ producuntur) tribuatur vis creandi; quod neq; fieri potest, ob rationes modo allegatas, neq; à Peripateticis asseritur. Quin imò acriter ipsi contendunt, quanquam Formæ à Generantibus fiant, non tamen ab ijs creari, neq; ipsarum productionem creationis nomine appellandam esse. Aiunt enim, creationem non esse nisi rerum per se subsistentium, ac proinde Formas (quæ omnes, Mentibus humanis exceptis, necessario Materiæ inhæreant, neq; per se subsistere possint) nequaquam creari, sed è Materiæ potentia educi; ac proinde quanquam è nihilo fiant eo respectu, quod de novo producantur ita, ut nihil ipsarum præextiterit; non tamen è nihilo fieri eo modo, quo è nihilo fiunt ea quæ creantur. Hæc est mirabilis illa solutio, cujus beneficio evadere se sperant ex hisce angustijs, ut ubi expressissime confessi sunt, Formas ex nihilo fieri, illis hoc rursus negare liceat, atq; sic evitare, ne Formas dicant creari. Sed præstiterit ipsos audire, suis verbis bellam hanc ac catam exceptionem explicantes. Fonseca quum posuisset hanc objectionem, Forma non producitur ex subjecto tanquam ex parte sua, neq; ex parte sua, quae prius in subjecto fuerit, quàm ipsa in subjecto est: ergo actio,
units.tr: If Forms come from nothing, and yet are made neither by another superior agent nor by God himself, then nothing else seems to remain except that the power of creating be attributed to the ordinary agents themselves, since it is by them that Forms are produced. This can be done neither on account of the reasons just alleged, nor is it asserted by the Peripatetics. Indeed they contend vigorously that, although Forms are made by the generating agents, they are not created by them, and their production should not be called creation. For they say that creation is only of things that subsist through themselves, and therefore Forms (all of which, except human minds, necessarily inhere in matter and cannot subsist through themselves) are by no means created, but are educed from the potency of matter. Accordingly, although they come from nothing in the respect that they are newly produced, so that nothing of them previously existed, they do not come from nothing in the way in which created things come from nothing. This is that wonderful solution by whose benefit they hope to escape these straits: when they have most expressly confessed that Forms come from nothing, they may then deny this again, and so avoid saying that Forms are created. But it would be better to hear them explaining this fine and cunning exception in their own words. When Fonseca had put forward this objection, A Form is not produced from the subject as from its own part, nor from its own part which was previously in the subject before it is in the subject: therefore the action,
Ch. I.

units.la: actio, qua ipsa incipit esse in subjecto, est Creatio: ita respondet, Formam, cum inducitur in subjectum, non fieri ex subjecto ut ex parte sua, aut ex parte sua prius existente in subjecto: verumtamen non ideo creari, nisi hujusmodi sit, ut possit suapte natura per se existere, cujusmodi est anima rationalis. nam cateras, etsi non fiunt ex subjecto ut ex parte sua, nec ex parte sua prius existente in subjecto, fieri tamen dependenter à subjecto; quocirca nec proprie fieri, quod Compositorum est proprium, nec proprie creari, ut animam rationalem. Pererius quum objecisset, Videtur Creatio effici ab agente naturali in generatione Formæ: nam per generationem, licet dicatur fieri Compositum, tamen Forma verè producitur, quæ cum ante generationem nec secundum se totam, nec secundum aliquam partem alicubi extiterit, sed prorsus nihil fuerit, cur non dicatur creari? Respondet: Habet sane generatio aliquam similitudinem creationis, propter eam rationem, quæ in objectione posita est. sed hoc interest, quia id quod creatur, non requirit illum subjectum, vel certe tantum ut recipiens, nec ejusmodi est, ut per affectiones & dispositiones ejus producatur id quod creari debet: at quod generatur, exigit necessario Materiam, tanquam id in quo ipsum recipiatur, sustentetur, & per cujus dispositiones & affectiones procreetur. Conimbricenses hanc formant objectionem: Quod creatur, non egreditur de potestate Materiæ, ut Philosophi una voce confitentur. at Forma omnes, si nihil earum prefuit, è nihilo fiunt; quod nihil est aliud quam creari: igitur nulla è Materiæ potestate egreditur. Respondent vero: Formas ante cujusq; rei exortum neq; actu existere, sic enim nihil de novo gigneretur; neq; prorsus non existere, alioqui jam aliquid Natura ex nihilo efficeret; sed esse potestate in Materia, & naturalium Causarum efficacitate de illius potentia ac quasi gremio exciri, & ad actum perfectionemq; adduci. Ut aliqua Forma de subjecti potentia educi dicatur, duplicem conditionem requiri, ac sufficere: unam, ut ad id naturalis potentia subjecto insit, ac Formæ privatio cum dispositionibus in ipso præsit; alteram, ut quod educi-
units.tr: The action by which a form itself begins to be in a subject is creation. Accordingly, he answers that a form, when it is introduced into a subject, is not made out of the subject as from its own part, nor out of a part of it already existing in the subject. Nevertheless it is not created unless it is of such a kind that it can by its own nature exist on its own, as the rational soul does. For the other forms, although they are not made out of the subject as from its own part, nor out of a part of it already existing in the subject, are still made dependently on the subject. Hence they are not properly made, which is proper to composites, nor properly created, as the rational soul is. When Pererius had objected, "Creation seems to be effected by a natural agent in the generation of a form, for through generation, although the composite is said to be made, the form is nonetheless truly produced. Since before generation it existed neither wholly in itself nor in any part somewhere, but was altogether nothing, why is it not said to be created?", he replies: generation certainly has some likeness to creation, for the reason stated in the objection. But there is this difference: what is created does not require that subject, or at most requires it only as a recipient, nor is it of such a kind that what is to be created is produced through the subject's affections and dispositions. What is generated, however, necessarily requires matter, as that in which the form is received and sustained, and by whose dispositions and affections it is brought forth. The Conimbricenses frame this objection: "What is created does not go forth from the power of matter, as the philosophers unanimously confess. But all forms, if none of them previously existed, are made from nothing, which is nothing other than being created. Therefore none goes forth from the power of matter." They reply, however, that forms before the rise of any thing neither actually exist (for thus nothing would be newly begotten), nor altogether do not exist (otherwise nature would now be producing something out of nothing). Rather, they are in potency in matter, and are drawn out of its potency, as it were out of its bosom, by the efficacy of natural causes, and brought to act and to perfection. For a form to be said to be educed from the potency of a subject, two conditions are required and sufficient: one, that a natural potency be present in the subject, with the privation of the form and its dispositions present in it; the other, that what is to be educed can neither be effected nor endure without the aid of such a subject.

units.la: Cap. I. marginal note: "ut hic nascitur et ibi crescit sic in campo sicut in sinu mater." (handwritten, not transcribed in full) educitur, sine talis subjecti adminiculo nec effici nec permanere possit. Itaq; nullam Formam, excepta humana, proprie fieri, quia effectio non nisi in rem per se subsistentem cadat; atq; ita nullam Formam effici e nihilo. praeterea id creari, quod fit e nihilo, hoc est, nullo praejacente subjecto, a quo esse ejus, quod fit, dependeat. liquere autem, quod omnes Formae naturales, excepta humana, a Materiae societate pendeant, cum extra illam subsistere non possint. Piccolomineus, Formas proprie non fieri, transire tamen ex non esse ad esse. itaq; fieri ex nihilo, & in nihilum redire, quatenus neq; fiunt ex aliquo; tanquam ex parte sui, neq; in illud resolvuntur per interitum; non fieri ex nihilo, quatenus contradistinguitur generatio a Creatione, quae non modo fit ex nihilo sui, sed ex nihilo absolute, cum neq; habeat terminum a quo, neq; subjectum, quod utrumq; requiritur in generatione Formarum, quae pro adverso termino habent privationem cum Forma antecedente, ac insuper non fiunt sine subjecta Materia, & praecurrente transmutatione. itaq; non fieri Formam ex nihilo ea significatione, qua ex nihilo fiunt ea quae creantur; & tamen vere ex nihilo fieri, cum ex nihilo sui producantur. & alibi rursus, Id quod fit, esse Compositum ex Materia & Forma, eiq; proprie competere principia Generationis, & de eo absolute nos dicere, non fieri ex nihilo, sed antecedere Materiam tanquam inchoationem ejus. Formam tamen quoq; aliquo modo fieri, quatenus est terminus ad quem Generationis, qui primo non erat, & deinde est; & cum ita fiat, partim fieri ex nihilo, quatenus nihil ejus antecedit, & per interitum in nihilum sui transit; partim non fieri ex nihilo, eo modo quo ea quae creentur, & ejus ortum contradistingui a Creatione, tum ex parte termini a quo, tum ex parte subjecti, quia pro creatione non requiritur subjectum, per cujus transmutationem, ab agente producatur Forma, ut requiritur pro generatione. ex parte autem termini a quo, quia pro creatione non reperitur terminus a quo, qui sit Forma antecedens, cui juncta sit privatio sequentis. Suarez sic objectionem concipit: Forma substantialis vel est aliquid ante generationem
units.tr: (Marginal note, handwritten: "As here it is born and there it grows, so in the field as in the mother's bosom.") It is educed, and cannot be effected or remain without the support of such a subject. Therefore no form except the human is properly made, because effection falls only upon a thing that subsists in itself; and thus no form is made out of nothing. Moreover, that is created which is made out of nothing, that is, with no preceding subject on which the being of what is made depends. It is clear, however, that all natural forms, except the human, depend on the company of matter, since they cannot subsist outside it. Piccolomini holds that forms are not properly made, yet they pass from non-being to being. Thus they are made out of nothing and return into nothing, inasmuch as they are not made from anything as from a part of themselves, nor are they resolved into it through perishing. Yet they are not made out of nothing in the sense in which generation is distinguished from creation, for creation is made not only out of nothing of itself but out of nothing absolutely, since it has neither a term from which nor a subject, both of which are required in the generation of forms. Forms have as their opposite term the privation together with the preceding form, and moreover they are not made without subject matter and a preceding change. Thus a form is not made out of nothing in the sense in which those things are made out of nothing that are created, and yet it is truly made out of nothing, since they are produced out of nothing of themselves. And elsewhere again: what is made is a composite of matter and form, and the principles of generation properly belong to it; and about it absolutely we say that it is not made out of nothing, but that matter precedes it as its beginning. Yet the form too is in some way made, inasmuch as it is the term to which generation tends, which at first was not and then is. And since it is so made, it is partly made out of nothing, inasmuch as nothing precedes it and it passes through perishing into its own nothing; and partly it is not made out of nothing in the way those things are that are created. Its origin is distinguished from creation both on the part of the term from which and on the part of the subject: for creation requires no subject through whose change the agent produces the form, as generation requires; and on the part of the term from which, because in creation no term from which is found, that is, no preceding form to which the privation of the following form is joined. Suárez conceives the objection thus: a substantial form either is something before generation, or nothing. If it is something, then a substantial form exists before it is made, but this is impossible, etc.

units.la: tionem rationem, vel nihil. si est aliquid, ergo est Forma substantialis antequam fiat: hoc autem est impossibile, &c. Si vero eligatur altera pars, nimirum Formam ante generationem nihil esse, sequitur Formam ex nihilo fieri, quod repugnat philosophorum axiomati, Ex nihilo nihil fit. Et respondet ad hunc modum: De omnibus aliis Formis substantialibus, praeter animas humanas, dicendum est, non fieri proprie ex nihilo, sed ex potentia praejacentis Materia educi; ideoque in effectione harum Formarum nihil fieri contra illud axioma, Ex nihilo nihil fit; si recte intelligatur. Nam fieri ex nihilo, duo dicit. unum est, fieri absolute & simpliciter: aliud est, quod talis effectio fit ex nihilo. Primum proprie dicitur de re subsistente, quia ejus est fieri, cujus est esse. id autem proprie est, quod subsistit, & habet esse. Ex hac ergo parte, Forme materiales non fiunt ex nihilo, quia proprie non fiunt. Sumendo ergo ipsum fieri in hac proprietate & rigore, sic fieri ex nihilo, est fieri secundum se totum, id est, nulla sui parte praesupposita, ex qua fiat. Et hac ratione res naturales, dum de novo fiunt, non fiunt e nihilo, quia fiunt ex praesupposita materia, & ita non fiunt secundum se totę. Forme autem harum rerum, quamvis revera totam suam entitatem de novo accipiant, quam antea non habebant, quia tamen non fiunt ut dictum est, ideo neque ex nihilo fiunt. Attamen, quia latiori modo sumendo verbum illud, fieri, negari non potest, quin Forma facta sit, eo modo quo nunc est, & antea non erat, ut probat etiam objectio proposita: ideo addendum est, sumto fieri in hac amplitudine, fieri ex nihilo non tantum negare habitudinem materialis. Causa intrinsece componentis id quod fit, sed etiam sustentantis Formam quae fit seu consit. Ex his ergo recte concluditur, Formas substantiales materiales non fieri ex nihilo, quia fiunt ex Materia, quae in suo genere per se concurrit & influit ad esse & fieri talium Formarum: quia sicut esse non possunt nisi affixae Materia, a qua sustentantur in esse; ita nec fieri possunt, nisi earum Effectio & generatio in eadem Materia sustentetur. Ex his etiam constat, proprie de his Formis dici non creari, sed educi de potentia Materiæ, nam cum illa Forma non fiant ex nihilo, non creantur; quia creari, est fieri ex nihilo, &c.
units.tr: or nothing. If it is something, then a substantial form exists before it is made; but this is impossible, etc. If, however, the other part is chosen, namely that the form before generation is nothing, it follows that the form is made out of nothing, which conflicts with the axiom of the philosophers, "Out of nothing, nothing is made." And he replies in this way: Concerning all other substantial forms, except human souls, it must be said that they are not properly made out of nothing, but are educed from the potency of pre-existing matter. Therefore in the effection of these forms nothing happens contrary to that axiom, "Out of nothing, nothing is made," if it is rightly understood. For to be made out of nothing says two things. One is to be made absolutely and simply; the other is that such an effection is made out of nothing. The first is properly said of a subsisting thing, because to be made belongs to that of which it is to be, and that is properly what subsists and has being. From this side, therefore, material forms are not made out of nothing, because they are not properly made. Taking "to be made" in this proper and strict sense, to be made out of nothing is to be made wholly of itself, that is, with no part presupposed from which it is made. For this reason natural things, when they newly come to be, are not made out of nothing, because they are made from a presupposed matter, and so are not made wholly of themselves. But the forms of these things, although in truth they receive their whole entity anew, which they did not have before, are nonetheless not made, as has been said, and therefore they are not made out of nothing either. Yet because, taking the word "to be made" in a wider sense, it cannot be denied that the form has been made in the state it now is in, and was not before, as the proposed objection also proves, it must be added that, taking "to be made" in this wider sense, to be made out of nothing denies not only the relation of the material cause, which intrinsically composes what is made, but also that of the cause sustaining the form that is made or comes to be. From these things it is rightly concluded that material substantial forms are not made out of nothing, because they are made from matter, which in its own kind concurs and contributes per se to the being and making of such forms. Just as they cannot exist except joined to matter, by which they are sustained in being, so neither can they be made unless their effection and generation is sustained in the same matter. From these things it is also established that of these forms it is properly said that they are not created but educed from the potency of matter. For since those forms are not made out of nothing, they are not created, because to be created is to be made out of nothing, etc.
Chapter I.

units.la: L. Prolixiores fuimus in allegandis diversorum autorum testimonijs ijsq; fusius recitandis, quia res, quam hic dicunt, adeò est absurda, tamq; evidentem continet contradictionem, ut sufficienter illam ob oculos proponere, sit illam refutare. Iamprimum quale quisumus illud est, quod sustinent dicere, Formas fieri è Materia seu subjecto, quia è Materiæ potentia educantur, quum tamen ex Materia non fabricentur Formæ, neq; ulla Materiæ pars assumatur ad Formarum constitutionem, sicuti ipsi asseveratissime contendunt. Et tamen non hoc tantum dicere audent, sed & eo progrediuntur, ut dicant, Formas è Materia fieri seu educi per ipsius transmutationem (uti cum apud alios, tum apud Piccolomineum lib. 1. de Creatione, cap. 5. & Fonsecam 5. Metaph. 2. quæst. 2. sect. 2. & Perer. 5. phys. 8. videre est) prorsus quasi sentirent, Materiam in Formas converti, seu Formas ex Materia in ipsas conversa fieri: quod tamen detestantur. Ut propterea summam mereantur reprehensionem, qui sic omnes loquendi leges pervertant, tamq; effræn em ac inusitatam sermonis licentiam usurpent, ut verba ipsorum eos præ se ferant sensus, à quibus sese esse alienissimos profiteantur: quod tamen ipsis necessario faciendum est, ut sic omnia turbent ac confundant, quo aliquid hinc fallsitati ac futilitati suorum dogmatum præsidij quærant, ne scilicet tam aperte illa in oculos incurrat, haec velut caligine offusa obcæcatos. Talis certe est etiam illa phrasis, qua Formas dicunt è Materia, seu è Materiæ potentia, educi, quum tamen prædicent, neq; totas Formas, neq; ullas ipsarum partes ullave rudimenta in Materia præcessisse, antequam ipsæ de novo simul totæ in ea producerentur.
units.tr: L. We have been rather lengthy in citing the testimonies of various authors and reciting them at some length, because the thing they say is so absurd and contains such an obvious contradiction that to set it plainly before the eyes is enough to refute it. First, what sort of thing is it that they maintain, that forms are made from matter or from the subject, because they are educed from the potency of matter, when in fact forms are not fabricated out of matter, and no part of matter is taken up into the constitution of the forms, as they themselves most emphatically contend? And yet they dare not only to say this, but they go further and say that forms are made or educed from matter through its transmutation (as can be seen both in others and in Piccolomini, De creatione, book 1, chapter 5, and Fonseca, Metaphysics 5, question 2, section 2, and Pererius, Physics 5, chapter 8), just as if they thought matter was converted into forms, or forms were made from matter converted into them; which nevertheless they detest. Therefore those deserve the greatest reproof who so pervert all the laws of speaking and take such an unbridled and unusual licence with language that their words display senses from which they profess themselves most alien. Yet they are necessarily obliged to do this, so that they may confuse and throw everything into disorder, and so seek some support for the falsity and futility of their doctrines from this, namely that such a thing might not run plainly into the eyes, but be blinded as if by a mist cast over it. Certainly such is also that phrase by which they say that forms are educed from matter, or from the potency of matter, when at the same time they affirm that neither whole forms nor any parts or rudiments of them had preceded in matter, before they were all produced anew together in it.

units.la: Nihil enim aliud dicere videmur (inquit Fonseca) quum Formam eductam esse de potentia Materiæ asserimus, quam id factum esse, ut ea, quæ prius non erat actu in Materia, sed potentiâ duntaxat, fit actu in illa: hoc est, si planis verbis idipsum eloquaris, Ut jam insit ea Forma, quæ prius non
units.tr: For we seem to say nothing else (says Fonseca) when we assert that a form is educed from the potency of matter, than that what previously was not actually in matter, but only potentially, is made actual in it: that is, if you say the same thing in plain words, that the form now is present in it which previously was not.
Chapter I.

units.la: non inerat, sed inesse poterat. Formam enim praefuisse in potentia Materiae, non significat, Formas prius aliqua ex parte in Materia latuisse, sed potuisse in Materia produci: quo respectu etiam Suarez dicit, Materiam solummodo continere Formam in potentia receptiva seu passiva. & similiter Piccolomineus ad quaestionem, Quommodo Forma possit educi ex Materia, si nec tota nec ejus portio in ea praeextitit: respondet, Formam dici educi, non quia praefuerit actu, sed quia praefuit potestate, & educitur ab agente, quatenus una cum Materia ab agente de novo producitur. Quae haec igitur est loquendi perversio, ut Forma dicatur educi e Materia, in qua nulla ipsius portio continetur; imo in qua continetur aliud, ipsi in tantum contrarium, ut simul subsistere nullo modo possint, nimirum privatio ipsius, & Forma opposita. Non enim solitaria unquam in Materia est illa potentia receptiva, sed haec duo (quamdiu Forma producenda nondum advenit) semper habet conjuncta; sicuti ab ipsis docetur. Itaque verissime dicta sunt illa apud Pererium: Quod vulgo dicitur, Formam educi ex Materia, nimis improprie dicitur: sonat enim illam segregationem Formarum Anaxagora, vel inchoationem quandam Formarum ab aliis introductam. quare magis proprie diceretur, Formam induci & gigni in Materia, quam ex ipsa educi. haec ille quidem dicit velut ex persona objicientis, ac proinde suam postea ijs apponit responsionem, sed nimis sane imbecillam. Non dicitur (inquit) Forma induci in Materia, nequis falso opinetur, Formam per se productam extrinsecus adjungi Materiae; sed dicitur educi ex Materia, ut Forma intelligatur produci cohaerens, imo immersa Materiae. Profecto si ob incommodum hic memoratum nolint dicere, Formam induci in Materiam; incommodum in objectione positum debuerat habere non minus momenti ad deterrendum ipsos ab hac phrasi, ne dicerent Formas ex Materia educi; quia his verbis videtur plane innui, quod Formae, vel totae, vel ex parte saltem, in Materia praefuerint. Quandoquidem enim id quod non inest, non potest educi; quando aliquid dicitur eductum, omnino infertur, quod prius fuerit in eo, unde eductum memoratur. Certe ut animae rationales dicantur è Materia seu è Materiae potentia educi, ne ipsi quidem tolerare volunt, idq; ob hanc rationem, quod (ut ipse Suarez loquitur) nihil educitur, nisi ex eo in quo continetur. Ast apertum est, nihilo plus aliarum Formarum, quàm animae rationalis, contineri in Materia, antequàm in ipsa producantur. Quod vero animae humanae seorsim factae, postea corpori uniuntur, aliae Formae vero non nisi in ipsis subjectis seu ipsa Materia gigni valent; propterea non magis dicendae sunt è Materia educi: quum hoc non fiat, quia Materia ipsas magis continet, quam animas rationales, sed quia ipsarum haec natura est, ut non queant per se subsistere (prout ipsi docent) ac proinde neq; per se produci. Si igitur illa potentia seu capacitas, quae est in Materia ad recipiendas animas humanas, non sufficit, ipsorum judicio, ut hae dicantur ex eâ educi, quia nimirum in ea non continentur: ne illa quidem potentia seu capacitas, quae est in Materia ad recipiendas alias Formas, sufficere potest, ut ipsae dicantur ex Materiâ educi: quia licet hoc inter se differant istae Formae, quod aliae per se productae, postea Materiae uniuntur, aliae verò eo ipso, quòd producuntur, uniuntur, quia nimirum in ipsa Materia producuntur; in hoc tamen conveniunt utræq;, quod antequam fierent, nequaquam in Materia continebantur, neq; ante ipsarum ortum, quicquam ipsarum in Materia praecessit; ut in hoc quidem par atq; eadem fit utrarumq; ratio. quare neque unae magis quàm alterae dicendae sunt ex Materia educi; si verum est (uti est verissimum, atq; ipsi fatentur) quod nihil possit educi ex eo, in quo non continebatur.
units.tr: Nor was it in it, but it could be in it. For to say that the form pre-existed in the potency of matter does not mean that forms previously lay hidden in some part of matter, but that they could be produced in matter. In this sense Suarez also says that matter contains the form only in a receptive or passive potency. Likewise Piccolomini, to the question How can a form be educed from matter, if neither the whole form nor any portion of it pre-existed in it?, answers: The form is said to be educed not because it existed actually, but because it existed potentially, and it is educed by the agent insofar as it is newly produced by the agent together with the matter. What kind of perversion of speech is this, that a form is said to be educed from matter in which no part of it is contained? Indeed, matter contains something else which is so contrary to it that the two cannot subsist together in any way: namely, its privation and the opposite form. For that receptive potency is never found alone in matter; as long as the form to be produced has not yet arrived, matter always has these two conjoined, as they themselves teach. Therefore, those words of Pererius are altogether true: What is commonly said, that a form is educed from matter, is spoken far too improperly. For it suggests the separation of forms as in Anaxagoras, or a certain initiation of forms introduced by others. Therefore it would be more properly said that a form is induced and begotten in matter than that it is educed from it. He says this indeed as if speaking in the person of an objector, and afterwards he adds his own reply to it, but a truly very feeble one: It is not said (he says) that the form is induced into matter, lest anyone falsely suppose that a form produced in itself is added to matter from outside; rather it is said to be educed from matter, so that the form is understood to be produced cohering with, indeed immersed in, the matter. Certainly, if they are unwilling to say that a form is induced into matter because of the inconvenience mentioned here, then the inconvenience raised in the objection ought to have been of no less weight in deterring them from this phrase, so that they would not say that forms are educed from matter. For these words clearly seem to imply that the forms, either wholly or at least in part, previously existed in matter. For since what is not in a thing cannot be educed, whenever something is said to be educed, it is wholly implied that it was previously in that from which it is said to be educed. Certainly, they themselves do not want to say that rational souls are educed from matter, or from the potency of matter, and they give this reason: because (as Suarez himself puts it) nothing is educed except from that in which it is contained. But it is plain that no more of the other forms than of the rational soul is contained in matter before they are produced in it. And because human souls, made separately, are afterwards united to the body, whereas the other forms can come into being only in their subjects, that is, in matter itself, they are not on that account to be said to be educed from matter any more. This does not happen because matter contains those forms more than it contains rational souls, but because it is the nature of those forms that they cannot subsist by themselves (as they teach), and so cannot be produced by themselves either. Therefore, if that potency or capacity which is in matter for receiving human souls does not suffice, in their judgment, for these souls to be said to be educed from it, because they are not contained in it, then that potency or capacity which is in matter for receiving other forms cannot suffice either for those forms to be said to be educed from matter. For although these forms differ in this respect, that some are produced by themselves and afterwards united to matter, while others are united by the very fact that they are produced, because they are produced in matter itself, yet both agree in this, that before they came to be, they were in no way contained in matter, and before their origin nothing of them preceded in matter. In this respect, therefore, the reasoning is exactly the same for both. Hence neither kind is to be said to be educed from matter any more than the other, if it is true (as it is most true, and as they themselves confess) that nothing can be educed from that in which it was not contained.

units.la: LI. Sunt haec adeo evidentia, ut ipse Scaliger, devotissimus alioqui Peripati cliens, ac summus passim maximarum in ea ineptiarum admirator, hanc tamen phrasin minime concoquere potuerit, neq; admittere ut Formae dicantur è Materia educi, sed judicarit dicendum potius esse, eas è potentia agentis educi, atq; in Materiam introduci: uti satis clare excipere licet ex ijs, quae Exerc. 6. ab
units.tr: LI. These things are so evident that Scaliger himself, otherwise a most devoted client of the Peripatetics, and everywhere a great admirer of the greatest absurdities in them, could nevertheless by no means digest this phrase, nor admit that forms are said to be educed from matter, but judged that they should rather be said to be educed from the potency of the agent and introduced into matter. This can be gathered clearly enough from what he writes in Exercitation 6 (Exerc. 6. ab

units.la: Disp. 15.2,3. ab eo scribuntur. namque sectione ejus secundâ sic ait: Neque enim verum est, Formas esse in Materiae potestate. De Formis loquor iis, quae Materiis aequivocis imponuntur; qualis est muris Forma, quae navalibus quisquilijs putrefactis inditur. non est ea, inquam, Forma in sími potestate, aut sordium illarum, nisi sit ejusmodi potestas, sicuti dicebamus, recipiendi: sed in agentis vi sita est. & rursus sectione quinta, Educitur ergo de agentis potestate Forma; Forma enim, quae ad id usque momenti fuerat in agentis potestate, producitur ab ipso agente, sicuti Forma scamni à fabro, & sic actu ut sit, fit atque ab eo in Materiam introducitur. Videtur quidem haec ad solas aequivocas generationes astringere, atque revera ita facit, quippe qui diserte testatur, se de iis tantum Formis loqui, quae Materiis aequivocis imponuntur; & praeterea addit, Univocas quidem Formas in Materia potestate contineri, puta in semine canino canis Formam. Sed aut seipsum non intellexit, aut sciens ambiguitate lusit, has duas generationes inter se comparando, qua in quisquilias imponitur Forma muris, & qua è semine canino generatur canis. Etenim si in semine canis, & quorumcunque animalium ac stirpium è semine nasci solitorum, integra Forma reapse atque actu continetur (sicuti Scaliger sentit, contra vulgatiorem Peripateticorum doctrinam) non illa proprie est canis generatio, quando è semine canino fit canis, sed quando ipsum semen caninum fit, seu quando in Materiam Forma canis imponitur, quum omnes in universum Peripatetici doceant, generationem substantialem à Formae introductione totam pendere, ac tunc vere & proprie rem dici generatam, quando Forma in subjectum est introducta; quae ipsa est Scaligeri quoq; sententia. Est autem generatio (inquit in comment. ad 6. Caus. 13.) cujusq; rei, Formae ultimae indivisibilis & momentanea introductio. & alibi, Introductâ Formâ in Materiam, cessat motus ad generationem. ac rursus, Ante generationem, id est, momentum illud, quo introductâ Formâ res est id quod est, multi fiunt motus. Et magis ad rem, quae nunc in manu est, dicit com. ad 4. Caus. 7. Se-
units.tr: Disp. 15.2,3. by him are written.) For in his second section he says thus: "For it is not true that forms are in the power of matter. I speak of those forms which are imposed on equivocal matters, such as the form of a mouse, which is put into rotten naval rubbish. That form, I say, is not in the power of the filth, unless there is such a power of receiving, as we were saying; but it lies in the force of the agent." And again in the fifth section: "A form is therefore educed from the power of the agent; for the form, which until that moment was in the power of the agent, is produced by the agent itself, just as the form of a bench is produced by the carpenter; and so it is made actual and is introduced by it into matter." This seems indeed to confine itself to equivocal generations alone, and in fact it does so, since he expressly testifies that he speaks only of those forms which are imposed on equivocal matters; and he adds besides that univocal forms are indeed contained in matter potentially, for example the form of a dog in the seed of a dog. But either he did not understand himself, or knowingly played on the ambiguity, by comparing these two kinds of generation with each other: that in which the form of a mouse is imposed on rubbish, and that in which a dog is generated from the seed of a dog. For if the whole form is actually and in fact contained in the seed of a dog, and in the seed of whatever animals and plants are wont to be born from seed (as Scaliger holds, against the more common doctrine of the Peripatetics), then it is not properly the generation of a dog when a dog comes from the dog's seed, but when the dog's seed itself comes to be, or when the form of the dog is imposed on matter. For all the Peripatetics in general teach that substantial generation depends wholly on the introduction of the form, and that a thing is then truly and properly said to be generated when the form has been introduced into the subject; and this is also Scaliger's own opinion. Generation, he says in his commentary on Causes 13, is the indivisible and momentary introduction of the ultimate form of anything. And elsewhere: "When the form has been introduced into matter, the motion towards generation ceases." And again: "Before generation, that is, at that moment by which, once the form is introduced, the thing is what it is, many motions take place." And more to the point of the matter now in hand, he says in his commentary on Causes 7: Se-

units.la: 7. Semen non corrumpi, quum ex eo fit animal aut planta, sed perfici. semen enim esse totum animal inarticulatum. itemq; alibi, Neq; bornum triticum gignitur, quum a terra prodit e semine, sed cum semen concreatur in spica: neq; pullus, quum excluditur, sed quum ovum, ex quo postea fit, perfectum est. Hisce ergo constitutis, inæqualis atq; incogitans est illa comparatio, qua, ut ostendatur non eandem esse æquivocæ atq; univocæ generationis rationem, quantum ad Formæ e Materia eductionem, semen canis confertur cum fimo, e quo mus producitur. unum enim considerat, uti jam habens Formam, alterum vero ut habiturum. ast ut justa sit comparatio, fimus nondum habens Formam debet conferri non cum semine, sed cum Materia seminis, in quam Forma seminis nondum est introducta: aut semen jam Formam canis possidens conferendum est cum quisquilijs jam Formam muris adeptis. Hoc pacto si comparatio instituatur (ut institui certe debet) aparebit Scaligerum temere illam inter æquivoca atq; univoca differentiam constituisse, & vel horum quoque Formam non e Materia educi, sed in Materiam introduci; aut ne illorum quidem Formam introduci, sed educi. Namq; si Forma canis recte dicitur e semine educi, quia in eo continetur; eodem etiam jure Forma muris rite dicetur educi e fimo, quando ea prius in fimum ad æquivoco generante impositâ, corpus postea dearticulatur, quandoquidem & ipsa in fimo continebatur. Sin vero respectus habeatur ad ipsam Formæ introductionem (quam Scaliger alijque Peripatetici habent pro vera ac propria generatione) semen canis nihilo magis continebatur in eâ Materiâ, in quam ipsâ introductâ, semen canis constitutum est, quam Forma muris in fimo continebatur: ac proinde ratio postulat, ut si in æquivocis generationibus non bene dicitur Forma ex Materiæ potestate educi, sed dicenda est educi e potentia agentis, atq; in Materiam induci; idem quoque de univocis generationibus statuatur. Quanquam autem absurdam hanc phrasin, qua Formæ dicuntur educi e Materia, in qua nihil ipsarum continebatur, hic
units.tr: 7. "The seed is not corrupted when an animal or a plant comes from it, but is perfected, for the seed is the whole animal in an unarticulated state." And elsewhere: "Nor is the grain of wheat generated when it comes up out of the earth from the seed, but when the seed is formed together in the ear; nor is the chick generated when it is hatched, but when the egg, from which it afterwards comes, is complete." Given these premises, that comparison is unequal and ill considered, by which, to show that the generation of equivocal and univocal things does not follow the same method as regards the drawing of form out of matter, the seed of a dog is compared with dung, from which a mouse is produced. For it considers one thing as already possessing the form, and the other as going to possess it. But for the comparison to be just, the dung, not yet possessing the form, ought to be compared not with the seed but with the matter of the seed, into which the form of the seed has not yet been introduced; or else the seed already possessing the form of a dog should be compared with the refuse that has already acquired the form of a mouse. If the comparison is set up in this way (as it certainly ought to be), it will appear that Scaliger rashly drew that distinction between equivocal and univocal things, and that the forms of these too are not drawn out of matter but introduced into matter, or rather that the forms of neither are introduced but drawn out. For if the form of a dog is rightly said to be drawn out of the seed because it is contained in it, then by the same right the form of a mouse will also be properly said to be drawn out of the dung, when, after the equivocal generating agent has been placed in the dung, the body is afterwards disarticulated, since the form too was contained in the dung. But if we look to the introduction of the form itself (which Scaliger and the other Peripatetics hold to be true and proper generation), the form of the dog was no more contained in that matter, into which, once the form was introduced, the seed of the dog was constituted, than the form of the mouse was contained in the dung. Accordingly reason requires that, if in equivocal generations it is not rightly said that a form is drawn out of the power of matter, but that it must be said to be drawn out of the power of the agent and induced into matter, the same should also be held of univocal generations. Although, however, this absurd phrase, by which forms are said to be drawn out of matter in which none of them was contained, here

units.la: Comm. ad Aristotelis de Plantis: 0 inanimata vivunt; animal ad quaedam animalia seminaria seu reticulata aut vel incorporata sive Ioanne. Ut Elbaneso Sbotzo-botzo. hic reprehendit atq; rejicit Scaliger ; pro solita tamen inconstantia alibi interdum eam ut probam absq; hæsitatione usurpat. namq; commentario in Hippocratem de insomniis scribit, Formarum omnia plena esse, ac de potentia Materiæ eas elici à tribus rebus inter se ordinatis, &c. quanquam hoc quidem novum non est, quum scripta Scaligeri (quod monstri simile sit in tanto viro) innumeris passim contradictionibus scateant.
units.tr: Commentary on Aristotle's book On Plants: "Things without life live"; the animal is to certain animals that are seminal or reticulated, or incorporated, or ... (the text is corrupted here; the rest of the gloss is unintelligible). Scaliger rejects and criticises this here, yet, with his customary inconsistency, elsewhere sometimes uses it without hesitation as sound. For in his commentary on Hippocrates' book On Dreams he writes, "All things are full of forms, and they are drawn out of the power of matter by three things ordered among themselves," etc. This, however, is not new, since the writings of Scaliger (a monstrous thing in so great a man) everywhere abound in countless contradictions.

units.la: LII. Duo autem ea, de quibus hactenus egimus, quan- quam perabsurda, non sunt maximum peccatum, quod hic peccant Peripatetici.
units.tr: LII. Although the two points we have so far discussed are very absurd, they are not the greatest error into which the Peripatetics fall here.

units.la: Aliud hisce longe gravius, & omnino portento propius est, quod quum apertissimis verbis plenissime profiteantur, Formas è nihilo fieri; eo tamen provehuntur incogitantiæ, ne dicamus insaniæ, ut simul atque uno spiritu tamen afferant, ac hominibus se persuadere posse putent, eas è nihilo nequaquam fieri; quæ duo simul stare non magis possunt, quàm meridies cum media nocte. Quanquam enim inter fieri è nihilo, &, non fieri è nihilo, possit certo quodam casu dari aliquid intermedium, ita ut dici possit, rem neq; absolute è nihilo fieri, neq; non ex nihilo, videlicet si Compositum aliquod partim ex nihilo fiat, partim ex præjacenti, de quo tunc utrumq; verum erit, & factum illud esse ex nihilo, & non esse ex nihilo factum, nimirum loquendo secundum quid: attamen si vel de substantia simplici, vel de composita secundum omnes partes suas sumta sermo sit, tunc nullo pacto fieri potest, ut res illa & ex nihilo facta sit, & non ex nihilo; sed alterutro istorum posito, alterum necessario removetur; ut si verum est, factam esse ex nihilo, penitus falsum sit, non esse ex nihilo factam: & contra. Sed videamus, quale id sit, cujus fiducia afferere audent, Formas, quanquam è nihilo fiant, è nihilo tamen non fieri. Primò aiunt, non creari, nisi ea quæ per se valent subsistere, neq; effectionem ex nihilo cadere nisi in res per se existentes. Sane si hoc verum est, eodem jure Materiæ primæ creationem quoque denegent oportet, quippe qui ne illam quidem per se existere istere posse existimant; quum tamen illam creatam esse omnes unanimiter concedant Materia prima revera per naturam gigni non potest (inquit Piccolomineus) Theologi tamen recte noverunt, eam non per generationem, sed per creationem recepisse Principium. itemq; Suarez, Actio, qua fit Materia, est vera creatio. & hæc est communis omnium Peripateticorum doctrina, ijs duntaxat exceptis, qui ethnici, aut ethnicorum delirijs imbuti, mundum ab æterno fuisse cum Aristotele asserunt. Quodsi Materiam primam dicunt creatam fuisse, quo primum tempore facta est; non est cur Formas, quando ipsæ fiunt, à nihilo fieri negent ob hoc, quod per se subsistere non valent, quum ijs hoc sit cum Materia prima commune, quæ, ex ipsorum decretis, nihilo magis per se ac sine Forma subsistere valet, quam Formæ sine Materia. Alterum, quod hic asserunt, est, Ea quæ creantur, non requirere ullum subjectum, à quo pendeant in fieri & esse; propterèaque Formas (excepta mente humana) non creari, quum fiant dependenter à subjecto. Ast si dependenter ab alio fieri, satis Causæ est, quominus aliquid dicendum sit creari, seu è nihilo fieri; & hoc quoque respectu negare debebunt Materiam primam creatam esse. Etenim ipsi docent, quomodo Formæ in esse & fieri pendent à Materia, ita Materiam in fieri & esse à Formis pendere, cujus rei testem damus Fonsecam, ita hac de re loquentem: Dicendum est, Materiam naturaliter pendere in suo esse actuali à Formis substantialibus, & in fieri, & in conservari. ac mox rursus, Necessario efficitur, nullam Materiam aut fieri aut conservari posse sine Forma. plane igitur eodem modo Materia pendet à Forma, quo Formæ à Materia. quippe Formarum à Materia dependentiam Fonseca ibidem hisce verbis explicat, omnes Formæ inseparabiles pendent à Materia & in fieri & in conservari, neq; ullo modo fieri possunt aut conservari sine Materia. Quodsi igitur dicendum est Formas, quanquam è nihilo fiant, tamen è nihilo non fieri, seu non creari, quia nimirum dependenter ab alio fiunt; æquum est, ut eadem ratione Materiam primam negent creatam seu.
units.tr: There is another error, far more serious and almost monstrous, which is this: although they most plainly and fully profess that forms come from nothing, they are carried so far by thoughtlessness, not to say madness, that in the same breath they assert, and think they can persuade men, that forms by no means come from nothing. These two claims cannot stand together any more than midday and midnight can. For although between "to come from nothing" and "not to come from nothing" there may, in a certain case, be some intermediate thing, so that it can be said that a thing neither comes absolutely from nothing nor does not come from nothing (namely, if some composite thing is partly made from nothing and partly from something lying before it, in which case both will be true: that it has been made from nothing, and that it has not been made from nothing, speaking, of course, in a qualified sense), nevertheless, if the discussion concerns either a simple substance or a composite taken in all its parts, then by no means can it happen that the thing both has been made from nothing and has not been made from nothing; rather, once one of these is posited, the other is necessarily removed, so that if it is true that it has been made from nothing, it is wholly false that it has not been made from nothing, and conversely. But let us see what sort of thing it is on which they dare to assert with confidence that forms, although they come from nothing, do not come from nothing. First, they say that only those things are created which are able to subsist of themselves, and that production from nothing falls only upon things that exist in their own right. Indeed, if this is true, they must by the same right deny that prime matter was created either, since they judge that it too cannot exist of itself; yet all agree that it was created. "Prime matter cannot truly be generated by nature," says Piccolomini, "but the theologians have rightly recognised that it received its beginning not by generation but by creation." Likewise Suárez: "The action by which matter comes to be is a true creation." And this is the common doctrine of all the Peripatetics, except those who, being heathen or steeped in the heathen follies, assert with Aristotle that the world has existed from eternity. But if they say that prime matter was created, at the first moment it was made, there is no reason why they should deny that forms, when they come into being, are made from nothing on the ground that they cannot subsist of themselves, since in this respect they share a commonality with prime matter, which, by their own decrees, is no more able to subsist of itself and without form than forms are without matter. The second point they assert here is that things which are created do not require any subject on which they depend in becoming and in being; and therefore forms (apart from the human mind) are not created, since they come to be dependently on a subject. But if a thing comes to be dependently on another, that is reason enough why it cannot be said to be created, or made from nothing; and in this respect too they must deny that prime matter was created. For they themselves teach that, just as forms depend on matter both in being and in becoming, so matter depends on forms in becoming and in being; of which we give Fonseca as a witness, speaking thus on this matter: "It must be said that matter naturally depends in its actual being on substantial forms, both in becoming and in being preserved." And soon again: "It necessarily follows that no matter can either come to be or be preserved without a form." Plainly, then, matter depends on form in the same way as forms depend on matter; indeed Fonseca in the same place explains the dependence of forms on matter in these words: "All inseparable forms depend on matter both in becoming and in being preserved, nor can they in any way come to be or be preserved without matter." If therefore it must be said that forms, although they come from nothing, nevertheless do not come from nothing, or are not created, because they come to be dependently on another, it is fair that by the same reasoning they should deny that prime matter was created,

units.la: Comm. ad 1. phys. Text. 82. Disp. 15. sect. 3. §. 2. seu è nihilo factam, quanquam plane è nihilo facta sit; quippe & ipsa dependenter à Formis facta est, ex ipsorum decretis, ac plane consimilem in esse & fieri habet à Formis dependentiam, quam Formæ ab ipsa, imo majorem, si vera sunt, quæ ipsi de Materiæ primæ natura docent.
units.tr: Commentary on the first book of the Physics, text 82; Disputation 15, section 3, §2; or made from nothing, although it was plainly made from nothing. For it too was made dependently on forms, by their own decrees, and it has in becoming and in being a dependence on forms quite like that which forms have on it; indeed a greater one, if what they teach about the nature of prime matter is true.
Chapter I.

units.la: LIII. Præterea vulgaris Peripateticorum opinio est (uti videre est apud Fonsecam, Conimbricenses, Suarezium) Formas cœlestium corporum creatas fuisse. Ast quamcunq; à Materia dependentiam in esse & fieri sibi imaginantur in aliis Formis, eandem hic quoq; admittant necesse est: unde sequeretur, has quoq; Formas non creatas fuisse, sed è Materia eductas; si illis non quadrat creatio, quæ dependenter à Materia fiunt. Huic difficultati ut obviam eant, eo confugiunt ut dicant, Ad eductionem Formarum non sufficere, ut ipsæ fiant dependenter à subjecto, sed præterea requiri, ut subjectum præexistat. Et nonnulli quidem ad omnem Formarum eductionem requirunt, ut tempore subjectum præexistat. De horum numero sunt Conimbricenses, sicuti non obscure indicant verbis illis supra recitatis, ubi alteram conditionum ad eductionem necessariarum hanc faciunt, ut Formæ privatio cum dispositionibus in subjecto præsit. Et hoc repetunt 1. phys. 9. quæst.12. art. 5. Non recte ac proprie de Materiæ potestate educi censetur, nisi ea Forma, cujus privatio cum dispositionibus in Materia præfuit. atq; ob hoc negant, non modo cœlorum Formas, sed & illas aliorum compositorum, quæ in prima rerum molitione à Deo procreata sunt, fuisse de Materiæ potentia eductas; quia nimirum privatio ejusmodi Formarum nequaquam tunc in Materia præfuerit, quum tam ipsæ, quàm earum Materia, & Composita, eodem instanti à Deo producta fuerint. Et ita quoque sensit Piccolomineus, uti apparet ex differentia, quam constituit inter creationem & generationem, itidem superius recitatâ. Ast alij contra affirmant, ad eductionem Formarum minime esse necessarium, ut subjectum tempore præcedat Formam ex ipsa educendum; sed sufficere, ut natura praexistat. Ita Suarez, quum dixisset, Quando dicitur educi Forma de potentia Materiae, quia in potentia ejus continebatur, supponitur Materia prius existens in potentia ad Formam, quam illam actu habeat; mox longam instituit disputationem, ut probet, Ad veram eductionem necessarium non esse, ut Materia tempore antecedat sub privatione, sed satis esse quod antecedat ordine naturae, ac proinde concludit: Formas quoque Elementorum (quas illi, qui ad eductionem requirunt temporis prioritatem in subjecto, creatas esse contendunt non secus, quam illas coelorum) quae in mundi initio fecit Deus, non creatas fuisse, sed de Materiae potentia eductas; quia licet Materia illa tempore non antecesserit ut existens in potentia ad tales Formas, antecesserit tamen prioritate naturae. Et hoc quidem pacto stropha haec plane enervatur. Qui enim aiunt, ad eductionem esse necessariam temporis praexistentiam; aliis tunc hoc obtrudant, ubi omnibus suae sectae illud persuaserint. Si vero prioritas naturae sufficit, ut Forma dicatur de subjecto educi; nihil causae est, quin & coelorum Formas dicant de Materiae potentia eductas; quas tamen cuncti asserunt revera fuisse creatas. Namq; quod illi, qui ad eductionem negant requiri ut subjectum tempore praecedat, hic respondent, Materiam coeli non itidem, ut aliarum rerum Materiam, esse Formā suā priorem naturā; in eo plane antiquum servant, ut quidvis sibi dicere permittant, non curantes, an vel suis ipsorum decretis apertissime contradicant. Sane receptissimum est in Peripato, omne subjectum esse prius naturā eo, cujus subjectum est. quare hic mirabilem (ut alibi plerumque) pugnam videre est: quippe ijdem illi, qui coeli Materiam negant Formis suis priorem ordine naturae, eo ipso in loco, ubi hoc dicunt, prioritatem naturae ipsi concedunt: Ita enim Suarez, Materia coeli, licet secundum propriam rationem causandi dicatur prior naturā, tamen ut existens in potentia, & aliquo modo sub privatione, nullo modo dicitur natura prior: & ideo non habet eam prioritatem naturae, quae ad eductionem Forma necessaria existit. Mirabiles profecto artifices,
units.tr: LIII. Moreover, the common opinion of the Peripatetics is (as one may see in Fonseca, the Conimbricenses and Suarez) that the Forms of the heavenly bodies were created. But whatever dependence on Matter they imagine in the being and becoming of other Forms, they must necessarily admit the same here too. From this it would follow that these Forms too were not created but educed from Matter, since creation does not fit things that come to be dependently on Matter. To meet this difficulty, they take refuge in saying that for the eduction of Forms it is not enough that they come to be dependently on the subject, but that the subject must also pre-exist. Indeed some require that the subject pre-exist in time for every eduction of Forms. Among these are the Conimbricenses, as they clearly indicate in the words quoted above, where they make one of the conditions necessary for eduction that the privation of the Form, together with its dispositions, be present in the subject. They repeat this in On the Physics 9, question 12, article 5: It is not rightly and properly held that a form is educed from the power of Matter unless that form, whose privation together with its dispositions was present in the Matter. And so they deny that not only the Forms of the heavens but also those of the other composites, which were produced by God in the first construction of things, were educed from the power of Matter; because, of course, the privation of such Forms was in no way present in the Matter at that time, since both the Forms themselves and their Matter and the composites were produced by God in the same instant. Piccolomini too thought this way, as appears from the distinction he draws between creation and generation, cited above. But others, on the contrary, affirm that for the eduction of Forms it is by no means necessary that the subject precede in time the Form to be educed from it, but that it is enough that it pre-exist in nature. Thus Suarez, having said: When it is said that a Form is educed from the power of Matter, because it was contained in its power, it is supposed that the Matter existed earlier, in potency to the Form, before it had it in act; then soon he entered upon a long disputation to prove that for true eduction it is not necessary that the Matter precede in time under privation, but that it is enough that it precede in the order of nature; and accordingly he concludes that the Forms of the Elements too (which those who require temporal priority in the subject contend were created, no less than those of the heavens), which God made at the beginning of the world, were not created but educed from the power of Matter, because although that Matter did not precede in time as existing in potency to such Forms, it did precede them in the priority of nature. And in this way indeed this argument is wholly weakened.
