For those who say that temporal pre-existence is necessary for eduction should then press this on others, once they have persuaded all of their own sect of it. But if priority of nature suffices for a Form to be said to be educed from the subject, there is no reason why they should not also say that the Forms of the heavens were educed from the power of Matter, although all of them assert that these were in truth created. For what those who deny that the subject must precede in time reply here, namely that the Matter of the heaven is not, like the Matter of other things, prior in nature to its Form, is plainly a way of keeping to the old pattern of permitting themselves to say whatever they please, without caring whether they flatly contradict their own decisions. Indeed it is most widely accepted among the Peripatetics that every subject is prior in nature to that of which it is the subject. Hence here one may see a remarkable fight (as often elsewhere): the very same men who deny that the Matter of the heaven is prior in the order of nature to its Forms, in that very place where they say this, concede to it priority of nature. Thus Suarez: The Matter of the heaven, although according to its proper mode of causing it is said to be prior in nature, yet as existing in potency and in some way under privation, is in no way said to be prior in nature; and therefore it does not have that priority of nature which is required for the eduction of a Form. Truly marvellous craftsmen,

units.la: Disp.15.3.5. fices, quibus nihil arduum est, aut difficile, quiq; nullo metu in quasvis sese induant contradictiones; quippe quibus semper ad manum est bella ac cata aliqua distinctiuncula, cujus praesidio è quibusvis laqueis sese expediant. Sed ut haec valeant inter eos, quibus propositum est quidvis pati potius, quam à receptis semel positionibus recedere; ita apud illos, qui veritati simpliciter ac libere studient, ultro suam ipsorum futilitatem manifestant; ut supervacuum sit, ijs convincendis tempus terere. & immensi foret laboris, omnia sophismata prolixe velle persequi. Contenti igitur hac Suarezij confessione, qua Materiam coeli facit natura priorem Forma suâ, atq; ipsi relinquentes eam distinctionem, quod non sit ita prior natura, quomodo aliarum rerum Materiae, dicimus, quum tam coelorum, quam Elementorum in ipso mundi primordio factorum, par in hoc sit ratio, quod Materia ipsorum, quanquam Formis suis natura prior, tempore tamen non praecessit; vanam esse hanc quoq; exceptionem, quae non temporis prioritatem, sed prioritatem naturae exigit ad Formarum eductionem; quia inde sequeretur, non Elementorum tantum, sed & coelorum Formas fuisse non creatas, sed de Materiae potentia eductas; contra quam vult ipse Suarez. Atq; ex hisce satis apparet, quàm inania sint ea, quorum argumento Peripatetici audent Formas, quas è nihilo factas fatentur, rursus eximere ex earum rerum numero, quae creatae sint seu è nihilo factae: quippe quibus admissis sequeretur alias quoq; res diversas, quanquam è nihilo factas, creatas non fuisse; quas tamen ipsi creatas fuisse, constanter asseverant.
units.tr: Disp.15.3.5. ficers indeed, for whom nothing is arduous or difficult, and who fear no contradiction in putting themselves into any sort of argument whatever. For they always have at hand some neat and clever little distinction, by whose protection they extricate themselves from any snare. But although these tricks may serve among those who have resolved to suffer anything rather than depart from positions once accepted, among those who study the truth simply and freely they reveal their own futility of their own accord, so that it would be a waste of time to spend effort in refuting them, and it would be of immense labour to try to pursue every sophism at length. Therefore, content with this admission of Suarez, by which he makes the Matter of the heaven prior in nature to its Form, and leaving aside the distinction that it is not prior in nature in the way we say the Matter of other things is, since the reasoning for the heavenly and the elemental Matter alike, made at the very beginning of the world, is the same in this respect, namely that their Matter, although prior to its Forms in nature, did not precede them in time, I hold this further exception to be vain as well, which demands for the eduction of Forms not temporal priority but priority of nature. For it would follow from it that not only the Forms of the Elements but also those of the heavens were not created but educed from the power of Matter, against what Suarez himself wants. And from these things it sufficiently appears how empty are those arguments by which the Peripatetics dare to remove again from the number of things created, or made out of nothing, those Forms which they confess were made out of nothing. For if these were admitted it would follow that other diverse things, although made out of nothing, were not created; yet they constantly assert that these were created.
LIV.

units.la: LIV. Quodsi autem hisce omissis, non cum aliis ipsorum placitis comparemus, sed ad ipsam rei veritatem examinemus hoc dogma, quo Formae simul & è nihilo fieri, & non fieri è nihilo asseruntur; longe adhuc magis elucescet summa atq; immanis ipsius absurditas. Etenim omne ipsius firmamentum situm est in ea propositione à Suarezio propositâ, Fieri ex nihilo, duo dicit: unum est, fieri ipsum absolute
units.tr: LIV. But if we set these aside, and do not compare this dogma with their other opinions but examine it against the truth of the matter itself, the dogma by which Forms are asserted both to be made from nothing and not to be made from nothing, its sheer monstrous absurdity will appear even more clearly. For its whole support rests on the proposition put forward by Suárez: to be made from nothing says two things. One is that the thing is made absolutely.

units.la: LIV. Quodsi autem hisce omissis ... (marginal note: "Nov. ad Dominum ad ad rem agamus et consideremus") absolute & simpliciter; aliud est, quod talis effectio est ex nihilo: quæ propositio est salsissima, sumendo, fieri absolute & simpliciter, in eo sensu, quo Suarez aliique Peripatetici sumunt, pro, fieri aliquid seorsim per se, atque ut per se subsistat. ipso enim fieri ex nihilo haud aliud dicitur, nisi ejus rei, quæ fit, nullam partem præcessisse; si nimirum hoc quoq; secundum quid, & secundum eam portionem, qua ex nihilo facta est, intelligatur. Namq; si aliquis, loquendo de rebus, quæ secundum quid ex nihilo factæ sint, velit sustinere, dari res, quæ factæ sint ex nihilo, ac de quibus tamen non sit verum nullam earum partem præcessisse; is aut stupiditatem suam manifesto prodat, aut perversitatem, quippe sepositâ omni ambiguitate, & æqualiter utrobiq; loquendo, si verum est, hujusmodi rerum aliquam partem præcessisse, verum quoq; est, eas non ex nihilo factas: & si verum est, eas ex nihilo factas, verum quoq; est, earum nullam partem præcessisse. Etenim si de ijs secundum se totas sumtis loquamur; dici non potest, nullam earum partem præcessisse; sed neq; dici tum potest, eas è nihilo factas. sin vero de ijs loquamur secundum quid, & respiciendo ad portionem è nihilo factam; non magis verum de ijs est hoc respectu, quod è nihilo factæ sint, quàm quod nulla ipsarum pars præcesserit. Quare semper verum est, quod dicimus, fieri ex nihilo, unum hoc duntaxat dicere, nimirum quod rei ex nihilo factæ nulla pars præextiterit. & si res ex nihilo factæ per se subsistant, hoc tamen ad naturam seu essentiam ipsius fieri ex nihilo haudquaquam pertinet; quæ sibi nihilo secius constabit, etiamsi res ex nihilo facta non per se, sed in altero aut cum altero subsistat, atque alterius rei pars sit. Et quod nos hic dicimus, idem nobiscum universus mundus dicet, ijs tantum sepositis, qui præconceptis opinionibus mancipati, earum amore seipsos sponte ita excæcaverunt, ut videre non possint res cuivis etiam idiotæ clarissimas, qualis hæc est. nihil enim facilius intellectu est, quam quid sit, ex nihilo fieri; resq; per se adeo aperta est, ut nulla declaratione indigeat; ac nemo, qui communibus duntaxat notionibus sit præditus, dubitaturus sit, quin, fieri
units.tr: LIV. But if we set these aside ... (marginal note: "Let us come to the matter itself and consider it") absolutely and simply. The other is that such a making is from nothing. This proposition is very silly, if to be made absolutely and simply is taken in the sense in which Suárez and the other Peripatetics take it, namely, that something is made separately by itself and so as to subsist through itself. For to be made from nothing means only that no part of the thing made existed before it; and this holds, of course, if it is understood in a qualified way, with respect to that portion of it which was made from nothing. For if anyone, speaking of things that are made from nothing in a qualified sense, wishes to maintain that there are things made from nothing of which it is nonetheless not true that no part of them existed beforehand, he either betrays his stupidity or his perversity. For, setting aside all ambiguity and speaking equally in both cases: if it is true that some part of such a thing existed before, it is also true that the thing was not made from nothing; and if it is true that the thing was made from nothing, it is also true that no part of it existed before. Indeed, if we speak of such things taken wholly in themselves, it cannot be said that no part of them existed before, but neither can it then be said that they were made from nothing. But if we speak of them in a qualified way, with respect to the portion made from nothing, it is no more true of them in that respect that they were made from nothing than that no part of them preceded. Therefore what we say, to be made from nothing, is always true, and says only this: that no part of the thing made from nothing existed before it. And if things made from nothing subsist through themselves, this nonetheless has nothing to do with the nature or essence of being made from nothing; for that nature will remain the same even if a thing made from nothing subsists not through itself but in another or with another, and is a part of some other thing. And what we say here, the whole world will say with us, setting aside only those who, bound to preconceived opinions, have of their own accord so blinded themselves through love of them that they cannot see things that are most clear even to any layman, such as this one. For nothing is easier to understand than what it is to be made from nothing, and the thing is so plain in itself that it needs no explanation; and no one endowed with common notions alone will doubt that, to be made...
Chapter I.

units.la: fieri ex nihilo, sit, ita fieri, ut nihil rei prius fuerit; neq; amplius quicquam, vi istorum verborum, fieri ex nihilo, inferatur. Sane ut verè aliquid ex nihilo factum sit; non magis ad rem facit, per se subsistat, an secus; quàm idem hoc ad rem facit, ut vere ex alio factum sit. Itaque eodem jure, quo ipsi dicunt, quod fieri ex nihilo duo significet, & fieri ex non præexistenti, & fieri ita ut per se subsistat; dicere aliquis poterit, quod fieri ex aliquo duo significet, & fieri ex præexistenti, & fieri ita ut per se subsistat; unde sequeretur, ut quecunq; non per se subsistunt, neganda essent ex altero facta, etiamsi revera ex altero facta essent; quomodo ipsi negant ea, quæ non per se subsistunt, ex nihilo facta, etiamsi re vera ex nihilo facta sint, ac totam suam entitatem (ut ipsi loquuntur) de novo acceperint. Quod si in generatione hoc pro stolidissimo ipsi repudiaturi sunt; oportet tantundem quoq; faciant in creatione, atq; agnoscant, quod sicuti ad essentiam ipsius fieri ex aliquo non pertinet, per se an non per se subsistat res ex aliquo facta; ita neq; ad creationis ex nihilo essentiam pertineat, an res ex nihilo creata per se subsistat, vel secus. Verum quidem est, substantias omnes ex nihilo factas per se subsistere; sed hoc verum est, non quia ipsum fieri ex nihilo requirit, ut res ita facta per se subsistat, sed quia Deo non placuit res alias, quam quæ per se subsisterent, ex nihilo creare. itaq; nos, quibus hoc persuasum est, poteramus probabilius asserere, esse de ratione ipsius fieri è nihilo, ut res è nihilo facta per se subsistat, ac proinde negare, quod Formæ è nihilo fiant, quippe quæ per se non subsistant. ast eos ipsos, qui & alias res haud quaquam per se subsistentes, & Formas dicunt ex nihilo fieri; introducere hoc axioma, [quod pertineat ad essentiam ipsius fieri ex nihilo, ut res, quæ ex nihilo fit, per se subsistat;] plane est monstri simile, atque vesaniæ proximum; quum omisso responso, quod ab ipsa rei natura per se considerata suppeditatur, sufficiat illi objicere tot res ipsorum consessione ex nihilo factas, quæ tamen per se non subsistant.
units.tr: Being made from nothing means that the thing was made so that nothing of it existed before. Nor does the force of these words, made from nothing, imply anything further. Indeed, for something to be truly made from nothing, it makes no more difference whether it subsists by itself than it makes a difference, for it to be truly made from another. So by the same right that they claim being made from nothing has two meanings, namely being made from what does not pre-exist and being made so as to subsist by itself, someone could claim that being made from something has two meanings, namely being made from what pre-exists and being made so as to subsist by itself. It would follow that things which do not subsist by themselves must be denied to have been made from another, even if they really were made from another, just as they deny that things which do not subsist by themselves were made from nothing, even though they really were made from nothing and have received their whole entity (as they put it) anew. But if they will reject this as utterly foolish in the case of generation, they must do the same in the case of creation, and acknowledge that just as whether a thing made from something subsists by itself or not does not belong to the essence of being made from something, so neither does it belong to the essence of creation from nothing whether a thing created from nothing subsists by itself or not. It is true that all substances made from nothing subsist by themselves; but this is true not because being made from nothing requires that the thing so made subsist by itself, but because it did not please God to create from nothing any things other than those that would subsist by themselves. Therefore we, who are persuaded of this, could more probably assert that it belongs to the nature of being made from nothing that a thing made from nothing should subsist by itself, and so deny that Forms are made from nothing, since they do not subsist by themselves. But to introduce this axiom, [that it belongs to the essence of being made from nothing that the thing made from nothing subsist by itself], in the case of those who say that other things not at all subsisting by themselves, and Forms, are made from nothing, is plainly monstrous and close to madness. Setting aside the answer that is supplied by the very nature of the thing considered in itself, it would suffice to object to them that so many things, which by their own admission were made from nothing, nevertheless do not subsist by themselves.
LV. Although

units.la: LV. Acsi autem parum esset hæc vel amentia vel impudentia, qua duas propositiones tam directo contradictorias, [Quod Formæ fiant è nihilo; & quod non è nihilo fiant;] asserere non erubescunt: ulterius adhuc progrediuntur, aliamq; viam præcedenti mirabiliorem, seu potius monstruosiorem, insistunt, ut se expediant ex hac difficultate, quomodo substantiæ creatæ non exerceant vim creandi, si Formas substantiales procreant, & Formæ ex nihilo fiunt. Etenim pro secunda hujus nodi solutione afferunt, tantum abesse ut Formæ è nihilo fiant, ut ne fiant quidem omnino, aut saltem non proprie ac primario fiant. Et quia incredibilia videmur narrare, rursus, ut paulo ante fecimus, ipsorum verba apponemus, ubi hoc distincte declarant. Vicomercatus scribit, Formam non esse Principium rerum naturalium eodem modo ac Materiam, quum non sit aeterna, ut illa, sed tum esse incipiat aut desinat, cum res oriuntur aut occidunt. nullo enim temporis spatio eam ante rerum generationem existere, sed eodem temporis momento & Formam, & rem cujus Forma est, incipere existere, genitamq; dici. cum enim tot sint Formæ, quot res generabiles, & neq; absq; Materia esse queant, nec simul multæ in una Materiæ portione, necesse esse ut non sint aeternæ, sed incipiant esse, atq; oriantur. Nec tamen proprie aut gigni aut interire, propterea quod simplices sint, & Aristoteles multis in locis tradiderit, nihil nisi Compositum ex ea & Materia gigni. Incipere autem esse, cum antea non essent, & desinere, cum fuerint, tametsi nec oriantur nec intereant, nisi ortus & interitus vocabulis communiori significatione usurpatis. Perspicuum tamen esse, Formas naturales, cum antea non fuissent, esse incipere, &c. Toletus, Constare, quod Compositum Materiâ conficiatur & Formâ, & Materia sit ingenerabilis, Formæ verò de novo producantur. nihil enim earum præcedere in Materia, ante ipsarum introductionem. negandum tamen prorsus esse cum Aristotele, fieri Formas aut produci. id enim, quod primo & per se generatur & corrumpitur, esse Compositum ipsum, ita ut actio non terminetur primo, nisi in Compositum; fieri enim Leonem, aut ignem, non Formam, aut Materiam; quæ conclusio sit maxime xime tenenda, quum ex ea pendeant multa graves physicae determinationes. Itaq; Formam non produci ex se, sed comproduci ad productionem Compositi; quod idem sit, ac si dicas, actionem in ipsum Compositum terminari primo, & consequenter ac velint per accidens in ipsam Formam. ex quo pateat, quid sit, Formas educi de potentia Materia: non enim esse aliud, quàm eadem actione consequenter fieri & habere esse, qua fit Compositum. Cum igitur Composita fiant, non ex nihilo, sed ex Materia, Forma verò consequenter fiant & comproducantur, non creari Formas; quia creatio est actio, qua aliquid primo fit, Formæ verò non primo fiunt. hanc autem esse vim concessam agentibus naturalibus, ut Compositum producerent, ac simul immediate Formas comproducerent, quod non est creare. Suarez, Formam proprie ac per se fieri, falsum est, & repugnat revera Aristoteli; secundum quem proprie Forma dicitur congenerari. Ratio est, quia ejus est per se primo fieri, cujus est esse, cum fieri tendat ad esse: sed id proprie est, quod subsistit; ergo id proprie fit. sed hæ Formæ non subsistunt, sed Composita ex ipsis: ergo ad Composita proprie & principaliter terminatur actio. Confirmatur. n m actio est una, ut supponimus: ergo & terminus adaquatus unus. sed hic non potest esse Forma. quia Compositum re vera fit, & non est Forma. Majoris autem claritatis gratia distingui solet duplex terminus, scilicet ut quod & ut quo, seu qui absolute fit, vel quo aliud fit. Compositum ergo est terminus Qui seu Ut quod, quia illud per se primo fit: nam illud maxime intenditur per Generationem, & in illud ultimate terminatur generatio. Terminus autem Quo est Forma, quia fit ut per eam Compositum constituatur. Profecto intellectu facile est, quomodo his admissis vitetur illa difficultas, ne Causæ Generantes creare seu substantiam facere è nihilo dicendæ sint. Sed quomodo hæc duo stare simul possint, ut & Formæ fiant improprie, sive ne fiant quidem omnino, sicuti nonnulli ipsorum hic dicunt; & tamen fiant è nihilo, quod ipsi prius diserte fassi sunt; hoc verò omnem captum superat. & nisi ab hominibus, qui sibi ipsis sponte oculos eruunt, aut saltem occludunt, ne lucem rationis ac veritatis videant, tam vecors assertio proficisci nequaquam posset. Sane passim ita se gerunt, ut nihil ipsorum referre videatur, quàm falsum aliquid sit, quàm insipidum, quàm insulsum, dummodo Aristotelem ejus habeant autorem; utpote cujus omnia effata qualiacunq; pro oraculis venerari, ipsorum animo sedit. itaq; hoc quoq; ejus dictum, Sola Composita generari seu fieri; sine ulteriori disquisitione pro verissimo susceperunt; quum tamen aut ipsum necessario falsum esse debeat, aut falsa ipsius de Formis doctrina, quas in omni substantiæ generatione de novo vult fieri, atq; entitatem suam, quam prius non habebant, tunc demum accipere, quando ipsum Compositum generatur. Nullæ enim machinæ essecerint, ut utrumq; hoc simul esse verum queat.
units.tr: LV. But if this madness or shamelessness were not enough, by which they do not blush to assert two propositions so directly contradictory, [that Forms are made from nothing; and that they are not made from nothing], they go further still and take a path more wonderful than the previous one, or rather more monstrous, in order to extricate themselves from this difficulty: how created substances do not exercise the power of creating, if they produce substantial Forms, and Forms are made from nothing. For as the second solution of this knot, they affirm that Forms are so far from being made from nothing that they are not made at all, or at least not properly and primarily made. And because we seem to be relating incredible things, we will again, as we did a little earlier, set out their words where they state this clearly. Vicomercatus writes: The Form is not a principle of natural things in the same way as Matter, since it is not eternal as Matter is, but begins to be or ceases to be when things arise or perish. For it does not exist before the generation of the thing in any span of time, but at the same moment of time both the Form and the thing of which it is the Form begin to exist and are said to be generated. For since there are as many Forms as there are generable things, and they can be neither without Matter nor many together in one portion of Matter, it is necessary that they are not eternal but begin to be and arise. Yet they are not properly generated or destroyed, because they are simple, and Aristotle has taught in many places that only the Composite of it and Matter is generated. But to begin to be, when previously they were not, and to cease, when they have been, though they neither arise nor perish, unless the words arising and perishing are used in a more general sense. It is nevertheless evident that natural Forms, when previously they were not, begin to be, etc. Toletus: It is agreed that the Composite is made up of Matter and Form, and that Matter is ungenerable, but Forms are produced anew, for none of them preceded in Matter before their introduction. Yet it must altogether be denied, with Aristotle, that Forms are made or produced. For that which is primarily and per se generated and corrupted is the Composite itself, so that the action terminates primarily only in the Composite; for a lion or fire is made, not a Form or Matter. This conclusion is to be held most firmly, since many grave physical determinations depend on it. Therefore the Form is not produced of itself, but is co-produced with the production of the Composite; which is the same as saying that the action terminates primarily in the Composite itself, and consequently, as they wish, incidentally in the Form itself. From this it is clear what it is for Forms to be educed from the potency of Matter: for it is nothing other than that the Form consequently comes to be and has being by the same action by which the Composite is made. Since therefore Composites are made not from nothing but from Matter, while Forms are consequently made and co-produced, Forms are not created; for creation is an action by which something is made primarily, whereas Forms are not made primarily. Moreover, this is the power granted to natural agents: to produce the Composite and at the same time immediately co-produce the Forms, which is not to create. Suarez: That the Form is properly and per se made is false, and really contrary to Aristotle, according to whom the Form is properly said to be co-generated. The reason is that it belongs to that which is primarily made per se to be that which has being, since making tends toward being; but that which properly subsists is that which is; therefore that is properly made. But these Forms do not subsist; the Composites made of them do. Therefore the action terminates primarily and principally in the Composites. It is confirmed: since the action is one, as we suppose, its adequate term is also one; but this cannot be the Form, because the Composite is what really is made, and is not the Form. For the sake of greater clarity, a twofold term is usually distinguished, namely that which is made as what (the term Qui or ut quod), and that by which something is made (the term Quo). The Composite therefore is the term Qui, or ut quod, because that is primarily made per se; for that is chiefly aimed at through generation, and generation ultimately terminates in it. The term Quo is the Form, because it is made so that the Composite is constituted through it. Indeed it is easy to see how, once these things are admitted, that difficulty is avoided, namely that generating causes must not be said to create, or to make substance from nothing. But how these two can stand together, that Forms are made improperly, or not made at all, as some of them here say, and yet are made from nothing, which they previously expressly confessed, this surpasses all understanding. Unless it came from men who willingly tear out their own eyes, or at least shut them, lest they see the light of reason and truth, so frantic an assertion could in no way have arisen. Indeed, everywhere they conduct themselves as if it mattered nothing to them how false, how insipid, how silly a thing is, provided they have Aristotle as its author; for it has settled in their minds to revere as oracles all his sayings, whatever they are. Thus they have accepted without further inquiry this saying of his, Only Composites are generated or made, as most true; whereas either this must necessarily be false, or his doctrine of Forms is false, which in every generation of substance he holds must be made anew, and must then at last receive the entity it did not previously have, when the Composite itself is generated. For no machinery could bring it about that both of these should be true at once.
LVI.

units.la: Sed quia tanti faciunt hoc magistri sui dogma Peripatetici, ut ejus solius objectu putent sufficienter excusari monstruosissimas suas contradictiones, faciantq; vim sibi ipsis & aliis, ut credunt id, quod nemo nisi mente captus credere potest, Aliquid factum esse, cujus antea nihil erat, neq; tamen ex nihilo esse factum, imo ne factum quidem esse omnino; juvat paulo exactius illiud examinare, ut sic extrema ejus futilitas omnibus fiat tanto manifestior. Meminerit autem lector ejus, quod supra diximus, Aristotelem passim, dum Formam suam substantialem declarare nititur per exempla à Formis accidentalibus petita, eo prolabi imprudentem, ut quæcunq; istis competunt, illis etiam attribuat, ac si par esset utrarumq; conditio; indeq; ortum esse inter alia hoc axioma, Quod nec Forma nec Materia fiat aut intereat, sed Compositum tantum, quia neq; accidentales Formæ fiant aut intereant, sed Compositum ex ijs & Materia. ostendimus autem in ipsius exemplis, dupliciter ipsum errare: tum sumendo falsas hypotheses; tum eas, etiamsi verae essent, Formæ substantiali accommodando, cum nequaquam sit eadem substantiarum atq; accidentium ratio. nunc quædam ijs, quæ illic dicta sunt, addantur, ac paulo uberius Aristotelis exempla consideremus: septimo igitur Metaphysicorum, capite octavo,
units.tr: But since the Peripatetics hold this dogma of their master in such high regard that they think it alone is enough to excuse their monstrous contradictions, and since they do violence to themselves and to others by believing what no one but a madman could believe, that something has been made of which previously there was nothing, and yet it was not made out of nothing, indeed was not made at all, it is worth examining this a little more exactly, so that its extreme futility may become plainer to everyone. The reader should recall what we said above: that Aristotle, while trying to explain his substantial form through examples taken from accidental forms, carelessly slips into attributing to the former whatever belongs to the latter, as if the two were in the same condition. From this arose, among other things, the axiom that neither form nor matter is made or destroyed, but only the composite, because accidental forms are neither made nor destroyed, but the composite of them and matter. We showed from his own examples that he errs in two ways: first by taking false hypotheses, and second, even if they were true, by applying them to substantial form, since substances and accidents are by no means the same in nature. Now let some additions be made to what was said there, and let us consider Aristotle's examples a little more fully. In the eighth chapter of the seventh book of the Metaphysics, then, he proceeds thus to prove the thesis that form is not made.
Cap. I.

units.la: ad probandam hanc thesin, Formam non fieri, ita procedit: Qui facit globum aneum, sicuti non facit æs, ita neq; globum facit, nisi per accidens, quatenus nimirum formát æs in globi figuram. nam si globum absolute faceret, oporteret ut faceret ex alio (quia nimirum ex nihilo fieri nihil possit) & sic in infinitum abirent generationes. Ἐσσεὶ δὲ ὑπό ἄνος τε γίνεται τὸ γινόμενον, καὶ ἐκ ἄνος, ἡσὶ ὁ γίνεται· τοῦτο δ᾽ ἐστιν ἡ ἡ σφαῖρα, ἢ ὁ κύκλος, ἢ ὅτι ἔτυχε τῶν ἄλλων, ὥστε οὐδὲ τὸ ὑποκείμενον ποιεῖ τὸν χαλκὸν, οὕτως οὐδὲ τὴν σφαῖραν, εἰ μὴ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς, ὅτι ἡ χαλκῆ σφαῖρα, σφαῖρά ἐστιν, ἐκείνην δὲ ὃ ποιεῖ· τὸ γὰρ τοῦδε ποιεῖν, ἐν τῷ ὅλῳ ὑποκειμένῳ τοῦδε ποιεῖν ἐστὶ. λέγω δὲ ὅλ τὸν χαλκὸν σφαιροῦν ποιεῖν ἐστὶν, ὃ τὸ σφαιροῦν ἢ τὴν σφαῖραν ποιεῖν, ἀλλὰ ἕτερόν τι, οἷον τὸ εἶδος ζῷον ἐν ἄλλῳ. εἰ γὰρ ποιεῖ, ἐκ ἴνος ἂν ποιοῖ ἄλλο· τοῦτο γὰρ ὑπάρχει, οἷον ποιεῖν χαλκῆν σφαῖραν, τοῦτο δὲ οὕτως, οὐκ ἐκ τουδὶ, ὃ, ὅτι χαλκὸς, ζῶλι ποιεῖ, ὃ ἐστι σφαῖρα· εἰ οὖν ἡσὶ τοδὲ ποιεῖ αὐτὸ, δῆλον ὅτι ὀσαύτως ποιήσει, καὶ βαδιεῖ ταυ ἀι γενέσεις εἰς ἄπειρον.
units.tr: He who makes a bronze globe does not make the bronze, and so does not make the globe except accidentally, insofar as he shapes the bronze into the form of a globe. For if he made the globe absolutely, he would have to make it out of something else (since nothing can be made out of nothing), and the generations would go on to infinity. [Ἐσσεὶ δὲ ὑπό ἄνος τε γίνεται τὸ γινόμενον, καὶ ἐκ ἄνος, ἡσὶ ὁ γίνεται· τοῦτο δ᾽ ἐστιν ἡ ἡ σφαῖρα, ἢ ὁ κύκλος, ἢ ὅτι ἔτυχε τῶν ἄλλων, ὥστε οὐδὲ τὸ ὑποκείμενον ποιεῖ τὸν χαλκὸν, οὕτως οὐδὲ τὴν σφαῖραν, εἰ μὴ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς, ὅτι ἡ χαλκῆ σφαῖρα, σφαῖρά ἐστιν, ἐκείνην δὲ ὃ ποιεῖ· τὸ γὰρ τοῦδε ποιεῖν, ἐν τῷ ὅλῳ ὑποκειμένῳ τοῦδε ποιεῖν ἐστὶ.]

units.la: Quoniam autem id, quod fit, fit ab aliquo, & ex aliquo, & fit aliquid, verbi causâ globus, aut circulus, aut quippiam aliud: sicuti [efficiens] non facit subjectum, nempe æs, ita neque globum, nisi per accidens, quia globus eius, globum est. ipsam autem non facit. facere enim hoc aliquid, est ex toto subjecto hoc aliquid facere. Dico autem, quod æs rotundum facere, est; non rotunditatem, aut globum facere, sed aliud quid, nimirum Formam hanc in alio. si enim faceret [rotunditatem] ex aliquo alio faceret; hoc enim supponebatur, veluti facere aneum globum. hoc autem sic, quia ex hoc, quod est æs, facit hoc, quod est globus. si igitur & hoc ipsum facit, apparet quod similiter faciet, & generationes vadent in infinitum. Tenendum est in his Aristotelis verbis, quando Globum & Circulum fieri negat, non intelligere eum substantias illas, quæ vulgo sic nominantur, sed globositatem & circularitatem. hæc enim & fieri negat, & interire. itaq; eum, qui facit globum æneum, non facere globositatem, neq; globositatem in æs introducere, sed absolute facere æs globosum, aut globum æneum. Globositatem autem fieri negat propterea (ut paulo ante quoque attingebamus) quia quidcunq; fit, requirat Materiam è qua fiat, cum ex nihilo non possit quicquam fieri. Ἐν ἀκαιρίᾳ (inquit in conclusione hujus tractationis) ὃ γίγνομένου ὕλη ἔνεσι, in omni eo, quod fit, materia inest. & in capite praecedenti, Ἀδύνατον γενέσθαι, εἰ μηδὲν προϋπάρχοι. Impossibile est, aliquid fieri, si nihil praexistat. Iam si globositas fiat, quando fit globus æneus; quum non fiat ex ære (æs enim non esse Materiam globositatis, sed subjectum) requiri aliud quid, ex quo illa fiat. Τὸ δὲ σφαῖρα εἶναι ὅλως εἰ ἔστι γένεσις, ἐν ᾧ ὑπὸ ἐστι. Globositatis autem omnino si est generatio, ex aliquo erit aliquid, [hoc est, è subjecto fiet.] Iam quum hoc pacto semper debeat id, quod fit, esse Compositum è Materia & Forma, Δεῖ ὅσα ὁ γιγνόμενον ... aportebit enim semper id, quod fit, esse divisibile, & esse partim hoc, partim verò illud, hoc est, partim Materiam, partim verò Formam: infert, generationes sic abituras in infinitum. Quippe in globositate, si illa fiat, futuram Materiam & Formam. si autem fiat id, quod Formæ rationem obtinet in globositate, recursuram eandem difficultatem, quæ in globo æneo occurrebat. statuendam enim fore Materiam è qua illa Forma fiat. Illic autem iterum, eodem modo rem se habituram; & sic hanc difficultatem, semper ascendendo, in infinitum processuram. Summa totius disputationis (quæ etiam 12. Metaph. 3. breviter attingitur) huc redit. Quidcunq; fit, fieri ex aliqua Materia. itaq; non fieri accidentia, cum illa in Materia quidem fiant, è Materia vero nequaquam; sicut apertum sit, quando globus vel circulus fit ex ære. Etenim æs quidem fieri globosum vel circulare, ipsam autem globositatem aut circularitatem nequaquam fieri. Est igitur sententia Aristotelis, Accidentia non fieri, (& proinde neq; interire) sed fieri rem ipsam talia accidentia habentem. Φανερὸν ἄρα (inquit) ὅτι ὅτε τὸ εἶδος, ἢ ὅτι λἱπποῖς χρὴ καλεῖν τὴν ἐν ᾧ αἰσθητῷ μορφὴν, ὃ γίνεται, ἀλλ' ἔστιν αὐτῷ γένεσις, ἀλλὰ τι τὶ ἦν εἶν τοῦτο. Manifestum ergo est, quod Forma, aut quocunq; nomine appellare libeat rei sensibilis speciem, nequaquam fit, neq; est ipsius generatio, nequis [fit] esse hoc aliquid, sive quidditas. Quae verba non de sola Forma substantiali dicta esse, sed tum de illa, tum de Forma artificiali, tum de quibuscunq; accidentibus (quae cur Formae rationem obtinere velit, nunc non quaerimus: voluisse apertim est) verbis proxime sequentibus ita significat. Τοῦτο γὰρ ἔστιν ὃ ἐν ἄλλῳ γίνεται, ἢ ἀπὸ τέχνης, ἢ ἀπὸ φύσεως, ἢ ἀπὸ δυνάμεως. hoc enim est, quod in alio fit, aut ab arte, aut à natura, aut à facultate. Itaq; de omnibus illis tribus accipienda sunt etiam verba haec, praecedentibus patvo intervallo subjuncta: Φανερὸν δὲ ἐν τῶν εἰρημένων, ὅτι τὸ μὲν ὡς εἶδος ἢ ὡς οὐσία λεγόμενον, ὃ γίνεται· ἢ δὲ σύνολος, ἢ καθὸ ταύτην λεγομένη, γίνεται. Manifestum est ex dictis, id quod venit appellatione Formae aut essentiae, non fieri. sed concursus, qui hinc denominatur, fit. haec, inquimus, ille de Forma, tum substantiali, tum accidentali, vi illorum exemplorum globi aenei, vel circuli aenei, decernit.
units.tr: Since, however, that which is made is made by something and out of something, and becomes something, for example a globe, or a circle, or something else, just as the agent does not make the subject, namely the bronze, so neither does it make the globe, except accidentally, because the globe is of bronze; it does not make the globe itself. For to make this particular thing is to make it from a whole subject that is this particular thing. I say that to make the bronze round is not to make roundness, or to make a globe, but to make something else, namely this form in another thing. For if it did make it, it would make it out of something else; for this is presupposed, as when one makes a bronze globe. And this is so because from that which is bronze it makes that which is a globe. If, then, it makes this itself too, it is clear that it will make it in the same way, and the generations will go on to infinity. It must be borne in mind in these words of Aristotle that when he denies that a globe or circle is made, he does not mean those substances which are commonly so named, but globularity and circularity. For these he denies both to be made and to perish. So he means that the one who makes a bronze globe does not make globularity, nor introduce globularity into the bronze, but absolutely makes the bronze globular, or a bronze globe. Globularity, however, he denies to be made for the reason (as we touched on a little earlier) that whatever is made requires a matter from which it is made, since nothing can be made out of nothing. In all that is made, matter is present, he says in the conclusion of this discussion, and in the preceding chapter: It is impossible for anything to be made if nothing pre-exists. Now if globularity is made when a bronze globe is made, since it is not made out of the bronze (for bronze is not the matter of globularity but its subject), something else is required from which it is made. If there is generation of globularity at all, then something will come to be from something, [that is, it will be made from a subject]. Since in this way that which is made must always be a composite of matter and form, for that which is made must always be divisible, and be partly this and partly that, that is, partly matter and partly form, he concludes that the generations will go on to infinity. For in globularity, if it were made, there would be matter and form; and if that which holds the role of form in globularity were made, the same difficulty would recur that met us in the bronze globe, for a matter from which that form is made would have to be posited. And there again the thing would stand in the same way, and so this difficulty, always ascending, would proceed to infinity. The sum of the whole discussion (which is also briefly touched on in Metaphysics 12.3) comes to this: whatever is made is made from some matter. Accordingly accidents are not made, since they are indeed made in matter, but not out of matter, as is plain when a globe or circle is made out of bronze. For the bronze is indeed made globular or circular, but globularity or circularity itself is by no means made. Therefore Aristotle's opinion is that accidents are not made (and consequently do not perish), but that the thing itself is made, having such accidents. It is therefore manifest, he says, that the form, or whatever one likes to call the shape of a sensible thing, is not made, nor is it its generation, but the thing that is this particular thing, or its quiddity, is. That these words are said not of substantial form alone, but of both that form and artificial form, and of whatever accidents (why he wishes these to hold the role of form we are not now asking; that he wished it is clear), he indicates in the words that immediately follow: for this is what comes to be in another, either from art, or from nature, or from a faculty. Therefore these words, joined a little after the preceding ones, must be understood of all three: It is manifest from what has been said that what is called form or essence does not come to be, but the composite, which is named from it, comes to be. By these words, I say, he decides about that form, both substantial and accidental, by the force of those examples of the bronze globe or bronze circle.

units.la: LVII. Primo autem in hac tractatione observandum est, falsam esse illam hypothesin, qua sumitur, accidentia non fieri.
units.tr: LVII. First, then, in this discussion it must be noted that the hypothesis on which he relies, that accidents do not come into being, is false.

units.la: Namq; illa probatio, Si fiant, debere fieri è materia: omnino vana est, utpote ad solas substantias pertinens, quarum nulla (nisi immediate ab ipso Deo per creationem) fieri potest nisi ex Materia. aut accidentia & fiunt ex nihilo, & in nihilum abeunt rursus. falsitas autem hujus hypotheseos vel seipsam aperte prodit. Quomodo enim non fit globositas, quando fit globus aeneus? certe globositas non est nihil. aut si est aliquid (ut re vera est) necesse est facta sit, si ibi est, ubi antea non erat. Nam quod antea non extabat, si nunc existit, necesse est existendi Principium acceperit. at tale principium accipere, hoc est fieri. non igitur rectius loquatur in philosophia, qui dicat factum esse globum, quam qui factam esse globositatem. illud enim verum est ratione totius, hoc vero ratione Formæ, quæ compositi illius altera pars est. imo si non fit globositas, aliáve talis Forma, sed tantummodo compositum quid sibi volunt ista verba, ποιεῖν τ᾽ εἶδος ἐν ἄλλῳ· τ᾽ εἶδος ἔστιν ὁ ἐν ἄλλῳ γίνεται, ἢ ἀπὸ τέχνης, ἢ ἀπὸ φύσεως, ἢ δυνάμεως· εἰς τοῦτο τοῦτο τ᾽ εἶδος ποιεῖ. Formam facere in alio. Forma est quæ in alio fit, aut ab arte, aut a natura, aut a facultate. In hoc [subjectum] facit hanc Formam. & consimilia plura, in loco proxime citato ? en, diserte dicit, fieri Formam: ut propterea apertissime secum pugnet, dum eandem rem & ait & negat in eodem sermone. Itaq; ne minimam quidem verisimilitudinem habet hæc hypothesis, quæ accidentia negat fieri & interire, nisi ut simul ponatur, Accidentia non esse entia. Quod cum alibi diserte professus sit Aristoteles, non dubitamus, quin in hujus quoq; theseos disputatione eo respexerit, atque rem ita se habere suppositurit. Est quidem & hoc quoque falsum, uti alibi à nobis monstrabitur. Sed etiamsi Aristoteli hoc quoque concederetur; attamen ne sic quidem quod vult efficeret. Namq; hoc posito, facile quidem est ad intelligendum, quomodo accidentia non fiant, quando res aliqua fit, hisce vel illis accidentibus instructa: siquidem generatio non est nisi entis: accidentia autem (ut impræsentiarum quidem ipse vult; quum illa duo Axiomata, Accidentia esse entia; &, Accidentia non fieri, nequaquam possint simul consistere) non sunt Entia. Sed hoc supposito; quomodo inde sequatur, Formas quoque substantiales non fieri, in substantiarum generatione; hoc vero animo capere non possumus. De hisce enim (ex ipsius doctrina) diversissima res est; quippe quas non modo vult esse ens, sed multo magis ens, quam Materia, quæ vix entis aut substantiæ nomine digna sit: quare etiam Compositum totam suam essentiam à Forma accipiat. Omne autem ens vel æternum sit oportet, vel si aliquando non fuit, generatum sit: Hoc est enim generari, incipere esse, quod
units.tr: For that proof, If they come into being, they must come into being from matter, is utterly worthless, since it applies only to substances, none of which can come into being except from matter, unless it is made immediately by God himself through creation. Accidents both come from nothing and pass back into nothing. The falsity of this hypothesis reveals itself openly. For how is roundness not made when a bronze ball is made? Roundness is certainly not nothing. And if it is something (as in fact it is), it must have been made, since it is now where it was not before. For what did not exist before, if it now exists, must have received a principle of existence, and to receive such a principle is to be made. So he who says in philosophy that the ball has been made speaks no more correctly than he who says that the roundness has been made. The former is true with respect to the whole, the latter with respect to the form, which is the other part of that composite. Indeed, if roundness, or some such form, is not made, but only the composite, what do these words of his mean? [ποιεῖν τ᾽ εἶδος ἐν ἄλλῳ· τ᾽ εἶδός ἐστιν ὁ ἐν ἄλλῳ γίνεται, ἢ ἀπὸ τέχνης, ἢ ἀπὸ φύσεως, ἢ δυνάμεως· εἰς τοῦτο τοῦτο τ᾽ εἶδος ποιεῖ.] To make a form in another. A form is that which comes to be in another, either from art, or from nature, or from a faculty. Into this [subject] he makes this form. And many similar things in the passage just cited. Look, he plainly says that the form is made, so that he most openly contradicts himself, since in the same discourse he both affirms and denies the same thing. Accordingly, this hypothesis, which denies that accidents come into being and perish, has not even the slightest plausibility, unless it is also assumed that accidents are not beings. Although Aristotle has openly professed this elsewhere, we do not doubt that in the discussion of this thesis too he had this in view and supposed the matter to stand thus. Indeed this too is false, as we shall show elsewhere. But even if this were granted to Aristotle as well, he still would not achieve what he wants. For granting this, it is indeed easy to understand how accidents do not come into being when some thing is made furnished with these or those accidents, since generation belongs only to a being; but accidents (as he himself wishes at present, since the two axioms, that accidents are beings and that accidents do not come into being, can by no means stand together) are not beings. But given this supposition, we cannot grasp how it follows from it that substantial forms also do not come into being in the generation of substances. For about these, according to his own doctrine, the case is quite different; for he wants them to be not merely beings, but much more beings than matter, which is scarcely worthy of the name of being or substance. Hence even the composite receives its whole essence from the form. But every being must either be eternal, or, if at some time it did not exist, must have been generated. For this is what it is to be generated: to begin to be, which
Chapter I.

units.la: quod antea non erat. Si igitur hæc ab accidentibus similitudo valebit in Forma quoq; substantiali, ad probandum, quod non ipsa generetur, sed totum ᾱ συναλημμένον; concedant, ne illam quidem esse Ens, æque ac Accidentia non sunt Ens. Si vero hoc concedere noluerint, & defendant, Formam esse Ens, ac quidem nobilissimum: desinant posthac ingerere, eam non generari. nihil enim eos juvare possunt illæ similitudines, petitæ ab Accidentibus, quæ cum non sint Ens, mirum non est, si ne generentur quidem. Quod enim non est, quomodo esse inceperit? Formæ autem cum sint, necesse est habuerint essendi (ut sic dicamus) principium; & proinde generatæ sint. Nam quod antea non extabat, si nunc existit, necesse est existendi principium acceperit. ast tale principium accipere, hoc est (ut dicebamus) fieri vel generari; sicuti desinere esse, est corrumpi. Qui igitur dicit aliquid & incipere esse, & desinere, idque tamen & fieri negat, & interire; sibi ipsi manifestissime contradicit: quod facit Aristoteles ejusdem septimi Metaph. capite decimo quinto, in hæc verba: Εωσὶ δὲ ὀσία ἑτέρα, ᾱ, τε σύνολον, καὶ ὁ λόγος, λέγω δ᾽ ὅτι ἡ μὲν οὕτως ἔστιν οὐσία, σὺν τῇ ὕλῃ συναλημμένος ὁ λόγος, ἡ δὲ, ὁ λόγος ὅλως. ὅσα μὲν οὖν ἔστω λέγεται. τούτων μὲν ἔστι φθορὰ, καὶ γένεσις. τὸ δὲ λόγος ἔκ ἔστιν ἔστως, ὥστε φθείρεσθαι. ἀλλ᾽ ἡ γίνεται, ᾱ οἰκία εἶναι, ἀλλὰ τὸ τῆδε τῇ οἰκία ἀλλ᾽ ἄνευ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς εἰσὶ καὶ ἐκ εἰσί. λέγειν δ᾽ ὅτι δὲ εἶ ταῦτα γεννᾷ δὲ ποιεῖ. Quoniam autem diversimode sunt essentia ipsum Totum, & Ratio; hoc est, alinsmodi essentia est Ratio sumta cum ipsa Materia, alinsmodi ipsa per se Ratio, quæcunq; ergo illo modo dicentur, eorum est corruptio, ut & generatio. Ratio autem non ita se habet, ut corrumpatur; nam nec generatio ejus est. non enim fit esse domum, sed fit hæc domus. sed absq; generatione & corruptione sunt & non sunt [Formæ seu Rationes] ostensum enim est, quod nemo hæc generat sive facit. & rursus octavo Metaph. 5. Εωσὶ δ᾽ ἄνευ ἐνίων γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς εἰσὶ, καὶ οὐκ ἔσιν, οἷον αἱ σιγμαὶ εἴωθε αὐτῶν. εισιν, και ὅλως τὸ εἶδη και αι μορφαὶ· ὃ ΔΔ τὸ λευκὸν γίγνεται, ἀλλὰ τὸ ξύλον λευκόν. Quandoquidem nonnulla absq; generatione & corruptione sunt & non sunt, veluti puncta (si modo ipsa sunt) & universim species ac Forma, non enim albedo fit, sed lignum album. In quibus locis quum agat conjunctim de Formis substantialibus & accidentalibus, de illis hoc quidem peccat, de quo nunc agimus, quod eas neget generari & interire, quum fateatur, quod & incipiant esse, & desinant. de his vero nimis imprudenter ait, Eas esse & non esse; quum ipse Accidentia habeat pro non Entibus, omnesq; hæ similitudines, ab ijs petitæ, quod nimirum non fiant ipsa, sed τὸ συνειλημμένον, ipsum Totum sen Compositum, nitantur isto fundamento, Quod Accidentia non sint Entia. aut alioqui falsum de ijs quoque est, æque ac de Formis substantialibus, quod nec generentur, nec intereant, utrumq; enim fieri necesse est, si & ipsa sunt entia.
units.tr: that which did not exist before. If, then, this likeness drawn from accidents holds also for the substantial form, so that it is not the form itself that is generated but the whole synolon [τὸ συνειλημμένον], let them concede that the form is not a being either, just as accidents are not beings. But if they are unwilling to concede this, and maintain that the form is a being, and indeed a most noble one, let them stop insisting that it is not generated. For those similarities taken from accidents can do nothing to help them. Since accidents are not beings, it is no wonder if they are not generated either. For how can that which is not begin to be? Forms, however, since they are, must have had a beginning of being (so to speak), and therefore they must have been generated. For whatever did not exist before, if it now exists, must have received a beginning of existence. To receive such a beginning is, as we said, to be made or generated, just as to cease to be is to be corrupted. Therefore whoever says that something both begins to be and ceases to be, and yet denies that it is made and perishes, plainly contradicts himself. Aristotle does this in the fifteenth chapter of the seventh book of his Metaphysics, in these words: "Since the essence of the whole and the Ratio are different in their ways (I mean that the essence in one sense is the Ratio taken together with the Matter, and in another sense the Ratio alone), whatever is spoken of in the former way is subject to corruption and generation. The Ratio, however, does not stand in such a way that it can be corrupted, for it has no generation either. It is not made to be a house; rather, this house is made. Forms [or Rationes] are without generation and corruption, and they are and are not; for it has been shown that no one makes or produces them." Again, in the fifth chapter of the eighth book: "Some things are without generation and corruption, and are and are not, like points (if indeed they are) and species and Form universally; for whiteness does not come to be, but the white wood does." In these passages, where he treats together of substantial and accidental forms, he errs with regard to the forms of which we are now speaking, by denying that they are generated and perish, although he admits that they both begin to be and cease to be. And with regard to the others he speaks very carelessly, saying that they are and are not, since he himself regards accidents as non-beings. All these likenesses drawn from them, namely that things are not made but the synolon, that is, the whole or composite itself, rest on this foundation, that accidents are not beings. Otherwise, what is false of substantial forms is also false of them, namely that they are neither generated nor perish; for both must happen to them, if they too are beings.

units.la: LVIII. Sed alium adhuc ludum in hoc negotio dat mi- rabiliorem Aristoteles.
units.tr: LVIII. But Aristotle plays yet another, still more remarkable, game in this business.

units.la: Ac si enim capite octavo hujus septimi Metaph. istam thesin, Formam non fieri nec interire, sed Compositum; de ipsa substantiali Forma primario probasset, non in accidentalibus Formis probatam, (seu potius tentatam) ad substantialem transtulisset; ita loquitur capite nono, Non de substantia tantum hoc verum esse, quod Forma non fiat; sed & in omnibus Accidentibus eodem modo se rem habere. ita enim inquit: Οὐ μόνον δὲ περὶ οὐσίας δηλοῖ ὁ λόγος, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ μὴ γίνεσθαι τὸ εἶδος, ἀλλὰ περὶ πάντων ὁμοίως τῶν πρώτων κοινὸς ὁ λόγος, οἷον ποσοῦ, ποιοῦ, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων κατηγοριῶν. γίνεται γὰρ ὥσπερ ἡ χαλκῆ σφαῖρα, ἀλλ᾽ ἡ σφαῖρα, ὅδε χαλκός, καὶ ἐπὶ χαλκῆ γίνεται· ἀεὶ γὰρ δεῖ προϋπάρχειν τὴν ὕλην ἢ τὸ εἶδος, ὅταν δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ τί ἐστι, καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ποιοῦ, καὶ ποσοῦ, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὁμοίως κατηγοριῶν. ὃ γὰρ γίνεται τὸ ποιόν, ἀλλὰ τὸ ποιὸν ξύλον, ἢ ζῷον. Non de substantia tantum declarat sermo, quod non fiat Forma, sed similiter de omnibus bus primis communis est sermo, ut de Quanto, Quali, aliisq; categoriis. fiunt enim sicut aneus globus, sed non globus, neq; as, atq; exare fit. semper enim oportet prius existere Materiam, quam Formam. itidem autem [se res habet] quantum ad Quidditatem, & Qualitatem, & Quantitatem, & reliquas similiter categorias. non enim fit Qualitas, sed quale lignum aut animal. qua sane vel levitate vel obliviositate, in tantulo praesertim intervallo, vix major ulla cogitari potest. Et tamen Aristoteli nihil frequentius, quam ejusmodi jactationes & fluctationes pati, ut ipse videatur plerumque nescivisse, quid aut quomodo probandum haberet: ita & theses cum probationibus, & probationes cum thesibus confundit: sicuti hoc in loco, cum thesin illam, Quod Forma substantialis nec fiat, nec intereat, probandam suscepisset exemplo artificialium atque accidentalium Formarum, ac plurima jam in eum finem dixisset; adeo sui obliviscitur in sermonis progressu, ut plane contrario modo argumentetur, Formas accidentales non fieri, nec interire, quia neq; in substantiales Formas illud cadat: quum tamen illud de Formis substantialibus paradoxum sit ipsum τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ κείμενον, ac pro quo nullam aliam probationem affert unquam, nisi illam ab accidentibus petitam similitudinem. Gloriatur quidem plus semel, se planam fecisse hanc thesin, quod Forma substantialis nec oriatur nec occidat, ut 8. Metaph. 3. Δέδεικται δὲ καὶ διελήλυθται ἐν ἄλλοις, ὅτι οὐ ποιεῖ τὸ εἶδος οὐδὲ γεννᾶται, ἀλλὰ ποιεῖται τόδε, γίγνεται δὲ ὁ ἐκ τῶνδε. Ostensum est ac declaratum alibi, quod Formam nemo facit, quodq; ipsa non generatur, sed fit hoc aliquid; fit autem Compositum ex istis. Verum tamen est nullam uspiam ipsius probationem extare in ipsius scriptis, praeter egregiam istam ab Accidentium similitudine ductam: quæ aut falsa est, si accidentia sunt entia: aut si entia non sunt (quod ipse potius sensit) vera quidem est, sed ad Formam substantialem pessime accommodatur, sicuti paulo ante monstravimus. Itaq; pronuntiatum illud, primo physicorum positum, & plurimis in locis repetitum, Τὸ γιγνόμενον ἄπαν ἀεὶ σύνθετον.
units.tr: For if in the eighth chapter of this seventh book of the Metaphysics he had proved that thesis, that the form is not made nor perishes, but the composite does, concerning the substantial form itself as its primary subject, he would not have transferred to the substantial form a thesis proved (or rather attempted) only in the case of accidental forms. Yet in the ninth chapter he speaks thus: that this is true not only of substance, that the form is not made, but that the same holds in all accidents. For he says: "The account declares not only of substance that the form is not made, but the common account applies alike to all the first categories, such as quantity, quality and the other categories. For, as the bronze sphere comes to be, but not the sphere, and the bronze comes to be as well; for the matter or the form must always pre-exist. And so it is in the case of the what-it-is, and of quality, and quantity, and the other categories alike. For quality is not made, but the quality wood or animal." What levity or forgetfulness is this, which can hardly be imagined greater, especially over so small an interval! Yet nothing is more frequent with Aristotle than to suffer such tossings and wavering, so that he often seems not to have known what he had to prove or how to prove it. Thus he confuses theses with proofs and proofs with theses. So here: having undertaken to prove the thesis that a substantial form neither comes to be nor perishes, by the example of artificial and accidental forms, and having said many things to that end, he forgets himself so far in the course of his discourse that he argues in exactly the opposite way: accidental forms are not made or destroyed because this does not hold of substantial forms. Yet that is itself the paradox set down at the beginning, the very thing that is paradoxical concerning substantial forms, and for which he never offers any other proof than that likeness drawn from accidents. He does indeed boast more than once that he has made this thesis plain, that the substantial form neither arises nor perishes, as in the eighth book, chapter three: "It has been shown and explained elsewhere that no one makes the form, nor is it generated; rather, this particular thing is made, and it comes to be from these things." It is true, however, that no proof of it is found anywhere in his writings, apart from that excellent one drawn from the likeness of accidents. That proof is false if accidents are beings; or if they are not beings (which he himself rather thought), it is indeed true, but it is very badly applied to the substantial form, as we have shown a little above. And so that statement, placed first in the Physics and repeated in many places, Whatever is generated is always composite [Τὸ γιγνόμενον ἄπαν ἀεὶ σύνθετον].

units.la: Cap. 7. {Gr}ἀλλὰ ὄντος, Compositum esse semper id, quod generatur; cujus sensus est, neq; Materiam Compositi generari, neque Formam, quomodo ipse & alibi explicat, & 12 Metaph. cap. 3. Οὐ γίνεται οὔτε ἡ ὕλη, ὅτε τὸ εἶδος. Neq; Materia fit, neq; Forma: planissime falsum est, si datur talis Forma substantialis, qualem Aristoteles ponit.
units.tr: Chapter 7. Whatever is generated is always composite; its sense is that neither the matter of the composite is generated nor the form, as he explains both here and elsewhere, and in the third chapter of the twelfth book: "Neither matter is made, nor form" [Οὐ γίνεται οὔτε ἡ ὕλη, οὔτε τὸ εἶδος]. It is plainly false, if there is such a substantial form as Aristotle posits.
LIX.

units.la: Aristotelici tamen, ac si firmissimis & invictis argumentis illud stabiliviisset ipsorum praeceptor, ita ipsi illud credunt; ac tantum non pro oraculo recipiunt: unde praesidentia illa Scaligeri verba: Formam vero qui dicat generari, is sese in Philosophia parum prodat exercitatum; generatur namq; solum Compositum: quod toties dictum, repetitum, inculcatum est, ut fateri pigeat. itaq; sumunt hoc tanquam Principium demonstrationis, unde deducant bellas istas conclusiones, Formas, quanquam generentur, nec aeternae sint, proprie tamen non gigni, quia simplices sunt, & Aristoteles multis in locis tradiderit, quicquid gignitur Compositum esse, & ex Materia gigni; ut supra audivimus. Sed isti homines nimium facilies non debebant praeceptori suo tam leviter credere rem tanti momenti, qualis est Origo Formarum substantialium, quam nulla demonstratione astruxerat, sed sola comparatione, eaq; à rebus dissimillimis, Formis nimirum accidentalibus; neq; adeo seipsos excaecare, ut postquam rei evidentia coacti sunt fateri, Formas ex nihilo fieri: id quasi retractent, autoritate huius axiomatis, Quod Formae non generentur aut intereant, sed Compositum. Namq; si hoc verum est, Formae ne sunt quidem entia. Si autem sunt entia, & quidem adeo nobilia, ut totam Composito essentiam ipsae largiantur; omnino falsum est hoc axioma. Quod enim nunc est, & aliquando non fuit; factum sive generatum sit necesse est. Quum autem factae non sint ex praeexistenti sive Materia, sequitur ut factae sint ex nihilo, ac proinde creatae. Ubi ridere libet Peripateticorum insulsitatem, qui ubi se in hasce angustias adactos vident, ut fateri cogantur, Formas ex nihilo fieri; audent tamen id retraretractare rursus, præsidio futilium hujusmodi distinctiunculbalium; quas si ipsis vel maxime concederemus esse veras, nihil amplius inde lucrarentur, nisi ut seipsos falsi convincerent in eo, quod fatentur Formas è nihilo fieri. Si autem hoc est verum (uti omnino esse debet, si Formæ sunt substantiæ, neq; vetustiores Compositis, sed simul cum ipsis existere incipientes) falsum ac vanum est quidcunq; ab ijs porro adfertur, quo ista assertio infringatur. Quippe è nihilo fieri; & non è nihilo fieri, sunt contradictoria, inter quæ nullum datur medium; quare nullo pacto de quacunq; re utrumq; simul verum esse potest; sed inevitabilis necessitas urget, ut si aliquid factum sit ex nihilo, non sit ex aliquo factum; & contra. Sicuti igitur plane ineptiunt Peripatetici, quando coacti fateri, quod Formæ è nihilo fiant; negant rursus, eas ex nihilo fieri, quia nimirum per se non subsistant, atq; è Materiæ potentia educantur: ita multo ineptiunt magis, quando hoc ipsum negant ob alteram istam exceptionem, quia ne fiant quidem omnino; non fieri autem eas, probant hoc axiomate, quod neq; Materiam fieri aut interire dicit, neq; Formam, sed solum Compositum. hoc est enim, ignotum aut incertum probare per æque ignotum & incertum. imò notum & certum est, & eam assertionem, & hoc axioma, utraq; esse salsissima: quum & illa hoc solo subnitatur, & ipsum autem non habeat aliud fulcimentum, nisi nudam Aristotelis autoritatem, qui nullis unquam rationibus, sed solis similitudinibus, ijsq; propositio ipsius adversissimis, illud stabilire annisus est. Quam rem ita se habere, sicuti nos & antea, & hic fecimus planissimum; ita & ipsis promptum fuerat, idem deprehendere, si maluissent dicta ac decreta præceptoris examinare, quam pro oraculis venerari. Miserrimum igitur est hoc probationis genus, quo Formas non oriri ex nihilo excipitur, vi istius Axiomatis Aristotelici, quod vult, Sola composita generari & interire; quo pacto efficitur necessario, Formas non esse Ens: si vero sint Ens, ipsum est salsissimum: nisi si Formæ, æque ac Materia, præexistant, ac non tum demum, quando Compositum fit, initium
units.tr: Still, the Aristotelians believe this as if their master had established it with the firmest and unanswerable arguments, and they accept it almost as an oracle. Hence those well-known words of Scaliger: Whoever says that a form is generated shows himself to be little practised in philosophy; for only the composite is generated. This has been said, repeated and drummed in so often that one is ashamed to admit it. They therefore take this as the first principle of a demonstration, and from it they draw those fine conclusions: that forms, although they are generated and are not eternal, nevertheless are not properly begotten, because they are simple; and that Aristotle has taught in many places that whatever is begotten is composite and is generated from matter, as we heard above. But these men ought not to have been so easily credulous, nor to have believed their teacher so lightly on a matter of such weight as the origin of substantial forms, which he had established by no demonstration, but only by comparison, and that with very dissimilar things, namely accidental forms. Nor ought they to blind themselves, so that, after being compelled by the evidence of the thing to admit that forms come from nothing, they then try to take this back by appeal to the authority of this axiom, that forms are not generated or perish, but only the composite. For if this is true, forms are not even beings. But if they are beings, and indeed so noble that they bestow the whole essence on the composite, then this axiom is altogether false. For what now exists and did not exist before must necessarily have been made or generated. Since, however, forms were not made out of a pre-existing matter, it follows that they were made out of nothing, and therefore created. Here it is pleasant to laugh at the silliness of the Peripatetics, who, when they see themselves driven into these straits, so that they are forced to admit that forms come from nothing, nevertheless dare to retract this again, relying on futile quibbles of this kind. Even if we granted these quibbles to be wholly true, they would gain nothing from them except to convict themselves of falsehood in admitting that forms come from nothing. But if this is true (as it must be wholly true, if forms are substances, and are not older than the composites, but begin to exist together with them), then whatever is afterwards brought forward to overturn this assertion is false and empty. For to come from nothing and not to come from nothing are contradictories, between which there is no middle; therefore in no way can both be true at once of any thing. Rather, inescapable necessity forces us to conclude that if something has been made from nothing, it has not been made from something; and conversely. Just as the Peripatetics plainly talk nonsense when, compelled to admit that forms come from nothing, they then deny that they come from nothing, because they do not subsist of themselves but are educed from the potency of matter, so they talk far more nonsense when they deny the very point on the other exception, namely that forms do not come into being at all; and they prove that they are not generated by this axiom, which says that neither matter nor form is made or perishes, but only the composite. For this is to prove what is unknown or uncertain by something equally unknown and uncertain. Indeed, it is known and certain that both that assertion and this axiom are most false, since the one rests on this alone, while the axiom itself has no other support than the bare authority of Aristotle, who never tried to establish it by any reasons, but only by similitudes, and those most adverse to his own proposition. That this is so, as we have made most plain both before and here, was also readily within their power to discover, if they had preferred to examine their teacher's sayings and decrees rather than to revere them as oracles. The method of proof by which it is objected that forms do not arise from nothing, by the force of this Aristotelian axiom which says that only composites are generated and perish, is therefore most wretched; by it it follows necessarily that forms are not being, and if they are being, the axiom is most false, unless forms, like matter, pre-exist, and do not receive their beginning only when the composite comes into being, but are produced beforehand and taken up for the constitution of the composite. This is what not only the greater part of the Aristotelians, but Aristotle himself, most strongly abhors and rejects. But it seems that what happened to Aristotle here is what happens to him very often elsewhere, as we have noted in more than one place in this work: namely, that he takes up foreign doctrines which are directly and diametrically opposed to his own teaching, and accommodates them to his own traditions, with which they cannot in any way agree; and no greater carelessness in teaching can be found. For all the ancient philosophers before Aristotle (perhaps Plato alone excepted, who, however, does not seem to be excluded by us) did not know substantial forms; and they fashioned all composites, according to all their substantial parts, out of pre-existing things, namely out of simple bodies or elements, which they held to be free from all origin and to have existed from eternity. So in their school it was true to say that only composites are generated, since none of their parts came into being at that time, but already existing parts came together for their constitution. It is therefore probable that in their writings, where generations were discussed, this opinion was familiar; and Aristotle, having seized upon it in his own manner, rashly introduced it into his philosophy, whereas he ought to have considered that his own account is quite different, since he did not make composites entirely out of pre-existing things as they did, but taught that the chief part of them comes into being only when they themselves come into being. From this it would necessarily follow that not only composites are generated, but together with them that part too which, not existing before, begins to exist along with them. Therefore this saying ought to have been banished far from him and from his doctrine, as manifestly repugnant to it, and rejected, rather than inculcated so often as if it were his own and agreeing with him. But it was his undoing that he tried this first in accidental composites, as they are called, that is, those which are made up of a subject and the accidents inhering in it. In these, since he had succeeded well, namely with that hypothesis that accidents are not beings, he then transferred the same, without further inquiry, to substantial composites, as if whatever is true in the one case must be true in the other too; although their nature is most different, as is plain of itself, and becomes still clearer from what we have just said on this matter. Indeed, let Aristotle with his followers turn himself in every direction, he will never advance to the least probability in defending two propositions so mutually repugnant: that only composites are generated, and therefore forms are not generated; and that forms are something, indeed substances, which did not exist before the composite, but begin to be together with the composite itself.

units.la: Cap.I. tium sui accipiant, sed prius productæ, ad Compositi constitutionem assumantur: id quod non Aristotelicorum modo maxima pars, sed & ipse Aristoteles quam maxime abhorret atq; aversatur. Videtur autem Aristoteli hic accidisse id, quod alibi ipsi accidit quam sæpissime, & à nobis non uno hujus operis loco adnotatur; ut nimirum aliena dogmata, suæ doctrinæ directo atq; è diametro adversantia, pro suis usurpet, atq; ad suas traditiones, quibuscum stare nullo pacto queunt, accommodet; qua nulla major in docendo incogitantia reperiri potest. Etenim omnes prisci ante Aristotelem Philosophi (solo forsan Platone excepto; qui tamen ipse nobis excipiendus haud videtur) quum ignoraverint Formas substantiales; omniaq; Composita, secundum omnes sui partes substantiales, fabricaverint ex præexistentibus, nimirum ex corporibus simplicibus, seu ex Elementis, quæ ipsi omnis ortus expertia, ab æterno suisse statuebant; in ipsorum schola dictu verum erat, sola Composita generari; quippe quorum nullæ partes tunc demum fierent, sed prius existentes, ad ipsorum constitutionem concurrerent: ac proinde probabile est, in eorum scriptis, ubi de Generationibus ageretur, familiarem fuisse hanc sententiam: unde arreptam pro more suo Aristoteles, suæ Philosophiæ temere intulerit; quum debuerit considerare, longe aliam esse suam rationem, qui Composita non itidem, ac illi, ex præexistentibus tota procrearet, sed potissimam eorum partem tum demum, quando ipsa fiunt, fieri doceret; unde necessario sequeretur, non sola Composita generari, sed simul cum ipsis generari eam quoq; partem, quæ prius non existens, cum ipsis existere inciperet. quare dictum hoc debuit à se, atq; doctrina sua, utpote ipsi apertissime repugnans, procul relegare, atq; repudiare, ac non ut suum sibiq; congruum toties inculcare. Sed fraudi ipsi fuit, quod id tentaverit prius in Compositis accidentalibus, ut vocant; hoc est, ijs quæ ex subjecto & inhærentibus ipsi accidentibus constata sunt: in quibus quum ipsi probe succesisset, cum illa nimirum hypothesi Quod accidentia non sunt entia: inde porro, absq; ulteriori disquisitione, ad Composita substantialia transtulit; acsi quicquid in illis verum sit, in his quoq; verum esse debeat; quum tamen diversissima sit ipsorum ratio, sicuti per se liquet, & ex ijs, quæ modo super hac re diximus, amplius fit manifestum. Sane in omnia se vertat licet Aristoteles cum suis, nunquam vel ad minimam progredientur probabilitatem, in tuendis duabus hisce propositionibus adeo inter se repugnantibus, Quod sola Composita generentur, quodq; proinde non generentur Formæ; & Quod Formæ sint aliquid, imò quod sint substantiæ, quæ ante Compositum non extiterint, sed cum ipso Composito esse incipiant.
units.tr: Chapter I. ...receive their beginning of being, but are produced beforehand and taken up to make up the composite. The greater part of the Aristotelians abhor this, and Aristotle himself most of all. It seems that here Aristotle experienced what happens to him very often elsewhere, as we have noted more than once in this work: he takes over foreign doctrines that directly and flatly contradict his own teaching, and adapts them to his own positions, with which they cannot in any way agree. No greater carelessness in teaching can be found. For all the ancient philosophers before Aristotle (perhaps excepting Plato alone, who does not seem to me to be an exception that need be made) did not know substantial forms. They built all composites, in every substantial part, out of things that already existed, namely out of simple bodies or elements, which they held to be free from all origin and to have existed from eternity. In their school it was true to say only composites are generated, since none of their parts came into being then, but already existed and joined in forming the composite. It is therefore probable that this opinion was familiar in their writings wherever generation was discussed. Aristotle, in his usual way, seized on it and rashly introduced it into his own philosophy, when he ought to have considered that his own account is quite different. He did not build composites wholly out of pre-existing things as they did; he taught that their chief part is generated only when the composite itself comes to be. From this it would necessarily follow that not only composites are generated, but that along with them that part is also generated which, not existing before, begins to exist together with them. For this reason he ought to have set this saying far away from himself and from his doctrine, as being plainly opposed to it, and to have rejected it, rather than repeat it so often as if it agreed with him. But it did him harm that he first tried it on accidental composites, as they are called, that is, those made up of a subject and the accidents inhering in it. In these he succeeded well, namely under that hypothesis that accidents are not beings. From there he carried it over, without further inquiry, to substantial composites, as if whatever is true in the one case must also be true in the other, although their nature is most different, as is plain in itself and as becomes clearer from what we have just said on this matter. Indeed, however Aristotle and his followers may turn themselves about, they will never advance even to the smallest degree of probability in defending these two propositions, which are so much at odds with each other: that only composites are generated, and therefore forms are not generated; and that forms are something, indeed that they are substances, which did not exist before the composite but begin to be together with the composite itself.

units.la: LX. Est quidem usitatus hîc Aristotelicis alter paulo modestior hujus axiomatis, quod sola Composita generari dicit, explicandi modus; quo non quidem absolute negant Formas fieri, sed tantum dicunt, eas non fieri proprie ac per se, sed ad generationem Compositi congenerari seu confieri: quo loquendi genere etiamsi nonnulli promiscuè cum præcedenti utuntur, acsi nihil inter hæc interesset; alij tamen uti ab eo diversum, quomodo revera est, usurpant. Sed neq; isto modo explicata ista sententia, quæ sola Composita dicit generari, veritati est consentanea; & si esset, nihil inde juvarentur Peripatetici; qui tamen eandem inde expectant utilitatem, quam ab altera illa impudentiori explicatione, quæ vi hujus axiomatis Formas omnino fieri inficiatur. Quod ad expediendam hanc difficultatem, quomodo Formæ & substantiæ sint, & ex nihilo fiant; nihil juvet hæc evasio, quæ Formas non fieri primo ac per se, sed confieri dicit; ita ostendimus. Rem aliquam congenerari seu confieri, non significat (uti cuivis ex ipsa vocabuli vi per se apertum est) non fieri omnino, sed non primariâ operâ fieri; seu ita fieri, ut ipsius generatio non per se instituatur, verum ad alterius rei generationem sit veluti consectaria: quare etiam Suarez castigans Thomam, quòd vi istius axiomatis Aristotelici dixisset, Formas per accidens fieri; ait, samo modo hoc intelligi.
units.tr: LX. There is indeed another, somewhat more moderate way of explaining this axiom, which the Aristotelians use, saying that only composites are generated; by it they do not absolutely deny that forms come into being, but say only that they do not come into being properly and of themselves, but are co-generated or made together with the generation of the composite. Although some use this way of speaking indiscriminately with the former, as if there were no difference between them, others use it as different from it, as in fact it is. But neither is this opinion, explained in this way, which says that only composites are generated, consistent with the truth; and even if it were, the Peripatetics would gain nothing from it, although they expect from it the same advantage that they hope for from that other, more shameless explanation, by which, by force of this axiom, they deny that forms come into being at all. As for resolving this difficulty, of how forms are substances and yet come from nothing, this evasion helps nothing, which says that forms are not made primarily and of themselves, but are made together; as we have shown. To be co-generated or made together does not mean (as is plain to anyone from the very force of the word) not to be made at all, but not to be made by a primary operation; that is, to be made in such a way that its generation is not undertaken of itself, but is, as it were, a consequence of the generation of something else. For this reason Suárez, rebuking Thomas because, by force of this Aristotelian axiom, he had said that forms come into being per accidens, says that this must be understood in one way only.

units.la: Disp. 15. sect. 4. §. 4. telligendum esse, late utendo verbo per accidens, prout idem est quod cum alio. & praeterea non debere aliter hanc phrasin accipi, ex eo patet, quod non ipsi fieri absolute sumto, sed primo ac per se fieri oppōnitur. Iam si illud, quod congeneratur seu confit, quanquam secundaria opera fiat, fit tamen; aeque de ipso, ac de eo quod per se fit, quaeri potest, ex aliquo fiat, an ex nihilo: & quum nihil inter haec duo fit intermedium (uti supra diximus) necesse est ut ea, quae confiunt seu congenerantur, aeque perfecte vel ex aliquo fiant, vel ex nihilo, quam quae primo ac per se generantur. Si itaq; Formae ex non praeexistenti sive ex nihilo fiant; integra manet quaestio, quomodo hoc fieri queat, si Formae sunt substantiae, & substantia ex nihilo fieri non potest; quum illa generationis & congenerationis distinctio nihil ad hujus rei enodationem faciat, eaq; quae ex nihilo fiunt, non minus absolute & perfecte ex nihilo fiant, si alteri rei congenerentur, quam si generentur ipsa per se: quandoquidem ipsum fieri ex nihilo nullam habet latitudinem, nullamq; recipit variationem: quare omnia, quae ex nihilo fiunt, eodem modo ex nihilo fiant necesse est.
units.tr: Disp. 15. sect. 4. §. 4. It must be understood that the phrase "per accidens" is used broadly, in the sense in which it is the same as "together with another." Moreover, this phrase should not be taken in any other way, as is clear from the fact that it is opposed not to to be made taken absolutely, but to to be made primarily and per se. Now if that which is co-generated or composed, although it is made by a secondary operation, is nevertheless made, then about it, just as about that which is made per se, it can be asked whether it is made out of something or out of nothing. And since (as we said above) nothing intermediate lies between these two, it is necessary that those things which are composed or co-generated are made just as perfectly either out of something or out of nothing as those which are generated primarily and per se.
