If therefore Forms are made out of no pre-existing thing, or out of nothing, the question remains whole: how this can happen, if Forms are substances and a substance cannot be made out of nothing. For that distinction between generation and co-generation contributes nothing to the explanation of this matter, and things that are made out of nothing are made out of nothing no less absolutely and perfectly if they are co-generated with another thing than if they are generated per se. This is so because being made out of nothing itself has no latitude and admits no variation. Hence all things that are made out of nothing must necessarily be made out of nothing in the same way.
LXI.

units.la: Quod vero neq; veritati congruat haec expositio, Formas ad generationem Compositi congenerari dicit; & ipsum facile probari potest. Eorum enim, quae priora sunt, generatio prior esse debet; id autem, quod prius generatur, non potest dici congenerari alteri rei, cujus generatio est ipsius generatione posterior: sed si alterum horum fieri, alterum confieri dicendum est, ratio postulat, ut posteriora potius dicantur prioribus congenerari, quam contra. & nimis absurdum sit, dicere, quod res posterior primo generetur; res autem prior generetur non primo, seu secundario. Hisce ita constitutis, si docemus partes esse toto priores, ac proinde Formas esse priores Composito; scilicet attigerimus, atque confecerimus, Composita potius Formis, quam Formas Compositis dicendas congenerari. Quum ergo Prioritatis duo tantum sint modi, qui quidem ad praesens negotium faciant; una temporis, altera naturae: illa quidem temporis prioritate saepe partes constituentes esse Toto ex iplis constituto priores, per se apertum est: altera vero (quae magis huc facit) semper priores esse, vel ex ipso Aristotele doceri potest. Etenim in Postpraedicamentis, capite de Priori, secundum modum Prioritatis (qui, consensu interpretum, & ex ipsius loci evidentia, est prioritas naturae vulgo dicta) ita exponit, ut dicat ea esse hoc modo priora, quae non pendent ex aliis, sed ex quibus alia pendent, quomodo unum non pendet à duobus, sed duo pendent ab uno; quum unum esse queat, ut non sint duo: duo esse nequeant, quin sit unum, quum duo nihil sint aliud quam bis unum. Δεύτερον δὲ [ἕτερον ἑτέρᾳ πρότερον λέγεται] τὸ μὴ ἀναιρεφόμενον καθ' τὴν τῆς εἶναι ἀπολέλυσιν· ὅτου, τὸ ἐν τῶν δύο πρότερον. Λύσιν μὲν ὄντοιν, ἀναιρεῖ δυὰς τὸ ἓν εἶναι. ἐνὸς δὲ ὄντος, οὐ ἀναγκαῖον δύο εἶν. ὥστε οὖν ἀναιρεῖ ἀπὸ τὸ ἑνὸς ἡ ἀπολέλυσις τὸ εἶναι τὸ λοιπόν. Secundo [aliquid altero prius dicitur] quod non reciprocatur secundum existendi consecutionem. ut unum duobus est prius: nam si duo sunt, statim sequitur unum esse. quare non reciprocatur, ut, si unum sit, sequatur reliquum esse. Idem repetit, sed planioribus verbis, quinti Metaphysicorum undecimo: Τὰ δὲ καθ' φύσιν [πρότερα λέγεται] ὅσα ἐνδέχεται εἶναι ἄνευ ἄλλων, ἐκεῖνα δὲ ἄνευ ἐκείνων μή. Alia autem naturâ [priora dicuntur] quae ejusmodi sunt, ut sine aliis esse possint, non item sine eis alia. & in candem sententiam ibi ait, accidens esse ratione prius ipso toto, quod ex subjecto & accidente constat. Καὶ καθ' τὸν λόγον δὲ τὸ συμβεβηκὸς τῆς ὅλης πρότερον, οἷον τὸ μουσικὸν τῆς μουσικῆς ἀνθρώπου· ὁ γὰρ ἔσαι ὅλος ὁ λόγος ἄνευ τοῦ μέρους, καίτοι οὐκ ἐνδέχεται μουσικὸν εἶναι, οὐκ ὄντος μουσικῆς ζῴου. Ratione etiam accidens prius est toto ipso, ut musicum,homine musico. non enim erit tota ratio sine parte; tametsi fieri non potest, ut musicum sit, nisi aliquid sit musicum. ad quae verba ita Fonseca in commentariis, Etsi musicum est ratione posterius homine, ut accidens subjecto, tamen ut est pars hominis musici, prius est ratione quàm homo musicus. Ex hisce evidentissime sequitur, & quaevis partes totis suis, & Formas compositis esse natura priores, ex ipsius Aristotelis judicio; quod ipsum & Aristotelici non pauci aperte profitentur. Etenim Pererius ait, Prioritate naturae Formam sine dubio esse priorem composito; quia ordine naturae causa sit prior effectu, simplex composito, pars toto. Et similiter Mercenarius, In generatione ex Materia jam dispositā id, quod primo oritur, & in esse erumpit, Forma est. enimvero quum Forma ipsius compositi Causa sit, necessario ipsum praire debet: non prius inquam tempore, quoniam haec simul tempore sunt, sed natura & causalitate. Imo ipse Suarez, qui in hac tractatione ita loquitur, ut Formae prioritatem absolute neget, postea tamen Disputatione 26. sect. 2. diserte ait, generale illud Aristotelis pronunciatum, Causam esse naturā priorem effectu suo, in Forma quoque, non minus quàm in aliis Causis, verum esse; Formamq; naturā prius esse, quam Compositum. Si ergo non veritas modo, sed Aristoteles quoq; decernit, Partes atq; Elementa esse priora natura Totis atque Compositis; siq; id, quod naturā prius est, non potest esse generatione posterius eo, quod est naturā posterius; omnino absurdum dictu est, Compositum prius fieri quàm Formam; contraq; potius dicendum, Formam primò fieri, ac Compositum secundario. & si id, quod secundario fit, confit seu congeneratur ei quod fit primo, non Forma Composito, sed Compositum Formae congeneratur.
units.tr: That this explanation does not agree with the truth, when it says that Forms are co-generated with the generation of the Composite, can easily be proved. For the generation of those things that are prior must be prior; and that which is generated first cannot be said to be co-generated with another thing whose generation is later than its own. But if one of these is made and the other is made together with it, reason requires that the later things be said to be co-generated with the earlier, rather than the reverse. And it would be too absurd to say that a later thing is generated primarily, while an earlier thing is generated not primarily, that is, secondarily. With these things so established, if we teach that the parts are prior to the whole, and therefore that Forms are prior to the Composite, then clearly we have touched on and completed the point that the Composites should rather be said to be co-generated with the Forms than the Forms with the Composites. Since there are only two modes of priority that bear on the present matter, one of time and the other of nature, it is plainly evident that the constituent parts are often prior to the whole constituted from them in respect of time. But the other mode, which bears more on this point, can be shown to hold always, from Aristotle himself. For in the Postpraedicamenta, in the chapter on the Prior, he sets out the second mode of priority (which, by the agreement of the interpreters and by the plain sense of the passage, is the priority of nature commonly so called), and he explains it so that those things are prior in this way which do not depend on others, but on which others depend. Thus one does not depend on two, but two depend on one: one can be without there being two, but two cannot be without there being one, since two is nothing other than twice one. [Δεύτερον δὲ [ἕτερον ἑτέρᾳ πρότερον λέγεται] τὸ μὴ ἀναιρεφόμενον καθ' τὴν τῆς εἶναι ἀπολέλυσιν· ὅτου, τὸ ἐν τῶν δύο πρότερον. Λύσιν μὲν ὄντοιν, ἀναιρεῖ δυὰς τὸ ἓν εἶναι. ἐνὸς δὲ ὄντος, οὐ ἀναγκαῖον δύο εἶν. ὥστε οὖν ἀναιρεῖ ἀπὸ τὸ ἑνὸς ἡ ἀπολέλυσις τὸ εἶναι τὸ λοιπόν.] Secondly, [one thing is said to be prior to another] which is not reciprocated in the sequence of existence; as one is prior to two, for if there are two, it follows at once that there is one; so it is not reciprocated, so that if there is one, the other follows. He repeats the same thing, but in plainer words, in the eleventh chapter of the fifth book of the Metaphysics: [Τὰ δὲ καθ' φύσιν [πρότερα λέγεται] ὅσα ἐνδέχεται εἶναι ἄνευ ἄλλων, ἐκεῖνα δὲ ἄνευ ἐκείνων μή.] Things are called prior by nature which can be without others, but those others cannot be without them. And to the same effect he says there that an accident is prior in definition to the whole that consists of subject and accident. [Καὶ καθ' τὸν λόγον δὲ τὸ συμβεβηκὸς τῆς ὅλης πρότερον, οἷον τὸ μουσικὸν τῆς μουσικῆς ἀνθρώπου· ὁ γὰρ ἔσαι ὅλος ὁ λόγος ἄνευ τοῦ μέρους, καίτοι οὐκ ἐνδέχεται μουσικὸν εἶναι, οὐκ ὄντος μουσικῆς ζῴου.] In definition also the accident is prior to the whole itself, as the musical is prior to the musical man; for the whole definition will not be without the part, although it cannot be that the musical exists unless something is musical. On these words Fonseca says in his commentary: Although the musical is posterior to the man in definition, as an accident is to its subject, nevertheless insofar as it is a part of the musical man, it is prior in definition to the musical man. From these things it follows most evidently, from Aristotle's own judgement, that both the parts are prior by nature to their wholes and the Forms to the composites; and this is openly professed by not a few Aristotelians. For Pererius says: Without doubt the Form is prior to the composite in the priority of nature, because in the order of nature the cause is prior to the effect, the simple to the composite, the part to the whole. Similarly Mercenarius: In generation from matter already disposed, that which first arises and breaks forth into being is the Form. Indeed, since the Form is the cause of the composite itself, it must necessarily precede it: not prior in time, I say, for these are simultaneous in time, but prior in nature and in causality. Indeed Suarez himself, who in this treatise speaks in such a way that he absolutely denies the priority of the Form, afterwards nevertheless states plainly in Disputation 26, section 2, that the general pronouncement of Aristotle, that a cause is prior by nature to its effect, is true also of the Form no less than of the other causes, and that the Form is prior by nature to the composite. If therefore not only truth but Aristotle too decides that parts and elements are prior by nature to wholes and composites, and if that which is prior by nature cannot be posterior in generation to that which is posterior by nature, then it is wholly absurd to say that the composite is made before the Form; rather, on the contrary, it must be said that the Form is made first and the composite secondarily. And if that which is made secondarily is co-generated with that which is made first, then it is not the Form that is co-generated with the composite, but the composite with the Form.
LXII.

units.la: Ad eam verò rationem, quę à Suarezio aliisq; affertur, cur Compositum debeat primo fieri, Forma autem confieri; facilis est responsio. Ejus est (inquit) per se primò fieri, cujus est esse; idq; proprie est quod subsistit. Formae autem non subsistunt, sed Composita. ad quod nos breviter dicimus, non ea tantum esse proprie, quae subsistunt (quo pacto ab ipsis subsistendi vocabulum sumitur pro eo existendi modo, quo suppositā existunt) sed & ea, quae rerum ita subsistentium partes sunt. sane totum suppositi esse veluti precarium est, ac pendet à partibus ipsius essen-
units.tr: To the argument that Suárez and others bring forward, why the composite must come into being first and the form afterwards, the reply is easy. It belongs to that which is per se first to come into being, whose it is to be; and this is properly what subsists. But forms do not subsist; composites do. To this we briefly answer that not only those things are properly said to be which subsist (in which sense the word "subsist" is taken for that mode of existing by which things exist as supposits), but also those which are parts of things that subsist in this way. Indeed the whole supposit is, as it were, dependent, and hangs on the essential parts of itself,

units.la: {y} Dilucid. 48. & pro intentione. essentialibus, quum ipsarum partium esse non pendeat à Composito, sed ex sese sint id quod sunt, suumq; esse constituendum. Quamobrem Materia prima & Forma (si illæ sunt partes essentiales substantiarum compositarum, ut in Peripato supponitur) non modo sunt prius natura quam compositum, uti modo ostendimus; sed & magis proprie, quam ipsum: uti ex hac dissertatione liquet. nam quod non existunt per se (hoc est, ex eorum sensu, separata) hoc nihil ad rem facit, neq; vera rei essentia ex eo spectanda est, quod ita per se vel non per se existat, quum hoc nihil faciat ad verum rei esse constituendum aut variandum; cujus assertionis vel sola anima humana fidem fecerit, cujus una eademq; est essentia, quando corpori juncta, unum Compositum cum eo constituit; & quando ab eo sejuncta, per sese existit separata. Si ergo ejus est primò ac proprie fieri, quod primo ac proprie est; non Compositum primò ac proprie fit, sed ipsa Forma, quæ uti natura prior est Composito, ita & magis proprie est; quippe quidquid est, id est ex sese ac suopte marte, quum Compositum esse suum non ita habeat, sed totum dependens ac tanquam communicatum à partibus suis, quarum Peripatetici Formam dicunt esse præcipuam; adeo quidem ut multi ipsorum totam Compositi essentiam sive quidditatem, ut loquuntur, à Forma arcessant. Quodsi igitur actio, qua Forma fit, & qua Compositum, Formâ ad Materiam adjuncta, constituitur, una est, ut Suarezius supponit; non est ejus terminus adæquatus ipsum Compositum, sed Forma; quandoquidem illa & prius natura fit, & magis proprie, quàm Compositum, cujus productio & natura posterior est Formæ productione, & minus propria, quippe quod non ipsum per se producitur, sed ex partium prius productarum unione consurgit. Habent quidem & aliam pro se rationem, quæ breviter atq; obscurius à Suarezio in loco supra recitato tacta, apertius à Mercernario sic proponitur: Ab Aristotele dicitur Compositum primo ac per se generari & corrumpi, non quia prius origine oriatur aut intereat, quàm Forma;
units.tr: Dilucid. 48. & pro intentione. essential parts, since the being of those parts does not depend on the composite, but they are what they are of themselves and constitute their own being. Therefore prime matter and form (if these are the essential parts of compound substances, as is assumed in the Peripatetic school) are not only prior in nature to the composite, as we have just shown, but also exist more properly than it, as is clear from this discussion. For the fact that they do not exist per se (that is, separated, in their own sense) has nothing to do with the matter, nor is the true essence of a thing to be judged by whether it exists per se or not, since this contributes nothing to establishing or changing the true being of the thing. The human soul alone would be enough to prove this assertion: it is one and the same essence when joined to the body, where it constitutes one composite with it, and when separated from the body, where it exists on its own. If, then, it belongs to that which is first and properly to come into being to come into being first and properly, it is not the composite that comes into being first and properly, but the form itself, which, just as it is prior in nature to the composite, so also exists more properly. For whatever is, is from itself and by its own power; whereas the composite does not have its being in this way, but depends wholly, and as if received, from its parts, of which the Peripatetics say the form is the chief. So much so that many of them derive the whole essence or quiddity of the composite, as they put it, from the form. Therefore, if the action by which the form comes to be and by which the composite is constituted, the form being joined to matter, is one action, as Suárez supposes, its adequate term is not the composite itself but the form; since the form both comes into being prior in nature and more properly than the composite, whose production and nature is posterior to the production of the form, and less proper, because it is not produced per se but arises from the union of parts previously produced. Indeed they have another reason for their view, which Suárez touched on briefly and somewhat obscurely in the passage cited above, and which Mercernarius sets out more plainly thus: Aristotle says that the composite is generated and corrupted primarily and per se, not because it arises or perishes earlier in origin than the form;

units.la: Dilucid. 48. Forma; sed quoniam objectum est, quod primo & per se ab ipsa generatione respicitur. proinde Compositum dicitur primo & per se generari, ac objectum generationis esse, non autem Forma, tametsi Forma prius in actum erumpat intereat, quàm Compositum. Volunt nimirum, ipsum Compositum esse primarium generantis scopum, ac proinde ejus generationem primario ac per se intendi; generationem autem Formæ non propter se, sed propter ipsum Compositum, in quantum ad ejus generationem est necessaria, neq; generari Compositum potest, nisi ut Forma generetur. Sed hoc adeo eos non juvat, ut potius contrarium, quàm ipsi volunt, inde sequatur, videlicet generationem Compositi esse generatione Formæ posteriorem, idcircoq; non Formam Composito, sed Compositum Formæ comproduci: idq; ex receptissimo illo ac decantato Aristotelis axiomate, quo dicitur Finem, qui sit primus in intentione, esse ultimum in executione; quo ad propositam rem applicato, concludendum erit, quod, si Compositum est ultimus generantis finis, Forma autem subordinatus, Forma prius effici debeat à Generante (si non tempore, saltem ordine naturæ) quàm Compositum; quandoquidem illud, quod non propter se, sed alterius acquirendi aut producendi causa acquiritur aut producitur, omnino ordine acquisitionis vel productionis anteceedere oportet illud, cujus acquisitioni vel generationi inservit; uti & per se liquet, & illa Aristotelis de Fine doctrina manifesto flagitat.
units.tr: Dilucid. 48. Forma; but because it is the object which generation regards primarily and per se. Accordingly the composite is said to be generated primarily and per se, and to be the object of generation, and not the form, although the form breaks forth into actuality and perishes earlier than the composite. They want, of course, the composite itself to be the chief aim of the one generating, and so its generation to be intended primarily and per se; but the generation of the form is intended not for its own sake but for the sake of the composite, insofar as it is necessary for the composite's generation, and the composite cannot be generated unless the form is generated. But this does not help them at all; rather, from it follows the very opposite of what they wish: namely, that the generation of the composite is posterior to the generation of the form, and therefore the composite is not produced together with the form, but the form together with the composite. This follows from that most accepted and celebrated axiom of Aristotle, by which the end which is first in intention is last in execution. Applied to the matter at hand, it must be concluded that, if the composite is the ultimate end of the generating agent, and the form is subordinate, the form ought to be brought about by the generator before the composite (if not in time, at least in the order of nature); since that which is acquired or produced not for its own sake but for the sake of acquiring or producing something else must necessarily precede, in the order of acquisition or production, that to whose acquisition or generation it serves. This is both evident in itself and plainly demanded by Aristotle's doctrine of the end.

units.la: LXIII. Quandoquidem ergo ad tollendas aut minuendas illas de Formarum ortu difficultates, nihil plane faciunt, quæcunq; de Formarum è Materiæ potentia eductione, deq; earum comproductione, aliaq; in eandem rem comminſcuntur Peripatetici, sed vana ac frivola, summæq; absurditatis plena deprehenduntur, sicuti superiori sermone planum fecimus; omnino nihil aliud Aristotelicis restat, ad tuendam suam hanc doctrinam, quod Formæ & sunt Substantiæ, & tum demum fiunt, quando aliquid generatur, tur, idq; ex non praexistenti: quam ut ad Deum ipsum cum Philopono recurrant, ab eoq; dicant Formas in rerum generationibus creari; quod & Ramus vidit, ac propterea ipse secutus est, ut Formas ab ipso Deo ex nihilo fieri diceret: imo ostendere quoq; laborat, quod ipse Aristoteles ita senserit. sed hoc quidem inane est, cum sit omnibus, quicunq; Aristotelis scripta vel a limine salutarunt, quod ipse illam summa potentiam, substantias ex nihilo faciendi, nullo modo agnoverit, sed plane contrarium, docuerit, uti & alij ante ipsum Philosophi pleriq; omnes. & ipsis Peripateticis hoc optime compertum est, qui proinde ipsi quoq; damnant (uti & supra diximus) hanc Philoponi opinionem, & in quaevis potius incommoda se induant, quam ut huc consugiant, dicantq; Formas a Deo fieri: solis mentibus humanis exceptis, quas quotidie ad singulorum hominum productionem ab eo creari asserunt. De reliquis autem omnibus Formis contentissime negant, Dei omnipotentiam se ad earum productionem interponere: & sic omnem sibi ipsis viam intercludunt, ex hac difficultate evadendi; quum nulla creatura, ipsis itidem fatentibus, polleat hac vi, ut substantiam ex nihilo producere valeat; & Formae tamen e nihilo producantur, ex planissima ipsorum confessione, damnatis etiam omnibus ijs, qui in hoc ab ipsis dissentiunt, Formasq; ex praeexistenti fieri affirmant. Herculeum est igitur hoc contra Formas substantiales argumentum, ab earum origine desumtum; siquidem substantia nulla ex nihilo fieri potest, nisi a vi infinita, quam ab hoc negotio ipsi Aristotelici excludunt; & Formas ex nihilo fieri, ipsi fatentur; neq; quicquam efficiunt ineptissimis effugijs, quibus planissimae huic confessioni postea rursus obluctantur: quum nos planum fecerimus, quicquid ex nihilo fit, simpliciter & absq; ulla exceptione ex nihilo fieri debere.
units.tr: LXIII. Since, then, whatever the Peripatetics devise about the educing of forms from the potency of matter, and about their co-production, and whatever else they invent on the same point, does nothing at all to remove or lessen those difficulties about the origin of forms, but is found to be empty, frivolous and full of the greatest absurdity, as we have shown in our earlier discussion, nothing at all remains for the Aristotelians to defend this doctrine except that forms are substances, and that they come into being only when something is generated, and that out of nothing that previously existed. To escape this, they would have to take refuge with Philoponus in God himself, and say with him that forms are created by God in the generations of things; which Ramus also saw, and therefore followed, so as to say that forms are made by God himself out of nothing. Indeed, he even labours to show that Aristotle himself thought so. But this is empty, since it is obvious to everyone who has so much as glanced at Aristotle's writings that he did not acknowledge that supreme power of making substances out of nothing in any way, but taught plainly the contrary, as did most of the other philosophers before him. And this has been very well established even among the Peripatetics themselves, who therefore condemn (as we also said above) this opinion of Philoponus, and would rather bring upon themselves any inconvenience than take refuge in it and say that forms are made by God. The only exception is human minds, which they say are created by him every day in the production of each individual man. But concerning all the other forms they stoutly deny that God's omnipotence interposes itself in their production; and so they cut off for themselves every way of escaping this difficulty, since no creature, as they too confess, has the power to produce a substance out of nothing, and yet forms are produced out of nothing, by their own plainest confession, with all those condemned who differ from them on this point and affirm that forms come from something pre-existing. This argument against substantial forms, drawn from their origin, is therefore a Herculean one. For no substance can come from nothing except by infinite power, which the Aristotelians themselves exclude from this business; and they admit that forms come from nothing; nor do they achieve anything by the most inept evasions, by which they later struggle against this most plain confession. For we have shown that whatever comes from nothing must come from nothing simply and without any exception.

units.la: LXIV. Una videtur illis relicta ratio ad effugiendum ex his angustijs, si nimirum Alexandro accedant, qui nullam aliam agnoscit Formam, ne in hominibus quidem, nisi Formas Elementorum certa proportione in quocunq; misto concurrentium, atq; sua harmonia velut enam Formam constituentium. hoc enim si sequantur, non urgebuntur illa difficultate, ut substantiam creent ex nihlo. sed hæc opinio dum unam vitat absurditatem, in alias incidit complures, quas Aristotelica de Formis doctrina ferre nullo modo potest, unde & Peripatetici pleriq; illam damnant pro ineptissima, & quovis potius se redigi patiantur, quam ut illam approbent; qua in re sufficiet Scaligerum produxisse testem, qui & alibi multis in locis in Alexandri hanc opinionem invehitur, & præcipue Exerc. 307. 20. ubi hunc ad modum scribit: Sunt enim invenustissimi, insciitissimi, infelicissimi omnium mortalium, qui putant ex multiplici Materia (hoc enim sunt Elementa) atq; ejus Formis contaminatis, posse per se fieri Formam unam, quæ totius molis auter sit existendi, sine adventu Forma externa unius, qua totum illud in fide atq; officio continuitatis atq; unitatis contineatur. & multa addit in eandem sententiam. Nam de opinione illa, quam in Controversiis secutus est Cardanus, & Averroi quoq; ascribit, Formam Mixti inanimis, & similarium quoque partium in stirpibus & animalibus, esse Formam Elementi prædominantis, nihil attinet verba facere: essent enim omnia Mixta nihil nisi terra aut aqua, quippe in quibus terræ aut aquæ Forma prædominatur, argumento ipsius Cardani, qui Elementum illud dominari concludit, cujus motu Mixtum movetur. ast moventur omnia Mixta deorsum; qui motus cum soli terræ & aquæ competat, vel hujus vel illius Forma in omni Mixto prædominabitur; & quia Forma dat esse rei, necessario omnia Mixta erunt aut terra aut aqua, quum terræ vel aquæ Formam obtineant; quod delirium indignum est, de quo plura verba faciamus.
units.tr: LXIV. One way seems to be left to them for escaping these straits, namely if they go over to Alexander, who acknowledges no form other than the forms of the elements concurring in a certain proportion in any mixed body and constituting, by their harmony, as it were a single form. For if they follow this, they will not be pressed by that difficulty of creating substance out of nothing. But while this opinion avoids one absurdity, it falls into many others, which the Aristotelian doctrine of forms cannot bear in any way. Hence most Peripatetics condemn it as most inept, and would rather be reduced to anything than approve it. On this point it will be enough to have brought forward Scaliger as a witness, who attacks this opinion of Alexander in many places, and especially in Exercitationes 307, 20, where he writes thus: For they are the most graceless, most ignorant and most unfortunate of all mortals, who think that from a manifold matter (for this is what the elements are), and from their contaminated forms, one form can arise of itself, which is the cause of the existence of the whole mass, without the coming of one external form, by which the whole is held together in the bond and office of continuity and unity. And he adds much more to the same effect. As for the opinion which Cardano followed in his Controversies, and which he also ascribes to Averroes, namely that the form of an inanimate mixed body, and likewise of the similar parts in plants and animals, is the form of the predominant element, there is no need to speak of it. For then all mixed bodies would be nothing but earth or water, since in each the form of earth or water would predominate, as Cardano himself concludes from the argument that the element whose motion moves the mixed body is the one that dominates. But all mixed bodies move downward; and since this motion belongs only to earth and water, the form of one or the other will predominate in every mixed body; and because the form gives the thing its being, all mixed bodies will necessarily be either earth or water, since they hold the form of earth or water. This absurdity is unworthy of serious refutation, and we need not spend more words on it.

units.la: LXV. Et hactenus quidem de Formarum origine. sed & ab earundem interitu desumere licet eandem argumentationem. Etenim substantiam aliquam in nihilum redigi, æque est impossibile, atq; ex nihilo creari, nisi ab ipso & solo Deo. quare si Formæ in nihilum abeunt, neq; id fit ab ipso Deo (quod certe neq; est verisimile, stante hac mundi machina, quotidie aliquas ejus partes à Deo in nihilum reduci; neq; ab ipsis dicitur ulpiam) relinquitur, ut nequaquam sint substantiæ. quod per se evidens, juvat tamen ex ipso Scaligero amplius deducere. Is commentario in primum de Plantis probaturus ex Aristotelicis principijs animæ immortalitatem, ita fatur: Si è nihilo nihil fieri potest, igitur id quod est aliquid, in nihilum reverti nequit. par enim ratio creationis & corruptionis. Fraterea cum triplex substantia sit, Materia, Forma & Compositum utroq;, hoc quidem Compositum dicitur generari, Materiam scilicet ineunte Forma; eadem vero abeunte corrumpi. Sane ipsa Materia neutiquam per se corrumpitur, nempe semper obtinet suum & ·: sed per accidens corrumpitur, cum aliam subit Formam. at Forma quum longe sit nobilior quam Materia, tanto minus corrumpi illam decet. si enim quod fit, ut sit hoc, id est Materia ipsa, non abolebitur; tanto minus abolebitur quod facit ut illa sit hoc. Ad id confugient ut dicant in Materia potentiam reverti, unde etiam Formæ omnes educantur. sed cum Materia, quæ est ignobilior, existat aliquid actu semper; igitur extare quoq; semper actu Formam, quæ nobilior est, necesse est: præterea non esse Formas in Materia potestate, nisi quatenus earum susceptibilis est: hæc ille quidem non pro omni Forma, sed pro anima humana. quominus tamen cunctis Formis ista sint communia, causa dici nulla potest. quod cum ipse videret, neque tamen vellet alias Formas ab interitu Compositi manere, in fine disputationis illius ait, ista à se prolata, ut eorum, qui animæ immortalitatem negant, desperatam contumaciam quatefaceret, non quod ipse sic sentiret: sequeretur enim, Formas certo numero esse circumscriptas, id quod à Veritate prorsus penitusq; sit alienum. Nihil attinet nunc quærere, quam sapienter factum sit, tantam rem, quanta est animæ immortalitas, contra tam desperatæ contumaciæ adversarios, ejusmodi probare argumento, quod ipse pro vero admittere non audeas. hoc dicimus, sive ita senserit Scaliger, sive non, inevitabiliter sequi ut illa, quæ ibi dixit vera sint, non de anima tantum, sed de omni Forma, si Forma est substantia, itaq; & quæ alibi in eundem disputat finem, nihilo magis pro Anima faciunt, quam pro Forma, & si vera sunt de illa, sunt etiam de ista. ita enim argumentatur; Animam esse simplicem & omnis compositionis expertem; propterea cum è partibus non constet, ne in partes quidem resolubilem esse. & neq; ita posse corrumpi, ut in nihilum evanescat; quia sic è converso fieri etiam aliquid ex nihilo naturaliter posset, quod est contra decreta omnium Peripateticorum. hæc quin in omnes æque quadrent Formas, ac in mentes humanas, afferri nihil potest; ac propterea, si intereunte composito intereunt etiam Formæ, substantiæ non erant, siquidem in nihilum redigi substantia nequaquam potest. aut interire eas, tum sequitur necessario ex isto axiomate, Quod Formæ, præter Mentem, sunt inseparabiles, neque aliter nisi in subjecto subsistere ullo modo possunt: tum ab ipsis dicitur Peripateticis. Scribit enim Vicomercatus, Post rei interitum nullam manere Formam, excepta sola anima humana; & sic alij quoq; scribunt, Omnem Formam materialem esse interitui obnoxiam. materiales autem vocant Formas omnes præter Mentem. Pleriq; tamen silentio hunc scopulum prætervehuntur; & in fusissimis de Naturali philosophia tractationibus, inter innumeras, & sæpe admodum futiles quæstiones, verbum de hac re nullum faciunt, neq; omnino attingunt, quid de Formis fiat, ubi res, quarum Formæ sunt, intereunt. si tamen urgeantur, dicere aliud non poterunt, quam quod quidam eorum ingenue confessi sunt, Re intereunte, Formas unà interire. namq; si non intereunt, manent necesse est. aut manere neq; in Materia illa, quam prius informabant, neq; extra illam possunt. non in ipsa, quia Forma specifica nova introduci in Materiam ex eorum decretis non potest, nisi pristina prius aboleatur, non extra ipsam, cum statuant Formas esse inseparabiles. itaq; interire necesse est.
units.tr: LXV. So much for the origin of Forms. But the same argument can also be drawn from their destruction. For to reduce any substance to nothing is just as impossible as to create one out of nothing, except by God alone. So if Forms pass into nothing, and this does not happen through God himself (which is certainly unlikely, since, with the mechanism of the world as it is, some parts of it are not reduced to nothing by God every day, and nowhere is it said that they are), it follows that Forms are by no means substances. This is evident in itself, but it helps to draw the point further from Scaliger himself. In his commentary on the first book of the Plants, intending to prove from Aristotelian principles the immortality of the soul, he says: If nothing can come from nothing, then what is something cannot revert to nothing. For the reasoning of creation and corruption is parallel. Moreover, since substance is threefold, Matter, Form and the Composite of both, the Composite is said to be generated when Form is joined to Matter, and to be corrupted when Form departs. Matter itself is certainly not corrupted in itself, since it always keeps its own [nature]; it is corrupted only accidentally, when it takes on another Form. But since Form is far nobler than Matter, it is all the less fitting that Form should be corrupted. For if that by which a thing becomes this, namely Matter itself, will not be abolished, then all the less will be abolished that which makes Matter to be this. Here they will take refuge, saying that Matter returns to potentiality, from which all Forms are also drawn out. But since Matter, which is the less noble, always exists in some actuality, it is necessary that Form, which is nobler, also always exists in actuality. Further, Forms are not in Matter potentially except insofar as Matter is susceptible to them. Scaliger said this of the human soul, not of every Form. Yet no reason can be given why these things should not be common to all Forms. Seeing this himself, but not wishing that other Forms should remain after the destruction of the Composite, at the end of that disputation he says that he put forward these things in order to shake the stubborn despair of those who deny the immortality of the soul, and that he did not think so himself; for it would follow that Forms are bounded by a fixed number, which is wholly and utterly alien to the truth. There is no point now in asking how wisely it was done to prove so great a matter as the immortality of the soul, against such desperately stubborn opponents, by an argument which you yourself dare not admit as true. We say this: whether Scaliger thought so or not, it inevitably follows that what he said there is true not only of the soul but of every Form, if Form is a substance. And what he argues elsewhere to the same end helps the soul no more than it helps Form; and if it is true of the one, it is true of the other too. For he argues thus: The soul is simple and free of all composition; therefore, since it does not consist of parts, it cannot even be resolved into parts. Nor can it be corrupted so as to vanish into nothing; for in that case, conversely, something could also naturally come from nothing, which is contrary to the decrees of all the Peripatetics. Nothing can be brought forward to show that these things do not apply equally to all Forms as to human minds. Therefore, if Forms perish when the Composite perishes, they were not substances, since substance can by no means be reduced to nothing. Or, if they perish, it follows necessarily from this axiom, that Forms, apart from the Mind, are inseparable and cannot subsist in any way except in a subject: and this is also stated by the Peripatetics themselves. For Vicomercatus writes, After the destruction of a thing no Form remains, except the human soul alone; and others also write thus, that every material Form is liable to perish. They call all Forms except the Mind material. Yet most people slip past this rock in silence. In the most extensive treatises on natural philosophy, among countless and often very trifling questions, they say nothing at all on this matter, and do not touch on what becomes of Forms when the things of which they are Forms perish. Yet if they are pressed, they will be able to say nothing else than what some of them have frankly confessed: that when the thing perishes, the Forms perish with it. For if they do not perish, they must remain; but they can remain neither in that Matter which they previously informed, nor outside it. Not in it, because, by their decrees, a new specific Form cannot be introduced into Matter unless the former one is first abolished; not outside it, since they hold that Forms are inseparable. Therefore they must perish.

units.la: LXVI. Nimis autem est puerile, hunc nodum solvere axiomate isto Aristotelico, de quo supra tam multa diximus, mus, nimirum non Formæ aut Materiæ, sed composito, ut Generationem, ita & Corruptionem competere; propterea q; Materiam & Formam non nisi per accidens, ut generari, ita & corrumpi. hanc evasionem tanti facit Averroes, ut plurimis in locis illam repetiverit. sed nihil facilius, quam ipsius futilitatem ostendere. etenim de Materia prima quid sibi velint, quando eam interire negant composito intereunte, facile est intellectu. de Forma autem adeo est absurdum, ut quomodo id fiat, ne imaginari quidem possis. Materiam enim manere aiunt, & nihil aliud pati, nisi quod novam Formam induat. at Formam manere, aut per se existentem seorsim, aut immigrantem in Materiam novam, hoc vero ipsi pernegant. at si non manet, interit: aut quæ dementia est, fateri aliquid desinere esse, & negare tamen illud interire? Interit igitur Forma; & si interit, nihil nostra interest, per se an per accidens interire dicatur.
units.tr: LXVI. But it is extremely childish to untie this knot by that Aristotelian axiom, about which we have said so much above, namely that generation, and likewise corruption, belongs not to Form or Matter but to the Composite; and therefore Matter and Form are generated and corrupted only accidentally. Averroes sets great store by this evasion, and has repeated it in very many places. But nothing is easier than to show its futility. For what they mean about prime Matter, when they deny that it perishes when the Composite perishes, is easy to understand. But concerning Form it is so absurd that you cannot even imagine how it could happen. For they say that Matter remains and suffers nothing except that it puts on a new Form. But that Form remains, either existing by itself apart, or passing into a new Matter, this they flatly deny. But if it does not remain, it perishes. Or what madness is it to admit that something ceases to be, and yet deny that it perishes? Therefore Form perishes; and if it perishes, it makes no difference to us whether it is said to perish in itself or accidentally.

units.la: Et tamen hoc ipsum falsum est, interire illam per accidens, cum potius è contrario ipsum Compositum per accidens interire dicendum sit, quippe quod non interiret, si Forma maneret. interit igitur, quia Forma interit, & propterea interit per accidens, quippe interiens ad interitum alterius. & certe Compositum non est re ipsa aliquid extra partes componentes; neq; corpus naturale, ex Materia & Forma Compositum, est aliquid tertium ab illis, nisi in intellectu. revera enim nihil est aliud, nisi Materia Formæ juncta, ex Peripati decretis, propterea q; ne datur quidem ulla affectio, quæ primario sit ipsius, sed quicquid ipso fit, id fit aut ratione Materiæ, aut ratione Formæ, aut utriusq; simul. jam Materiæ neq; per se soli, neq; junctim cum Forma, competit aut ortus aut interitus, nisi improprie loquendo, quandoquidem & ante ortum Compositi ipsa erat, & post ejusdem obitum ipsa manet, ne mutationem quidem ullam passa essentialem, sicut ipsi docent. at Forma cum Composito & esse incipit & definit, neq; aliud est Compositi generatio & corruptio, quam ipsius Formæ in Materia ortus & obitus. tunc enim unamquamq; rem generatam esse dicunt, quando in Materia teria incipit existere talis Forma ; & tunc corruptam, quando Forma illius interijt. unde facile est colligere, rem prorsus contrario modo fe habere, quam Ariftoteles dixerit, & ortum atq; interitum ipsi Formæ primario ac per fe competere, Composito tantum per accidens, quippe quod nequaquam totum aut generetur aut corrumpatur, sed altera tantum fui parte, nimirum Formâ, quæ sola & principium habet & finem, cum neutrum cadat in Materiam, utpote æternam ex ipsorum sententia : quod adeo fequitur ex illis Principijs, ut ipse effugere nequiverit Ariftoteles, quin id aliquando confiteretur ; quod fecit undecimo Metaphysicorum planissimis verbis, Μᾶλλον ἀρχὴ κυριωτέρα τῆς ὕλης δόξειεν ἂν εἶναι τὸ εἶδος καὶ ἡ μορφὴ. τοῦτο δὲ φθαρτόν. ὅλως οὖν οὐκ ἔστιν αἴτιος οὐσία, χωριστὴ καὶ καθ' ἑαυτήν. Videtur principalius Principium, quam Materia, esse species & Forma. hoc autem est corruptibile, itaq; haudquaquam est essentia aterna, separabilis & per se [existens.] Phrasin autem, Per accidens, ita hic usurpamus, quomodo usurpatur in ista re ab ipso Aristotele, & Aristotelicis : quum alioquin haudquaquam probemus, ut ea, quæ necessariâ consequentiâ fiunt, per accidens fieri dicantur. sed cum balbis sæpe nobis, vel invitis, balbutiendum est, ut tanto melius eos in ruborem demus. Consectum igitur est, Formam interire & in nihilum recidere : sicuti antea probatum est, illam ex nihilo oriri
units.tr: And yet even this is false, that Form perishes accidentally, since it should rather be said, on the contrary, that the Composite itself perishes accidentally, since it would not perish if the Form remained. Therefore it perishes because the Form perishes, and so it perishes accidentally, as something that perishes through the destruction of another. Indeed the Composite is not in fact anything apart from its component parts; and a natural body, composed of Matter and Form, is not something third beside them, except in the intellect. For in reality it is nothing other than Matter joined to Form, according to the decrees of the Peripatetics; and therefore no affection at all belongs to it primarily; whatever happens to it happens either by reason of the Matter, or by reason of the Form, or of both together. Now neither Matter alone, nor Matter joined with Form, admits of origin or destruction, except in an improper sense, since it existed even before the origin of the Composite and remains after its end, not having suffered any essential change, as they themselves teach. But Form begins and ceases to be together with the Composite; and the generation and corruption of the Composite is nothing other than the origin and end of the Form itself in Matter. For they say that each thing is generated when such a Form begins to exist in Matter, and corrupted when its Form has perished. Hence it is easy to gather that the matter stands in a manner entirely opposite to what Aristotle said, and that origin and destruction belong primarily and in themselves to Form, and to the Composite only accidentally, since the whole is by no means generated or corrupted, but only one part of it, namely the Form, which alone has both beginning and end, since neither falls on Matter, which is eternal by their own opinion. This follows so necessarily from those principles that Aristotle himself could not escape admitting it at some point; which he did in the eleventh book of the Metaphysics, in the plainest words: Form and shape would seem to be a more principal principle than Matter. But this is corruptible. Therefore altogether there is no essence that is separable and existing by itself. [Μᾶλλον ἀρχὴ κυριωτέρα τῆς ὕλης δόξειεν ἂν εἶναι τὸ εἶδος καὶ ἡ μορφὴ. τοῦτο δὲ φθαρτόν. ὅλως οὖν οὐκ ἔστιν αἴτιος οὐσία, χωριστὴ καὶ καθ' ἑαυτήν.] I use the phrase per accidens here as it is used on this matter by Aristotle himself and the Aristotelians, although I do not in any way approve that things which follow by a necessary consequence should be said to happen accidentally. But since we must often stammer with stammerers, whether we like it or not, so that we may put them to shame all the more. It follows, then, that Form perishes and falls back into nothing, just as it was proved before that it arises out of nothing.
LXVII.

units.la: Libet autem tractationem hanc, de Formæ in nihilum redactione, concludere verbis Pererij, viri acutissimi, & Peripatetici percelebris, qui Physicæ lib. 5. cap. 8. expressis verbis dicit, omnes Formas physicas in rei interitu non solum separari à Materia, ut fit in anima rationali, sed penitus interire : nec tamen Forma naturalis interitum, esse annihilationem. Quæ verba profecto talia sunt, ut indignationem moveant vel moderatissimis viris. Quis enim non gravissime indignetur, magnos alioquin viros eo usque Θαυμασιῶς illi philosophiæ fascinandos sese præbere, uti ad tuenda vanissima ejus ac salsissima de-
units.tr: I would like to conclude this discussion of the reduction of form to nothing with the words of Pererius, a most acute man and a very famous Peripatetic, who in his Physics, book 5, chapter 8, says in so many words: all physical forms, at the destruction of a thing, are not only separated from matter, as happens with the rational soul, but utterly perish; and yet a natural form's perishing is not annihilation. These words are truly such that they stir indignation even in the most moderate men. For who would not be deeply indignant that great men, otherwise, should allow themselves to be so bewitched [Θαυμασιῶς] by that philosophy as to lend their efforts to defending its most empty and most absurd de-
Chapter I.

units.la: decreta, ea proferant, quæ nemo nisi vecors crediderit? Quis enim sibi persuaderi patiatur, posse aliquid penitus interire; & tamen talem interitum non esse redactionem in nihilum, aut (ut ipsi amant loqui) annihilationem? Sed audiamus mirificas sane rationes, quibus invercundum hoc effatum suffulciatur. prima est: Alioquin ejus quoq; generatio deberet dici creatio. cujus argumenti ineptia ex ijs, quæ supra diximus de Formarum origine, per se apparet. sive enim Forma abeat in nihilum, sive non abeat; ejus tamen ortus nullus relinquitur, nisi ut ex nihilo creetur: quandoquidem nulla substantia aliter nisi vel ex præexistenti fit, vel ex nihilo creatur; ipsi autem Formam ex præexistente fieri, acerrime negant; ut necessarium sit, si substantia est, ex nihilo creari: quod cum non fiat, neq; ipsi fieri velint, inde confecimus quod ipsa neqtiaquam sit substantia. Altera Pererij ratio, cur Forma, cum penitus intereat, tamen dici non possit, in nihilum redigi, hæc est: Quod per eandem vim & dispositiones, quibus una Forma deletur ex Materia, continuo excitatur altera inhærens in eadem Materia; & sic corruptionem naturalem semper immediate consequitur generatio: cum necesse non sit, ut annihilationem sequatur semper alterius rei productio. Prosecto tam inanis est hæc ratio, ut nos pudeat eam refellere. faciendum tamen est, cum jam suetum nobis sit; cum vanissimis opinionum & axiomatum larvis luctari. Dicimus igitur ad rem nihil pertinere, an aliquid in rei abolitæ locum succedat; neq; eo effici, quominus illa dici possit esse abolita penitus, &, si ita fors ferat, in nihilum redacta. alioqui ne aeris quidem frigus annihilatum erit (ut sic dicamus) quando à Sole vel igne calor in eum introducitur. namq; & hic abolitionem unius rei sequitur immediata alterius productio. Quod si ne accidentia quidem inveniunt à successore solatium aut auxilium, quominus in nihilum abierint; imo si hoc ipso in nihilum abierunt, quia successorem acceperunt; sane potiori jure id de substantijs dicendum erit. Si enim Formæ sunt substantiæ, neq; duæ Formæ possunt magis subsistere simul in una Materia. ria, quam summus calor & summum frigus eodem tempore in eodem subjecto; neq; tamen Formæ uni plus unâ assignatur Materia, è qua ubi emigraverit, nullum aliud in mundo pateat misellæ receptaculum: quis non videt, à succedente Forma adeo nullum esse pereunti Formæ præsidium, quominus in nihilum abeat; ut ex eo ipso, quod altera ipsi Forma successit, certissime concludere liceat, eam in nihilum redactam. eo ipso enim indivisibili temporis momento, quo nova Forma in Materiam fuit introducta, pristinam emigrare necesse erat. emigranti autem cum nullum alibi præsto esset domicilium, neq; consistere sola posset; nihil aliud relinquebatur, nisi ut in nihilum abiret. nimis igitur mirabiles sunt istæ præstigiæ, dicere, aliquid non esse ibi, ubi fuerat prius, neq; esse alibi uspiam in universa rerum natura, & non esse quicquam omnino; & tamen non in nihilum esse redactum. sed de Pererij verbis satis.
units.tr: Who would bring forward such things, which no one but a madman would believe? For who would allow himself to be persuaded that something can perish entirely, and yet that such a perishing is not a reduction into nothing, or (as they themselves like to say) an annihilation? But let us hear the truly marvellous reasons by which this shameless saying is propped up. The first is: Otherwise its generation too ought to be called creation. The absurdity of this argument is plain in itself from what we have said above about the origin of forms. For whether a form passes into nothing or does not, no origin for it remains except that it is created out of nothing. Since no substance comes into being except either from something pre-existing or out of nothing, and they most vehemently deny that a form comes from something pre-existing, it follows that, if a form is a substance, it must be created out of nothing. Since this does not happen, and they themselves do not wish it to happen, we conclude from this that it is by no means a substance. The second reason of Pereira, why a form, though it perishes entirely, cannot yet be said to be reduced into nothing, is this: Because by the same force and dispositions by which one form is destroyed from matter, another is at once brought forth, inhering in the same matter; and so generation always immediately follows natural corruption, since it is not necessary that the production of another thing should always follow an annihilation. Truly this reason is so empty that we are ashamed to refute it. Yet it must be done, since it is now our custom to wrestle with the most empty phantoms of opinions and axioms. We say, therefore, that it has nothing to do with the matter whether something takes the place of the thing destroyed; nor does this prevent that thing from being said to have been wholly abolished and, if so it should happen, reduced into nothing. Otherwise, the cold of the air would not be annihilated either (to speak thus) when heat is introduced into it by the sun or by fire; for here too the immediate production of one thing follows the abolition of another. But if accidents do not find any solace or help in their successor against passing into nothing; indeed, if they have passed into nothing for this very reason, that they received a successor, then surely the same must be said with greater right of substances. For if forms are substances, then two forms cannot subsist together in one matter any more than the greatest heat and the greatest cold can at the same time in the same subject; and yet no more than one matter is assigned to one form, and when it has emigrated from this, no other place of refuge in the world lies open to the poor thing. Who does not see that there is no protection for the perishing form against passing into nothing from the succeeding form, so that from the very fact that another form has succeeded it, we may most certainly conclude that it has been reduced into nothing? For at that very indivisible moment of time in which the new form was introduced into the matter, the former had to depart. But since, for the departing form, no other dwelling was at hand, and it could not subsist alone, nothing else was left but that it should pass into nothing. Those tricks are therefore too marvellous: to say that something is not there where it was before, and is nowhere else in the whole of nature, and is not anything at all; and yet has not been reduced into nothing. But enough about Pereira's words.

units.la: Quandoquidem igitur confecimus; Formam & oriri è nihilo, & in nihilum abire; cum neutrum cadat in substantiam (ex unanimi ipsorum quoq; Peripateticorum consensu) ut nimirum aut fiat ex nihilo, aut in nihilum abeat: efficitur necessario, Formam minime esse substantiam, proptereaq; vanam esse ac futilem totam Peripateticorum de Forma doctrinam, utpote nixam hoc fundamento, Quod Forma sit substantia.
units.tr: Since, therefore, we have concluded that a form both arises out of nothing and passes into nothing, and since neither of these can befall a substance (by the unanimous consent of the Peripatetics themselves), namely that it should either come from nothing or pass into nothing, it necessarily follows that a form is in no way a substance; and therefore the whole Peripatetic doctrine of form is vain and futile, being founded upon this foundation, that form is a substance.
LXVIII.

units.la: Namq; sensisse Averroem, quod ipsi attribuit Fernelius, propriam partium similarium Formam esse ipsius temperamenti rationem; veremur ut pro vero admittant Peripatetici. dixit id quidem tum alibi, tum præcipue 1. Coll. cap. 1. sed & contrarium dixit locis non paucioribus; & si non dixisset, erroris illum notassent haud dubie Aristotelici, quibus nihil ægrius est, quam quod Galenus nullam aliam agnoscit Formam, non in Elementis modo, sed & in Compositis, præter illas quatuor qualitates & illarum temperamentum: adeoq; hæc res cunctis videtur absurda, ut ne ipsi quidem Galenici audeant hic præceptoris sui partes tueri, sed eo deserto in Aristotelis castra
units.tr: For we fear that the Peripatetics will not admit as true that Averroes held what Fernelius attributes to him, namely that the proper form of similar parts is the very ratio of their temperament. He indeed said this both elsewhere and especially in the first Colliget, chapter 1. But he also said the contrary in not a few places; and if he had not said it, the Aristotelians, to whom nothing is more distasteful than that Galen acknowledges no other form, not only in the elements but also in compounds, except those four qualities and their temperament, would undoubtedly have marked him as in error. So absurd does this matter seem to all, that not even the Galenists themselves dare to defend their master's part here, but, deserting him, go over to the camp of Aristotle.
Chapter I.

units.la: stra transfugiant, aut omnes; aut maxima saltem pars. hoc ipsum tamen debuerat illis ansam haud spernendam ministrare, altius de fictitia illa Forma substantiali cogitandi, quam à tanto viro non repudiatam modo scirent, sed tanto-pere damnatam, ut indignam duxerit, cujus vel mentionem ullam faceret. namq; in immensa ista librorum turba, quae ad manus nostras pervenit, ne ipsum quidem nomen Formae Aristotelicae unquam comparet, nisi semel aut iterum. Per Totam enim Substantiam, & Proprietatem Substantiae, quam toties ad partes vocat, ubi cum sua Crasi expedire se in reddendis causis non potest, qui Formam intelligendam putet, haud satis se in scriptis ipsius versatum ostendat. utcunq; enim interdum Temperamentum & Totam Substantiam velut res admodum diversas inter se opponat, semper tamen eo revolvitur, ut haec rursus inter se confundat, quod jam ante nos annotavit, & exemplis aliquot docuit, magnum Medicinae columen Sennertus. idq; ut magis etiamnum constet, nos ijs, quae ab eo allata sunt, nonnulla adhuc addemus. Quarto simpl. cap. 15. diserte scribit, ut plus de hoc vel illo Elemento inest in aliquo Composito, ita exurgere illam substantiae proprietatem. Ενια μεν γὰρ πυρὸς ἔχει πλεῖον, ἢ τῶν ἄλλων στοιχείων, ἐνια δὲ ὕδατος, ἄλλα δὲ, εἰ οὕτως ἔτυχε, γῆς, ἔνια δὲ ἀέρος. ἐξ οὖν τοιαύτης ἀνισότητος αἱ τῶν κατὰ μέρος σωμάτων ἰδιότητες ἀποτελέσθησαν. Quaedam enim habent plus ignis, quam aliorum elementorum, quaedam plus aquae, alia, si ita usu veniat, plus terrae, quaedam autem aeris. ex tali igitur inaequalitate particularium corporum proprietates constituuntur. & qui passim totam alimentorum rationem, & cur illo, quo unum animalis genus nutritur, aliud nequaquam nutriri possit, referat ad κοινωνίαν τινὰ καὶ συγγένειαν καὶ οἰκειότητα ἐν ταῖς ποιότησι, communicationem quandam & affinitatem & familiaritatem in qualitatibus: & tertio Simpl. 6. dicat illam οἰκειότητα fieri κατὰ τὴν ἰδιότητα ὅλης ουσίας, secundum proprietatem totius substantiae: quod & repetit 4. simpl. 10. Τροφαὶ μόνα τὰ σύμφυλα καὶ οἰκεῖα ταῖς ὕλαις τῶν τρεφομένων οὐσίαις· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τῶν
units.tr: or all of them, or at least the greater part. Yet this very fact ought to have given them no small occasion to think more carefully about that fictitious "substantial form" of thinking, which they would have known was not only rejected but condemned so strongly by so great a man that he considered it unworthy of even a mention. For in that huge mass of books that has come into our hands, the very name of the Aristotelian Form never appears, except once or twice. Indeed, anyone who thinks the Form must be understood, when he so often appeals to "whole substance" and "property of substance," and cannot explain the causes with his own "mixture," shows that he is not well versed in Aristotle's writings. For although he sometimes sets temperament and whole substance against each other as things quite different, he always returns to confusing them again, as the great pillar of medicine, Sennertus, already noted before us and showed by several examples. So that this may be even clearer, we will add some further points to those he has brought forward. In the fourth book of Simple Medicines, chapter 15, he writes plainly that as more of this or that element is present in a compound, so that property of the substance arises. [Some things have more of fire than of the other elements, some more of water, others, as it happens, more of earth, and some of air. From such inequality the properties of particular bodies are produced.] Some things have more fire than the other elements, some more water, others, if it so happens, more earth, and some more air. Therefore the properties of particular bodies are constituted from such inequality. And he who everywhere refers the whole account of foods, and why one animal kind can be nourished by one thing and another cannot be nourished at all, to [κοινωνίαν τινὰ καὶ συγγένειαν καὶ οἰκειότητα ἐν ταῖς ποιότησι] a certain communion, kinship and affinity in the qualities; and in the third book of Simples, chapter 6, says that this affinity comes about [κατὰ τὴν ἰδιότητα ὅλης οὐσίας] according to the property of the whole substance; which he repeats in the fourth book of Simples, chapter 10: [Τροφαὶ μόνα τὰ σύμφυλα καὶ οἰκεῖα ταῖς ὕλαις τῶν τρεφομένων οὐσίαις] Only those things are foods which are congenial and familiar to the material substances of what is nourished.

units.la: 2. Facul. nat. 10 / 7. de usu par. 8. τῶν ἐλεσμάτων καὶ τῶν φαρμάκων ἐχ' ἓν εἶδος ἁπασι τοῖς ζῴοις· ἐσὶ καὶ ἃ γὰρ τὴν οἰκείαν ἑκάσου αὐτῶν ὄσιαν τε ἅμα καὶ διάθεσιν ἡλεταί τε καὶ ὠφελεῖται πρὸς ἀμφοῖν. Ea sola alimentorum vicem prabent, qua sunt cognata & familiaria totis substantiis eorum qua nutriuntur. ideoq; non est omnibus animalibus unum idemq; ciborum atq; medicamentorum genus. quippe ipsorum unumquodq; pro peculiari substantia simul atq; dispositione deleetetur & juvatur ab ambobus: alibi tamen hanc totius substantiae affinitatem ad temperamenti leges revocat. Εωειδὴ τὰ μὲν μᾶλλόν ἐσιν οἰκεῖα τῇ τῶ σώματος ἡμῶν φύσει, τὰ δὲ ἥττον, καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν τῇδε τῇ συζυγία τ' κράσεως, τὰ δὲ ἐν τῇδε. Quandoquidem alia sunt magis familiaria naturis corporum nostrorum, alia vero minus: & alia quidem in hac temperamenti conjugatione, alia vero in alia. & capite sequenti nihil nisi calorem, frigus, humiditatem, & siccitatem crepat, quorum moderatione aut excessu fiat, ut aliud aliis sit familiare alimentum, vel secus. Similiter cum 5. simpl. 1. dixisset, Deleteria, sicut & purgantia omnia, & antidotorum ac attrahentium pleraq;, ἀλλοιεῖν καθ' ὅλην ἑαυτῶν τὴν ὄσίαν, alterare secundum totam sui substantiam, quod & repetit cap. 17. inquiens attrahentia illa agere οἰκειότητι ποιότητος, ὅτω γε ἐδὲν ἄλλο ἐσὶν, ἢ ἀμοιότητι τ' ὅλης ὄσίας. proprietate qualitatis, quod nihil aliud sit, quam totius substantia similitudine. quam totius substantiæ similitudinem, mox directo opponit crasi, quippe Antidota ἀλλοιοῦν ἢ τοι κατὰ ἓνα ποιότητα μίαν, ἢ συζυγίαν ἐκ δυοῖν, ἢ κατὰ τὰς ὅλας ὄσιας: alterare aut secundum unam aliquam qualitatem, aut conjugationem ex duabus, aut secundum totas substantias: eodem tamen in loco ad temperamentum rursus recurrit, εἰδέναι χρὴ τὰς ἁπλοποιείας ἀπάτας δυνάμεις ἐνωλιλοιάτας ὄσης τῇ κράσει τοῖς ὑπ' αὐτῶν βλαπτομένοις σώμασι: sciendum est, omnes lethiferas qualitates maxime contrarias esse temperamento corporum, quae ab ipsis laduntur. E quibus satis apparet, eum ex aliorum sententia locutum esse libro περὶ συσάσεως cap. 11. quando ait
units.tr: Book 2 of On the Natural Faculties, ch. 10 / Book 7 of On the Use of the Parts, ch. 8: [τῶν ἐλεσμάτων καὶ τῶν φαρμάκων ἐχ' ἓν εἶδος ἁπασι τοῖς ζῴοις· ἐσὶ καὶ ἃ γὰρ τὴν οἰκείαν ἑκάσου αὐτῶν ὄσιαν τε ἅμα καὶ διάθεσιν ἡλεταί τε καὶ ὠφελεῖται πρὸς ἀμφοῖν] Those alone supply the role of food which are akin and familiar to the whole substances of the things nourished. Therefore not all animals have one and the same kind of food and medicines; for each of them is delighted and benefited by both, according to its own peculiar substance and disposition. Elsewhere, however, he refers this affinity of the whole substance back to the laws of temperament: [Ἐπειδὴ τὰ μὲν μᾶλλόν ἐστιν οἰκεῖα τῇ τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν φύσει, τὰ δὲ ἥττον, καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν τῇδε τῇ συζυγίᾳ τῆς κράσεως, τὰ δὲ ἐν τῇδε] Since some things are more familiar to the natures of our bodies, others less, and some in this conjugation of temperament, others in that. And in the following chapter he chatters about nothing but heat, cold, moisture and dryness, by whose moderation or excess it comes about that one food is familiar to one body and another to another, or not. Similarly, when in the fifth book of Simples, chapter 1, he had said that all deadly things, like purgatives, and most antidotes and attractives, [ἀλλοιεῖν καθ' ὅλην ἑαυτῶν τὴν οὐσίαν] alter according to their whole substance, which he also repeats in chapter 17, saying that those attractives act [οἰκειότητι ποιότητος], which is nothing other than [ἀμοιότητι τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας]: by the proprietary quality, which is nothing else than the likeness of the whole substance. He soon directly opposes this likeness of the whole substance to temperament, since antidotes alter either according to one single quality, or a conjunction of two, or according to the whole substances: to alter either according to one quality, or a conjugation of two, or according to whole substances. Yet in the same place he returns again to temperament: [εἰδέναι χρὴ τὰς ἁπλοποιείας ἀπάσας δυνάμεις ἐναντιωτάτας ὑπάρχειν τῇ κράσει τοῖς ὑπ' αὐτῶν βλαπτομένοις σώμασι] one must know that all deadly qualities are most contrary to the temperament of the bodies which are harmed by them. From these things it sufficiently appears that he spoke in accordance with the opinion of others in the book [περὶ συστάσεως], chapter 11, when he says
Chapter I.

units.la: alt τὴν ὕλην ἀσίων συνίστασθαι ἐκ συναμφοτέρων, τοῦ τε εἴδους, καὶ ἢ ὑποδεχομένης αὐτὸ ὕλης· totam substantiam constare ex duobus, è Forma, atq; ex Materia ipsam suscipiente, quæ verba videntur omnino Aristotelicam Formam approbare. reverâ tamen nec illic quidem aliam intelligit Formam, quam temperamentum, quod evidenter apparet ex his verbis; χερὶ γὰρ ὁ μόνον, οἷς ἀέρες καὶ ψυχρὸς καὶ ξηρὸς καὶ ὑγρὸς περιφερομένων, ἑκάστου τε γίνεται μορίου, ἐγνωκέναι τὸν ἰατρὸν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅσα ἐστὶ λίθος ἐστελλόντα, ὡς μὲν τῶν ὀστῶν ἐστι πεῖρα, οἷς δὲ τῶν σαρκῶν τε καὶ νεύρων καὶ φλεβῶν, ἑκάστου τε τῶν ἄλλων τῶν ἀτλῶν. Oportet enim medicum nosse, non modo quod calido, frigido, humido, atq; sicco inter se contemperatis, unaquæq; pars sit, sed & specialiter inquirere, quod sit temperamentum ossium, qualeq; illud carnium, nervorum, venarum, & uniuscujusq; similarium. Alias autem per τὸ εἶδος intelligit non Aristotelicam sed Democriteam Formam, τὸ σχῆμα nimirum καὶ τὴν σύνθεσιν, figuram atq; compositionem, quod apparebit, siquis cap. 12. & 13. sexti de Usu partium legerit: ubi longo sermonis tractu de Causis agens, quatuor illis, quas ipse ponit, Scopo, Efficienti, Materiæ, Instrumentis, vix dignam putat quæ annumeretur quintam hanc, quam τὸ καθ' ὃ καὶ τὴν καθ' ὃ τὸ εἶδος αἰτίαν, id secundum quod, & formalem Causam, appellat. qualia etiam sexti de Sanitate tuenda capite tertio ab ipso proferuntur.
units.tr: Galen says that the substance of a thing is composed of two things together, the form and the matter that receives it [τὴν ὕλην ... συνίστασθαι ἐκ συναμφοτέρων, τοῦ τε εἴδους, καὶ ... ὑποδεχομένης αὐτὸ ὕλης]. Words like these seem wholly to approve the Aristotelian Form: that the whole substance consists of two things, of Form and of the Matter that receives it. In truth, however, even there he understands by Form nothing other than temperament, as is clear from these words: [χρὴ γὰρ τὸν ἰατρὸν ... ἐγνωκέναι]: It is necessary for the physician to know not only how each part is constituted by the hot, cold, moist and dry in mutual mixture, but also to inquire specifically what the temperament of the bones is, and what that of the flesh, nerves and veins is, and of each of the similar parts. But by [τὸ εἶδος] he understands not the Aristotelian but the Democritean Form, namely [τὸ σχῆμα καὶ τὴν σύνθεσιν], figure and composition. This will be apparent to anyone who reads chapters 12 and 13 of the sixth book On the Use of the Parts. There, treating of Causes at length, he thinks that the four he himself lists (Purpose, Efficient, Matter, Instruments) are scarcely worth adding to them this fifth, which he calls [τὸ καθ' ὃ καὶ τὴν καθ' ὃ τὸ εἶδος αἰτίαν], that according to which, and the formal Cause. He puts forward similar things in the third chapter of the sixth book On Preserving Health.

units.la: LXIX. Cum igitur viderent tum Medici tum Philosophi, repudiatam fuisse & Galeno Formam substantialem, in suspicionem venire debuerant, non sine Causa factum id ab ipso fuisse. Quanquam enim nos nullius hominis auctoritatem in quacunq; Philosophiæ parte valere quicquam volimus, nisi quatenus argumentis tueri se ipsam potest; cum illis tamen alia res est, qui omnia autoritatibus metiuntur. quare illi in tanti momenti re tanti viri judicium non debuerant ita neglectui habere; qui præsertim nec primus nec solus hoc Formæ commentum rejecit: quandoquidem dem universa Stoicorum secta illam similiter damnavit, quamquam informem illam Materiam primam cum Aristotele agnoscerent. Attamen & ex illa communi Materia quatuor Elementa, & ex Elementis omnia fabricabant, ablq; ulla Forma substantiali, sola novarum qualitatum introductione contenti: quæ ipsa Platonis quoq; fuit Philosophia, uti ex Timæo clare apparet, quicquid Aristotelici in contrarium dicant. Non solus igitur Galenus, sed cum Stoicis secutus Platonem, veteresq; Philosophos ad unum omnes, quorum nemo istam substantialem Formam agnovit, hac in parte ab Aristotele discessit. neq; obest, quod à veritate & ipse non minus aberraverit cum sua Crasi, quam Peripatus cum Forma substantiali. facilius enim est, etiam maximis ingenijs, commissos ab aliis errores animadvertere, quam Verum invenire, inq; eorum locum substituere. Scimus quidem mancipia Aristotelicorum deliriorum solere amarulento dente Galenum proscindere, quod avidissimus carpendi se meliorem, sola obtrectandi prurigine, non Veritatis amore, in Aristotelem incursaverit, quoties aliquid in ipso redarguit. ast non Galenum, sed ipsos calumniandi studio nimium indulsisse, satis notum est omnibus, qui in Galenicis scriptis versati. quippe quod de seipso prædicat, ὅτι ἀνούλους ὀνομάζει τὰς ἑαυτῶν ἀναγορεύοντας ἀπό ἕνος ἀνδρὸς, ἐκλέγοι δὲ τὰ παρ' ἑκάστοις καλὰ, quod servos nominet eos, qui ab ullo viro denominationem sibi assumunt, quodq; eligat quæ apud unumquemq; egregia sint, apparet illum re ipsa studuisse implere: & si non semper optima elegit, non ipse, sed communis mortalium cœcitas accusetur. fecit quod in se erat: elegit quæ optima ipsi videbantur; neq; quicquam ipsi propterea minus placuit, quia Aristoteli placuerat, si verum id esse judicaret. imo in talibus solet cum perhonorifica mentione laudare Aristotelem ejusdem sententiæ autorem. & venia illi esse debuit Aristotelem reprehendendi, qui ne Hippocratem quidem (cui tantum ipse tribuit, quantum nemo ignorat) sustineat parcere, ubi ipsum Veritati parum consentanea locutum esse existmat: præsertim cum illa, in quibus Aristotelem castigat, sint pleraq;
units.tr: LXIX. Since physicians and philosophers both saw that Galen had also rejected the substantial Form, they ought to have suspected that he had not done so without reason. For although we want the authority of no man to count for anything in any part of philosophy, except insofar as it can defend itself by arguments, the matter is different for those who measure everything by authorities. Therefore they ought not to have disregarded the judgment of so great a man on a matter of such importance, especially since he was neither the first nor the only one to reject this invention of Form. The whole school of the Stoics likewise condemned it, although they acknowledged with Aristotle that formless First Matter. Yet even from that common Matter they built the four Elements, and from the Elements everything else, without any substantial Form, content only with the introduction of new qualities. This was also the philosophy of Plato himself, as is clear from the Timaeus, whatever the Aristotelians say to the contrary. Therefore it was not Galen alone, but Galen following the Stoics and Plato, and all the ancient philosophers without exception, none of whom recognised that substantial Form, who departed from Aristotle on this point. Nor does it count against him that he himself strayed from the truth no less with his own Crasis than the Peripatetics did with the substantial Form. For it is easier, even for the greatest minds, to notice errors committed by others than to discover the Truth and put something in its place. We know indeed that the slaves of Aristotelian nonsense are wont to tear at Galen with a bitter tooth, saying that he, most eager to carp and to appear the better man, attacked Aristotle whenever he refuted something in him, from a mere itch to disparage and not from love of Truth. But that it was not Galen but they themselves who indulged too much in the eagerness to slander is well known to all who are versed in Galen's writings. For what he says of himself, that [ὅτι δούλους ὀνομάζει τοὺς ἑαυτοὺς ἀπό ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς ὀνομάζειν ἀναγορεύοντας, ἐκλέγοι δὲ τὰ παρ' ἑκάστοις καλά], that he calls slaves those who take a name for themselves from any one man, and that he chooses what is excellent in each, shows that in fact he aimed to do exactly this. And if he did not always choose the best, the blame lies not with him but with the common blindness of mortals. He did what was in him to do: he chose what seemed best to himself. Nor did anything please him less merely because it had pleased Aristotle, if he judged it to be true. Indeed, in such cases he usually praises Aristotle with most honourable mention as the author of the same opinion. And Aristotle ought to have been allowed to be rebuked by him, since Aristotle does not even spare Hippocrates (to whom Galen attributed as much as nobody doubts), when he thinks Hippocrates has said something little consonant with the truth; especially since those things for which he castigates Aristotle are for the most part
Chapter I.

units.la: pleraq; adeo enormia ac portentosa, ut ipsa illa monstra, in quæ sententias Prisco-rum nequaquam ita pravas, sæpè etiam optimás, passim transformavit ac deformavit Aristoteles, aut æquent, aut antegredian-tur; quicquid obstinati nugentur pro suo Præceptore ac contra Galenum Peripatetici. Et quam non obtrectandi studio ista coarguerit Galenus, vel hinc apparet, quod tam pauca attigit è tam grandi sylva. certe præter illa, quæ nos toto hoc opere, ipsa instituti hujus necessitate coacti, in medium producimus, tot adhuc Aristotelis errores supersunt, ut magnum ijs volumen implere possemus, neq; tamen quicquam eorum, quæ Ramus aut alij ante nos exagitaverunt, attingeremus. Sed & à candore nostro plurimum abest illa alienam Famam ex professo traducendi rabies, & ab instituto nostro, cum propositum nobis sit, Veritatem docere, non aliena errata πεϱιϱ-ϱεινγμαλίσαι, illis tantum exceptis, quæ nisi demoliamur, nostra introducere non possumus.
units.tr: for the most part so enormous and monstrous that they equal or surpass those very monsters into which Aristotle, in many places, transformed and deformed the opinions of the ancients, which were by no means so perverse, and often most excellent. Whatever the obstinate Peripatetics babble on behalf of their Master and against Galen. And that Galen did not expose these things out of a desire to disparage is clear even from this: that he touched on so few things out of so great a forest. Certainly, apart from those things which we, compelled by the necessity of this very undertaking, bring forward throughout this whole work, there still remain so many errors of Aristotle that we could fill a large volume with them, and yet we would not touch on any of those which Ramus or others before us have attacked. But that rage of deliberately tearing apart another's reputation is also far from our candour, and far from our purpose, since we intend to teach the Truth, not to go round picking at the errors of others; except for those which, unless we demolish them, we cannot introduce our own.

units.la: Et eundem quoq; Galeni animum fuisse, nemo nisi odio & iræ indulgens negabit; ac proinde ille, qui & vivebat eo tempore, quo Peripatetica Philosophia summopere in scholis florebat, & amicis ex illa secta utebatur quam conjunctissimis, & permulta ejus placita retinebat ac sequebatur, nunquam principale hoc illius caput sustulisset, nisi multæ magnæq; absurditates, quibus id est implicatum, hoc ipsi suasissent. quod tamen non in eum finem proserimus, ac si Galeni de Forma judicium pro argumento valere deberet. imo nisi aliunde, ac solidis rationibus, fecimus planissimum, Formam Aristotelicam esse figmentum merum, fidem nullam aut nobis aut ipsi haberi postulamus.
units.tr: And that Galen had this same mind no one will deny, unless he indulges in hatred and anger. Accordingly, he who lived at the time when Peripatetic philosophy flourished greatly in the schools, who used as friends the most intimate men of that sect, and who retained and followed many of its tenets, would never have abolished this principal point of theirs, unless many great absurdities, in which it is entangled, had persuaded him to do so. Yet we do not put this forward to such an end, as if Galen's judgment about Form ought to count as an argument. Indeed, unless we have made it perfectly plain from other sources and on solid reasons that the Aristotelian Form is a mere fiction, we demand that no trust be placed either in us or in him.
LXX.

units.la: Iis autem ex abundanti addatur locus ille ex Aristotele, ubi Formam statuens extrinsecus advenire, & esse aliquid per se subsistens, etiam priusquam compositum constituere incipiat, apertissimè suis de Forma placitis ipse contradicit, inter quæ Inseparabilitas est unum ex præcipuis, sicut omnibus notum est, qui Peripateticam Philosophiam vel à limine tantum salutaverunt, & nos jam antea attigimus. Est autem ille locus in primo de partibus, cap. 1. ubi longa oratione deducit, Animæ consideratio-nem ad Naturalem philosophum pertinere, quia Naturæ vocabulum etiamsi Materiæ quoq; tribuatur, præcipue tamen Formæ competat, quæ etiam sit φύσις ὡς ἡ κινήσεως, ὡς τέλος, & tanquam Causa movens, & tanquam finis, Forma autem in animalibus sit Anima, aut Animæ pars una, vel plures. non dicit Animam simpliciter, quia τὸ νοητικὸν facultatem intelligendi vi præditam, diserte excludit, quippe quod non sit κινήσεως ἀρχή, principium motus. itaq; vult tribus tantum illis Animæ partibus (partes ipse appellat) competere, ut Natura sint ac dicantur, Vegetativæ, Sensitivæ, ac loco motivæ: quarum unaquæq; sit Principium certi motus, prima αὔξησεως, augmenti, altera ἀλλοιώσεως, alterationis, (quam recte hoc, ipsius discipuli viderint) tertia φορᾶς, lationis. Hisce ita constitutis, pergit, hoc motus Principium ac Causam nos habere ex Universo, sicuti indidem habemus Elementa, è quibus corpora nostra constata sunt, φαίνεται γὰρ ὥσπερ ἐν τοῖς τεχνασοῖς ἐσὶν ἡ τέχνη, οὕτως ἐν αὐτοῖς τοῖς πράγμασιν ἄλλη ὡς ἀρχὴ αἰτίᾳ τιαύτη, ἣν ἔχομεν, καθάπερ τ' δεμιόν καὶ τ' ψυχὴν, ἐν τῷ παντός. Apparet enim, sicut in arte factis est ars, sic in ipsis rebus [naturalibus] aliud quoddam Principium & Causa ejusmodi, quam habeamus ex Universo, itidem ac calidum & frigidum. Verba sunt apertissima, neq; ullus patet effugio aut excusationi locus. neque enim de Mente hæc intelligi possunt, quam expressissimis verbis ibi negat, esse tale motus Principium, ac sunt reliquæ Animæ partes; neq; de spiritu illo cœlesti, quem Animæ ac Corporis vinculum facere solet: quia Spiritus ille non est ipsi Anima, aut Animæ pars; & propterea non illud motus Principium.
units.tr: To these, moreover, let us add that passage from Aristotle where, positing that the Form comes in from outside and is something subsisting in itself even before it begins to constitute the composite, he plainly contradicts his own opinions about Form. Among these, inseparability is one of the chief, as is known to all who have so much as greeted Peripatetic philosophy at the threshold, and as we have already touched upon. The passage is in the first book On the Parts of Animals, chapter 1, where in a long discourse he argues that the consideration of the soul belongs to the natural philosopher, because the word nature, though it is also applied to matter, belongs chiefly to form, which is nature as the principle of motion, as the end, and as the moving cause and the final cause. In animals, form is the soul, or one or more parts of the soul. He does not say simply "the soul," because he plainly excludes the intellect, the faculty of understanding, since it is not a principle of motion. He therefore holds that only those three parts of the soul (as he calls them parts) are natures and are said to be natures: the vegetative, the sensitive, and the locomotive. Each of these is a principle of a certain motion: the first of growth, the second of alteration (which his own disciples rightly saw), the third of locomotion. Having laid this down, he goes on to say that we have this principle and cause of motion from the universe, just as we have from it the elements of which our bodies are made.
