"For it is evident that, just as in the products of art there is an art, so in the things themselves [natural things] there is another principle and cause of this kind, which we have from the universe, just as we have the hot and the cold." These words are most plain, and there is no room for escape or excuse. They cannot be understood of the mind, which he expressly denies to be such a principle of motion as the other parts of the soul are, nor of that heavenly spirit which is wont to make the bond between soul and body, because that spirit is not the soul itself or a part of the soul, and therefore is not a principle of motion.

units.la: Videtur quidem in prioribus istius disputationis verbis tanquam dubitabundus in incerto posuisse, ipsáne anima sit Forma animalis, an aliquid præter ipsam, sed ipsi tamen conjunctum individuo nexu, spiritum illum haud dubie innuens ἄλλον τοίνυν δὲ ἐν ὀρθῶς λέγεσι, καὶ
units.tr: In the earlier words of this discussion he seems to have put himself, as though in doubt and uncertain, whether the soul itself is the form of the animal, or something besides the soul yet joined to the individual by a bond, clearly hinting at that spirit. "But they speak rightly in another way" [ἄλλον τοίνυν δὲ ἐν ὀρθῶς λέγεσι], and the Greek text here is too corrupted in the scan to be recovered.

units.la: x quo Ywe; x ultima, o plura, ulla, ipsam, mille, vuiva
units.tr: [The Greek of this line is so garbled in the scan that it cannot be read; its sense belongs to Aristotle's continuing discussion of the parts of the animal.]

units.la: χαὶ ὃ͂λ. λεγ͂λέον ὡς τοιοῦτον τὸ ζῷον, ηφ͂ τᾷ ἐκείνῳ, καὶ ᾧ καὶ ποῖόν ἢ τῶν μορίων ἕκαστον, ἂ͂ ὡς ἡμῖν περὶ ἴσ͂ ἐιὰ ὰς τ͂ ηλίνης, εἰ δὲ τοῦτό ἐστι ψυχὴ, ἡ ψυχῆς μέσς, ἡ μὲν ἄνευ ψυχῆς. ἀπολλύσης γὰρ ἀνέ ζῷόν ἐστιν, ὅλε τῶν μορίων ὅλὴν τὸ αὐτὸ λείπεται, πλὴν ζῷ σχήματι μόνον.
units.tr: [The Greek of this line is badly garbled in the scan; from what can be made out, it continues Aristotle's argument that the whole is called an animal in such a way, not by reference to that part, and that each of the members is what it is, as in the case of a bed, and that if this is the soul, or a part of the soul, or is not without soul.] For when the soul is lost, the animal is no longer an animal, and the members are not the same, except in shape only.

units.la: Liquet itaq; quod non recte dicant, & quod dicendum sit, quod ejusmodi est animal; ac de ipso, quid sit ac quale quid unumquodq; membrum, sicuti & de Forma lecti, si modo hoc est anima, aut animæ pars, aut non absq; anima. sane ubi abierit, non amplius animal est, neq; ullum membrum relinquitur idem; nisi figura duntaxat. sed in progressu satis mentem suam aperit, neq; aliud quid ab ipsa anima ad illam dignitatem admittit, ut sit animalis Forma & Natura.
units.tr: It is clear, then, that they do not speak correctly, and that it must be said that the animal is of such a kind; and about it, what it is, and what sort of thing each member is, just as about the form of a bed, if indeed this is the soul, or a part of the soul, or not without the soul. Certainly, when the soul has departed, the animal is no longer an animal, and no member remains the same, except in figure only. But in the course of his discussion he makes his mind sufficiently clear: he admits nothing other than the soul itself to that dignity of being the form and nature of the animal.

units.la: Cum autem dicat, nos habere hanc Naturam ἐν τῷ παντὸς, omnino sensit, eam aliquid fuisse, etiam antea quam nos illam haberemus. Non enim hæc ita exponere licet, ac si id intellexisset tantum de ratione effectionis, ut τὰ πᾶσι sit cœlum, quod & alibi sic appellat; & multis in locis vult concurrere ad rerum generationem. hæc, inquimus, expositio locum habere non potest, ob adjuncta illa verba, καθάπερ τὸ ἄερμὸν καὶ τὸ ψυχρόν, quæ etiam cogunt τὰ πᾶν non de cœlo accipi; sed de Universitate rerum. non enim è cœlo veniunt Elementa in mixta (cum ibi nulla sint Aristoteli.) sed è mole Universi. Apparet igitur vel ex ipso Aristotele, quid de Forma illa substantiali inseparabili sentiendum sit, cui ipse tam parum confisus sit, ut pro ea nescio quid extrinsecus arcessitum in mista introduxerit, quod ejus officio fungeretur. Nam quæ de Animalium Forma dixit, generaliter ad omnes aliarum rerum Formas transferri nihil vetat, cum nullam hic differentiam constituant Peripatetici, & omnem Animæ aut partem aut speciem, præter solam Mentem, faciant ejusdem conditionis, ac Formam aliam quamcunque, quantum ad existentiam earum, ortumq; ac interitum attinet. itaq; ut reliquas Formas, ita Animas quoq; illas & è Materiæ potestate educi, & Materiæ illigatas, sive ut, ipsi loquuntur, materiales esse volunt, & inseparabiles: quæ omnia hoc Aristotelis telis loco planissime evertuntur. Neq; ab eo multum abludunt illa, quæ Exerc. 307. scripsit Scaliger, Non animam modo & mentem humanam, sed omnem cujuscunq; perfecte mixti Formam esse naturam quintam & rem cœlestem, longe aliam à quatuor Elementis. quanquam admirari licet, cur imperfecte mixta, & ipsa Elementa non sit prosecutus pari liberalitate; præsertim qui ita ægre ferret Averroem diminutas Formas Elementis assignare, quas propterea non debuit ipse è reliquarum Formarum societate velut in exilium miserias proturbare. Sed ut hoc ipsi donemus, sequitur ex illis verbis; Omnes perfecte mistorum Formas, æque ac Mentem, individuo illo Materiæ nexu nequaquam teneri, sed & separabiles esse, & separari re vera, ac post compositi interitum superesse; siquidem Mentem esse immortalem, atq; à morte manere, putat abunde probari ex hoc Principio, Quod ipsa est quinta natura, & res cœlestis: nullam enim naturam cœlestem esse corruptibilem.
units.tr: Since, however, he says that we have this nature in the universe [ἐν τῷ παντός], he plainly understood that it was something even before we had it. Nor can these words be expounded as though he meant only the manner of production, so that the all [τὰ πᾶν] is the heaven, which he elsewhere also calls by that name, and in many places he wants the heavens to concur in the generation of things. This exposition, we say, cannot stand, because of the added words, just as the hot and the cold [καθάπερ τὸ θερμὸν καὶ τὸ ψυχρόν], which also force us to take the all not of the heaven but of the totality of things. For the elements do not come into mixed bodies from the heaven (since for Aristotle there are no elements there), but from the mass of the universe. It appears, then, even from Aristotle himself, what is to be thought of that substantial and inseparable form, in which he so little trusted that, in place of it, he introduced into mixed bodies some thing brought in from outside to perform its office. For what he said of the forms of animals, there is nothing to prevent our transferring generally to the forms of all other things, since the Peripatetics make no difference here, and they make every soul, or part or kind of soul, except the mind alone, of the same condition as any other form, so far as their existence, origin and perishing are concerned. Thus, as with the other forms, so with these souls too, they want them both to be educed from the power of matter, and to be bound to matter, or, as they themselves put it, to be material, and inseparable. All of this is most plainly overthrown by this passage of Aristotle. Nor is what Scaliger wrote in Exercise 307 far from him: not only the human soul and mind, but the form of every perfectly mixed thing is a fifth nature and a heavenly thing, far different from the four elements. Although one may wonder why he did not follow the same generosity with imperfectly mixed bodies and the elements themselves, especially since he took it so ill that Averroes assigned diminished forms to the elements, which for that reason he ought not to have driven out of the company of the other forms into a kind of exile. But granting him this, it follows from those words that the forms of all perfectly mixed bodies, like the mind, are by no means held by that individual bond to matter, but are also separable, and in fact are separated, and survive the destruction of the composite. For he thinks it is sufficiently proved that the mind is immortal and remains after death, from this principle: because it is a fifth nature and a heavenly thing, and no heavenly nature is corruptible.

units.la: LXXI. Ut igitur sepoimamus multas illas ac maximas planeq; inextricabiles difficultates atq; absurditates, ex ipsa Peripateticorum de Formis doctrina orientes, eamq; inseparabiliter comitantes, quarum unaquæq; per se sufficit ad eas plane abrogandas, atq; de medio tollendas: qua fronte tantum in Philosophia caput, atq; est illud de Substantialibus Formis, obtrudi mundo potest ob solam Aristotelis autoritatem (quippe nullo alio ipsâ fundamento nituntur, uti superior sermo declaravit) qui quum eam in Mundum primus omnium mortalium introduxerit, non modo nullis eam argumentis astruxit, sed & ipse alicubi ea planis verbis tradit, quæ præcipuis suis de ea decretis apertissime repugnent: sicuti hoc loco ea dicit, unde liquido sequitur (quod alibi, ubi suam de Formis doctrinam pertractat, summopere abhorret) Formas omnes & ante compositi ortum existere, & post ejusdem obitum manere: sicuti & Scaliger, tenacissimus alioquin atq; pugnacissimus totius Aristotelicæ de Formis doctrinæ, uti & reliquorum Peripatetiscomniorum, sectator ac defensor, hunc tantum in propria Sect. 20. in princip. pria schola solæcissimum commisisse deprehenditur. Certe præstitisset tales Formas semper ab ijs traditas fuisse. Potuissent enim & defendere illas sine ulla ingenti absurditate, & omnes illas difficultates, in quas nunc cum illa sua commentitia Forma se ipsos conjiciunt, effugissent; præsertim illam omnium maximam, quod substantiæ & oriantur è nihilo, & in nihilum revertantur: & metui Scaligeri; Quod sic darentur Formæ certo numero circumscriptæ, facile erat mederi: siquidem animæ plantarum, bestiarum, hominum (præter Mentes: coecutiunt enim, qui unam tantum in homine animam, neque aliam quàm immortalem, vident) nequaquam sunt certo numero circumscriptæ, & tamen existunt, antequam in corpora sua ingrediantur, manentq;, postquam ex ijs emigraverint: neq; ob hoc est una generalis Mundi anima, quam invitissima Veritate introductam fuisse in Philosophiam, nos libro quarto prolixè monstraturi sumus. Quomodo autem sublatâ Animâ Mundi, verum tamen illud sit, quod nos de animis dicimus; ejus rei explicatio debetur alteri itidem hujus operis loco, ubi animarum conditio ex professo excutietur. Si itaq; talem invexisset Formam Aristoteles, qualem isto loco videtur animo concepisse, multo firmior erat futura ipsius philosophia, neq; ita subversu facilis, utpote veritati longe proximior; quanquam ne sic quidem ex toto vera. Est enim in plerisq; perfecte mistis talis aliqua natura, multorum effectuum, quos Formæ ascribere ipsi solent, autor; quæ propterea, ut & stirpium ac animantium animæ, Formæ appellationem sustinere quodammodo posset; quanquam multæ aliæ conditiones illi desunt, quas Formæ suæ ascribunt Peripatetici, cum tamen neq; has habeat, neq; illas, utpote quæ nihil est ipsa, sicuti superiori sermone abunde est demonstratum: unde novum quoq; exurgit contra Materiam primam argumentum, quippe quæ sublatâ Formâ esse nulla potest; quod per se ita perspicuum est, ut probationis non indigeat, & satis sit verbo id indicasse.
units.tr: LXXI. Setting aside, then, those many and very great, indeed altogether inextricable, difficulties and absurdities that arise from the Peripatetic doctrine of forms itself and accompany it inseparably, each of which is by itself enough to abolish them completely and remove them from the field, with what face can this chief head of philosophy, namely the doctrine of substantial forms, be thrust upon the world on the sole authority of Aristotle? (For, as the foregoing discussion has shown, it rests on no other foundation.) He, although he was the first of all mortals to introduce it into the world, not only supported it by no arguments, but himself in places delivers it in plain words which most openly contradict his own principal decrees about it. Thus here he says things from which it clearly follows (what he greatly shrinks from elsewhere, where he treats his own doctrine of forms) that all forms exist even before the origin of the composite and remain after its death. Scaliger too, otherwise the most stubborn and combative follower and defender of the whole Aristotelian doctrine of forms, as also of all the rest of the Peripatetics, is found to have committed this solecism only in his own school, in Section 20 at the beginning. Certainly it would have been better had such forms always been handed down by them. For they could have defended them without any great absurdity, and would have escaped all those difficulties into which they now throw themselves with that fictitious form of theirs, especially the greatest of all, that substances both arise from nothing and return into nothing. And Scaliger's fear, that if forms were given in this way they would be confined to a certain number, was easy to remedy. For the souls of plants, beasts and men (except the minds: those are blind who see only one soul in man, and not another besides the immortal one) are by no means confined to a certain number, and yet they exist before they enter their bodies, and remain after they have emigrated from them. Nor, on account of this, is there one general soul of the world, which, introduced into philosophy against the strongest truth, we shall at length show in the fourth book. How, however, with the soul of the world removed, what we say about souls can still be true, the explanation of that matter is owed to another place of this work, where the condition of souls will be examined expressly. If, then, Aristotle had introduced such a form as he seems to have conceived in mind in this place, his philosophy would have been far firmer and not so easily overthrown, as being much closer to the truth, although even so it would not be wholly true. For in most perfectly mixed bodies there is some such nature, the author of many effects which the Peripatetics are wont to ascribe to forms; and this, like the souls of plants and animals, could in some way bear the name of form. Yet many other conditions which the Peripatetics ascribe to their forms are lacking in it, while it has neither these nor those, since it is nothing in itself, as has been abundantly demonstrated in the foregoing discourse. Hence also there arises a new argument against prime matter, since without form it can by no means exist; this is so self-evident that it needs no proof, and it is enough to have indicated it in a word.
SECTIO
SECTION FOUR.
ON PRIVATION.

units.la: I. Aristotelis sententia de Privatione. II. Privatio everti-tur ex Aristotelica Principiorum descriptione. III. Ridiculæ expositiones, quibus Aristotelici illud Aristotelis dictum, Principia semper manere oportet, in alium sensum trahunt. IV. Vanitas istius effugiy, quòd Privatio, etiamsi non componat res ipsas, componat generationes rerum; sive quod sit Principium generationis & rei generandæ, non rei genitæ. V. Examinatur alterum commentum, quod dicit Privationem esse Principium rerum; non ut partem componentem, sed ut terminum à quo. VI. Privatio non potest esse Principium, cum sit nihil omnino. VII. Privationem consistere cum Forma expellenda (quod multi dicunt Peripatetici) absurdum esse ostenditur. Vana distinctio inter Negationem & Privationem. Privationis non possunt esse ullæ differentiæ. VIII. Conimbricensium somnium, Privationem in instanti tantum existere, & rursus evanescere. IX. Privationis στέρησις ipse agnoscit Aristoteles; & tamen ejus inventionem, tanquam placlari mysterij, magna sibi gloriæ ascribit. X. Privatio nihil, quum nunquam existat. XI. Privatio non contraria Formæ. XII. Vana distinctio inter Privationem, & Materiæ potentiam. immodestia Scaligeri adversus eos qui Privationem tollunt; quumtamen ipse fatetur alibi, Privationem nihil esse. Ina-nis Conimbricensium conatus, negantium Privationem esse ens intentionale.
units.tr: I. Aristotle's opinion on privation. II. Privation is overturned by Aristotle's own description of the principles. III. The ridiculous explanations by which the Aristotelians twist Aristotle's saying, "the principles must always remain," into another sense. IV. The vanity of the escape that privation, even if it does not compose things themselves, composes their generation; or that it is the principle of generation and of the thing to be generated, not of the thing generated. V. The other fiction is examined, which says that privation is the principle of things, not as a component part but as the terminus from which. VI. Privation cannot be a principle, since it is absolutely nothing. VII. That privation coexists with the form to be expelled (as many Peripatetics say) is shown to be absurd. The empty distinction between negation and privation. Privation cannot have any differences. VIII. The dream of the Conimbricenses, that privation exists only in an instant and then vanishes again. IX. Aristotle himself acknowledges the privation [στέρησις], yet he claims for himself great glory for its discovery, as if it were a mystery of great importance. X. Privation is nothing, since it never exists. XI. Privation is not contrary to form. XII. The empty distinction between privation and the potency of matter. The arrogance of Scaliger against those who abolish privation, although he himself elsewhere admits that privation is nothing. The futile effort of the Conimbricenses, who deny that privation is an intentional being.

units.la: I. NUnc tempestivum erit, ad tertium Aristotelis Prin-cipium transire, nempe Privationem: quanquam fortassis nonnullis videbitur supervacuus hic labor, cum sublatâ Materiâ primâ & Formâ, sponte illam evanescere sit.
units.tr: Now it will be timely to pass on to Aristotle's third principle, namely privation. Yet to some this labour may seem superfluous, since once matter and form are removed, privation evidently vanishes of its own accord.
Chapter I.

units.la: sit necesse, sed nihil nocuerit, ipsam quoq; per se seorsim examinare, ut tanto magis appareat, qualis hactenus philosophia regnum obtinuerit. Privationis necessitatem in rebus naturalibus ut probaret, plurimum termonis insumsit Aristoteles in primo physicorum, & similia postea rursus per totam sparsit Metaphysicam. ita autem instituit probationem suam. In omni Generatione aliquid fit quod prius non erat. illa autem mutatio non fit ratione Materiae, quippe quae in se ipsa semper eadem manet, sed ratione Formae. omnis autem mutatio fit ex contrariis. oportet igitur in Materia ante illius Formae introductionem aliquid praefuisse ipsi Formae contrarium, in cujus locum Forma successerit. non enim ipsa ex se invicem fiunt contraria, sed Materia, quae utriq; suscipiendo aeque habilis sit, altero deperdito alterum acquirit. Quum autem substantiae non sint inter se contrariae, ac proinde una Forma nequeat alteri Formae esse contraria: Privationem Formae dicit esse illud contrarium Formae oppositum, inter quam ac Formam exerceatur generationis substantialis vicissitudo, sicuti reliquae quoq; generationes inter sua quaeq; contraria exerceantur. Quomodo igitur in aliis mutationibus Formam introducendam praecedat in subjecto Forma contraria; ita in generatione substantiarum asserit introductionem Formae substantialis necessario in eadem Materia praecedere Privationem; quae sit absentia Formae generandae, cum adjuncta aptitudine ad eam recipiendam. Haec summatim est Aristotelis de Privatione doctrina; contra quam nos sic argumentabimur; ac si Materia prima ac Forma nondum a nobis essent eversa. ut tanto magis hujus commentitij Principij vanitas deprehendatur.
units.tr: it is necessary, but it will do no harm to examine privation also by itself and separately, so that it may appear all the more clearly what kind of philosophy has hitherto held sway. In order to prove the necessity of privation in natural things, Aristotle spent a great deal of discussion in the first book of the Physics, and afterwards scattered similar material through the whole of the Metaphysics. He set out his proof as follows. In every generation something comes to be that did not exist before. This change does not occur by reason of the matter, which in itself always remains the same, but by reason of the form. Every change, however, proceeds from contraries. It is necessary, therefore, that before the introduction of that form there was present in the matter something contrary to the form, into whose place the form succeeded. For the forms do not become contraries of one another; rather, the matter, which is equally apt to receive either, acquires the one when it has lost the other. Since substances are not contrary to one another, and so one form cannot be contrary to another form, he says that privation of the form is the opposite contrary to the form, and that the alternation of substantial generation takes place between privation and form, just as the other generations take place between their own contraries. Therefore, just as in other changes a contrary form in the subject precedes the introduction of the form, so in the generation of substances he asserts that privation, which is the absence of the form to be generated together with an aptitude for receiving it, necessarily precedes the introduction of the substantial form in the same matter. This is in brief Aristotle's doctrine of privation. Against it we shall argue as follows, as if prime matter and form had not yet been overthrown by us, so that the vanity of this fictitious principle may be detected all the more.
II.

units.la: Dicimus igitur Privationem malo consilio inter Principia esse relatam ab Aristotele, qui hanc ipse fecit Principiorum proprietatem, ut res, quarum sunt Principia, ex ijs fiant ac constent. ita enim I. Physic. quinto ait. Δεῖ τὰς ἀρχὰς μήτε ἐξ ἀλλήλων εἶναι, μήτε ἐξ ἄλλων, ἀλλὰ ἐκ τῶν ὄντων. oportet principia neque ex se mutuo esse, neque ex aliis, sed ex ipsis omnia. & adhuc clarius ejusdem libri capite septimo: Εἰ γὰρ εἰσὶν αἰτίαι καὶ ἀρχαὶ τῶν φύσει ὄντων, ἐξ ὧν πρώτων εἰσὶ καὶ γεγόνασι, Siquidem rerum natura constantium Causæ atque Principia ea sunt, ex quibus primis constant atque orta sunt. Et eodem spectat, quod capite sexto dicit, Τὰς δὲ ἀρχὰς ἀεὶ δεῖ μένειν, Principia semper manere oportet: quod idem est, acsi diceret, Quamdiu res manet, Principia ipsam constituentia debere manere, quippe quæ ita essentiales ipsius partes sunt, ut sine iis nec constitui nec manere aut perseverare ullo pacto queat. Iam ex Privatione res non gignuntur aut constant, neque Privatio semper manet, quum & ipse 1. phys. 7. satis clare innuat, & omnes ejus sectatores magno consensu affirmant, Privationem non manere in re genita, sed adveniente Forma evanescere. Aut igitur falsam tradidit Aristoteles Principiorum descriptionem, perperamque hoc iis attribuit, ut semper manerent, utque res ex ipsis fierent & constarent; aut male inter Principia ascripsit Privationem, è qua res nequaquam fiunt & constant, & quæ nequaquam in rebus manet.
units.tr: We say, then, that Aristotle wrongly placed Privation among the principles. He himself made this a property of principles: the things whose principles they are come to be from them and consist of them. For in the fifth chapter of the first book of the Physics he says: "The principles must be neither from one another, nor from other things, but from the things that are" [Δεῖ τὰς ἀρχὰς μήτε ἐξ ἀλλήλων εἶναι, μήτε ἐξ ἄλλων, ἀλλὰ ἐκ τῶν ὄντων]. And more clearly still in the seventh chapter of the same book: "For if there are causes and principles of natural things, it is from these first things that they come to be and have come to be" [Εἰ γὰρ εἰσὶν αἰτίαι καὶ ἀρχαὶ τῶν φύσει ὄντων, ἐξ ὧν πρώτων εἰσὶ καὶ γεγόνασι]: Since the causes and principles of things that consist by nature are those from which they consist and have arisen as first things. To the same point belongs what he says in the sixth chapter: "The principles must always remain" [Τὰς δὲ ἀρχὰς ἀεὶ δεῖ μένειν], The principles must always remain. This amounts to saying: as long as a thing remains, the principles constituting it must remain, since they are its essential parts, and without them it can in no way be constituted, remain or persist. Now things are not generated from Privation, nor do they consist of it, and Privation does not always remain. Aristotle himself indicates this quite clearly in the first book of the Physics, chapter seven, and all his followers agree that Privation does not remain in a thing once it has come into being, but vanishes when the Form arrives. Either, then, Aristotle gave a false description of principles and wrongly attributed to them that they should always remain and that things should come to be and consist of them; or he wrongly ranked Privation among the principles, although things by no means come to be and consist of it, and it by no means remains in things.

units.la: III. Aristotelicis quidem aliter videtur, & manifestissimæ huic contradictioni se mederi posse non desperant; quod ut faciant, multa & mirifica excogitant, sed admodum sane futilia, uti ex sequentibus apparebit. Etenim quantum ad illum locum, quod dicitur, quod Principia semper manere oporteat; verum ac genuinum sensum, qui ex illis verbis sponte fluit, nequaquam admittentes, aliam atque alienissimam ipsius expositionem comminiscuntur, eaque in re haud parum inter se dissentiunt, quum varij varias explicationes, diversissimas ac plurimum inter se discrepantes, afferant: quæ cujusmodi sint, facile erit judicium facere ex duabus illis, quas Conimbricenses ut omnium optimas selegerunt. Prima est, Manere Principia, non omnia, sed quæ in rei compositionem coeunt. sed hoc ex illo loco haberi non potest; imo contrarium prorsus apparet, cum tota illa priore capitis parte loquatur Aristoteles tantum de
units.tr: III. The Aristotelians, indeed, see the matter differently, and they do not despair of being able to remedy this very plain contradiction. To do so they devise many clever-sounding but really quite trifling arguments, as will become clear from what follows. For, as regards the passage stating that principles ought always to remain, they do not admit the true and genuine sense that flows spontaneously from those words, but contrive another, quite alien, explanation of it. In this they disagree considerably among themselves, since different men offer different explanations, very diverse and mostly at odds with one another. The kind of explanations these are can easily be judged from the two which the Conimbricenses chose as the best of all. The first is: "The principles remain, not all of them, but those which come together into the composition of the thing." But this cannot be drawn from that passage; on the contrary, the opposite appears quite plainly, since the whole earlier part of that chapter speaks of Aristotle's concern only with the two contrary principles, Form and Privation, while he has not yet said anything about the third principle, namely Matter. So if this condition applies to Matter, about which he has so far said scarcely a word, it ought much more to apply to the other two principles, of which he speaks there.
Chapter II.

units.la: de duobus Principijs contrarijs, Forma & Privatione, quum de tertio principio, nimirum Materia, nihil adhuc constituerit: itaq; si haec conditio competit Materiae, de qua vix ullum adhuc verbum fecit, multo magis competere debet reliquis duobus Principijs, de quibus illic ex professo agitur. Altera solutio à Conimbricensibus posita, est, quod verba illa, oportet principia manere, ita explicanda sint, Quod omnia tria debeant concurrere ad singularum rerum generationem: quae solutio risu diluenda est, quippe contrarium dicens iis verbis, quorum explicationem profitetur. revera enim hoc dicit, Non esse necessarium ut Principia maneant in re generata, cum sufficiat illa concurrere ad ejus generationem. At Aristoteles non dicit, quod debeant concurrere, sed quod debeant manere. Et nihilo meliores esse reliquas quoq; expositiones, tum illam Alexandri, qui, Principia semper manere, in hoc sensu intellexit, quod Principia aeterna sint; neq; eam Averrois (quam secutus est Mercenarius Dilucid. 9.) quae istorum verborum hunc dicit esse germanum intellectum, Quod semper debeant manere in ratione principij, & ex alijs minime fieri; ita ut, Principia semper manere, nihil aliud sit, quàm Principia ex alijs non fieri: unusquisque, sobrie ista considerans, nullo negotio percipiet; & ex ijs quoque, quae alij Peripatetici, alijs expositionibus addicti, contra istas disputant, poterit intelligere: ut nobis necesse non sit, pluribus commonstrare earum vanitatem; quam tamen ut alibi passim, ita hic effugere non valent Peripatetici, quamdiu summae Aristotelis inconstantiae summam suam pertinaciam adjungunt, ut quidvis pati, ac in quavis se malint vertere, quàm veram ipsi medicinam adhibere; ut quando adeo fluctuatur, ac sibi ipsi aperte repugnat, atq; ἀσύστατος statuit, detegerent ipsius vanitatem, aut saltem agnoscerent, eumq; sic agentem deserarent: à quo tantum absunt, ut nulla tam absurda tamq; inconcinna in eo occurrant, quae non propugnare atq; inter se conciliare adnitantur: quod dum agunt, plane nugas agant necesse est.
units.tr: about the two contrary principles, form and privation, since he had as yet laid down nothing about the third principle, namely matter. So if this condition applies to matter, of which he has barely said a word so far, it must apply far more to the other two principles, of which he treats there expressly. Another solution put forward by the Conimbricenses is that the words "principles ought to remain" must be explained thus: that all three ought to concur in the generation of each thing. This solution should be laughed away, since it says the opposite of the words whose explanation it professes. For in truth it says this: that it is not necessary for the principles to remain in the thing generated, since it is enough that they concur in its generation. But Aristotle does not say that they ought to concur, but that they ought to remain. Nor are the remaining expositions any better: that of Alexander, who understood "principles always remain" to mean that the principles are eternal; nor that of Averroes (which Mercenarius followed in the ninth of the Dilucidationes), which says that the true meaning of those words is that they should always remain as principles and are not made at all from others, so that "principles always remain" is nothing other than "principles are not made from others." Anyone who considers these things soberly will perceive it without any trouble; and from the things which other Peripatetics, attached to other expositions, argue against these, he will be able to understand it as well. So it is not necessary for us to demonstrate their vanity at length. Yet the Peripatetics cannot escape this here, any more than they do everywhere else, so long as they join their own great stubbornness to Aristotle's great inconsistency. They would rather suffer anything and turn themselves in any direction than apply the true remedy to him. Since he so wavers, and so plainly contradicts himself, and lays down things that do not hang together, they ought to have detected his vanity, or at least acknowledged it, and abandoned him in his conduct. Far from it, they strive to defend and reconcile with one another every absurd and incongruous thing that occurs in him. In doing this they must necessarily be talking sheer nonsense.
IV. Whereby
Chapter I.

units.la: IV. Quomodo autem, ut Aristotelem à contradictione vindicent, ac Privationem salvis omnibus ipsius dictis in Principiorum numero retineant, valde incongruas istius sententiæ, Quod Principia semper manere oporteat, expositiones moliuntur Peripatetici; ita istud quoq; dictum, quo ex Principijs res fieri ac constare dicit Aristoteles, non minus mirabiliter intorquent, quo ejus vim effugiant, neq; propter ipsum cogantur fateri, quod Privationem male principijs annumeravit ipsorum Præceptor, legesq; Principiorum à se ipso scriptas eo violavit; quum omnes pro confesso ponant, quod Privatio non veniat in rerum compositionem, quodq; res minime ex ea constent. Et duabus quidem hic utuntur solutionibus, quibus efficere se posse sperant, ut quamvis Privatio non ingreditur rerum compositionem, in eam tamen quadrare valeat ista sententia, quâ definivit Aristoteles, Res ex principijs fieri. Primo aiunt, Privationem esse Principium intrinsecum productionis naturalis, etiamsi non sit ipsius Compositi; & quanquam rei ortæ principium nuncupari non possit, quum in ea non permaneat, sed accedente Forma abboleatur, esse tamen Principium ipsius generationis. Admitto (inquit Toletus 1. Phys. quæst. 11.) omnia Principia componere, sed generationem & mutationem rei: at vero rem ipsam tantum duo componunt, puta Materia & Forma, privatio vero non: unde est intrinsecum generationis Principium (& hoc sufficit) non autem ipsius rei. Et similiter Vicomercatus, Quemadmodum artus à re, qua oritur, differt, tametsi ad eam referatur, in eamq; desinat, ita & ejus principium aliquod esse potest, quod rei genitæ non erit. Quid autem sibi velint per hæc, quod Privatio sit Principium generationis, non rei genitæ, breviter indicat Toletus, aiens quod sit Principium rei in fieri, non rei factæ; & prolixius declarat Vicomercatus, Privationem esse rei partem, dum oritur nondumq; perfecta est; ipso ortus momento terminari. itaq; rei, quamdiu fit, partem dici posse: mox tamen ubi genita est, & complementum suum nacta, desinere in ea esse ut partem, utpote Formæ adventu deperditam: ad quod nos ita respondemus. Cum unaquaq; res per Formam sit id quod est, ne esse quidem omnino, quamdiu Formam non accepit: ast non entis partes esse non possunt. & si pars est rei, non est pars rei quæ generatur, sed ejus quæ interit, cum ipsi fateantur, simulatque introducitur Forma, Privationem evanescere. & si illa sunt rei partes, quæ ipsi inerant, antequam fieret hoc aliquid per novam Formam, Forma amissa erit rei genitæ pars, quippe quæ in Materia fuit ad illud usq; momentum, quo nova Forma introducebatur. Si igitur, esse generationis principium est (ut ipsi explicant) esse principium rei dum generatur; male aiunt privationem esse principium generationis rerum, seu principium rerum dum generantur. Quanquam enim duplex statuitur generatio; quarum altera, quæ est velut præparatio quædam ad prioris Formæ abjectionem, & novæ acquisitionem, habet aliquod temporis spatium, ac non subjecto tota, sed veluti per gradus peragitur; generatio tamen proprie dicta, ipsa nimirum Formæ introductio, non fit aliquo temporis tractu, sed in individuali momento, secundum ipsorum placita: ipso autem illo momento, quo Forma introducitur, privatio esse definit. Quodsi igitur, dum privatio est, res nondum est, neq; in totum, neq; ex parte (quum res non per partes, sed repente integras generari statuant) & simulatq; res esse incipit, privatio confestim aboletur atq; evanescit: nullo jure dicunt, privationem esse rei partem, dum generatur; atq; ita dicendo, suis ipsorum de Forma ac Generatione decretis evidenter contradicunt.
units.tr: IV. The Peripatetics, however, work out very strained explanations in order to clear Aristotle of contradiction and to keep privation among the principles while leaving all his statements intact. They are equally ingenious in bending his words that things come into being and consist of principles, so that they may escape its force without being compelled to admit that their master wrongly counted privation among the principles and violated the rules of principles he himself had laid down. Everyone grants that privation does not enter into the composition of things and that things are by no means made up of it. Here they use two solutions, by which they hope to show that, although privation does not enter into the composition of things, this statement by which Aristotle defined things as coming from principles can still fit it. First, they say that privation is the intrinsic principle of natural production, even if it is not a part of the composite itself; and although it cannot be called a principle of the thing that has come into being, since it does not remain in it but is destroyed when the Form arrives, it is still the principle of the generation itself. "I admit," says Toletus (on Physics 1, question 11), "that all principles compose, but the generation and change of a thing, not the thing itself. Only two things compose the thing itself, namely Matter and Form, and privation does not. So it is an intrinsic principle of generation (and that is enough), but not of the thing itself." Vicomercatus says similarly: "Just as the limb differs from the thing from which it arises, even though it is related to it and ends in it, so it can be some principle of that thing which will not be part of the thing once generated." What they mean by saying that privation is the principle of generation but not of the thing generated is briefly indicated by Toletus, who says it is the principle of a thing in the process of becoming, not of a thing already made. Vicomercatus explains it at more length: privation is a part of the thing while it is arising and not yet perfected, and it ends at the very moment of its coming into being; so it can be called a part of the thing while it is coming to be, but as soon as it has been generated and has attained its completion, it ceases to be in it as a part, having been lost by the arrival of the Form. To this we reply as follows. Since each thing is what it is through its Form, it does not even fully exist as long as it has not received the Form; but non-being cannot be a part. And if privation is a part of the thing, it is a part not of the thing being generated but of the thing that perishes, since they themselves admit that privation vanishes as soon as the Form is introduced. And if those things are the parts of a thing which were in it before this particular thing came to be through the new Form, then the Form lost will be a part of the thing generated, since it was in the Matter up to that very moment when the new Form was introduced. So if the principle of generation is (as they explain) the principle of the thing while it is being generated, they are wrong to say that privation is the principle of the generation of things, or the principle of things while they are being generated. For although two kinds of generation are recognised, one of which is a kind of preparation for the casting off of the former Form and the acquisition of the new, and takes some span of time, and is carried through not all at once but by degrees, yet generation properly so called, namely the introduction of the Form itself, does not take place over any stretch of time but in an indivisible moment, according to their own opinions. And at that very moment when the Form is introduced, privation ceases to exist. So if, while privation exists, the thing does not yet exist, either wholly or in part (since they hold that things are generated not part by part but suddenly whole), and as soon as the thing begins to exist, privation is at once destroyed and vanishes, then they are wrong to say that privation is a part of the thing while it is being generated; and in saying so they plainly contradict their own decrees about Form and Generation.

units.la: V. Alter modus, quo illam Principiorum conditionem, quòd res ex ijs fiant & constent, Privationi aptare student Aristotelici, in eo consistit, quod dicant in illis verbis, Principia neq; ex se invicem fiunt, neq; ex aliis, sed ex ijs omnia, voculam, Ex, æquivoce sumi, ita ut illa duo priora ex, dicant habitudinem partis componentis; tertium ex dicat habitudinem termini; ut illorum verborum, Et ex ipsis omnia fiunt, sensus sit, Aut ex partibus, ut ex Materia & Forma, Tolet. 1. phys. quæst. 11. Forma, aut ex termino, ut ex Privatione. quippe Privationem esse terminum à quo ipsius generationis, & sic Principium rei genitæ. Id unde per se generatio proficiscitur (inquiunt Conimbricenses) verè ac proprie principium illius est, ac proinde Privatio est principium per se generationis, quum generatio per se oriatur à privatione, quia generatio est progressio à non esse ad esse, ut à termino à quo; qui terminus quum non sit Materia (siquidem terminus, à quo res oritur, utpote Forma geniti contrarius, non manet: Materia autem semper manet) consequens fit, ut sit ipsa forma privatio. Sed hæc distinctio, quod fieri ex in illa Principiorum definitione dupliciter sumendum sit, (pro fieri ex aliquo, vel tanquam parte componente, vel tanquam termino à quo) ex ipso Aristotele haberi non potest, qui in illo libro verbum faciat nullum termini à quo, aut quod privatio concurrat ad generationem tanquam terminus à quo. & si recte dicitur, fieri res ex aliquo, tanquam termino à quo, inepta est illa Aristotelis interrogatio 1 phys. 6. πῶς ἐκ μὴ ὄντων οὐσία ἂν εἴη; quomodo ex non substantis substantia fieret? Præterea si satis est Privationi ut rei Principium dicatur, quia res ex ea generetur, tanquam ex termino à quo; nihil impedit, quin ipsius quoq; Formæ Principium dicatur, cum & Forma fiat ex ex Privatione, ut ex termino à quo, sicuti ex nocte fit dies, atq; ex tenebris lumen. Ast si hoc recipiatur, & si vocula, ex, ita late sumatur in illa Principiorum descriptione, non constabit illa conditio, quam ipsis ibi attribuit Aristoteles, Non fieri ex se mutuo.
units.tr: V. The second way in which the Aristotelians try to fit privation to that condition of the principles, that things come from them and consist of them, lies in this: they say that in the words "Principles do not come from one another, nor from other things, but all things come from them," the little word "from" is taken equivocally. The first two uses of "from" express the relation of a component part, while the third expresses the relation of a terminus; so the sense of the words "and all things come from them" is: either from parts, as from Matter and Form (Toletus, on Physics 1, question 11), or from a terminus, as from privation, since privation is the terminus a quo of generation and so a principle of the thing generated. "That from which generation proceeds of itself," say the Conimbricenses, "is truly and properly its principle, and therefore privation is the principle of generation per se, since generation per se arises from privation, because generation is a progression from non-being to being, as from a terminus a quo." Since this terminus is not Matter (for the terminus from which a thing arises, being contrary to the Form of what is generated, does not remain, whereas Matter always remains), it follows that privation itself is the form. But this distinction, that "coming from" in that definition of principles must be taken in two ways (either as coming from something as a component part, or as coming from a terminus a quo), cannot be found in Aristotle himself, who in that book says nothing about a terminus a quo, or about privation concurring in generation as a terminus a quo. And if it is rightly said that a thing comes from something as from a terminus a quo, then Aristotle's question in Physics 1, chapter 6, is pointless: "πῶς ἐκ μὴ ὄντων οὐσία ἂν εἴη" [how could a substance come from non-substances?]. Moreover, if it is enough for privation to be called a principle of a thing because the thing is generated from it as from a terminus a quo, nothing prevents the Form itself from being called a principle too, since the Form also comes from privation as from a terminus a quo, just as day comes from night and light from darkness. But if this is accepted, and if the little word "from" is so widely taken in that definition of principles, then the condition Aristotle lays down there, that principles do not come from one another, will not hold.
VI.

units.la: Sed ut hæc omittamus, atq; ipsis concedamus, ut particulam hanc pro libitu explicent, aliamque prioribus locis, aliam posteriore significationem ipsi attribuant: quomodo erit principium alterius rei, quæ non est ipsa quicquam. Non esse quicquam, ipse fatetur Aristoteles, qui dicit eam esse μὴ ὄν, neq; id per accidens, sicuti Materia est, ἓν ὄν, sed simpliciter & per se, quippe quæ nullo pacto sit substantia, sicut illa. Ast non ens nequit esse Principium entis, neq; nihil potest conferre quippiam ad corporis naturalis generationem, nedum ut ejus Principium statui mereatur: nimis enim vanum est, quod afferunt Conimbricenses, Quanquam ens non possit dependere à non ente, ut ab influente aut ab impartiente aliquod esse, posse tamen ab ea dependere, tanquam à termino, atque ut ab eo, quod essentialiter ad suum conceptum requirit. Profecto & locum omnis res essentialiter ad sui conceptum requirit, quippe sine quo fieri nullo modo potest, quare & illum facere Principium debuerant. neque est quod causentur, disparem esse loci ac Privationis rationem, cum ille sit extra rem, haec vero intra ipsam: neque enim intra ipsam esse potest, neque extra, quod est nihil omnino. & si vel maxime esset aliquid, non tamen esset quid internum, cum dicant esse terminum à quo: talis autem terminus non est intra rem ipsam: & quomodo sit intra eam, cum qua aut in qua: ne ad minimum quidem temporis momentum subsistere potest, ut ipsi dicunt.
units.tr: But let us set these things aside and grant them the freedom to explain this particle as they please, giving it one meaning in the earlier places and another in the later. In what way will there then be a principle of some other thing that is not anything itself? Aristotle himself admits that privation is not anything: he says it is a not-being [μὴ ὄν], and not a being in an incidental sense [ἓν ὄν] as matter is, but simply and per se, since it is in no way a substance as matter is. But a non-being cannot be the principle of a being, nor can it contribute anything to the generation of a natural body, much less deserve to be counted as its principle. What the Conimbricenses allege is quite empty: Although a being cannot depend on a non-being as on something that influences or imparts some being, it can nevertheless depend on it as on a terminus, and as on that which it essentially requires for its concept. Certainly every thing essentially requires place for its concept, since it cannot come to be in any way without it; so they too ought to have made place a principle. Nor is there reason for them to plead that the manner of place differs from that of privation, since place is outside the thing and privation within it. For privation can be neither within the thing nor outside it, since it is nothing at all. And even if it were something, it would not be something internal, since they call it a terminus from which, and such a terminus is not within the thing itself. How can it be within that with which or in which it is? It cannot subsist even for the smallest moment of time, as they themselves say.

units.la: VII. Quanquam mirum est, tantam intercedere Privationi inimicitiam cum Forma illa, cui viam & aditum munivit ad Materiam, & nullam intercedere cum ipsa, cui exitium molitur: quae tamen adeo ipsam non aspernatur, ut uno in contubernio admodum socialiter vivant; ubi altera illa Forma, quae tantum ipsi beneficium debet, ne ad punctum quidem temporis consortium ipsius vult tolerare. etenim si privatio non est cum illa Forma, cui interficiendae navat operam, non est unquam omnino. oporteret enim dari tempus aliquod, in quo Materia post amissionem prioris Formae, & ante susceptionem novae, omni prorsus Forma careret; quod validissime omnes negant Peripatetici, asserentes Materiam ne indivisibili quidem temporis momento posse sine Forma subsistere. cum itaque in instanti fiat prioris Formae excessus, & novae introductio, Privatio autem cum illa Forma, ad quam habet relationem, non possit consistere: oportet aut non sit unquam, aut sit cum priore Forma. & hoc posterius multi affirmant Peripatetici, Simplicius, Piccolomineus, Zabarella, Vicomercatus, Toletus;
units.tr: VII. Although it is strange that privation should bear such enmity toward that form, to which it has paved the way and access into matter, and bear no enmity toward the form it plots to destroy. Yet it does not so despise that form that they do not live together in one lodging quite sociably, while that other form, which owes privation only a kindness, will not tolerate its company even for a moment of time. For if privation is not with the form against which it labours to destroy, it never exists at all. There would have to be some time in which matter, after losing the former form and before receiving the new one, would be wholly without form. All the Peripatetics most strongly deny this, asserting that matter cannot subsist without form even for an indivisible moment of time. Since therefore the departure of the former form and the introduction of the new take place in an instant, and privation cannot subsist without the form to which it is related, it must either never exist or exist together with the former form. Many Peripatetics affirm this latter: Simplicius, Piccolomini, Zabarella, Vicomercatus, Toletus;
Cap. I.

units.la: Toletus; nempe, Privationem in subjecto, in quo inest, ponere aliquam Formam positivam, aut contrariam, aut aliquo modo oppositam Formae producendae. & hoc coguntur dicere necessario, quippe qui statuant, Omnem generationem praesupponere aliquod compositum, ex quo res generanda per transmutationem fiat, cum Materia nuda non subjiciatur actioni agentis, quod debet generare. imo Zabarelle adeo necessaria conjuncta est Privationi Forma, ut dicat ex Materia nuda & penitus inaffecta, si daretur, fore ut nihil penitus generari posset, quia apta non esset ad sustinendam actionem agentis. Sed aeque absurdum esse, ut conjungatur huic Formae, quam ut illi, facile monstrare possumus. Dicendum enim est, aut unicam tantum esse Privationem, omni Formae contrariam, aut plures esse Privationes, ita ut alia alij Formae sit contraria. Prius si dicant, per se evidens est, quod cum una Forma non possit Privatio magis constare, quam cum alia, si omnibus simpliciter adversatur, contraria autem in eodem subjecto simul morari non possunt. necesse igitur est, ut dicant alterum. Et hoc quidem dicunt omnes, quippe nullo modo cupientes admittere, quod Privatio idem sit cum negatione. hanc enim, quae sit universalis omnium Formarum absentia, & nihil sit, ac esse penitus tollat, & solum removeat, nec quicquam ponat, multum differre a Privatione, quae connotet subjectum definitum: esse enim absentiam Formae in subjecto apto recipere Formam, & habilitatem ad id habenti: namq; eam importare potentiam quandam proximam in eo subjecto, in quo inest, ad eam Formam, cujus est Privatio. itaq; duplicem esse Privationem, aliam in Materia prima, quae dicit potentiam primam ad quamlibet Formam, & unam tantum esse hanc; aliam in Materia proxima ad quamlibet Formam, quae sit terminus propinquus generationis: & hanc esse multiplicem, sicuti multiplex est Forma introducenda. Sed haec Privationis multiplicitas (ut sic dicamus) facile everti potest, & proinde totum hoc de Privatione commentum, quae absq; illa proxima potentia non differet à negatione, quod tantopere ipsi reformidant. Etenim illæ potentiæ proximæ ad certas Formas suscipiendas, dicunt differentias Privationis. Ast in Privationem non cadunt differentiæ, quippe quæ est non ens, non entis autem nec sunt nec esse possunt ullæ differentiæ. nec est quod cavillentur, non ens multipliciter sumi: nos enim capimus pro eo, quod simpliciter & absolute non est quicquam omnino; quod à nobis sumi debere si negaverint, tanquam ὃ ἐν ἀρχῇ, meditentur jam non quid nobis, sed quid Aristoteli respondeant, cujus hoc est axioma, & Privationem esse non ens simpliciter, quippe quæ nec substantia sit nec accidens; & propterea non admittere ullas differentias. Οὐκ ἔστι δὲ διαφορὰ στερήσεως, ἡ στέρησις. ἀδύνατον γὰρ εἶναι τῆς μὴ ὄντος. non est differentia privationis, inquantum est privatio. impossibile enim est, ut sint species non entis. & in quarto Phys. quoq; contra eos, qui ponebant vacuum, ob motum, ita argumentatur, ut dicat, Posito vacuo contrarium prorsus sequi, quam ipsi volunt. necesse enim esse, ut in vacuo omnia quiescant, quia non erit, quorsum moveantur; quia inanis nullæ sint differentiæ. in vacuo necesse est quiescere. non enim est, quò magis aut minus movebitur. inquantum enim vacuum, non habet differentiam. Dicent; Privationis nullas esse differentias per se, sed ratione Formarum, quibus opponuntur; & sic revera differre Privationes Formarum, quomodo realiter differunt Privationes habituum, & diversa est Privatio lucis à Privatione saporis. sed hoc pacto etiam negationis erunt differentiæ. non potest enim ulla negatio physica esse indefinita, sed necesse est semper exprimatur id, cujus est negatio, ut cum aqua negatur esse amara aut calida. & sic Causam nullam habebunt, cur negationem tam enixe à Privatione separent. nam quantum ad potentiam proximam attinet, illa non est à Privatione, sed ipsius Materiæ: & quod aer tenebrosus habet potentiam proximam ad suscipiendum lumen, hoc non habet à tenebris, quippe quæ potius deberent obsistere luci, propter contrarietatem; cum privatio sit habitui ac Formæ contraria, ex decretis Aristotelis non dabunt nobis vitio, quod exemplum sumimus ab accidentibus, cum Aristoteli & ipsis nihil sit magis solenne, quam generationem & corruptionem substantialem exemplis generationum & corruptionum accidentalium declarare. Et cum illa proxima potentia ac aptitudo sit accidens aliquod in Materia non coæternum ipsi, sicuti generalis illa potentia, quam Materiæ primæ attribuunt, & semper manere volunt, sub quacunq; Forma, sed per vices & orietur in ea, & interiens, Privatio ipsius causa esse nequit, cum omne accidens (ex ipsorum doctrina) fluat ab aliqua Forma.
units.tr: Toletus; namely, that privation, in the subject in which it inheres, posits some positive form, either contrary to or in some way opposed to the form to be produced. They are necessarily compelled to say this, since they hold that every generation presupposes some composite from which the thing to be generated arises by transmutation, bare matter not being subjected to the action of the agent that is to generate. Indeed Zabarella is so necessarily bound to privation together with form that he says that if bare matter, wholly unaffected, were given, nothing at all could be generated, because it would not be fit to sustain the action of the agent. But we can easily show that it is equally absurd for privation to be joined to this form as to that one. For we must say either that there is only one privation, contrary to every form, or that there are several privations, so that one is contrary to one form and another to another. If they take the first, it is self-evident that, since one form can no more sustain privation than another if privation simply opposes all forms, and contraries cannot abide together in the same subject, they must say the second. And indeed all of them say this, since they are in no way willing to admit that privation is the same as negation. For negation, which is the universal absence of all forms, is nothing, wholly removes being, and posits nothing; it is said to differ greatly from privation, which connotes a definite subject. Privation is the absence of a form in a subject apt to receive it, and a readiness in the one who has it, for it implies a certain proximate power in the subject in which it inheres toward that form of which it is the privation. Thus they say there is a twofold privation: one in prime matter, which signifies the first power toward any form, and this alone is one; another in proximate matter toward any form, which is the nearer terminus of generation, and this is multiple, just as the form to be introduced is multiple. But this multiplicity of privation (so to speak) can easily be overturned, and so this whole fiction about privation, which without that proximate power would not differ from negation, is one they dread so greatly. For those proximate powers toward certain forms to be received are said to be the differences of privation. But differences do not fall upon privation, since it is a non-being, and there are, or can be, no differences of non-being. Nor is there reason for them to quibble that non-being is taken in many senses. We understand it as that which simply and absolutely is nothing at all. If they deny that we must take it this way, as the starting point of the matter, they will be pondering not what they answer to us but what they answer to Aristotle, whose axiom this is: that privation is simply non-being, since it is neither substance nor accident, and therefore admits no differences. [Οὐκ ἔστι δὲ διαφορὰ στερήσεως, ἡ στέρησις. ἀδύνατον γὰρ εἶναι τῆς μὴ ὄντος.] There is no difference of privation, insofar as it is privation. For it is impossible that there be species of non-being. And in the fourth book of the Physics, too, against those who posited a void in order to explain motion, he argues that if a void is posited the very opposite of what they want follows: in a void all things must be at rest, since there will be no reason for them to move in one direction rather than another, because a void has no differences. In a void it is necessary to be at rest. For there is no direction in which it will move more or less, insofar as it is void, it has no difference. They will say that privations have no differences in themselves, but only by reason of the forms to which they are opposed, and that thus privations of forms really differ just as privations of habits differ, and the privation of light is different from the privation of taste. But in this way negations too will have differences. For no physical negation can be indefinite; it is always necessary that that of which it is the negation be expressed, as when water is denied to be bitter or warm. And so they will have no cause to separate negation so earnestly from privation. As far as proximate power is concerned, that does not come from privation but from matter itself. And that a shadowy air has a proximate power to receive light, it does not have from the darkness, which should rather resist light because of contrariety, since privation is contrary to habit and form. By Aristotle's decrees they will not fault us for taking our example from accidents, since nothing is more customary for Aristotle and for them than to explain substantial generation and corruption by the examples of accidental generations and corruptions. And since that proximate power and aptitude is an accident in matter, not coeternal with it, like that general power which they attribute to prime matter and want to remain always under any form, but which arises and passes away in it by turns, privation cannot be its cause, since every accident (by their own doctrine) flows from some form.

units.la: Et si vel maxime ipsa per se Privatio esset causa istius affectionis, esset tamen plane inefficax, quia obscuraretur à contraria affectione, Materiæ impressa à Forma præsenti. cum enim dicant omnem Formam quærere sui perpetuitatem, & totam Materiam esse in Formæ imperio ac potestate, haud dubie Materiam ita disponet, ut velit præsenti suo statu contenta, novationem nullam appetere; neq; causa ulla est, cur affectio à Privatione fluens debeat esse potentior illâ, quæ fluit ab ipsa præsenti Forma, imo cur hæc illam non penitus expellat, & veluti perpetuo edicto extra fines suos relegeret, quippe cum Materia, ex eo quod absentium Formarum Privationem in se cohibet, actum Formæ, cui velut matrimonio conjuncta erat, repudiet, ut actum Formæ, quo caret, admittat, ita adulterina quadam ratione maleficium committens; quæ sunt ipsa Conimbricensium verba. nullum igitur relinquitur tempus quo unquam sit Privatio. siquidem cum illa Forma, cujus est Privatio, consistere posse ipsi negant Peripatetici: cum præcedenti non posse morari nos ostendimus, quia generalis Privatio omni æque Formæ contraria est; particularis Privatio neq; datur, & si daretur, Forma per illam abolenda nullo modo eam secum in eodem subjecto tolerare vellet.
units.tr: And even if privation itself were the cause of this affection, it would nonetheless be wholly ineffective, because it would be overpowered by the contrary affection, impressed upon matter by the present form. For since they say that every form seeks its own perpetuity, and that all matter is under the command and power of the form, without doubt the form will so dispose matter that, content with its present state, it desires no change at all. Nor is there any reason why an affection flowing from privation should be stronger than that which flows from the present form itself; indeed, why the latter would not utterly expel the former and banish it beyond its borders, as by a perpetual edict. For matter, since it holds within itself the privation of absent forms, rejects the act of the form to which it was joined as by marriage, in order to admit the act of the form it lacks, and so commits a kind of adulterous wrong; these are the very words of the Conimbricenses. Therefore no time remains at which privation ever exists. For since the Peripatetics deny that the form whose privation it is can coexist with it, and we have shown that privation cannot remain together with the preceding form, because general privation is equally contrary to every form, and particular privation is not given at all; and even if it were given, the form about to be destroyed by it would by no means be willing to tolerate it alongside itself in the same subject.

units.la: VIII. Et certe ipsi quoq; Conimbrincenses, soli fere inter
units.tr: VIII. And indeed the Conimbricenses themselves, almost alone among those Peripatetics we know,

units.la: {E e} inter eos quos novimus Peripateticos, non audent dicere, quod Privatio introducendæ Formæ sit cum priori Forma conjuncta, quanquam paulo aliud ob argumentum; quia cum Privatio sit negatio Formæ in subjecto natura apto ante punctum generationis Materia non est apta ad Formam, cum nondum habeat dispositionum omnium apparatum ad eam excipiendam, non possit Privatio tempore antecedenti esse in Materia. hæc quidem velut ab aliis objecta dicunt, volentibus probare nunquam dari Privationem. sed ipsorum responsio eodem recidit. nam quanquam dicunt Materiam, quamdiu Formam non habet, esse illa absolute privatam, aptamque ex sese ad eam excipiendam; addunt tamen, Quod proximam & completam aptitudinem tunc solum obtineat, cum perventum fuit ad terminum complementumq; omnium accidentium, quibus ab agente disponitur, qui terminus in ipso tantum generationis momento datur. itaq; in ipso puncto generationis Materiæ, antequam Formam recipiat, inesse summam aptitudinem ad eam recipiendam, quæ sit exactissima Formæ Privatio: Nec repugnare, quod in eodem instanti temporis secundum aliam & aliam considerationem detur in Materia & Privatio Formæ, & ipsa Forma; licet talis Privatio in eodem instanti reipsa ac simpliciter aboleatur.
units.tr: Among those Peripatetics we know, they do not dare to say that the privation of the form to be introduced is conjoined with the prior form. Their reason is a little different: since privation is the negation of a form in a subject naturally apt for it, before the point of generation the matter is not apt for the form, since it does not yet have the full apparatus of dispositions needed to receive it; so privation cannot exist in the matter at an earlier time. They say these things as though objected by others, who wish to prove that privation never exists at all. But their own reply comes to the same thing. For although they say that matter, as long as it does not have the form, is absolutely deprived of it and apt of itself to receive it, they add that it obtains proximate and complete aptitude only when it has reached the term and completion of all the accidents by which it is disposed by the agent, and this term is given only in the very moment of generation. Thus at the very point of generation, before matter receives the form, the highest aptitude to receive it is present in it, and this is the most exact privation of the form. And they say there is nothing contradictory in the same instant of time that, according to one consideration and then another, both privation of the form and the form itself are present in the matter, although such a privation is really and simply abolished in that same instant.

units.la: Profecto piget tædetq; tantis ineptijs an delirijs confutandis diutius immorari. sed cum hæc ipsa plus quam febriculosa somnia per immensi temporis præscriptionem tam alte hominum animis insederint, ut præ ijs sanam doctrinam contumacissime refspuant, devorandum nobis est hoc tædium, & prolixe refutanda illa, de quibus apud animos à præjudicio liberos vix tria verba commutare opus esset; cum Luciani Veræ narrationes non contineant majora portenta in Historia, quam pleraq; Aristotelica dogmata in Philosophia: quæ dum mordicus retinent Peripatetici, necesse est ab uno absurdo ad aliud absurdum trudantur (falsas enim theses nisi falsis argumentis tueri haud promtum est; &, quod Asclepiadæ olim exprobabat Galenus, Οὐχ ὅτι μαχητικῶς δογμάτων ὑπολαμβάνοντι χρη- ὀμένων [?] σάμενόν τινα, μὴ ὃ καλαγέλασον ἀνρισυεσθαι παντλαχοῦ ἣν fieri non potest, quin qui pravis dogmatum hypothesibus nitur, undequaq; ridiculus inveniatur) & non modo cum Veritate, quacum semper male ijs convenit, sed & secum ipsis pugnent passim. Quale enim hoc est, quod hic nugantur Conimbricenses, in eodem instanti & gigni Privationem, & aboleri, & Formam introduci, si satis est dicere, quod hæc non repugnant secundum aliam atq; aliam consideration̄, eodem jure nihil non dicere licebit. & si hæc non è diametro repugnant doctrinæ Aristotelicæ, qua τὸ νῦν statuitur indivisibile, non repugnat etiam, dicere, quod summus calor ac summum frigus possint esse simul in eodem subjecto.
units.tr: Truly it irks and wearies me to spend longer refuting such absurdities and delirium. But since these dreams, more than feverish, have so deeply settled in men's minds through the prescription of immense time that they most obstinately reject sound doctrine in their favour, we must endure this tedium and refute at length things which, among minds free from prejudice, would scarcely need three words to dispose of. Lucian's True Histories contain no greater prodigies in their story than most of the Aristotelian dogmas contain in philosophy. While the Peripatetics cling to these with their teeth, they must be driven from one absurdity to another. For it is not easy to defend false theses except with false arguments; and as Galen once reproached the followers of Asclepiades, [Οὐχ ὅτι μαχητικῶς δογμάτων ὑπολαμβάνοντι χρη- ὀμένων [?] σάμενόν τινα, μὴ ὃ καλαγέλασον ἀνρισυεσθαι παντλαχοῦ ἣν] it cannot be but that whoever leans on the corrupt hypotheses of doctrines will be found ridiculous everywhere. And they conflict not only with the truth, with which they never agree, but also with themselves, everywhere. For what is this trifling of the Conimbricenses, that privation is both generated and abolished in the same instant, and the form introduced at that same instant? If it is enough to say that these things do not conflict when considered in different ways, then by the same right one may say anything at all. And if these things do not directly conflict with Aristotelian doctrine, by which the now [τὸ νῦν] is held to be indivisible, then it does not conflict either to say that the greatest heat and the greatest cold can be together in the same subject.

units.la: IX. Et quid disputamus diutius contra Privationem, cum ipse Aristoteles in eodem illo libro, ubi tam operose illam astruit, satis manifesto illam repudiet. Quippe dicit Causas & Principia, è quibus res essentialiter constent ac genitæ sint, esse Materiam & Formam. Φανερὸν οὖν, ὡς εἴπερ εἰσὶν αἰτίαι καὶ αρχαὶ τῶν φύσει ὄντων, ἐξ ὧν πρώτων εἰσί καὶ γεγόνασι, μὴ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς, ἀλλ' ἕκαστον ὃ λέγεται καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν, ὅτι γίγνεται ἀπὸν ἐκ τε τῆς ὑποκειμένης καὶ τῆς μορφῆς. Manifestum igitur est, siquidem rerum naturâ constantium Causa sunt ac Principia, ex quibus primis constant atq; orta sunt, non per accidens, sed unumquodq; quod dicitur secundum essentiam, omnia fieri ex Subjecto atq; Forma. non esse modo dicit res ex his duobus Principijs, sed & generari, ut appareat futilitas istius distinctionis, quod Privatio non sit Principium essentiæ, sed generationis. & postea addit, Καὶ ἅπλου ἐστιν, ὅτι ἀεὶ ὑποκειμένη ἐν τοῖς ἐναντίοις, καὶ τὰ ἐναντία δύο εἶναι. τρόπον δέ τινα ἄλλον ἐκ ἀναγκαῖον ἱκανὸν ἦ ἕσαι ἡ ἕτερον τῶν ἐναντίων ποιεῖν τῇ ἀπουσίᾳ καὶ παρουσίᾳ τὴν μεταβολήν. Et apertum est, quod oporteat aliquid esse subjectum contrarijs, & contraria duo esse. alio autem modo non est hoc necesse. alterum enim contrariorum sufficiet ad faciendam faciendam mutationem suâ absentiâ & præsentiâ. quibus verbis suam ipsius levitatem prodit quam apertissime, qui hoc pro Principio necessario invexerit in Philosophiam, quod non esse necessarium ipse ultro ac gratis fateatur, quia sola Materia cum Forma sufficiat: qui tamen alibi præceptorem suum Platonem, hoc ipsum dicentem, ac Privationem à generatione excludentem, graviter incessat: & in eodem isto primo physicorum, paulo post supraposita verba, acriter invehatur in priscos philosophos, quod ob Privationem ignoratam in tam crassum prolapsi sint errorem, ut simpliciter negarent quicquam fieri, quandoquidem absq; illius mysterij cognitione non poterant comprehendere, quomodo aliquid fieret ἐκ μὴ ὄντος, ex non ente. Hoc autem se invenisse, & introducta Privatione monstrasse; nihil quidem fieri simpliciter ἐκ μὴ ὄντος, fieri tamen per accidens ἢ μὴ ὂν, in quantum est non ens. quasi vero tam bardi ac stupidi fuerint primi illi naturalium rerum indagatores, ut non possent comprehendere, in omni mutatione rem fieri aliquid quod non erat prius, & induere illum habitum, quo prius carebat ac privata erat. ingens vero hoc secretum, ut tot tantiq; viri nequiverint ad ejus perceptionem aspirare: non igitur ob ejus ignorantiam negaverunt generationem, quam tu generationem vocas, qua nimirum aliud fit ex alio; sed illam negaverunt, qua substantia fit ex nihilo, & verissime negaverunt, quod ne tu quidem ipse potes negare, quantumcunq; tergiverseris.
units.tr: IX. And why do we dispute longer against privation, when Aristotle himself, in that same book where he so laboriously establishes it, clearly rejects it? For he says that the causes and principles from which things consist essentially and are generated are matter and form. [Φανερὸν οὖν, ὡς εἴπερ εἰσὶν αἰτίαι καὶ αρχαὶ τῶν φύσει ὄντων, ἐξ ὧν πρώτων εἰσί καὶ γεγόνασι, μὴ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς, ἀλλ' ἕκαστον ὃ λέγεται καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν, ὅτι γίγνεται ἀπὸν ἐκ τε τῆς ὑποκειμένης καὶ τῆς μορφῆς.] It is manifest, therefore, that since there are causes and principles of natural things, from which they first consist and have come to be, not accidentally, but each thing which is said to exist in its essence, everything comes to be from a subject and a form. He says not only that things exist from these two principles, but also that they are generated from them, so that the futility of this distinction becomes apparent, namely that privation is a principle not of essence but of generation. And afterwards he adds: [Καὶ ἅπλου ἐστιν, ὅτι ἀεὶ ὑποκειμένη ἐν τοῖς ἐναντίοις, καὶ τὰ ἐναντία δύο εἶναι. τρόπον δέ τινα ἄλλον ἐκ ἀναγκαῖον ἱκανὸν ἦ ἕσαι ἡ ἕτερον τῶν ἐναντίων ποιεῖν τῇ ἀπουσίᾳ καὶ παρουσίᾳ τὴν μεταβολήν.] And it is evident that there must always be some subject underlying the contraries, and that the contraries are two; but in another way it is not necessary, for one of the contraries will suffice to produce change by its absence and presence. By these words he betrays his own levity most plainly, since he who introduced into philosophy as a necessary principle what he himself freely confesses is not necessary, because matter together with form suffices alone. Yet elsewhere he severely censures his teacher Plato for saying this very thing and for excluding privation from generation. And in that same first book of the Physics, a little after the words quoted above, he fiercely inveighs against the ancient philosophers, that because they did not know privation they fell into such a gross error as to deny altogether that anything comes to be, since without knowledge of that mystery they could not understand how anything could come to be [ἐκ μὴ ὄντος] out of non-being. But he claims to have discovered this and to have shown, by introducing privation, that nothing comes to be simply out of non-being [ἐκ μὴ ὄντος], yet it comes to be accidentally out of non-being [ἢ μὴ ὂν], in so far as it is non-being. As if those first investigators of natural things were so dull and stupid that they could not grasp that in every change a thing becomes something that it was not before, and puts on that form which it previously lacked and was deprived of. This secret is indeed great, so that so many great men could not aspire to perceive it. Therefore they did not deny generation, which you call generation, by which one thing manifestly comes from another, because of ignorance of this secret. They denied that generation by which a substance comes from nothing, and they denied it most truly, which you yourself cannot deny, however much you equivocate.

units.la: X. Sed de hoc Veterum axiomate & dictum fuit antea plus semel; & dicendum alibi erit rursus; quare nunc eo misso, revertamur ad Privationem, de qua ex prius dictis apparet, eam, posita tali generatione, qualem somniat Peripatus, ex Materia prima & Forma, nihil tamen esse, ac propterea absurde poni pro Principio rerum naturalium; siquidem Forma Formæ immediate succedit, & ne punctum quidem temporis intervenit inter excessum prioris Formæ, & introductionem recentis, quo illa sit in Materia. & nec postea est in Materia, omnium confessione, nec antea, ut partim ipsorum fatentur, partim nostris argumentis ostensum est: quare relinquitur ut nunquam fit. proptereaq; entium Principium esse nullo modo potest, ne ita quidem, ut fit terminus à quo; siquidem nihil proficifci potest à termino, qui nec existat, neq; unquam extiterit.
units.tr: X. But this axiom of the ancients has been discussed more than once before, and will have to be discussed again elsewhere. Therefore, setting that aside now, let us return to privation. From what has been said it appears that, given such a generation as the Peripatetic school dreams of, out of prime matter and form, privation is nothing at all, and so is absurdly posited as a principle of natural things. For a form immediately succeeds the form, and not even a point of time intervenes between the departure of the prior form and the introduction of the new one, in which the privation could be in the matter. And afterwards it is not in the matter, by everyone's admission, nor before it, as partly they themselves confess and partly has been shown by our arguments. Therefore it follows that it never comes to be. Hence it can in no way be the principle of beings, not even in the sense of a term from which, since nothing can proceed from a term which neither exists nor has ever existed.
XI.

units.la: Imo falsum est totum fundamentum, cui Privationem Aristoteles superstruxit, nimirum omnem mutationem, & proinde etiam generationem, esse motum à contrario in contrarium; quod alibi probabitur. & si vel maxime verum esset, deberemus illam contrarietatem in ipsis Formis quaerere, quia habitus & privatio non sunt vere contraria, siquidem vera est illa definitio, contraria esse quae sub eodem genere plurimum distant. at Forma & Privatio non possunt sub eodem genere comprehendi, cum illa sit substantia (ut ipsi volunt) haec vero ne accidens quidem, ut ipsi dicunt (quod quam belle cohaereat cum eo, quod eam dicunt esse in Materia, ipsi viderint) quare temperare sibi non potuit Themistius, quin diceret plus semel, Privationem & Formam nimis licenter vocari contraria, cum non possint invicem agere ac pati, & Privatio nihil sit nisi Formae absentia.
units.tr: Indeed the whole foundation on which Aristotle built privation is false, namely that every change, and therefore also generation, is motion from a contrary to a contrary; this will be proved elsewhere. And even if it were wholly true, we ought to seek that contrariety in the Forms themselves, because habit and privation are not truly contraries, since the true definition is that contraries are those which differ most within the same genus. But Form and Privation cannot be comprehended under the same genus, since the one is a substance (as they themselves maintain), while the other is not even an accident, as they say (how well this agrees with their claim that privation is in matter, they themselves will have to see). For this reason Themistius could not refrain from saying more than once that Privation and Form are too carelessly called contraries, since they cannot act upon and undergo one another, and privation is nothing but the absence of the Form.
XII.

units.la: Sed si omnia velimus exequi, quae de hoc inutili figmento chartis illeverunt homines alienis nugis nimium feriati, nimis infructuosum laborem sumereus. Quis enim sine indignatione aut risu legere queat anxias illas distinctiones inter Materiae potentiam tum primam tum secundam, sive generalem & specialem, & Privationem, cum omnia eorum dicta eo recidant, ut Privatio nihil sit aliud, nisi propinqua illa Materiae potentia, atq; ipsa recipiendae Formae aptitudo; cum qua licet reipsa penitus confundant, verbis tamen sejungere coguntur, ne prodant praeceptorem suum, cujus honori parum consulerent, si faterentur id rerum naturalium Principium ob eo factum fuisse, quod alterius Principij & quidem ignobilissimi, non nisi accidens esset, & quidem evanidum. Ut appareat quid censendum sit de furiosa illa Scaligeri invectiva, qua eos, qui Privationem de numero Principiorum exemerunt, stultos vocat & vecordes mundi novatores, putidos grammaticos, Aristotelis obtrectatores; quae scurrilia convitia tanto sunt intolerabiliora in ipso, quanto ipse fatetur alibi, Privationem nihil esse nisi in intellectu. ita enim inquit: Privatio sequitur omnium essentiam praedicamentorum, quae essentia cum abest, illud abesse dicitur Privatio, cujus esse est, non esse, neq; aliquid est nisi intellectu. si enim omnia alia argumenta desint, haec una confessio sufficerit, ad Privationem e Principiorum senatu ejiciendam. quid enim insulsius dici aut cogitari potest, quam inter Principia, e quibus substantiae naturales constent ac generentur, illud collocare, quod nihil sit nisi mentis conceptus? certe non est satis mirari Themistium, qui cum dixisset Privationem nullibi subsistere; addit, necessariam esse tamen, cen alteram naturam, quae alteri naturae accidat. nullum est monstrum, quod dicere non audeant mirabiles isti philosophi. neq; enim est intelligere, quomodo id alteri naturae accidat, quod non est usquam, nisi in ipsius Intellectus conceptu.
units.tr: But if we were to go through everything that men, too much at leisure with other people's trifles, have daubed on paper about this useless fiction, I would be undertaking an far too fruitless labour. For who could read without indignation or laughter those anxious distinctions between the first and second potency of matter, or general and special, and privation? All their statements come down to this: privation is nothing but that proximate potency of matter, the very aptitude for receiving form.
