Although in reality they utterly confuse the two, they are forced to separate them in words, lest they betray their teacher, whose honour they would do little to serve if they admitted that this was a principle of natural things because of another principle, and indeed a most ignoble one, which would be merely an accident, and a fleeting one at that. This shows what we should think of that frenzied invective of Scaliger, in which he calls those who have removed privation from the number of principles foolish and deranged innovators of the world, stinking grammarians, and detractors of Aristotle. These scurrilous insults are all the more intolerable in him, since he elsewhere admits that privation is nothing except in the intellect. For he says: Privation follows the essence of all the categories; when that essence is absent, the absence is called privation, whose being is non-being, and which is nothing except in the intellect. Even if all other arguments were lacking, this one confession would be enough to expel privation from the senate of principles. For what can be said or thought more silly than to place among the principles from which natural substances consist and are generated that which is nothing but a concept of the mind? Certainly one cannot sufficiently marvel at Themistius, who, having said that privation nowhere subsists, adds that it is nevertheless necessary, as another nature which accrues to another nature. There is no monstrosity these marvellous philosophers do not dare to utter. For it is not understandable how that which is nowhere, except in the concept of the intellect itself, could accrue to another nature.

units.la: Negant quidem hoc multi Peripatetici, Privationes in sola mentis notione esse, inter quos sunt Conimbricenses. sed nihil solidi afferunt, quo negationem suam tueantur. omnis enim eorum probatio petita est ex illis Aristotelis verbis, Quod Forma & Privatio versantur circa idem subjectum. ergo [inquiunt] quoties in tempore a natura constituto subjectum Forma caruerit, inerit ei Formae Privatio: hoc autem contingit seclusa qualibet mentis actione: igitur Privatio inest in rebus formaliter sine intellectu. sed haec consequentia nihili est, cum ipsi fateantur, subjectum nunquam vel ad minimum temporis punctum Forma carere. & sua ipsorum dicta verbis sequentibus manifestissime evertunt, quando Privationi omnem denegant existentiam; quia cum existentia positivum quippiam sit, fieri non potest, ut negationem re ipsa proprie
units.tr: Indeed, many Peripatetics deny that privations are in the mere notion of the mind, among them the Conimbricenses. But they bring forward nothing solid to defend their denial. For their whole proof is drawn from those words of Aristotle, that form and privation are concerned with the same subject. Therefore, [they say], whenever within a time fixed by nature the subject has lacked form, privation is inherent in it as form; but this happens apart from any action of the mind; therefore privation exists in things formally without the intellect. But this inference is worthless, since they themselves admit that the subject never lacks form, not even for the smallest point of time. Moreover, their own statements in the following words most clearly overturn it, when they deny that privation has any existence at all; for since existence is something positive, it cannot happen that a negation actually informs a thing properly.

units.la: Manuscript annotations in the margins and below the text are handwritten and are not transcribed. prie informet. Sed jam ἄλλᾳ βοηθείᾳ; verbum non amplius addimus de Privatione. & sicui haec omnia nondum satisfaciunt (animis enim pertinaciter in aliqua secta obfirmatis nulla rationum momenta satisfacere queant) ille Materiam primam & Formam substantialem asserat prius à nostris objectionibus, & postea super Privatione pedem nobiscum conferat. namq; illis sublatis hanc ne ipsi quidem posuerint Peripatetici.
units.tr: Yet now by another aid [ἄλλῃ βοηθείᾳ], we add no further word about privation. And if all these things still do not satisfy anyone (for those whose minds are stubbornly fixed in some sect cannot be satisfied by any weight of arguments), let him first assert prime matter and substantial form against our objections, and afterwards let him join issue with us about privation. For once these are removed, not even the Peripatetics themselves would posit privation.
FIFTH SECTION.

units.la: Transitur ad examinandam Aristotelis sententiam de Causis. Principia sua Aristoteles & Aristotelici etiam Elementa vocant. A Causis potius quam à Principiis incipere debuerat Aristoteles. II. Aristotelis scopus in tractatione de Principiis ac Causis. III. In quibus culpemus tractationem Aristotelis de Causis, in secundo Physicorum institutam. IV. Vanitas istius axiomatis, Efficiens, Formam & Finem, idem esse in naturalibus. V. Difficultas, quomodo Agentia naturalia, cognitionis expertia, agant propter finem: & Aristotelis ad eam responsio. VI. Cavillatoria vanitas istius responsi; aliag in eo absurda. VII. Quod Aristoteles statuit, Naturam agere propter finem; in eo nihil novi dixit, quum recepta Veterum haec fuerit sententia. VIII. Vera Veterum assertio, Agentia naturalia agere ex congenitâ necessitate: explicatur. IX. Aristotelis inconstantia: sententiam modo dictam maligne detorquet. X. Incusatur Aristoteles, quod nihil de natura ac modo operandi Finalis Causae tradiderit. Absurda plerorumq; Aristotelicorum opinio, Finem agere secundum esse regale. XI. Absurditas Peripateticorum, negantium Causalitatem Finis consistere in motu, quo ciet appetitum. Finis non est peculiare Causae genus, sed Efficientis quaedam species. XII. Aliy defectus in hac tractatione de Fine. Epilogus totius disqui-
units.tr: We pass to an examination of Aristotle's doctrine of causes. Aristotle and the Aristotelians also call their principles "elements." Aristotle ought to have begun with causes rather than with principles. (II) Aristotle's aim in his treatment of principles and causes. (III) The points in which we find fault with Aristotle's treatment of causes, set out in the second book of the Physics. (IV) The vanity of the axiom that the efficient, the form and the end are the same in natural things. (V) The difficulty of how natural agents, which lack knowledge, act for an end, and Aristotle's answer to it. (VI) The trifling vanity of that answer, and other absurdities in it. (VII) What Aristotle laid down, that nature acts for an end: in this he said nothing new, since this was the accepted opinion of the ancients. (VIII) The true assertion of the ancients, that natural agents act from innate necessity, is explained. (IX) Aristotle's inconsistency: he twists the opinion just mentioned in a malicious way. (X) Aristotle is accused of having handed down nothing about the nature and mode of operation of the final cause; and the absurd opinion of most Aristotelians, that the end acts by royal authority. (XI) The absurdity of the Peripatetics, who deny that the causality of the end consists in the motion by which it stirs up appetite. The end is not a peculiar kind of cause, but a certain species of the efficient. (XII) Other defects in this treatment of the end. Epilogue of the whole disquisition.

units.la: Sect. V. Cap. I. De quisitionis de Principijs Aristotelicis.
units.tr: Sect. V. Cap. I. On the Inquiry into Aristotle's Principles

units.la: I. HActenus igitur Aristotelis de internis rerum Principijs, è quibus constent ac generentur, sententiam exanimavimus, & quæ ille tria ponit, Materiam primam, Formam, & Privationem, nulla esse omnino ostendimus. nunc consequens esset, ut nostram de Principijs opinionem aperiremus: sed quia adeo conjuncta est apud Aristotelem Principiorum ac Causarum tractatio, ut divelli sine maxima perturbatione non possint, statuimus prius ipsius de Causis quoq; placita perpendere; & sic postea nostram de Principis ac Causis sententiam proponere. Repetendum autem nobis est, quod supra attigimus, Principium ac Causam nihil prorsus differre Aristoteli, ac passim in omnibus ejus scriptis pro eodem usurpari promiscue, & & perfaps etiam utrumq;, simul jungi plane synonymos, neq; alia cum significatione, quam si alterutrum tantum positum esset; ut non posset dici, alterum altero esse generalius, aut hoc sub illo comprehendi. in solo primo Physicorum discrimen invexit, & Principij vocabulum duobus illis, Materiæ & Formæ (addita etiam Privatione, sed quæ in Materiæ ratione intelligenda sit) proprie assignavit, exclusò Efficiente ac Fine, & solo Causæ nomine ijs relicto; quod prioribus illis, quanquam peculiariter attributa ijs Principij appellatione, non auferret: sicut è secundo physicorum apparet, ubi, quemadmodum semper alibi, in Causarum enumeratione Materiam & Formam de novo posuit. Ex his itaque sequitur, in illis libris generalius esse Aristoteli Causæ quam Principij vocabulum, cum hoc sub comprehenderit, non contra. & Principij vocabulum hoc pacto usurpatum, nihil differt ab Elemento; quomodo ipse Elementi vocabulum usurpat, non modo de Materia secunda, & de ijs, quæ vulgo Elementa dicuntur, sed & de Materia prima ac Forma, imo & de Privatione. itaque ipse in primo physicorum semel iterumq; στοιχεῖον pro ἀρχὴ posuit, cap. 6. Τὸ μὲν οὖν τρία φάσκειν τὰ στοιχεῖα εἶναι, λόξειεν ἂν ἔχειν ἱκανὸν λόγον. Τὸ δὲ πλείω τρισὶν, ὀυκέτι. Dicere igitur, quòd quòd tria sint Elementa, videtur aliquam rationem habere: plura autem tribus, nequaquam. & mox, ὅτι μὲν οὖν οὔτε ἐν τῷ στοιχεῖον, οὔτε πολεῖα λυσιν ἢ τριῶν, φανερόν. Quod igitur neq; unum sit Elementum, neq; plura duobus aut tribus, manifestum est. & 12. Metaph. 4. ὥσε στοιχεῖα μὲν κατὰ ἀναλογίαν τρία, αἴτια δὲ καὶ ἀρχαὶ τέσσαρες. Itaq; Elementa quidem secundum analogiam tria sunt, Causa autem & Principia quatuor. (ubi Principij vocabulum latius usurpat, ut Causæ synonymum) Et quanquam Privationi non competit Elementi definitio, cum non sit rei pars, extenditur tamen ad eam ex accidenti, quia quatenus est Principium internum, est eadem cum Materia; & aliquo modo Forma, inquit Piccolomineus; quod quale sit, hic non discutiemus, cum nunc tantum velimus ostendere, Principij vocabulum, quatenus tribus illis attribuitur, nihil ab Elemento differre. & certe iltis, præsertim Materiæ & Formæ (si talia essent, ac ab ipso ponuntur) omnino competit Elementi definitio ab ipso tradita 5. Metaph. 3. ἐξ οὗ γίγνεται πρώτου ἐνυπάρχοντος, ἀδιαιρέτου τῷ εἴδει ex quo compositum est primo inexistente, indivisibili secundum speciem, non solis Elementis corporeis; ut asseverat etiam a Piccolomineus. Imò b Averroes dicit Elementum in propria significatione sumtum, de Causis intrinsecis, Materia & Forma, dici; quod secutus est & c Zabarella ita etiam d Scaliger, Sane Forma Elementum est. & c alibi, Materia & Forma, compositi partes atq; Elementa sunt. & Exerc. 364. 2. Elementum, ex quo quid constituitur, duplex, Materia & Forma. cum igitur Principia (ut hic sumuntur) non differant ab Elementis; hinc quoq; sequitur, Causam ipsi latius patere quam Principium, in hoc primo Physicorum libro; quare quod propositum à maxime generalibus incipere, non præstitit. Non tamen hoc dicimus, quod ab Efficiente & Fine potius, quam a Materia & Forma ordiri Physicam debuerit, sed quod propositæ in Principio rerum naturalium Causæ, ita illi partiendæ fuerint, ut diceret duas istarum peculiariter hoc sibi nomen vindicare; reliquas duas, etiamsi & ipsæ generico hoc nomine
units.tr: I. Hitherto, then, we have examined Aristotle's opinion about the internal principles of things, out of which they consist and are generated, and we have shown that the three he posits, prime matter, form and privation, are not principles at all. It would now follow that we set out our own opinion about principles. But since Aristotle's treatment of principles and causes is so closely bound together that they cannot be separated without great confusion, we resolved first to weigh his views on causes as well, and afterwards to propose our own view of principles and causes. We must, however, repeat what we touched on above: for Aristotle, principle and cause differ in no way at all. Throughout his writings they are used interchangeably, and perhaps both are even joined together as plain synonyms, with no other meaning than if only one of them had been set down. So one cannot say that one is more general than the other, or that one is contained under the other. He introduced a distinction only in the first book of the Physics. There he properly assigned the word principle to the two, matter and form (privation being added too, though it is to be understood in the sense of matter), leaving out the efficient and final causes and keeping for them the name cause alone. This does not take the name principle away from the former two, though it is attributed to them in a special way. This appears from the second book of the Physics, where, as everywhere else, he again posits matter and form in his enumeration of causes. It follows from this that in those books the word cause is more general for Aristotle than the word principle, since he includes principle under cause, not the reverse. And the word principle, used in this way, differs in nothing from element. Aristotle himself uses the word element not only of secondary matter and of those things commonly called elements, but also of prime matter and form, and even of privation. Thus in the first book of the Physics, ch. 6, he once and again puts στοιχεῖον [element] for ἀρχή [principle]: To say that there are three elements seems to have some reasonable account; but to say more than three, by no means. And soon after: That there is neither one element nor more than two or three is clear. And in Metaphysics 12, text 4: So there are three elements according to analogy, but four causes and principles. (Here he uses the word principle more widely, as a synonym of cause.) And although the definition of element does not fit privation, since it is not a part of a thing, it is nonetheless extended to it by accident, because insofar as it is an internal principle it is the same as matter, and in some way form, says Piccolomini. What sort of thing that is we will not discuss here, since we wish only to show that the word principle, insofar as it is attributed to those three, differs in nothing from element. Certainly the definition of element that he gives in Metaphysics 5, text 3, applies wholly to them, especially to matter and form (if they were such things, as he posits them): that from which a thing is made, first inhering in it, indivisible in species, and not only to corporeal elements; as Piccolomini also asserts. Indeed Averroes says that element, taken in its proper sense, is said of the intrinsic causes, matter and form; Zabarella followed him in this, and so did Scaliger: Surely form is an element. And elsewhere: Matter and form are the parts and elements of a compound. And in Exercitationes 364, section 2: Element, that out of which something is constituted, is twofold: matter and form. Since therefore principles (as they are taken here) do not differ from elements, it also follows from this that in this first book of the Physics cause extends more widely than principle; which is why he did not achieve what he proposed, to begin from the most general things. Yet we do not say that Physics ought to have begun from the efficient and final causes rather than from matter and form. Rather, the causes proposed in the principles of natural things ought to have been divided in such a way that he said two of them claim this name for themselves in a special way, while the other two, although they are also commonly called by the general name

units.la: 1 Phys. text. 99. in dubit. mine vocari consueverint, magis tamen speciali Principiorum nomine gaudere. & sic deinde nihilominus à Principiorum pertractatione potuisset incipere, Efficiente & Fine in secundum librum, sicuti nunc quoq; fecit, rejectis: ubi tunc non opus habuisset Materiam & Formam otiose de novo repetere. & sic plurimos bonos viros, sectatores atq; interpretes suos, magna molestia liberasset, qui nunc causam istius repetitionis dum exquirunt, mira sibi somnia confingunt, sicuti ante latius executi sumus.
units.tr: 1 Phys. text. 99. in doubt. (the marginal reference) by the general name, nonetheless enjoy the more specific name of principles. And so he could nevertheless have begun the treatment of principles from there, rejecting the efficient and final causes to the second book, as he now also did. Then he would not have needed to repeat matter and form idly once more. And so he would have spared many good men, his followers and interpreters, great trouble. Those who now try to find out the reason for this repetition devise strange fancies for themselves, as we have explained more fully before.

units.la: II. Porro ut hoc mittamus, Aristotelis scopus in tractatione Principiorum ac Causarum (de quo tot tamq; differentientes sunt ipsius interpretum opiniones) hic videtur fuisse. Primo tradere voluit interna rerum Principia, è quibus constant atq; generantur. & quia duplex est eorum consideratio, vel quatenus partes rerum sunt atq; Elementa, vel quatenus operationum authores; priore quidem respectu de ijs egit prius, in primo libro physicorum; altero, in principio secundi, sub nomine Naturæ, quod ijs competat, quatenus effectiones ab ijs proficiscuntur. Tunc denum transiit ad Principia externa, Causam efficientem & finalem; de quibus solis cum illic verba facere debuisset, Materiam & Formam cum ijs rursus supervacue posuit.
units.tr: II. Moreover, to set this aside, Aristotle's aim in treating principles and causes (about which the opinions of his interpreters are so many and so varied) seems to have been this. First, he wished to set out the internal principles of things, out of which they consist and are generated. And since these can be considered in two ways, either insofar as they are parts and elements of things, or insofar as they are the authors of operations, he dealt with them first in the first book of the Physics from the former standpoint, and from the latter at the beginning of the second book, under the name of Nature, which belongs to them insofar as effects proceed from them. Only then did he pass to the external principles, the efficient and final causes. Since he ought to have spoken of these alone at that point, he superfluously posited matter and form again along with them.

units.la: Hæc est Aristotelis methodus, qua rerum naturalium Principia & Causas executus est in duobus primis physicorum libris, per se bona satis; hoc vitij habens, quod in principio dicere neglexit, quomodo se haberent Principia ad Causas, & quid inter hæc duo interesset, quodq; Materiam & Formam inter Causas non recte repetivit. absq; hoc methodus illa est proba, quanquam non exactissima, si ad ipsius scita exigatur; cum dicat, in principio primi physicorum, non modo à maxime generalibus, sed & ab omnium primis ordiendam esse Physicam: Causa autem Efficiens est magis prima, quam Materia aut Forma; imo & Finis quoque, ex ipsius doctrina. Non tamen, ut ipsa nobis non multum displicet, ita & res quæ eâ tractantur. namq; illo ordine agi de rerum naturalium Causis & Principijs; possumus quodammodo probare, Principia ipsa & Causas ab Aristotele tradita, nequaquam: cum partim falsa sint, partim manca, quae ab ipso traduntur & de Principijs quidem generationis ac constitutionis, jam dixi-mus. sed neq; placent nobis, quae de ijsdem tradit, quate-nus sint Principia operationum, & Naturae nomine ab ipso insigniuntur; quod postea peculiari ac prolixa tractatione (ita enim rei dignitas postulat) persecuturi su-mus.
units.tr: This is Aristotle's method by which he worked through the principles and causes of natural things in the first two books of the Physics. In itself it is good enough, but it has the fault that at the beginning he neglected to say how principles stand in relation to causes, and what difference there is between these two, and that he wrongly repeated matter and form among the causes. Apart from this, the method is sound, though not most exact, if it is measured against his own rules. For he says, at the beginning of the first book of the Physics, that Physics must begin not only from the most general things but from the very first of all. Yet the efficient cause is prior to matter or form, and indeed the final cause too, according to his own teaching. Nor, although we do not much dislike the method itself, do we find the things treated by it to be the same. For although one can, in a way, approve of Aristotle's treatment of the causes and principles of natural things in that order, we cannot approve the principles and causes he delivers. Some are false and some are incomplete. I have already said this about the principles of generation and constitution. Nor do we like what he says about the same things insofar as they are principles of operations, and which he marks with the name of Nature. We shall pursue this in a separate and extended treatment, since the importance of the matter demands it.

units.la: III. Restat igitur imprsenti, ut de Causis quid dicatur ab Aristotele perpendamus: ubi inprimis id nobis displicet, quod ita levi pede illas pertransiverit. Quanquam enim, aggressurus Caularum explicationem, dicat id necessarium esse, ut ortum ac interitum, omnesq; naturales mutationes ad eas referre sciamus; ita tamen laxe id fecit ac negligenter, ac si in tyrocinio Logicae, non in Disciplina Naturali versaretur; quod de Efficienti praecipue intelligi volumus: quam nequaquam subjecto suo accommodavit, aut accommodare aggressus est, adeoq; oscitanter eam transcurrit, ut fere nihil aliud de ea dicat, nisi quum Caesarum sint quatuor genera, unam de isto numero esse Causam Efficientem. & de Finali quoq; Causa diligentiam haud multo majorem praestitit. de Materia & Forma paucissima delibavit, sed ea ipsa sint nimia, cum nullum de ijs verbum hic facere debuerit, utpote de quibus antea tam verbose seorsim egerit. Itaq; multi accusant Aristotelem, quod illa de Causis in secundo physicorum tractatio nequaquam physica sit, sed logica penitus. & ipse Zabarella, qui multum laborat, ut ostendat, rite & loco dicta esse, quae ibi de causis dixit Aristoteles, fateri tamen cogitur, Quod de illa tractatione, quae in primo libro habetur, dicere possumus, nos per eam cognovisse primas Causas rerum naturalium; sed de illa, quae habetur in secundo libro, nihil tale dicere nos posse, quia per eam nullas cognoscimus rerum naturalium Causas, ex quarum notitia aliorum cognitionem adipiscamur: namq; co in loco agi tantum de gene-
units.tr: III. It remains, then, for the present, that we weigh what Aristotle says about causes. Here, above all, we dislike the fact that he passed over them so lightly. For although, when about to explain the causes, he says it is necessary to know that all birth and death, and all natural changes, are to be referred to them, he did this so loosely and carelessly, as if he were occupied with the rudiments of Logic and not with Natural Philosophy. We wish this to be understood especially of the efficient cause. He did not fit it to its subject at all, nor did he attempt to do so, and he runs through it so carelessly that he says almost nothing about it except that since there are four kinds of causes, one of this number is the efficient cause. He also showed no much greater diligence about the final cause. He touched very briefly on matter and form, but even these are excessive, since he ought not to have said a word about them here, having already treated them so verbosely and separately before. So many accuse Aristotle that his treatment of causes in the second book of the Physics is not physical at all, but wholly logical. And Zabarella himself, who labours hard to show that what Aristotle said there about causes was rightly said and in its proper place, is nonetheless forced to admit this: what we can say about the treatment found in the first book, that through it we have come to know the first causes of natural things; but about that found in the second book we cannot say any such thing, because through it we know no causes of natural things, from whose knowledge we might gain knowledge of others. For that place deals only with the kinds...
Enig-hentery
Chapter I.

units.la: generibus modifq; causarum, non de causis illis affectuum naturalium. & Simplicius, tam pauca, ac tam parum ad propositum quae facerent, de Efficienti Causa dicta videns, in eam venit opinionem, ut crederet, Aristotelis intentionem fuisse, ut de solo Fine ageret; & quia Finis Causae species sit, per eam occasionem de Causis in genere nonnulla locutum esse.
units.tr: of the kinds and modes of causes, not of those causes of natural affections. And Simplicius, seeing that so few things, and those so little to the point, had been said about the efficient cause, came to the opinion that Aristotle's intention was to treat only of the final cause. Because the final cause is a kind of cause, he thought that on that occasion Aristotle had said some things about causes in general.

units.la: IV. Nimis igitur leviter Efficientem causam transcurrit Aristoteles, neq; eam physicè accommodavit; quippe non amplius quàm nominans ipsam: quum plurima, ac scitu perquàm digna & necessaria, de ipsa dicenda sint Physico, qui muneri suo vel tolerabiliter velit satisfacere. quin interdum velut somnians, ita de ipsa loquitur; quippe tria haec, Formam, Finem, Efficiens, unum & idem esse in naturalibus. sic enim ait. 2. Phys. 7: Sæpe tria ista in unum veniunt. & clarius 2. de Anim. 4. Ὁμως δ' ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τὰς δι' ἡμένης τρεῖς τέρπως αἰτίας. Attamen anima secundum triplicem illum modum Causa est, namq; & Principium motus est hæc, & Causa finalis; & tanquam essentia corporum naturalium causa est anima. quæ verba nimis odiosâ ludunt homonymia. Animam enim esse Efficiens, nemo sanus negaverit. namque & actiones omnes ab ipsa fluunt, & corpus ipsa fabricavit, quod ut verissimum est, ita ipse quoq; sensisse videtur. 7. Metaph. 9. qua de re alibi agendum erit. Propterea tamen ipsa Efficiens Plantæ aut animalis, cujus Anima est, dici nullo pacto debet. non enim corpus tantum est animal aut planta, sed corpus animæ junctum; propterea quoq; quando Efficiens quæritur, non solius corporis Efficiens afferendus est, sed totius, hoc est, ipsius quoq; Animæ. & quanquam Anima, quæ erat in femine canis, corpus ipsius architectata est; quando tamen de Efficiente canis quæstio est; non Anima alleganda est, sed illud, quod ipsam quoq; animam fecit, & semini implantavit, ac viribus illis donavit, ut ex femine corpus sibi moliri ipsa posset, non enim seipsam anima fecit, sed cum aliquando non esset, à Principio Efficienti ut esset accepit; propterea̛q; animalis Efficiens Anima dici non meretur, cum ipsa, nobilissima animalis pars, aliud Efficiens agnoscat; quod ut per se manifestum est, ita ipsi quoq; alicubi testatum, illis verbis, ῥεντᾶ δ᾽ ἀ̓ῤ̓ὲν αὑτὸ ἑαυτὸ. Nihil autem generat seipsum. Itaq; prorsus absurda est illa sententia, Animam esse Efficiens animalium. Et secundo physicorum mirificos dat lusus, in explicatione istius theleos supra citatæ, ἐχεσθαι τὰ τέλεια εἰς τ᾽ ἐν πόλεσι. cum enim dicendum illi esset, quo pacto Anima esset ejusdem rei Forma & Efficiens, eo revolvitur ut dicat, Efficiens esse idem specie cum Forma. τὸ μὲν ᾧ εἶδει, καὶ τ᾽ ὃν ἐνεκα, ἐν εἶσι. τ᾽ δὲ ὅθεν ἡ μίνησις πρῶτον, ὥσπερ εἶδει τ᾽ αὐτὸ τόπος· ἄνθρωπος ἢ ἄνθρωπον γεννᾷ. Etenim Forma & Causa finalis, idem sunt. id autem, unde motus primò est, idem specie est cum hisce. namq; homo hominem generat, ut esse idem non est aliud, quam esse specie idem, omnino recte dixerit, Animam esse idem cum Efficiente, sed si plurimum inter hæc interest, temere illud posuit, quod explicando ipse everteret. namq; si homo generat hominem, non generat homo seipsum, ac proinde Anima hominis non est hominis Efficiens, ejusdem niminum hominis. namcum de uno quæritur, de alio respondere, sophistæ potius est, captionum laqueos nectentis, quam Philosophi veritatem docere profitentis. itaq; frivolum dictu est, Efficiens esse idem quod τὸ εἶδος; Formam, quia sit idem ᾧ εἶδει, specie. in ista enim τὸ εἶδος homonymia fundatum est hoc axioma, qua sane & alibi abutitur, ut quod dicendum suscepera̛t περὶ τῶ̃ εἴδους in significatione Formæ; id de eo explicet in significatione speciei; vel contra. itaq; plane extra chorum saltat, dum istam affert probationem, cur Forma & Efficiens sint unum; quia sunt unum specie; ad quod suis ipsi verbis respondemus; Οὐκ ἐν ἀπαυλα, ὧν μία ἡ οὐσία, ἀλλὰ πολλὰ καὶ διάφορα. Non sunt unum omnia, quorum eadem est substantia, seu essentia; sed multa & differentia. Averroes tamen (cui pessima quaeque in Aristotele maxime placuerunt) non dubitavit hoc tanquam probatum à praeceptore usurpare. scribit enim, Quod Causa formalis, finalis, & movens, sint idem secundum subjectum, nec differant nisi secundum modum: & alibi quoque similia repetit: estque hoc axioma apud reliquos quoque Peripateticos vulgatum & receptum.
units.tr: IV. Aristotle therefore passes over the efficient cause too lightly and does not treat it in a physical way. He does no more than name it, though many things about it are worth knowing and necessary, and must be said by a natural philosopher who wishes at least tolerably to discharge his duty. Indeed, sometimes, as if dreaming, he speaks of it in such a way that these three, Form, End and Efficient, are one and the same in natural things. For he says in Physics 2: Often these three come to one. And more clearly in De Anima 2.4: Ὁμως δ' ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τὰς δι' ἡμένης τρεῖς τέρπως αἰτίας. Yet the soul is a cause in that threefold manner, for it is both the principle of motion and the final cause, and as the essence of natural bodies the soul is their cause. These words play with a most odious homonymy. For no sane person will deny that the soul is an efficient cause: all actions flow from it, and it fashioned the body, which, as it is most true, so it also seems to have perceived. See Metaphysics 7.9, a matter to be treated elsewhere. Nevertheless, the efficient cause of a plant or animal, of which the soul is the form, ought by no means to be called the soul. For an animal or plant is not merely the body, but the body joined to the soul. Therefore also, when the efficient cause is asked, the efficient cause must be given not of the body alone but of the whole, that is, of the soul too. And although the soul that was in the seed of a dog shaped its body, when the question concerns the efficient cause of the dog, it is not the soul that is to be adduced, but that which made the soul itself and implanted it in the seed, and endowed it with those powers so that it could build a body for itself out of the seed. For the soul did not make itself; though at one time it did not exist, it received its being from an efficient principle. Therefore the efficient cause of an animal does not deserve to be called the soul, since the soul, the most noble part of the animal, itself acknowledges another efficient cause. This is manifest in itself, and it is attested elsewhere in these words: ῥεντᾶ δ᾽ ἀ̓ῤ̓ὲν αὑτὸ ἑαυτὸ. Nothing generates itself. Therefore that opinion, that the soul is the efficient cause of animals, is utterly absurd. And in the second book of the Physics he plays wonderful games in explaining the saying cited above, ἐχεσθαι τὰ τέλεια εἰς τ᾽ ἐν πόλεσι. For when he ought to say how the soul is the form and the efficient cause of the same thing, he turns back and says that the efficient cause is the same in species as the form: τὸ μὲν ᾧ εἶδει, καὶ τ᾽ ὃν ἐνεκα, ἐν εἶσι. τ᾽ δὲ ὅθεν ἡ μίνησις πρῶτον, ὥσπερ εἶδει τ᾽ αὐτὸ τόπος· ἄνθρωπος ἢ ἄνθρωπον γεννᾷ. For the form and the final cause are the same. That from which motion first comes is the same in species as these: man begets man. He could rightly have said that the soul is the same as the efficient cause; but if there is a great difference between these, he rashly posited it, and in explaining it he overturns it himself. For if man begets man, man does not beget himself, and so the soul of man is not the efficient cause of man, that is, of the same man. When one asks about one thing, to answer about another belongs rather to a sophist, weaving the snares of captious arguments, than to a philosopher who professes to teach the truth. Therefore it is a frivolous claim that the efficient cause is the same as τὸ εἶδος, the form, because it is the same ᾧ εἶδει, in species. For this axiom rests on the homonymy of τὸ εἶδος, and he surely abuses it elsewhere too: what he undertook to say περὶ τοῦ εἴδους in the sense of form, he explains in the sense of species, or the reverse. So he plainly dances outside the chorus when he offers this proof that form and efficient cause are one, namely that they are one in species. To this we answer in his own words: Οὐκ ἐν ἀπαυλα, ὧν μία ἡ οὐσία, ἀλλὰ πολλὰ καὶ διάφορα. Not all things of which the substance is one are one, but many and different. Averroes, however (to whom the worst things in Aristotle especially pleased), did not hesitate to use this as if it had been proved by the master. For he writes: That the formal, final and moving causes are the same according to subject, and differ only according to mode. He repeats similar things elsewhere, and this axiom is common and accepted among the other Peripatetics as well.
V.

units.la: Profecto saepe ita agit Aristoteles, ut non tam docere, quam ludere velle videatur, ac captata ambiguitate, sophisticas captiunculas nectere: quod non modo in cudendo hoc axiomate, quod tria in unum saepe veniant, sed & alibi rursus in secundo hoc physicorum libro ipsi accidit, in solvenda quadam circa Causam Finalem objectione; quomodo agentia naturalia, quae id quod faciunt, sine cognitione faciunt, agant propter Finem, quum hoc videatur iis tantum competere, quae cum cognitione & ratiocinatione agunt. Etenim id, cujus gratia aliquid fit, scopi rationem obtinet: atque hac appellatione à Philosophis usici solet, uti videmus inter alios fecisse Galenum lexti de Usu partium, cap. 12 & 13, ubi plurimum de hac Causa sermonem habet. & frivola est illa inter scopum, & Finem, seu τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα, distinctio, à Scaligero tradita, quod nimirum scopus sit opera sive officium; finis, quod movet artificem ad operam, id est opera perfectio. operam quidem movere etiam artificem, sed non simpliciter, quia movet propterea quod movetur, nec primo, quia finis primo movet. Inanis, inquimus, est illa distinctio, neque ipsa actio sive opera, ut ipse vocat, est scopus, sed medium, & iter, quo ad scopum & finem pervenitur. & propterea non modo non movet primo, sed ne secundario quidem: namque medici scopus non est medicari, sed id quod medicando obtineri potest, sive id sit sanitas, sive duntaxat morbi levamentum. etenim scopus (nisi omnino pervertere velimus ordinem loquendi) est id quod expetitur & intenditur; non autem per se expetitur ulla earum actionum, quae aliquid efficere natae sunt, sed illud ipsum, quod ab iis efficitur. neq;
units.tr: Indeed, Aristotle often argues in a way that seems to aim less at teaching than at playing, and by seizing on an ambiguity he weaves sophistical little tricks. This happens to him not only in coining the axiom that three things often come to one, but also elsewhere, in the second book of his Physics, in resolving an objection about the Final Cause. The objection asks how natural agents, which do what they do without knowledge, can act for an end, since this seems to belong only to those who act with knowledge and reasoning. For that for whose sake a thing is done holds the place of a goal (scopus), and philosophers commonly use this term, as Galen among others did in his book on the Use of the Parts, chapters 12 and 13, where he speaks at length about this cause. The distinction between goal and end, or τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα [that for the sake of which], handed down by Scaliger, is worthless. He says that "the goal is the work or function, the end is what moves the craftsman to the work, that is, the perfection of the work. The craftsman is indeed moved to the work, but not simply, because he is moved by what is moved, and not first, because the end moves first." We reply that this distinction is empty. The action or work, as he calls it, is not the goal but the means and the route by which the goal and end are reached. Therefore it not only does not move first, it does not even move secondarily. For the physician's goal is not to practise medicine, but what can be obtained by practising it, whether that is health or merely the relief of the disease. Indeed, unless we want to pervert the ordinary use of words entirely, the goal is what is desired and aimed at. None of those actions which are made to produce something is desired for its own sake; rather, what is produced by them is. Nor

units.la: 12. Metaph. com. 6. neq; si aliquid, quod intendebamus, non assequimur, propterea minus est ἕνεκα illius actionis, quae propter illud suscepta erat. & tame mirabilis est illa distinctio apud autorem Introductionis, Id quod optatur, & non attingitur, dici scopum; dum vero attingitur, dici finem; quasi vero id, quod attingitur, propterea scopi nomen amittere debeat. itaq; superfluam illam subtilitatem merito repudiant a Piccolomineus & b Sennertus; neque scopus quidquam omnino differt ab eo, quod aliter finis sive τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα b appellari solet. Iam scopum sibi proponere, eumq; sibi feriendum destinare, sicuti in scopo proprie dicto fieri sine cognitione haudquaquam potest; ita & in scopo metaphorico locum id habere videtur, quum propterea praecipue Finis scopi nomine afficiatur, quod Agens eum sibi assequendum proponat, actionesq; suas ad eum dirigat ac collimet. Hinc porro oritur difficultas, quomodo agentia naturalia, cognitionis expertia, dicantur agere propter Finem, quum eum sibi proponere, sequeq; ac suas operationes ita ad eum dirigere non valeant. Hanc objectionem ut solvat Aristoteles, ait, non opus esse ut id, quod propter Finem operatur, deliberatione utatur, quum ars non deliberet, & tamen propter Finem agat. eandem autem esse hic naturae, quam artis, rationem. ἄτοπον δὲ, τὸ μὴ ὀιεσθαι ἕνεκά του γίνεσθαι, ἐὰν μὴ ἰδωσι τὸ πινὸν βουλευσάμενον. καίτοι καὶ ἡ τέχνη ὁ βουλεύεται. καὶ ἡ εἰ ἐνῇν ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ ἡ ναυπηγικὴ, ὁμοίως ἂν τῇ φύσει ἐποίει. ὥστε εἰ ἐν τῇ τέχνῃ ἔνεστι τὸ ἕνεκά του, καὶ τῇ φύσει ἔνεστι. μάλιστα δὲ δῆλον, ὅταν ἰς ἰατρεύῃ αὑτὸς ἑαυτόν. τοῦτο γὰρ ἔοικεν ἡ φύσις. Absurdum autem est, putare rem non fieri alicujus gratia, si non videant causam moventem deliberare. namq; & ars non deliberat. si enim in ligno inesset ars fabricandi naves, eodem modo, ac natura, ageret. itaq; si arti inest hoc, ut alicujus gratia operetur, etiam naturae inest. maxime autem manifestum hoc est, si aliquis sibi ipsi medeatur. huic enim similis est natura. An idonea sit haec responsio, & an absurditati, quam alteri parti impingit, ipsa non multo magis
units.tr: (12. Metaph. com. 6.) nor, if we do not attain what we were aiming at, is the action undertaken for its sake any less "for the sake of" that thing. Yet the distinction in the author of the Introduction is remarkable: "What is wished for and not attained is called the goal; but when it is attained, it is called the end." As if what is attained should therefore lose the name of goal! So Piccolomini and Sennert rightly reject that superfluous subtlety. The goal differs in no way from what is otherwise commonly called the end, or τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα. Now, to set a goal before oneself and to fix it as the mark to be struck is something that cannot happen without knowledge in the proper sense of a goal. So too in the metaphorical sense of a goal it seems to have its place, since the end is especially called a goal because the agent sets it before himself to attain, and directs and aims his actions at it. From this arises the difficulty of how natural agents, lacking knowledge, can be said to act for an end, since they cannot set it before themselves, or direct themselves and their operations to it in this way. To resolve this objection Aristotle says that it is not necessary that what works for an end should use deliberation, since art does not deliberate and yet acts for an end; and that the reasoning in nature is the same as in art. ἄτοπον δὲ, τὸ μὴ οἴεσθαι ἕνεκά του γίνεσθαι, ἐὰν μὴ ἴδωσι τὸ κινοῦν βουλευσάμενον. καίτοι καὶ ἡ τέχνη οὐ βουλεύεται. καὶ εἰ ἐνῆν ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ ἡ ναυπηγικὴ, ὁμοίως ἂν τῇ φύσει ἐποίει. ὥστε εἰ ἐν τῇ τέχνῃ ἔνεστι τὸ ἕνεκά του, καὶ τῇ φύσει ἔνεστι. μάλιστα δὲ δῆλον, ὅταν ἰατρεύῃ αὑτὸς ἑαυτόν. τοῦτο γὰρ ἔοικεν ἡ φύσις. It is absurd to think that a thing is not done for the sake of something unless one sees the moving cause deliberating. For art too does not deliberate. And if the shipbuilding art were in the wood, it would act in the same way as nature. So if the "for the sake of" is present in art, it is present in nature too. This is most evident when someone heals himself, for nature is like that. Whether this answer is apt, and whether it is much more closely related to the absurdity it charges upon the other side, and in more ways than one, nobody who weighs it carefully can doubt.

units.la: a Introd. 23. b I. Inst. 1. gis sit affinis, & quidem non uno modo; nemo, qui eam perpenderit, poterit dubitare.
units.tr: a Introd. 23. b I. Inst. 1. Nobody who weighs it carefully can doubt that the answer is not apt, and that it is closely akin to the absurdity it imputes to the other party, and indeed in more than one way.

units.la: VI. Sane, qui hanc moverunt dubitationem, quomodo agentia naturalia agant propter Finem, quum ita agere, proprium sit ijs, quae cum deliberatione agunt; non aliud ijs verbis voluerunt, quam ad actiones non temerarias nec fortuitas, sed quae in certum Finem tendunt, necessarium esse, ut Finis sit praecognitus, atq; appetatur, ac proinde actio cum certa intentione ad eum assequendum dirigatur: quae suppositio veritati est omnino consentanea, nec à quoquam negari potest, fatentibus ipsis Aristotelicis, è quibus sufficiat nominasse Suarezium, qui diserte ait, Ut finis causet, necessarium omnino esse, ut praecognitus sit; hancq; esse omnium philosophorum receptam sententiam: & saepe quidem fieri, ut finis causet, quando non existit; nunquam autem, si non sit cognitus. Sed Aristoteles cavillationis ansam invenit in ambiguitate vocis βουλεύεσθαι, deliberare; quia deliberatio intelligi solet de ijs rebus, quae in utrumq; agitari ac ventilari ita solent, ut quaeratur, utrum potius faciendum sit; & quod agendum est, hoc potius an illo modo agi debeat: quod certe concedimus Aristoteli, in artibus plerumq; locum non habere; quum in magna illarum parte artificibus absq; ulla consultatione certum sit, quid ac quomodo agere debeant. Sed haec non est sola vocis βουλεύεσθαι significatio, quippe quae saepissime etiam sumitur pro eo, quod est, in animo habere, & certo consilio apud se statuere; quo pacto non est ut artifex ἄνευ βουλεύσεως operetur, sed quotiescunq; aliquid agere aggreditur, necesse est ut constitutum apud se habeat, quid agere velit, certaq; intentione in illud, quod agendum sibi proposuit, feratur. Solutio igitur haec, quae nihil impedire ait, quominus natura agat propter certum Finem, quanquam non adhibita deliberatione, quia & ars agat ob Finem, nec tamen deliberet; absurda est, quippe vocabulum Deliberationis in diverso sumens sensu, quàm autores objectionis sumi id voluerunt: quorum non alia mens fuit, nisi
units.tr: VI. Certainly those who raised this doubt, how natural agents act for an end when acting in such a way is proper only to those who act with deliberation, meant nothing else by these words than this: for actions that are not rash or accidental, but tend toward a certain end, it is necessary that the end be foreknown and desired, and so the action be directed with a definite intention toward attaining it. This supposition is wholly in harmony with the truth, and it cannot be denied by anyone, the Aristotelians themselves admitting it. Among them it is enough to name Suárez, who plainly says: For the end to cause, it is wholly necessary that it be foreknown; and he says this is the common opinion of all philosophers. And it often happens that the end causes when it does not exist, but never if it is not known. But Aristotle found an occasion for cavilling in the ambiguity of the word βουλεύεσθαι, to deliberate. For deliberation is usually understood of those matters which are usually debated and weighed on both sides, so that one asks whether a thing should rather be done, and whether it should be done this way or that. We certainly grant to Aristotle that in the arts this generally has no place, since in a great part of them it is certain to craftsmen, without any consultation, what they should do and how. But this is not the only meaning of the word βουλεύεσθαι, since it is very often taken to mean to have in mind, and to settle in one's own counsel with a fixed purpose. In this sense the craftsman does not work without deliberation; rather, whenever he sets about doing something, it is necessary that he have settled in himself what he wishes to do, and be carried with a definite intention toward what he has proposed to do. This solution, then, which says that nothing prevents nature from acting for a certain end, although without deliberation, because art too acts for an end without deliberating, is absurd. It takes the word "deliberation" in a different sense from that in which the authors of the objection meant it to be taken. Their mind was none other than

units.la: {x} finis requirit ut concludantur. nisi ea, quæ alicujus gratia agunt, agere certa ratione; quærendo porrò, quomodo agentia naturalia possint agere certa ratione, quum ipsa sint rationis expertia. Nam quod agant certa ratione, nemo nisi demens negaverit; omnesq; sani cerebri concesserint, quod & in hoc. 2. Physicorum tantopere inculcat Aristoteles, & repetit quarti de Gener. Anim. secundo, Omnia, quæ natura fiunt, non secus quam quæ arte, certa ratione fieri: sed hoc non tollit dubitationem, quomodo ratione agant, quæ carent ratione. Sane Galenus, si quisquam unquam Philosophus, & vidit, & acerrime defendit, naturæ opera ob certum Finem fieri, suamq; illis rationem exactissime constare: ac summam in ijs non potentiam modo, sed & sapientiam, pleno ore passim depradicat. hoc autem adeò non minuit ipsi hunc scrupulum, ut nemo sollicitius ipso quæsiverit, quo pacto tam sapienter agat natura; ὃ μόνον ἓν οὖσε ΘΦΗ, ἀλλὰ ΝΟΥ ΠΑΝΤΑΠΑΣΙΝ ἄλογος, non modo non sapiens, sed omnino rationis expers: sicuti hæc de re loquitur in libro de Formatione fœtus, ubi plurimis verbis tractat præsentem difficultatem. ad quam solvendam profecto nihil facit hæc Aristotelis responsio, utpote cavillatio mera, non ipsam rem enodare laborantis, sed unius verbi, quod in ea proponenda adhibitum fuit, ambiguitate abutentis, indeq; ludicram hanc captiunculam exsculpentis. cui hoc præterea absurditatis accedit, quod ea huc congeruntur ab Aristotele, quæ cum propositá quæstione ne minimam quidem habent affinitatem. Namq; suppositio illa (admodum sane inficeta) de naupegica existente in ligno, uti & exemplum medici curantis seipsum, fortassis aliquid faciant ad declarandum, quomodo natura sit Principium internum operationum. quam autem lucem afferant ad explanandum; quomodo natura, rationis expers, agat tamen cum ratione, ne oculatissimi quidem videre possunt. ut mirari liceret, quomodo Aristoteli in mentem venire potuerit, hæc isto loco assuere; nisi si passim ejus scripta scaterent ejusmodi exemplis, quæ rebus, ad quarum illustrationem ipsa adhibet, tenebras longe majores offundunt; utpote adeo obscura, atq;
units.tr: {x} the end requires that they be concluded: unless those who act for an end act by a certain reason. Asking further, how natural agents can act by a certain reason when they are devoid of reason. For that they act by a certain reason, no one but a madman would deny, and all sane minds would grant it; Aristotle inculcates this so strongly in the second book of the Physics, and repeats it in the second book of the Generation of Animals: All things that nature makes are made by a certain reason, no less than those made by art. But this does not remove the doubt of how those things which lack reason act by reason. Indeed Galen, if any philosopher ever did, both saw and most vigorously defended that the works of nature are made for a certain end, and their reason is most exactly consistent; and everywhere he proclaims with full voice the great power and wisdom in them. Yet this does not diminish the scruple for him at all; no one has inquired more anxiously than he how nature acts so wisely; he says that it is not only alive, but altogether irrational (ὃ μόνον ἓν οὖσε ΘΦΗ, ἀλλὰ ΝΟΥ ΠΑΝΤΑΠΑΣΙΝ ἄλογος) not only not wise, but wholly devoid of reason, as he speaks on this matter in his book on the Formation of the Foetus, where in very many words he treats the present difficulty. To resolve it, Aristotle's answer does nothing at all; it is mere cavilling, not untangling the matter itself, but abusing the ambiguity of one word used in proposing the question, and from it carving out this playful little trick. Added to this is the absurdity that Aristotle heaps here things that have not even the slightest affinity with the question proposed. For that supposition (quite insipid indeed) about the shipbuilding art existing in the wood, and the example of the physician healing himself, may perhaps do something to show how nature is an internal principle of operations. But what light they cast on explaining how nature, devoid of reason, nevertheless acts with reason, even the sharpest-sighted cannot see. One might wonder how it came into Aristotle's mind to insert these things at this point, unless his writings everywhere abounded with examples of this kind, which pour far greater darkness over the things they are brought in to illustrate, being so obscure, and

units.la: Gg atq; à proposito in tantum discrepantia, ut diligentissimi quoq; atq; addictissimi ejus interpretes, ubi plus satis suadaverunt, cogantur re infecta discedere, neq; alterum alteri queant accommodare: aut si quid afferunt, ( uti in desperatissimis quoq; locis afferre tamen aliquid semper satagunt ) frigidissima loquantur, & quæ nemini libere ac sane judicanti queant persuaderi. unde etiam fit, ut intestinis inter se discordijs collidantur, dum alius aliud commiscitur, ac socij commenta repudiat, ipse nihilo saniora apportans: cujus rei specimen rursus habemus mox post hunc ipsum locum, videlicet capite nono, ubi ad illa verba, Ἐστὶ ἡ ψυχὴ &c. ita Conimbricenses; Adverte, non parum esse difficultatis & dissensionis in explicando exemplo mathematico, quod hic Aristoteles adhibuit. & ejusmodi exempla innumera in omnibus Aristotelis libris Physicis ac Metaphysicis sparsa sunt. sed hoc quidem nunc omittatur: atque ad propositum de Fine sermonem revertamur.
units.tr: ...and so far at odds with his purpose that even his most diligent and devoted interpreters, when they have labored hard, are forced to give up without result and cannot reconcile one with another. Or if they offer anything (as they always strive to offer something even in the most desperate passages), they say very frigid things, which cannot be persuaded to anyone who judges freely and soundly. Hence it also happens that they clash in internal discords among themselves, while one adds one thing and another rejects his fellow's inventions, bringing forth nothing sounder himself. We have an example of this again soon after this very passage, namely in chapter nine, where at the words Ἐστὶ ἡ ψυχὴ [Esti hē psychē] etc. the Conimbricenses say: Note that there is no small difficulty and disagreement in explaining the mathematical example which Aristotle uses here. And innumerable examples of this kind are scattered throughout all Aristotle's Physical and Metaphysical books. But let this be passed over for now, and let us return to our subject of End.

units.la: VII. Profecto hoc quidem recte Aristoteles, quod na- turam alicujus gratia agere sentit, atq; opera ipsius nequaquam esse fortuita, sed certa ac summa ratione con- stantia.
units.tr: VII. Certainly Aristotle is right in this, that he perceives nature to act for the sake of something, and that its works are by no means accidental, but constant by a certain and supreme reason.

units.la: in quo tamen non putamus eum quicquam novi attulisse, neq; quicquam abstrusi aut obscuri. namq; res adeo est evidens, & ita in oculos sponte incurrit, ut negari haud possit, nisi summa cum stoliditate ac vecordia. Extitit quidem post Aristotelem Epicurus, qui brutam hanc opinionem, qua omnia naturæ opera casu fieri, neq; certum in Finem spectare asseritur, auderet profiteri; è cujus schola Lucretius pro magno damnat errore, siquis oculos factos dicat, ut ijs videremus, aut pedes, ut ijs progrederemur, aut manus, ut ijs res apprehenderemus; eósque, qui sic statuunt, perversam ait ac præposteram inire rationem. & pergit: Nil adeo natum est in corpore, ut uti possemus: sed quod natum est, id procreat usum. ac postea repetit, prius ipsa Nata, dedere sue post notitiam utilitatis. concludit; ita, Quare etiam atq; etiam procul est, ut credere credere possis Utilitatis ob officium potuisse creari (videlicet sensus ac membra) quam dementissimam ac plane pecuinam sententiam amplexus etiam fuit, atq; ab Epicuro acceptam, sectæ suæ tradidit Medicus Asclepiades; quem Galenus in plurimis locis divini operis De usu partium, præsertim vero libro undecimo, nervosissime impugnavit atq; expugnavit. Sed qui ante Aristotelem fœdum hunc errorem erraverit, neminem putamus fuisse celebriorum Philosophorum. Quanquam enim vel ex Platonis nono de legibus constet, jam olim fuisse nonnullos, qui ita sentirent, ut & ipsam mundi originem fortuitis Materiæ motionibus ferrent acceptam & omnem deinceps generationem ab eodem fonte repeterent: priscos tamen illos atq; præclaros philosophos, Parmenidem, Anaxagoram, Democritum, Empedoclem, cæterosq; fuisse ab hoc crimine immunes, casumq; & fortunam à natura relegasse, vel ex ipsius Aristotelis testimonio constat, qui hujus libri cap. 4. scribit, Ἀπορήσειεν ἄν τις, ἆρα ποτὲ ἀρχὴ ... τῶν ἀρχαίων ... τὰ αἴτια ... περὶ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς λέγων, περὶ τύχης ... ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἔοικεν, ... ἀπὸ τύχης. Dubitare autem licet, quare nemo veterum sapientum, generationis ac interitus causas differens, de fortuna quicquam definiverit. Sed, ut videtur, ne illi quidem putabant quippiam fortuito fieri. quæ sane veriora, quàm quod ibidem, non multo post hæc verba, Empedocli affingit, quod dixerit, Τὰ μέρια τῶν ζώων ἀπὸ τύχης γενέσθαι τὰ πλέκτα, plerasq; animalium partes fortuito factas fuisse.
units.tr: Yet we do not think he has brought forward anything new in this, nor anything abstruse or obscure. For the matter is so evident, and so spontaneously strikes the eyes, that it cannot be denied except by the utmost stupidity and madness. Epicurus did indeed come after Aristotle, who dared to profess that brutish opinion by which all the works of nature are said to come about by chance and not to aim at a certain end. From his school Lucretius condemns as a great error anyone who says that eyes were made so that we might see with them, or feet so that we might walk with them, or hands so that we might grasp things with them; and he says that those who so judge enter upon a perverse and preposterous reasoning. He goes on: Nothing is so born in the body that we might use it, but what is born produces the use. And afterwards he repeats: Things were first born, and only afterwards did they give rise to knowledge of their usefulness. He concludes: Therefore it is far, far from credible that the senses and limbs could have been created for the sake of the office of usefulness. Embracing this most senseless and plainly brutish opinion, and receiving it from Epicurus, the physician Asclepiades handed it down to his sect; Galen attacked and overthrew it most vigorously in very many places of his divine work On the Use of the Parts, especially in the eleventh book. But we do not think that anyone among the more famous philosophers before Aristotle fell into this foul error. For although it is evident even from Plato's ninth book of the Laws that some had long before held this view, namely that the very origin of the world was brought about by chance motions of matter and that all subsequent generation was derived from the same source, yet that those ancient and distinguished philosophers, Parmenides, Anaxagoras, Democritus, Empedocles and the rest, were free from this charge, and banished chance and fortune from nature, is clear from Aristotle's own testimony, who in chapter 4 of this book writes: One might doubt whether ever the principle... of the ancients... the causes... speaking of generation and corruption, of fortune... but, as it seems, ... from fortune. It is fair to ask why none of the wise men of old, in discussing the causes of generation and destruction, has defined anything about fortune. But, as it seems, not even they thought that anything happens by chance. These words are certainly more true than what he attributes to Empedocles shortly afterwards, namely that he said τὰ μέρια τῶν ζώων ἀπὸ τύχης γενέσθαι τὰ πλέκτα [ta merea tōn zōiōn apo tychēs genesthai ta plekta], that most parts of animals came about by chance.
VIII.

units.la: Sicut autem nihil novi hac in parte attulit Aristoteles, neq; aliud dixit, quàm quod cum per se clarum, tum plerisq; ante ipsum Veteribus jam dictum fuerat; ita longe post illos est, quantum ad difficultatem illam modo tactam, quomodo natura, quum rationis expers sit, agat tamen propter Finem. Ad hoc enim nihil ipse affert (sicuti vidimus) præter inanem captionem, quæ ad rem illustrandam nihil plane faciat: Veteres autem, si non omnes, at nonnulli rem acu tetigerunt. Quippe aiunt, agentia
units.tr: Just as Aristotle brought forward nothing new in this respect, and said nothing other than what was both clear in itself and had already been said by most of the ancients before him, so, as regards the difficulty just touched upon, how nature, although it lacks reason, nevertheless acts for the sake of an end, he is far behind them. For he himself offers nothing on this point (as we have seen) beyond an empty sophism, which does nothing at all to illustrate the matter. The ancients, however, if not all, at least some, hit the mark. For they say that agents...
Chapter I.

units.la: agentia naturalia sic agere, quia sic agere nata sunt, & quia ipsis necessitas sic agendi imposita est; quod ipse testatur Aristoteles his verbis: Εἰς ταύτην τὴν αἰτίαν ἀνάγκαι πάντες, ὅτι ἐπειδὴ ὁ ἥλιος τοιοῦτος πέφυκε, καὶ ὁ ψυχρὸν, καὶ ἕκαστον δὴ τῶν τοιούτων, ταχὺ ἐξανάγκης ἐστὶ καὶ γίνεται καὶ πέφυκε. Omnes ad hanc Causam reducunt; quòd quandoquidem tale natum est calidum, & frigidum, & unumquodq; ejusmodi rerum, hæc necessario sint, & fiant, ac nata sint: quæ sane sententia verissima est, si recte explicetur; quod nimirum, sicuti calida necessario calefaciunt, & frigida frigefaciunt, ita omnia agentia naturalia necessario agant id quod agunt, & eo modo ac agunt; quia ipsis vis sic agendi indita est, ac congenita.
units.tr: Natural agents act in this way because they are born to act so, and because the necessity of acting thus has been imposed on them. Aristotle himself testifies to this in these words: "For this cause all men refer it to necessity, since the sun is of such a nature, and the cold, and each of such things, are by necessity and come to be and are born [Εἰς ταύτην τὴν αἰτίαν ἀνάγκαι πάντες, ὅτι ἐπειδὴ ὁ ἥλιος τοιοῦτος πέφυκε, καὶ ὁ ψυχρὸν, καὶ ἕκαστον δὴ τῶν τοιούτων, ταχὺ ἐξανάγκης ἐστὶ καὶ γίνεται καὶ πέφυκε]." All refer this to one cause: since hot things are born of such a nature, and cold things, and each thing of this kind, these things necessarily are, and come to be, and are born so. This opinion is most true, if it is rightly explained: namely, that just as hot things necessarily heat and cold things necessarily cool, so all natural agents necessarily do what they do, and in the way they do it, because a power of acting in this way has been implanted in them and is innate to them.

units.la: Quum enim agant propter certum Finem, & ad ita agendum requiratur ut Finis præcognitus sit, atq; intendatur; quod ipsa facere non valent, quum ratione ac cognitione in totum careant: alterutrum necesse est, ut Causa superior, atq; ratione prædita (sive ipse Deus, sive, ut vocant, Intelligentiæ) vel cooperetur ijs, atq; ad omnes ipsorum actiones concurrat, easq;, quod ipsa facere non possunt, ad certum Finem dirigat; quomodo nimirum magister pueri scribere discentis manum sua manu apprehensam dirigit, ut certos atq; destinatos literarum ductus efformet: vel ut cuiq; agenti naturali simpliciter eas vires indiderit, quibus ad Finem, sibi quidem præcognitum ac destinatum, ipsi autem agenti ignotum, perveniret; ut quanquam ipsa nesciant, quid agant ac propter quid, & quis actionis sive operationis suæ exitus sit futurus, certus tamen illis scopus sit propositus, quem sua actione debeant attingere, ac quem, viribus suis utendo, attactura sint nihilo secius, neq; minus certo, quam si cognitione prædita essent, eumq; sibi ipsa proponerent: sicuti asinus molarius operæ suæ scopo, qui est comminutio frumenti, æque satisfacit cum ista ignoratione, asi eum vel maxime cognitum haberet, sciretq; se propterea circumcursare, ut frumentum commoleretur. Horum modorum alterum necessario amplecti debent, quotquot Agentia naturalia, cognitionis exortia, propter certum Finem, & alicujus gratia operari fatentur. Et prior quidem modus plurimos omni ævo Aristotelicos habuit, à quibus foveretur, totaq; fere scholasticorum (ut vocatur) turba eo concessit; qui & ipsum Aristotelem eo pertrahunt. in quo tamen falluntur, quum neque hoc in libro (ubi locus erat cummaxime) verbulum ea de re ullum faciat; neq; ij loci, quos in hoc allegant (ut quod primi de cœlo capite quarto, Deum & naturam conjungit, dicens nihil facere frustra; quodq; alibi plus semel ait, naturam nihil frustra aut temere agere) eum habeant sensum: sicuti & nos alibi oportuniore loco declaraturi sumus, & nonnulli de ipsis Peripateticis agnoscunt; inter quos Pererius verè scribit; Intelligentias secundum Aristotelem non alio modo movere aut regere res sublunares, quàm per motum ac lumen cœli. Sed quum hic modus à vero alienus sit, ob rationes postmodo à nobis exponendas; relinquitur ut alter modus sequendus sit; utq; agentia naturalia dicantur ob Finem operari propterea, quia tales vires à Conditore suo acceperunt, ac necessitas ita operandi ipsis ab eo imposita est. [Quodsi Veteres illi insitas hasce facultates necessario sic operandi, ut ad certum Finem certo perveniatur, Materiæ sponte insitas putaverunt, non à Deo creatore inditas; in eo sane graviter erraverunt, atq; castigationem merentur. Ad veritatem tamen sic quoq; propius accesserunt quam Aristoteles, qui de duobus illis modis (præter quos haud alius hic datur) neq; priorem amplectitur, neq; hunc secundum; sed rem hanc, quomodo agentia naturalia propter Finem agant, plane indecisam relinquit, ludicra tantum & captiosa responsiuncula eam diluisse contentus.
units.tr: For since they act for a certain end, and to act thus it is required that the end be known in advance and aimed at, which they themselves cannot do, since they are wholly without reason and knowledge, it is necessary that one of two things be the case: either a superior cause, endowed with reason (whether God himself or, as they call them, the Intelligences), cooperates with them and concurs in all their actions, and directs them, which they cannot do themselves, to a certain end, just as a teacher guides the hand of a boy learning to write, taking it in his own hand, so that it forms the fixed and determined strokes of the letters; or else he has simply imparted to each natural agent those powers by which it reaches an end that is known in advance and determined by him, but unknown to the agent itself. So although they do not know what they are doing, or for what reason, or what the outcome of their action or operation will be, nevertheless a certain goal is set before them, which by their action they must attain, and which, by using their powers, they will reach no less surely than if they were endowed with knowledge and proposed it to themselves. Thus a mill-ass, in its work, satisfies the goal of its labour, which is the grinding of grain, just as well with that ignorance, as if it had the goal fully known and knew that it must therefore go round and round so that the grain might be ground. Whoever professes that natural agents, which lack knowledge, act for a certain end and for the sake of something, must necessarily embrace one of these two ways. The first way has had very many adherents in every age among the Aristotelians, and the whole throng of the so-called Schoolmen has largely gone over to it, and they drag Aristotle himself into it. Yet in this they are mistaken, since he does not say a single word about this matter in this book, where the place was most fitting, nor do those passages which they cite (such as the one in the first book of On the Heavens, chapter four, where he joins God and nature, saying that nothing is done in vain, and his statement elsewhere more than once that nature does nothing in vain or at random) have that meaning, as we shall show in a more suitable place, and as some of the Peripatetics themselves acknowledge; among them Pereira rightly writes: "According to Aristotle, the Intelligences move and govern sublunary things in no other way than through the motion and light of the heavens." But since this way is foreign to the truth, for reasons that we shall set out later, it remains that the other way must be followed, and that natural agents are said to act for an end because they have received such powers from their Creator, and a necessity of acting thus has been imposed on them by him. [If those ancient thinkers believed that these faculties, which necessarily act so that a certain end is surely reached, were implanted in matter of itself and not implanted by God the Creator, they certainly erred gravely and deserve censure. Yet in this respect too they came closer to the truth than Aristotle, who, of those two ways (beyond which no other is given here), embraces neither the first nor this second; but leaves this matter, of how natural agents act for an end, wholly undecided, content to dispose of it by some playful and captious little answer.]
IX.

units.la: Sed insignem sane, ut alibi sæpissime, ita hic Aristotelis inconstantiam est animadvertere; qui hanc opinionem, quod agentia naturalia faciant omnia ὅτι ἀεὶ τὸ πέφυκε, sive per congenitam necessitatem, aliquanto post, quam eam ex veterum sententia proposuit, rursus velut suam ac propriam promit, hisce verbis: ἀνάγκη ὡς πρᾶττε- τα,
units.tr: But it is truly a remarkable inconsistency of Aristotle, as so often elsewhere, to note here: he proposes this opinion, that natural agents do all things "always as they are born [ὅτι ἀεὶ τὸ πέφυκε]," or "through innate necessity," as the opinion of the ancients, and then a little later he again brings it forward as though it were his own and proper, in these words: "necessity... as things are done [ἀνάγκη ὡς πρᾶττεταιπαι]"

units.la: Handwritten marginal annotations in the right margin (manuscript Latin and Greek notes, not transcribed). παι, ὅτω πέφυκε. καὶ ὡς πέφυκεν, ἂν μὴ ἐμποδίζῃ, ὅτω πράττεσθαι. unumquodq; ergo, quomodo agitur, sic agi natum est: & quomodo natum est agi, ita agitur, nisi quid impediat. Et tamen postea toto capite nono impugnat hanc sententiam, facitq; eos, qui eam tuentur, extirpare Finem & τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα ex natura; acsi propterea, quia dicunt naturalia agentia necessario agere id quod agunt, dicerent, actiones eorum ad nullum certum Finem dirigi; quod & in aliis multis suorum librorum locis repetit. Sed hæc male colligit, neq; ex eo, quod agentia naturalia dicuntur agere ex congenita necessitate, statim sequitur, ea non agere ob certum Finem. Exempli gratia, qui hominis dentes anteriores acutos, molares planos ac latos factos dicit, quia vis illa formatrix, quæ dentium fabricationi præsidet, necessario alios dentes sic habentes, alios vero aliter, efficit; non propterea dicit, dentes non esse cum ista varietate factos ad commodiorem cibi commolitionem: sed hoc tantummodo dicit, facultatem illam huic quidem scopo satisfacere; non tamen propterea sic operari, quia sic manducationis utilitas & commoditas requirebat (quum nullam istius rei cognitionem habeat, utpote omnis cognitionis expers) sed quia πέφυκεν ὅτω ποιεῖν, nata est sic agere, ut ipsius actio necessario hunc Finem attingat: idq; moderatione superioris Agentis, qui cum hunc Finem & cognosceret, & obtineri vellet, Agens hoc inferius ita instituit, ut sic operetur ex necessitate, quomodo operaretur μετὰ βουλεύσεως atq; ex destinatione, si ratione atq; cognitione præditum foret. Ipse tamen Aristoteles longe aliter torquet hanc, quam veteres isti physici loquebantur, necessitatem, aitq; eò redire, ac si quis diceret parietem ita factum; quia quæ gravia erant, sponte ac necessario in inferiorem locum descenderunt; quæ leviora, superiorem occuparunt. νῦν δὲ οἴονται τ' ἐξ ἀνάγκης εἶν ἐν τῇ γενέσει, ὥσπερ ἂν εἴ τις τὸν τοῖχον γεγεννῆσθαι ἐξ ἀνάγκης νομίζοι, ὅτι τὰ μὲν βαρέα κάτω πέφυκε φέρεσθαι, τὰ δὲ κοῦφα ἐπιπολῆς. διὸ οἱ λίθοι μὲν κάτω, καὶ τὰ ἀεμέλια· ἡ δὲ γῆ ἄνω, δι᾽ τὴν κουφότητα· ἐπιπολῆς δὲ μάλιστα τὰ ξύλα. κουφότατα γάρ. Nunc enim putant necessitatem esse in generatione ita, ac si quis existimaret parietem necessario factum esse, quia gravia nata sunt deorsum ferri, levia autem sursum: quare lapides quidem & fundamenta sint inferius: terra autem superius, ob levitatem: ligna vero maxime in summo, quum sint levissima. Sed, ô bone, (respondere illi possent) non hæc, quam tu nobis affingis, est illa necessitas, de qua nos loquimur, sed alia longe diversa: quod in tuo ipsius exemplo facile est nobis declarare. Quomodo enim faber parietem ita ædificat, partesq; ejus sic disponit, quia sic melius ipsi videtur, atq; usus ita requirit; ita si ars parietem ita ædificandi posset lapidibus atq; lignis indi (cujusmodi suppositione tu ipse in hac tractatione uteris) sic quidem ut hoc tantum modo, & non alio, posset parietem ejusq; partes extruere atq; disponere; recte diceremus parietem necessario ita factum fuisse, quia Principium ædificativum ita erat determinatum, ac veluti circumscriptum, ut non posset aliter ædificare, quippe insitam habens necessitatem ita ædificandi. Hanc igitur volumus in rerum generationibus intelligi necessitatem, non quæ à proprio ac spontaneo ipsius Materiæ motu pendeat, sed quæ à certa ac congenita Principiorum effectivorum, Materiam regentium, facultate pendeat. Sane hanc fuisse istorum Philosophorum mentem, quoad necessitatem in generationibus, longe est credibilius, quam quę illis attribuitur ab Aristotele, qui minimum sane exercitatus est in bonis atq; probis, aut saltem non valde improbabilibus Priscorum sententijs, in aliena atq; oppido quàm monstrosa figmenta detorquendis. Quod Aristoteles omnino ita senserunt, quomodo eos hic sensisse facit Aristoteles, attamen ne sic quidem pejori sunt loco, quantum ad præsentem quæstionem, quam ipse, qui contentus dixisse, quod actiones agentium naturalium non sint temerariæ, nec fortuitæ, sed certos Fines, ad quos perveniant, habeant propositos; in medio reliquit hanc difficultatem, quomodo res cognitionis expertes possint actiones suas ad certos
units.tr: [Handwritten marginal annotations in the right margin (manuscript Latin and Greek notes, not transcribed).] "As each thing is done, so it is born to be done [ὅτω πέφυκε]. And as it is born to be, so it is done, unless something impedes it [ἂν μὴ ἐμποδίζῃ, ὅτω πράττεσθαι]." Therefore, each thing is born to be done in the way it is done: and as it is born to be done, so it is done, unless something impedes it. And yet afterwards, throughout the whole ninth chapter, he attacks this opinion, and makes those who defend it do away with the end and the "for the sake of which [τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα]" in nature; as if, because they say that natural agents necessarily do what they do, they were saying that their actions are directed to no certain end; which he also repeats in many other places of his books. But he draws this conclusion badly, nor does it follow straightway, from the fact that natural agents are said to act from innate necessity, that they do not act for a certain end. For example, one who says that the front teeth of a man are made sharp and the molars flat and broad, because that forming power which presides over the making of teeth necessarily produces some teeth of this kind and others of another kind, does not therefore say that the teeth were not made with this variety for the more convenient grinding of food; he says only this, that that faculty does satisfy this purpose, yet does not act so for this reason, that the usefulness and convenience of chewing required it (since it has no knowledge of that matter, being devoid of all knowledge), but because it is born to produce [πέφυκεν ὅτω ποιεῖν], that is, it is born to act so that its action necessarily attains this end. And this occurs by the governance of a superior Agent, who, both knowing this end and wishing it to be obtained, arranged this inferior agent so that it operates from necessity in the same way as it would operate "with deliberation [μετὰ βουλεύσεως]" and from a purpose, if it were endowed with reason and knowledge. Aristotle himself, however, twists this necessity, of which those ancient natural philosophers spoke, quite differently, and says it comes to the same as if someone should say that a wall was made by necessity, because heavy things are naturally carried downwards and light things upwards. [Νῦν δὲ οἴονται τ' ἐξ ἀνάγκης εἶν ἐν τῇ γενέσει, ὥσπερ ἂν εἴ τις τὸν τοῖχον γεγεννῆσθαι ἐξ ἀνάγκης νομίζοι, ὅτι τὰ μὲν βαρέα κάτω πέφυκε φέρεσθαι, τὰ δὲ κοῦφα ἐπιπολῆς. διὸ οἱ λίθοι μὲν κάτω, καὶ τὰ ἀεμέλια· ἡ δὲ γῆ ἄνω, δι᾽ τὴν κουφότητα· ἐπιπολῆς δὲ μάλιστα τὰ ξύλα. κουφότατα γάρ.] For now they think that there is necessity in generation, just as if someone should suppose that a wall had come to be by necessity, because heavy things are naturally carried downwards and light things upwards: so that stones and foundations are below, but earth above, on account of its lightness; and wood especially on top, since it is the lightest. But, good sir, they might answer him, that this is not the necessity of which we speak, which you attribute to us, but a different and quite diverse one; as is easy to show from your own example. For just as a builder constructs a wall and arranges its parts in such a way because it seems better to him and use requires it; so if the art of building a wall could be implanted in stones and wood (which supposition you yourself use in this treatment), so that it could build and arrange the wall and its parts only in this one way and in no other, we would rightly say that the wall was necessarily made so, because the building principle was so determined, and as it were circumscribed, that it could not build otherwise, having an innate necessity of building thus. This, then, is the necessity we wish to be understood in the generation of things: not that which depends on the proper and spontaneous motion of matter itself, but that which depends on a fixed and innate faculty of the effective principles that govern matter. Certainly it is far more credible that this was the mind of those philosophers concerning necessity in generation than the view attributed to them by Aristotle, who was indeed little practised in the good and upright, or at least not very improbable, opinions of the ancients, and in twisting their views into alien and quite monstrous fictions. Even if the ancients thought as Aristotle makes them think here, they are nonetheless in no worse position, as regards the present question, than he himself, who, content to have said that the actions of natural agents are not rash or fortuitous, but have certain ends set before them to which they attain, leaves in the middle this difficulty of how things lacking knowledge can direct their actions to certain ends (which is entirely the work of reason and intellect), and does not contribute anything to its explanation.

units.la: × qui aut monstrosi ipsius ædificationis, sit antitheo aut secundum ipsum sit ædificationis aut, parsicillum sit pictor, aut secundum sit faber. ∧ citandi et laudando. certos Fines dirigere (quod omnino est rationis & intellectus opus) neq; ad ejus enodationem quicquam omnino attulit, quum tamen hic proprius esset ejus pertractandę ac decidendæ locus.
units.tr: ...whether, in the building of a house, the one who makes it is the architect, or, according to him, the builder; or whether the painter is the one who paints, or, according to him, the carpenter. Quoted and praised. He brought nothing at all to the explanation of how they direct their actions to certain ends (which is entirely a work of reason and intellect), although this was the proper place to treat and settle it.

units.la: X. Sed & de natura hujus Causæ, ac modo operandi, dictum aliquid oportuit. quanquam enim ad aliam forte scientiam plenior istius negotij disquisitio pertinet, omnino tamen & physiologo aliquid de ea dicere opportunum est, ne rem tanti in sua disciplina usus, ac Finalem Causam in Physica ipse facit Aristoteles, totam aliunde emendicare habeat necesse: & qui tantum sermonis in libris hisce physicis insumsisset de loco, tempore, infinito, alijsq; rebus, ad investigandas corporum naturalium generationes non admodum necessarijs, excusatius ac majori jure aliquam saltem in eo operam posuisset, ut ejus Causæ, cujus summam in physiologia dignitatem toties ac tantopere nobis commendat, conditionem ac naturam quadamtenus saltem nobis explicaret. Iam vero non modo hic non fecit istuc, sed ne alibi quidem uspiam: ac proinde uberem, pro more suo, discipulis dubitationum atq; rixarum messem reliquit, qui multum in eo æstuant, ac inter se digladiantur, utrum Finis moveat, ac Causæ vim obtineat, secundum esse suum reale an secundum esse (ut vocant) intentionale. Et quanquam res, sobrie considerantibus, ita plana fit, ut nullus videatur relinqui dubitandi locus, utrum ex duobus sequendum fit; longe tamen major numerus abijt in deteriorem partem, ac statuit Finem movere secundum esse reale; quod sane non parvam habet absurditatem. Sæpe enim id, quod Finis rationem obtinet, atq; ob quod actio suscipitur, nondum existit in rerum natura, sed illa ipsa actione producendum est: imo interdum non modo nondum est, sed ne futurum quidem est, atq; aliquando ne esse quidem potest. Dictu autem absurdum est, ejusmodi res movere per esse suum reale, quod ipsæ nullum habent, quum ipsæ realiter non existant. Ipsis quidem pro nihilo est, Gordium hunc nodum solvere (sicuti mirifici sane sunt homines,
units.tr: X. But something also had to be said about the nature of this cause and its mode of operation. For although a fuller inquiry into this matter perhaps belongs to another science, it is still fitting for the natural philosopher to say something about it, so that he would not have to beg the whole account of a matter of such importance to his own discipline from elsewhere, especially since Aristotle himself makes the final cause central in Physics.
