Whoever spent so many words in these physical books on place, time, the infinite and other things not very necessary for investigating the generation of natural bodies would have been more excusable, and with greater right, if he had taken at least some pains to explain to us, at least in some measure, the condition and nature of that cause whose supreme dignity in physiology he so often and so strongly commends. Yet not only has he not done this here, he has not done it anywhere else either. And so, in his usual way, he has left his disciples a rich harvest of doubts and quarrels, who labour greatly over the matter and fight among themselves over whether the end moves and holds the power of a cause according to its real being, or according to its so-called intentional being. And although the matter, for those who consider it soberly, is so plain that no room for doubt seems to remain as to which of the two should be followed, a far greater number have gone over to the worse side and decided that the end moves according to its real being, which certainly carries no small absurdity. For often that which holds the place of an end, and for the sake of which an action is undertaken, does not yet exist in the nature of things, but must be produced by that very action; indeed sometimes it not only does not yet exist, but is not even going to exist, and at times cannot exist at all. Yet it is absurd to say that such things move by a real being which they do not have at all, since they do not actually exist. For these men it is nothing to untie this Gordian knot (as indeed they are marvellous men,

units.la: Cap.I. homines, & quibus nihil tam arduum aut desperatum occurrit, ad quod non aliquid in promtu habeant: quum semel apud se statuerint, hypotheses suas custodire, quidcunq; tandem ipsis futurum sit) ac explicare, quomodo id, quod non est omnino, possit aliquid agere realiter, & secundum esse suum reale. Aiunt enim, se intelligere illud esse reale, non quod est verum & positivum Ens, & non dependens ab intellectus notione; sed ita fuse, ut complectatur omne esse, quod quoquo modo est possibile obtineri, vel saltem tanquam possibile aut non impossibile offertur appetitui, sive positivum aliquid sit, sive habeat esse in rebus, sive in sola mente; prout tamen praedictam possibilitatem vel non impossibilitatem in ordine ad possessionem induit. sed ludunt certe nimis proterviter in vocabulis, qui id vocant Esse reale, quod nihil sit positivum, neque habeat esse in rebus, sed in sola mente, atq; ab intellectus notione dependeat. nam si hoc non est Ens intentionale, cui omnia ista competunt, nullum profecto est in Mundo. nam quod ad ista probanda dicunt, Rem, quae Finis dicitur, secundum id, tanquam secundum rationem formalem causandi, movere, quod cum obtinetur, desiderium satiat: hoc autem non convenire ei secundum esse, quod habet in mente, quia sic appetitum acuit, non explet, sed secundum esse reale, quo adepto quiescit agens: neq; esse objectivum Finis expeti aut procurari ab agente, neq; agrotum desiderare esse intentionale valetudinis, sed esse reale: speciosa quidem sunt, sed errore plena, in quem impulsi sunt, dum speciem rei animo oblatam, à re ipsa non discernunt. Certum enim est, nos appetere res, ut realiter subsistunt, non ut in mentis conceptibus foventur. Attamen id, a quo movemur ad appetendum, non est res ipsa, sed species rei animo obversans; quam speciem esse ens rationis, non reale, neq; ipsi negare queunt. Et res haec declarari potest exemplo: qui amat alterum, non ab ipso movetur, aut ab esse ejus reali, sed ab ejus specie, hoc est ab esse ejus intentionali; idq; inde manifestum est, quod amamus etiam absentes, imo jam mortuos, ita ut multi charorum morte sublatorum desiderio contabescant: cujus amoris ac desiderij causa non est esse reale, quod ipsi tunc nullum habent, sed esse intentionale, species nimirum ipsorum, animo amantium impressa. neque est quod cavillentur, animas a morte manere. non enim anima hic inter mortales est amoris objectum, sed homo integer, ex anima & corpore compositus: & si alterutrum seorsim amatur, corpori saepius quam animae hoc accidit, & corporis magis quam animae amatoribus illud evenit, quod hic dicimus. Quod si res realiter existens, non tamen movet animum secundum esse suum reale, sed secundum esse intentionale; multo minus id fecerint Fines, qui plerumque esse reale nullum habent, nisi postquam ab agente id acceperunt, quippe qui agentis actioni non praexistunt, sed ab eo efficiuntur. & certe sibi ipsis contradicunt, qui itidem dicant, Et si Finis, cum actu causat, non existat secundum esse, quod habet in rebus, existere tamen secundum esse intentionale, quod in mente obtinet, dum apprehenditur, quae apprehensio sit conditio, sine qua Finis suam causalitatem exercere non possit. Itemque motionem, qua res sub ratione convenientis appetitui objecta, ipsum allicit, esse rationem causandi Finalis Causae. hujusmodi enim species appetitui objecta non est ipsum esse reale objecti; ac proinde verum non est, quod dicunt Finis rationem formalem causandi, esse ipsius ens reale: idque non modo sincerae rationis dictamini, sed & ipsorum confessioni, vel invitis expressae, adversari deprehenditur.
units.tr: Chapter I. men, to whom nothing is so difficult or hopeless that they do not have something ready to hand, once they have settled in their own minds to defend their hypotheses, whatever may become of them; they explain how that which does not exist at all can act really and according to its real being. For they say that they understand that real being not as a true and positive entity, independent of the notion of the intellect, but so broadly that it embraces every being that can in any way be obtained, or at least is offered to the appetite as possible or not impossible, whether it is something positive, has being in things, or exists only in the mind; insofar as it takes on this possibility or non-impossibility in relation to possession. But they certainly play too boldly with words when they call real being that which is not positive, does not have being in things, but only in the mind, and depends on the notion of the intellect. For if this is not intentional being, to which all these things belong, then there is certainly no such thing in the world. As for what they say to prove these points, that the thing called the End moves by that, as by its formal reason for causing, which, when it is obtained, satisfies desire; but this does not belong to it according to the being it has in the mind, because so it sharpens the appetite rather than satisfying it, but according to its real being, on attaining which the agent rests; nor does the objective being of the End get sought or pursued by the agent, nor does the sick man desire the intentional being of health, but its real being: these are plausible, but full of error, into which they have been driven, while they do not distinguish the appearance of a thing presented to the mind from the thing itself. For it is certain that we desire things as they really subsist, not as they are cherished in the concepts of the mind. Yet that by which we are moved to desire is not the thing itself, but the appearance of the thing hovering before the mind; this appearance they cannot deny to be a being of reason, not a real one. And this matter can be made clear by an example: he who loves another is not moved by that person, or by his real being, but by his image, that is, by his intentional being; and this is evident from the fact that we love even the absent, indeed the already dead, so that many waste away with longing for loved ones taken by death. The cause of this love and desire is not real being, which they then have not at all, but intentional being, namely their images impressed on the minds of those who love. Nor is there reason for them to cavil that souls remain after death. For the soul is not here among mortals the object of love, but the whole man, composed of soul and body; and if either is loved separately, this happens more often with the body than with the soul, and what we say here happens more to lovers of the body than of the soul. But if a really existing thing moves the mind not according to its real being but according to its intentional being, much less will Ends do so, which for the most part have no real being until after they have received it from the agent, since they do not pre-exist the agent's action but are brought into being by it. And certainly those contradict themselves who likewise say: Even if the End, when it causes in act, does not exist according to the being it has in things, it still exists according to the intentional being it obtains in the mind, while it is apprehended; which apprehension is a condition without which the End cannot exercise its causality. Likewise that the motion by which a thing, presented to the appetite under the aspect of the suitable, attracts it, is the reason for causing of the Final Cause. For such an appearance presented to the appetite is not the real being of the object itself; and therefore it is not true, as they say, that the formal reason for causing the End is its real entity; and this is found to be opposed not only to the dictate of sound reason, but also to their own confession, expressed even against their will.
XI.

units.la: Sicuti autem discipulis male hac in parte cum suo silentio consuluit Aristoteles, ita nihilo melius de ijs meruit, aut plus adjumenti attulit, quantum ad alteram quaestionem, ingentem sane ac difficillimam, uti ipsis videtur; quippe quae aut omnino tollit Finem e Causarum numero, aut saltem efficit, non constituere eum peculiare Causae genus, sed ad Efficiens esse reducendum. Etenim duobus tantum modis Finis considerari potest; vel ut est ultimum simpliciter, atque id in quod actio desinit, & quod ab agente tante tandem vel efficitur; vel acquiritur: vel ut movet ap- petitum agentis, eumq; ad se obtinendum excitat. Sed utrumvis horum elegerint, aqua ipsis herebit. Priori enim modo, Finis nequaquam Causæ, sed effecti duntaxat rationem obtinet, uti per se perspicuum est, atq; ipsi fatentur. Altero autem modo ipsi quoq; aiunt, Finem obtinere rationem efficientis. Finis (inquit Toletus) si consideretur in ratione objecti moventis intellectum & appetitum nostrum ad operandum, habet rationem Causæ Efficientis; quum objectum ad potentiam apprehensivam & appetitivam se habeat ut Agens. taliaq; passim est apud alios Peripateticos reperire. Et hoc adeo in confesso ponunt, ut proinde omnes absq; ulla cunctatione pronuntient, In hoc non consistere rationem Finis, neq; eum Causæ locum obtinere, in quantum movet appetitum: quo certe nihil mirabilius cogitari potest. nam si Finis non est Causa; quatenus movet, non est Causa omnino; quum omnis Causa necessario aliquam debeat habere effectionem, quo Causæ nomen meretur. Fini autem non alia relinquitur effectio, nisi illa, quia Agens movet, ejusq; appetitum excitat ad se persequendum. quare qui Fini hoc eripiunt, neq; Finalis causæ rationem in eo consistere volunt, nihil sibi reliqui faciunt, ob quod Finem in Causarum censum recipiant. Sane tam inextricabilia sunt, quæ in hoc negotio proferunt Peripatetici, adeoq; cum veritate ac inter se pugnantia; ut vix animo capere queamus, quomodo fieri potuerit, ut viri non dicimus acuti ac docti, sed vel communi sensu præditi, animo suo quiescerint imperare, ut ejusmodi opinionum monstra crederent, atq; aliis credenda proponerent. Sed non tam ipsorum hæc culpa est, ac rei, quam tuendam susceperunt, quxq; aliter defendi non potest, nisi ut quis monstrosis ejusmodi assertionibus atq; contradictionibus se involvat. Hujus enim difficultatis unicum remedium est in eo, quod tantopere ipsi reformidant, nimirum quod Finis non peculiare aliquod Causæ genus constituat, sed ad Efficiens pertineat, ejusq; quedam species sit; quanquam
units.tr: Just as Aristotle has served his disciples badly in this part with his silence, so he has deserved no better of them, nor brought them more help, on the second question, which is very great and most difficult, as they themselves think. For he either removes the End altogether from the number of causes, or at least makes it so that it does not constitute a peculiar kind of cause but must be reduced to the Efficient. The End can be considered in only two ways: either as the ultimate thing, the point at which the action ends, and which is at length brought about or acquired by the agent; or as it moves the agent's appetite and stirs it to obtain it. But whichever of these they choose, they will stick fast in the mud. In the first way, the End obtains the character not of a cause at all but only of an effect, as is evident in itself, and as they themselves confess. In the second way, they also say that the End obtains the character of an efficient cause. "The End (says Toletus), if it is considered as the object moving our intellect and appetite to act, has the character of an efficient cause, since the object stands to the apprehensive and appetitive power as an agent does." Such things are found everywhere among the other Peripatetics. They put this so much beyond dispute that they all, without any hesitation, pronounce: "The character of End does not consist in this, nor does it hold the place of a cause, insofar as it moves the appetite." Nothing more astonishing than this can be imagined. For if the End is not a cause insofar as it moves, it is not a cause at all, since every cause must have some effectiveness by which it deserves the name of cause. But to the End no effectiveness is left except that it moves the agent and excites its appetite to pursue it. Therefore those who snatch this from the End, and do not want the character of final cause to consist in it, leave themselves nothing by which they could reckon the End among the causes. Indeed, what the Peripatetics put forward in this business is so inextricable, and so at odds with the truth and with itself, that we can scarcely grasp how it could have happened that men not merely sharp and learned, but endowed with common sense, let their minds rest so far as to believe such monsters of opinion and to propose them to others to be believed. But this fault is not so much theirs as that of the thing they undertook to defend, which cannot be defended in any other way than by entangling oneself in monstrous assertions and contradictions of this kind. For the only remedy for this difficulty is that which they so greatly dread: namely, that the End does not constitute some peculiar kind of cause, but belongs to the Efficient and is a certain species of it; although
2 Phys. quæst. 14.

units.la: quam longe diversa ab Efficiente vero ac proprie dicto: quum effectio ipsius sit duntaxat metaphorica, ac proprie loquendo non efficiat quicquam omnino (quantum quidem ad animi impulsionem attinet.) sed totum hoc, quod efficere ipse dicitur, sit actio ipsius animi seipsum libere ac sponte moventis: qua de re alias plura dicentur. Hanc rem (cognitu non adeo difficilem, si quis paulo diligentius eam rimetur) si ignoravit Aristoteles, tanti nominis Philosophus, effugere non potest quin reprehensione dignus sit. Si autem cognovit eam, multo majorem castigationem meretur, qui eam non patefecerit: quod si fecisset, sectatores suos à magno labore, à-q; multis & ingentibus absurditatibus, in quas nunc prolapsi sunt, liberasset.
units.tr: it is far different from the true and properly so called Efficient, since its causing is merely metaphorical, and properly speaking it effects nothing at all (so far as the impulse of the mind is concerned). Rather, all that is said to be effected by it is the action of the mind itself, moving itself freely and spontaneously. More will be said about this elsewhere. If Aristotle, a philosopher of such renown, was ignorant of this matter (which is not very difficult to know, if anyone examines it a little more diligently), he cannot escape being worthy of reproof. But if he knew it, he deserves much greater censure for not having revealed it. For if he had revealed it, he would have freed his followers from great labour, and from many huge absurdities into which they have now fallen.

units.la: XII. Quodsi autem vel maxime & hæc, & alia, quæ prius attigimus, de Fine pervidisset ac tradidisset, ne sic quidem erat ut pensum suum se absolvisse, propositoque satisfecisse arbitraretur: quum instituta in hoc libro de Causis, in quantum ad Physicum earum consideratio pertinet, tractatio requireret præterea, ut aliquid de diversis Finium generibus diceret; ac nos edoceret, omnesne æqualiter ad Physicam spectent; paremq; in rerum generationibus vim ac dignitatem obtineant; an verò diversa sit eorum ratio: et siqua hac in parte inter ipsos intercedat differentia, quinam præcipue ac primario cadant sub physici consideratione, quive minus exactam ipsius contemplationem requirant. Hæc aliáque plura de Fine dicenda fuerunt Aristoteli in hoc secundo Physicorum, quem librum ex professo pertractandis Causis, (inquantum Physiologi interest eas cognoscere ad investigandas rerum generationes) dicavit: quum nunc paucissima dixerit de illo, uti & de Efficiente; ac ne minimam quidem partem ejus disquisitionis, quæ ipsi hic incumbebat, impleverit: quod sicuti jam nunc partim apparet ex ijs, quæ à nobis ea de re dicta sunt; ita multo fiet manifestius, si ea, quæ ipse in hoc libro de Causis perstrinxit, cum ijs, quę nos postea super hoc negotio edissertaturi sumus, conferantur: quando ex ipsa comparatione clarissime dilucescet, quam immani laborét defectu, quàmq; extreme jejunus sit ac mancus Aristotelicus hic de Causis naturalibus sermo.
units.tr: XII. Yet even if he had fully perceived and handed down these things, and the others we touched on earlier about the End, he still would not have thought that he had completed his task and satisfied his purpose. The treatment of causes set out in this book, insofar as their consideration belongs to the natural philosopher, requires him also to say something about the different kinds of ends: whether all of them pertain equally to physics and hold equal force and dignity in the generation of things, or whether their character is different; and if any difference lies between them in this respect, which of them chiefly and primarily fall under physical consideration, and which require a less exact examination. These and many other things about the End should have been said by Aristotle in this second book of the Physics, which he expressly devoted to treating causes, insofar as it concerns the physiologist to know them for investigating the generation of things. Yet he has now said very little about it, as also about the Efficient, and has not fulfilled even the smallest part of the inquiry that lay upon him here. As this partly appears now from what we have said on the matter, so it will become much more manifest if what he touched on about causes in this book is compared with what we shall set out later on this subject. For from that very comparison it will shine most clearly how great the lack of labour is, and how extremely meagre and defective this Aristotelian discourse on natural causes is.

units.la: Et sic quidem modus fiat huic examini Aristotelicæ de Principijs ac Causis Doctrinæ: in quo mirum videri non debet, si qua prolixius à nobis fuerunt tractata; quum summa hic Peripateticæ Philosophiæ capita versentur, quibus reliqua omnia superstructa sunt; quæq; proinde non nimis strictim aut perfunctorie delibanda fuerunt. Quum enim ista secta per tot secula tantam habuerit celebritatem, ut hodieq; vel ob hanc solam causam, maximè nimirum vetustatis prærogativam, plurimorum animis pertinacissime insederit, qui infelicissimo judicio contemnentes seculi sui felicitatem, & præfracta admodum pertinacia obdurati ad defensionem veterum nugarum, oculos adversus Veritatem occludunt, seq; ipsos perpetua rerum ignoratione condemnant: non erat satis, breviter ipsorum errores perstringere, sed præcipui saltem ad vivum fuerunt resecandi, cunctæq; absurditates ex ipsis pullulantes, evidenter ob oculos ponendæ, atque suis quæq; rationibus coarguendæ, ut appareret nihil à nobis leviter factum, neque novandi studio, sed multis atq; gravissimis de causis nos eam repudiasse philosophiam, quæ uti ex nugis atq; commentis conflata fere tota est, ita in ipso statim limine erroribus tota implicatur: ad quorum nonnullos digitum ante hac intendit Ramus, sed cursim nimis atq; ἐνδλεῶς omina delibans, utpote Aristotelis vitia magis, quam Aristotelicæ philosophiæ defectus detegere allaborans. Recenter autem vir magni spiritus Sebastianus Basso valde animose versatus est in hoc argumento, ut Aristotelicæ Philosophiæ Principia refutaret. in cujus tamen labore non debuisse nos acquiescere, facile erit cuivis animadvertere, qui hæc nostra cum ipsius scriptis contulerit. Quippe nec omnia, de quibus nos egimus, attigit; & in ijs, quæ juxta nobiscum pertractavit, etiamsi multa ac bona (præsertim in disputatione contra Formam) dixerit, nobis plurima reliquit dicenda. Quare omnino de novo suscipiendum nobis fuit hoc fundamentorum Aristotelicæ Philosophiæ examen; à quo nunc tempestivum erit ad nostram de Principijs & Causis sententiam aperiendam transfire.
units.tr: And so this examination of the Aristotelian doctrine of principles and causes has been carried out in this way. In it, it should not seem strange if some matters have been treated by us at greater length, since the chief heads of Peripatetic philosophy are at issue here, and all the rest are built upon them; these therefore were not to be touched on too narrowly or perfunctorily. For this sect has had such celebrity through so many centuries that even today, for this reason alone, chiefly its prerogative of antiquity, it has settled very obstinately in the minds of very many. These men, with most unhappy judgment, despise the felicity of their own age, and, hardened in a very stubborn pertinacity in defence of old trifles, close their eyes against Truth and condemn themselves to perpetual ignorance of things. It was not enough to touch briefly on their errors; the chief ones had to be cut out to the quick, and all the absurdities sprouting from them had to be set plainly before the eyes and refuted each with its own reasons. This was so that it would appear that nothing was done by us lightly or from a desire for novelty, but that for many and most weighty reasons we have rejected that philosophy which, as it is almost wholly compounded of trifles and fictions, so at its very threshold is entirely entangled in errors. To some of these errors Ramus pointed his finger before, but touching on the matters too cursorily and superficially [ἐνδλεῶς], as one labouring to uncover the faults of Aristotle rather than the defects of Aristotelian philosophy. Recently, however, the man of great spirit Sebastian Basso has dealt with this subject very boldly, in order to refute the principles of Aristotelian philosophy. Anyone who compares our writings with his will easily notice that we ought not to have rested content with his labour. For he has not touched on all the matters we have treated, and in those he has handled alongside us, although he has said much that is good (especially in the disputation against Form), he has left us very much to say. Hence this examination of the foundations of Aristotelian philosophy had to be undertaken afresh by us altogether. From it we may now opportunely pass on to set forth our opinion on Principles and Causes.

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM. DE PRINCIPIIS AC CAVSIS NOSTRA SENTENTIA.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. OUR OPINION CONCERNING PRINCIPLES AND CAUSES.
FIRST SECTION.

units.la: I. Notio ac vis vocabuli Principij in vulgato loquendi usu. Principium & Initium, idem. II. Suarezij fluctuationes, super primaria ac vulgata hujus vocis notione. Primus in ordine loci non recte dicitur Principium eorum, qui post ipsum: III. Ita neq; Primogenitus, Principium dicendus reliquorum liberorum. Hebraica vox Reschith, multo latius patet, quam Graeca ἀρχὴ, aut Latina Principium. IV. Philosophicus vocis Principij usus, incertissimus apud Aristotelem, atq; ad plurimas diversissimas res promiscue accommodatus. V. Enumeratio significationum hujus vocabuli, non rite facta ab Aristotele in initio quinti Metaphysicorum. VI. Ineptissimus Aristotelicorum conatus, ad distorquendum illud magistri sui dictum, ubi conceptis verbis fatetur, Causam & Principium reciproce dici. VII. Censura Aristotelis, super isto vocum abusu vaga atq; incertissime ipsius in libris Physicis & Metaphysicis fluctuationes. Immethodica Aristotelis indocendo ratio, à Scaligero castigata: idemq; adhuc acrius ab eo factum per latus Theophrasti. Rami tamen intemperantia in lacerando Aristotele, non approbata.
units.tr: I. The meaning and force of the word Principle in common usage. Principium & Initium are the same thing. II. Suárez's wavering over the primary and common meaning of this word. The first in order of place is not rightly called the principle of those who come after him. III. Likewise the firstborn cannot be called the principle of the other children. The Hebrew word Reschith has a much wider range than the Greek ἀρχὴ or the Latin Principium. IV. The philosophical use of the word Principle is most uncertain in Aristotle and is applied indiscriminately to very many quite different things. V. Aristotle's enumeration of the meanings of this word, made at the beginning of the fifth book of the Metaphysics, is not done properly. VI. The most absurd attempt of the Aristotelians to twist their master's saying, where he states in so many words that Cause and Principle are said reciprocally. VII. Aristotle's criticism of this vague abuse of words, and his very uncertain wavering in the Physics and Metaphysics. Aristotle's unmethodical way of teaching, rebuked by Scaliger, and attacked even more sharply by him on the side of Theophrastus. Ramus's intemperance in tearing Aristotle apart, however, is not approved.

units.la: VIII. Vera notio vocis Principij in Philosophia.
units.tr: VIII. The true notion of the word Principle in Philosophy.

units.la: PRincipij vocabulum è medio desumtum, suo proposito accommodaverunt, qui rerum originem primi indagare aggressi sunt prisci Philosophi. Neq; enim in vulgata loquendi consuetudine eum habet usum, quem ab ipsis accepit: sed eodem modo ac Finis, qui est ipsius correlativum, ita ipsum quoq; de Dimensionibus tantum usurpatur, ita ut in quantitate continua id sit Principium & Finis, quod in discreta est Primum & Ultimum. néque vero omni competit quantitati continuae, sed lineae tantum & tempori: neque ulli rei tribuitur Principium aut Finis, nisi quatenus longitudinem habet, aut in spatio aut in tempore; quod in plerisq; manifestum, verum etiam est in ijs, ubi minime videtur. nam & Principium libri dicitur non alio respectu, nisi ratione longitudinis: quam qui in libro videre non potest, nequeat etiam in Maeandro, Serpentinis, Glomis, Spiris, quorum nullum habet suam in directum protensam longitudinem, & longitudinem tamen habent ista omnia certissimam. sic etiam bello, miseriis, felicitati, Principium & Finis competit ratione longitudinis, quam in tempore obtinent; idemq; de actionibus quoq; & passionibus cunctis, quae aliquam habent durationem, dictum esto. & tale Principium & Finis non est aliquid extra rem ipsam, sed cum ipsa, & in ipsa. neq; enim rei Principium statim potest, nisi ubi jam est aliquid de ipsa, neque Finis, nisi ubi adhuc est (nam quod interdum illud, quod post rem ipsam est, Finis ejus vocatur, ut si gaudium vocest tristitiae Finem, minus exacte loquentium est) sensile enim Principium intelligimus, non punctum aliquod indivisibile. Et quidem videntur Principium & Finis opposita sita esse sub uno genere Extremitatis; ut Principium sit extremitas rei incipientis, quomodo Finis est extremitas rei definentis: quod & Aristoteles agnovit, quando dixit ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἀρχὴ, πέρας [?] τὸ δὲ πέρας, ὃ πᾶν ἀρχή. Principium est extremitas quaedam: non autem omnis extremitas est Principium. eodem spectant illa tertij Physicorum quarto, τῶν δ' ἀπείρων οὐκ ἔστιν ἀρχή. εἰ γὰρ ἂν αὐτῶ πέρας. Infiniti nullum est Principium: esset enim extremitas ipsius. Sumpsit autem à Platone, cujus haec est in Parmenide sententia: Καὶ μὴν τελευτὴ γε ἢ ἀρχὴ, πέρας ἐκάστου: Finis & Principium sunt cujusq; rei extremitas. Illa autem significatio, qua Principium rei dicitur id, quod primum in ea fit, quomodo carina navis, & fundamentum domus Principium appellare solent, ad primam ejus notionem pertinet. ejusmodi enim res dicuntur Principia, habita ratione temporis. sunt enim in Principio istius temporis, quod faciendae toti rei impenditur. & eadem ratione Principium alicujus scientiae dicitur ea pars, unde primum auspicari solent, qui eam tradunt & discunt: quopacto physiologia est Principium Medicinae; & orthographia, principium Grammaticae. hunc igitur usum Principij atq; initij (nam de Fine non est ut nunc dicamus) cum invenissent primi philosophi, ad aliam illud peculiarem notionem transtulerunt. Principium & initium conjungimus, quia duobus istis vocabulis unica res significatur, ut vel ex Graeca lingua apparet, quae non nisi unum vocabulum hic habet, ἀρχὴ, quod Latinè utrovis istorum apte exprimitur: quare etiam Cicero & Seneca in philosophicis Initia rerum & Principia indifferenter dicunt. Videtur quidem aliquod discrimen constitui posse, ut initium actionibus tantum accommodetur, principium reliquis. sed loquendi usus non agnoscit talè discrimen: atque ut Hebraeis Reschith & Techilla, ita Latinis Initium ac Principium promiscuè usurpantur. Quia tamen Latinis Philosophis Principij tantum vocabulum placuit, non Initij, ad illum usum, ad quem Graeci philosophi vocem ἀρχὴ transtulerunt, nos illos hac in re sequemur; quippe quibus non placet novare quicquam, ubi novandi nulla necessitas incumbit.
units.tr: The word Principle was taken from ordinary life and adapted to their purpose by the ancient philosophers who set out to investigate the first origin of things. For it does not have in common speech the sense they gave it. Rather, just as End, which is its correlative, is used only of dimensions, so that in continuous quantity that is the Principle and End which in discrete quantity is the First and the Last, so too Principle and End belong only to a line and to time, and are not ascribed to any thing except insofar as it has length, either in space or in time. This is plain in most cases, but it is also true in cases where it seems least obvious. For the Principle of a book is spoken of on no other ground than its length; whoever cannot see this in a book could not see it in a meander, a serpentine, a clew, or a coil, none of which has its length stretched out in a straight line, and yet all of these have a very definite length. So too Principle and End belong to war, to miseries, and to happiness on account of the length they have in time; and the same is to be said of all actions and passions that have some duration. Such a Principle and End is not something outside the thing itself, but is with it and in it. For the Principle of a thing can exist only where something of it already exists, and the End only where it still exists. (For it is sometimes called the End of a thing when what comes after the thing is named its End, as when joy is called the end of sadness; but that is the way of speaking of people who are not exact.) For we understand a sensible Principle, not some indivisible point. And indeed Principle and End seem to be placed as opposites under one genus of Extremity, so that a Principle is the extremity of a thing that begins, just as an End is the extremity of a thing that ends. Aristotle also recognised this when he said: "For the beginning is a limit [ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἀρχὴ πέρας], and the limit is that of which the whole is a beginning [τὸ δὲ πέρας, οὗ πᾶν ἀρχή]." A Principle is a certain extremity, but not every extremity is a Principle. To the same point are those words in the fourth chapter of the third book of the Physics: "Of the infinite there is no beginning [τῶν δ' ἀπείρων οὐκ ἔστιν ἀρχή]; for then it would have a limit [εἰ γὰρ ἂν αὐτῶ πέρας]." The infinite has no Principle, for the Principle would be its extremity. He took this from Plato, whose view in the Parmenides is this: "And indeed the end or the beginning is the limit of each thing [Καὶ μὴν τελευτὴ γε ἢ ἀρχὴ, πέρας ἐκάστου]." The End and the Principle are the extremity of each thing. That sense, however, in which the Principle of a thing is called that which comes first in it, as people are accustomed to call the keel of a ship or the foundation of a house its Principle, belongs to the first notion of the word. For such things are called Principles with respect to time: they lie at the beginning of the time spent on making the whole thing. In the same way the part of any science with which those who teach and learn it usually begin is called the Principle of that science; thus physiology is the Principle of medicine, and orthography the Principle of grammar. Having found this use of Principle and beginning (for we are not now speaking of End), the first philosophers transferred it to a different and special sense. We join Principle and beginning because one and the same thing is signified by these two words, as is clear even from the Greek language, which has only one word here, ἀρχὴ, and this is aptly rendered in Latin by either of them. For this reason Cicero and Seneca, in their philosophical works, use Initia rerum & Principia interchangeably. It might seem that a distinction could be made, so that initium is applied only to actions and principium to other things. But common usage does not recognise such a distinction; just as the Hebrews use Reschith & Techilla, so the Latins use Initium ac Principium indiscriminately. Nevertheless, since the Latin philosophers preferred the word Principium alone, and not Initium, for that sense to which the Greek philosophers applied the word ἀρχὴ, we shall follow them in this matter; for they did not wish to introduce any novelty where there was no pressing need for it.
Chapter II.

units.la: II. Et haec quidem de vocabulo Principij praefari placuit, deqʒ vulgato ipsius usu, super quo multa turbat Suarez, aiens latissimum esse, & variis modis posse multiplicari: quum tamen omnes modi, tum quos ipse affert, tum quos a se omitti significat, commode ad duo illa capita a nobis posita possint revocari, illis duntaxat exceptis, qui plane fictitij sunt, sicuti quum ait, In ordine loci eum, qui sedet primus, dici principium caeterorum, falsum enim hoc est, & nemo ita loquitur. Nam quod Aristoteles ait, Ταυτὸ λέγω πρῶτον καὶ ἀρχὴν, idem dico primum & principium, aliam habet mentem, & neqʒ de Principio vulgari, neqʒ de Philosophico aut Physico ab eo prolatum est, sed de Dialectico. Omne quidem principium (nimirum in vulgari significatione) est primum ejus rei, cujus principium dicitur: non tamen, quicquid primum est, potest propterea principium appellari: quum illa (ut sic dicamus) primitas, quae in ordine loci consistit, omnino sit a Principij notione aliena.
units.tr: II. I have thought it right to say these things by way of preface about the word principium and its common usage, on which Suarez makes a great fuss, claiming that it is very broad and can be multiplied in various ways. Yet all the senses, both those he himself brings forward and those he says he has left out, can conveniently be traced back to the two heads we have set down, except for those that are plainly invented, such as when he says: in the order of place, the one who sits first is called the principle of the others. This is false, and nobody speaks like that. For what Aristotle says, Ταυτὸ λέγω πρῶτον καὶ ἀρχὴν [idem dico primum & principium, I say the same thing: first and principle], has a different meaning. He did not say it about the common principle, nor about the philosophical or physical principle, but about the dialectical one. Every principle (in the common sense, of course) is the first of the thing of which it is called the principle. But not everything that is first can for that reason be called a principle, since that primacy, so to speak, which consists in order of place, is wholly alien to the notion of principle.

units.la: III. Ita etiam neque primogenitus quidem recte dicatur Principium liberorum, & ne in vulgari quidem sermone hoc fieri solet, contra quam Suarez asserit. Locutus quidem sic est Vetus Scripturae interpres, Genes. 49. 3. & Deuter. 21. 17. sed decepit eum ambiguitas vocis Hebraicae Reschith, quae ita Principium significat, ut significet etiam alia, quae nullo modo vi Graecae vocis, ἀρχὴ, aut Latinae, Principium, continentur. Durissimus enim fit sermo, & consuetudinem Latinę Graecaq; linguae planissime violans, si quis pro primitijs dicat ἀρχὴν aut Principium. Ast Hebraeis illae non aliud nomen, quam Reschith habent, ut cuivis istius linguae perito notum est. Reschith etiam illis dicitur, quod in quaq; re praecipuum est ac principale, ut Amos 6. 6. Reschith schemanim, primarium unguentorum, id est, unguentum primarium, pro quo Vetus transtulit, Optimum unguentum. & in ejusdem capitis versu primo: reschith haggoiim, præcipuum gentium, id est, gens præcipua. Sic Iob 40. 14. elephas dicitur reschith darce el, præcipuum operum Dei, id est, unum de præcipuis operibus. & sic vulgatissimum illud verbum, Principium sapientiæ est timor Domini, quod in Hebraico est, Reschith chochmæ Jirath Adonai, Timor Domini, sive pietas, est præcipua sapientia. Alio etiamnum modo Reschith Hebraeis dicitur, primus alicujus rei inceptor, sive autor. sic enim Prov. 17. 14. reschith madon, quod Vetus convertit, Caput jurgiorum, à Rabbi Salomone Jarchi, doctissimo commentatore, exponitur, Hammatchil bammeriba, qui litem incipit. Quum igitur Reschith habeat tot significationes, quas Latina voce Principij nequicquam exprimas, non est ut Scripturæ testimonio confirmetur, Primogenitum, rite dici Principium liberorum. Videtur autem exponendum, Primitiæ liberorum: quod non mirabitur, qui legerit apud Hieremiam Prophetam illa verba, Israel sacer Domino, primitiæ frugum ejus, qua phrasi in Novo fœdere etiam Christus vocatur ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων, primitiæ defunctorum, 1 Cor. 15. vers. 20. & 23. & familia Stephanæ, ἀπαρχὴ τῆς Ἀχαΐας, primitiæ Achaiæ. Falsum igitur est hoc Suarezij exemplum: ac falsum quoq; alterum, quod è Damasceno ponens, ipse etiam rejicienti quam approbanti proximior videtur, nimirum, Regem dici principium eorum quibus præest: nisi si Principium capias pro Principe, quod in Latina lingua plane inusitatum in Græca fit interdum, ut ἀρχὴ pro ἀρχῶν ponatur: sed plane ridiculum est, in philosophia ejusmodi amphibologijs ludere. ubi enim quæritur, quotupliciter vel in vulgo, vel apud philosophos, dicatur ἀρχὴ, uti Principium significat, insulse isti disquisitioni immiscetur: altera illa diversissima significatio, quæ imperium aut magistratum, vel eum qui imperio aut magistratu fungitur, denotat. Namq; Aristoteles sane hic excusandus videtur, qui & ipse τὰς κατὰ πόλεις ἀρχὰς Urbium magistratus affert, ubi de multiplici hujus vocis usu tractat; sed alia ratione, quatenus nimirum Magistratus sum sunt species Efficientis: omnis autem Efficiens principij philosophice sumti species est.
units.tr: III. Likewise, the firstborn cannot rightly be called the principle of his children, and this is not even the usual way of speaking in ordinary language, contrary to what Suarez asserts. The ancient interpreter of Scripture did indeed speak in this way, at Genesis 49:3 and Deuteronomy 21:17, but he was misled by the ambiguity of the Hebrew word Reschith, which means principle in such a way that it also means other things that are in no way contained in the force of the Greek word ἀρχὴ or the Latin principium. For it becomes a very harsh way of speaking, and one that plainly violates the usage of both Latin and Greek, if someone calls the firstfruits ἀρχὴν or principium. But the Hebrews have no other name for them than Reschith, as is well known to anyone skilled in that language. Reschith is also used by them of what is chief and principal in any matter, as at Amos 6:6, Reschith schemanim, the chief of ointments, that is, the chief ointment, which the Ancient translator rendered as "the best ointment." And in the first verse of the same chapter: reschith haggoiim, the chief of the nations, that is, the principal nation. So at Job 40:14 the elephant is called reschith darce el, the chief of the works of God, that is, one of the chief works. And so too that very familiar saying, "The principle of wisdom is the fear of the Lord," which in Hebrew is Reschith chochmæ Jirath Adonai, the fear of the Lord, or piety, is the chief wisdom. There is yet another way in which the Hebrews use Reschith: for the first initiator or author of anything. Thus at Proverbs 17:14, reschith madon, which the Ancient translator rendered "the head of strife," is explained by Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, the most learned commentator, as Hammatchil bammeriba, the one who begins the quarrel. Since Reschith therefore has so many meanings, which the Latin word principium cannot possibly express, it cannot be confirmed by the testimony of Scripture that the firstborn is rightly called the principle of his children. It seems rather that it should be rendered "the firstfruits of his children." No one will be surprised at this who has read in the prophet Jeremiah those words, Israel is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his increase; and in the New Covenant too Christ is called by this expression ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor. 15:20 and 23), and the household of Stephanas is called ἀπαρχὴ τῆς Ἀχαΐας, the firstfruits of Achaia. So Suarez's example is false. Also false is the other one, which he takes from Damascene, and which seems closer to those who reject it than to those who approve it, namely, that a king is called the principle of those over whom he rules, unless one takes principium to mean prince. That is plainly unusual in Latin, though in Greek it happens sometimes, that ἀρχὴ is put for ἀρχῶν. But it is quite ridiculous to play with such ambiguities in philosophy. For when the question is in how many senses ἀρχὴ is used, whether in common speech or among the philosophers, in which it means principle, it is foolish to mix in that other, very different meaning, which denotes command or magistracy, or the one who holds command or magistracy. Aristotle, indeed, seems to deserve pardon here, since he himself also cites τὰς κατὰ πόλεις ἀρχὰς [the magistracies of cities] when treating of the many uses of this word. But he does so for another reason, namely, because magistrates are species of the efficient cause, and every efficient cause is a species of principle taken in the philosophical sense.

units.la: IV. Porro cum vulgari huius vocabuli usu, de quo hactenus dictum, magnam habet similitudinem philosophicus ejusdem significatus: qui cum unus debeat esse & certus, magnopere sane culpandus est Aristoteles, qui in suis scriptis ita laxe & promiscue eo usus est, ut praeter illam vulgarem notionem, de qua modo egimus, illud adhibeat passim novem aut decem adhuc aliis inter se diversis significationibus; ita ut divinandum sit, ubicunque hoc vocabulum occurrit, quid per illud in eo loco voluerit intelligi. hoc ne quis calumniam putet, appositis testimonijs docebimus. 1. Facit Principij vocabulum generalius quam Causa, quippe cujus ambitu & omnes Causae, & alia praeterea continentur. Privationem enim inter Principia numerat; inter Causas vero nunquam, nisi 12. Metaphysicorum 2. ad quem locum omnes dicunt interpretes (quos etiam sequitur Suarez) Aristotelem ibi improprie Causae nomen usurpasse, atq; vulgari modo, prout Causa dicitur, quicquid ad aliud quovis modo requiritur. 2. Alibi vero passim illa duo, ἀρχαὶ καὶ αἰτίαι, usurpat plane pro synonymis, ac si nullum prorsus discrimen inter illa intercederet; & proinde nihil referat, sive utrumq; nomen conjunctim, sive alterutrum separatim ponatur. itaq; secundo Physic. in proœmio tractationis de Causis, cum dixisset necessarium esse in unaquaq; scientia, scire τὸ διότι περὶ ἑκάστου, καὶ τὴν πρώτην αἰτίαν; propter quid unumquodq; est, & primam ejus causam, subjungit, idem faciendum quoq; in physicis, ὅταν εἰδῶμεν τὰς ἀρχάς, ἀνάγειν εἰς αὐτὰς πειρώμεθα τὰ ζητούμενα ἕκαστον, ut cognitis ipsorum Causis conemur ad eas reducere unumquodq; eorum quae quaeruntur. item quarto de Gener. Animal. in fine. Δεῖ δὲ γίνεσθαι πολλὰς ἀρχάς; αἱ τὰς γενέσεις τὰς καλὰς φύσιν καὶ τὰς φθορὰς ἐμποδίζουσι, πολλάκις αἴτιον τὸν παρὰ φύσιν συμπίπτοντα ἐστί; quia multa existunt principia, natura-les
units.tr: IV. Moreover, since the philosophical meaning of this word has a great resemblance to the common usage of which we have spoken so far, and since that meaning ought to be one and fixed, Aristotle is greatly to be blamed, for in his writings he uses it so loosely and indiscriminately that, besides that common notion we have just discussed, he employs it everywhere with nine or ten other meanings that differ from one another. So that wherever this word occurs one must guess what he meant by it in that place. Lest anyone think this a calumny, we will show it by citing passages. 1. The word principium is more general than cause, for its scope includes all causes and, in addition, other things. For he counts privation among the principles, but never among the causes, except at Metaphysics 12, chapter 2. In that passage all the commentators (whom Suarez also follows) say that Aristotle there improperly used the name of cause, in the common way, in which whatever is required in any way for something else is called a cause. 2. Elsewhere, however, he everywhere uses those two words, ἀρχαὶ καὶ αἰτίαι [principles and causes], as plain synonyms, as if no difference at all lay between them. Therefore it makes no difference whether the two names are put together or either one is put by itself. So in Physics 2, at the beginning of the treatment of causes, after saying that in every science it is necessary to know τὸ διότι περὶ ἑκάστου, καὶ τὴν πρώτην αἰτίαν [the why of each thing, and its first cause], he adds that the same must be done also in physics: ὅταν εἰδῶμεν τὰς ἀρχάς, ἀνάγειν εἰς αὐτὰς πειρώμεθα τὰ ζητούμενα ἕκαστον [when we know the principles, we try to reduce each of the things sought to them], so that, once their causes are known, we try to refer each of the things sought to them. Likewise in Generation of Animals 4, at the end: Δεῖ δὲ γίνεσθαι πολλὰς ἀρχάς; αἱ τὰς γενέσεις τὰς καλὰς φύσιν καὶ τὰς φθορὰς ἐμποδίζουσι, πολλάκις αἴτιον τὸν παρὰ φύσιν συμπίπτοντα ἐστί [there must be many principles; those which hinder the natural generations and corruptions are often the cause of what happens contrary to nature]: for there are many principles, natural

units.la: Disp.12. sect.1. §.29. les ortus & interitus impedientia, saepe causae sunt eorum Cap.II. qua contra naturam eveniunt. Hic cum secundo de Part. Animal. septimo dixisset, περὶ τούτων ἐν τοῖς τῶν νόσων ἀρχαῖς ἀρμόττει λέγειν, de his convenit agere in principiis morborum: nihil aliud intellexit per Morborum principia, quam quae alias Morborum causae dicuntur. & passim loci occurrunt, ubi ἀρχὰς καὶ αἰτίας ut ταυτόδυναμοῦντα conjungit. de quorum numero & hic est. ὅσε στοιχεῖα μὲν, τρία. αἴτιαι δὲ καὶ ἀρχαὶ τέτταρες. itaque Elementa quidem sunt tria: Causae autem & Principia quatuor. 12. Metaph. 4. Alias vero uni alicui ex illis suis quatuor causis hoc nomen facit peculiare, modo Efficienti, modo Materiae, modo Fini. nam de Forma nihil attinet dicere, quandoquidem dictum de eo satis est antea, quomodo ipsi, cum Materia prima, & Privatione, hoc nomen peculiariter attribuerit. 3. Pro Efficiente usurpavit primo de Ortu & Interitu septimo. Ἡ ἀρχὴ, πρώτη τῶν αἰτίων. nam Principium; est prima Causarum. item in hisce. Τὸ δυνάμενον πέτλειν σπέρμα ἔχον ἀρχὴν εἶδος, ἄρρεν. λέγω δ' ἀρχὴν ὁ τοιαύτην, ἐξ ἧς ὥσπερ ὕλης γίνεται τοιοῦτον, οὖν γεννᾶν, ἀλλὰ τὴν κίνησιν πρώτην. Id quod potest coquere semen habens Principium speciei, mas est. dico autem Principium non tale, e quo tanquam e Materia fit tale, ac est ipsum generans, sed primum movens. b Ἐσὶ δὲ ἡ σελήνη ἀρχὴ διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸν ἥλιον κοινωνίαν. Est autem luna Principium ob communicationem cum sole. c Τῆς δὲ τῶν ἄστρων τοπῶν περιφορᾶς, ἴαχα ἂν ἐτέραι ἵνες εἶεν ἀρχαί. Circularis motus astrorum fortasse quaedam alia sunt Principia. d Τὶ μάλιστα ὁ πειῶν τὸ πάσχοντος, καὶ ἡ ἀρχὴ ὅ ὕλης. Praestantius est agens patiente, & Principium Materia. Ἡ μὲν οὖν τέχνη, ἀρχὴ ἐν ἄλλῳ. Ars est principium in alio. & 9. Metaph. 12. Αἱ τέχναι, ἀρχαὶ μεταβλητικαί εἰσι. 4. Pro Materia seu Elementis posuit in hisce: a Τόσων οὖν ταῦτα στοιχεῖα καὶ ἀρχαί. Horum igitur ista sunt Elementa & Principia. dicit haec de calido & frigido, e quibus caro & ossa componantur. b Τὰς ἀρχὰς, ἰὰ καλούμενα ὑπὸ ὕ-λων.
units.tr: Disp. 12, sect. 1, §29. Chap. II. things that hinder birth and death are often the causes of what happens contrary to nature. Here, when in the seventh book of On the Parts of Animals he had said: περὶ τούτων ἐν τοῖς τῶν νόσων ἀρχαῖς ἀρμόττει λέγειν [it is fitting to speak of these in the principles of diseases], it is fitting to treat of these in the principles of diseases, he understood nothing else by the principles of diseases than what are elsewhere called the causes of diseases. And everywhere there are passages where he joins ἀρχὰς καὶ αἰτίας as things of equal force. Of their number is this one too: ὅσε στοιχεῖα μὲν, τρία. αἴτιαι δὲ καὶ ἀρχαὶ τέτταρες [there are three elements, but four causes and principles]: so there are three elements, but four causes and principles, Metaphysics 12, chapter 4. 3. In other places, however, he gives this name peculiarly to one of his four causes: sometimes to the efficient, sometimes to the matter, sometimes to the end. As for the form, there is no need to say anything, since enough has been said about it earlier, and how he has ascribed this name peculiarly to it, together with prime matter and privation. 4. He used it for the efficient cause, first in On Generation and Corruption, book 7: ἡ ἀρχὴ, πρώτη τῶν αἰτίων [the principle is the first of the causes]: for the principle is the first of the causes. Likewise in the same work: τὸ δυνάμενον πέτλειν σπέρμα ἔχον ἀρχὴν εἶδος, ἄρρεν. λέγω δ' ἀρχὴν ὁ τοιαύτην, ἐξ ἧς ὥσπερ ὕλης γίνεται τοιοῦτον, οὖν γεννᾶν, ἀλλὰ τὴν κίνησιν πρώτην [that which can concoct seed having the principle of the species is the male; I call principle not such a one from which something comes as from matter, but the first mover]: that which can concoct seed, having the principle of the species, is male. I call a principle not that from which such a thing comes as from matter, but that which generates it, that is, the first mover. Also: Ἐσὶ δὲ ἡ σελήνη ἀρχὴ διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸν ἥλιον κοινωνίαν [the moon is a principle because of its association with the sun]: the moon is a principle because of its association with the sun. Also: Τῆς δὲ τῶν ἄστρων τοπῶν περιφορᾶς, ἴαχα ἂν ἐτέραι ἵνες εἶεν ἀρχαί [perhaps there are other principles of the circular motion of the stars]: perhaps the circular motion of the stars has certain other principles. Also: Τί μάλιστα ὁ πειῶν τὸ πάσχοντος, καὶ ἡ ἀρχὴ ὅ ὕλης [the agent is more excellent than the patient, and the principle is the matter]: the agent is more excellent than the patient, and the principle is the matter. Ἡ μὲν οὖν τέχνη, ἀρχὴ ἐν ἄλλῳ [art is a principle in another]: art is a principle in another; and in Metaphysics 9, chapter 12: Αἱ τέχναι, ἀρχαὶ μεταβλητικαί εἰσι [the arts are principles of change]. 4. For matter or the elements he used it in these passages: Τόσων οὖν ταῦτα στοιχεῖα καὶ ἀρχαί [these, then, are the elements and principles of these things]: these, then, are the elements and principles of these things. He says this of hot and cold, from which flesh and bones are composed. Τὰς ἀρχὰς, ἰὰ καλούμενα ὑπὸ ὕ-λων [the principles, which are called by the matters]
Chap. II.

units.la: νων στοιχεῖα. Principia, quae à nonnullis vocantur Elementa: c Ὁι μὲν οὖν τὰ πρῶτα ἀρχὰς νομῑ στοιχεῖα καλῶς ἔχει λέγειν, ἔσω συνομολογούμενοι, ἐξ ὧν μεταβάλλοντων, ἢ καὶ σύγκρισιν νομ̄ διάκρισιν ἢ καὶ ἄλλην μεταβολὴν, συμβαίνει γένεσιν εἶν καὶ Φθορὰν. In confesso igitur sit, quod rectè Principia et elementa dicantur prima illa, è quibus mutatis, per seu conoretionem et discretionem, seu per quā aliam mutationē, accidit ortum & interitum fieri. 5. Pro Fine sumit 9. Metaph. Ἀ πᾶν ἐπ' ἀρχὴν βαδίζει τ' γιγνόμενον καὶ Τέλος. ἀρχὴ δὲ τ' οὐ ἕνεκα: Omne ortum vadit ad Principium, & ad Finem. Id enim, cujus gratia aliquid fit, Principium est. 6. Praeterea usurpat interdum pro eo, quod Latine Rudimentum dicas; illud nimirum è quo quaeq; res oritur, & in quo primam existentiam accepit; quale in plerisq; est semen, in alijs quid analogum. exempla sunt in hisce: ᾳ Τὰ ζῷα καὶ τὰ φυτὰ, ἀμφοτέρα γεννητικά. γεννητικὰ δ' ἐν τῶν ἀρχῶν, οἷον τ' σπέρματος. αὕτη γὰρ ὡς ἀρχή. τ' δὲ μετὰ τὰς ἀρχὰς, οὕτως ἔχει. ὡς γὰρ ἂν ἔχωσιν αἱ ἀρχαί, οὕτω καὶ τὰ ἐν τῶν ἀρχῶν ἔχει. Animalia et stirpes, ambo sunt generativa; & quidē generativa è Principijs, veluti arbor fit è semine. hoc enim est Principium quoddam. quod autem Principia consequitur, perinde se habet. prout enim se habent Principia, ita et ea se habent, quae ex Principijs fiunt. ᵇ Τῶν μὲν οὖν μικρῶν, καὶ ὅσα γίνεται μὴ ἐξ ἀλλήλων, αἴτιον τοιαῦτα γίνεσθαι, οἷα ἐξ ἀσχῆς ἐγεννήθησαν, ἡ τὸ σπέρματος μικρό-της. τὸ γὰρ ἐλάττονος, καὶ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐλάττων. Parvorum igitur, eorumq; quae non ex se invicem fiunt, Causa est (ut talia fiant; qualia à principio genita sunt) seminis exilitas. minoris enim & principium minus est. in quo loco, verbis proxime antecedentibus; duo diversa hujus vocabuli significata ridicule confundit. ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἀρχὴ, παντὸς ἔργου μέγιστον· ἡμῶν γάρ. τὸ δὲ σπέρμα, ἀρχὴ. Principium enim est cujusq; operis maximum, utpote dimidium ipsius. semen autem est Principium: in hac autem oratione praeter illam absurditatem, quod quae de Principio in una significatione dicta sunt; illi in altera significatione applicat; altera altera etiam inest, quod pro verbiale dictum hyperbolicum, sumit pro certo axiomate: unde deberet tequi, Semen, aut analogum, habere dimidiam magnitudinem ejus, quod ex eo nasciturum est. nisi si in animo habuit Formam suam substantialem, cujus ratione mereatur semen τ' ἥμου dici, aut plus quoque: quo respexerit & istis verbis, Ἡ ἀρχὴ δυνάμει μέιζων ἢ μεγέθει. διὸ τὸ γὰρ ἐν ἀρχῇ μικρὸν ἐν τῇ τελευτῇ γίνεται παμμέγεθες. Principium maius est potestate, quàm magnitudine. propterea quod in Principio parvum est, in Fine fit maximum. sed Formam τοῦ γεννωμένου σώματος, corporis quod nasciturum est, esse in semine aut analogo, acriter negat permagna pars Peripateticorum. In hac significatione frequens est Theophrasto Principij vocabulum, ut 1. Caus. 4. Ῥᾷδιον γεννῆσαι τὰ ἀτελέστερα, ᾧ ἀπὸ ἐλάττονος ἀρχῆς. Facilius est gignere imperfectiora, & à minori Principio. 7. Alias per Principium id designant, quod Medicis vulgata phrasi Pars Princeps dicitur: quia nimirum quasi imperium habeant in vitam ejusmodi partes. exempla sunt haec: Ενια τῶν μοςίων, ἀρ- χαί εισιν. ἀρχῆς δὲ νινυθείσης, ἀναγκη πολλὰ μεθίσασθαι τῶν ἀκολουθούντων. Quedam partes sunt Principia. Principio autem moto necesse est multa de consequentibus dimoveri. Rationem hujus usurpationis ibidem indicat his verbis: ἐν τῇ ἀρχῇ καὶ τοῦ μοςίω τοῦ ἔχοντα τὴν ἀ φυσικὴς δεμότιος ἀρχήν. in principio, inq; parte habente caloris naturalis principatum. quasi diceret ἀρχὴν esse μοςίον ἔχον ἀρχὴν: quare eodem in loco pro eodem dicit etiam μοςίον ἐπίχαιρον, Ενὸς δὲ μορίς ἐπικαίρῳ μεταβάλλοντος ὅλη ἡ οὐσία τὸ ζῷον πολὺ τοῦ εἴδει ἑτερέψ. Una præcipua parte immutata, tota animalis constitutio multum specie differt. Hoc sensu Theophrastus dixit, Αἱ ἐίζαι ἀρχαί ῥίζες τῶν δένδρων. Radices sunt quaedam Principia arborum. Interdum sumit pro parte, quæ prima formatur (qui usus à vulgari non multum abhorret) Ἀρχὴ ἡ πρῶτα τῶν ὁμοίων καὶ τῶν ἀνομοίων. Cor est Principium similium & dissimilimum. 8. Imo & pro parte, à qua alię exoriuntur:
units.tr: Principles, which some call elements [ἀρχῶν στοιχεῖα]. Principles, which by some are called elements: (c) Those who call the first things principles speak well, since they agree that from them, by their change, whether by composition and separation or by some other change, coming-to-be and passing-away take place [Ὁι μὲν οὖν τὰ πρῶτα ἀρχὰς νομίζοντες στοιχεῖα καλῶς ἔχει λέγειν, ἔσω συνομολογούμενοι, ἐξ ὧν μεταβαλλόντων, ἢ καὶ σύγκρισιν καὶ διάκρισιν ἢ καὶ ἄλλην μεταβολὴν, συμβαίνει γένεσιν εἶναι καὶ φθοράν]. It is granted, therefore, that those first things are rightly called principles and elements, from which, when they are changed by composition and separation or by some other change, coming-to-be and passing-away come about. (5) He takes principle for end, in Metaphysics 9: Everything that comes to be proceeds toward a principle and an end; and the principle is that for the sake of which [Ἁ πᾶν ἐπ' ἀρχὴν βαδίζει τὸ γιγνόμενον καὶ τέλος. ἀρχὴ δὲ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα]. Everything that comes to be goes toward a principle and an end. For the principle is that for whose sake a thing is. (6) Moreover, he sometimes uses the word for what in Latin you would call the rudiment, namely that from which each thing arises and in which it first receives its existence; in most things this is the seed, in others something analogous. Examples are these: (α) Animals and plants are both generative; and that which is generative arises from principles, as a tree comes from a seed. For this is a kind of principle. What follows the principles is related to them in the same way: as the principles are, so also are the things that come from the principles. [Τὰ ζῷα καὶ τὰ φυτὰ, ἀμφοτέρα γεννητικά. γεννητικὰ δ' ἐν τῶν ἀρχῶν, οἷον τὸ ἐκ σπέρματος ἀπὸ δένδρου. αὕτη γὰρ ὡς ἀρχή. τὰ δὲ μετὰ τὰς ἀρχὰς, οὕτως ἔχει. ὡς γὰρ ἂν ἔχωσιν αἱ ἀρχαί, οὕτω καὶ τὰ ἐκ τῶν ἀρχῶν ἔχει.] (β) Of small things, and of those that do not arise from one another, the cause of their being such as they are, as those that were begotten from their principle, is the smallness of the seed. For the principle of the smaller thing is also smaller. [Τῶν μὲν οὖν μικρῶν, καὶ ὅσα γίνεται μὴ ἐξ ἀλλήλων, αἴτιον τοιαῦτα γίνεσθαι, οἷα ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐγεννήθησαν, ἡ τοῦ σπέρματος μικρότης. τὸ γὰρ ἐλάττονος, καὶ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐλάττων.] In this passage, with the words immediately preceding, he ridiculously confuses two different meanings of this word. [ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἀρχὴ, παντὸς ἔργου μέγιστον· ἡμῖσυ γάρ. τὸ δὲ σπέρμα, ἀρχὴ.] For the principle is the greatest part of every work, since it is half of it. And the seed is a principle. In this sentence, besides the absurdity that what was said of the principle in one sense he applies to another sense, there is also this: he takes a verbal, hyperbolic saying for a certain axiom. Hence the seed, or what is analogous to it, ought to have half the size of what is to be born from it, unless perhaps he had in mind its substantial form, on account of which the seed may be called half, or even more. He may also have had in view these words: "The principle is greater in power than in magnitude, for what is small in the principle becomes very large in the end." Yet a very large part of the Peripatetics vigorously deny that the form of the body that is to be born is in the seed or the analogue. In this sense the word principle is frequent in Theophrastus, as in Causes 1.4: [Ῥᾷδιον γεννῆσαι τὰ ἀτελέστερα, ᾧ ἀπὸ ἐλάττονος ἀρχῆς.] It is easier to beget the less perfect things, and from a smaller principle. (7) At other times they designate by principle that part which in the common medical phrase is called the leading part, because such parts hold, as it were, a rule over life of this kind. Examples are these: [Ἔνια τῶν μορίων, ἀρχαί εἰσιν. ἀρχῆς δὲ κινηθείσης, ἀναγκαῖον πολλὰ μεταβάλλεσθαι τῶν ἀκολουθούντων.] Some parts are principles. When the principle is moved, many of the things that follow must necessarily be moved. He indicates the reason for this usage in the same place, in these words: [ἐν τῇ ἀρχῇ καὶ τοῦ μορίου τοῦ ἔχοντος τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς φυσικῆς θερμότητος.] in the principle, that is, in the part holding the principality of natural heat. As if he were saying that the principle is a part holding a principle; hence in the same place he also calls by the same name a part that is pre-eminent: [Ἑνὸς δὲ μορίου ἐπικαίρου μεταβάλλοντος ὅλη ἡ οὐσία τοῦ ζῴου πολὺ τῷ εἴδει ἑτέρα.] When one principal part is changed, the whole constitution of the animal becomes very different in kind. In this sense Theophrastus said: [Αἱ ῥίζαι ἀρχαὶ ῥίζες τῶν δένδρων.] Roots are certain principles of trees. Sometimes he takes it for the part that is formed first (a usage not far removed from the common one): [Ἀρχὴ ἡ πρῶτα τῶν ὁμοίων καὶ τῶν ἀνομοίων.] The heart is the principle of things similar and dissimilar. (8) Indeed, he also takes it for the part from which the others arise:
Chapter II.

units.la: oriuntur; quo pacto ejusdem libri capite octavo dicit Cor esse ἀρχὴν τῆς αἵματος καὶ τῶν φλεβῶν. Principium sanguinis & venarum. quod etiam dicitur 3. de Part. 4. cum subjunctis verbis, quæ rationem hujus appellationis ostendunt: ἡ δὲ ναρδία τῶν φλεβῶν ἀρχή. φαίνονται γὰρ ἐν ταύτης οὖσα, καὶ οὐ δι' αὐτῆς. Cor autem est Principium venarum. apparet enim quod ex ipso sint, & non per ipsum. 9. Alibi vero pro parte præcipua sumit, non quod principatum obtineat, sed quoad molem, aut ob alias utilitates. ita 2. de Part. anim. 8. dicit Carnem esse ἀρχὴν καὶ σῶμα τῶν ζώων. Principium & corpus animalium. & alibi dicit, Τὴν τοῦ αἵματος φύσιν, καὶ τὴν τῶν φλεβῶν, ἀρχῇ ἐοικέναι. naturam sanguinis & venarum, Principij instar se habere. 10. Est & ubi ἀρχὴν usurpat pro eo, quod vulgo subjectum dicitur. ita certe sumit 12. Probl 2. ubi dicens bonum odorem non ita bene percipi, siquis nimis aut prope aut procul à re odorata absit, ait: Neque prope constituto Principio, plurimum est, neque valde longe.
units.tr: arise; in the same book's eighth chapter he says the heart is the principle of the blood and the veins [ἀρχὴν τῆς αἵματος καὶ τῶν φλεβῶν]. The principle of the blood and of the veins. He also says this in On the Parts of Animals, book 3, chapter 4, with the words that follow, which explain the reason for the name: "But the heart is the principle of the veins. For they appear to arise from it, and not through it" [ἡ δὲ ναρδία τῶν φλεβῶν ἀρχή. φαίνονται γὰρ ἐν ταύτης οὖσα, καὶ οὐ δι' αὐτῆς]. But the heart is the principle of the veins. For it appears that they come from it, and not through it. 9. Elsewhere, however, he takes it for the chief part, not because it holds the principal place, but with regard to bulk or for other uses. Thus in On the Parts of Animals, book 2, chapter 8, he says flesh is the principle and body of animals [ἀρχὴν καὶ σῶμα τῶν ζώων]. The principle and body of animals. And elsewhere he says that the nature of the blood and that of the veins are like a principle [ἀρχῇ ἐοικέναι]: the nature of the blood and of the veins stands in the manner of a principle. 10. There is also a place where he uses ἀρχή for what is commonly called the subject. He certainly takes it so in Problems, section 12, question 2, where, saying that a good smell is not perceived well if one is either too near to or too far from the odorous thing, he says: Neither when the principle is set near is there much, nor when it is very far away.

units.la: V. Tot significationibus hoc vocabulum passim adhibet Aristoteles, & alijs adhuc pluribus, uti comperiet quisquunq; ejus scripta evolverit; in quæ omnia non optime quadrat illa nota, τὸ πρῶτον ἐν ᾧ ἔσιν ἢ γίνεται ἢ γινώσκεται: esse primum, unde quid aut est, aut fit, aut cognoscitur. quam tamen vult πασῶν κοινὴν εἶναι τῶν ἀρχῶν communem esse omnium Principiorum, 5. Metaph. 1. quo in loco varias hujus vocabuli significationes enumerat. Est autem illa enumeratio non uno modo culpanda: ait enim Principium esse, ὅθεν ἂν ἡς τὸ πράγματος μηνδείκνυ πρῶτον, unde aliquid primo movetur, ut longitudinis & viæ: vel ὅθεν ἂν κάλλιστα ἕκαστον γένοιτο, unde quidq; rectissime incipitur, ut in disciplinis interdum ab eo incipitur, quod non est rei Principium, ἀλλ' ὅθεν εὰς ἂν μάθοι: vel ὅθεν πρῶτον γίνεται ἐνυπάρχοντος, quod in quaq; re primum fit, ut carina in navi: vel, ὅθεν πρῶτον ἡ κίνησις ἀρχεῖ, unde primum motus incipit, quomodo parentes sint Principium liberorum, & convitium pugnæ: vel, οὖ κ᾿ξ̓ προαίρεσιν γίνεσθαι τὰ κινούμενα, cujus arbitrio res geruntur; ut magistratus & principes, itemq; artes: vel, ὅθεν γνωσὸν τ᾿ πρᾶγμα πρῶτον, unde res primò cognoscibilis, quomodo hypotheses sint principia demonstrationum. deinde adhuc duo addit, Materiam sive Elementum, & Finem, sic inquiens: ἡ γὰρ φύσις ἀρχὴ, καὶ τὸ στοιχεῖον, καὶ διανοια, καὶ ἡ προαίρεσις, καὶ οὐσία, καὶ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα: & natura est Principium, & Elementum, & mens, & propositum, & essentia, & id cujus gratia quid fit: ubi fortasse per οὐσίαν intellexerit Formam. & sic in universum novem erunt Principiorum species illic ab ipso enumeratæ. Ast mirum sane est, quod non paucas earum significationum, in quibus hoc vocabulum usurpare ipse solet (ut ostendimus) in isto catalogo omiserit, cum tamen adeo liberalis fuerit in recensendo Principiorum numero, ut ea quoque distraxerit, quæ conjungi omnino postulabant; & Parentes fecerit unam Principij speciem; Magistratus & Artes, alteram: cum utraq; sub una & communi Efficientis ratione sibi Principij nomen vendicent. Imo illud quoq; erratum ejus non parvum est, quod tres illas Principij species, quas primo loco posuit, huc attulerit; siquidem istarum significationum hic nullus erat commemorandi locus, ubi Philosophicè duntaxat Principij significationes erant exponendæ, vel ipso mox teste, quando ait, Causæ vocabulum æque late patere, ac Principij. ἰσχὺς δὲ νοῦ τὰ αἴτια λέγεται. πάντα γὰρ τὰ αἴτια ἀρχαί. totidem modis & causa dicuntur. omnes enim Causæ sunt Principia. hoc enim falsum, si omnes Principij significationes ibi recitatas respexeris. quippe tres illæ priores nullo pacto ad ullam quatuor Causarum ab ipso assignatarum revocari possunt. ut neque illa, qua hypotheses demonstrationum vocantur Principia. Ista igitur quatuor perperam, ipso judice, illic adducta sunt. reliqua omnia quæ illic nominat, præter Elementum & Formam, ad Efficiens pertinent. Ut igitur verum esset quod ipse dicit, Principium & Causam æque
units.tr: V. Aristotle uses this word everywhere with so many meanings, and with many more besides, as anyone will find who goes through his writings. That well-known definition, "the first thing in which something is, or comes to be, or is known" [τὸ πρῶτον ἐν ᾧ ἔστιν ἢ γίνεται ἢ γινώσκεται], does not fit all of these very well: the first thing from which something is, or is made, or is known. Yet he wants this to be common to all principles [πασῶν κοινὴν εἶναι τῶν ἀρχῶν], common to all principles, in Metaphysics, book 5, chapter 1, where he lists the various meanings of this word. But that enumeration is open to criticism in more ways than one. For he says a principle is that from which a thing is first moved, as of length and of a road; or that from which each thing can best come to be, from which anything is most rightly begun, as in the disciplines one sometimes begins from that which is not the principle of the thing itself, but from where one may most easily learn it; or that from which something first comes to be when it is present in it, what is first made in each thing, as the keel in a ship; or that from which motion first begins, as parents are the principle of children, and the start of a fight; or that by whose choice things in motion are done, as magistrates and rulers, and likewise the arts; or that from which the thing is first knowable, as hypotheses are the principles of demonstrations. Then he adds two more, matter or element, and end, saying: "for nature is a principle, and element, and mind, and purpose, and essence, and that for the sake of which something is" [ἡ γὰρ φύσις ἀρχὴ, καὶ τὸ στοιχεῖον, καὶ διάνοια, καὶ ἡ προαίρεσις, καὶ οὐσία, καὶ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα]. Here, perhaps by essence he understood form. And so in all there will be nine species of principles enumerated by him there. But it is certainly strange that in this catalogue he has omitted not a few of the meanings in which he himself is accustomed to use this word (as we have shown), although he was so generous in counting the principles that he also split up those which absolutely ought to be joined; he made parents one species of principle and magistrates and arts another, though both claim the name of principle under one common reason of efficient cause. Moreover, this is no small error of his: he brought in here those three species of principle which he put first. For there was no place for mentioning these meanings here, where only the philosophical senses of principle were to be explained, as he himself bears witness soon after, when he says that the word cause extends as widely as principle: "the power of mind is called cause [ἰσχὺς δὲ νοῦ τὰ αἴτια λέγεται]; for all causes are principles [πάντα γὰρ τὰ αἴτια ἀρχαί]." Cause is said in as many ways as principle; for all causes are principles. This is false, however, if you consider all the meanings of principle recited there. For those first three cannot in any way be traced back to any of the four causes he assigned, nor can that sense in which hypotheses of demonstrations are called principles. Those four, then, were wrongly brought in there, by his own judgment. All the rest he names there, except element and form, pertain to the efficient cause. So, for what he himself says, that principle and cause are equally...
