Chapter II.

units.la: æque latè patere; debuerat illorum quatuor priorum non meminisse. Quanquam ne sic quidem effugisset reprehensionem. Sic enim eadem est utriusq; vocabuli vis, Principij & Causæ, & æque amplus utriusq; ambitus; quorsum attinebat de utroq; seorsim dicere, & Principiorum prius, deinde Causarum species distincta tractatione perlequi: cum potuerit longe minori & ipsius labore, & lectorum tædio, utrumq; conjungere, & quidcunq; de eorum notione ac speciebus dicendum erat, simul ac semel expedire.
units.tr: would have extended just as widely. He ought not to have mentioned those first four at all. Yet even so he would not have escaped criticism. For the force of the two words, Principle and Cause, is the same, and their scope is equally broad. What was the point of treating each separately, and then working through the kinds of principles and the kinds of causes in distinct discussions, when he could have joined the two with far less effort for himself and far less tedium for his readers, and dealt in one go with whatever had to be said about their meaning and their kinds?

units.la: VI. Namq; ridere sane libet inanem Interpretum conatum, qui nullum non movent lapidem, ut negent Aristotelem hic dicere, quod causa æque late patear ac Principium. Itaque verba illa, quæ apertissime dicunt id, quod ipsi postea dictum negant, alius aliter torquet. Quod Aristoteles plane dicit (ait Fonseca) tot modis dici Causas, quot Principia, intelligendum est negative, quasi dicat, non pluribus dici Causam quam Principium. hoc est, (ut Suarez amplius exponit) Causam non dici aliis modis quam his, quibus dicitur Principium, licet non necesse sit dici omnibus illis modis. Alij aiunt, Causam hic ab Aristotele sumi lato & vulgari modo, non ita arcte, ut quando de quatuor illis dicitur. Alensis vero exponit; Tot modis dici Principium, quot dicitur Causa, quia omnis Causa est Principium; ita ut post enumeratas significationes Principij subjunxerit Aristoteles quasi generalem regulam, qua Principium etiam dicitur omnibus modis, quibus dicitur Causa, quamvis non illis solis. Thomas vero ea verba sic explicat, quasi eorum sensus sit, principij acceptiones ibi enumeratas omnes convenire causæ, quamvis non sub eadem ratione: nam ex causa incipit motus; & sic de aliis. Et hanc expositionem amplectitur ipse Suarez, eamque amplius enarrat ad hunc modum: Juxta hanc expositionem (inquit) probatio Aristotelis aliter est inducenda, scilicet, ut inde confirmet, illas acceptiones habere locum in principio, quia etiam locum habent in causa, quia omnis causa principium est: inde tamen non sequitur, causam & principium reciproce dici, quia licet acceptiones ibi enumerata rata secundum alias rationes possint causa accommodari, tamen principium latius patet, quia dicitur omnibus illis modis, quibus dicitur causa, & secundum propriam rationem causae; & preterea dicitur alijs modis secundum generalem principij rationem. Sed has omnes expositiones esse totidem depravationes, verba Aristotelis manifestissime pervertentes, in proclivi est ostendere. Et de secunda quidem, ipsi fatentur Fonseca atque Suarez esse absurdam, & aperte contra mentem Aristotelis pugnare. Etiam tertiam, quanquam vehementer illi faveat, rejicere cogitur Suarez, quia non possit accommodari ad Aristotelis verba. Quantum ad primam, quae est Fonsecae, & à qua Suarez quoque ostendit se non esse alienum; & illa planissime contradicit verbis, quorum expositionem profitetur. quis enim tam bardus est, qui sibi persuaderi patiatur, quando aliquid dicitur totidem modis accipi, quot aliud hoc significare, non totidem modis, sed non pluribus? quod eodem redit, ac si dicas, totidem modis significare, paucioribus modis, qua expositione ineptius nihil cogitari potest. Sed non minus inepta est ratio, quam ipsi praetexit Fonseca, quamque tanti facit Suarez, ut dicat illam videri cogere ad admittendam hanc expositionem, licet proprietas huius vocis, tot modis, ipsi videatur refragari. Ratio autem haec est; quod post illa verba, Totidem modis causa quoque dicitur; subjungatur, Quoniam omnes causa principia sunt: ex qua ratione (inquiunt) ineptissime inferretur, causam dici omnibus modis, quibus dicitur Principium: esset enim argumentatio à superiori ad inferius affirmative, ut si quis colligeret, Omnis substantia est ens: ergo quot modis dicitur Ens, totidem dicitur substantia. sed haec ratio nulla est. primo enim nihil vetat, quo minus concedamus id quod ipsi inferunt, vitiosam fore Aristotelis illationem sub ista argumentationis forma. non enim hoc insolens est Aristoteli ut ἀσύνταξία loquatur. Non est necesse tamen, ut eo confugiamus; sed dicimus alterum illud membrum priori subjunctum esse, ad mentem suam clarius exprimendam, quasi deceret: Totidem modis, quot dicitur Principium, dicitur etiam Causa; quod ne cui videatur durum ob finem, quem
units.tr: VI. Indeed, it is certainly amusing to watch the empty efforts of the interpreters, who move every stone to deny that Aristotle here says that cause extends as widely as principle. So each of them twists those words, which most plainly say what they later deny, in his own way. What Aristotle plainly says (says Fonseca) that causes are spoken of in as many ways as principles, must be understood negatively, as if he meant that cause is not spoken of in more ways than principle. That is, (as Suarez explains at greater length) cause is not spoken of in any other ways than those in which principle is spoken of, although it is not necessary that it be spoken of in all those ways. Others say that cause is taken here by Aristotle in a broad and ordinary sense, not so strictly as when it is said of those four. Alensis, however, explains: As many ways as cause is spoken of, so many ways is principle spoken of, because every cause is a principle; so that after listing the meanings of principle, Aristotle added, as it were a general rule, that principle is also spoken of in all the ways in which cause is spoken of, although not only in those. Thomas explains the words in this way, as if their sense were that all the senses of principle listed there apply to cause, although not under the same aspect: for motion begins from a cause, and so on with the others. Suarez himself embraces this explanation and expounds it further in this manner: According to this explanation (he says), Aristotle's proof must be drawn differently, namely, so that he may confirm from it that those senses have a place in principle because they also have a place in cause, since every cause is a principle. Yet it does not follow from this that cause and principle are said reciprocally, because although the senses listed there can be fitted to cause on other grounds, principle nonetheless has a wider range, since it is said in all those ways in which cause is said, and according to the proper notion of cause; and besides, it is said in other ways according to the general notion of principle. But it is easy to show that all these explanations are so many distortions, plainly perverting the words of Aristotle. As for the second, Fonseca and Suarez themselves admit that it is absurd and clearly opposed to Aristotle's meaning. Suarez is also forced to reject the third, although he strongly favours it, because it cannot be fitted to Aristotle's words. As for the first, which is Fonseca's, and to which Suarez also shows he is not averse, it plainly contradicts the words whose explanation it claims to give. For who is so dull as to allow himself to be persuaded that when something is said to be taken in as many ways as another thing signifies, it is not taken in as many ways but in no more? This comes to the same as saying that it signifies as many ways, in fewer ways, and no explanation more absurd than this can be imagined. Yet the reasoning that Fonseca puts forward is no less absurd, and Suarez sets such store by it that he says it seems to compel the admission of this explanation, although the proper sense of this phrase, as many ways, seems to him to oppose it. The reasoning is this: after the words, Cause too is spoken of in as many ways, there follows, since all causes are principles; from which reasoning (they say) it would most absurdly be inferred that cause is spoken of in all the ways in which principle is spoken of. For this would be an affirmative argument from the higher to the lower, as if someone were to conclude, Every substance is a being; therefore, in as many ways as being is spoken of, so many ways is substance spoken of. But this reasoning is worthless. For, first, nothing prevents us from granting what they infer, that Aristotle's inference in that form of argument would be faulty. For it is not unusual for Aristotle to speak asyntaxia [ἀσύνταξία], that is, in a loose construction. There is no need, however, to take refuge in that; we say instead that the second clause is added to the first in order to express his meaning more clearly, as if he should say: As many ways as principle is spoken of, so many ways cause is also spoken of; and lest this seem harsh to anyone, because of the purpose which
Chapter II.

units.la: quem inter causas numero, quum tamen videatur cum ipsius natura pugnare, ut sit Principium: assero tamen illum quoque esse Principium, ac proinde omnes Causas esse Principia: hæc est vera illorum verborum, Omnes enim Causæ, Principia, expositio, aut saltem æque verisimilis, ac ulla alia; ideoque cadit argumentum ex iis desumptum à Fonseca, à Suarezio; qui eo solo argumento, quod hæc verba cum præcedentibus non satis apte videbantur congruere, ausi sunt fabricari aut amplecti absurdissimam illam interpretationem, quod Totidem modis significet Pluribus modis: cujus perversionis insulsitatem vel puer deprehendat. Quantum vero ad Thomam attinet; argute ille quidem, sed parum probabiliter. Nulla enim est hæc consequentia: motus fit à causa: igitur principium viæ, unde motus incipit, potest quodammodo appellari viæ causa, aut Efficiens: ab Efficiente enim fit motus. Et æque absurdum sit, Carinam appellare Efficientem navis, quia fiat ab Efficiente. Et sic de cæteris. Miros autem hic Suarez ludos dat, qui cum profiteatur se hanc Thomæ expositionem amplecti, ita eam enarrat, ut fiat diversissima. Eo enim evadit ipsius oratio, ut dicat, eam esse verborum Aristotelis mentem, Quod principium dicatur omnibus illis modis, quot causa, non autem Causa omnibus modis, quibus principium. quam ipsam quoque expositionem palam respuunt verba textus, siquidem in eo non dicitur Principium dici totidem modis, quot dicitur causa, sed causam dici totidem modis, quot dicitur Principium. Cum itaque commenta mera sint, quæcunq; ad hunc locum afferunt interpretes, insoluta manet, ac veritatem habet objectio, quam hinc sibi formavit Fonseca, Aristotelem hic plane asserere, tot modis hic dici causam quot principium, propterea que dubium non esse, quin sentiat æque late patere causam ac principium. Si enim putaret latius patere Principium, non minus falso diceret, tot modis dici causam quot principium, quam si affirmaret; tot esse homines, quot animalia. Et sane non hoc tantum loco istud dixit Aristoteles, Causam & Principium æque late patere. ut enim nunc omittamus locos superius adductos ubi illum hæc.
units.tr: whom I count among the causes, although he seems to be at odds with his very nature as a principle. Still I maintain that he too is a principle, and therefore that all causes are principles. This is the true sense of those words, All causes, principles, exposition, or at least equally probable as any other. So the argument drawn from them by Fonseca and Suárez falls away. They, on the sole ground that these words did not seem to fit well with what precedes, ventured to invent or adopt that most absurd interpretation, that as many ways means in more ways. Even a boy could detect the silliness of this distortion. As for Thomas, he is clever, but not very convincing. For this inference does not hold: motion comes from a cause; therefore the starting point of a journey, from which the motion begins, can in some sense be called the cause or efficient of the journey, since motion comes from an efficient. It would be just as absurd to call the keel the efficient of the ship because it is made by an efficient. And so with the rest. Suárez, however, plays strange tricks here. Although he professes to embrace Thomas's exposition, he explains it in such a way that it becomes quite different. His words come to this: that it is Aristotle's meaning that principle is said in all the ways that cause is, but not cause in all the ways that principle is. The very wording of the text openly rejects this exposition too, since there it is not said that principle is said as many ways as cause, but that cause is said as many ways as principle. Since, then, the comments that the interpreters bring to this passage are pure fabrications, the objection that Fonseca formed from it remains unanswered and holds good: that Aristotle here plainly asserts that cause is said in as many ways here as principle, and so there is no doubt that he thinks cause extends as widely as principle. For if he thought that principle extended more widely, he would be no less wrong to say that cause is said in as many ways as principle than if he affirmed that there are as many men as animals. And indeed Aristotle said this not only in this place, that cause and principle extend equally widely. To pass over for now the passages cited above where he says this.
J. Metaph. i. q. 7. sect. 2.

units.la: hæc duo vocabula promiscue usurpare monstravimus; 4. Metaph. 2. ait, ita inter se comparari causam & principium, quomodo ens & unum, Τὸ ὂν καὶ τὸ ἓν ταὐτὸν, καὶ μία φύσις, ᾧ ἀκολουθεῖν ἀλλήλοις, ὥστε ἀρχὴ καὶ αἴτιον,
units.tr: We have shown that these two words are used interchangeably. In Metaphysics 4 he says that cause and principle are related to each other as being and one are: [Τὸ ὂν καὶ τὸ ἓν ταὐτὸν, καὶ μία φύσις, ᾧ ἀκολουθεῖν ἀλλήλοις, ὥστε ἀρχὴ καὶ αἴτιον].

units.la: Ens & unum sunt idem, & una natura, eo quod se invicem consequantur, itidem ac principium & causa, quibus verbis planius nihil dici potest, ad significandum, quod Causa & Principium inter se reciprocentur. Nam quantum ad strophas illas, ad quas ex more suo hic quoque confugiunt Expositores, ut vim tam aperti loci effugiant, ac præceptorem suum aliud loqui faciant, quam quod loqui ipse voluit; adeo sunt, ut semper, frigidæ ac ridiculæ, ut pigeat illas huc referre, aut refellere. sufficit enim civili illas bello permittere, atque invicem conficiendas dare. non magis enim cum verbis Aristotelis pugnant omnes illæ, quam ipsæ inter se. quæ enim solutio uni cata videtur & lepida, illam alter absurdam judicat & insulsam. Estque sane hoc perpetuum illorum hominum, qui adeo serviliter Aristoteli sacramento dixerunt, fatum, ut dum præceptorem ab antilogijs vindicare contendunt, sibique consentanea ubique loqui cogunt, ipsi in maximas ac manifestissimas incidant absurditates; quum possent longe leviori negotio se expedire, ubicunque tale aliquid in eo occurrit quod cum ipsius placitis minus bene quadrat, fatendo ingenue, illum sibi ipsi contradicere, propterea que non quid ibi, sed quid alibi dicat, attendendum esse. Sed illis hoc facere non permittit sacrosancta Magistri Majestas, quam vilem ac protritam futuram vident, si ipsi hoc iter ingrediantur, quum innumeris antilogijs scateant ipsius scripta. quas omnes cum excusare ac conciliare nitantur, mirum non est, si ad summas ipsi ineptias redigantur. Sed hi homines, quandoquidem ita ipsi volunt, infelicitati suæ relinquendi sunt.
units.tr: Being and one are the same, and one nature, in that they follow each other, just as principle and cause do. Nothing could be said more plainly than these words to show that cause and principle are interchangeable. As for those subtle turns to which the commentators, as usual, retreat here, in order to escape the force of so clear a passage and make their teacher say something other than what he wished to say, they are always so cold and ridiculous that it is tiresome either to cite them here or to refute them. It is enough to let them wage their civil war and destroy one another. For all of them contradict the words of Aristotle no more than they contradict each other. The solution that one finds neat and witty, another judges absurd and silly. And it is indeed the constant fate of those men, who have so slavishly sworn allegiance to Aristotle, that while they strive to defend their master against contradictions, and force him to say everywhere what agrees with itself, they fall themselves into the greatest and most obvious absurdities. Yet they could extricate themselves with far less trouble wherever something occurs in him that agrees poorly with his own opinions, by frankly confessing that he contradicts himself, and that therefore one must attend not to what he says there, but to what he says elsewhere. But the sacrosanct majesty of the Master does not allow them to do this, for they see that if they took this path he would be shown to be cheap and worn out, since his writings abound in countless contradictions. Since they struggle to excuse and reconcile all of these, it is no wonder if they are reduced to the greatest silliness. But these men, since they wish it so, must be left to their unhappiness.

units.la: VII. Hoc tamen sciant, non habere ipsos justam querendi de nobis Causam, qui sicuti in alijs fere cunctis Physiologiæ partibus, ita in hac quoque de Principijs ac Causis tractatione deseruimus ipsorum præceptorem, apud quem
units.tr: VII. Yet let them know that they have no just ground for complaint against us. Just as we have departed from their teacher in nearly all the other parts of natural philosophy, so we have done in this treatment of principles and causes, in which he was

units.la: Cap. II. quem non modo falsa sunt; quæ de re ipsa tradidit (quo de satis in superiori capite dictum est) sed & tam immanis in vocabulis hallucinatio, ut ea non modo ad plurimas & diversissimas significationes passim in suis scriptis adhibeat, lectori divinandum relinquens, quomodo quoquo in loco accipienda sint; sed & ibi, ubi ex professo de ipsorum vi ac significatione agit, adeo & se ipsum contradictione, & negotium totum partim absurdis, partim supervacuis atq; à proposito alienis divisionibus intricet, ut nulla major liberalibus atq; erectis ingenijs crux figi possit, quam ut ejusmodi sententiæ rimentur.
units.tr: Chapter II. not only false in what he taught about the matter itself (on which enough was said in the previous chapter), but he is also so monstrous in his confusion of words that he uses them everywhere in his writings in very many and widely differing senses, leaving it to the reader to guess how they are to be taken in any given place. And even where he treats their force and meaning expressly, he so entangles both himself in contradiction and the whole matter in divisions that are partly absurd, partly superfluous and foreign to the purpose, that no greater cross could be set up for liberal and lofty minds than to search out such opinions.

units.la: Ut tamen condonandum quodammodo Ramo videatur, si intemperantius subinde Aristotelem incessit, præsertim in Physicis & Metaphysicis; qui libri adeo scatent toti istis non modo falsis, sed amethodis prorsus atq; pugnantibus sermonibus, ut vel adamantinam patientiam expugnare, atq; contra se irritare possint. Et quisquis ita affectus est, ut servili alienorum dogmatum necessitati manifestam audeat anteponere veritatem (quod paucissimi hactenus cum ratione facere sustinuerunt aut sciverunt) fateatur necesse est, pessime de Re philosophica meritum esse Aristotelem cum libris istis Physicis ac Metaphysicis, quæ & veritatis vix scintillam habent, & præterea falsas atq; absurdissimas theses tanta enarrant cum fluctuatione & confusione, ut videantur ad aliud nihil comparata esse, nisi ut animos hominum atq; ingenia non modo erroribus penitus involverent, sed & infinito in plerisq; rimandi ipsam autoris sententiam labore, miserrime exercerent atq; attererent.
units.tr: Yet it may seem somewhat forgivable to Ramus if he attacked Aristotle rather intemperately at times, especially in the Physics and Metaphysics. These books so abound throughout, not only in falsehoods but in utterly disorderly and contradictory discourses, that they could overcome even adamantine patience and provoke it against them. And whoever is so disposed as to dare to put manifest truth before the slavish necessity of other men's doctrines (which very few have hitherto ventured or known how to do rationally) must confess that Aristotle has deserved very badly of philosophy through these Physical and Metaphysical books. They scarcely have a spark of truth, and moreover they recount false and most absurd theses with such wavering and confusion that they seem to have been composed for nothing else than to bury men's minds and wits not only in errors, but also to wear them out and exhaust them most wretchedly, with infinite labour in most cases in tracking down the author's own meaning.

units.la: Nihil hic à nobis frustra dici, testantur enormia illa atq; ridicula opinionum portenta, quæ ex Aristotelicis fundamentis necessario sequentia, tantum abest ut sectatores ejus ad sanam mentem redire, atq; de ejusmodi fundamentis attentius cogitare faciant, ut illa pro verissimis axiomatis unanimiter excipiant omnes, atq; alijs obtrudant; ob illud ipsum, quod ex ipsis hypothesibus sequuntur: cum pleraq; eorum talia sint, ut si quis Peripateticis figmentis non imbutus ea audiat, juraturus sit, nisi ab insanis talia pronunciari aut credi non posse. Testantur rursus ex altera parte id quod nos dicimus, innumerabiles atq; acerrimæ summorum Peripateticorum de præcipuis quibusq; suæ disciplinæ capitibus concertationes, unoquoq; Aristotelem in suis partibus collocante, atq; suam sententiam in ipsius scriptis contineri affirmante: cujus rei, ut & præcedentis, multa ac magna jam dedimus specimina, plura procedente opere, atq; sic effiagitante nostri instituti ratione (cum veritatem introducere, nisi exagitatis atq; sublatis erroribus non polfimus) exhibituri. Certe immodicus ille Aristotelis admirator atq; laudator & animosissimus omnium ipsius figmentorum propugnator Scaliger, altero tamen illo, quod hic attigimus, scriptorum ipsius vitio, incertissima nimirum atq; inconditissima fluctuatione, tantopere offensus fuit, ut non raro ipsum super hoc culpaverit, partim quidem tacite sua in ipsum dicta jaciens, partim nomine quoque ipsius expresso; in ijs commentariis, quos ad Theophrasti de Causis libros scripsit. Confusa (inquit) non raro capita, haud facile tam apud hunc, quam etiam apud Præceptorem, explicari possunt. & alibi, Prisci illi viri, domiforis magni nominis, methodos quidem docuere nos, nobisq; earum curam injecere; ipsi plerumq; nullam aut perexiguam habuere. Ac rursus, Sane laxiuscula fuit veterum Philosophia multis in locis, quasi non nisi cognitionis jecerit fundamenta. Libro etiam tertio, capite quarto Aristotelem perstringit, quod incondita sint ejus & fluctuantes in topicis ac metaphysicis vestigationes. Sic libro sexto, capite tertio, hoc est peculiare vitium Peripateticis, ut non semper statuant, quid in animo certi habeant, sed simul cum discipulo venentur conclusiones. sic pene per totos Metaphysica libros. Et libro sexto, capite decimo quinto, Utinam vero unum quempiam ex Scotistis & Waterististis audirem tractantem hæc: paucissimis verbis plura, meliora, ordinatiora, quasi ex rebus ipsis expicta, longe commodius perciperemus. Ceterum isti Graeci semper in suis disputationibus jactationem patiuntur; id quod ad fastidium vexati, ad fastidium monimus. Ac rursus eodem libro, capite decimo nono. Simillimas labyrinthis animadvertimus apud hos Graecas errationes. videntur enim tanquam clausis oculis circumferre se, quoad ostium nancisci antur. interea offendunt saepe ipsi; auditorem vero ad cruces sistunt. Et multo plura haud dubie dicturus fuerat de hoc argumento, nisi eum pudor deterruisset. Qui enim ubiq; se profiteatur Aristotelis discipulum, idq; sibi gloriae ducat; non potuit non contentissime ipsius honorem tueri, ac vitia dissimulare; quanquam ipsorum enormitas omnem interdum ejus patientiam ac dissimulandi studium expugnavit, & velut invito justas expressit querelas. Sed quam non ausus est in praeceptore nisi parce & carptim exercere censuram, illam in discipulum ejus Theophrastum plenissime destrinxit: quem acriter persaepe & acerbe, nec sane immerito castigat. at nihil est eorum, quae in ipso reprehendit, quod non & in Aristotelem aeque bono jure dici possit. Fuit enim non degener discipulus, eamque scribendi formam, quam a magistro acceperat, ad vivum suis scriptis expressit; quae adeo Aristoteli placuerunt, ut ob illa, qui prius Tyrtamus dicebatur, Theophrastum appellaverit, quasi divina quadam disserendi ac scribendi facultate praeditum; quare ex universa quoque sectatorum suorum cohorte hunc potissimum delegit loci sui ac magisterij successorem. Et qui utriusque scripta contulerit, inveniet eadem prorsus vena utraque fluere, nisi quod amoenior & aliquando copiosior paulo est Theophrastus. Quaecunque igitur in hoc culpat Scaliger, quantum ad methodum & docendi modum, eadem omnia in Aristotelem quoque ab eo dicta existimare debemus. Sunt autem illa ejusmodi, ut nos omnino clementes Aristotelicorum vitiorum exagitatores debeamus videri, si cum tali censore conferamur: id quod manifestum erit cuivis, si aliquot ipsius locos e modo dictis commentarijs ascribamus. In praefatione igitur conqueritur, non pauca a Theophrasto coacervata, alia repetita, plurima inculcata, nec pauciora prapostera. Et mox, Multa confundit, multa repetit: quaedam tam perplexe & misere tractat, at explicatio longe majorem pariat dubitationem, quam ipsa quaestio. stio. Alibi, solere perplexissime & morosissime implicare potius quam explicare quaestiones. Et rursus, Plane subsultare ipsius disceptationes, & hoc vitium ipsi maxime peculiare esse, ut perplexissime doceat. Acutiora judicia nunquam satis conqueri posse de istius viri securitate. Item, Autorem eum meritum esse non de nobis, ut speremus ab eo doceri nos posse: caeterum nobis plus esse laborandum ad sententiarum perceptionem, quam ipse in scribendo sumserit opera. omnino vero indignum esse, quem in scripturis nostris illo modo imitemur. In hisce verbis qui non Aristoteleum aeque ac Theophrasteum scribendi genus vivis coloribus delineatum videat, illum quavis talpa caeciorem esse oportet. Et cum ita se res habeat, nemo nobis vitio vertere potest, quod non ipsarum modo rerum falsitatem, sed perplexissimam quoque & morosissimam docendi rationem in Aristotele culpamus. Peccavisse tamen Ramum quoque nimia Aristotelem insectandi immodestia, haud gravate concedimus; quandoquidem multa mala multis bonis pensavit, & non prava tantum atq; damnosa scripta, sed & egregia atq; fructuosa nobis reliquit; ut oporteat nos & pro hisce gratias agere, & eorundem respectu, aequanimiores nos ipsi atq; ignoscibiliores, in quibus peccavit, praebere; ijs duntaxat exceptis, ubi non ignorantia, sed malitia erravit. Quod enim veterum sententias in ejusmodi portenta convertit, ac potius pervertit, de quibus illi ne per somnium quidem cogitaverant, ut tanto majorem & favorabiliorem haberet eos, insectandi praetextum, (quod fecit nimis quam saepe) prosecto veniam nullam meretur: ut neq; in ijs, ubi cum errore insignis aliquarimpietas conjuncta est. In aliis vero erratis, quantum vel ad res ipsas, vel earum tradendarum modum, quanquam & creberrima illa sunt & gravissima, clementer tractari meretur, ita ut vitia quidem ipsa, quoties id res poscit, suis coloribus depicta detegantur, & quantum satis sit refellantur; convitijs vero in ipsum autorem, & acerbis insectationibus abstineatur. Nobis enim vehementer placuit semper illud Nostri Senis, qui de veterum erroribus loquens alicubi, sic infit: Μεμφόμενοι μὲν ἀδίκως ... ἀξιόν ἐστιν, ἐι μὴ ἐΛωνύΗσαν ἐξευρεῖν ἐπαινέσαι ὡς μᾶλλον πάντας, ὅτι ἀλλ' ἐπεχειρήσαντο ζητῆσαι. Nullum ipsorum culpare aequum est, quod non potuerint invenire; sed potius omnes laudare, quod saltem aggressi sunt quaerere. Itemq; illud Senecae, qui opiniones Veterum parum exactas suisse dicens, & rudes, ac circa verum erravisse; illis tamen, si quid inventum est, referri vult acceptum. Magni enim animi rem fuisse, rerum naturae latebras dimovere, nec contentum exteriori ejus superficie, in ipsius secreta descendere. plurimum ad inveniendum contulisse, qui speravit reperiri posse. itaq; cum excusatione veteres audiendos esse.
units.tr: Nothing is said here by us without cause. The monstrous and ridiculous opinions that follow necessarily from Aristotelian foundations bear witness to this. Far from bringing his followers back to sound judgment or making them think more carefully about those foundations, these consequences lead them to accept the same things unanimously as the most certain axioms and to press them on others, for the very reason that they follow from those hypotheses. Most of them are such that anyone who has not been steeped in Peripatetic fictions and hears them would swear that they could not be pronounced or believed except by madmen. On the other hand, the countless and most bitter disputes among the leading Peripatetics over the chief points of their discipline likewise confirm what we say. Each places Aristotle on his own side and asserts that his own opinion is contained in Aristotle's writings. Of this, as of what came before, we have already given many large examples, and as the plan of our work requires (since we cannot introduce truth unless errors are first shaken out and removed), we shall give more as the work proceeds. Certainly that immoderate admirer and praiser of Aristotle, and most spirited defender of all his fictions, Scaliger, was nevertheless so offended by the other fault of his writings, which we have touched on here, namely their most uncertain and disorderly confusion, that he often blamed him for it. He did this partly by tacitly casting his remarks against him, and partly by naming him openly, in the commentaries he wrote on the books of Theophrastus' On Causes. The confused chapters (he says) can not easily be explained, not often with this man, but also with the Teacher. And elsewhere: Those ancient men, great in name, indeed taught us methods and put the care of them into our hands, but they themselves for the most part had none, or very little. And again: Surely the philosophy of the ancients was rather loose in many places, as if it had laid only the foundations of knowledge. In the third book, chapter four, he also censures Aristotle because his investigations in the Topics and Metaphysics are disorderly and wavering. So in the sixth book, chapter three: This is a peculiar vice of the Peripatetics, that they do not always settle what they really hold in mind, but hunt for conclusions together with the student. So almost throughout the books of the Metaphysics. And in the sixth book, chapter fifteen: Would that I might hear some one of the Scotists and Waterists treating these matters: in very few words I would more conveniently grasp many things that are better and more orderly, as if drawn from the things themselves. Moreover those Greeks always suffer boasting in their disputations: which, vexed to disgust, we warn to disgust. And again in the same book, chapter nineteen: We notice wanderings among these Greeks most like labyrinths. For they seem to go about as with closed eyes, until they find a door. Meanwhile they often stumble themselves, and bring the listener to crosses. He would undoubtedly have said much more on this subject, had shame not restrained him. For one who everywhere professes himself a disciple of Aristotle, and counts this a glory, could not but defend his honour most zealously and dissemble his faults. Yet the enormity of those faults sometimes overcame all his forbearance and his will to dissemble, and as if against his will they drew from him just complaints. But while he did not dare to exercise censure on the teacher except sparingly and piecemeal, he fully lashed it upon his disciple Theophrastus, whom he rebukes sharply and very often bitterly, and not undeservedly. Yet there is nothing among those things he reproves in him which could not with equal good right be said of Aristotle. For Theophrastus was no degenerate disciple, and he expressed in his own writings to the life the style of writing he had received from his master. These pleased Aristotle so much that because of them he called Theophrastus, who had before been named Tyrtamus, by the name of "divine speaker," as if endowed with a certain divine faculty of discourse and writing. For this reason he chose him above the whole band of his followers as the successor of his place and teaching. And whoever compares the writings of the two will find that both flow from exactly the same vein, except that Theophrastus is somewhat more pleasant and at times a little fuller. Therefore, whatever Scaliger blames in Theophrastus, as regards method and manner of teaching, we ought to suppose he has said equally of Aristotle too. Such are these faults that we who criticise Aristotle's errors ought to appear altogether gentle when compared with such a censor. This will be plain to anyone if we quote some of his passages from the commentaries just mentioned. In the preface, then, he complains that not a few things are heaped together by Theophrastus, some repeated, very many thrust in, and no fewer put in the wrong order. And soon after: He confuses many things, repeats many, and treats some so perplexedly and wretchedly that the explanation produces far more doubt than the question itself. Elsewhere: he is accustomed to entangle questions most perplexingly and most tediously, rather than to explain them. And again: his disputations plainly stagger, and this vice is especially peculiar to him, that he teaches most perplexingly. One can never complain enough of the sharper judgments about that man's carelessness. Likewise: That author deserves that we should not hope to be taught by him; but we have to labour more to grasp his opinions than he himself spent effort in writing. It is altogether unworthy that we should imitate him in that way in our writings. Whoever does not see in these words a picture, in vivid colours, of the Aristotelian as well as the Theophrastean manner of writing must be blinder than any mole. And since this is so, no one can fault us for condemning in Aristotle not only the falsity of the matters themselves but also the most perplexing and tedious manner of teaching. Yet we readily concede that Ramus also sinned by his excessive immodesty in attacking Aristotle. For he balanced many evils with many goods, and left us not only corrupt and harmful writings but also excellent and profitable ones. Therefore we ought both to give thanks for these, and in view of them to show ourselves more even-tempered and more forgiving toward the errors in which he sinned, excepting only those cases where he erred not from ignorance but from malice. For he turned the opinions of the ancients into such monstrosities, or rather perverted them, that they had never even dreamed of them, in order to have a greater and more favourable pretext for attacking them. (And he did this only too often.) Such conduct deserves no pardon at all, especially where some notable impiety is joined to the error. In other errors, however, whether as regards the matters themselves or their manner of presentation, although these are very frequent and very grave, he deserves to be treated gently. So the faults themselves may be exposed, painted in their own colours whenever the matter requires, and refuted as far as is sufficient, but abuse aimed at the author himself and bitter attacks must be refrained from. For we have always been greatly pleased by that saying of our own Sen. who, speaking somewhere of the errors of the ancients, begins thus: Μεμφόμενοι μὲν ἀδίκως ... ἀξιόν ἐστιν, εἰ μὴ ἐξευρεῖν ἠδυνήθησαν, ἐπαινέσαι ὡς μᾶλλον πάντας, ὅτι ἀλλ' ἐπεχειρήσαντο ζητῆσαι. [Blaming them unjustly ... it is worthy, if they were not able to discover, to praise them all the more, because they at least attempted to seek.] No one of them is fair to blame for not having been able to find; rather all are to be praised, because at least they set out to seek. Likewise is that saying of Seneca, who says the opinions of the ancients were not very exact, and rough, and went astray about the truth; yet he wills that whatever has been discovered by them be credited to them. For, he says, it was the mark of a great mind to remove the hiding places of nature's secrets, and not to be content with her outward surface but to descend into her inmost secrets. Whoever hoped that something could be found has contributed much to discovery. Therefore the ancients are to be heard with indulgence.

units.la: VIII. Ut igitur ex hoc diverticulo in viam rursus redeamus; sua certa ac physiologica vocabulo Principij significatio, non ex Aristotele, (qui ipse scivit nunquam, si ex scriptis ejus haurienda est ipsius mens) quis proprius esset ac genuinus hujus dictionis in Philosophia usus ( sicuti modo ostendimus) sed ex ipsa rei veritate assignanda est. quod ut recte faciamus, repetendum est, quod supra diximus, philosophicae hujus vocabuli notioni magnam intercedere cum vulgari ejusdem usurpatione cognationem. neq; sane fieri aliter potest. Quum enim hoc vocabulum non sit de numero eorum, quae Casu aequivoca dicuntur in scholis, quemadmodum Gallus & avis nomen est, & nationis, & sacerdotis: sed deliberato consilio secundaria haec significatio invecta sit a priscis illis viris, qui vocabulum e medio sumtum ad usus suos accommodaverunt; necesse est id fecerint ratione alicujus convenientiae, quam in utroq; Principiorum genere perspexerint: ac proinde ratio Principij vulgaris analogice Principio philosophico competat. Est autem ratio Principij vulgaris, (sicuti ex ijs, quae dicta sunt superius, apparet) Esse id, unde res cujus principium dicitur, incipit: nimirum, vel secundum longitudinem, vel secundum durationem, sicuti antea latius declaravimus. hanc rationem Principio quoq; philosophico quodammodo, & per analogiam, competere; sic discere licet. [Quidquid non est aeternum, aliquando non fuit, & cum non effet prius, esse postea incepit. Ast incipere esse, nihil est aliud, quam quod Oriri aut Nasci vulgo dicimus. Illas igitur res, unde res aliqua oritur, Principia ipsius vocaverunt Prisci, quia & ab illis res incipiunt. Sicuti vero in hoc conveniunt utraq; Principia,quod ab ijs res incipiunt (in quo ratio analogiæ consistit) ita in eo discrepant, quod admodum diversus est in utrisq; incipiendi modus. namq; ab altero principio initium dimensionis res ducunt; ab altero initium Essendi, ut sic dicamus, trahunt. potest itaq; talis assignari Principij Philosophici definitio. Principia rei sunt res, per quas factum est, ut ipsa, cum non esset prius, esse postea inceperit. vel brevius sic, Principia rei sunt res, per quas ipsa ortum accepit. Sic igitur vestigando, quo respectu sumptam à vulgo Principij dictionem, ad usus suos converterint prisci philosophi, veram Principij philosophici rationem invenimus. Nunc porro tota ipsius natura ac vis latius nobis explicanda est, in qua re ita progrediemur, ut primo numerum principiorum rimemur, & an omnia omnibus rebus competant, dispiciamus. Posteriore autem loco proprietates, quas Principijs in universum attribuit Aristoteles examinabimus, & quatenus Principijs veris congruant, consider abimus.
units.tr: VIII. To return, then, from this digression to the main road: the proper and genuine meaning of this word "principle" in philosophy (as we have just shown) is not to be taken from Aristotle, who never knew it himself, if his mind is to be drawn from his writings, but must be assigned from the truth of the matter itself. To do this rightly, we must repeat what we said above: there is a great affinity between the philosophical notion of this word and its common use. Nor can it really be otherwise. For since this word does not belong to the class of words that are called equivocal by chance in the schools (as "cock" is the name of a bird, of a nation and of a priest), but the secondary meaning was introduced by deliberate design by those early men, who took the word from common use and adapted it to their own purposes, they must have done so on the basis of some correspondence which they saw in each kind of principle; and so the common definition of principle fits the philosophical principle by analogy. Now the common definition of principle is (as appears from what was said earlier): that from which the thing whose principle it is said to be begins to be. That is, either in respect of length or in respect of duration, as we explained more fully before. That this definition likewise fits the philosophical principle, in a certain way and by analogy, may be learned thus. [Whatever is not eternal once was not, and since it was not before, it began to be afterwards. But to begin to be is nothing other than what we commonly call arising or being born. Those things, therefore, out of which some thing arises, the early writers called its principles, because from them the thing begins.] Just as the two kinds of principle agree in this, that things begin from them (and in this lies the basis of the analogy), so they differ in this, that the manner of beginning is quite different in each. For from the one kind of principle things derive a beginning of extension; from the other they draw a beginning of being, so to speak. Thus such a definition of the philosophical principle can be assigned: The principles of a thing are those things through which it came about that the thing, since it was not before, afterwards began to be. Or more briefly: The principles of a thing are those things through which it has received its origin. Thus, by inquiring in what respect the early philosophers took the common term "principle" and turned it to their own uses, we find the true account of the philosophical principle. Now its whole nature and force must be explained more fully, and in doing so we shall proceed so as first to inquire into the number of principles and to examine whether all of them belong to all things. In the second place we shall examine the properties which Aristotle attributes to principles in general, and consider how far they agree with true principles.
SECTIO SECUNDA.
ON THE NUMBER OF PRINCIPLES.
