units.tr: division of parts is not rightly made, which is shown from the fact that the differences they assign between essential parts and integral parts cannot stand. VII. The difference offered by Zabarella, to which Suárez opposes a passage saying the plain opposite. VIII. Suárez's opinion, that in every composition there is found something material and something formal, is weighed. The ridiculous opinion that the whole stands in the place of a form. IX. The absurdity of this fiction is shown. X. The distinction between parts laid down by Zabarella is overturned. XI. A composite does not arise from potency and act. XII. Our division of parts: quantitative parts. XIII. Scaliger denies that qualities can be intended and remitted, with a ridiculous argument; his most absurd opinion on the intension of qualities. XIV. It is further maintained that degrees of intension are not to be counted as quantitative parts. XV. The property and characteristic of quantitative parts. XVI. Dissimilar parts, opposed to quantitative ones: their distinction into essential and conforming parts. XVII. The name of "natural" parts also belongs to conforming parts, and more so than to the preceding. XVIII. If any dissimilar part is removed, the whole is either destroyed or violated. What mutilations the wholes of dissimilar things can sustain, and to what extent. XIX. Aristotle's teaching on mutilated things and mutilation is set out. XX. It is examined. XXI. Accidental composites are also mutilated. It is further explained in what the reason of mutilation consists. XXII. Partition is always to be made into proximate parts. XXIII. The distinction of parts delivered by us is briefly applied to artificial and fortuitous composites. XXIV. The various modes of composition of essential parts. Accidents are not united except by the union of a subject. XXV. Suárez's contrary opinion, that certain accidents inhere in other accidents; it is examined. XXVI. Scaliger's opinion, that all accidents are composed of potency and act. XXVII. It is overthrown. XXVIII. Against Suárez it is shown that the subject is not the matter of accidents.
IN
Chapter II.

units.la: IN disquisitione illa, qua numerus Principiorum quæritur, primo se offert Efficiens. Quum enim nulla res effi-cere se ipsam possit (quod adeo est evidens, ut probari non debeat, neq; refelli is, qui id negaverit, utpote indignus, cujus ratio habeatur) necessario eam debet præce-dere Efficiens, quod sua vi producere possit, atq; facere ut sit, cum non esset prius: ac proinde id omnino inter Principia, & quidem primo loco, collocandum est. Sunt autem multæ res, quibus solum hoc Principium competit; tem multæ res, quibus solum hoc Principium competit; illa nimirum, quæ compositionis essentialis expertia, sim-plicissimâ essentiâ constant: hæc enim cum simpliciter fi-ant, non nisi Principio producente opus habent. At compositorum alia est ratio, quippe quæ non ita simpliciter fiunt, sed per partium componentium coalitionem. Quum enim nihil aliud sit compositum, quam Partium componentium unio, aut potius ipsæ partes unitæ; ac sine partibus suis esse ac subsistere nequaquam possit: ne oriri quidem sine ipsis poterit; quum oriri nihil sit aliud, quam incipere esse. Omnino igitur, ut compositum existere incipiat, partes ipsum componentes concurrere, atq; inter se uniri necesse est; unde sequitur, ut Partes Compositi, pro Principijs ipsius habendæ sint. Itaq; Composita præter Effectivum Principium, aliud insuper Principium habent, ni-mirum Compositivum: quod Principium Elementi quoque nomine indigetare licet. Namq; Elementa rei sunt id, è quo res ipsa componitur, hoc est, partes rei. Loquimur autem nunc de partibus rei essentialibus, non integrantibus (ut vocari vulgo solent) quandoquidem compositio è partibus In-tegrantibus non obstat, quo minus totum integrale possit esse simplex. Partes enim integrales omnes ejusdem sunt inter se naturæ, sicuti in corporibus primis, ut aqua & aëre, itemq; compositis homogeneis, ut carne & ossè, videre est; quæ om-nia, ac similia, non stat per partes integrales, quo minus sint essentialiter simplicia. Talia tamen non sunt, quia præter istam compositionem, habent etiam alteram illam è partibus essen-tialibus, quæ cum simplicitate consistere nequaquam potest, quum
units.tr: In that inquiry into how many Principles there are, the Efficient presents itself first. For since no thing can make itself (which is so evident that it need not be proved, and he who denies it is not to be refuted, being unworthy of having his reasoning considered), the Efficient must necessarily precede the thing, being able by its own power to produce it and bring it about that it exists when it did not exist before. Therefore this must be counted among the Principles, and indeed in first place. There are, however, many things to which this Principle alone belongs: namely those which, free of essential composition, consist of a wholly simple essence. For these, since they come into being simply, need only a producing Principle. Composite things, however, are different, since they do not come into being simply but through the coming together of their component parts. For since a composite is nothing other than the union of its component parts, or rather the parts themselves united, and since it can by no means exist or subsist without its parts, it cannot even arise without them, since to arise is nothing other than to begin to be. Altogether, then, for a composite to begin to exist, its component parts must concur and be united with one another. Whence it follows that the parts of a composite must be regarded as its Principles. Thus composites have, besides the Efficient Principle, another Principle as well, namely the Compositive, which may also be called by the name of Element. For elements are that out of which a thing is composed, that is, the parts of a thing. We are speaking now, however, of essential parts, not integral parts (as they are commonly called), since composition out of integral parts does not prevent a integral whole from being simple. For integral parts are all of the same nature among themselves, as can be seen in primary bodies such as water and air, and in homogeneous composites such as flesh and bone. All these things, and similar ones, do not, by their integral parts, stand in the way of their being essentially simple. Such things are not simple, however, because besides that composition they also have the other composition out of essential parts, which cannot consist with simplicity, since...
Chapter II.

units.la: quum partes essentiales necessario diversæ sint inter se essentiæ, cujus rei in anima & corpore, quæ partes sunt essentiales ipsius animalis, manifestum exemplum habemus. sed de hac re, ut de nomine ipso Integralis, (quod nequaquam nobis placet) mox plura dicturi sumus.
units.tr: Since essential parts are necessarily different in essence from one another, we have a clear example of this in soul and body, which are the essential parts of the animal itself. But concerning this matter, as also concerning the word "integral" itself (which does not please us at all), we shall say more shortly.

units.la: Vt sciamus igitur, unum ne an duo habeat Principia unaquæq; res, sciendum prius est, simplex ne sit, an composita. Simplex enim si est, simplicitate scilicet essentiali, solum effectivum Principium agnoscet. sin vero composita est, præter Efficiens, etiam Elementa, (nimirum illas partes, è quibus componitur) pro Principijs habebit. Hujus autem generis sunt substantiæ, quæ ad unam omnes, (nullâ, præter Deum, exceptâ) ex Materia constant & Natura, non modo hæ nostrates & corruptibiles, sed & cœlum, ac cœlestia imò ipsi quoq; Angeli, atq; Mentes humanæ: id quod impræsens ita supponentes, in tractatione de Natura, volente Deo, probatum dabimus: ubi etiam planum fiet, quid per Naturam intelligamus, videlicet rem non solo nomine à formâ Aristotelica diversam, sed reali ac peringenti discrimine ab ea differentem. Materiam autem dicimus, non illam commentitiam, quæ Materia prima Peripateticis dicitur (hanc enim supra ipsi explosimus) sed aliam longe diversam, sicuti suo in loco postea declarabimus.
units.tr: So that we may know whether each thing has one principle or two, we must first know whether it is simple or composite. For if it is simple, that is, simple in essence, it will acknowledge only an efficient principle. But if it is composite, then besides the efficient principle it will also have elements (namely the parts of which it is composed) as principles. Of this kind are all substances, which, with the sole exception of God, all consist of matter and nature: not only these earthly and corruptible things, but also the heavens and heavenly things, and indeed the angels themselves and human minds. Supposing this for now, we will prove it in the treatise on Nature, God willing, where it will also become plain what we mean by Nature: namely a thing differing from the Aristotelian form not merely in name but by a real and striking distinction. We speak of matter, however, not of that fictitious matter which the Peripatetics call prime matter (for we have already rejected this above), but of another, far different matter, as we shall declare later in its proper place.

units.la: Quum igitur omnis substantia sit composita, duplex Principium necessario obtinet, Effectivum, & utrumq; Compositivum, Materiam ac Naturam: quæ duæ partes etiamsi diversissimæ sint conditionis (altera enim Substantia est, altera Accidens) non tamen duo diversa Principiorum genera constituunt; quippe quæ in ista diversitate, conveniant in eo, cujus ratione Principiorum appellationem sortiuntur; quod est, substantiam, cujus Principia dicuntur componere. Quandoquidem, ergo ad componendam Substantiam ex æquo utraq; concurrit (sive enim hæc desit, sive illa, Compositi ortus æquè impedietur) uno communi Principiorum Componentium nomine utraq; censenda est: sicuti rursus ubi multæ materiæ assumuntur ad Compositum aliquod constituendum, non aliter, quam ut una totius Materia, omnes illæ materiæ simul junctæ considerantur. de qua Materia notandum quoq; est, si considere-
units.tr: Since therefore every substance is composite, it necessarily has a twofold principle: the efficient, and the component principles, matter and nature. Although these two parts are of very different condition (one is a substance, the other an accident), they do not constitute two different kinds of principles. For in this difference they agree in that by which they obtain the name of principles, namely that they compose the substance whose principles they are. Since therefore both concur equally in composing the substance (for if either is lacking, the coming-into-being of the composite is equally prevented), both are to be reckoned under one common name of component principles; just as again, when many matters are taken up to constitute some composite, they are considered as one matter of the whole, all those matters joined together. Concerning this matter it should also be noted that, if it is considered separately,
Chapter II.

units.la: consideretur seorsim, habere & ipsam Principium Compositivum. quum enim concipiatur sub ratione unius, unum autem è multis fieri non possit, nisi per compositionem; apparet & illam Materiam, è diversis materijs conflatam, esse quasi quoddam compositum. & quum partes illam componentes sint Essentiales (quacunq; enim earum sublata, Essentia ejus læditur) pro Principio compositivo omnino sunt habendæ.
units.tr: it also has a composing principle. For since it is conceived under the aspect of one thing, and one thing cannot be made from many except by composition, it is evident that this matter, fused together from diverse matters, is also in a way a composite. And since the parts composing it are essential (for if any of them is removed, its essence is harmed), it must altogether be held to be a composing principle.

units.la: II. Substantiæ igitur omnes utroq; Principio indigent, Effectivo, & Componenti, quum nulla ipsarum sit absolutè simplex. Accidentium autem non una est ratio propterea q; in universum determinari de ijs non potest, quod vel unum Principium habeant; vel utrumq;. Nam pleraq; quidem ipsorum sunt absolutè simplicia, omnisq; compositionis essentialis expertia, nihil præter simplicem Essentiam habent: quæ proinde solum desiderare Principium Effectivum; ex antedictis patet. Alia autem composita sunt, atq; ex diversorum accidentium unione emergunt, quæ proinde indigent utroq; Principio, æque ac Substantiæ, Effectivo, & Compositivo, ut ortum accipere possint. Prioris generis exempla recensere nihil attinet, cum obvia passim sint, de quibus nemo controversiam moveat; ut calor, frigus, lumen, aliaq; innumera: Sed & composita quænam sint, facile est intellectu; quæcunq; nimirum è variorum accidentium concursu constant, seu potius, quæ nihil sunt aliud, quam ipse variorum Accidentium concursus. nihil enim refert, hoc ne an illo modo dicas, sicuti & in substantijs eodem redit, dicasne corpus humanum, verbi gratia, esse concursum capitis, thoracis, ventris, artuum, aliorumq; membrorum, an ex illarum partium concursu constare. Quippe Totum sive Compositum est quidem aliquid diversum à singulis partibus suis seorsim consideratis: idem verò est cum illis simul sumptis, unitisq; quod etiamsi controversum est, major tamen & melior philosophorum pars nobiscum sentit, & ita sentiendum esse, Toletus firmis argumentis convincit. Omne itaq; compositum est concursus suorum Elementorum, sive partium componentium; & quod idem est, ex concursu suorum Elementorum hoc est, ex Elementis suis inter se concurrentibus, constat; neq; aliud est, quam ipsa Elementa concurrentia, sive unita. Quippe concursum cum dicimus, non intelligimus fortuitam conglomerationem, sed decentem ac ordinatam partium inter se conspirantium adunationem. Sunt autem Accidentium compositorum duo genera. alia enim ex accidentium congenerum, alia ex diversi generum concursu oriuntur. E congeneribus Accidentibus illa constare dicimus, quae constant ex Accidentibus idem genus proximum sortitis Inter haec primo loco collocare possumus figuras, quae omnes in universum (recta simplici duntaxat excepta) sunt compositae ex aliis figuris. Multo autem magis composita est figura corporum organicorum, verbi gratia, corporis humani. Etenim totum corpus quatenus unum compositum, unam figuram habet. sed quomodo ipsius unitas ex partium diversarum concursu nata est atq; constat, ita & figura ipsius non simpliciter una est, sed ex diversarum cuiusq; partis figurarum adunatione consistit. Ita multarum rerum sapores sunt compositi. alia enim ex acido & dulci, alia ex acido & amaro, alia ex dulci & amaro, alia ex dulci, amaro, acido, conflatum habent saporem, multaq; aliae saporum permixtiones dantur, quas hic omnes enarrare, nequaquam est necesse. In omnibus autem illis idem tenendum est, quod de figuris modo dicebamus, saporem totius esse omnes illos partium sapores simul sumptos atq; inter se unitos. Idem quoq; de coloribus deq; odoribus habendum est. quacunq; enim alium in alia parte colorem habent, aut odorem, illorum universus vel color, vel odor, compositus est. Sic etiam multi habitus, multae itidem potentiae naturales, ex diversorum habituum, ac diversarum potentiarum collectione aut concursu constant. nulla enim fere est ars aut scientia, in qua non diversi habitus inveniantur. omnes tamen illi habitus simul sumpti unam tantum artem, aut unam scientiam, hoc est, unum habitum constituunt. idemq; de multis quoq; vitijs ac virtutibus verum est: & pariter tum nutriens animae facultas, tum sentiens, tum intelligens, multas quaeq; ambitu suo facultates tates comprehendunt, ex quibus concurrentibus atq; adunatis ipsæ constant. hi autem habitus compositi, hæq; potentiæ, partim ad prius genus Accidentium compositorum, quæ nimirum constant ex accidentibus congeneribus, pertinent; partim vero ad alterum. Non enim omnes habitus, omnesq; potentiæ, quæ aliquem superiorem habitum, aut aliquem superiorem potentiam constituunt, sub eodem genere proximo semper comprehenduntur. Ad secundum etiam Accidentium compositorum genus pertinet Natura, quæ nihil est aliud, quam coetus proprietatum omnium congenitarum; istarum autem proprietatum multæ sub diversis admodum generibus continentur. qua de re in tertio libro fusè tractabitur. Ejusdem classis est & Sanitas, quæ ipsa quoq; accidentium diversigenerum est concursus. sanitas enim totius corporis, in singularum partium sanitate consistit. omnium autem partium non eadem est ratio recte se habendi, ac proinde aliter hæc, aliter illa affecta esse postulat, ut sanitatem suam habeat. illæ autem diversæ diversarum partium sanitates, concursu suo unam constituunt totius sanitatem. imò sanitas, si quis recte rem perpendat, nihil aliud est, quam ipsa Natura, ac solo nomine, aut saltem non plus quam externo respectu, ab ea differt, nimirum in subjectis sanitatis capacibus, sive quibus sanitas tribui solet. Quanquam enim omnis sanitas est natura, non omnis natura est sanitas, quum plurima habeant Naturam, quibus sanitas tribui non potest. sed de hac re fusius infra tractabitur. hujus quoq; ordinis est Pulchritudo, quæ ex debito partium situ, & accurata figura, atq; bono colore, aut bonis coloribus consurgit. hæc igitur sunt Accidentia composita, quæ sicuti non subsistunt nisi per partium suarum unionem, ita neq; oriri possunt, nisi ex illarum concursu: atq; propetera illas pro altero sui principio, nimirum compositivo, agnoscunt.
units.tr: II. All substances therefore need both principles, the efficient and the composing, since none of them is absolutely simple. But there is not one account of accidents, so that one cannot determine in general whether they have one principle or both. For most of them are absolutely simple, free of every essential composition, and have nothing but a simple essence; these therefore require only an efficient principle, as is clear from what was said above. Others, however, are composite and arise from the union of diverse accidents, and so they need both principles, as substances do, the efficient and the composing, in order to come into being. It is pointless to list examples of the former kind, since they are everywhere obvious and no one disputes them: heat, cold, light, and countless others. But what the composites are is easy to grasp: namely whatever consists of the concurrence of various accidents, or rather, what is nothing other than that very concurrence. For it makes no difference whether you put it this way or that, just as in substances it comes to the same thing: whether you say the human body, for instance, is the concurrence of head, chest, belly, limbs and other members, or that it consists of the concurrence of those parts. For the whole or composite is indeed something different from its individual parts considered separately; but it is the same as those parts taken together and united. Although this is disputed, a greater and better part of philosophers agrees with us, and Toletus convinces us by firm arguments that it must be thought so. Every composite, therefore, is the concurrence of its elements or component parts; and, which is the same thing, it consists of the concurrence of its elements, that is, of its elements concurring with one another, and it is nothing other than the elements themselves concurring, or united. For when we say concurrence, we do not mean a chance conglomeration, but a fitting and orderly union of parts agreeing with one another. There are two kinds of composite accidents: some arise from the concurrence of accidents of the same kind, others from the concurrence of accidents of different kinds. We say that those consist of accidents of the same kind which consist of accidents having the same proximate genus. Among these, we may first place figures, all of which in general (except the straight line alone) are composed of other figures. Much more composite, however, is the figure of organic bodies, for instance the human body. For the whole body, as one composite, has one figure. But just as its unity arises and consists from the concurrence of diverse parts, so its figure is not simply one, but consists of the union of the figures of each of its diverse parts. Thus the tastes of many things are composite: some consist of sour and sweet, some of sour and bitter, some of sweet and bitter, some of sweet, bitter and sour mixed together; and many other mixtures of tastes exist, which it is not at all necessary to enumerate here. In all of these, however, the same must be held as we were just saying about figures: the taste of the whole is all those tastes of the parts taken together and united with one another. The same is to be held about colours and odours. For whatever colour or odour they have in one part and another, the whole colour or odour is composite. So also many habits and many natural powers consist of the collection or concurrence of diverse habits and diverse powers. For there is hardly any art or science in which diverse habits are not found; yet all those habits taken together constitute only one art, or one science, that is, one habit. The same is true of many vices and virtues; and likewise the nutritive faculty of the soul, the sensitive, and the intellective each comprise within their compass many faculties, and they consist of these concurring and united. These composite habits and powers, however, partly belong to the first kind of composite accidents, which of course consist of accidents of the same kind; partly to the other. For not all habits and all powers which constitute some higher habit or higher power are always comprehended under the same proximate genus. To the second kind of composite accidents belongs also Nature, which is nothing other than the collection of all innate properties; and many of these properties are contained under very diverse genera, a matter to be treated at length in the third book. Health is of the same class, which is likewise a concurrence of accidents of diverse kinds. For the health of the whole body consists in the health of each single part; but the right disposition of all the parts is not the same, and so one requires this part to be disposed in one way and that part in another in order to have its health. Those diverse healths of diverse parts, by their concurrence, constitute one health of the whole. Indeed health, if one considers the matter rightly, is nothing other than Nature itself, and differs from it only in name, or at least by no more than an external relation, namely in the subjects capable of health, or to which health is usually ascribed. For although all health is nature, not all nature is health, since many things have a nature to which health cannot be ascribed. But this will be treated more fully below. Of this order too is Beauty, which arises from the due position of parts, an accurate figure, and a good colour or good colours. These, then, are the composite accidents: just as they do not subsist except through the union of their parts, so neither can they arise except from the concurrence of those parts; and therefore they acknowledge those parts as their other principle, namely the composing one.

units.la: III. Porrò cum dixerimus supra, duplicem esse compositionem, è partibus integralibus, & essentialibus; paulo accuratius nobis hoc negotium enucleandum est, tum ut expeditius in substantijs discernere unusquisq; possit, quenam ipsarum compositio sit hujus generis, quæ illius; tum ut constet quoq;, hanc Accidentium compositionem essentialem esse, non Integralem. Tractant quidem & Peripatetici de hac Materia, tum in Logicis, tum in Metaphysicis: sed nihil hactenus apud quenquam, quod animum expleret, ac Veritati probe concordaret, invenire potuimus. Namq; Aristotelem ipsum quod attinet, is sibi, ut semper, similis est, qui in duobus illis capitibus quinti Metaphysicorum, in quibus de Partibus & de Toto agit, admodum confuse & sine delectu congerat illa, è quibus nemo fiat doctior.
units.tr: III. Having said above that there are two kinds of composition, from integral parts and from essential parts, we must now work out this matter a little more carefully. This will let each reader more readily distinguish in substances which composition belongs to which kind, and it will also make clear that this composition of accidents is essential, not integral. The Peripatetics do treat this subject, both in their Logic and in their Metaphysics, but so far we have been unable to find anything in any of them that satisfies the mind or agrees properly with the truth. As for Aristotle himself, he is as always like himself: in the two chapters of the fifth book of the Metaphysics, where he treats of parts and of the whole, he heaps together, quite confusedly and without selection, things from which no one becomes any wiser.

units.la: Antequam autem nostram super hac re sententiam exprómamus, volumus prius vulgarem de ea doctrinam breviter examinare. Illa secundum Fonsecam ita se habet. Partes reales aut Essentiales sunt, aut Integrantes. Essentiales vero ac reipsa essentiam componunt, suntq; Materia & Forma. atq; ad hanc divisionem revocantur partes compositi accidentalis: ea enim & figurarum in hisce alia pars Materia, & alia Forma analoga est. Partes integrantes sunt ea, quibus tota aliqua magnitudo aut multitudo extensa est: suntq; aut similares, ejusdem natura ac appellationis cum toto, ut partes carnis, & partes aquæ; aut dissimilares, ut membra corporis humani, partes domus, ordines Reipublicæ. Ad partes integrantes revocantur etiam Potestates sive Vires rerum: quia ut res extensa constat partibus integrantibus, sic res, quæ multa potest (quomodo animus habet intellectum & voluntatem) constat suis viribus potentiisve, quoad totam potestatem.
units.tr: Before we set out our own opinion on this matter, we wish first to examine briefly the common doctrine about it. According to Fonseca it stands as follows: Real parts are either essential or integrating. Essential parts truly compose the essence, and they are matter and form; and to this division are referred the parts of an accidental compound, for among these too one part is analogous to matter and another to form, as in figures. Integrating parts are those by which some whole magnitude or multitude is extended; and they are either similar, of the same nature and name as the whole, such as the parts of flesh and the parts of water; or dissimilar, such as the members of the human body, the parts of a house, and the orders of a commonwealth. The powers or faculties of things are also referred to integrating parts, because just as an extended thing consists of integrating parts, so a thing that has many powers (as the mind has understanding and will) consists of its powers or faculties, with respect to its whole capacity.

units.la: Hæc ibi Fonseca, estq; recepta apud omnes Peripateticos hæc partium realium (namq; de Partibus rationis, Genere & Differentia, nihil attinet dicere) divisio: in qua nos id primum culpamus, quod Materiam tantum & Formam, atq; analoga, pro partibus essentialibus habent. namq; etiamsi per Materiam & Formam intelligas non illa duo commenta à nobis explosa, sed Meteriam veram, & Naturam (quæ aliquo modo Formæ respondet) non
units.tr: So far Fonseca, and this division of real parts (for there is no need to say anything about parts of reason, genus and difference) is accepted by all the Peripatetics. In it we first blame this: they take only matter and form, together with the analogous things, as essential parts. For even if by matter and form you understand not those two inventions which we have cast out, but true matter and nature (which in some way corresponds to form), still these alone, and the analogous things, should not be regarded as essential parts,

units.la: {x} pro Ms. facus. Hac Accidentium... non potest saltem capitali. non tamen hæc tantum, & analoga, pro partibus essentialibus habenda sunt, quum multæ dentur partes essentiales, in quibus ista analogia, ut altera se habeat instar Materiæ, altera instar Formæ seu Naturæ, frustra quæratur; sicuti in accidentibus illis compositis paulo ante enumeratis (quorum partes certe sunt essentiales) manifestum est. Sed multo etiam magis in altero membro peccant, non in re tantum, sed & in nomine ipso. Partes enim integrantes cur appellari debeant hæ magis, quam præcedentes, nihil causæ est. Quippe ratio nominis haud alia dari potest, nisi quod integrant rem, sive integritatem rei constituunt. ast hoc faciunt essentiales quoq; partes. Totum enim seu integrum dicitur compositum, quod habet omnes partes sibi debitas, οὗ μηδὲν ἄπωτσι μέρος, cujus nulla pars abest. Omnes igitur cujuscunq; (Totius sive Integri) partes, sunt partes integrantes: quippe integritatem sui compositi unaquæq; per se constituit. Non magis igitur partibus quantitativis (namq; & sic appellare vulgo solent) quam essentialibus competit Integrantium appellatio. Imo sunt inter illas, quæ ne possunt quidem recte ita dici. Quum enim integrum hoc sit, quod habet omnes partes sibi debitas; quomodo integrum hoc dicetur, cui nullæ certæ partes debentur? talia autem sunt omnia Elementa, ac corpora similaria, quæ ex natura sua, definitam magnitudinem non habent, ac proinde neque certas partes sibi vendicant. & tantum quidem de nomine. Quoad vero rem ipsam; per summam imprudentiam partes similares & dissimilares in idem construuntur. dissimilaribus enim partibus injuriam facit, qui eas magnitudinem tantum aut multitudinem Totius, sive Totum quatenus magnum aut multum, constituere dicit: quam tamen constitutionem adeo propriam faciunt partibus integrantibus, ut eam non modo in definitione, aut descriptione, vel solam vel præcipue exprimant, sed eodem respectu eas Quantitativas quoque & Materiales promiscue appellent: plane ut significent, earum, quatenus partes sunt, non
units.tr: {x} the manuscript reads "facus" ... This composition of accidents ... cannot at least be principal. Yet these are not the only essential parts, since there are many essential parts in which that analogy, one part standing as matter and another as form or nature, is sought in vain; as is clear in those composite accidents listed a little above, whose parts are certainly essential. But they err far more in the second member, not only in the thing but in the very name. For there is no reason why these should be called integrating parts rather than the preceding ones. Indeed the reason for the name can be nothing other than that they integrate a thing, or constitute the integrity of a thing; but essential parts do this too. For a whole or entire thing is said to be a compound which has all the parts due to it, οὗ μηδὲν ἄπεστι μέρος [of which no part is absent], of which no part is missing. So all the parts of any whole or entire thing are integrating parts, since each by itself constitutes the integrity of its compound. The name of integrating parts therefore belongs no more to quantitative parts (for so the common people are accustomed to call them) than to essential parts. Indeed among the former there are some that cannot even be properly so called. For since that is whole which has all the parts due to it, how will that be called whole to which no definite parts are due? Yet such are all the elements and similar bodies, which by their nature do not have a fixed magnitude and so do not claim any definite parts for themselves. So much for the name. As for the thing itself, through great imprudence, similar and dissimilar parts are lumped together. For he does an injustice to dissimilar parts who says that they constitute only the magnitude or multitude of the whole, or the whole as large or many; yet they make this constitution so peculiar to integrating parts that they not only express it alone, or chiefly, in their definition or description, but also, in the same respect, call them quantitative and material without distinction. Plainly they mean that the function of these parts, insofar as they are parts, is nothing other than to integrate or fill out the mere bulk and quantity of matter, and to make it larger or smaller by their presence or absence.

units.la: Physi. 7. Metaph. 26. non aliud esse officium, quàm solam materiæ molem atq; quantitatem integrare seu explere, eamq; majorem duntaxat aut minorem sua præsentia aut absentia facere : id quod verum in similaribus ( quibus propterea Quantitativarum nomen, quanquam, ut alia multa in Philosophia, horridum & barbarum, optime quadrare existimamus ) in dissimilaribus plenum esse dicimus summæ absurditatis. Quanta enim stupiditas est, profiteri quod caput aut cor solam corporis quantitatem vel molem constituant? imò quæ imprudentia de quibuscunq; organis, etiam queis corpus carere sine pernicie possit, qualia sunt manus & pedes, hoc ipsum affirmare? certe qui non videt vel hasce partes, vel illas, longe alium ac nobiliorem præstare usum, quam ut ijs præsentibus corpus duntaxat majus, ablatisq; minus fiat, is neq; lucem videat in meridie.
units.tr: Physics 7; Metaphysics 26. This is true of similar parts (for which we think the name of quantitative parts, though it is, like many other terms in philosophy, harsh and barbarous, fits very well), but to say it of dissimilar parts we declare to be utterly absurd. For how great is the stupidity of professing that the head or heart constitutes only the quantity or bulk of the body? Or how great the imprudence of affirming this of any organs, even those the body could lack without harm, such as the hands and feet? Certainly whoever does not see that these parts, or those, perform a far different and nobler function than merely making the body larger when they are present and smaller when they are removed, could not see light at noon.
IV.

units.la: Nullo igitur modo tolerari potest hæc consuetudo, qua partes omnes, essentiam rei non constituentes, uno communi Integrantium, Quantitativarum, & Materialium nomine comprehenduntur. posteriores enim duæ appellationes nullo modo partibus dissimilaribus competunt; ac proinde ne prima quidem, si eodem cum illis sensu ( ut vulgo omnes faciunt ) sumatur. Si vero ipsam hujus vocis vim spectes, quæcunq; alicujus integri aut totius partes istuc nomen merentur, ac proinde non hisce magis quam Essentialibus competit, sicuti modo declaravimus. Potest quidem & alia hujus nominis ratio afferri, ut nimirum illæ peculiariter dicantur partes integrantes, quæ constituunt tale totum sive integrum, quod potest esse non integrum, hoc est, in quod cadit mutilatio. Quædam enim sunt ejusmodi, ut nisi tota sint, ne possint quidem esse omnino; quomodo animal quodcunq;, si vel corpus tollas, vel animam, statim pereat necesse est. alia vero ita se habent, ut violationem integritatis suæ sustineant, & ablata quoq; aliqua parte, maneant tamen; quomodo corpus, ablata manu aut pede, mutilum quidem fit, sed corporis tamen appellationem atq; naturam retinet. Quanquam igitur quavis cujuscunq;
units.tr: Therefore this usage cannot be tolerated in any way, by which all parts that do not constitute the essence of a thing are comprehended under one common name of integral, quantitative, and material parts. For the latter two appellations apply in no way to dissimilar parts, and so not even the first, if it is taken in the same sense as the others, as everyone commonly does. But if you consider the force of the word itself, whatever parts of some whole or integral deserve that name, and so it applies no more to these than to essential parts, as we have just shown. Another reason for the name can indeed be given, namely that those are peculiarly called integral parts which constitute such a whole or integral as can be not-whole, that is, which admit of mutilation. For some parts are of such a kind that, unless they are entire, they cannot exist at all; thus any animal whatever must straightway perish if you take away either its body or its soul. Others, however, are such that they sustain a violation of their integrity and remain even when some part has been removed; thus a body, with a hand or foot cut off, becomes indeed mutilated, but still keeps the name and nature of body. Although, therefore, any parts of any whole or integral...

units.la: * quovis pacto nullo modo separari. juscunq; Totius aut Integri partes, sunt integrantes, spectato primario hujus vocis usu; non negamus tamen, quin suo quodam jure, & hac contemplatione, quam nunc diximus, peculiariter Integrantium nomine donari possint illae partes, quae constituunt totum aliquod mutilationis capax; non tamen omnes, sed illae duntaxat, quibus ablatis res integritatem suam ita amittit, ut ipsa non intereat. Namq; in tali quoq; composito partes Principales (ut caput, thorax, venter) non alia ratione Integrantes appellari debent aut possunt, quam qua animae duę, & corpus, sunt partes integrantes hominis. Quamobrem ne hoc quidem modo sumptum istud vocabulum, rectè omnibus illis partibus, quę essentiam non constituunt, attribuunt; quum neq; similaribus competat (Elementa enim, aliaq; similaria non mutilari, planum est, & Aristoteles fatetur, sicuti mox videbimus). neq; dissimilaribus cunctis, sed ijs duntaxat, quae sint minus principales.
units.tr: in no way separable in any manner, are integral parts when the primary use of this word is considered. We do not deny, however, that by their own right, and in the light of the consideration we have just stated, those parts which constitute some whole capable of mutilation may be peculiarly given the name of integral parts; yet not all of them, but only those with whose removal the thing loses its integrity in such a way that it does not itself perish. For in such a composite too, the principal parts (such as head, chest, and belly) ought not, or cannot, be called integral in any other way than that in which the two souls and the body are integral parts of man. Wherefore not even in this sense is the word rightly attributed to all those parts which do not constitute the essence: it applies neither to similar parts (for it is plain that elements and other similar parts are not mutilated, as Aristotle admits, as we shall soon see), nor to all dissimilar parts, but only to those which are less principal.
V.

units.la: Porrò longè alium, quam reliqui Peripatetici, huic voci usum assignat Petrus Molinæus, qui & alias in instituenda partium divisione aliquid peculiare videtur habere. Totum enim aliud dividi dicit in partes materiales, aliud in formales. Partes formales intelligit eas, quæ alijs sunt partes Metaphysicæ, seu Logicæ (quas nos, utpote non reales partes, sed rationis, à nostra consideratione rejecimus) ut apparet ex exemplo quod affert. Animal enim & rationale dicit esse partes formales seu essentiales hominis: ubi essentiales non ita dicit, quomodo alij; quippe qui vere essentiales hominis partes, animam & corpus, in censu materialium partium collocet & tamen partes artificialia constituentes, quas ad Essentiales illi revocant, ipse hisce Essentialibus sive formalibus à se dictis annumerat. addens enim secundum exemplum, ait Materiam ac structuram esse partes formales domus. Partes reliquas omnes appellat Materiales, easq; definit, Quæ situ differunt, & in quas totum dividitur actu. deinde adhibet vulgatam distinctionem, qua partes materiales aliæ sint homogeneæ, aliæ heterogeneæ.
units.tr: Moreover, Petrus Molinaeus assigns to this word a use quite different from that of the other Peripatetics, and in drawing up his division of parts he seems to have something peculiar of his own. For he says that one whole is divided into material parts and another into formal parts. By formal parts he means those which are, for others, parts of metaphysics or logic (which we, as not real parts but parts of reason, have rejected from our consideration), as appears from the example he gives. For he says that animal and rational are the formal or essential parts of a human being; where he does not use essential in the way others do. For while he places the true essential parts of a human being, soul and body, among the material parts, yet he counts among his essential or formal parts, as he has called them, those parts which others refer to the essential ones and which constitute artificial things. For in giving a second example he says that matter and structure are the formal parts of a house. All the remaining parts he calls material, and he defines them as those which differ in position, and into which the whole is actually divided. Then he applies the common distinction, by which some material parts are homogeneous and others heterogeneous.
Log. I. 2. cap. 9.
Cap. II.

units.la: nex. Heterogeneas autem distinguit in Integrantes seu proximas, & in non Integrantes seu remotas: ita ut integrantes sint, in quas totum proximè dividitur, ut animal in corpus & animam, civitas Romana in plebem, equites, patricios; non integrantes, ut civitatis partes minutiores sunt tribus, curia, familia. In qua divisione non parva reprehensione dignum est, quod cum Materiam ac Formam Aristotelicam ipse receperit, ut quisquam alius (quod vel ex ista Logica certissimo constat) non expresserit ad utram classem, formaliumne an materialium partium, illas referendas censuerit. ambigendi enim occasio est, quod artificialia (in quibus subjectum se habere instar Materiæ, figuram instar Formæ, reliqui Peripatetici profitentur, & cum ijs ipse quoq;, sicuti ex hujus libri capite decimo apparet) cum formalibus numerat, animam vero & corpus (quorum alterum esse Materiam, alterum Formam, omnes similiter dicunt) cum materialibus; quod sane nullo modo est ferendum, ut anima & corpus pro materialibus hominis partibus habeantur.
units.tr: nex. He divides heterogeneous parts into integrating, or proximate, parts and non-integrating, or remote, parts. Integrating parts are those into which a whole is divided immediately, as an animal is divided into body and soul, or the Roman state into the plebs, the knights and the patricians. Non-integrating parts are smaller parts of a state, such as the tribe, the curia and the family. In this division there is no small fault to find: although he has adopted the Aristotelian matter and form, he has not stated, as no one else has (and this is clear even from this Logic), to which class he thinks they belong, the formal parts or the material parts. There is room for doubt, because he counts artificial things among the formal parts, though the other Peripatetics declare that in them the subject stands in the place of matter and the shape in the place of form, and he himself agrees with them, as appears from the tenth chapter of this book. Yet he counts soul and body among the material parts, though all say alike that one of them is matter and the other form. This certainly cannot be tolerated, that soul and body should be held to be material parts of man.

units.la: etiamsi enim altera conditio in definitione posita, ijs competat, posse actu dividi (namq; alteram conditionem, etiamsi non minus veram, ipse non admiserit, qui cum majori Peripateticorum parte opinetur animam esse totam in toto) hoc non sufficit, ad hanc ipsis appellationem conciliandam, quum alias habeant ac nobiliores conditiones sub ea ratione, qua partes sunt, nimirum ipsam hominis essentiam constituendi. Recta autem ratio non patitur, ut nobilioribus rei conditionibus insuper habitis, à viliori aliqua nomen ijs imponatur. atq; ob eandem causam æque peccat ipse, Partes dissimilares materialibus accensendo (quanquam & situ differant, & actu dividi possint) quam illi, qui ijs hoc nominis dant, quatenus Materiæ molem integrant. Porrò quod solis proximis cujusq; rei partibus attribuit Integrantium appellationem; ne hoc quidem rationem habet, non magis quam si solas partes proximas vellet partium nomine donare. Agnoscimus quidem, rem aliquam posse dici quodammodo integram, etiamsi aliqua partium remotarum ei desit, ut si homo manu careat. quippe, ut antea diximus, integrum id est, quod habet omnes partes sibi debitas, ac propterea homo est integer, qui habet animam & corpus, sive illud integrum sit, sive mutilum. proprie tamen & absolute illa res integra non est; cujus aliqua pars est mutila, ut in prædicto exemplo patet. mutilus enim est homo, cui manus abest: sicuti mutila est manus, quæ articulum alicujus digiti amisit, quanquam articulus non sit proxima manus pars, sed ipsius digiti. itaq; etiam articulus est pars manum integrans, & manus est pars hominem integrans: sed sicuti hoc respectu partes sunt remotæ (proxime enim articulus est pars digiti, & manus est pars corporis) ita non nisi remote hæc hominem, & illE manum integrat. Eodem igitur jure, quo partes aliæ dicuntur proximæ, aliæ remotæ, etiam aliæ proxime integrantes, aliæ remote integrantes dicantur. hoc tamen recte Molinæus, quod hoc quoq; partium discrimen (alijs fere neglectum) quo aliæ sint propinquæ, aliæ remotæ, attigit. est enim hoc discrimen omnino necessarium, atq; non parvi momenti, quippe quod non observatum, magnæ confusionis causa esse potest, qua de re mox plura dicturi sumus.
units.tr: For even if the other condition in the definition, that of being able to be actually divided, applies to them (since he does not admit that other condition, which is no less true, he who with the greater part of the Peripatetics holds that the soul is wholly in the whole), this is not enough to earn them this name, since they have other and nobler conditions under the aspect in which they are parts, namely that of constituting the very essence of man. Right reason does not allow that a name taken from some baser condition should be imposed on a thing while its nobler conditions are disregarded. For the same reason he errs as much in counting dissimilar parts among the material parts (although they differ in position and can be actually divided) as those do who give them this name insofar as they make up the bulk of matter. Furthermore, his assigning the name of integrating parts only to the proximate parts of each thing has no more reason behind it than if he wished to give the name of parts only to the proximate parts. We grant indeed that a thing may be called in some sense whole even if some of its remote parts are lacking to it, as when a man lacks a hand. For, as we said before, that is whole which has all the parts due to it, and therefore a man is whole who has soul and body, whether he is maimed or not. Properly and absolutely, however, that thing is not whole of which some part is maimed, as is clear in the example given. For a man who lacks a hand is maimed, just as a hand that has lost the joint of a finger is maimed, although the joint is not a proximate part of the hand but of the finger. So the joint is indeed a part integrating the hand, and the hand is a part integrating the man; but just as in this respect they are remote parts (for the joint is immediately a part of the finger, and the hand is immediately a part of the body), so these integrate the man and that the hand only remotely. By the same right, then, by which some parts are called proximate and others remote, some may also be called proximately integrating and others remotely integrating. Molina, however, rightly touched on this distinction of parts (which others have mostly neglected), by which some are near and others far. For this distinction is wholly necessary and of no small importance, since if it is not observed it can be a cause of great confusion, a matter on which we are about to say more shortly.

units.la: VI. Porro quam ridicula sit illa à Peripateticis allata distinctio partium in Essentiales & Integrales, præterquam quod ex supradictis abunde liquet, inde quoq; discas, quod nequeunt se in assignando inter utrasq; discrimine probabiliter saltem expedire. Docebimus hoc ex Toleto, qui cum dixisset partes integrantes valde differre à partibus substantiæ rei, tres hasce differentias ponit: 1. Quod partes integrantes sæpe sint similares; partes autem substantiæ semper dissimilares. 2. Quod pars integralis non habet eundem adæquate locum cum altera, nec pars est in loco totius: sicuti ulnæ una medietas, adæquate non est ubi altera, nec est in toto loco ubi totum: cum circa partes substantiæ contra se res habeat. in quo enim loco adæquate est Materia, ibi esse Formam, & in toto loco, in quo compositum est, ibi & Materiam & Formam esse. 3. Quod partes integrantes possint separatim consistere, ut duæ ligni partes: 6 Phys. quæst. 1.
units.tr: VI. Furthermore, how ridiculous is that distinction of parts into essential and integral, brought forward by the Peripatetics, is clear enough from what has been said above; one may also learn it from this, that they cannot, in assigning a distinction between the two, extricate themselves even probably. We shall show this from Toletus, who, after saying that integrating parts differ greatly from the parts of a thing's substance, sets down three differences: (1) integrating parts are often similar, whereas parts of substance are always dissimilar; (2) an integral part does not occupy exactly the same place as another, nor is a part in the place of the whole, as one half of a cubit is not exactly where the other half is, nor is it in the whole place where the whole is; but with the parts of substance the case is otherwise, for where matter is exactly located, there form is too, and in the whole place in which the compound is, both matter and form are there; (3) integrating parts can exist separately, as two parts of wood. 6 Phys. quæst. 1.
Chapter II.

units.la: partes: ast neq; Formam neq; Materiam per se esse posse. Hæ sunt differentiæ à Toleto assignatæ, quæ quam sint probæ, nunc ostendemus. Prima sane non est melior, quam siquis hominem à brutis discriminaret eo, quod ipse sit bipes. sicuti enim hæc differentia esset vitiosa, quia non generalis (nam & bruta multa, ut aves, sunt bipedia) ita hæc quoque. namq; & integrantium partium multæ sunt dissimilares, quod & ipse agnoscere cogitur. ait enim, hoc in viventibus locum non habere, neq; quamlibet hominis partem esse hominem, sicuti quælibet aquæ pars est aqua. Secunda differentia neq; ipsa procedit, & vel solum ab anima ac corpore exemplum illam destruat. neq; enim verum est, quod in eodem adæquate loco, ubi est corpus, sit anima, cum animæ locus sit ipsum corpus, aut saltem in corpore. quam quidem assertionem scimus magnas pati difficultates, ac plerosq; omnis ævi non philosophos modo, sed & Theologos, in contrarium ire, ac fidenter asseverare, quod anima sit tota in toto. sed eos plurimum errare, ac Aristotelico commento de Forma substantiali (cui hoc itidem tribuunt multi Peripatetici, & cujus speciem faciunt animam) aliisq; ratiunculis parum solidis à vero abreptos fuisse, suo loco demonstrabimus. Quantum vero ad posteriorem hujus secundæ differentiæ partem; falsum est, partes integrales simul sumtas non esse in eodem loco, in quo totum est: quippe cum totum nihil sit aliud (sicuti ipse contra eos, qui id negant, defendit Toletus) quam omnes partes simul sumtæ. si vero istorum verborum mens est, integrantium partium quamcunq; non esse in eodem loco, in quo totum est; ne in essentialibus quidem hoc perpetuum est; sicuti ex ijs, quæ modo de anima & corpore dicebamus, apparet. & eorundem exemplo tertia quoq; differentia evertitur. namq; & Mens, & corpus, quæ partes sunt essentiales, possunt separatim consistere, ac re vera consistunt, ubi per mortem distrahuntur. nam quod ad illos attinet, qui corpus mortui non esse corpus asserunt, nisi homonymice, eos planissime delirare, supra satis ostendimus.
units.tr: Neither the Form nor the Matter can exist by itself. These are the differences Toletus assigned, and we will now show how sound they are. The first is no better than if someone distinguished man from the brutes by saying that he is two-footed. Just as that difference would be faulty because it is not general (for many brutes, such as birds, are also two-footed), so is this one. For many integral parts are also dissimilar, which Toletus himself is forced to acknowledge. He says that this does not apply to living things, and that no part of a man is a man, as every part of water is water. The second difference does not hold either, and its own example, taken from soul and body, destroys it. For it is not true that the soul is in the same place as the body, adequately, since the place of the soul is the body itself, or at least is in the body. We know that this assertion faces great difficulties, and that most philosophers of every age, and not only philosophers but theologians too, take the opposite view and confidently assert that the soul is wholly in the whole body. But we will show in its place that they err greatly, and that they have been carried away from the truth by the Aristotelian fiction of substantial form (to which many Peripatetics also attribute this, and of which they make the soul a species) and by other rather unsound little arguments. As for the latter part of this second difference: it is false that integral parts taken together are not in the same place in which the whole is, since the whole is nothing other than all its parts taken together (as Toletus himself defends against those who deny it). But if the meaning of these words is that any integral parts whatever are not in the place where the whole is, then this is not constant even in essential parts, as is clear from what we were just saying about soul and body. By the same example the third difference is also overturned. For both mind and body, which are essential parts, can exist separately, and in fact do so when they are parted by death. As for those who assert that a dead body is not a body except homonymously, we have already shown sufficiently above that they rave quite plainly.
× Equivocally

units.la: VII. Differentiae igitur inter partes Essentiales & Integrantes à Toleto assignatae stare non possunt, quum aut non verae sint, aut non universales. Nihilo autem firmius aut melius est discrimen à Zabarella constitutum, qui ita hanc rem expedire conatus est, ut asseveret, hoc esse inter partes essentiales & quantitativas discrimen, quod partes quantitativae sint ejusdem ordinis & naturae, nec una dicatur esse magis actu quam alia, vel magis potestate quam alia, ut in homine pes & manus. At partes essentiales habere inter se ordinem perfectibilis, & perficientis, & unam ad aliam dirigi; ut Materiam ad Formam, ut potentiam ad actum, & perfectibile ad persectionem, & contentum ad continens. nolumus hic carpere sermonem admodum imprudentem, quod partes omnes dissimilaris quoq; corporis dicat esse ejusdem inter se ordinis & naturae: quae verba, si quis ea accipiat ita uti sonant, plena sunt falsitatis; ac contenti sumus ea sic intelligere, quomodo ipse ea interpretatur, quod una non sit magis actu quam alia, quodq; inter se non habeant ordinem perfectibilis & perficientis. Quod verum sit nec nenos mox dispiciemus: Peripateticis omnibus non probari, certi sumus. Plane enim contrarium asserit Suarez asserens, In omni compositione esse aliquid, quod sit fundamentum & inchoatio rei, & aliquid quod sit terminus & consummatio rei; & ideo aliquid semper considerari ut Materiam, & aliquid ut Formam rei. quod adeo verum sit, ut etiam in compositione e partibus integrantibus, quae maxime materialis esse videatur, semper una pars consideretur ut Materia, & altera ut Forma: idq; clarius apparere in rebus heterogeneis. sic enim in homine caput esse velut Formam aliarum partium, & in artificialibus tectum esse velut Formam edificii. & addit quoq; rationem, cur sic esse debeat, Quia nimirum compositio e Materia & Forma sit prima compositio realis, & maxime propria ac per se. Ideo per quandam analogiam ad illam compositionem, debere omnem aliam compositionem declarari, quia Materia sit quiddam informe, & imperfectum, & inchoatio quaedam & super-
units.tr: VII. The differences between essential and integral parts assigned by Toletus therefore cannot stand, since they are either not true or not universal. But the distinction set up by Zabarella is no firmer or better. He tried to settle the matter by asserting that this is the distinction between essential and quantitative parts: quantitative parts are of the same order and nature, and one is not said to be more actual than another, or more potential than another, as in a man the foot and the hand. But essential parts have among themselves the order of the perfectible and the perfecting, and are directed one to another: as matter to form, as potency to act, the perfectible to perfection, and the contained to the container. We do not wish to pick apart here an expression that is quite ill-considered, namely that he says all the parts even of a dissimilar body are of the same order and nature among themselves. If anyone takes these words as they sound, they are full of falsity; we are content to understand them as he himself interprets them, that one part is not more actual than another, and that they do not have among themselves the order of perfectible and perfecting. Whether this is true we shall soon examine; we are certain it is not approved by all the Peripatetics. Suárez plainly asserts the contrary, saying: In every composition there is something which is the foundation and beginning of the thing, and something which is the term and consummation of the thing; and so something is always considered as matter, and something as form of the thing. This is so true that even in a composition of integral parts, which seems most material, one part is always considered as matter and another as form; and this appears more clearly in heterogeneous things. For in man the head is, as it were, the form of the other parts, and in artificial things the roof is, as it were, the form of the building. He also adds the reason why it must be so: Because the composition of matter and form is the first real composition, and the most proper and per se. Therefore, by a certain analogy, every other composition ought to be explained in terms of that one, since matter is something formless and imperfect, a kind of beginning and super-
Chapter II.

units.la: imperfectio naturæ; Forma vero sit quasi pulchritudo, & perfectio, ac consummatio naturæ. Hæc cum ex diametro repugnent ijs, quæ de Partibus Integrantibus seu Quantitativis tradit Zabarella; palam est, si vera sint, differentiam ab ipso constitutam funditus convelli.
units.tr: imperfection of nature. The form, however, is as it were the beauty, perfection and completion of nature. Since these ideas flatly contradict what Zabarella teaches about integral or quantitative parts, it is plain that, if they were true, the distinction he establishes would be utterly overthrown.

units.la: VIII. Pro veris tamen illa ne nos quidem habemus, neq; nobis persuaderi patimur, in omni composito inveniri aliquid, quod se habeat instar Materiæ, & aliquid quod instar Formæ. Reclamant enim & composita Accidentalia, sive Accidentia composita, in quorum plerisq; nihil tale cernere est; & manifestius etiam composita similaria, quorum omnes partes cum sint omni ex parte exactissime inter se similes, ne imaginari quidem in illis licet hanc differentiam, quod aliæ se habeant instar materiæ, & aliæ instar formæ. Est hoc ita apertum, ut non potuerit id non videre Suarez, qui tamen propositum non mutat ob hanc difficultatem, sed solvere eam aggreditur, idq; eo modo, ut & hic putet imaginem ejus, quam dixerat, diversæ habitudinis reperiri, sed longe alio modo quam in heterogeneis. non enim, ut istic, partem aliquam principalem vult obtinere formæ vicem, sed sed ipsum Totum. In rebus Homogeneis (inquit) ubi inter partes non potest distingui illa diversa habitudo, propter earum similitudinem & uniformitatem omnes partes dicuntur esse materia totius, compositum autem comparari ut forma ad singulas partes. Hæc ubi legimus, vix est ut risum teneamus: & tamen communis est hæc inter Peripateticos sententia, quod Totum se habeat instar formæ, nisi quod non de Homogeneis tantum compositis hoc dicunt, sed & de omnibus in universum. Ita enim Thomas, & ex eo Toletus, Totum habet rationem formæ, respectu partium, partes vero rationem materiæ. Zabarella hoc ipso in loco, e quo illa paulo ante posita depromebamus, Ultima perfectio, quæ alias omnes complet, dicitur alias omnes continere, & tenere locum totius: reliquæ autem essentiales partes ab ea continentur, ab ea sumunt nomen, & esse, & definitionem, & sunt loco materia & partis, respectu illius
units.tr: VIII. We, however, do not accept these doctrines as true, nor do we allow ourselves to be persuaded that in every composite there is found something that stands in the place of matter and something that stands in the place of form. For accidental composites, or composite accidents, object, and in most of them one can discern nothing of the kind. And even more plainly the similar composites, whose parts are in every respect most exactly like one another, do not allow us even to imagine this distinction, that some parts stand in the place of matter and others in the place of form. This is so obvious that Suarez could not have failed to see it. Yet he does not change his position because of this difficulty, but undertakes to resolve it, in such a way that he too thinks that an image of the diverse relation he had described is found here, but in a very different manner from that found in heterogeneous things. For he does not wish, as there, some principal part to take the role of form, but the whole itself. In homogeneous things (he says), where that diverse relation cannot be distinguished among the parts, because of their likeness and uniformity, all the parts are said to be the matter of the whole, while the composite is compared to each part as form. When we read this, we can scarcely keep from laughing. Yet this opinion is common among the Peripatetics, that the whole stands in the place of form, except that they do not say this only of homogeneous composites but of all composites in general. Thus Thomas, and after him Toletus: The whole has the character of form with respect to the parts, while the parts have the character of matter. Zabarella, in the very passage from which we drew the statement quoted a little earlier: The ultimate perfection, which completes all the others, is said to contain all of them and to hold the place of the whole; the remaining essential parts are contained by it, take from it their name, their being and their definition, and are in the place of matter and of part with respect to it

units.la: 3. Phys. ad text. 77. illius, quia illa sola simpliciter locum tenet formæ; forma autem est totum, materia verò pars. Et Averroes 7. Metaph. comm. 35. Respectum partium ad totum, esse respectum materiæ ad formam: respectum vero totius ad partes, esse respectum formæ ad Materiam: qualia & alibi iterat. Habent autem ducem hujus sententiæ ipsum Aristotelem, qui ut partes, Materialis, ita Totum & compositionem Formalis causæ rationem obtinere scribit. Τούτων δὲ τὰ μὲν ὡς ὑπομενόμενον, οἷον τὰ μέρη. τὰ δὲ ὡς τὶ ἦν εἶν, ὡς τε ὅλον, καὶ ἡ σύνθεσις, καὶ τὸ εἶδος. Horum verò quædam se habet instar subjecti, uti partes: alia verò instar essentiæ, ut totum, & compositio, & forma. ad quæ verba ita Conimbricenses, Tria refert ad genus causæ formalis, nimirum totum, compositionem, & formam. Mirificè autem (etsi non præter morem suum) Totum & Compositionem seperatim tanquam duas diversas res recensèt, quum haud dubie eandem rem sub utroq; vocabulo intellexerit. Nam quod ijdem Conimbricenses ex Alensi asserunt, eum vocare Totum, id quod coalescit ex partibus, ordine duntaxat quodam inter se junctis, ut exercitus; compositionem verò id, quod componitur ex partibus, non solum ordinem aliquem habentibus, sed in unam aliquam formam coeuntibus, ut domus: frivolum est, neq; ullum vel à ratione, vel ab ipsius Aristotelis consuetudine prætextum habet. Porrò quod hic dicitur, Partes se habere instar Materiæ, (unde alterum illud, Quod Totum sit ut forma, sequitur) attingit etiam in principio primi de Gener. Anim. ἡ ὕλη τῆς ζῴοις τὰ μέρη, παντὶ μὲν ὅλῳ τὰ ἀνομοιομερῆ. Partes sunt materia animalibus, omni quidem Toti dissimilares, &c. Ex quibus satis apparet, & receptam esse inter Aristotelicos, & ab ipso Aristotele fluxisse hanc sententiam, quod Totum, respectu suarum partium, sit instar Formæ. Quanquam autem & ipse, & illorum plerique; indefinite atq; generaliter loquantur, sunt tamen & alij, qui hoc non quidem ad solum totum Homogeneum cum Suarezio, attamen ad Totum Integrale ipsis dictum duntaxat revocent; de quorum numero est Archangelus Mercenarius, ita hac de re scribens: Per
units.tr: 3. Phys. ad text. 77. with respect to it, because it alone holds the place of form in the strict sense; the form, however, is the whole, and the matter is the part. And Averroes, 7 Metaph. comm. 35: The relation of the parts to the whole is a relation of matter to form; the relation of the whole to the parts is a relation of form to matter; which he also repeats elsewhere. The leader of this opinion is Aristotle himself, who writes that the parts have the character of the material cause, and the whole and the composition that of the formal cause. [Τούτων δὲ τὰ μὲν ὡς ὑπομενόμενον, οἷον τὰ μέρη. τὰ δὲ ὡς τὶ ἦν εἶναι, ὡς τὸ ὅλον, καὶ ἡ σύνθεσις, καὶ τὸ εἶδος.] Of these, some stand as the underlying subject, such as the parts; others as the essence, such as the whole, the composition and the form. To these words the Conimbricenses say: He refers three things to the genus of formal cause, namely the whole, the composition and the form. Remarkably, though not contrary to his usual custom, he lists the whole and the composition separately, as two different things, when he undoubtedly understood the same thing under either word. For what the same Conimbricenses report from Alensis, that he calls the whole that which coheres out of parts joined merely in some order among themselves, as an army; and the composition that which is composed of parts not only having some order but coming together into one form, as a house: this is trifling, and has no pretext either in reason or in Aristotle's own usage. Moreover, what is said here, that the parts stand as matter (from which the other statement, that the whole is as form, follows), is also touched on at the beginning of the first book On the Generation of Animals: [ἡ ὕλη τῆς ζῴοις τὰ μέρη, παντὶ μὲν ὅλῳ τὰ ἀνομοιομερῆ.] The parts are the matter of animals, the non-homogeneous parts being dissimilar to every whole, etc. From these passages it sufficiently appears that this opinion, that the whole stands in the place of form with respect to its parts, is both accepted among the Aristotelians and has flowed from Aristotle himself. Although he and most of them speak indefinitely and generally, there are nevertheless others who, with Suarez, restrict this not to the homogeneous whole alone but to the integral whole as they call it; among their number is Archangelus Mercenarius, who writes on this matter as follows: By

units.la: Per totum, intellexit totum integrale. Nam sicuti partes integrantes, ut caput, manus, & brachia, respectu totius, materiæ rationem habent, ita totum integrale, cum sit absolutio & consummatio quædam partium, Formæ rationem habet. Certum est autem, quod hujusmodi comparatio non fit inter totum essentiale, & partes essentiales, utpote Materiam & Formam; quoniam Forma, ratione totius compositi, rationem non habet Materiæ & subjecti, à quo.
units.tr: "Whole" means the integral whole. For just as integral parts, such as the head, hands and arms, stand to the whole in the relation of matter, so the integral whole, since it is a certain completion and perfection of its parts, has the relation of form. It is certain, however, that this kind of comparison does not hold between an essential whole and its essential parts, such as matter and form, since form, in relation to the composite whole, does not have the relation of matter and of that which is subject to it.

units.la: IX. Non satis igitur super hac re inter ipsos convenit, quum alij de quovis Toto dicant, alij de Integrali tantum, nonnulli de solo Homogeneo, quod se habeat tanquam Forma. Sed absurdam esse quamcunq; istarum opinionum, ac proinde omnes quoq; simul, in proclivi est ostendere. Si enim partes cujusvis Totius se habent ut Materia, & Totum ipsum ut Forma sequitur Totum ipsum non esse Totum, sed partem alterius Totius, quod nimirum ex illa compositione Partium ac Totius constituatur. Materia enim & Forma, in ipsorum schola, inter se junctæ, efficiunt compositum, quod nec Materia sit, nec Forma, sed tertium quid, ex illis inter se unitis consurgens. Necesse igitur est, ut in alijs quoq; rebus, ubi aliud est instar Materiæ, aliud instar Formæ, eodem modo se res habeat, atq; ex iis duobus invicem adunatis constituatur tertium quid, ab utroq; separatim sumpto diversum: ac proinde Totum non erit Totum, sed alterius Totius pars, quomodo Forma non est nisi pars Totius, quod cum sua Materia constituit. id quod si est absurdissimum, pro absurdo quoq; repudiandum est hoc dogma, quod Partes se habeant ad Totum, ut Materia; & Totum ad partes, ut Forma. Hoc enim posito, illud quoq; ponatur necesse est. Et sic apparet, veritati parum consentaneum esse illud Suarezij, quod in omni compositione sit aliquid quasi materiale, & aliquid quasi formale: quum in Compositis similaribus, ubi omnium partium eadem est ratio, nihil tale ostendi possit: perfugium autem illud, Quod omnes simul partes sint instar Materiæ, & Compositum instar Formæ; per ea, quæ nunc diximus, interclusum sit.
units.tr: IX. Therefore the parties do not sufficiently agree among themselves on this matter: some say that anything whatever is a whole, others only an integral whole, and some only a homogeneous whole, which stands as form. But it is easy to show that each of these opinions is absurd, and therefore all of them taken together are absurd. For if the parts of any whole stand as matter, and the whole itself as form, it follows that the whole is not a whole but a part of another whole, which is evidently constituted by that composition of parts and whole. For in their own school, matter and form, joined together, make a composite which is neither matter nor form but a third thing arising from their union. It is necessary, therefore, that in other things too, where one thing is like matter and another like form, the thing should be related in the same way, and that from these two things united together a third thing should be constituted, different from each taken separately. And so the whole will not be a whole but a part of another whole, just as form is only a part of the whole which it constitutes together with its matter. If this is most absurd, then this dogma, that the parts stand to the whole as matter, and the whole to the parts as form, must also be rejected as absurd. For once this is posited, that too must necessarily be posited. And so it appears that the saying of Suarez, that in every composition there is something material and something formal, agrees little with the truth: since in similar composites, where all the parts have the same character, nothing of that kind can be shown. And the refuge of saying that all the parts together are like matter and the composite like form is cut off by what we have just said.

units.la: X. Concedimus itaq; Zabarellæ id quod supponit, Partium Quantitativarum unam non esse magis actu quam aliam, neq; unam ab altera perfici.
units.tr: X. We therefore grant to Zabarella what he supposes: that of quantitative parts, one is not more actual than another, nor is one perfected by another.

units.la: Inde tamen non sequitur, bonam esse quam assignat inter partes Essentiales & Quantitativas differentiam. Nam quod ille ait, in partibus Essentialibus rem contrario modo se habere, id vero nos negamus, asserimusq;, nec illarum unam esse magis actu quam alteram, neq; unam ab alia perfici. Quantum ad prius; partes in potentia non possunt compositum sive totum in actu constituere. Si itaq; compositum quodcunq; in actu futurum est, omnes quoq; ipsius partes proximæ in actu sint necesse est. & hoc nemo ipsorum Peripateticorum negaverit; qui etiamsi soleant dicere, quod partes sint entia in potentia, id non aliter intelligunt, nisi quod non sunt entia per se subsistentia. de solis partibus continui Homogenei lis est, quas aliqui dicunt non esse actu partes, quamdiu sunt in Toto, sed ratione duntaxat, aut designatione. Sed alij has quoq; esse actu partes affirmant, in quibus est Fonseca. Partes integrantes, inquit, totius Homogenei, & si ante consideration em aut designationem actualem non sunt actu distinctæ, ut entia quædam, sunt tamen distinctæ, ut partes ejusdem entis. Cujuscunq; igitur Compositi partes, ac proinde etiam essentialis, sunt actu: & si omnes sunt actu, non est cur unam magis actu esse dicamus quam aliam.
units.tr: Nevertheless it does not follow that the difference he assigns between essential and quantitative parts is sound. For what he says, that in essential parts the matter is otherwise, we deny; and we assert that neither is one of them more actual than the other, nor is one perfected by another. As to the first point: parts in potency cannot constitute a composite or whole in act. If, then, any composite is to be actual, all its proximate parts must necessarily be actual too. And none of the Peripatetics themselves will deny this; although they are accustomed to say that the parts are beings in potency, they understand this only in the sense that they are not beings subsisting through themselves. The dispute concerns only the parts of a homogeneous continuum, which some say are not actually parts while they are within the whole, but only parts in thought or by designation. But others affirm that these too are actually parts, among them Fonseca: The integral parts of a homogeneous whole, he says, even if before actual consideration or designation they are not actually distinct, as certain beings are, are nonetheless distinct, as parts of the same being. Therefore the parts of any composite, and so also the essential parts, are actual; and if all are actual, there is no reason to say that one is more actual than another.

units.la: Quod si quis pro Zabarella respondeat; Materiam Compositi esse quidem actu, sed habere à Forma quod sit actu; is sciat, ista somnia de Materia prima, quæ per se non sit aliud quam ens in potentia, & per formam substantialem actuetur, nobis, qui utramq;, & Materiam primam, & Formam substantialem (sola anima, quam ipsi quoq; formis accensent, excepta; id quod plus semel monuimus) firmis argumentis evertimus, non posse obtrudi. Et cum alterum illud, quod Materia sit perfectibile, forma autem perficiens, ab eodem fonte manet, eodem quoq; responso diluitur. Forma enim (hoc est, Anima aut Natura: aliam enim nos Formam non agnoscimus) non perficit Materiam, non magis quam Materia perficit Formam, sed utraq; in suo genere perfecta, totum
units.tr: But if anyone, in reply to Zabarella, says that the matter of the composite is indeed actual, but has its actuality from the form, let him know that those dreams about prime matter, which in itself is nothing but a being in potency and is actuated through a substantial form, cannot be imposed on us, who have overthrown with firm arguments both prime matter and substantial form (excepting only the soul, which they too count among the forms; as we have said more than once). And the other claim, that matter is perfectible and form perfecting, remains from the same source and is refuted by the same answer. For form (that is, soul or nature, for we recognize no other form) does not perfect matter, any more than matter perfects form; rather each, perfect in its own kind, together perfects the whole

units.la: Metaph. 6. q. 6. sect. 3. totum simul perficiunt. Concedimus quidem Formam, id est, Animam, & Naturam (hanc tamen non omnium) esse digniorem Compositi partem, quare etiam perfectior dici quodammodo potest (quanquam proprie non potest aliud alio dici perfectius, nisi in ijs, quæ sunt ejusdem speciei) sed inde non sequitur, quod ipsa Materiam perficiat. & si vel maxime sequeretur, nihil tamen hoc prodesset Zabarellæ. sic enim rediret sententia Suarezij; quia eodem jure tunc caput quoq;& cor possent dici perficere reliqua membra, quippe quibus ipsa similiter sunt digniora ac persectior. ipse autem in hoc constituebat partium Integralium atq; Essentialium discrimen, quod harum alia aliam perficeret, illarum vero nequaquam.
units.tr: Metaph. 6. q. 6. sect. 3. the whole. We grant indeed that form, that is soul and nature (though not nature of all things), is the more worthy part of the composite, and so can in a way be called more perfect (although strictly speaking one thing cannot be called more perfect than another except among things of the same species); but it does not follow from this that the form perfects the matter. And even if it did follow, this would not help Zabarella at all. For the opinion of Suarez would then return; since by the same right the head and heart could be said to perfect the other members, because they are similarly more worthy and more perfect than them. But he himself located the distinction between integral and essential parts in this: that one of these perfects another, whereas those in no way do.
XI.

units.la: Quod vero addit Zabarella de Potentiâ & Actu, ne hoc quidem officit quicquam ijs, quæ hactenus diximus. Scimus quidem tritam admodum esse sententiam, quod Potentiæ à suis Actibus perficiantur; sed quæ nobis non probatur: neq; ullo modo admittimus, actum recipi in potentiam, ut cum ea unum compositum constituat. Quantum enim ad potentiam receptivam, seu passivam, in educatione de potentia in actum non ipsa potentia patitur, aut mutatur, sed subjectum illa potentia præditum. non enim, quando aqua calefit, calor introducitur in potentiam illam, quam habet aqua, ut possit calefieri, sed in ipsam per se aquam; sicuti sigilli imago in ipsam proxime ceram imprimitur, non in potentiam illam, cujus ratione habilis est cera ad omnem figuram recipiendam: quòmodo etiam ab Aristotele dictum, ἐνάσχ ἡ ἐντελέχεια ἐν τῷ δυνάμει ὑπάρχοντι καὶ τῇ οὐσίᾳ ὕλῃ πέφυκε γίνεσθαι. ejusdem actus in eo quod est potentia, inq; propriâ Materiâ producì nata est. actum dicit fieri non in ipsa potentia, sed in eo quod est potentiâ. quanquam ibidem pro solita inconstantia & fluctuatione, illa etiam dicit, unde contrarium concludatur. Non posse autem fieri compositum ex tali Potentia, & Actu ipsius, non magis quam ex Ente & nihilo, Suarez quoq; profitetur. Sed neq; potentia Acti-
units.tr: What Zabarella adds about potency and act does not in the least weaken what we have said so far. We know that the saying that potencies are perfected by their acts is quite commonplace, but we do not accept it, and we in no way admit that an act is received into a potency so as to form one compound with it. For as regards a receptive or passive potency, when a thing is brought from potency into act, it is not the potency itself that suffers or is changed, but the subject endowed with that potency. When water is heated, the heat is not introduced into that potency which water has of being heated, but into the water itself. Just as the image of a seal is impressed on the wax itself, not on that potency by which the wax is apt to receive every shape. Aristotle also says this: the actuality is naturally produced in that which is potential and in the underlying matter [ἐνάσχ ἡ ἐντελέχεια ἐν τῷ δυνάμει ὑπάρχοντι καὶ τῇ οὐσίᾳ ὕλῃ πέφυκε γίνεσθαι]. He says the act comes to be not in the potency itself but in that which is potential. Yet in the same place, with his usual inconsistency and wavering, he also says things from which the contrary may be concluded.
