Suárez too professes that a compound cannot be made from such a potency and its act, no more than from being and nothing. But neither is active potency

units.la: * ἡ ντελέχεια, μὴ ποιότης va componitur cum suo actu; quippe cujus actus nihil aliud est quam actio. Actio autem non est nisi accidentalis ac temporarius modus agentis: & talis Modus non facit compositum, cum eo, cujus est modus: de qua re alias dicetur. Et non dari ullam talem compositionem ex potentia & actu, confirmari etiam potest eo argumento, quo omne compositum est aliquid diversum à partibus componentibus per se consideratis, & tertium quid, ex ipsarum unione consurgens. quale autem sit illud tertium, quod è conjunctione potentiae (vel receptivae vel activae) & actus exurgat, ne imaginari quidem licet. Quamobrem ne hic quidem habet quicquam Zabarella, ad differentiam illam inter Partes Essentiales atq; Integrales stabiliendam.
units.tr: * [ἡ ἐντελέχεια, μὴ ποιότης] is compounded with its own act, for its act is nothing other than action. Action, however, is only an accidental and temporary mode of the agent, and such a mode does not make a compound with that of which it is the mode. This matter will be discussed elsewhere. That no such compound arises from potency and act can also be confirmed by the argument that every compound is something different from its component parts considered in themselves, a third thing arising from their union. But what that third thing is which would arise from the conjunction of a potency (whether receptive or active) and an act, we cannot even imagine. Therefore Zabarella has nothing here either to establish that distinction between essential and integral parts.

units.la: Mirum vero est, cur Continens & Contentum hic quoq; afferat, tanquam partes Essentiales, quae inter se habeant ordinem Perfectibilis & Perficientis. nullum enim aliud est Continens & Contentum, de quibus hoc dici possit, praeter Materiam & Formam: de quibus dixit Aristoteles, quod Forma continet Materiam (quanquam potius contra est. namq; & anima continetur à corpore, & natura à subjecto.) Ast illas jam nominatim posuit: ut valde superflua sit (etiamsi verum esset quod Materia à Forma contineatur) haec repetitio. Si vero non eo respexit, manifesto falsa dixit, Continens & Contentum esse partes Essentiales, quarum una perficiatur ab altera. Namq; & quodvis Totum continet suas partes; & non perficit illas, sed potius ab illis perficitur. Totum enim non est perfectum, nisi omnes partes suas habeat: quo respectu dixit Aristoteles, Totum & Perfectum aut idem esse, aut fere idem. Τὸ ὅλον, καὶ τὸ τέλεον, ἢ τὸ αὐτὸ πάμπαν, ἢ σύνεσγυς τῇ φύσει ἐσί. Atq; hinc evertitur quartum exemplum à Zabarella positum; cujus mirifica hic est oratio: quippe cum dixisset, partes essentiales se habere ut perficiens & perfectibile, inter alia exempla partium ita se respicientium ipsum quoque perficiens & perfectibile ponit. Sed eum peccare, qui ea, quae proprie ita se habent, numeret inter partes Essentiales, ex proxime dictis de Toto, quod à partibus suis perficitur, apparet. Et tantum quidem de recepta apud Peripateticos partium in Integrales (quas easdem & Quantitativas & Materiales vocant) ac Essentiales divisione dictum esto. Nunc tempus erit propriam super hoc negotio sententiam declarare.
units.tr: It is indeed strange why he also brings forward the container and the contained here, as essential parts that stand to one another in the relation of perfectible and perfecting. For there is no other pair of container and contained of which this can be said, apart from matter and form. Aristotle said of these that form contains matter (though it is rather the reverse, for the soul is contained by the body and the nature by the subject). But he had already named these two explicitly, so that this repetition is very superfluous, even if it were true that matter is contained by form. If, however, he did not have this in mind, he manifestly said something false, that container and contained are essential parts, one of which is perfected by the other. For every whole contains its parts, and does not perfect them; rather it is perfected by them. For a whole is not complete unless it has all its parts, and in this respect Aristotle said that the whole and the perfect are either the same or nearly the same. [Τὸ ὅλον, καὶ τὸ τέλεον, ἢ τὸ αὐτὸ πάμπαν, ἢ σύνεσγυς τῇ φύσει ἐσί.] From this the fourth example put forward by Zabarella is overturned. His language here is remarkable, for having said that essential parts stand as perfecting and perfectible, among other examples of parts so related he also puts forward perfecting and perfectible themselves. But that he errs in counting among essential parts those things which properly stand in this relation appears from what was just said about the whole, which is perfected by its parts. And let this suffice on the division of parts into integral (which they also call quantitative and material) and essential, as received among the Peripatetics. Now it will be the time to set out our own opinion on this matter.

units.la: XII. Partes alias Dissimilares esse dicimus, alias Quan- titativas.
units.tr: XII. We say that some parts are dissimilar, others quantitative.

units.la: Quantitativæ partes sunt, quarum appositione & ablatione nihil aliud acquirit aut amittit Totum, cujus illæ dicuntur partes, nisi quod majus fit aut minus. Tales partes habent omnia Elementa; item corpora similaria, ut caro, lignum, aurum, si indefinite, & absq; certæ molis aut figuræ circumscriptione considerentur. Accidentia etiam habent ejusmodi partes, non omnia, sed sensibilia duntaxat, neq; ea cuncta: quippe figura ijs caret, nisi recta simplex; quum aliæ omnes figuræ constent è partibus dissimilaribus. Reliqua autem habent partes quantitativas, quando enim secatur corpus tali aliqua qualitate præditum, una etiam secari qualitatem ipsam, manifestum est. Quod si quis dicat, secari tales qualitates per accidens, quia secantur ad sectionem subjecti (id quod Averroës alicubi dicit, & ex Aristotele profitetur Zabarella, consentientibus ipsi plerisq; Peripateticis) is sciat, nihil hoc referre. non minus enim vere fiunt, quæ fiunt isto modo, quem illi appellant per Accidens, imò quæ certo per Accidens fiunt, quàm quæ fiunt primario, ac per se. fieri enim per accidens, non infert alteritatem (ut sic dicamus) in actione aut passione quæ fit, inq; earum terminis, sed in modo quo fiunt: qua de re & supra diximus nonnihil, & alibi plura erunt dicenda. Non magis autem secantur Accidentia per accidens, quia secantur cum subjecto, neq; aliter nisi cum subjecto secari possunt, quam sunt aut producuntur per accidens, quia producuntur & sunt in subjecto, neq; aliter quam in subjecto esse aut produci queunt. Et dantur tamen alij quoq; modi, quibus proximè ac per se, non communicante subjecto, partes quantitativas amittunt aut acquirunt accidentia; sicuti manifestum est in ijs, quæ calescunt, aut frigescunt. gefiunt per partes, ac minutatim, ut si cylindrum ferreum altera extremitate in ignem immittas: prius enim calescet pars igni proxima, ac deinceps vicinæ, donec totum ferrum incaluerit: quod ferrum ita calefactum si rursus altera duntaxat extremitate in frigidam immergas, frigus item successive in ipsum introducetur. Sæpè etiam videmus in panno aliquo lineo, laneove aut sericeo, colorem deperdi in certis partibus, quum in reliquis salvus maneat: quod sicuti interdum fit deperditione substantiæ colorem conferentis (quo pacto ad præsentem contemplationem non pertinet) ita non raro fit simplici alteratione; & tunc est hujus ordinis. Etenim in tali subjecto minus tunc est istius qualitatis, quam ante illam jacturam: quod qui negare ausit, illi liceat eodem jure affirmare, non plus caloris esse in massa ferrea candenti mille librarum, quam in frustulo unius drachmæ, aut quam in una scintilla. Distinguendum autem diligenter est inter gradus caloris, & partes. plures enim pauciorve partes esse nequeunt, nisi in pluribus aut paucioribus partibus subjecti. intensior autem vel remissior gradus in unam eandemque partem introducitur. & quod de calore diximus, idem de aliis quoque qualitatibus sensibilibus dictum esto. Et plurimum hæc differre, inde quoque liquet, quod quum partes quantitativas non habeant nisi qualitates sensibiles, gradus intensionis & remissionis cadunt in omnes omnino qualitates, solâ & hic figurâ exceptâ. Vbi igitur est intensior gradus caloris, majorem liceat dicere calorem, quam ubi est remissior; non tamen putandum est, plures esse partes caloris, in intensiore gradu, quam in remissiore. non enim gradus gradui apponitur, ut pars parti, neque inferior gradus superiori coalescit, sed in eo obliteratur. eque enim simplex est supremus caloris, & alterius cujusque qualitatis intensibilis, gradus, quam infimus.
units.tr: Quantitative parts are those by whose addition or removal the whole of which they are called parts acquires or loses nothing except that it becomes greater or smaller. All elements have such parts, and likewise the similar bodies, such as flesh, wood, and gold, if they are considered indefinitely and without circumscription of a certain mass or shape. Accidents also have such parts, not all of them but only the sensible ones, and not all of these: shape, for instance, lacks them, unless it is a straight line, since all other shapes consist of dissimilar parts. The remaining accidents, however, have quantitative parts, for it is clear that when a body endowed with some such quality is cut, the quality itself is also cut. If someone says that such qualities are cut only accidentally, because they are cut along with the division of the subject (which Averroes says somewhere, and Zabarella professes from Aristotle, with most of the Peripatetics agreeing), let him know that this makes no difference. Those things that happen in this way, which they call accidental, are no less truly done than those that happen primarily and per se; indeed they are certainly no less real than what happens accidentally in a certain way. For happening accidentally does not imply a difference (so to speak) in the action or passion that takes place, or in its terms, but in the manner in which it happens. We have said something about this matter above, and more will be said elsewhere. Accidents are not cut accidentally any more because they are cut together with the subject, nor can they be divided in any other way than together with the subject, than they are or are produced accidentally because they are produced and exist in a subject, and cannot exist or be produced otherwise than in a subject. Yet there are also other modes by which accidents lose or acquire quantitative parts proximately and per se, without the subject being involved; as is evident in things that grow warm or grow cold. These change part by part, and gradually: for example, if you thrust one end of an iron cylinder into the fire, the part nearest the fire will become hot first, and then the neighbouring parts, until the whole iron has been heated. If you then dip only one end of that heated iron into cold water, cold is likewise introduced into it successively. We often also see in some cloth of linen, wool, or silk that its colour is lost in certain parts while it remains intact in the others. As this sometimes happens through the loss of the substance that imparts the colour (in which way it does not belong to the present discussion), so it often happens through a simple alteration, and then it is of this kind. For in such a subject there is then less of that quality than before the loss. Whoever dares to deny this may by the same right affirm that there is no more heat in a white-hot iron mass of a thousand pounds than in a little fragment of one drachm, or than in a single spark. One must carefully distinguish between degrees of heat and parts. For there can be more or fewer parts only if there are more or fewer parts of the subject. A more intense or more remiss degree, however, is introduced into one and the same part. What we have said of heat, let the same be said of the other sensible qualities too. That these differ greatly is also clear from the fact that, since they have quantitative parts only as sensible qualities, degrees of intensity and remission apply to all qualities without exception, shape alone excepted here as well. Where, then, there is a more intense degree of heat, one may say there is more heat than where there is a more remiss degree; yet it should not be thought that there are more parts of heat in the more intense degree than in the more remiss. For degree is not added to degree as part to part, nor does the lower degree coalesce with the higher, but is obliterated in it. For the highest degree of heat, and of any other intensible quality, is as simple as the lowest.

units.la: XIII. Non enim audiendus est Scaliger, qui hac in re ab Aristotele dissentiens (à quo vel in minimis rebus, & nequaquam huic comparandis, dissensisse, capitale est misello Cardano, quoties huic dictatori videtur) ausus est negare receptissi-
units.tr: XIII. Scaliger is not to be heard, for he dissents from Aristotle on this point (and it is a capital offence for poor Cardanus to dissent from this dictator even in the smallest matters, which are in no way comparable to this), and he dares to deny the most ## Chapter II.

units.la: receptissimum axioma, & innixum manifestissimæ experientiæ, atq; in omni vitæ parte se ingerenti, intensionem, inquimus, qualitatum: quam qui tuentur, cum crassis ac plebijs ait sordescere: vocatoq; lectore ad altiorem contemplationem, ait nullum calorem (caloris enim exemplo utitur) majorem esse, eo modo, quo dicunt, calorem intendi. Illa enim intendi, quorum extrema coguntur longius distare; quod in calore fieri non possit, ne metaphorice quidem. Quæ sane de vocabulo ipso satagentia risu digna est; quasi vero quisquam unquam ita deliraßet, ut putaret intendi qualitates ita, quomodo funes intenduntur. sed in febriculosa hac circa voces ac phrases vulgo usitatas diligentia, mirum quantum ille vir sibi placuerit: à quo parum sibi cavit Cicero, & probatissimi quiq; scriptores Latini, quando familiariter usurpant illas loquendi formulas, ut dicant aliquem intendere curam, animum, mentem, aciem, & similia; quorum tamen nullum intenditur ita, quomodo funis, ut extremitates cogantur longius distare. Neque talem consiliarium habuit Plato, quando dixit, Τὸ θυμοειδὲς μᾶλλον ἐπιτάδειν τοῦ λέοντος, συλληπότερον τε καὶ χαλεπώτερον γίγνεσθαι. Partem irascibilem, magis insensam quam par est, duriorem ac difficiliorem fieri, & in aliis mille locis, ubi hoc verbum ad eundem modum usurpat; quod cum ipso faciunt passim alij quoq; scriptores Græci. Sed missa lite de vocabulo, rem ipsam videamus.
units.tr: received axiom, resting on the most manifest experience and intruding into every part of life: the intension, I mean, of qualities. Those who uphold it, he says, smack of the common and vulgar. Calling his reader up to a loftier contemplation, he says that no heat (for he takes heat as his example) is greater in the way they say heat is intensified. For those things are intended whose extremities are forced to stand farther apart, which cannot happen in heat, not even metaphorically. This is indeed laughable, busying itself with the word alone, as if anyone had ever been so mad as to think that qualities are intended the way cords are stretched. But in this feverish care over words and commonly used phrases, it is remarkable how well pleased that man was with himself. Cicero was not so careful, nor were the most approved Latin writers, when they freely use such forms of speech as to intend one's care, mind, attention, or keen sight, and the like; yet none of these is intended as a cord is, so that its extremities are forced farther apart. Nor did Plato have such an adviser when he said [Τὸ θυμοειδὲς μᾶλλον ἐπιτάδειν τοῦ λέοντος, συλληπότερον τε καὶ χαλεπώτερον γίγνεσθαι]: the irascible part, more hostile than is right, becomes harsher and more difficult. He uses the word in the same way in a thousand other places, and other Greek writers do the same everywhere. But setting aside the quarrel over the word, let us look at the thing itself.

units.la: Quod intensio in qualitatibus dicitur, id accretionem esse dicit, sicut & quantitatis. accretionem autem fieri vel ipsius corporis calidi condensatione, ut si ferri calidi partes quatuor malleo condensatæ cogant in unum. sic enim fore, ut quadruplicetur calor ille, quum ignis quatuor partes in unam coierint. unamquamq; enim ferri particulam habuisse partem unam ignis, per quam caleret. adunatis igitur quatuor ipsius ferri partibus, quatuor quoq; ignis partes adunatas esse. quare eosdem esse caloris gradus, qui erant prius, sed ob conjunctionem efficaciores. Posse quoq; unam eandemq; ferri partem fieri calidiorem, non propter condensationem, sed quia quatuor ignis partes successive in eam introductæ sint. Ista est Scaligeri circa qualitatum intensionem, aut, ut ipse vocat, accretionem sententia, non uno modo ridicula. Futilius enim nihil cogitari potest (vel ipso Aristotele iudice, qui 1. de Generat. & Corr. 8. prolixe impugnat eos, qui omnem alterationem fieri per poros asseverabant) quam quod in ea corpora, quae calefiunt, vult ipsam ignis substantiam introduci: quod delirium deliravit etiam Suessanus, quippe qui dixerit (si vera de eo refert Zabarella) aquam ferventem non esse calidam. sed videri calidam, propter vapores, (hoc est, ex mente Scaligeri, particulas ignis) in ea existentes. quod ita refellit Zabarella, ut dicat eos qui hoc statuunt, alterationem tollere de rebus: quod Scaliger facit planissime cum suis illis ignis particulis, quas in ferrum introducit, ut illud calefaciat. & ne quid de summa futilitate (tanto sane viro indigna in negotio tam manifesto) reliquum faciat: objectionem Cardani, quod sic duae substantiae forent in aere, verbi causa, ignito; ita solvit, ut dicat, ignem in concavitatibus aeris hospitari, sicut aqua facit in concavitatibus panni vel spongiae. Sed ut in aere ac ferro tale quid fieri possit. multa sunt, in quibus id locum habere non potest. Et praeterea ipsa ignis natura aliam adhuc suppeditat validiorem rationem, cur calefactio hoc pacto fieri nequeat; sicuti in tractatione de Oleo, libro sequenti exhibenda ubi prolixe hac de re disputandum est, clarum fiet.
units.tr: What is called intension in qualities, he says, is accretion, just as it is in quantity. Accretion occurs either by condensation of the hot body itself, as when the four parts of hot iron are pressed together by a hammer into one. For that heat would thus be quadrupled, once the four parts of fire have come together. For each little particle of iron, he holds, had one part of fire by which it was hot; so when the four parts of the iron are joined, the four parts of fire are joined as well. Therefore the degrees of heat are the same as before, but more effective because of the conjunction. It is also possible for one and the same part of iron to become hotter, not through condensation but because four parts of fire have been introduced into it successively. This is Scaliger's opinion on the intension of qualities, or, as he calls it, accretion, and it is not ridiculous in only one way. Nothing more trifling can be imagined (even by the judgement of Aristotle himself, who in De Generatione et Corruptione 1.8 at length attacks those who asserted that all alteration occurs through pores) than that he wants the very substance of fire to be introduced into the bodies that are heated. Suessanus also raved in this madness, since he said (if Zabarella reports him truly) that boiling water is not hot, but only seems hot because of the vapours (that is, in Scaliger's sense, particles of fire) present in it. Zabarella refutes this by saying that those who hold it do away with alteration in things. Scaliger does exactly this quite plainly with those particles of fire of his, which he introduces into the iron to heat it. And so that he may leave nothing of utter triviality (unworthy of so great a man in a matter so manifest), he answers Cardano's objection, that in this way there would be two substances together in air, for example in burning air, by saying that fire lodges in the hollows of air, just as water does in the hollows of cloth or sponge. But although something of this kind might happen in air and iron, there are many cases in which it cannot take place. Moreover, the very nature of fire supplies yet another and stronger reason why heating cannot happen in this way; this will become clear in the treatment of Oil in the following book, where the matter must be disputed at length.

units.la: Quinimo ut vel maxime Scaligero concederetur, quod de calefactione per ignis introductionem, & de intensione caloris per partium condensationem, vel plurium ignis partium introductionem, contendit; plurimae tamen sunt qualitates, in quibus ne fingi quidem potest, earum intensionem ad eundem modum fieri. Ut enim unum de innumeris exemplum delegamus, non erit, credimus, Stoicus, ut praeceptori suo neget, alios alijs posse magis justos esse, vel minus, & proinde unum eundemq; hominem posse fieri se ipso justiorem. Pervelimus igitur scire, quaenam sit illa substantia αὐτοδιχαιοσύνη, Platonicarum Idearum sororcula, cujus partium introductione sicuti anima fiat insita, ita si plures ejusdem partes introducantur, fiat
units.tr: Indeed, even if we were to grant Scaliger as fully as possible what he contends about heating through the introduction of fire, and about the intension of heat through condensation of parts or the introduction of several parts of fire, there are still very many qualities in which it cannot even be imagined that their intension occurs in the same way. To choose one example out of countless, I believe the Stoic would not deny to his teacher that some men can be more just than others, or less so, and therefore that one and the same man can become more just than himself. We would very much like to know, then, what that substance self-justice [αὐτοδιχαιοσύνη] is, the little sister of the Platonic Ideas, by the introduction of whose parts, as the soul is made to be implanted, so if several parts of the same are introduced, it becomes
Chapter II.

units.la: fiat justior. Ex duobus enim illis modis, quibus aliquid dicebat fieri calidius, vel sui condensatione, vel plurium ignis partium introductione; prior saltem hic locum non habet, neq; enim dixerit, animam fieri justiorem, si quatuor ipsius partes in unum coeant. Sed & posterior modus æque est puerilis. Videndum igitur ipsi fuerit, quem velit hic tertium modum excogitare, quo in anima fiat justitiæ accretio. Quippe non de calore tantum, sed de qualitatibus in universum pronuntiat; Non intensionem earum fieri, sed accretionem.
units.tr: become more just. For of the two ways by which he said something became hotter, either by its condensation or by the introduction of several parts of fire, the first at least has no place here, for he would not say that the soul becomes more just if its four parts come together into one. But the second way is equally childish. It must therefore be seen what third way he wishes to devise here, by which an increase of justice comes about in the soul. For he pronounces not only about heat but about qualities in general: that what happens to them is not an intensification but an accretion.

units.la: XIV. Non igitur per novarum partium appositionem Qualitates intenduntur, sed imperfectioris gradus persectione. Hoc enim voluit Deus Qualitatibus proprium esse, ut possent in se ipsis atq; essentialiter perfectiores esse & imperfectiores: quod ne recipiant, in causa multis est Aristotelis illud decretum, quo scisçit; Essentias rerum se habere instar numerorum; in quos sicuti non cadit magis & minus, ita neq; in illas cadere. Sed non videtur ille latius hoc extendisse, quam ad Formas substantiales. Si vero de accidentalibus quoq; formis hoc ipsum protulit; rem dixit vel sola experientia refutandam. quare in re adeo manifesta non debebat illos à veritate admittenda deterrere unius viri autoritas. Certissimo enim comperimus quotidie, unam eandemq; qualitatem posse magis aut minus esse perfectam. Et hæc est perfectio proprie dicta, non illa altera, quæ in omnium partium, unum totum componentium, præsentia consistit. Ista enim non tam perfectio est, quam integritas; quanquam potest aliquo etiam modo Persectio appellari. Proprie autem Perfectio in solis qualitatibus locum habet. illa enim qualitas, quæ in summo gradu, qui ejus naturaliter esse potest, constituta est, perfecta est; à quo quantum recedit, tantum abest à perfectione. Et sic etiam composita proprie perfecta aut imperfecta non dicuntur, nisi ratione perfectarum aut imperfectarum in ijs qualitatum. Gradus igitur Qualitatum, qui in earum intensione consistunt, confundendi non sunt cum partibus earundem × Sub gluten vel minus accidentis ... subiecta magis minus tardit ... (handwritten marginal note) rundem quantitativis, neq; pro partibus illi habendi.
units.tr: XIV. Qualities are therefore not intensified by the addition of new parts, but by the perfecting of a more imperfect degree. For God willed this to be proper to qualities, that they can become more perfect and less perfect in themselves and essentially. That they do not admit this is, for many, due to that decree of Aristotle by which he declared that the essences of things stand like numbers: just as more and less do not apply to numbers, so they do not apply to essences. But he does not seem to have extended this further than to substantial forms. If, however, he also said this of accidental forms, he said something that experience alone refutes. So in a matter so manifest, the authority of one man ought not to deter them from accepting the truth. For we most certainly learn every day that one and the same quality can be more or less perfect. And this is perfection properly so called, not that other kind, which consists in the presence of all the parts that make up one whole. For that is less a perfection than an integrity, although it can in some way also be called perfection. Properly, however, perfection has a place only in qualities. For that quality which is set at the highest degree that is naturally possible for it is perfect, and the further it recedes from this, the further it is from perfection. And so also composites are not properly called perfect or imperfect, except by reason of the perfect or imperfect qualities in them. The degrees of qualities, which consist in their intension, are therefore not to be confused with the quantitative parts of those same qualities, nor are they to be regarded as parts of them. (Marginal note, garbled in the scan: "… under the gluten or less of the accident … the subject more or less … ")
Chapter II.

units.la: XV. Est autem partium Quantitativarum, tum in substantiis, tum in accidentibus, haec conditio, (qua tanquam certissimo κριτηρίω internoscì queant, atq; à partibus essentialibus discerni) quod earum apposizione aut detractione Totum quantitativum non aliam patitur mutationem, nisi quod majus fit aut minus. Unde etiam sequitur, partes quantitativas omnes esse inter se similes. nisi enim hoc sit, non potest esse uniforme ipsum Totum. & si Totum diversiforme est, fieri nequit quin aliquarum partium ablatione aliam, quàm secundum solam quantitatem, patiatur mutationem. Est autem nonnulla Partium Quantitativarum in eo differentia, quod nonnullae post divisionem à Toto, eandem servant essentiam, quam habebant, dum Toti essent conjunctae; aliae vero nequaquam. Priores non modo omnes inter se sunt similes, sed & cum Toto eandem habet Essentiam, adeo ut definitio Totius competat cuicunq; parti à Toto separatae, & per se existenti. sic enim omnia, quae in definitione aquae vel auri exprimuntur, aeque inveniuntur in quavis minima particula, aut gutta, quam in tota massa aut mole, à qua ipsa ablata est. hoc autem nequaquam competit iis, quas in secundo loco posuimus. tales autem sunt, partes animarum plerarumque. Plerarumq; dicimus, non omnium: sunt enim stirpes, quarum animae partes habent non modo inter se, sed & toti similes, ideoq; in apospasmatis manentes, ibiq; integrarum animarum conditionem servantes. quales etiam sunt fortasse nonnullorum insectorum animae. Aliarum autem stirpium, & plerorumq; insectorum, omniumq; animalium perfectorum animae (excepta Mente, quae nullam patitur actualem divisionem, non magis quam Angeli) quanquam partes habent invicem similes, propterea q; earum amissione aut acquisitione majores tantum aut minores fiant; partes tamen illae, simulatq; à Toto separatae sunt, desinunt esse quod erant, depositâq; totâ natura, qua participabant dum Toti erant junctae, redeunt ad statum simplicis Elementi. menti, ejus nimirum, ex quo omnes animæ per naturæ introductionem constituuntur. Quod autem de hisce animabus dicimus, eas è partibus quantitativis componi, id non de ipsis integris intelligendum est, sed Ꝑ tantum duntaxat. Etenim hæ omnes animæ, si universæ considerentur, composita sunt dissimilaria, atq; è partibus plurimum inter se diversis constituuntur. Namq; ea animæ pars, quæ in iecore radices egit, (ut sic dicamus) plurimum differt ab ea, quæ in testibus habitat. utraq; autem non parum diversa est ab ea portione, quæ vel in corde vel in cerebro domicilium sortita est. Omnes autem hæ multum sunt diversæ ab ea parte, quæ per totam venarum capacitatem fusa est. Et in plantis quoq; (ijs duntaxat exceptis, quarum è quovis apospasmate integra rursus planta nasci potest) idem quoq; obtinet per analogiam, quanquam non cum tanta varietate: quæ omnia, nova sane, & in Lyceo inaudita, faciemus suo loco planissima. Quod igitur dicimus de hisce animabus, earum partes esse quantitativas; id non de partibus ipsas totas constituentibus, sed de partium partibus, ijs nimirum, quæ magnas has atq; diversiformes portiones constituunt, accipiendum est. In quibus autem partibus non invenitur generalis illa conditio, hic à nobis assignata, ut omnes sint inter se similes, utq; earum accessu aut abscessu compositum duntaxat majus fiat aut minus; eas certum est, non esse Quantitativas, sed alterius conditionis: quæ quot qualseque sint, nunc videbimus.
units.tr: XV. The condition of quantitative parts, both in substances and in accidents, is this (by which, as by a most certain criterion, they can be recognised and distinguished from essential parts): that by the addition or removal of them the quantitative whole undergoes no other change except that it becomes greater or smaller. Hence it also follows that all quantitative parts are similar to one another. For unless this were so, the whole itself could not be uniform; and if the whole is of diverse form, it cannot be that by the removal of some parts it undergoes a change other than in quantity alone. There is, however, a certain difference among quantitative parts in this respect: some, after separation from the whole, keep the same essence that they had while they were joined to the whole; others by no means do. The former are not only all similar to one another, but also have the same essence as the whole, so that the definition of the whole applies to any part separated from the whole and existing on its own. For all the things expressed in the definition of water or of gold are found equally in any smallest particle or drop as in the whole mass or bulk from which it was taken. This, however, by no means applies to those we have placed in the second group. Such are the parts of most souls. I say most, not all: for there are plants whose souls have parts that are similar not only to one another but also to the whole, and therefore remain in the cuttings, preserving there the condition of complete souls; such perhaps are also the souls of some insects. But the parts of the souls of other plants, and of most insects, and of all perfect animals (except the Mind, which admits no actual division, no more than an angel does), although they are similar to one another, and therefore become greater or smaller only by the loss or gain of them, nevertheless those parts, as soon as they are separated from the whole, cease to be what they were, and, having put off the whole nature in which they shared while they were joined to the whole, they return to the state of a simple element, namely that element from which all souls are constituted by the introduction of nature. And what we say about these souls, that they are composed of quantitative parts, is to be understood not of the complete souls themselves, but only of their parts. For all these souls, if considered as a whole, are dissimilar composites, made up of parts that differ greatly from one another. For that part of the soul which has taken root in the liver, so to speak, differs greatly from that which dwells in the testicles; and both differ not a little from that portion which has its seat either in the heart or in the brain. All of these, moreover, differ much from that part which is spread through the whole capacity of the veins. And in plants also (except those whose complete plant can grow again from any cutting) the same holds by analogy, although not with so great a variety. All these things, indeed new and never heard of in the Lyceum, we shall make very plain in their place. What we say about these souls, then, that their parts are quantitative, is to be understood not of the parts that constitute the whole souls, but of the parts of those parts, namely those which make up these large and diversely formed portions. In those parts, however, in which we do not find the general condition assigned here by us, that all are similar to one another, and that by their addition or removal the composite is only made greater or smaller, it is certain that they are not quantitative but of another kind; what and how many these are, we shall now see.
XVI.

units.la: Partes dissimilares duorum sunt in universum generum, Essentiales, & Conformantes. Essentiales vocamus, quæ ipsam rei Essentiam constituunt, quomodo anima & corpus constituunt animal vel plantam: Conformantes vero, quæ inserviunt vel totius corporis, vel alterius partis conformationi, quomodo caput est pars conformans corporis; facies, capitis; nasus facici; nares, nasi; similares, ipsarum narium. Nullæ autem partes Dissimilares excogitari possunt, quæ non ad alterutram harum speciem revocandę sint. & quum partes conformantes non dentur (sicut ex ipso nomine apparet) nisi in corporibus certam conformationem sortitis, sequitur, accidentia omnia, quæ concursu suo aliud accidens componunt, esse partes essentiales. atq; eodem modo liquet, pro partibus, Essentialibus haberi quoq; debere Materiam & Naturam, tum in Angelis, tum in anima quacunq; : itemq; animam & corpus, tum in animalibus, tum in plantis. neq; enim vel plantæ vel animantes certam habent conformationem, quatenus ex anima & corpore constant, sed καθὸ τι, quatenus altera ipsorum pars essentialis, videlicet ipsum corpus, certo modo est conformata; sicuti manifeste in morte apparet, ubi separatâ à corpore animâ, eadem manet, quæ in vivente erat, totius conformatio. Sicuti autem hoc clarum est, ita clarum quoq; est, & utramq; illam partem essentialem, Materiam & Naturam, in corporibus quoq; Conformatis reperiri, & Partes eorundem conformantes pro essentialibus habendas non esse. Quantum ad prius; cum universa corporis moles ex partibus similaribus constet, ipsæ autem partes similares ex Elementis; Elementa autem, quomodocunq; inter se miscentur, ne unam quidem partem similarem constituere possint, nisi aliæ extrinsecus qualitates accedant; apparet plus in similaribus esse, quam nudam Materiam, è sex Elementis seu corporibus simplicibus conflatam. Ast hoc quod in ijs plus est, est ipsa Natura. Porro Natura hæc in duo summa capita scinditur. altera enim sui parte Materiam intrinsecus afficit, altera extrinsecus disponit. prior pars fere consistit in qualitatibus tertiæ classis, inq; ipso substantiæ modo, ex certa Elementorum proportione debitaq; mixtione consurgenti, per quæ fit ut caro sit caro, & os sit os; itidemq; de cæteris partibus similaribus. altera verò Naturæ pars, extrinsecus disponens, in conformatione consistit. Usurpamus autem vocabulum conformationis non in angusta illa significatione, qua in Physiologia & Pathologia à medicis sumi solet, ubi partium organicarum compositionem in hisce quatuor consistere dicentes, Certo numero, Conveniente magnitudine, Debito
units.tr: Dissimilar parts are of two general kinds: essential and conforming. We call essential those parts which constitute the very essence of a thing, as the soul and the body constitute an animal or a plant. Conforming parts are those which serve the conformation either of the whole body or of another part: the head is a conforming part of the body, the face of the head, the nose of the face, the nostrils of the nose, and the similar parts of the nostrils themselves. No dissimilar parts can be devised which must not be referred to one or other of these kinds. And since conforming parts exist (as the name itself shows) only in bodies that have obtained a certain conformation, it follows that all accidents which by their concurrence compose some other accident are essential parts. In the same way it is clear that matter and nature must be counted among essential parts, both in angels and in every soul; and likewise soul and body, both in animals and in plants. For plants and animals do not have a definite conformation insofar as they consist of soul and body, but in a certain respect [καθὸ τι], insofar as their other essential part, namely the body itself, is conformed in a certain way. This is plainly seen in death, where, with the soul separated from the body, the conformation of the whole remains what it was in the living thing. But just as this is clear, so it is also clear that both those essential parts, matter and nature, are found in conformed bodies too, and that their conforming parts are not to be held as essential. As to the former: since the whole mass of a body consists of similar parts, and the similar parts themselves of elements, and the elements, however they are mixed together, could not constitute even one similar part unless other qualities were added from outside, it appears that there is more in similar parts than bare matter compounded of the six elements or simple bodies. But that which is more in them is nature itself. Further, this nature is divided into two chief heads: one part of it acts on the matter from within, the other arranges it from without. The former part consists almost in the qualities of the third class, and in the very mode of substance arising from a definite proportion of elements and a due mixture, through which flesh is flesh and bone is bone; and likewise with the other similar parts. The other part of nature, arranging from without, consists in conformation. We use the word conformation, however, not in the narrow sense in which physicians are wont to use it in physiology and pathology, where, saying that the composition of organic parts consists in these four things, a certain number, a convenient size, due
Chapter II.

units.la: Debito situ, & Conformatione, sub Conformatione figuram decentem, Cavitatem aut Soliditatem, & superficiei lævitatem vel asperitatem complectuntur: sed tum hæc, tum priora illa omnia sub hac appellatione, quæ apud Galenum quoq; non raro ita late usurpatur, comprehendimus. Sicuti igitur ab interna Naturæ parte habet unaquæq; pars similaris, ut tale vel tale substantiæ genus constituat: ita ab externa ejusdem parte habet suam Conformationem. Et quum partes omnes organicæ, quas ita Medici vocant, ex similaribus constent, sicuti majora organa proxime è minoribus organis, & totum corpus immediatè ex majoribus organis constituitur; apparet totius corporis conformationem à partium similarium conformatione pendere. & cum illarum conformatio proficiscatur à naturæ ea parte, quam exteriorem vocavimus, liquet partes conformantes pro essentialibus haberi non debere, quum ipsarum conformatio sit quasi essentiæ consectaria; quippe quæ ab altera duntaxat Essentiæ parte, nimirum Naturâ, neq; eâ totâ proficiscatur. Ex dictis autem satis apparet, quare Conformantes dicamus partes, non Organicas, vocabulo Medicis usitato. Etenim organicas partes ita dicere illi solent, ut similaribus opponant: & quanquam eorum nonnulli aliquas etiam similares partes, ut ossa, in organicarum censum recipiant, reliquas tamen & ipsi quoq; ab earum numero excludunt. Usurpandum igitur nobis fuit vocabulum, quod latius pateret; quodq; ambitu suo non organicas modo, sed & similares omnes complecteretur. Quanquam enim similares partes per internam illam Naturam nullis certis conformationis terminis circumscribuntur; quum tamen in corporibus viventium, cum interna Naturæ externam habeant conjunctam, ejusq; ratione certæ conformationi ita astringantur, ut omnium organorum totiusq; corporis conformatio ab earum conformatione manet; nullo modo ipsæ extra partium conformantium numerum fuerunt rejiciendæ; sed primæ in illo ordine collocandæ. Itaq; non est, quod quisquam miretur, quum Partes Essentiales & Conformantes uno generico Dissimilarium vocabulo comprehenderimus, quo jure postea Similares Conformantibus annumeraverimus. Hoc enim facimus ea ratione, qua licet similares sint per internam sui Naturam, dissimilares tamen sunt, quantum ad exteriorem suæ Naturæ partem. Imo & priori modo possunt certo respectu dici dissimilares, si ipsæ similares inter sese, sive aliæ similares cum aliis conferantur. Sic enim per internam quoq; sui naturam sunt invicem dissimiles, non minus quam caput est dissimile manibus, aut thorax ventri.
units.tr: due position, and conformation, they understand by conformation a fitting figure, hollowness or solidity, and smoothness or roughness of surface. But we include both these and all those former things under this name, which Galen too often uses so broadly. Just as, therefore, each similar part has from the internal part of nature its ability to constitute this or that kind of substance, so from its external part it has its conformation. And since all the parts which physicians call organic consist of similar parts, just as larger organs are formed immediately from smaller organs and the whole body immediately from larger organs, it appears that the conformation of the whole body depends on the conformation of the similar parts. And since their conformation proceeds from that part of nature which we called external, it is clear that conforming parts should not be held as essential, since their conformation is, as it were, a consequence of essence, inasmuch as it proceeds from only one part of the essence, namely nature, and not from all of it. From what has been said it is sufficiently clear why we call them conforming parts rather than organic parts, the term in use among physicians. For they usually speak of organic parts so as to set them against similar parts; and although some of them also admit certain similar parts, such as bones, into the number of organic parts, yet they too exclude the rest. So we had to use a word of wider scope, one which would embrace not only organic but all similar parts. For although similar parts are not bounded by any fixed limits of conformation through their internal nature, yet since in the bodies of living things they have their external nature conjoined with the internal, and by reason of it are so bound to a certain conformation that the conformation of all organs and of the whole body remains dependent on theirs, they ought in no way to be rejected from the number of conforming parts, but placed first in that order. So there is no reason for anyone to wonder that, when we comprehend essential and conforming parts under the one generic term of dissimilar parts, we afterwards rightly count similar parts among the conforming ones. For we do this on the ground that, although they are similar by their internal nature, they are dissimilar as regards the external part of their nature. Indeed, in the former way too they can in a certain respect be called dissimilar, if similar parts are compared with one another or with other similar parts. For thus too, by their internal nature, they are unlike one another, no less than the head is unlike the hands or the chest unlike the belly.

units.la: XVII. Monemus autem porrò, Partes conformantes nobis dictas posse suo jure etiam Partes Naturales dici: ut corpora, quæ ex illis constant, Tota Naturalia. neq; putandum est, nimis laxam esse hanc appellationem. nulla enim Tota sunt in mundo, præter corpora Naturaliter certam conformationem sortita, quæ ipsa, Tota Naturalia, aut quorum Partes, Partes Naturales dici merentur. Nam Tota quantitativa, (qualia sunt animarum magnæ illæ portiones, de quibus modo dicebamus, ac nonnullæ animæ integræ; itemq; Elementa, ac mixta similaria non Conformata, ut metalla, lapides, varia terrarum ac salium genera) quanquam sunt Corpora Naturalia, Tota tamen Naturalia non sunt; quum nullis Naturæ suæ legibus certam molem, certumq; partium numerum aut situm habeant sibi præfinitum. idcirco quæcunq; ipsis addantur aut demantur partes, Natura ipsorum una eademq; manet, neq; ullam patitur mutationem. At in Totis Conformatis longe aliter se res habet. omnia enim illic per Naturam sunt definita, nihilq; illis vel addi, vel demi, aut aliter mutari potest, quin ad ipsam Naturam novatio illa redundet. Quippe quum Natura nihil sit aliud, quàm concursus proprietatum speciei debitarum (qua de re suo loco plenius a nobis agetur) interq; illas proprietates in corporibus conformatis hæ quoq; sint, Tales habere partes, talem partium numerum, talem proportionem, talem situm, talem connexionem, & quæcunq; ad absolvendam Totius conformationem spectant: in quacunq; harum conditionum aliqua mutatio fiat, cum ipsius Naturæ damno
units.tr: XVII. We further note that the conforming parts we have described may rightly also be called natural parts, so that the bodies composed of them are natural wholes. Nor should this name be thought too loose. For there are no wholes in the world except bodies that have obtained a certain conformation by nature; these themselves deserve to be called natural wholes, or their parts natural parts. For quantitative wholes (such as those great portions of souls of which we were just speaking, and some entire souls; likewise elements and unconformed mixed similar bodies, such as metals, stones, and various kinds of earths and salts), although they are natural bodies, are not natural wholes, since by no laws of their nature do they have a definite mass, or a definite number or position of parts prescribed to them. Hence, whatever parts are added to them or taken from them, their nature remains one and the same and suffers no change. But in conformed wholes the case is quite different. For everything there is defined by nature, and nothing can be added to them, taken from them, or otherwise changed without that change redounding upon the nature itself. For since nature is nothing other than the concurrence of the properties of a due kind (which we will treat more fully in its place), and among those properties in conformed bodies are these too: to have such parts, such a number of parts, such a proportion, such a position, such a connection, and whatever else pertains to the completion of the conformation of the whole; whenever any change occurs in any of these conditions, there is damage to the nature itself
Chapter II.

units.la: no illa mutatio est conjuncta. atq; hoc respectu tum ipsæ partes Conformantes; tum tota Conformata, Partes Naturales, & Tota Naturalia rite dicantur; quum hoc nomen ita sit illis proprium, ut omnibus alijs sit incommunicábile. Animis enim, Elementisq; & similaribus non conformatis, haud competere, modo ostendimus. sed neq; Totis aut Partibus Essentialibus competit, ut Naturalia aut Naturales dicantur. Quod enim homo, verbi gratia, ex corpore, & anima gemina, bruta atq; immortali, constat, non Naturæ, sed Essentiæ ratione fit, ideoq; homo, quatenus ex tribus illis partibus constat, non est Totum Naturale, sed Totum Essentiale, ac proinde partes quoq; illæ, non partes Naturales, sed partes Essentiales. sic in Animis & Angelis Materia & Natura partes non sunt Naturales, sed Essentiales. neq; enim ratione Naturæ fit, ut ibi sit Materia, sed ratione Essentiæ, quæ ad integritatem sui & Materiam postulat & Naturam. quare ipsa quoq; Natura non sui ipsius ratione ibi est, sed ratione Essentiæ, ad quam integrandam ipsa est necessaria. & hæc eadem de Materia quoq; & Natura Corporis Conformati vera sunt. ut enim tale corpus esse possit, & Materia desideratur & Natura. quod vero corpus sit tale, ex talibus partibus factum, atq; taliter conformatum; hoc totum ad Naturam pertinet: quum omnes istæ conditiones in ipsius Naturæ Essentia sint inclusæ, atq; ad integritatem ipsius necessariæ. quacunq; igitur istarum conditionum mutata, ipsius essentiam atq; integritatem lædi necesse est. Et sic patet, verum esse, quod dicebamus, Tota Conformata, ritè etiam Tota Naturalia, & Partes Conformantes, Partes Naturales dici posse. quare etiam fraudi nobis esse non debet, si ad priorem istam appellationem haud semper nos astringimus, sed promiscue modo unam, modo alteram usurpamus, quoties res feret, ut de istis partibus loquamur.
units.tr: is joined to that change. In this respect, both the constituent parts themselves and the whole they constitute may rightly be called natural parts and natural wholes, since this name belongs so properly to them that it cannot be shared with any others. We have already shown that it does not belong to souls, to elements, or to non-constituted similar bodies. Nor does it belong to wholes or parts that are essential, so that they might be called natural. For that man, for example, consists of a body and a twofold soul, both rational and immortal, does not come about by reason of Nature but by reason of Essence. Therefore man, insofar as he consists of those three parts, is not a natural whole but an essential whole, and consequently those parts too are not natural parts but essential parts. So in souls and angels, matter and nature are not natural parts but essential parts. For matter is there not by reason of Nature but by reason of Essence, which requires both matter and nature for its own completeness. The same things are true of the matter and nature of a constituted body. For matter and nature are required in order that such a body may exist. But that the body is such, made of such parts and so constituted, pertains to Nature as a whole, since all these conditions are included in the Essence of Nature itself and are necessary for its completeness. Therefore, if any of these conditions is changed, its essence and completeness must necessarily be harmed. And thus it is clear that what we said is true: the constituted wholes can also rightly be called natural wholes, and the constituent parts natural parts. Hence we ought not be blamed if we do not always keep to that first designation, but use now one term and now the other, interchangeably, whenever the matter requires us to speak of those parts.
XVIII.

units.la: Communis autem est utrisq; partibus dissimilaribus conditio (quod vel solo nomine innuitur) ut omnes sint inter se dissimiles. Sicuti autem commune est utriq; huic partium generi, ut inter se sint dissimiles, (namq; & manus manui, & pes pedi est dissimilis aliquo respectu) commune ipsis quoq; est, ut quacunq; ipsarum ablata, Totum ipsum aut pereat, aut violetur. Quantum ad composita Essentialia; alia sunt ejus conditionis, ut ne esse quidem possint, nisi sint integra, & idcirco quacunq; parte sublatâ, ipsa intereant necessario: alia vero sustinent aliquam partium jacturam, possuntq; esse non integra. prioris generis sunt, quæcunq; ex anima & corpore, & quæcunq; ex Materia & Natura constant. Posterioris generis sunt Accidentia pleraq; composita, omnesq; Materiæ compositæ. quum enim ad corpora viventium (ut & aliarum rerum) constituenda non unum aliquod Elementum assumatur; sed Materia illa, quæ cum Natura Totum constituit, sit ex cœtu variorum Elementorum composita; cujusq; elementi portio est istius Materiæ pars essentialis: & quacunq; una istarum sublata, non ipsa materia tollitur, sed tantum mutilatur. Eadem vero est & Totius Naturalis ratio. Neq; enim illud statim interit, parte aliqua naturali ablata, sed mutilum fit. Et hæc vero, & illa, non unius tantum partis, sed & plurium jacturam sustinent; antequam pereant, & nomen suum amittant: terminus autem vix alius statui videtur posse, nisi ut ne plus auferatur, quam relinquatur: imo ut plus relinquatur, quam tollatur. Totorum autem Conformatorum seu Naturalium duplex hic est consideratio. si enim considerentur ut talia simpliciter, nihil habent hic peculiare, valetq; in ijs conditio proximè dicta. namq; & corde evulso, & capite amputato, non tamen definit esse corpus. namque & cadaver, cui caput ablatum est, corpus tamen dicimus, sed truncum. Truncatio autem est nihil aliud, quam species quædam mutilationis; qualis est mancitas, quæ consistit in manus ablatione, & luscitia, quæ alterius oculi est amissio. Si vero consideratur corpus, ut vivens atq; animæ organon, tunc certæ sunt in eo partes, quarum vel unicâ ablatâ, totum destruitur. tales sunt majores illæ, caput, thorax, venter; tum minores, cerebrum, cor, jecur (quæ tria tali quodam respectu Partes Principes vulgo
units.tr: Dissimilar parts share a common condition (which is indicated by the very name) that they are all unlike one another. Just as it is common to this kind of part that they are unlike one another (for hand is unlike hand, and foot unlike foot, in some respect), so too it is common to them that when any one of them is removed, the whole itself either perishes or is damaged. As for essential composites, some are of such a kind that they could not exist at all unless they were complete, and therefore, if any part is removed, they necessarily perish. Others, however, can bear the loss of some parts and can exist without being complete. Of the first kind are all those composed of soul and body, and all those composed of matter and nature. Of the second kind are most accidental composites, and all composite matters. For since no single element is taken to constitute the bodies of living things (or of other things), but that matter which together with nature makes up the whole is composed of a mass of various elements, and a portion of each element is an essential part of that matter, then when any one of these is removed, the matter itself is not destroyed but only mutilated. The same is true of a natural whole. For it does not immediately perish when some natural part is removed, but becomes mutilated. And these, both the matter and the natural whole, bear the loss not of one part only but of several before they perish and lose their name. The limit, however, seems scarcely able to be set otherwise than that not more is taken away than is left; indeed, that more is left than is taken away. There is a twofold consideration of constituted or natural wholes. If they are considered simply as such, there is nothing peculiar here, and the condition just stated applies to them. For even when the heart is torn out or the head cut off, the body does not cease to be a body; we still call a corpse from which the head has been removed a body, though a trunk. Truncation, moreover, is nothing other than a kind of mutilation; such as maimedness, which consists in the removal of a hand, and one-eyedness, which is the loss of one eye. But if the body is considered as living and as the instrument of the soul, then there are certain parts in it such that if even one of them is removed, the whole is destroyed. Such are the greater ones: head, chest, and belly; and the lesser ones: brain, heart, and liver (which three, in a certain respect, are commonly called principal parts).
Chapter II.

units.la: vulgo à Medicis dicuntur) itémque pulmones, ventriculus, intestina, aliaque partes. harum enim quavis sublata, definit corpus posse animæ instrumentum esse. Duplex igitur videtur mutilationis terminus assignari posse: unus generalis, ut plus relinquatur quam tollitur: alter Corporibus organicis animæ sociatis peculiaris, ut ne tollatur pars aliqua ad vitam necessaria.
units.tr: ...as they are commonly called by physicians), and likewise the lungs, the stomach, the intestines, and other parts. For when any one of these is removed, the body ceases to be able to serve as the instrument of the soul. There seem to be two limits that can be assigned to mutilation: one general, that more is left than is taken away; the other peculiar to organic bodies joined to a soul, that no part necessary for life is removed.

units.la: XIX. Ex hisce autem facile est juvare aut corrigere Aristotelem, qui explanaturus quid sit Mutilum, per magnas verborum ambages nihil tandem aliud colligit, nisi grammaticam de hujus vocis usu observatiunculam. Requirit enim ut Mutilum, seu potius Mutilabile, sit quantum, & divisibile, & totum. κολοβὸν δὲ λέγεται τῶν ποσῶν, ὃ τ' τυχὸν, ἀλλὰ μεριςόν τε αὐτὸ δεῖ εἶναι, καὶ ὅλον. Mutilum in quantis dicitur, non quodvis eorum, sed oportet ut & divisibile sit illud, & totum. item, ut plus relinquatur quam aufertur. Ιζν τ' κολόβωμα καὶ τ' λοιπὸν ὁλόττος ἐςίν. Id, cujus ablatione aliquid mutilum fit, & id quod relinquitur, nunquam aqualia sunt. ac quinto loco, Ut essentia maneat: Τὴν οὐσίαν δεῖ μένειν. εἰ νύλιξ κολοβὸς, ἔτι δεῖ εἶναι νύλιχα. Essentiam manere oportet. si calix est mutilus, oportet ut adhuc calix sit. Fonseca in explicanda Aristotelis mente sicuti primam ac secundam conditionem pro una habet, ita etiam tertiam cum quarta ac quinta confundit, atq; ex tribus unam facit. Secunda conditio est, inquit, ut sit totum, hoc est, tanto majus ipso mutilamine, ut idem adhuc secundum substantiam censeri possit. sed non cepit, quid Aristoteles hic voluerit per vocem ὅλον, quodtamen facillimum erat excipere è fine præcedentis capitis, ubi dictum, Id, cujus partes nullum certum situm habent aut desiderant, Omne dici; ubi vero contra se res habet, Totum. Ὁσων μὴ ποιεῖ ἡ θέσις διαφορὰν, πᾶν λέγεται. ὅσων δὲ ποιεῖ, ὅλον. Ea, quorum differentiam non facit situs, dicuntur Omne. in quibus autem facit [situs differentiam,] Totum [dicuntur.] Quando igitur requirit, ut mutilabile tilabile
units.tr: XIX. From these points it is easy to help or correct Aristotle, who, meaning to explain what the mutilated is, after long verbal circumlocutions finally gathers nothing except a small grammatical observation on the use of this word. For he requires that the mutilated, or rather what can be mutilated, be a quantity, and divisible, and a whole. [κολοβὸν δὲ λέγεται τῶν ποσῶν, ὃ τ' τυχὸν, ἀλλὰ μεριςόν τε αὐτὸ δεῖ εἶναι, καὶ ὅλον.] Among quantities, the mutilated is so called not of just any kind, but it must be divisible and a whole. Likewise, that more is left than is taken away. [Ιζν τ' κολόβωμα καὶ τ' λοιπὸν ὁλόττος ἐςίν.] That from whose removal something becomes mutilated, and what remains, are never equal. And fifthly, that the essence remain: [Τὴν οὐσίαν δεῖ μένειν. εἰ νύλιξ κολοβὸς, ἔτι δεῖ εἶναι νύλιχα.] The essence must remain; if a cup is mutilated, it must still be a cup. Fonseca, in explaining Aristotle's meaning, treats the first and second conditions as one, and in the same way confuses the third with the fourth and fifth, and so makes one out of three. The second condition, he says, is that it be a whole, that is, so much greater than the mutilation itself that it can still be judged the same in substance. But he did not grasp what Aristotle meant here by the word ὅλον, which could easily have been gathered from the end of the preceding chapter, where it is said that those things whose parts have no fixed position or require none are called "all"; but where the case is otherwise, "whole." [Ὁσων μὴ ποιεῖ ἡ θέσις διαφορὰν, πᾶν λέγεται. ὅσων δὲ ποιεῖ, ὅλον.] Those things whose differences are not made by position are called "all." Those in which position makes a difference are called "whole." Therefore, when he requires that what can be mutilated be a whole, mutilable

units.la: In Com. ad locum. tilabile sit ὅλον, hoc vult, ut habeat partes situ differentes; quod mox etiam repetit, & apertius exprimit, Ολως ἂν μὴ ποιεῖ ἡ θέσις διαφορὰν, ψιλὸν κολοβὸν, οἷον ὕδωρ, ἢ πῦρ, ἀλλὰ δεῖ τοιαῦτα εἶναι, ἃ κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν θέσιν ἔχει. In universum nihil eorum, in quibus situs non facit differentiam, mutilum est, uti aqua, aut ignis: sed oportet ut talia sint, quae ratione essentiae [certum partium] situm habeant. paulo post vocem ὅλα eodem sensu rursus usurpat, Οὐδ' ὅλα ὅλα, ἀλλὰ ταῦτα ὁταν μοίρας στερήσει κολοβά. Sed nec ipsa tota cujusvis partis ablatione fiunt mutila. Sexta ac septima conditio est, ut sint dissimilaria, ac continua, ἀνομοιομερῆ, καὶ συνεχῆ. Octava, ut non auferatur pars principalis, κυρία τῆς οὐσίας. Nona, ut promineat in re. Αν τρυπηθῇ ἡ κύλιξ, ὁ κολοβὸς, ἀλλ' ἂν τι ᾖ, καὶ ἀπεσήμειον ἔχει. Calix non fit mutilus, si perforetur, sed si [auferatur] ansa, aut [alia] quaedam extremitas. Decima ac ultima conditio est, ut pars, quae aufertur, sit talis extremitas, quae renasci non possit, καὶ τοῦτο ὁ πᾶν, ἀλλ' ὃ μὴ ἔχει γένεσιν. ἀφαιρεθὲν· διὰ τοῦτο οἱ φαλακροὶ ὁ κολοβοί. Eaque non omnis, sed quae ablata non habet generationem [i.e. regenerari nequit.] propterea calvi non sunt mutili. quae postrema verba hoc miri habent, quod prae se ferunt, in calvis semper pilos renasci posse, cum tamen in paucissimis renascantur, & in plerisque (ut qui per aetatem crines amiserunt) ne renasci quidem possint. Nam quod Fonseca, excusando magistro, ait, Etiamsi raro in calvis capilli renascantur, tamen spectata hominum natura nihil esse, cur renasci non possint; non possumus scire, quibus ille oculis spectaverit hominum naturam, ut hoc in ea inveniret, quod in maxima calvorum parte falsum esse, omnis aevi ac loci clamat experientia. Cautior itaque est altera excusatio, Quod Aristoteles intelligere potuit calvos ex morbo, qui saepe sanantur. sed hoc mittentes, atque Aristoteli condonantes, rem ipsam videamus.
units.tr: (In the commentary on the passage.) ...must be a whole, he means that it must have parts differing in position. This he repeats soon after, and expresses more plainly: [Ολως ἂν μὴ ποιεῖ ἡ θέσις διαφορὰν, ψιλὸν κολοβὸν, οἷον ὕδωρ, ἢ πῦρ, ἀλλὰ δεῖ τοιαῦτα εἶναι, ἃ κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν θέσιν ἔχει.] In general, nothing in which position makes no difference is mutilated, such as water or fire; but such things must be those which have a position according to their own nature, with certain parts placed in order by their essence. A little later he again uses the word ὅλα in the same sense: [Οὐδ' ὅλα ὅλα, ἀλλὰ ταῦτα ὁταν μοίρας στερήσει κολοβά.] But wholes are not mutilated as wholes, but those things are mutilated when they are deprived of a part. The sixth and seventh conditions are that the parts be dissimilar and continuous: [ἀνομοιομερῆ, καὶ συνεχῆ]. The eighth, that the principal part of the essence, [κυρία τῆς οὐσίας], not be removed. The ninth, that it stand out in the thing: [Αν τρυπηθῇ ἡ κύλιξ, ὁ κολοβὸς, ἀλλ' ἂν τι ᾖ, καὶ ἀπεσήμειον ἔχει.] A cup does not become mutilated if it is pierced, but if [a handle] or some [other] projecting extremity is removed. The tenth and last condition is that the part removed be such an extremity as cannot grow back, [καὶ τοῦτο ὁ πᾶν, ἀλλ' ὃ μὴ ἔχει γένεσιν. ἀφαιρεθὲν· διὰ τοῦτο οἱ φαλακροὶ ὁ κολοβοί.] and this not every extremity, but that which, once removed, has no generation [i.e., cannot be regenerated]. For this reason the bald are not mutilated. These last words have a remarkable feature: they imply that hair can always grow back on bald heads, whereas in fact it grows back in very few cases, and in most (those who have lost their hair with age) it cannot grow back at all. For Fonseca, excusing his master, says: Even though hair rarely grows back on the bald, yet, considering human nature, there is no reason why it should not be able to grow back. We cannot know with what eyes he looked at human nature, so as to find this in it, when the experience of every age and place cries out that it is false for the greater part of the bald. The other excuse is therefore more cautious: Aristotle could have understood the bald to be those afflicted by a disease, which often is cured. But setting this aside, and pardoning Aristotle, let us look at the matter itself.

units.la: XX. Nemo ista de Mutilo legens, non aliquid Philosophici
units.tr: XX. No one reading these things about the mutilated fails to find something philosophical...
Chapter II.

units.la: phici in ijs latere existimet. nihil tamen esse nisi grammaticam observatiunculam, ex nona conditione apparet, quam praecedentibus cunctis ita superaddit, ut ipsas sine ea nequaquam esse idoneas judicet; quia fieri possit, ut omnia prius dicta in aliqua re inveniantur, quae tamen mutila esse aut fieri non possit, nisi nona haec conditio accedat. at ea plane de medio petita est, neque aliud docet, quam quomodo in vulgato loquendi usu istud vocabulum usurpetur. ibi enim certum est, mutilum seu κολοβὸν id fere dici, quod aliquam extremitatem amisit, sicuti illi, qui in Graecis autoribus versati sunt, noverunt: & notabilis est ad hanc rem locus Galeni, libro 14. de Methodo medendi, cap. 16. Κολο-βάμαῖα ὀνομάζεσι τὰ χεῖλη ἢ πτέρυγιον εἶνὸς ἢ ὠὺς ἐλλείπουσα, Mutilamina appellant, labij, aut alae nasi, aut auris defectum. quanquam non est hoc adeo perpetuum, ut non ad alia quoque interdum transferatur, sicuti exemplis vel ex ipso Aristotele petitis docere est. quippe de internis non minus quam externis partibus hoc usurpat Quarto de Part. 13. aiens, Τὸ δὲ τῶν ἰχθύων γένος ἔλλ μᾶλλον κεκολόβωται τῶν ἐντὸς μορίων. ὅτε γὰρ σπέλη, ὅτε χεῖρας, ὅτε πτέρυγας ἔχουσι. Piscium genus magis adhuc mutilum est [partibus externis] quam partibus internis. namque nec crura habent, nec manus, nec alas. in quibus verbis cum dicat, pisces magis etiamnum mutilos esse quantum ad externas partes, quam quantum ad internas; quumq; mutilationem, aut potius (ut sic dicamus) mutilitatem externam opponat internae, omnino intrinsecus mutilos esse pisces innuit; quia nimirum, uti dixerat supra, ἄπαξων τὴν τῶν σπλάγχνων ἓν ἔχουσι φύσιν, omnem viscerum non habent naturam. Alibi vero mirabili admodum ratione, mutilam esse dicit testudinum naturam, quia habeant vesicam, quae alia φολιδωτὰ, aveseq; & pisces careant. Οὐδὲν ἔχει τῶν τῶν κύσιν, ἀλλὰ ἐπὶ χελῶναι τῶν φολιδωτῶν, καὶ ἐν τούτῳ ἡ φύσις κεκολόβωται μόνον. Nullum horum habet vesicam, prater testudinem in genere crustatorum: atque in his solis natura mutila est. Sed etiamsi perpetuae esset veritatis ista observatio, non dicimus, quae utilitas, eam afferre in philosophiam? sed hoc rogamus, & indignamur, si nihil nisi grammaticum praestare voluit in hac de mutilo tractatione, cur tanto verborum ambitu uti voluerit, ac tot conditionibus obtundere lectorem, quum & decima contineatur in nona (nemo enim vulgo pilos pro parte habet) & omnes praecedentes; praeter octavam (quae eadem est cum quinta) ac sextam. Et sexta quidem vera non est. potest enim & similare corpus, aeque ac dissimilare, habere extremitates extantes; quarum ablatione fiat mutila, sicuti in ossibus est manifestum. reliquas autem omnes conditiones sola nona in se complectitur, ut ipsa pro omnibus potuerit sufficere, neque necesse fuerit eas tam verbose ennumerare. Quae enim res extremitates habet a reliquo corpore extantes, eam necesse est quantam esse, ac divisibilem, partesque situ differentes habere, & majorem esse corpore, quam appendicibus (quis enim unquam vidit rem contrario modo se habentem?) & continuam. Pertot ambages igitur non plus dixit, quam si simpliciter dixisset, Rem mutilam fieri, quando extremitas ejus a reliquo corpore extans, quae non sit principalis Totius pars (ut caput) auferetur.
units.tr: think there is anything philosophical in them. Yet it is nothing but a small grammatical observation, as appears from the ninth condition, which he adds to all the preceding ones in such a way that he judges they are not fit without it, since it could happen that all the things said before are found in some thing which nevertheless cannot be, or be made, mutilated unless this ninth condition is added. But that condition is plainly taken from common usage, and teaches only how this word is used in ordinary speech. For it is certain there that mutilated (or κολοβόν) is commonly said of what has lost some extremity, as those versed in Greek authors know. A notable passage on this point is in Galen, book 14 of the Method of Healing, chapter 16: "They call the lips, or a wing of the nose, or an ear that is lacking, mutilated parts, or a defect of the ear." [Κολο-βάμαῖα ὀνομάζεσι τὰ χεῖλη ἢ πτέρυγιον εἶνὸς ἢ ὠὺς ἐλλείπουσα] Yet this usage is not so fixed that it is never transferred to other things, as examples taken even from Aristotle himself show. Indeed he uses the word of internal parts no less than of external ones, in book 4 of On the Parts of Animals, chapter 13, saying: "The kind of fishes is more mutilated [in its external parts] than in its internal parts, for they have neither legs, nor hands, nor wings." [Τὸ δὲ τῶν ἰχθύων γένος ἔλλ μᾶλλον κεκολόβωται τῶν ἐντὸς μορίων. ὅτε γὰρ σπέλη, ὅτε χεῖρας, ὅτε πτέρυγας ἔχουσι.] In these words, since he says that fishes are more mutilated as to external parts than as to internal ones, and since he opposes external mutilation, or rather (so to speak) mutilatedness, to internal, he clearly implies that fishes are mutilated inwardly as well; because, as he said above, they do not have the whole nature of the viscera [ἄπαξων τὴν τῶν σπλάγχνων ἓν ἔχουσι φύσιν]. Elsewhere, in a most remarkable way, he says that the nature of tortoises is mutilated because they have a bladder, which the scaly animals and the birds and fishes lack: "None of these has a bladder, except the tortoise among the crustaceans; and in these alone nature is mutilated." [Οὐδὲν ἔχει τῶν τῶν κύσιν, ἀλλὰ ἐπὶ χελῶναι τῶν φολιδωτῶν, καὶ ἐν τούτῳ ἡ φύσις κεκολόβωται μόνον.] But even if this observation were a perpetual truth, we ask, what use does it bring to philosophy? Yet this we ask, and we are indignant, if he meant to offer nothing but a grammatical point in this treatment of the mutilated, why he chose to use such a wordy circumlocution and to weary the reader with so many conditions, since the tenth is contained in the ninth (for no one commonly counts hairs as a part), and all the preceding ones, except the eighth (which is the same as the fifth) and the sixth. And the sixth is indeed not true: for a similar body, just as a dissimilar one, can have projecting extremities, by whose removal it becomes mutilated, as is evident in bones. But the ninth condition alone embraces all the others in itself, so that it could have sufficed for them all, and it would not have been necessary to enumerate them so verbosely. For whatever thing has extremities projecting from the rest of the body must be of some size, and divisible, and have parts differing in position, and be larger than its appendages (for who has ever seen a thing in the opposite arrangement?), and be continuous. So, through so many roundabouts he said no more than if he had simply said: a thing becomes mutilated when an extremity of it, projecting from the rest of the body and not a principal part of the whole (such as the head), is removed.

units.la: Quod si quis contendat, non Grammaticè tantum, sed & Philosophicè hanc vocem per istas octo priores conditiones ab Aristotele explicatam; & declaratum, quid sit Mutilum, quatenus Toti opponitur in prima significatione capite 26. posita: Ὅλον λέγεται δ᾽ μηδὲν ἀπέσι μέρος, ἐξ ὧν λέγεται φ᾽ ὅλον φύσει, Totum dicitur, cui nulla abest earum partium, è quibus naturaliter constare dicitur, quae est Fonsecae in commentario ad hunc locum sententia: & sic quoq; inutilem verbositatem culpari necesse est. Quomodo enim Totum sive Integrum breviter definiverat, Illud à quo nulla earum partium abest, ex quibus natura Totum nominatur; ita poterat & de Mutilo definire, esse illud, in quo aliqua pars naturaliter debita, quae sine pernicie Totius abesse potest, desideratur. nunc vero cum illa verbositate, praeterquam quod eandem rem bis dixit, in quinta & octava conditione, veritatis quoq; damnum fecit, ad sola corpora accommodando, ut possint mutilari, sicuti ex septima conditione apparet; quum tamen & in accidentia composita, quorum illa est conditio, ut possint aliquam sui partem amittere, revera mutilatio cadat.
units.tr: But if someone contends that this word, explained by Aristotle through these first eight conditions, is not only grammatical but also philosophical, and that he has declared what the mutilated is insofar as it is opposed to the whole, in the first sense set down in chapter 26: "A whole is said of that from which no part is absent of those from which it is said naturally to be a whole. [Ὅλον λέγεται δ᾽ μηδὲν ἀπέσι μέρος, ἐξ ὧν λέγεται φ᾽ ὅλον φύσει] A whole is said of that to which none of the parts is absent, of which it is naturally said to consist," which is Fonseca's opinion in his commentary on this passage, then it is necessary that this useless wordiness be blamed as well. For just as he had briefly defined the whole, or the complete, as that from which none of those parts is absent of which the thing is naturally called a whole, so he could also have defined the mutilated as that in which some part naturally due, which can be absent without ruin to the whole, is lacking. But as it is, with that verbosity, besides saying the same thing twice in the fifth and eighth conditions, he has also done harm to the truth, by fitting it only to bodies, so that they alone can be mutilated, as appears from the seventh condition; whereas mutilation also falls upon composite accidents, the condition of which is that they can lose some part of themselves.

units.la: XXI. Videtur quidem hoc negare Fonseca, inquiens, Neminem dicturum, concentum mutilum, nisi per translationem. sed hoc exemplum non est accommodatum. namq; neq; per translationem quidem mutilum dicere concentum licet, quum sit de ijs rebus, quæ omnino mutilari non possunt. quod & ipse hic dicit Aristoteles, ἡ γὰρ ἁρμονία κολοβὸς γίνεται. Harmonia nequit mutila fieri. Nequit autem mutilari, quia in nullius est potestate, ut partes ejus separet. quis enim separaverit partes soni? concentus autem est soni genus. quod si quis pauciores fides aut intendat aut pulset, is non mutilat harmoniam, sed aliam adornat. Ea autem Accidentia, quæ possunt aliquam sui partem essentialem deperdere, non metaphoricè, sed maximè proprie sunt mutila, tali aliqua parte ablata, non minus quam corpus quodvis: sicuti è diverso integra sunt, juxta cum substantijs, quando omnes partes suas habent.
units.tr: XXI. Fonseca indeed seems to deny this, saying: "No one will call a concord mutilated, except by a figure of speech." But this example is not suitable. For not even by a figure of speech is it permitted to call a concord mutilated, since it belongs to those things which cannot be mutilated at all. Aristotle himself says this here: "For harmony becomes mutilated." [ἡ γὰρ ἁρμονία κολοβὸς γίνεται] Harmony cannot be made mutilated. It cannot be mutilated because it is not in anyone's power to separate its parts; for who could separate the parts of a sound? Yet concord is a kind of sound. And if someone tunes or plucks fewer strings, he does not mutilate the harmony but produces another. But those accidents which can lose some essential part of themselves are mutilated not metaphorically but most properly, when some such part is removed, no less than any body whatever; just as, on the contrary, they are whole when they have all their parts, in the same way as substances are.

units.la: Declaratio igitur hujus rei, quid Mutilum dici debeat, sita est in eo partium dissimilarium discrimine, supra à nobis tradito, quod nimirum aliæ sint absolutè necessariæ, ita ut sine ijs, aut quacunq; ipsarum, res esse nullo modo possit; aliæ vero non ita simpliciter requisitæ, quin aliquibus ipsarum carere Compositum sine interitu possit. Ubi enim priori modo se habent partes, ibi mutilatio locum non habet, quum res ex talibus partibus composita, esse, nisi tota sit, non queat: quale aliquid in quinta & octava conditione (quæ eodem recidunt) significasse Aristoteles videri possit: quanquam probabilius est, ob exemplum octavæ conditioni appositum; quod per Partes principales intellexerit eas, quas in corpore organico absolute ad vivendum necessarias esse diximus. Quæ vero componuntur ex partibus essentialibus secundi modi, ea quum possint esse non integra, mutilationem admittunt; quum esse mutilum, nihil sit aliud (quod & Fonseca vidit) quam non esse integrum. Quot autem ac quas partes tollere licèat, ut res non pereat, atq; ita non mutila sit, sed nulla, vix aliter in universum est determinare (sicuti jam diximus) nisi per illam conditionem, quam & Aristoteles inter suas conditiones quarto loco posuit, Ut plus relinquatur, quam auferatur. Et in his duabus duntaxat Mutili conditionibus, ab ipso positis, ut & in sexta, aliquod est operæ pretium: reliquæ vix ullam habent utilitatem, quippe partim superfluæ, partim non generales, partim à vero alienæ. Et tantum quidem de Mutilis ac Mutilatione per occasionem dictum esto.
units.tr: The explanation of this matter, then, of what ought to be called mutilated, lies in the distinction between dissimilar parts which we have set out above: namely, that some are absolutely necessary, so that without them, or without any one of them, the thing cannot exist in any way; while others are not so simply required that the composite cannot lack some of them without perishing. For where the parts are in the first manner, there mutilation has no place, since a thing composed of such parts cannot exist unless it is whole; and Aristotle might seem to have meant something of this kind in the fifth and eighth conditions (which come to the same thing); although it is more probable, on account of the example added to the eighth condition, that by principal parts he understood those which we said are absolutely necessary for living in an organic body. But things composed of essential parts of the second kind, since they can exist unimpaired, admit of mutilation, since to be mutilated is nothing other than not to be whole (as Fonseca also saw). But how many and which parts may be removed without the thing perishing, and so be not mutilated but nothing, it is hardly possible to determine in general otherwise than (as we have already said) by that condition which Aristotle too placed fourth among his conditions: that more remains than is taken away. And in these two conditions only of the mutilated, set down by him, as also in the sixth, there is some value; the rest have hardly any usefulness, being partly superfluous, partly not general, partly foreign to the truth. And let so much be said about the mutilated and mutilation, by way of digression.

units.la: XXII. Appendicis loco ad hanc de Partibus tractationem adjicere libet admonitionem, ut in partiendis rebus ab oculos semper habeatur distinctio illa, quam supra è Molinæo attigimus, Partium proximarum & remotarum; quippe cujus neglectus, magnæ sæpe confusionis causa esse possit. Est autem usus hujus discriminis, non in Totis homogeneis seu quantitativis, quandoquidem omnes ibi partes sunt æquè propinquæ, sed tum in Essentialibus, tum in Naturalibus Totis.
