Pleraq; enim istorum è partibus constant, quæ & ipsæ rursus è partibus sunt compositæ. quæ partium partes etiamsi suo jure possunt etiam Totius partes dici, non sunt tamen ipsius partes proximæ, sed remotæ, quippe quæ Totum non componunt per se, sed interventu illarum partium, quæ ex illis componuntur. Exempli gratia; partes hominis Essentiales proximæ sunt, anima gemina, & corpus. horum trium unumquodq; rursus componitur ex Materia & Natura. Natura autem cujusq; nec ipsa componitur è partibus simplicibus, sed ex ejusmodi, quæ ipsæ rursus in alias partes dividuntur. Sic in partibus Conformantibus, corpus humanum proxime dividitur in Caput, Thoracem, Ventrem, Manus, & Pedes; intelligendo nimirum per Manus & Pedes, totos illos artus, quorum extremitates sunt Manus & Pedes proprie dicti: ita enim medici veteres loqui solent, sicuti doctissimus Anatomicorum Andreas Laurentius recte annotavit. Quia autem longum foret ac molestum, singulas istas partes subdividere, sumamus solam Manum,in ea quoq; servantes, ut ex singulis divisionibus unam tantum partem persequamur. Manus partes proximæ sunt (ex Hippocratis atq; Galeni divisione) βραχίων, πῆχυς, ἀγκών, brachium, cubitus, summa manus. Manus summa partes habet tres, carpum, metacarpium, & digitos. quisq; digitus constat ex cute, ungue, ossibus, musculis. Musculos componunt membranæ, vasa, tendines, caro. in carne autem sistendum est, quum infra illam nullæ sint partes Naturales, e quibus ipsa componatur. Fibræ enim, partes sunt quantitativæ, quarum ablatione aut additione caro non aliam patitur mutationem, nisi quod majorem acquirit aut minorem quantitatem. Et hæc satis sint in exemplum, atq; ad demonstrandum, quomodo in proximas semper partes resolutio facienda sit: unde etiam discere est, ubi de partibus rem componentibus, vel Essentialibus, vel Conformantibus seu Naturalibus, quæritur, proximas partes quæri.
units.tr: XXII. As an appendix to this treatment of parts, I should like to add a warning: when dividing things, one must always keep in view the distinction, which I touched on above from Molinaeus, between nearer and more remote parts. Neglecting it can often cause great confusion. This distinction has no use in homogeneous or quantitative wholes, since all their parts are equally near. It applies to essential and natural wholes. Most of these consist of parts, which are themselves in turn composed of parts. These parts of parts may rightly be called parts of the whole, but they are not its nearer parts, only its remote ones, because they do not compose the whole directly but through the intervention of those parts that are composed of them. For example, the nearer essential parts of man are the twofold soul and the body. Each of these three is in turn composed of matter and nature. But the nature of each is not itself made of simple parts; it is made of such parts as are again divided into further parts. So in the conforming parts, the human body is directly divided into head, thorax, belly, hands and feet. Here, of course, by hands and feet I mean the whole limbs whose extremities are the hands and feet properly so called, for this is how the old physicians were accustomed to speak, as the most learned anatomist Andreas Laurentius rightly noted. But since it would be long and tiresome to subdivide each of these parts, let us take the hand alone, keeping to the rule that from each division we follow only one part. According to the division of Hippocrates and Galen, the nearer parts of the hand are the upper arm [βραχίων], the forearm [πῆχυς], the elbow [ἀγκών], that is, the brachium, the cubit, and the top of the hand. The top of the hand has three parts: the carpus, the metacarpus, and the fingers. Each finger consists of skin, nail, bones and muscles. The muscles are composed of membranes, vessels, tendons and flesh. But we must stop at flesh, since below it there are no natural parts out of which it is composed. For fibres are quantitative parts, and by taking away or adding them flesh suffers no change other than acquiring a greater or lesser quantity. Let these examples suffice to show how the resolution must always be made into nearer parts; hence one may also learn that when the question concerns the parts that compose a thing, whether essential or conforming (that is, natural), it is the nearer parts that are sought.
XXIII.

units.la: Quanquam autem nos ea, quæ de Partium discrimine hic diximus, Compositis tantum Naturalibus accommodavimus, (quod sufficiebat pro nostro scopo, atq; hujus operis conditione) facile tamen est, illa ad Artificiosa quoq; & Fortuita Composita accommodare: quod etiamsi Logicum magis est quam Physicum, quamobrem jure à nobis omitti poterat, volumus tamen verbo delibare. Monemus igitur, facilè unumquemq; sese expediturum in discriminandis ejusmodi compositis, eorumq; partibus, si partium characterismos, à nobis datos, ijs adaptet. Quæ enim composita fortuita aut artificiosa deprehendet ejus conditionis, ut partibus additis aut detractis nihil eis nisi in magnitudine accedat aut decedat, ea sciat è partibus constare quantitativis. Talia sunt, verbi gratia, Fascis lignorum, acervus lapidum aut frumenti, grex pecorum, coetus hominum. in quorum plerisq; hoc observandum est, ablationem partium debere sisti, antequam ad minimas partes ventum sit. non enim, ut Elementa & similaria sub minimis portiunculis nomen suum tuentur, ita & illa. Quanquam enim nullam certam & definitam habeant magnitudinem, mini-
units.tr: Although we have applied what we have said here about the distinction of parts only to natural composites (which was enough for our purpose and for the plan of this work), it is still easy to apply these points to artificial and accidental composites as well. This is more a matter for logic than for physics, so we could rightly have left it out, but we want to touch on it briefly. We advise, then, that anyone will easily distinguish such composites and their parts if he fits to them the marks of parts that we have given. Whatever artificial or accidental composites he finds to be of such a kind that adding or removing parts changes them only in size, let him know that they consist of quantitative parts. Examples are a bundle of sticks, a heap of stones or grain, a flock of sheep, a crowd of men. In most of these one must observe that the removal of parts must stop before one comes to the smallest parts. For these do not keep their name down to the smallest particles as the elements and similar parts do. Although they have no certain and definite magnitude, there is a least mag-

units.la: {x} Souris écorchée. {x} filosè, conduite, canaux, tuyaux. ma tamen quædam est magnitudo, ultra quam si procedatur, demendo partes, subsistere non poterunt. duo enim boves aut oves gregem, & quatuor aut quinq; tritici grana, acervum non constituunt. & si quis de his ambigat unum saltem pecus, gregis; aut unum granum, acervi nomen sustinere nequit. Habent autem hoc ista quantitativa cum nonnullis quantitativis naturalibus commune, videlicet cum animis, aut (si quis ita mavult) animabus. namq; & illæ subsistere non valent, si nimium carpantur. Quum autem partium quantitativarum hæc quoq; sit conditio, ut omnes sint inter se similes; hinc liquet, si vel fasces, vel acervus, vel grex, vel cœtus ex dissimilibus constet, non debere illa composita pro quantitativis haberi, sed magis pro dissimilaribus. ablatione enim partium, ipsa rei essentia immutatur. advertendum tamen hic est discrimen inter partes proximas & remotas. verbi gratia, sit grex, qui è decem bubus, totidem asinis, totidem mulis constet; non quodvis illorum animalium est pars essentialis totius cœtus, sed totus ille numerus congenerum animalium. cum itaq; animalia, si quæ demantur, non demantur proxime à toto grege, sed à grege illo partiali, totius gregis parte essentiali; singulorum animalium ablatio essentiam gregis non lædit, quamdiu aliqua ejusdem generis in eo relinquuntur. si vero omnes, quæ sunt ejusdem speciei, simul tollantur, tunc ipsa totius gregis essentia damnum patitur. & quod de grege diximus, idem de variis quoq; hominum cœtibus dictum esto; qui cœtus possunt esse diversigeneres multis respectibus, sexuum, ætatum, ordinum, functionum, aliorum. Artificialia autem pleraq; Totis Naturalibus magis respondent; quum pleraq; artes materiales in eo consistant, ut subjectum suum certo modo conformeant; quare abiata aliqua parte, compositi conformationem lædi necesse est. Latius hæc persequi, non fert animus, quum ad nostrum institutum parum faciant; à quo magis etiamnum abhorret, easdem hasce partium divisiones Compositis intensionalibus, ut numeris, alijsq;, accommodare. Itaq; hæc quidem prætereuntes, illa autem breviter perstrinxisse contenti; ad propositum nunc regredimur.
units.tr: {x} Flayed mouse. {x} Philosophy, conduct, channels, pipes. nitude, beyond which, if one proceeds by removing parts, they cannot subsist. For two oxen or two sheep do not make a herd, and four or five grains of wheat do not make a heap; and if anyone doubts this, one animal alone is not a herd, and one grain cannot bear the name of a heap. These quantitative composites have this in common with some natural quantitative things, namely with souls (or, if anyone prefers, animas): for these too cannot subsist if they are too much cut down. Since this is also the condition of quantitative parts, that they should all be like one another, it is clear that if a bundle, a heap, a flock or a crowd is made up of unlike things, these composites should not be held to be quantitative but rather dissimilar. For by removing parts the very essence of the thing is changed. Yet here one must note the difference between proximate and remote parts. For example, let there be a flock made up of ten oxen, as many asses and as many mules. Not any one of those animals is an essential part of the whole crowd, but that whole number of animals of the same kind is. Since therefore the animals, if any are taken away, are not taken away immediately from the whole flock but from that partial flock, an essential part of the whole flock, the removal of single animals does not harm the essence of the flock as long as some of the same kind remain in it. But if all that belong to the same species are taken away together, then the essence of the whole flock itself suffers loss. What we have said of a flock should be taken to hold also of the various crowds of men, which can be of different kinds in many respects: of sexes, ages, orders, functions, and others. Moreover, most artificial things correspond more to whole natural things, since most material arts consist in shaping their subject in a certain way; so when some part is taken away, the shape of the composite must necessarily be harmed. I do not feel inclined to pursue these matters at greater length, since they contribute little to our plan; and I shrink all the more from applying these same divisions of parts to intensional composites, such as numbers and others. So, passing over these matters and content to have touched on them briefly, we now return to our proposal.
Chapter II.

units.la: XXIV. Ex iis, quae de Partium discrimine diximus, clarum est, Accidentium Compositorum partes, esse Essentiales, ac proinde Accidentibus Compositis non unicum tantum Principium Effectivum, sed & Compositivum assignandum esse. Diximus enim, quaecunque essentialiter concurrunt ad rem aliquam componendam, ea uno communi Elementorum sive Principiorum componentium nomine censenda esse. Sive enim Elementa sint ejusdem ordinis seu Praedicamenti, sive diversorum, illud ad praesens negotium nihil attinet. Ad illud enim, ut idem Principiorum nomen participent, sufficit, ea pariter ad componendam rei essentiam concurrere. fit autem ille concursus varijs modis. nam si utraque aut omnes partes sint substantiae, uniuntur illae vel per contiguitatem & mutuum contactum, veluti Elementa inter se mixta ad unam aliquam Materiam constituendam; vel in modum continentis & contenti: ita enim animae corporibus uniuntur, ut ijs contineantur sive includantur; quod à Peripati quidem decretis (ut omnia fere nostra abhorret plurimum: sed firmis atq; evidentibus argumentis suo loco à nobis probabitur. Si vero altera Essentialium partium sit Substantia, altera Accidens; hoc illi inhaerere necesse est, ut Compositio habeat. Accidentium vero concursus non aliter fieri potest, nisi quod uno communi subjecto utantur. aliter enim illa uniri, nisi per unitatem subiecti, cui ipsa simul inhaereant, non possunt. Et hoc ipsum Aristoteles quoq; alicubi professus est. Ita enim ille in quarto Metaphysicorum: Τὸ συμβεβηκὸς οὐ συμβεβηκὸς συμβεβηκὸς, εἰ μὴ ὅτι ἄμφω συμβέβηκε τινί, Accidens non accidit accidenti, nisi quatenus ambo eidem [subjecto] accidunt. ac magna Aristotelicorum pars in ea est sententia, ut dicant, unum accidens non posse esse alterius accidentis subjectum: de quorum numero est & Scaliger, ut è multis ipsius locis apparet. Comment. in 4. Caus. Non accidenti accidit accidens, sed utrumq; speciei. & adhuc apertius alibi: Nullum accidens alteri accidit accidenti, sed utrumq; subjecta communi se competit, sunt boni praestant.
units.tr: 24. From what we have said about the distinction of parts, it is clear that the parts of composite accidents are essential, and therefore composite accidents must be assigned not only a single efficient principle but also a compositive one. For we have said that whatever concurs essentially to compose a thing is to be counted under the one common name of elements or component principles. Whether the elements belong to the same order or category, or to different ones, does not matter to the present business. For to share the common name of principles, it is enough that they concur together to compose the essence of the thing. This concurrence takes place in various ways. If both or all the parts are substances, they are united either by contiguity and mutual contact, as elements mixed together to make up a single matter, or in the manner of container and contained: thus souls are joined to bodies in such a way that they are contained or enclosed by them. This the Peripatetic doctrines teach (though, as with almost all our own positions, it is greatly at odds with them), but we shall prove it by firm and evident arguments in its proper place. If, however, one of the essential parts is a substance and the other an accident, the accident must inhere in the substance for there to be a composition. The concurrence of accidents, moreover, cannot take place in any way other than by their using one common subject. For they cannot be united in any other way, except through the unity of the subject in which they inhere together. Aristotle himself also professed this somewhere. For thus he says in the fourth book of the Metaphysics: "An accident does not accident an accident, unless both accident to something" [Τὸ συμβεβηκὸς οὐ συμβεβηκὸς συμβεβηκὸς, εἰ μὴ ὅτι ἄμφω συμβέβηκε τινί], that is, an accident does not befall an accident, unless both befall the same [subject]. And a large part of the Aristotelians hold this opinion, that one accident cannot be the subject of another accident. Scaliger is among their number, as appears from many of his passages. In his Commentary on the Fourth Causes: "An accident does not befall an accident, but both belong to a species." And more openly elsewhere: "No accident befalls another accident, but both pertain to one common subject; these are good and excellent points."

units.la: XXV. Pleriq; tamen Aristotelici, (non obstante isto Aristotelis dicto modo posito, id quod alio detorquent, ne ab ipso dissentire videantur) in diversa sunt opinione, atq; omnino statuunt, unum accidens posse in altero accidenti tanquam in subjecto proximo inesse. Inter hos est Suarezius, qui hanc rem ex professo tractat Disputationis 14. Sectione quarta: ubi tria argumenta, ad tuendam istam opinionem, ab ipso asseruntur. Primum est, Omnia accidentia corporalia inesse substantiae media quantitate, id quod ait, videri experientia probari. nam albedinem in superficie extendi, & calorem similiter, cum per corpus diffunditur, in quantitate ejus extendi. Alterum petit a quibusdam Accidentibus, quae non sunt res omnino distinctae ab Accidentibus in quibus fundantur, sed modi eorum, ut est figura respectu quantitatis, & motus, & ubi seu praesentia localis respectu ejusdem, & relatio (si est modus diversus) respectu sui fundamenti. Tertium ducit a Spiritualibus Accidentibus (ut & Materialibus, quae proportionem cum illis habent) in quibus hoc ait esse certissimum. necessarium enim esse, ut habitus operativi immediatè inhaerant in potentijs, ad quas juvandas ordinantur: & hac ratione scientiam recipi in intellectu, ac species in potentia cognoscente. Et sic etiam Theologos dicere, quod fides sit in intellectu, & charitas in voluntate. eandem quoque vel majorem rationem esse de actibus vitalibus, quae essentialiter sint actus immanentes, unde necesse sit recipi immediate in proximo principio, à quo procedunt.
units.tr: 25. Most Aristotelians, however (not withstanding the saying of Aristotle just cited, which they twist to other meanings so as not to seem to dissent from him), are of a different opinion, and altogether maintain that one accident can inhere in another accident as in its nearest subject. Among these is Suarez, who treats this matter expressly in Disputation 14, Section 4, where he sets out three arguments in defence of that opinion. The first is: All corporeal accidents inhere in substance through the medium of quantity, which he says is seen to be proved by experience: for whiteness spreads over a surface, and heat likewise, when it diffuses through a body, extends through its quantity. The second he draws from certain accidents which are not things altogether distinct from the accidents in which they are grounded, but modes of them, such as figure with respect to quantity, motion, place or local presence with respect to the same, and relation (if it is a distinct mode) with respect to its foundation. The third he derives from spiritual accidents (as also from material ones, which have a proportion to them), in which he says this is most certain: that operative habits must inhere immediately in the powers to which they are ordained to assist; and in this way science is received in the intellect, and species in the knowing power. And so, he says, theologians also say that faith is in the intellect and charity in the will. The same or even greater reason holds, he says, for vital acts, which are essentially immanent acts, and so must be received immediately in the proximate principle from which they proceed.

units.la: Sed haec partim ejusmodi sunt, ut nihil nobis adversentur; partim autem à veritate sunt aliena. Quantum enim ad illa, quae in tertia classe ponit Suarez, etiamsi ea omnia essent certissima, atq; ita in ijs se res haberet, ac ipse asserit (id quod impraesens non est nobis discutiendum) nihilominus staret axioma nostrum, quippe non universim à nobis conceptum, sed cum peculiari respectu ad ea accidentia, è quorum coetu atq; congerie natura componitur, ac quae ad originem atq; primam rerum naturalium constitutionem concurrunt. Ista autem, quae hic à Suarezio memorantur, alterius sunt generis, neq; rebus primitus constituendis inserviunt, sed rebus jam constitutis atq; existentibus demum accedunt. De relatione autem quod dicit Suarez, multo minus huic pertinet, quum ne sit quidem ens Physicum relatio, sed mere Logicum, praeterea[?] adeo incertum est, quod in hoc exemplo ponitur, ut ne ipse quidem Suarez audeat id pro certo affirmare. Sed & Figura, Modus, atq; Ubi, non sunt accidentia per se, sed modi tantum accidentis, ut ipse vult: quod ipsum si vel maxime verum esset (quum revera non alicujus Accidentis, sed ipsius Substantiae isti sint modi) staret tamen quod diximus, Accidens non accidere accidenti: quippe id intellectum volumus non de ejusmodi accidentibus, quae duntaxat modi sunt aliorum accidentium (qualia, certè dantur, ut visibilitas in colore, aliaq; similia) sed quae realia sunt accidentia per se, suamq; sibi essentiam habent, ab alterius accidentis essentia nequaquam dependentem.
units.tr: But these arguments are partly of such a kind that they do nothing against us, and partly are alien to the truth. For as to those which Suarez places in the third class, even if they were all most certain, and things were so in them as he asserts (which is not for us to discuss at present), our axiom would still stand, since it is not conceived by us universally, but with a particular reference to those accidents out of whose company and heap nature is composed, and which concur to the origin and first constitution of natural things. But those that Suarez here mentions are of another kind, and do not serve to constitute things in the first place, but come to things already constituted and existing. As for the relation that Suarez mentions, it bears even less on this matter, since relation is not a physical being at all but merely logical. Besides, what is put forward as an example here is so uncertain that Suarez himself does not dare to affirm it as certain. But figure, mode and place are not accidents in their own right but merely modes of an accident, as he himself holds. Even if this were most true (since in truth these are modes not of some accident but of substance itself), what we have said would still stand: that an accident does not befall an accident. For we wish this to be understood not of such accidents as are merely modes of other accidents (of which there certainly are some, such as visibility in colour, and other similar things), but of accidents which are real and accidents in their own right, having their own essence and not depending on the essence of another accident.

units.la: Quantum vero ad Accidentia corporalia; supponit hic Suarez (quod & in ijs supponit, de quibus jam nunc diximus) Quantitatem esse Accidens Materiae inhaerens, realiter ab ipsa distinctum: quo etiam dato, ne sic quidem satis firmum esset, quod dicitur, Accidentia corporalia substantiae medio Accidente, nimirum quantitate, inhaerere. Non enim sequitur: Quantitas est accidens, & in omni corpore est quantitas: ergo quaecunque passiones corpori accidunt, accidunt ipsi ratione aut interventu quantitatis. Hoc enim non debebant sibi sumere, sed probare: quod cum non faciant, ignoscent nobis, si eadem facilitate illud negamus, quod ab ipsis asseritur. Sed & gravem praeterea habemus rationem, cur illud negemus. Quantitas enim non est Accidens, neque substantia est quanta, quia ipsi inhaereat accidens, quod quantitas vocetur, sed per se, & essentialiter: quā de re cum alibi agendum sit, non est ut hic plura verba fiant.
units.tr: As for corporeal accidents, Suarez here presupposes (as he also does in those matters of which we have just spoken) that quantity is an accident inhering in matter, really distinct from it. Even granting this, it would not be firm enough that corporeal accidents inhere in substance through the intermediate accident, namely quantity. For it does not follow: quantity is an accident, and in every body there is quantity; therefore whatever affections befall a body befall it by reason of, or through the intervention of, quantity. For they ought not to assume this but to prove it; and since they do not do so, they will pardon us if with equal ease we deny what they assert. But we have, besides, a weighty reason for denying it. For quantity is not an accident, nor is substance quantified because an accident inheres in it which is called quantity, but through itself and essentially. This matter must be treated elsewhere, so there is no need to say more about it here.

units.la: Quod si igitur Quantitas non est Accidens omnino (id quod & de Peripateticis quamplurimi juxta nobiscum sentiunt) non erit sane alterius Accidentis subjectum; ac proinde corruit haec probatio: quae nequicquam confirmatur ex mysterio Eucharistiae, ubi in quantitate separata inhaerant accidentia: tale enim mysterium nos nullum agnoscimus, imò illam doctrinam habemus pro immani atq; crassissimo errore: de qua re nos plura alias.
units.tr: If then quantity is not an accident at all (which very many of the Peripatetics also think, agreeing with us), it will certainly not be the subject of another accident; and therefore this proof collapses. It is vainly confirmed from the mystery of the Eucharist, where accidents inhere in separated quantity. For we acknowledge no such mystery; indeed we hold that doctrine to be a monstrous and very gross error. We shall say more about this elsewhere.

units.la: [Marginal handwritten annotations are not printed text and are not transcribed here.] non dicemus, cum ad Theologiam tota pertineat. hoc tantum dicimus, fieri eam à Deo non posse, nisi ut totam Naturam destruat. quomodo enim quantitas separetur à suo subiecto, in quo nulla inest? inesse enim nequit, cum quantitas non sit ens substantiæ inhærens, sed quidem duntaxat modus substantiæ: cuius rei pleniorem disputationem alteri loco, ut diximus, reservamus. Atq; ex his satis apparet, causam non esse, cur quisquam de hoc nostro axiomate, quo Accidens accidenti tanquam subiecto inhærere negamus, dubitet ob ea, quæ in contrariu n à Suarezio disputantur: quum eorum alia veritatem non habeant, alia vero ad præsentem disquisitionem minime pertineant, ac proinde contra nos non faciant, qui de solis Accidentibus realibus, suamq; propriam essentiam sortitis, & quidem ijs duntaxat, quæ ad rerum naturalium ortum concurrunt, hanc assertionem intelligi volumus. &sic ratum manet, quod dicebamus; Non dari Accidens compositum, nisi quatenus Accidentia componentia uni communi subiecto inhærent.
units.tr: [Marginal handwritten annotations are not printed text and are not transcribed here.] We shall not say more, since it belongs wholly to theology. We say only this: that it cannot be done by God unless he destroys all of nature. For how can quantity be separated from its subject, in which it is not present? It cannot be present in it, since quantity is not a being inhering in substance but merely a mode of substance; a fuller discussion of this matter we reserve, as we said, for another place. And from these things it sufficiently appears that there is no reason why anyone should doubt this axiom of ours, by which we deny that an accident can inhere in an accident as in a subject, because of those things which Suarez disputes to the contrary. For some of them do not have truth, and others do not pertain to the present inquiry, and therefore do not work against us. We wish this assertion to be understood only of real accidents which possess their own essence, and indeed only of those which concur to the origin of natural things. And so it remains established, as we were saying: there is no composite accident, except insofar as the component accidents inhere in one common subject.

units.la: XXVI. Sed opponit se ex alia parte Scaliger, qui aliam adhuc tradit Accidentium compositionem, ut ab hac nostra, ita ab illa altera, de qua è Suarezio diximus, diversam. Omnia enim Accidentia ipse ex Esse & Essentia componit. Utitur autem hisce vocabulis suo quodam proprio ac peculiari modo, non quomodo vulgo solent Peripatetici, inter quos sufficienter disputari solet, an detur compositio ex Esse & Essentia. quippe per Essentiam intelligunt ipsum rei τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι; per Esse vero, actualem ejus existentiam: sicuti videre est tum apud alios, tum apud Suarezium Disp. 31. ubi verbose tota hæc disputatio (quam nescias morosiorem-ne dicas an inutiliorem) agitatur. Scaliger autem non sic hæc intelligit, sed alio quodam modo, sicuti apparet ex ipsius verbis, quæ huc ascripsimus. Commentario in sextum Theophrasti de Causis Plantarum, Accidens, inquit, non habet Materiam, sed esse; non Formam, sed Essentiam. esse saporis est, hoc ipsum quod ipsa Mixtio; essentia vero id, quod ex ipsa Mixtione constatur. sic ingenijs acrioribus Esse
units.tr: XXVI. But Scaliger opposes us from another quarter. He sets out yet another composition of accidents, different both from ours and from the one we took from Suárez. For he composes all accidents out of Esse and Essence. He uses these words, however, in a peculiar way of his own, not as the Peripatetics commonly do, among whom it is customary to argue at length whether there is a composition of Esse and Essence. They understand by Essence the very what-it-was-to-be-the-thing (τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι), and by Esse its actual existence. This may be seen both in others and in Suárez, Disp. 31, where the whole disputation is pursued at great length (you would not know whether to call it more tedious or more useless). Scaliger, however, does not understand these terms in this way but in another manner, as appears from his own words, which we have quoted here. In his commentary on the sixth book of Theophrastus, On the Causes of Plants, he says: "An accident has no matter but esse; no form but essence. The esse of a flavour is the mixture itself; its essence is what is constituted from the mixture itself. Thus for sharper minds, esse
Chapter II.

units.la: Esse sanitatis est ipse concursus atq; cætus qualitatum: Essentia, est ipsa qualitas, quæ creatur ex consensu illo, ab ipse deinde Esse, & ab ipsa Essentia saporis, procedit proprius affectus, qui est certa ratio movendi gustum. & Exercitatione 325. alijs verbis eandem rem docens, statuit, Accidentia omnia habere suam Essentiam, constatam ex potentia & actu; hoc est habere aliquid internum tanquam potentiam, & aliquid tanquam Formam, qua sint hoc quod sint. è quibus verbis apparet, illum in hoc negotio parum sibi constare de usu vocis Essentiæ. namq; hic Essentiam vocat, totum id quod sunt Accidentia. In priori autem loco Essentiam ita dicit, tanquam si esset pars tantum eorum. quippe quod illic Essentiam, id hic Actum dicit; sicuti Potentiam, quod illic Esse. quod enim priori loco dicit, Accidentia constare ex Esse & Essentia, respondet ijs, quæ hic asseruntur, Accidentium Essentiam è Potentia & Actu esse constatam. quod idem est, ac si diceret, in omni Accidente esse aliquid, quod se habeat instar Materiæ substantialis, & aliquid, quod instar Formæ substantialis, è quibus duobus inter se unitis consurgat unum totum Accidens, quomodo ex Materia & Forma dicunt consurgere unam totam substantiam. Potentiam enim non ita hic intelligit, quomodo illud in Potentia esse dicitur, quod nondum habet actualem ullam existentiam. ex tali enim Potentia, & Actu illi opposito, fieri aliquod compositum, non dicunt Peripatetici, idq; fieri posse, expresse negat Suarez. Respexit igitur cum hac phrasi Scaliger illud Peripateticorum dogma, quod Materia & Forma sint duæ substantiæ incompletæ, ita ut Materia se habeat instar Potentiæ, Forma instar actus; quorum unione, congesso compositum substantiale constituatur: cujus compositionis proportionem dicunt etiam esse in compositione ex genere & differentia. namq; etiam genus & differentia comparari ut potentiam & actum, per se ordinata ad constituendum unum in suo genere completum. atq; hoc pacto dicunt Angelos quoq; componi ex actu & potentia, quatenus componuntur ex genere & differentia, sicut homo componitur. nitur ex animali & rationali. sed hanc ex potentia generis, & actu differentiæ, compositionem fatentur esse non realem, sed mere rationalem; ut certe est. Scaliger autem non talem, sed realem Accidentium compositionem inculcat. quanquam enim Exerc. 325. nonnulla admiscet de illa rationali Accidentium compositione ex Genere & Differentia (cui nos neq; in Accidentibus, neq; in substantijs refragamur, quanquam eam à Physica, utpote Logicam duntaxat & intentionalem, rejicimus) realem tamen compositionem ipsum intelligere, multa ibidem scripta manifeste evincunt, è quibus sufficiat hæc apponere in specimen: Quamobrem colorem dicemus habere subjectam substantiam, cui inhaeret: in se verò, & potentiam & actum, ex quo unum fit in subjecto, & à subjecto. ex qua Essentia producitur proprium illud, visile. & ille quoq; locus è commentarijs ad Theophrastum adeo est clarus, ut non relinquat ullam dubitationem, quin de reali compositione sermo sit.
units.tr: is the very concurrence and assembly of the qualities. Essence is the quality itself, which is created from that agreement. From the esse itself, and from the essence of the flavour, there proceeds a proper affect, which is a certain manner of moving the taste." And in Exercitation 325, teaching the same thing in other words, he lays down that "all accidents have their own essence, made up of potency and act; that is, they have something within as potency, and something as form, by which they are what they are." From these words it appears that he was rather inconsistent in this matter about the use of the word Essence. Here he calls Essence the whole of what accidents are, but in the earlier passage he speaks of it as if it were only a part of them. For what there he calls Essence, here he calls Act; and what there he calls Esse, here he calls Potency. What he says in the earlier place, that accidents consist of Esse and Essence, corresponds to what is asserted here, that the essence of accidents is made up of potency and act. This is the same as saying that in every accident there is something which stands in the place of substantial matter, and something which stands in the place of substantial form, and that from the union of these two a single whole accident arises, just as they say a single whole substance arises from matter and form. For he does not understand "potency" here in the sense in which that is said to be "in potency" which does not yet have any actual existence. The Peripatetics do not say that a compound arises from such a potency and its opposite act, and Suárez expressly denies that this can happen. Scaliger, then, with this phrasing, had in view the Peripatetic dogma that matter and form are two incomplete substances, such that matter stands as potency and form as act, and from their union a substantial compound is constituted. They say the proportion of this composition is also found in the composition from genus and difference, for genus and difference too are compared as potency and act, ordered by themselves to constitute one thing complete in its own kind. In this way they say angels too are composed of act and potency, insofar as they are composed of genus and difference, just as man is composed of animal and rational. But they admit that this composition from the potency of the genus and the act of the difference is not real but merely rational, as it certainly is. Scaliger, however, insists not on such a composition but on a real composition of accidents. Although in Exercitation 325 he mixes in some remarks about that rational composition of accidents from genus and difference (to which we object neither in accidents nor in substances, although we reject it from Physics, as merely logical and intentional), the many things written there clearly prove that he means a real composition. Of these it will suffice to set down this one sample: "Wherefore we shall say that colour has a subject substance in which it inheres; but in itself it has both potency and act, from which one thing arises in the subject and from the subject. From this Essence there is produced that proper thing, the visible." And that passage from the commentaries on Theophrastus is so clear that it leaves no doubt that the discussion concerns a real composition.

units.la: XXVII. Quanquam autem in hac opinione plurimum sibi placet Scaliger de ingenij acumine; manifeste tamen falsa est. Illud quidem, quod ab Essentia Accidentis procedere ait proprium affectum, qualis in sapore fit, Movere gustum, in colore visibilitas, tolerari quodammodo potest, si commode intelligatur, ut nimirum Proprius affectus non sit Accidens aliquod, quod alteri accidenti accidat, sed essentialis modus ejus. tales enim modos dari, ut in substantijs, ita in accidentibus, qui non sint aliquid realiter ab ipsis diversum, sed plane essentiales, alibi docebimus. verbum tamen Procedendi nequaquam hic quadrat, neq; commode adhiberi potest: & multo etiam minus, alterum illud Producendi, quod in eadem re usurpat. Quantum verò ad rem ipsam attinet, atq; ad realem illam Accidentium è Potentia & Actu compositionem; plurimum ea à veritate abhorret. id quod vel ipse intellexisset, si hoc suum commentum explorasset in alijs Accidentibus ipsi notioribus, qualia sunt calor & frigus. magnopere enim velimus scire, quod
units.tr: XXVII. Although Scaliger takes great pleasure in the keenness of his wit in this opinion, it is nonetheless manifestly false. That he says a proper affect proceeds from the essence of an accident, such as moving the taste in the case of flavour, or visibility in the case of colour, can be tolerated to some degree if it is understood properly: namely, that the proper affect is not some accident which befalls another accident, but an essential mode of it. For such modes exist in accidents as in substances, which are not really something distinct from them but plainly essential, as we shall teach elsewhere. However, the verb "to proceed" does not fit here at all, nor can it be used suitably; and still less the other verb, "to produce", which he uses for the same thing. As for the matter itself, and that real composition of accidents out of potency and act, it is very far from the truth. He himself would have understood this if he had tested his opinion on other accidents better known to him, such as heat and cold. For we would very much like to know, quod
Chapter II.

units.la: quod assignaturus ifuerit Esse caloris, ab Essentia caloris diversum, è quo Esse, & è qua Essentia totus ipse calor conflaretur. Nunc autem commentum vero vacuum expertus est in exemplis æque falsis, saporis & coloris; in quorum Accidentium origine, essentia, & proximo subjecto, non plus ipse vidit, quam cæcus lucis videt media nocte. secutus enim Aristotelem & Galenum, receptamq; totæ Peripato sententiam, putavit utrumq; ex Mixtione oriri, sicut de sapore planum faciunt vel ipsa verba superius ex ipso allegata, ut alios innumeros ex iisdem commentariis locos, ubi idem prodit, non sit opus advocare. de colore verò & multa in eodem opere, & Exercitatio 325. docent, illumrita sensisse, quod calor ex elementorum mixtione oriatur, sed cum luce; quam etiam ad saporis generationem adhibet, sed alio respectu, quatenus nimirum calefacit. quod absurdissimum commentum tam vehementer illi arrisit, ut temperare nequiverit, quin illud pro subtilissimo, marginali nota extolleret. qua ratione tantum non interclusit sibi ignorantiæ veniam, quam promeritus videbatur aperta confessione, sect. 4. ubi ait. Quid sit color, haud facile est definire. latet enim natura hæc, sicut & alia rerum species, in profundissima caligine inscitiæ humanæ, hic sane verum dixit, & justissimam habuit hujus sive querelæ sive confessionis occasionem. omnino enim Cimmeriæ ipsi tenebræ fuerunt, quemadmodum in alia pleraq; Naturæ parte, ita in exploratione Coloris & Saporis; sicuti ex iis, quæ in secundo ac tertio hujus operis libro (quorum in hoc de essentia, in illo de subjecto horum aliorumq; accidentium nobis erit pertractandum) dicentur, manifestum fiet.
units.tr: what he would have assigned as the Being of heat, different from the Essence of heat, out of which Being and Essence the whole of heat itself would be put together. But now he has tried his fiction in examples just as false, those of taste and colour. On the origin, essence and proximate subject of these accidents he saw no more than a blind man sees of light at midnight. For, following Aristotle and Galen and the view received throughout the whole Peripatetic school, he thought that both arise from mixture, as the very words quoted from him above on taste make plain; there is no need to call up the countless other passages from the same commentaries where the same view appears. But concerning colour, both in the same work and in Exercise 325, they teach that he understood the matter quite wrongly, holding that heat arises from the mixture of the elements, but with light, which he also uses for the generation of taste, though in another respect, namely insofar as it warms. This most absurd fiction pleased him so greatly that he could not refrain from extolling it in a marginal note as most subtle. By this means he almost cut off for himself the pardon for ignorance which he seemed to have earned by an open confession, in section 4, where he says: "What colour is, is not easy to define. For this nature lies hidden, like other kinds of things, in the deepest darkness of human ignorance." Here he certainly spoke the truth, and he had a most just occasion for this complaint or confession. For indeed Cimmerian darkness was all around him, as in most other parts of nature, so in the investigation of colour and taste; as will become clear from what will be said in the second and third books of this work (of which the essence is to be treated in the one, and the subject of these and other accidents in the other).

units.la: Propius ad verum accedunt, quæ de sanitate dicit: nam si pro Qualitatum substitutus Accidentium (namq; & alia, præter qualitates, Accidentia, si non realia, saltem ab ipso pro realibus habita, ad sanitatis integritatem requiruntur) vera est sententia. Omnino enim Sanitas est certorum Accidentium concursus. hoc tamen exemplum nequicquam ab eo adhibetur; ad astruendum, quod omnia Accidentia è Potentia & Actu compositam habeant Essentiam. tiam. Etenim cum in prioribus exemplis conatus sit ostendere, Accidentis essentiam, sive totum ipsum Accidens, ex illis duabus partibus, potentiali & actuali, componi: hic omnes partes componentes habet pro potentia; pro Actu autem non aliquam e partibus, sed ipsum compositum: quem errorem non est ut hic denuo refutemus, quum supra in eadem hac sectione alterum plane consimilem refutaverimus in Suarezio; qui cum assereret, in omni compositione esse aliquid simile materiae, & aliquid simile formae, hoc est (ex consuetudine Peripateticorum, quam alibi ipse, & hic sequitur Scaliger.) aliquid potentiale, & aliquid actuale: illud in Homogeneis probaturus, non partes partibus, uti in heterogeneis fecerat, opponebat, quarum aliae pro Materia, aliae pro Forma essent; sed omnes simul partes, materia; ipsum autem compositum, formae vicem obtinere ajebat. Cui errori cum plane similem errorem hic erret Scaliger, non est ut actum agamus, ea, quae semel jam dicta sunt, repetendo.
units.tr: Closer to the truth is what he says about health. For if "accidents" is substituted for "qualities" (since other accidents besides qualities, if not real, at least regarded by him as real, are required for the integrity of health), his view is true. Indeed health is altogether a concurrence of certain accidents. Yet this example is adduced by him to no purpose, in order to establish that all accidents have an Essence composed of Potency and Act. For although in the earlier examples he tried to show that the essence of an accident, or the whole accident itself, is composed of those two parts, the potential and the actual, here he takes all the component parts as the potency, and for the act not some one of the parts but the composite itself. We need not refute this error again here, since above in this same section we have already refuted a quite similar one in Suarez. He asserted that in every composition there is something like matter and something like form, that is (following the custom of the Peripatetics, which he himself follows elsewhere and here Scaliger follows), something potential and something actual. In proving this for homogeneous things, instead of setting part against part as he had done for heterogeneous things, some of which would be matter and others form, he set all the parts together as matter, and said the composite itself takes the place of form. Since Scaliger here falls into an error quite similar to this, there is no need to act at length, repeating what has already been said.

units.la: Apparet igitur hanc Accidentium Compositionem, à Scaligero confictam, esse admodum futilem, cum neq; illius eam argumentorum momentis stabiliat; & exempla, quae pro omni probatione affert, manifestae falsitatis convincantur. Et sic relinquitur, ut verum sit, quod dicebamus, nullam esse Accidentium compositionem, nisi quatenus in uno subjecto concurrunt. Quare sequitur etiam, ut sicuti Accidentia simplicia solum agnoscunt Principium Efficiens, ita Accidentia componentia, praeter Efficiens, alterum quoq; habeant Principium, Constitutivum, nimirum, ipsa Accidentia particularia, sive (si ita loqui liceret) partialia.
units.tr: It therefore appears that this composition of accidents, invented by Scaliger, is quite worthless, since it is supported neither by the weight of his arguments, and the examples he brings forward as all his proof are shown to be manifestly false. And so it remains true, as we were saying, that there is no composition of accidents except insofar as they concur in one subject. It follows also that, just as simple accidents recognise only an Efficient Principle, so composite accidents, besides the Efficient, must also have another Principle, a Constitutive one, namely the particular accidents themselves, or (if one may so speak) the partial accidents.

units.la: XXVIII. Quod si auscultare Suarezio velimus, ipsum quoq; Subjectum inter Principia Accidentium erit collocandum. Materia enim rei, inter Principia locum tenet: ipse autem acriter contendit, subjectum esse Materiam Accidentis. Tractat de hac re Disp.14. sect.1. aitq; Subjectum esse revera causam Materialem Accidentis, quandoquidem ab illo dependet Accidens. Entitatem enim accidentalem per se subsistere
units.tr: XXVIII. But if we are willing to listen to Suarez, the Subject itself must also be placed among the Principles of accidents. For the matter of a thing holds a place among the Principles, and he vehemently contends that the subject is the matter of the accident. He treats this matter in Disputation 14, section 1, and says: "The subject is in truth the material cause of the accident, since the accident depends on it. For an accidental entity cannot subsist of itself."
Chapter II.

units.la: subsistere non posse, sed indigere subjecto, in quo sustentetur, & ideo indigere causa materiali, tanquam necessaria ex natura rei, ut subsistere possit, cum Accidentis sit, inesse in ipsa autem ratione inhaerendi, includi subjectum, & consequenter materialem causam: quae non sit modo materialis causa Accidentis quoad Unionem, sed & quoad Entitatem, quam in suo genere causet mediante unione; neque esse causam solum in facto esse, sed etiam in fieri. unumquodque enim Accidens pendere ab aliquo subjecto in fieri, atq; ita habere materialem causam sua effectionis, eo modo quo fieri naturaliter potest. Sed his omnibus non plus probatur, quam quod Accidens existere per se non possit, ac propterea subjectum requirat, in quo insit. inde tamen non sequitur, subjectum illud esse causam materialem ipsius accidentis.
units.tr: to subsist, but needs a subject in which it is sustained, and so needs a material cause, as something necessary from the nature of the thing, in order to subsist. Since it is an accident, to inhere is part of its very nature, and so the subject, and consequently a material cause, is included in that nature. This cause is material not only for the accident's union but also for its being, which it brings about in its own kind through the union. It is the cause not only in existing but also in coming to be. For every accident depends on some subject in its coming to be, and so has a material cause of its production, in the way such things can naturally come about. But all this proves no more than that an accident cannot exist by itself and therefore requires a subject in which it inheres. Yet it does not follow from this that the subject is the material cause of the accident itself.

units.la: Et in proclivi est ostendere, quod subjectum male appelletur Materia Accidentis. hoc enim fieri omnino praeter mentem Aristotelis (cujus autoritatem isti profitentur sese sequi) claret ex definitione Materiae, quam 1. Physic. 9. & 5. Metaph. 2. tradit hunc in modum; Τὸ πρῶτον ὑποκείμενον ἐξ ὧν γίνεταί ἐνυπάρχοντος, id quod primum subjacet unicuique, ex quo fit inexistente. quae definitio falsa est; aut falsum est, Subjectum esse Materiam Accidentis. nemo enim inter ipsos ferat dicentem, quod Accidens fiat ex subjecto inexistente. namq; Accidens fieri è subjecto, quanquam dictu absurdum est, ipsi tamen, aut ipsorum plerique non repudiaverint. somniant enim, Accidentia educi è potentia subjecti, atq; eo respectu non dubitaverint dicere, Accidens fieri è subjecto: quandoquidem ne de Forma quidem verentur ita loqui. Ait enim Suarez, Materiam ex qua dici, vel respectu compositi quod ex illa constat; vel respectu Formae, quae ex illa educitur. Sed quanquam hoc sibi permittant, non tamen sibi permittunt, ut dicant, Accidens fieri ex subjecto inexistente. ast hoc necesse erat, ex Aristotelis definitione. Et quam absonum sit, Subjectum dicere Materiam Accidentis, ex eo apparet, quod in tota Disputatione decimaquarta, quam impendit isti quaestioni de causa materiali accidentium, vix semel audet dicere, subjectum esse materiam accidentium, sed pro materia semper dicit causam materialem: quum tamen revera nihil intersit apud ipsos, hocne an illud dicas: quomodo etiam causam formalem & finalem pro forma & fine dicunt. Quanquam igitur revera idem sit in Peripato, Materiamne dicas an Causam materialem; maluit tamen hoc, quam illo modo dicere, quia minus eminere videtur istius opinionis absurditas, si subjectum dicatur Materialis causa Accidentium, quam si simpliciter eorum materia dicatur. hoc autem consilio Suarezium usurpasse istam phrasin, inde apparet, quod non semel aut iterum, sed creberrime in ista disputatione hanc rem inculcans, quod Subjectum sit Materia Accidentium, perpetuo hoc servat (uno duntaxat aut altero loco excepto) ut subjectum appellet non materiam Accidentium, sed Causam Materialem. Quid opus igitur est, ut demonstremus istius opinionis absurditatem, quae tanta est, ut ipse cujus autor vereatur planis verbis, quod sentit, proferre? Porro inepte subjectum appellari Accidentis materiam, praeterquam quod suam absurditatem abunde prae se fert, ostendimus ex eo, quod nequaquam Subjecto competit, ut Accidentis principium dicatur. Ast si materia est, est principium, cum omnis materia sit principium. Non posse autem subjectum dici Accidentis principium, apparet ex definitione Principij, quam ex ipsa rei natura deprompsimus. Quippe Principium definiebatur id, a quo res originem suam accepit. Accidens autem non accipit originem suam a subjecto, sed in subjecto. Fatemur quidem, Accidens non posse subsistere nisi in subjecto, ideoque non posse produci nisi in subjecto. sed hoc argumento si subjectum inter Principia allegimus, nihil obstat quin & locum eidem allegamus. aeque enim impossibile est, ut res sit aut fiat non in loco, quam ut Accidens sit aut fiat non in subjecto. itaque incassum laborat Suarezius, qui ad probandum, quod subjectum Accidentium sit eorundem causa materialis, hoc solo utitur argumento, idque iterum ac iterum repetit, Quod Accidens necessario insit in subjecto: sicuti ex ipsius verbis, quae supra posuimus, apparet.
units.tr: And it is easy to show that the subject is wrongly called the matter of the accident. That this is entirely contrary to the mind of Aristotle, whose authority these men profess to follow, is clear from the definition of matter which he gives in Physics 1.9 and Metaphysics 5.2, in this way: that which is first underlying each thing, from which it comes to be by being in it [Τὸ πρῶτον ὑποκείμενον ἐξ ὧν γίνεταί ἐνυπάρχοντος]. Either this definition is false, or it is false that the subject is the matter of the accident. For no one among them would tolerate someone saying that an accident comes to be from an inhering subject. Yet that an accident comes to be from its subject, however absurd it sounds, is not rejected by them, or at least by most of them. For they dream that accidents are educed from the potency of the subject, and with respect to this they do not hesitate to say that the accident comes to be from the subject, since they do not even shrink from speaking this way about form. For Suarez says that matter from which is said either with respect to the composite which consists of it, or with respect to the form which is educed from it. But although they allow themselves this, they do not allow themselves to say that the accident comes to be from its inhering subject; yet this would have to follow from Aristotle's definition. And how absurd it is to call the subject the matter of the accident appears from the fact that throughout the whole fourteenth disputation, which he devotes to this question about the material cause of accidents, he scarcely once dares to say that the subject is the matter of accidents, but always speaks of the material cause in place of matter. Yet in truth, among these men, it makes no difference whether you say this or that; just as they also say the formal and final causes in place of form and end. Although, therefore, in the Peripatetic school it is really the same whether you say matter or material cause, he preferred the latter, because the absurdity of this opinion seems less glaring if the subject is called the material cause of accidents than if it is simply called their matter. That Suarez used this phrase deliberately is clear from the fact that, though he repeatedly and constantly inculcates in this disputation that the subject is the matter of accidents, he consistently (with only one or at most two exceptions) calls the subject not the matter of accidents but their material cause. Why then is there need for us to demonstrate the absurdity of this opinion, which is so great that its own author shrinks from stating what he thinks in plain words? Moreover, that it is inappropriate to call the subject the matter of an accident, apart from the absurdity it plainly displays, we show from the fact that it does not in any way belong to the subject to be called a principle of the accident. For if it is matter, it is a principle, since all matter is a principle. But that the subject cannot be called a principle of the accident is clear from the definition of principle which we drew from the very nature of the thing. For a principle was defined as that from which a thing has its origin. But an accident does not receive its origin from the subject, but in the subject. We admit indeed that an accident cannot subsist except in a subject, and therefore cannot be produced except in a subject. But if on this argument we count the subject among the principles, nothing prevents us from counting place among them too. For it is just as impossible for a thing to be or to come to be not in a place as for an accident to be or to come to be not in a subject. So Suarez labours in vain when, to prove that the subject is the material cause of accidents, he uses only this argument, and repeats it again and again: that an accident necessarily inheres in a subject. This is clear from his own words which we quoted above.

units.la: {x} Unde ita alij subjectum substantia substituitur accidentia labetur accidentia.
units.tr: {x} Hence others hold that substance is put in place as the subject, and that accidents slip away.
Chapter II.

units.la: Poterat autem tribus verbis tota hæc res expediri, quod Subjectum non sit Materia Accidentium. Etenim ipsa Materiæ ratio in eo consistit (sicuti per se manifestum est) ut res, cujus Materia esse dicitur, ex ea tanquam parte, aut partibus, componatur. Accidens autem non componi ex Materia, ipse asseverat Suarez. namq; §. 3. ait, Entitatem accidentalem in abstracto sumptam non habere Causam materialem, ex qua intrinsece componatur, sed in concreto: hoc est, habere Materiam, in qua sustentetur, non è qua componatur. ac rursus §. 7. Accidens, quoad suam Entitatem accidentalem precise & abstracte sumtam, habere Causam materialem, non ex qua componatur, sed à qua sustentetur in suo esse. & prolixe ac strenue impugnat eos, qui dixerunt Accidentia è propria Materia & Forma componi. Male igitur Accidenti tribuit Materiam, quod ex Materia componi ipse negat. & melius Scaliger, Humorem esse Saporis subjectum, non Materiam. accidentia enim Materiam non habere. & Alibi, Accidentia non habere Formam, quia ne Materiam quidem, sed tantum Essentiam.
units.tr: The whole matter could have been settled in three words: the subject is not the matter of the accidents. For the very notion of matter consists in this (as is plain in itself): that a thing of which something is said to be the matter is composed of that matter as one part, or several parts. Suarez himself asserts that accidents are not composed of matter. For in §3 he says that an accidental entity taken in the abstract does not have a material cause from which it is intrinsically composed, but only in the concrete; that is, it has a matter in which it is sustained, not one out of which it is composed. And again in §7: an accident, taken precisely and abstractly as to its accidental entity, has a material cause not from which it is composed but by which it is sustained in its being. He also attacks at length and vigorously those who have said that accidents are composed of their own matter and form. Suarez therefore wrongly assigns matter to the accident, when he himself denies that it is composed of matter. Scaliger puts it better: moisture is the subject of flavour, not its matter, for accidents do not have matter. And elsewhere: accidents do not have a form, since they do not even have matter, but only essence.

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA. De Principijs, Stoicorum, & Platonis, Priscorumq; opin- iones, quatenus cum nostra Sententia conveniant aut dis- cordent.
units.tr: THIRD SECTION. On the principles of the Stoics and Plato, and the opinions of the ancients, insofar as they agree with or differ from our view.

units.la: Plato & Stoici posuerunt utrumq; Principium, Effectivum, & Compositivum. II. Priscos non solum Materiale Principium, quod Aristoteles ijs obicit, sed & Efsectivum nominasse demonstratur. III. Deum Mundi effectorem agnoverunt Prisci. IV. Ipsius Aristotelis testimonijs diluitur ista calumnia, qua veteres dicit Efficiens de rebus sustulisse. V. Aristotelis prurigo, Vetustos Philosophos calumniandi, insigni Parmenidis exemplo ostenditur. VI. Calumnia hujus, Quod Veteres non posuerint Efficiens; origo detegitur. VII. Efficiens
units.tr: Plato and the Stoics posited both principles, the efficient and the compositive. II. It is shown that the ancients named not only a material principle, which Aristotle objects to them, but also an efficient one. III. The ancients acknowledged God as the maker of the world. IV. This calumny, that the ancients removed the efficient cause from things, is refuted by Aristotle's own testimonies. V. Aristotle's itch to calumniate the ancient philosophers is shown by the notable example of Parmenides. VI. The origin of this calumny, that the ancients did not posit an efficient cause, is uncovered. VII. Efficient

units.la: Comm. in 6. Cauf. 12. Exerc 248.16. ens quoq; Principij nomine insigniverunt Veteres. VIII. Quorsum opiniones Priscorum, ubi nobis concordant, producamus. IX. Divisio Principiorum, à Peripateticis post Aristotelem facta, quid boni aut mali habeat. X. Principia Aristotelica, incorporeis accommodari non possunt. XI. Videri Veteres non solam Materiam pro Principio compositivo habuisse, sed & alterum Principium compositivum quodammodo attigisse. XII. Aristoteles Veteribus falsam hic opinionem affingit, sibi ipsi contradicit. XIII. Raritatem ac Densitatem pro Principijs habuerunt Veteres, qui unicam uniformem Materiam statuebant. XIV. An alij quoq; Veteres, multiformis Materiae autores, Principij compositivi alteram partem aliquatenus agnoverint. Veterum peccata circa hoc de Principijs negotium.
units.tr: Comm. in 6. Cauf. 12. Exerc 248.16. ens, too, the ancients also marked with the name of principle. VIII. Why we bring forward the opinions of the ancients where they agree with us. IX. The division of principles made by the Peripatetics after Aristotle, and what good or harm it contains. X. Aristotelian principles cannot be applied to incorporeal things. XI. It seems that the ancients did not hold only matter as the compositive principle, but also touched in some way on a second compositive principle. XII. Aristotle here attributes to the ancients a false opinion and contradicts himself. XIII. Those ancients who held a single uniform matter regarded rarity and density as principles. XIV. Whether other ancients, authors of a multiform matter, also acknowledged in some measure the other part of the compositive principle. The errors of the ancients concerning this business of principles.

units.la: DUo esse rerum Principia, Effectivum & Compositivum, in praecedenti sectione monstratum fuit. Consentiunt autem nobis, quantum ad hunc Principiorum numerum & Stoici, & Plato, & Prisci illi fere omnes, qui ante Platonem fuerunt. De Stoicis testatur Laërtius: Δοκεῖ δὲ αὐτοῖς, τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν ὅλων εἶναι δύο, τὸ ποιοῦν, καὶ τὸ πάσχον. Statuunt duo esse Principia universitatis rerum, Effectivum, & Passivum. Itemq; de Platone, Δύο δὲ τῶν πάντων ἀπέφηνεν ἀρχὰς, Θεὸν (ὃν καὶ Νοῦν προσαγορεύει, καὶ Αἴτιον) καὶ ὕλην. Duo declaravit universi esse Principia, Deum (quem & Mentem appellat, & Causam) ac Materiam. Quanquam autem non de singularum rerum, sed de Universi, sive Mundi ortu loquatur Laërtius, qui à duobus illis Principijs, Effectivo sive Deo, & Compositivo, sive Materia, fiat Stoicis & Platoni; non est tamen ut putet quisquam, aut hunc aut illos Mundo duntaxat illa Principiorum genera adhibuisse, ac non alijs quoq; rebus omnibus, quae quotidie oriuntur. Sed praecipuum opus sibi nominandum putavit Laërtius, in quo demonstraret, quid de Principijs Plato & Stoici sensissent: quia quae Principia Toti Mundo assignant, ea intellectu facile cile erat, reliquis quoq; rebus attributa ab ijs fuisse. Certè Seneca epistola 65. quanquam ista Initia (sic ipse vocat ἀρχὰς) Vniversis sive Mundo præcipue accommodat, generalem tamen esse hanc Stoicorum super omni aliarum quoq; rerum ortu sententiam, ut duo hæc Principiorum genera, Efficientis & Materiæ, ad eum requirant, manifeste ostendit. Dicunt Stoici nostri (inquit) duo esse in rerum Natura, ex quibus omnia fiant, Causam, & Materiam. Materia jacet iners, res ad omnia parata, cessatura, si nemo moveat. Causa autem, id est ratio, Materiam format, & quocunq; vult versat: ex illa, varia opera producit. Esse ergo debet, unde aliquid fiat; deinde, à quo fiat: hoc Causa est, illud Materia. Hæc de Universo à se dicta profitetur. Deinde subjungit, in artibus eodem modo fieri. Statuam enim & Materiam habuisse, quæ pateretur artificium; & artificem, qui Materiæ daret faciem. Serinonem vero obsignat generali hac clausula: Eadem conditio rerum omnium est: ex eo constant quod fit, & ex eo quod facit. (ubi excusari aut castigari debet catachresis in verbo Constant commissa.) & eandem quoq; Platonis mentem fuisse, ut non Mundo tantum, sed & corporibus omnibus (corporum enim Principia duntaxat & illi & Stoicis memorata sunt; qua de re dicetur infra) duo illa Principia, Efficiens & Materiam, assignaret, vel ex Timæo apparet. Ibi enim sicuti Universo Summum Deum & Materiæ inordinatę Chaos pro Principijs attribuit; ita alia corpora omnia à Dijs minoribus ex adunatis Elementorum portiunculis conflata esse scribit.
units.tr: That there are two principles of things, the effective and the compositive, was shown in the preceding section. The Stoics, Plato, and almost all those ancient thinkers who lived before Plato agree with us as to this number of principles. Concerning the Stoics, Laertius bears witness: "They hold that the principles of the universe are two, the active and the passive" [Δοκεῖ δὲ αὐτοῖς, τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν ὅλων εἶναι δύο, τὸ ποιοῦν, καὶ τὸ πάσχον]. They state that there are two principles of the whole universe, the Effective and the Passive. Likewise of Plato: "He declared the principles of all things to be two, God (whom he also calls Mind and Cause) and matter" [Δύο δὲ τῶν πάντων ἀπέφηνεν ἀρχὰς, Θεὸν (ὃν καὶ Νοῦν προσαγορεύει, καὶ Αἴτιον) καὶ ὕλην]. He declared that there are two principles of the universe, God (whom he calls also Mind and Cause) and Matter. Although Laertius speaks not of the origin of individual things but of the origin of the universe, or the world, which for the Stoics and Plato proceeds from those two principles, the effective, or God, and the compositive, or matter, nobody should think that either they or these men applied those kinds of principles only to the world, and not also to all the other things that come into being every day. But Laertius thought fit to name a special work in which he would show what Plato and the Stoics had thought about principles, because whatever principles they assigned to the whole world, it was easy to understand that they had attributed the same to the rest of things. Certainly Seneca, in Epistle 65, although he applies these beginnings (so he himself calls them, ἀρχάς) chiefly to the universe or the world, clearly shows that the Stoics' view on the origin of all other things is general, so that these two kinds of principle, of the efficient and of matter, are required for it. Our Stoics say (he says) that there are two things in the nature of things from which all things come, a cause and matter. Matter lies inert, ready for everything, and will remain idle unless someone moves it. The cause, that is reason, shapes matter and turns it wherever it wishes: from it it produces various works. There must therefore be that from which something is made, and then that by which it is made: the latter is the cause, the former matter. These things he professes to have said of the universe. Then he adds that in the arts it happens in the same way: for there is a statue and matter that undergoes the craft, and an artisan who gives shape to the matter. He seals the discourse with this general clause: The condition of all things is the same: they consist of that which is made and of that by which it is made. (Where the catachresis committed in the word consist should be excused or corrected.) And that Plato's mind was the same, that he assigned those two principles, the efficient and matter, not only to the world but to all bodies (for only the principles of bodies were mentioned by him and by the Stoics; this will be discussed below), appears also from the Timaeus. For there, just as he attributes to the universe the supreme God and disordered Chaos of matter as principles, so he writes that all other bodies were compounded by the lesser gods from gathered little portions of the elements.

units.la: II. Sed quemadmodum planum est de Platone & Stoicis, quod eundem nobiscum Principiorum numerum statuerint; ita, quod dicebamus, Priscos quoq; idem fecisse, dubitationem pati videtur, utiq; si audire velimus Aristotelem, qui expresse scribit 1. Metaph. 3. plerosq; ipsorum solum Materiale Principium agnovisse. Οἱ μὲν πρῶτοι φιλοσοφήσαντες, inquit, οἱ πλεῖστοι τὰς ἐν ὕλης εἶδει μόνον ἐνόμισαν ἀρχὰς εἶναι πάντων.
units.tr: II. But just as it is plain about Plato and the Stoics that they posited the same number of principles as we do, so the other point I was making, that the ancients also did the same, seems open to doubt, at least if we are willing to hear Aristotle, who expressly writes in Metaphysics 1, chapter 3, that most of them acknowledged only a material principle. "The first philosophers," he says, "for the most part thought that the principles of all things were only in the form of matter" [Οἱ μὲν πρῶτοι φιλοσοφήσαντες, οἱ πλεῖστοι τὰς ἐν ὕλης εἶδει μόνον ἐνόμισαν ἀρχὰς εἶναι πάντων].

units.la: Pleriq; eorum, qui Primi philosophas losophati sunt, solum Materiale Principium statuerunt, quod & repetit cap. 7. Περὶ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς ἐπιχειροῦντες τὰς αἰτίας λέγειν, καὶ περὶ πάντων φυσιολογοῦντες, τὴν κινήσεως αἴτιον ἀναιροῦσι. Generationis ac Corruptionis causas explicare aggressi, ac omnium naturam inquirentes, causam moventem tollunt. Nam quod iis, qui non unam aliquam Materiam primam, sed multiplicem statuebant, imponere solet, eos multa fecisse Principia, id fundamento caret. Qui enim variam diversiformem statuerunt rerum Materiam, non tamen multiplicaverunt Principia, neq; multa fecerunt Principia Materialia, sed unum Principium in diversas species distinxerunt: quomodo nos unicum tantum ponimus Principium compositivum, sub quo non modo sex diversas Materiae species, sed & alia multa, quae Materiae nomine nequaquam censeri possunt, comprehendimus: quomodo etiam varios atq; admodum numerosos Efficientes sub uno summo ac generali Principij Effectivi appellatione complectimur. Quantum vero ad priorem illam ac principalem criminationem, quod Principium Efficiens non agnoverint maxima pars veterum Physiologorum, ea haud dubie falsa est, sive de particulari singularum rerum, sive de universali ipsius Mundi generatione hoc intelligas. Nam quantum ad priorem: quis credere sustineat, magnos illos viros, Thaletem, Anaximenem, Diogenem Apolloniatem, Hippasum, Heraclitum (quos omnes in illo loco 1. Metaph. 3. hujus criminis reos peragit) adeo delirasse, ut nescirent (quod ne pueri quidem nescire possunt) in omni mutatione requiri τὴν ἑτέραν ἀρχὴν, ὅθεν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως, ἐπιδλὰν τὸ ὑποκείμενον ὁ πιεῖ αὐτὸ μεταδάλλειν ἑαυτό, Alterum principium, unde proficiscitur origo motus: quandoquidem subjectum non facit seipsum mutari: quae sunt ipsius verba in eadem tractatione, ubi ait Anaxagoram, & Empedoclem, aliosq; ipsa rei evidentia coactos, Principium Effectivum Materiali adjunxisse? Quod si est hoc ita evidens (ut est certè evidentissimum) Materiam non posse ipsam se movere, ac propterea non posse quicquam ex ea generari, nisi vi Effectiva in eam agente; quomodo
units.tr: Most of those who first philosophised posited only a material principle, which he also repeats in chapter 7 of On Generation and Corruption: "Attempting to explain the causes of generation and corruption, and investigating nature in all things, they abolish the moving cause" [Περὶ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς ἐπιχειροῦντες τὰς αἰτίας λέγειν, καὶ περὶ πάντων φυσιολογοῦντες, τὴν κινήσεως αἴτιον ἀναιροῦσι]. Having undertaken to explain the causes of generation and corruption, and inquiring into the nature of all things, they remove the moving cause. For the charge that he is wont to bring against those who posited not one single primary matter but a manifold one, that they posited many principles, has no foundation. For those who posited a varied and diversiform matter of things did not multiply principles, nor did they make many material principles, but they divided one principle into diverse species: just as we posit only one compositive principle, under which we comprehend not only six diverse species of matter but also many other things that cannot at all be counted under the name of matter; just as we also embrace various and very numerous efficient causes under the one supreme and general name of the efficient principle. As to his first and principal accusation, that the greater part of the ancient natural philosophers did not acknowledge an efficient principle, that is undoubtedly false, whether you understand this of the particular generation of individual things or of the universal generation of the world itself. For as to the first: who could bring himself to believe that those great men, Thales, Anaximenes, Diogenes of Apollonia, Hippasus, Heraclitus (all of whom he charges with this crime in that passage of Metaphysics 1, chapter 3), were so mad as not to know (which not even boys can fail to know) that in every change there is required "the other principle, whence comes the origin of motion, since the subject does not make itself change" [τὴν ἑτέραν ἀρχὴν, ὅθεν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως, ἐπειδὰν τὸ ὑποκείμενον αὐτὸ μεταβάλλειν ἑαυτό]; these are his own words in the same treatise, where he says that Anaxagoras and Empedocles, and others compelled by the very evidence of the thing, added an effective principle to the material one? But if this is so evident (as it is most evidently), that matter cannot move itself, and therefore nothing can be generated from it unless an effective force acts upon it, how
Chapter II.

units.la: quomodo tanti viri, qui Naturæ penetralia scrutari primi sunt aggressi, quiverunt adeo bruti esse, ut ipsos hoc lateret, utq; putarent ex sola per se Materia, nullo accedente Efficiente, omnia procreari? Aut quomodo fit verisimile, eos negasse, quod parentes & genitores sint suorum fœtuum Efficientes, tum in animalibus, tum in plantis? id quod ne ipse quidem Epicurus negavit? Proinde nimium credulus Magistro suo fuit Toletus, quum scripsit, Antiquos in sola Mundi constitutione adhibuisse causam Efficientem; in generationibus autem particularibus nequaquam ea usos esse, sed ad solam Materiam recurrisse; quæ sane calumnia si aliunde non possit, ex primo de Anima abunde diluitur. ibi enim toto capite secundo ita enarrantur Veterum de Anima sententiæ, ut appareat, quod omnes eam fecerint omnis motus autorem, ac consequenter etiam generationis. quod si autem animæ generationem retulerunt acceptam, fallum est, saltem in animatis, quod Efficientem à generationibus exclauserint, solaq; Materia fuerint contenti. Si igitur verum est crimen, ijs ab ipso impactum, quod Principium Effectivum non agnoverint; omnino intelligi debet de prima illa rerum Effectione, per quam omnia constituta, eamq; vim, ut ipsa quoq; efficere aliquid deinceps possent, nacta sunt. & ita sane exponit Fonseca (plane contrario modo quam Toletus) aiens, nequaquam ita intelligendum esse Aristotelem, quasi crederet, Veteres non agnovisse, causas efficientes particulares, sed de primo Efficiente illum loqui. At sic quoq; falsum esse, quod Veteribus impingit, vel ex ipsius scriptis evidentissime colligi potest: quandoquidem passim ea scribit, è quibus appareat, vix quenquam eorum, qui ante ipsum fuissent, Philosophorum, Deum ab opificio Mundi penitus exclusisse; falsamq; illam ac stultam opinionem, quæ Mundum facit æternum, & ἀγέννητον, ab ipso primo in Philosophiam fuisse introductam. namq; in primo de Coelo, capite decimo, diserte scribit, omnes Philosophos, qui ante ipsum fuerunt, sensisse, Mundum non ab æterno fuisse sed originem habuisse. idemq; etiam testatur in principio octavi Physicorum, Ἐιναι μὲν οὖν κίνησιν, πάντες φασίν. οἵν οἱ περὶ φύσεως ἢ λέγοντες, καὶ ἡ κόσμοποιεῖν. Esse mo-tum, omnes aiunt qui de natura aliquid dicunt, quia mundum faciunt. [hoc est, factum docent] adeo ut appareat, quod & illos falso accusaverit, & illi crimini, quod alijs injuria inurit, ipse manifestissime sit obnoxius.
units.tr: How could such great men, who were the first to undertake to probe the innermost secrets of Nature, have been so dull that they failed to notice this, and thought that everything was produced from matter alone, through itself, with no efficient cause coming in? Or how is it likely that they denied that parents and begetters are the efficient causes of their offspring, both in animals and in plants, something that not even Epicurus himself denied? Therefore Toletus was too credulous toward his master when he wrote that the ancients employed an efficient cause only in the constitution of the world, but in particular generations they did not use one at all and had recourse to matter alone. If this slander cannot be refuted elsewhere, it is amply refuted from the first book On the Soul. For there, throughout the second chapter, the opinions of the ancients about the soul are set out in such a way that it appears they all made the soul the author of every motion, and consequently of generation too. But if they referred the generation of the soul to something received from elsewhere, it is false, at least in the case of living things, that they excluded the efficient cause from generations and were content with matter alone. If, therefore, the charge he brought against them is true, that they did not acknowledge an efficient principle, it must be understood entirely of that first making of things, by which all things were constituted and received the power by which they could afterwards bring something about themselves. And Fonseca explains it so, in a way quite opposite to Toletus, saying: Aristotle is by no means to be understood as if he believed that the ancients had not recognised particular efficient causes, but he is speaking of the first Efficient. But that even so the charge he lays against the ancients is false can be most clearly gathered from his own writings. For he writes in many places things from which it appears that scarcely any of the philosophers who preceded him had entirely excluded God from the making of the world, and that the false and foolish opinion which makes the world eternal and ungenerated [ἀγέννητον] was first introduced into philosophy by himself. For in the first book On the Heavens, chapter ten, he expressly writes that all the philosophers who came before him held that the world had not existed from eternity but had an origin. He also testifies to the same at the beginning of the eighth book of the Physics: That there is motion, all say who speak about nature, because they make the world [Ἐιναι μὲν οὖν κίνησιν, πάντες φασίν. οἵν οἱ περὶ φύσεως ἢ λέγοντες, καὶ ἡ κόσμοποιεῖν] [that is, they teach that it was made]. So it appears that he falsely accused them, and that he is himself most manifestly liable to the very charge which he unjustly brings against others.

units.la: III. Profecto cum Mundum habuisse initium, neq; ab æterno fuisse, asseruerint omnes fere, qui ante ipsum Physiologiam tractarunt, necesse est aut Effectorem adhibuerint, aut fortuita Materiæ conglomeratione omnia extitisse statuerint. Sed hoc de fortuito rerum ortu delirium etiamsi jam olim magnam apud vulgus habuit jactationem, sicuti ex Platonis Sophista, & Decimo de Legibus constat, primus tamen in Philosophiam videtur invexisse stultissimus Epicurus. De prisicis enim illis fere constat, quod Deum statuerint Mundi Effectorem. Namq; de Thalete expresse scribit Lacrtius, quod solitus sit dictitare, Mundum esse ποίημα θεοῦ, Dei opus. De Empedoclis quoq; Philia, & de Anaxagoræ Mente nota res est. & de Democrito testatur Aristoteles, quod eodem fere modo, atq; Anaxagoras, Mentem sive Animam Universo præfecerit: ut appareat Epicurum, qui magnam Physiologiæ suæ partem Democrito suffuratus est, illud fœdissimum delirium, de spontaneo Mundi ortu, ab eo nequaquam hausisse. Et quantum ad illos attinet, de quibus hodie nominatim nulla litterarum monumenta certiores nos reddunt, quid de Mundi generatione senserint; pro omnibus respondebit unus ipsius Aristotelis locus, è secundo Physicorum, ubi illustrissimum Veteribus cunctis super hac re testimonium perhibet. quippe incusat eos, quod in rimandis atq; exponendis rerum causis nullum Casui sive Fortunæ locum fecerint, adeoq; ne vel ullam quidem ipsius mentionem habuerint. Καὶ ἀποφήσειεν ἂν ὡς, καὶ τί ποτε οὐδεὶς τῶν ἀρχαίων σοφῶν τὰ αἴτια περὶ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς λέγων, περὶ τύχης οὐδὲν διώρισεν, ἀλλ', ὡς ἔοικεν, οὐδὲν ὤοντο οὐδ' ἐκεῖνοι εἶν ἀπὸ τύχης. Dubitare licet, quare nemo Veterum Sapientum, generationis ac corruptionis causas pertractans, de Fortuna aliquid definiverit. Sed videtur
units.tr: III. Indeed, since almost all who treated natural philosophy before him asserted that the world had a beginning and had not existed from eternity, they must either have posited a Maker or held that everything came into being through a chance conglomeration of matter.
