But this madness about a chance origin of things, although it long ago enjoyed great vogue among the common people, as is clear from Plato's Sophist and the tenth book of the Laws, nevertheless seems to have been first introduced into philosophy by the most foolish Epicurus. For it is fairly well established that those early men held God to be the Maker of the world. Laertius expressly writes of Thales that he used to say the world is a work of God [ποίημα θεοῦ]. The matter of Empedocles' Love (Philia) and of Anaxagoras' Mind is well known. Aristotle testifies that Democritus, in much the same way as Anaxagoras, set Mind or Soul over the universe; so it appears that Epicurus, who stole a great part of his physics from Democritus, did not at all draw from him that most foul madness about the spontaneous origin of the world. As for those men about whom no written records today tell us for certain what they thought of the generation of the world, one passage of Aristotle himself, from the second book of the Physics, will answer for all of them, for there he bears the most illustrious testimony of all to the ancients on this matter. For he accuses them of having given no place to chance or fortune in searching out and explaining the causes of things, and so of not even having made any mention of it at all. One may wonder why none of the ancient sages, when treating the causes of generation and corruption, defined anything about chance. But it seems [Καὶ ἀποφήσειεν ἂν ὡς, καὶ τί ποτε οὐδεὶς τῶν ἀρχαίων σοφῶν τὰ αἴτια περὶ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς λέγων, περὶ τύχης οὐδὲν διώρισεν, ἀλλ', ὡς ἔοικεν, οὐδὲν ὤοντο οὐδ' ἐκεῖνοι εἶν ἀπὸ τύχης].

units.la: S f 3 sibi putavisse, nihil casu fieri. Qui igitur nihil omnino opinabantur casu fieri, quomodo ipsum hoc Universum casu factum esse opinari potuerunt? certe sine summa impudentia asseri hoc non potest; neq; cuiquam cordato fiat verisimile, eos viros, qui ab omni quotidiana generatione exulare fortunam voluerunt, eam generando Universo praefecisse. Nam quod ipse ait, nonnullos eorum, qui nec animalia, neq; plantas nisi à certis efficientibus produci volebant, ita male sanos fuisse, ut cœli totiusq; mundi ortum fortunæ & τοῦ αὐτομάτου referrent acceptum (id quod scribit secundi physicorum quarto) haud gravate credimus, in medio vulgo semper fuisse, qui ita sentirent, non paucos. De illustribus autem illis viris, qui rerum ortum primi scrutati sunt, quenquam ita excordem fuisse, ut id assereret, nobis non fit verisimile; cum nemo id, quod sciamus, tradat, ne ipse quidem Aristoteles, utut Veterum calumniae deditus: qui neq; alibi usquam id expresse prodidit, & hoc in loco simpliciter dicit, aliquos ita existimare, non expresso, quinam isti sint, qui ita opinentur.
units.tr: S f 3 to have thought that nothing happens by chance. How, then, could they suppose that this very universe was made by chance, when they thought that nothing at all happens by chance? Surely this cannot be asserted without the greatest impudence, nor does it seem likely to any sensible person that those men, who wanted fortune banished from every daily generation, put it in charge of generating the universe. For as to his saying that some of them, who would not allow animals or plants to be produced except by definite efficient causes, were so unsound in mind as to refer the origin of the heavens and of the whole world to fortune and to [τοῦ αὐτομάτου] (as he writes in the fourth chapter of the second book of the Physics), we readily believe that there were always not a few among the common crowd who thought in this way. But concerning those illustrious men who first investigated the origin of things, it does not seem likely to us that any of them was so senseless as to assert this, since no one, so far as we know, hands it down, not even Aristotle himself, however given he was to slandering the ancients. He nowhere else expressly reports it, and in this place he simply says that some think so, without specifying who those are who hold this opinion.
IV.

units.la: Utrocunq; igitur modo interpreteris illam Aristotelis in Veteres criminationem, quod Principium Effectivum non agnoverint, sive de particulari generatione, sive de Universali; falsa esse deprehenditur. imo ad illam coarguendam sufficere poterat unicus hic è principio quinti de Generatione Animalium locus, ubi in universum de Priscorum Philosophorum circa rerum Principia sententia loquens, dicit, eos Formalis quidem & Finalis causæ nullam habuisse rationem, sed Efficientem duntaxat & Materiam consideralle, Οἱ δ' ἀρχαῖοι φυσιολόγοι τὸ συναμφότερον ὠνόμασαν. Τοῦτο δ' αἴτιον, ὅτι οὐχ ἑώρων τὰ πλείους ὄντας τὰς αἰτίας, ἀλλὰ μόνον τὴν τῆς ὕλης, καὶ τὴν τῆς κινήσεως. τὴν δὲ τοῦ λόγου, καὶ τὴν τοῦ τέλους, ἀνεπισκέπτως εἶχον. Priscii autem physiologi contrarium opinati sunt. cujus rei causa est, quòd non videbant plures esse causas, sed materialem duntaxat, & efficientem. formalis autem ac finalis ipsis in mentem non venit. in quibus verbis cum fateatur priscos phyli-
units.tr: However one interprets Aristotle's charge against the ancients, that they did not recognize the efficient principle, whether in particular generation or in universal generation, it is shown to be false. Indeed, the single passage at the beginning of the fifth book of the Generation of Animals would have been enough to refute it. There, speaking generally of the opinion of the earlier philosophers about the principles of things, he says that they took no account of the formal and final causes, but considered only the efficient cause and the matter: "The early natural philosophers gave the name of both together" [Οἱ δ' ἀρχαῖοι φυσιολόγοι τὸ συναμφότερον ὠνόμασαν]. "The reason for this is that they did not see that there are several causes, but only the cause of matter and the cause of motion. They were careless about the cause of the form and the cause of the end" [Τοῦτο δ' αἴτιον, ὅτι οὐχ ἑώρων τὰ πλείους ὄντας τὰς αἰτίας, ἀλλὰ μόνον τὴν τῆς ὕλης, καὶ τὴν τῆς κινήσεως. τὴν δὲ τοῦ λόγου, καὶ τὴν τοῦ τέλους, ἀνεπισκέπτως εἶχον]. The early natural philosophers, however, thought otherwise. The reason is that they did not see that there are several causes, but only the material and the efficient. The formal and the final cause never came into their minds. In these words, since he admits that the early phys-

units.la: × Nog ordine, o ex ordine, nog via, o Rationes.
units.tr: Neither in order, nor out of order; neither by way, nor by reasons.
Chapter II.

units.la: physiologos, in tractando rerum ortu, non Materiae tantum, sed & Efficientis rationem habuisse; quid aliud quam ipse falsitatis condemnat illam contra eos in primo Metaphysicorum institutam accusationem? Imo alibi adhuc expressius dicit, eos in omni generatione, tum illa Mundi, tum quotidiana, utrumq; Principium, Effectivum & Materiale, adhibuisse. Οἱ μὲν οὖν ἀρχαῖοι καὶ πρῶτοι φιλοσοφήσαντες περὶ φύσεως, περὶ δὲ ὕλης ἀρχῆς ἡσθῆ δὲ τὴν αὐτῆς αἰτίας ἐσκόπευν, τίς καὶ πῶς ἐν ταύτης γίνεται τὸ ὅλον, καὶ τίνῳ κινήσεως, οἷον νείκος, ἢ φιλίας ἢ νοῦς, ἢ τὸ αὐτόματον. Τῆς δὲ ὑποκειμένης ὕλης τοιάνδε τινὰ φύσιν ἔχουσης ἐξ ἀνάγκης, οἷον τὸ μὲν πυρὸς θερμὸν, τῆς δὲ γῆς ψυχρὸν, τὸ μὲν κοῦφον, τῆς δὲ βαρὺ. ὅτως δὴ καὶ τὸν κόσμον γεννῶσι. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ περὶ τὴν τῶν ζῴων καὶ τῶν φυτῶν γένεσιν λέγουσι.
units.tr: The physicists, in treating the origin of things, took account not only of the material cause but also of the efficient cause. What else does he himself condemn, in the first book of the Metaphysics, than the accusation brought there against them, which he calls false? Indeed, he says even more explicitly elsewhere that in every generation, both that of the world and the daily kind, they employed both principles, the efficient and the material. The earliest philosophers of nature, then, sought the principle of matter, and they inquired into the cause of the thing itself: what and how the whole comes to be from it, and by what motion, such as strife, or friendship, or mind, or chance. But since the underlying matter has by necessity such a nature, as fire being hot, earth cold, the one light and the other heavy, thus they also generate the world. They speak in the same way about the generation of animals and plants. [Οἱ μὲν οὖν ἀρχαῖοι καὶ πρῶτοι φιλοσοφήσαντες περὶ φύσεως, περὶ δὲ ὕλης ἀρχῆς ἡσθῆ δὲ τὴν αὐτῆς αἰτίας ἐσκόπευν, τίς καὶ πῶς ἐν ταύτης γίνεται τὸ ὅλον, καὶ τίνῳ κινήσεως, οἷον νείκος, ἢ φιλίας ἢ νοῦς, ἢ τὸ αὐτόματον. Τῆς δὲ ὑποκειμένης ὕλης τοιάνδε τινὰ φύσιν ἔχουσης ἐξ ἀνάγκης, οἷον τὸ μὲν πυρὸς θερμὸν, τῆς δὲ γῆς ψυχρὸν, τὸ μὲν κοῦφον, τῆς δὲ βαρὺ. ὅτως δὴ καὶ τὸν κόσμον γεννῶσι. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ περὶ τὴν τῶν ζῴων καὶ τῶν φυτῶν γένεσιν λέγουσι.]

units.la: Prisci, ac qui primi de natura philosophati sunt, de materiali principio, deq; istiusmodi causa inquirebant, qualis esset, ac quomodo ex ea fieret Universum, & quo movente, puta lite, aut amicitia, aut mente, aut forte: subjecta autem Materia talem quandam naturam habente necessario, puta quod ignis sit calidus, terra autem frigida; illeq; levis, & hac gravis. ita enim & mundum generant. similiter autem & de animalium ac stirpium ortu dicunt. quibus verbis nihil clarius dici potest ad absolvendos prisicos ab hoc crimine, quod Efficiciens de rebus sustulerint. Quanquam enim unius tantum alteriusq;, Anaxagorae, & Empedoclis, sententiam de Efficiente tangit; id tamen non fieri nisi in exemplum, atq; de reliquis quoq; tantundem intelligendum esse, facile evincunt illa prius à nobis dicta, & ipsa quoq; prima hujus testimonij verba, quae in generale de omnibus priscis philosophis loquuntur. Quod vero & τὸ αὐτόματον recensent inter Efficientes ab aliquibus ipsorum positos; parum probabilia loquitur, siquis attendat testimonio, quod ex ipsius secundo physicorum paulo ante depromebamus.
units.tr: The ancients, and those who first philosophised about nature, inquired into the material principle and into the cause of such a kind, what it was and how the Universe came to be out of it, and by what mover, namely strife, or friendship, or mind, or chance. But the underlying matter, having necessarily such a nature, namely that fire is hot and earth cold, the one light and the other heavy, is what they generate the world from. They speak in the same way about the origin of animals and plants. No words could be clearer than these for absolving the ancients of the charge that they removed the efficient cause from things. For although he touches on the opinion about the efficient cause of only one or two, Anaxagoras and Empedocles, this was done merely as an example, and it is easily proved that the same must be understood of the rest, both from what we said earlier and from the first words of this testimony itself, which speak in general of all the ancient philosophers. As for his listing chance [τὸ αὐτόματον] among the efficient causes posited by some of them, he speaks with little probability, if one considers the testimony which I quoted a little earlier from his second book of the Physics.

units.la: Incusat quidem Veteres in eodem loco primi de Part. Animal. 1. Quod qualitatibus illis Materiae plus justo attribuerint, eisq; acceptas retulerint varias conformationis Effecti-
units.tr: Indeed, in the same place, in the first book of the Parts of Animals, he accuses the ancients of attributing too much to those qualities of matter, and of ascribing to them the various effective causes of the formation [of living things].
Chapter II.

units.la: Effectiones, quæ nequaquam illis, sed Efficienti erant assignandæ. & vera eum loqui hac in parte, non dubitamus; consideratò, quod & Anaxagoræ consimile vitium objicit in Phœdone Plato, & quod generaliter in Timæo vetustiores se physiologos castigat, tanquam qui maximam Essectuum partem illis Qualitatibus ascriberent. Sed inde tamen inferendum plus non erat, nisi quod Efficienti causæ à se positæ minus tribuerent Prisci, quam deberent: id quod longe aliud est, quam Efficiens in totum tollere. Quin ipsas illas qualitates, quanquam in Materia sitas, tamen pro Efficientis specie habebant; ac proinde etiamsi non aliquos tantum, sed omnes effectus illis attribuissent; ne sic quidem culpari jure poterant, quod Principium Efsectivum nullum, ac solum Materiale ponerent; sed quod errarent in Efficiente assignando: quomodo Plato in Timæo eos, qui sic facerent, dicit errare in eo, quod Co-efficiens & Instrumentarium agens in ipsius principalis Agentis locum surrogarent. & ipse quoque alibi, ubi de eadem hac Priscorum, qualitatibus Materiæ effectivis tantum tribuentium, opinione tractat, fatetur eos Efficiens posuisse in eo tantum ipsos culpans, quod Efficienti Instrumentario transcriberent Efficientis Principalis dignitatem. Τὰς δυνάμεις ἀποδιδόασι τοῖς σώμασι, δι' ὰς γεννῶσι λίαν ὀργανικῶς. Facultates assignant corporibus, per quas generant nimis instrumentarie, quid autem sit illud ὀργανικῶς γεννᾶν, sic explicat, Ἐπεὶ γὰρ πέφυκεν, ὡς φασι, τὸ μὲν θερμὸν διακρίνειν, τὸ δὲ ψυχρὸν συνιστάναι, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἕκαστον, τὸ μὲν ποιεῖν, τὸ δὲ πάσχειν, ἐν τούτων λέγοσι, καὶ διὰ τούτων, ἅπαντα τἆλλα γίνεσθαι καὶ φθείρεσθαι. Quandoquidem natum est, ut inquiunt, calidum secernere, frigidum cogere, aliorumq; unumquodq; hoc vel illud facere aut pati; ex his ac per hæc dicunt omnia alia oriri & interire. Omnibus igitur modis vim veritati facit Aristoteles, quando Veteres arguit, quod Efficiens de rebus statuerint.
units.tr: These are effects that were in no way to be assigned to those qualities but to the efficient cause. We do not doubt that he speaks truly on this point, since Plato in the Phaedo brings the same kind of charge against Anaxagoras, and since in the Timaeus he generally rebukes the older natural philosophers for ascribing the greater part of effects to qualities. But nothing more could be inferred from this than that the ancients attributed too little to the efficient cause they had posited, which is quite different from abolishing the efficient cause altogether. Indeed, even though those qualities were located in matter, the ancients still regarded them as a kind of efficient cause. Therefore, even if they had ascribed not just some but all effects to them, they still could not justly be blamed for positing no efficient principle and only a material one. Their fault lay rather in their mistake about the efficient cause. So Plato in the Timaeus says that those who did this erred in putting a co-efficient and instrumental agent in the place of the principal agent. Elsewhere, where he treats this same opinion of the ancients, who gave only an efficient role to the qualities of matter, he admits that they did posit an efficient cause, blaming them only for transferring the dignity of the principal efficient cause to an instrumental one. Facultates assignant corporibus, per quas generant nimis instrumentarie [Τὰς δυνάμεις ἀποδιδόασι τοῖς σώμασι, δι' ὰς γεννῶσι λίαν ὀργανικῶς]: they assign faculties to bodies, through which they generate too instrumentally. What he means by generating instrumentally he explains thus: since it is natural, as they say, for the hot to separate and the cold to condense, and each of the others to do or suffer this or that; from these and through these they say all other things arise and perish [Ἐπεὶ γὰρ πέφυκεν, ὡς φασι, τὸ μὲν θερμὸν διακρίνειν, τὸ δὲ ψυχρὸν συνιστάναι, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἕκαστον, τὸ μὲν ποιεῖν, τὸ δὲ πάσχειν, ἐν τούτων λέγοσι, καὶ διὰ τούτων, ἅπαντα τἆλλα γίνεσθαι καὶ φθείρεσθαι]. In every way, then, Aristotle does violence to the truth when he accuses the ancients of positing an efficient cause of things.

units.la: V. Sed Aristoteli nihil frequentius, quam priscis Philosophis
units.tr: V. But nothing is more common with Aristotle than to attach to the early philosophers monstrous opinions of this kind,
Chapter II.

units.la: sophis ejusmodi opinionum monstra affingere, quæ si vera essent, oporteret eos non modo non doctos & sapientes, sed plane bardos & blennos fuisse; & tamen rursus alijs in locis ea prodere, unde talium criminationum falsitas liquidissimo revincatur. cujus rei, in hoc ipso de Principijs negotio, insigne præ cæteris habemus exemplum in Parmenide. qui cum Deum faceret omnium rerum Principium Effectivum, quem appellat Ens unum, Immobile, infinitum, nec genitum, nec interiturum; Principium autem Materiale statueret ignem & terram: Aristoteles initio primi Physicorum ipsi hoc imponit, ac si illud Unum immobile faceret Principium non Effectivum, sed Materiale; super quo acriter eum incessit, dicens quod ἐρισικῶς συλλογίζεται, καὶ ἄνευ λογικῆς ἀπολυθεῖσα λαμβάνει, litigiose ratiocinatur, falsaq; & perperam collecta assumit: ut ne disputandum quidem adversus illum sit in Physica, non magis quam Geometræ πρὸς τὸν ἀνελόντα τὰς ἀρχάς. adversus eum, qui principia tollit. Ast in ipso illo libro postea fatetur, Parmenidem alia Principia pro rerum Elementis ac Materia agnovisse, ignem & terram; quanquam ne illo quidem in loco calumnia sua (cui illis ipsis in verbis manifeste contradiceret) potuit abstinere. sic enim ait: Πάντες δὴ τ' ἀντία ἀρχὰς ποιοῦσιν, οἵτε λέγοντες ὅτι ἐν τῷ πᾶν καὶ μὴ κινούμενον. καὶ ᾗ παρμενίδης ψυχρὸν καὶ θερμὸν ἀρχὰς ποιεῖ. ταῦτα δὲ πρὸς ἀγορεύει πῦρ καὶ γῆν. Omnes autem opposita contraria faciunt principia, etiam qui dicunt universum esse unum ac immobile. namq; Parmenides frigidum & calidum facit principia, eaq; appellat ignem & teram. & talia etiam primo Metaph. 5. ab eo scribuntur. Vbi sane ridere libet Toleti conatum, qui cum videret Aristotelem manifestissime sibi contradicere, dum Parmenidi tam pugnantes tribuit opiniones, ut modo aiat eum statuere unum Principium materiale immobile, modo duo contraria ignem & terram; præceptori subsidium fert cum hac stropha, quod Parmenides scripserit duum generum libros, alios vulgares, accuratiores alios; quorum in his unum dixerit esse rerum Principium, in illis vero duo. sed hoc figmentum cum careat
units.tr: Sophists of this kind attribute to them such monstrous opinions that, if they were true, these men would have been not only unlearned and unwise but plainly dullards and fools. Yet elsewhere they set out the very passages by which the falsity of such accusations is most clearly refuted. In this matter of the Principles we have a notable example, outstanding above the rest, in Parmenides. Although he made God the efficient principle of all things, calling him the One Being, immobile, infinite, neither begotten nor perishable, and posited fire and earth as the material principles, Aristotle at the beginning of the first book of the Physics charges him with making that immobile One a material principle rather than an efficient one. He attacks him sharply for this, saying that he reasons contentiously [ἐρισικῶς συλλογίζεται] and, not using logic, takes for granted what is false and wrongly inferred [καὶ ἄνευ λογικῆς ἀπολυθεῖσα λαμβάνει]. So one should not even dispute with him in Physics, any more than a geometer disputes with one who removes the principles [πρὸς τὸν ἀνελόντα τὰς ἀρχάς], that is, against one who abolishes principles. Yet in the same book he later confesses that Parmenides acknowledged other principles, fire and earth, as the elements and matter of things. Even in that passage, however, he could not refrain from his calumny, which he plainly contradicts in those very words. For he says: "All, indeed, make opposite contraries their principles, even those who say that the universe is one and immobile [Πάντες δὴ τ' ἀντία ἀρχὰς ποιοῦσιν, οἵτε λέγοντες ὅτι ἐν τῷ πᾶν καὶ μὴ κινούμενον]. For Parmenides makes the cold and the hot into principles, and calls them fire and earth [καὶ ᾗ παρμενίδης ψυχρὸν καὶ θερμὸν ἀρχὰς ποιεῖ. ταῦτα δὲ πρὸς ἀγορεύει πῦρ καὶ γῆν]." Aristotle says similar things elsewhere too, in the fifth chapter of the first book of the Metaphysics. Here it is indeed amusing to see the effort of Toletus, who, seeing that Aristotle plainly contradicts himself in ascribing to Parmenides opinions so conflicting, that now he says he posited a single immobile material principle and now two contraries, fire and earth, comes to his master's aid with this quibble: that Parmenides wrote books of two kinds, some popular and others more exact, and that in the latter he said there is one principle of things, but in the former two. But this fiction, since it lacks

units.la: Cap. 5. reat testimonio antiquitatis, frustra aut Toletus aut Pholoponus (qui ipsi hoc suggessit) postulant, ut ipsis hoc credamus. & neq; credunt sibi ipsis, ideoq; alteras copias circumspiciunt, dicentes, Quod duo ista Principia posuerit secundum apparentiam, quae erant unum secundum existentiam. in quo commento quum non modo non existat, sed ne appareat quidem hilum veritatis, nos illo refellendo superse-dere constituimus.
units.tr: Cap. 5. Lacking the testimony of antiquity, the claim of either Toletus or Philoponus (who himself suggested it) is put forward in vain, asking us to believe it. They do not trust it themselves, and so they look around for other support, saying: that he posited these two principles according to appearance, while according to existence they were one. Since this invention not only does not exist but does not show even a trace of truth, we have decided to set it aside without refuting it.

units.la: Quod autem Parmenides per illud unum infinitum nihil intellexerit aliud, nisi ipsum Deum Omnipotentem, omnium rerum Effectorem, aperte decla-rat ipse Aristoteles, 3. Phys. 4: aiens maximam veterum Physiologorum partem Infiniti nomine Deum designasse, quotquot nimirum nullo eum peculiari appellatione (ut Anaxagoras, Mentis, & Empedocles, Philiae) insigniebant; in quo numero Parmenides comprehensus est. Quod autem illud Infinitum habuerint pro Principio Mundi Essectivo, haud obscure colligas ex iis, quae ibidem ex ipsorum sententia de illo dicit. Διὸ, καὶ θάνατον λέγομεν, ὃ τοῦ-της ἀρχὴ, ἀλλ' αὐτὴ τῶν ἄλλων εἶν λοιπὸν, καὶ πάντα ἐπέχειν καὶ πάντα κυβερνᾶν, ὡς φασὶν, ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐπειδὴ ... Quare, ut dicimus, hujus principium non est, sed ipsum videtur esse principium aliorum, & continere omnia, omniaq; regere, sicuti aiunt, quicunq; non faciunt alias causas praeter infinitum (puta Mentem, aut Amicitiam) aiunt hoc esse Numen, utpote immortale, & interitus expers: sicuti inquit Anaximander, ac plerique Physiologi. Ex hujusmodi autem locis (ut id obiter annotemus) observare possunt Aristotelici, causam se habere nullam, cur debeant nobis succensere, qui toties dissentiamus ab ipsorum Magistro; quum & ipse à cunctis ante ipsum Philosophis dissenserit. neq; contentus ab ijs dissentire in illis, quae revera ipsi senserant; quaesivit etiam quomodo ab ijs dissen-tiret, ubi plane ipsorum sequebatur opinionem; idq; cum damno ipsorum ac dedecore, sententiam eorum per manifestissimam calumniam in ea detorquendo commenta, de quibus illi nunquam, ne per somnum quidem, cogitaverant. Qui enim Primum Movens non mobile introductus erat in Physicam, ac plurima de eo verba facturus, tanquam de primario Physiologiae capite, ac cognitu inprimis necessario; Parmenidem, ob idem illud Principium in Physicam introductum, hostilem in modum exagitavit; quod ut faceret cum aliquo praetextu, invitissima veritate confuxit, quod illo Principio Parmenides pro Materiali usus fuerit: qua de re a Ramo etiam in scholis Physicis multa dicta sunt. Porro minus mirum est, quod de Veteribus illis, quorum partim nihil scripserant, partim pauca, & quae non admodum manibus hominum tererentur, ausus sit confingere Aristoteles, quod Principium Essectivum nullum posuissent, quum veritas non sit, idem de Praeceptore suo Platone alicubi prodere: quum & a plurimis condiscipulis suis, in quibus secta Platonica florebat tunc cum maxime, posset mendacij convinci; & in omnium manibus versarentur ejus scripta, in quorum infinitis locis contrarium apertissime Plato profiteretur, ita ut nemo, qui illa vel a limine unquam salutasset, posset ignorare, salsissimam esse istam criminationem. Sed quum inferius in hoc ipso capite hac de re agendum nobis sit, hic eam missam facimus. Impraesens sufficit monstrasse, injuria accusatos ab Aristotele Priscos illos, ac si pleriq; ipsorum alterum tantum Principium, videlicet Materiale, posuissent, quum illi utrumq; posuerint, & hoc, & Effectivum.
units.tr: That Parmenides understood by that one infinite nothing other than God Almighty, the Maker of all things, Aristotle himself openly declares in Physics 3, chapter 4. He says that most of the ancient natural philosophers designated God by the name of the Infinite, namely all those who did not mark him with any particular appellation (as Anaxagoras did with Mind, and Empedocles with Love), and Parmenides is included among them. That they held this Infinite to be the efficient principle of the world you may readily gather from what Aristotle there reports of their opinion about it: "Διὸ, καὶ θάνατον λέγομεν, ὃ τοῦ-της ἀρχὴ, ἀλλ' αὐτὴ τῶν ἄλλων εἶν λοιπὸν, καὶ πάντα ἐπέχειν καὶ πάντα κυβερνᾶν, ὡς φασὶν, ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐπειδὴ ..." ["Therefore, as we say, it has no beginning, but itself seems to be the beginning of other things and to embrace all things and govern all things, as they say, from the beginning ..."]. Aristotle goes on: those who do not posit any causes besides the infinite (such as Mind or Friendship) say that this is the Deity, as being immortal and free from decay, as Anaximander and most of the natural philosophers say. From passages like these (let us note this in passing) the Aristotelians may see that they have no reason to be angry with us, who so often dissent from their own Master, since he himself dissented from all the philosophers before him. Nor was he content to dissent from them in matters where they had truly held his own view; he also sought out ways to dissent from them where he plainly followed their opinion, and that to their loss and shame, distorting their doctrine by the most evident calumny into notions of which they had never, not even in their sleep, thought. For when the Prime Mover that is not moved had been introduced into Physics, and he was going to say very much about it as the chief topic of natural philosophy and especially necessary to know, he savagely attacked Parmenides for introducing the same principle into Physics. In order to do so under some pretext, he twisted, against the plainest truth, the claim that Parmenides used that principle as a material one; on this matter Ramus also said much in the physics schools. Moreover, it is less surprising that Aristotle ventured to invent, about those ancients (some of whom had written nothing, and others little, and works not much handled by people), that they posited no efficient principle, when the same thing about his own teacher Plato he has stated somewhere, though it is not true; he could have been convicted of lying by very many of his fellow students, among whom the Platonic school was then flourishing most of all, and his writings were in everyone's hands, in countless places of which Plato openly professes the contrary, so that no one who had ever so much as greeted them from the threshold could fail to know that this accusation is most absurd. But since we must treat this matter further below in this same chapter, we set it aside here. For the present it is enough to have shown that those ancients were wrongly accused by Aristotle as if most of them had posited only one principle, namely the material, when in fact they posited both, both this and the efficient.
VI.

units.la: Quod vero non posuerint tantum utrumque, sed & Principij nomine utrumq; affecerint; id non minus clarum est. Et de Materia quidem non licet dubitare. quippe non modo pro Principio eam habuerunt, sed vix alio quam generali Principij nomine eam affecerunt, quum non haberent, quomodo aliter eam appellarent; quandoquidem illa vocabula, ὕλη & σοιχεῖον, illum usum, ad quem postea translata sunt in Philosophiam, ipsorum tempore nec dum acceperant, sicuti libro sequente declarabitur. & hinc quoq; praecipuam Aristoteles arripuit occasionem eos criminandi, quod solam Materiam Principium facerent: quum tamen omni tempore satis vulgatus hic mos fuerit, ut alicui speciei, quæ peculiari nomine careret, ipsum genericum nomen tanquam proprium (absq; tamen aliarum specierum præjudicio) attribueretur: cujus rei ex ipsius scriptis possent exempla non pauca adduci: ita nimirum alicubi ἰχθύν, sub cujus vocis ambitu omnium piscium species comprehenduntur, uni cuidam speciei, pro qua propriùm nomen non inveniebat, facit peculiare. Ridet quidem hoc Scaliger (licet hoc ipsi; per quem alijs ne mutire quidem contra Aristotelem licet) sed irrisus causam nullam se habere scivisset, si tantùm reputasset, quam Gallina in communi Græcæ linguæ consuetudine habeat appellationem, certè hæc avium species commune toti generi nomen ipsa tanquam peculiare possidet. & alia ad hunc modum sunt complura. Et quid opus est longius exempla petere, quum ipsa Philosophia Peripatetica ijs abundet? Elementorum enim vocem esse generalem ad omnia, è quibus res componitur, ac propterea Materiæ quoq; Primæ & Formæ competere, fatentur ipsi. & tamen notum, solis quatuor simplicibus corporibus, quæ tanquam Materiam ad constituenda mixta concurrere dicunt, hanc appellationem velut propriam attribui. Et in ipsa Principij voce (de quâ nunc agimus) nonne idem jus usurpavit Aristoteles? Sanè non Materiam modò Primam, Formamq; ac Privationem, sed & alia hujus vocis ambitu comprehendi, ipsē non dissicetur; & tamen tribus illis peculiariter assignavit hanc Principiorum appellationem: ut nihil nunc dicamus de abusu illo, quo multis quoq; alijs rebus proprium subinde fecit hoc vocabulum; quo de satis multa dicta fuerunt prius. Causam igitur nullam habuit Aristoteles, cur ex eo, quòd genericò Principij vocabulo alteram Principiorum speciem, videlicet Materiam, indigetare soliti sunt Veres Physiologi, strueret hanc calumniam, quod solam Materiam pro Principio habuerint.
units.tr: That they did not merely posit both, but also applied the name of "principle" to both, is no less clear. There can be no doubt about matter. They did not only regard it as a principle; they could hardly have given it any name other than the general name of principle, since they had no other term by which to call it. The words hylē and stoicheion [ὕλη, στοιχεῖον] had not yet acquired in their time the philosophical sense to which they were later transferred, as will be shown in the following book. Hence Aristotle also seized on his chief pretext for accusing them, namely that they made matter alone a principle. Yet it has always been common practice to give the generic name, as if it were a proper name, to a species that lacks a name of its own (without prejudice, of course, to the other species). Examples of this can be cited from Aristotle's own writings in no small number. Thus somewhere he makes ichthys [ἰχθύς], a word under which all species of fish are comprehended, into the peculiar name of one particular species for which he had no proper name. Scaliger laughs at this (although he is a man by whom others are not permitted even to murmur against Aristotle), but he would have seen that the mockery had no basis if he had only considered what name the hen has in common Greek usage. Certainly this species of bird keeps for itself, as if it were a peculiar name, the name common to the whole genus. There are many other instances of this kind. And why seek examples at greater length, when the Peripatetic philosophy itself abounds in them? They themselves admit that the word element is general, applying to all the things from which a thing is composed, and that it therefore also belongs to prime matter and to form. Yet it is well known that this name is attributed as if it were proper to the four simple bodies alone, which they say concur as matter to constitute mixed bodies. And did not Aristotle claim the same right in the very word principle (which we are now discussing)? Surely he does not deny that prime matter, form and privation, and also other things, are comprehended within the range of this word; yet he assigned the name of principles to those three in particular. We need not now speak of that abuse by which he often made this word peculiar to many other things, of which enough has been said before. Aristotle therefore had no reason for bringing this charge, that the old natural philosophers had posited only matter as a principle, merely because they were accustomed to call matter, one species of principle, by the generic name of principle.

units.la: VII. Quod vero Efficiens quoq; Principij nomine insigniverint, non est dubitandum. solet quidem Aristoteles tria illa vocabula, Principium, Causa, Elementum, confundere, unumq; pro altero promiscue usurpare, ac proinde etiam, ubi Veterum de Principijs opiniones recitat, non Principia tantum, sed & Causas, & Elementa vocare; quomodo 1. Metaphysicor. ait Anaxagoram ponere duo Elementa, Mentem atq; Homoiomeriam: & de Materia passim ita loquitur, ut dicat, Veteres illam Causam agnovisse: quum tamen non sit verisimile, aut Veteres illos Materiae nomen Causae, aut Anaxagoram Menti, Elementi nomen impositisse. sed ex suo sensu ista locutus est Aristoteles, quasi diceret, ex numero earum rerum, quae mihi modo Principia, modo Causae, interdum Elementa dicuntur, has aut illas Pristi agnoverunt. quare inde concludere non licet, quod istae appellationes Veteribus ita fuerint usurpatae, quomodo Aristoteles in suis scriptis, ubi eorum sententiae tractantur, eas usurpat. & sic neq; ex illis locis, ubi Aristoteles de Efficiente opiniones Veterum recitans, illud Principium vocat, colligi firmiter potest, Efficiens Veteribus Principium dictum fuisse. Sed alij extant loci, è quibus id hauriatur. Etenim ab aliquo Veterum aut Materiam Causae, aut Efficiens Elementi nomine affectum fuisse, nusquam, quod sciamus, prodit: Principij autem appellationem Efficienti ab ijs tributam fuisse, est ubi expresse profiteatur. namq; primo de Anima capite secundo ait Animam Heraclito Principium dictam fuisse; & primo Physicorum tantundem de Empedoclea Amicitia ac Lite (quae duo pro Causis Efficientibus ab Empedocle habita fuisse, notum est) testatur. Etenim Veterum consensum advocans ad confirmationem suae sententiae, Quod Principia debeant esse contraria, sic inquit, πάντες Τὰ στοιχεῖα, καὶ Τὰς ὑπ' αὐτῶν καλυμένας ἀρχὰς, καίτοι ἄνευ λόγου ἀδέντες, ὅμως τ' ἀναντίᾳ λέγουσι: Omnes Elementa & vocata ab ipsis Principia, quanquam ea sine ratione ponant, contraria tamen esse dicunt: & paucis interjectis ita pergit: ὁι μὲν γὰρ θερμὸν καὶ ψυχρὸν, οἱ δὲ ὑγρὸν καὶ
units.tr: VII. That they also marked the efficient cause with the name of principle is not to be doubted. Aristotle is indeed accustomed to confuse those three words, principle, cause and element, and to use one for another indiscriminately. Accordingly, when he recounts the opinions of the ancients about principles, he calls them not only principles but also causes and elements. Thus in the first book of the Metaphysics he says that Anaxagoras posited two elements, Mind and the homoeomeries. And he speaks of matter throughout as if he means that the ancients recognised it as a cause, although it is not likely that those ancients gave matter the name of cause, or that Anaxagoras gave the name of element to Mind. Aristotle spoke these things according to his own meaning, as if he were saying: "Of the things that are now called by me principles, now causes, and sometimes elements, the ancients recognised these or those." It is therefore not permissible to conclude from this that these terms were used by the ancients in the same way as Aristotle uses them in his writings, where he treats their opinions. Nor can it firmly be inferred from those passages, where Aristotle, reciting the opinions of the ancients about the efficient cause, calls it a principle, that the efficient cause was called a principle by the ancients. But other passages exist from which this may be drawn. For it does not appear anywhere, so far as we know, that any of the ancients designated either matter as cause or the efficient as element. But there are places where it is expressly stated that the name of principle was attributed to the efficient cause by them. For in the first book On the Soul, chapter two, he says that Heraclitus called the soul a principle; and in the first book of the Physics he testifies to the same effect about Empedocles' Friendship and Strife, which, as is known, Empedocles regarded as efficient causes. For in calling on the consensus of the ancients to confirm his view that principles must be contraries, he says: "Everyone, although they posit the elements and the things called principles by them without reason, nonetheless say that they are contraries" [πάντες τὰ στοιχεῖα, καὶ τὰς ὑπ' αὐτῶν καλουμένας ἀρχάς, καίτοι ἄνευ λόγου τιθέντες, ὅμως τἀναντία λέγουσι]. And after a few words he goes on: "For some posit the hot and the cold, others the moist and the dry" [οἱ μὲν γὰρ θερμὸν καὶ ψυχρόν, οἱ δὲ ὑγρὸν καὶ]

units.la: * cerebro καὶ ξηρὸν, ἕτερον δὲ ψυχρὸν καὶ ἄξιον, ὁ δὲ νεῖκος καὶ φιλίαν, αἰτίας ἂν ἔχοντα τῆς γενέσεως[?]. Alij enim calidum & frigidum, alij humidum & siccum, alij par & impar, alij Amicitiam & Litem, ponunt causas generationis. Quod ista Oppositorum paria Causas vocat & Elementa, de suo facit, ea ratione quam modo diximus. sed diserte scribit, quod ab ipsis, qui ea ponebant, Principia vocata sint. & cum ea, quae hic ponuntur, partim Materiae, partim Efficientis locum obtineant, ex mente eorum à quibus introducta sunt; apparet itidem ex hoc loco, quod utrumq; Veteres illi, & Materiam, & Efficiens, sub una communi Principij appellatione comprehenderint.
units.tr: ξηρὸν, ἕτερον δὲ ψυχρὸν καὶ ἄξιον, ὁ δὲ νεῖκος καὶ φιλίαν, αἰτίας ἂν ἔχοντα τῆς γενέσεως[?] "and the dry; others the cold and the ... ; others Strife and Friendship, as causes of generation." [Alij enim calidum & frigidum, alij humidum & siccum, alij par & impar, alij Amicitiam & Litem, ponunt causas generationis.] That he calls these pairs of opposites causes and elements, he does on his own account, for the reason we have just mentioned. But he clearly writes that they were called principles by those who posited them. And since the things posited here partly take the place of matter and partly of the efficient cause, according to the mind of those who introduced them, it appears from this passage as well that the ancients comprehended both matter and the efficient cause under one common name of principle.

units.la: VIII. Plura hujusmodi testimonia ex Aristotele, & ex aliis quoq; autoribus, colligi possent, per quae appareret, Veteres illos Efficientem & Materiam communi Principiorum appellatione affecisse. Sed non libet laborem aut tempus perdere in re minime necessaria. Est enim hoc satis per se evidens iis, qui Veterum scripta legerunt: quod si vero aliquis hoc neget; id nos parum moramur, neq; videmus pretium operae, in eo ad contrariam sententiam perducendo sumendae. Non enim ullum in eo robur ponimus, aut ad stabiliendam nostram de Principijs opinionem producimus Veterum consensum: sed ut homines videant, nos nequaquam novandi studio, aut dissentiendi prurigine ad hunc Philosophiae Reformandae laborem accessisse; qui tantum absumus, ut dissimulemus, sicubi Veteres idem nobiscum sentiunt; ut ipsi id profiteamur, ac prae nobis feramus. Quod si quis aut hic, aut alibi, ubi Veteres nobiscum sentire autumamus, docere potest, aliter se rem habere, faciet id volentibus nobis: qui nihilo propterea minus in sententia nostra perseverabimus, nisi si ostendi simul potest, nos à Veritate aberrare; quod siquis praestet, libenter nos in viam reduci patiemur, & Reductori quoque gratias habebimus.
units.tr: VIII. Many more testimonies of this kind could be gathered from Aristotle and from other authors too, by which it would appear that the ancients gave the efficient cause and matter the common name of principles. But I do not wish to waste labour or time on a matter that is in no way necessary. For this is sufficiently evident in itself to those who have read the writings of the ancients. If anyone should deny it, we do not dwell on him much, nor do we see any point in undertaking to lead him to the contrary opinion. For we do not rest any strength in this, nor do we bring forward the consensus of the ancients to establish our opinion about principles. Rather, we wish men to see that we have not come to this labour of reforming philosophy from any zeal for novelty or itch for disagreement. We are so far from concealing it where the ancients agree with us that we ourselves profess it and proclaim it. But if anyone can show, either here or elsewhere where we think the ancients agree with us, that the matter stands otherwise, he will be doing us a service, and we shall nonetheless persist in our opinion, unless it can at the same time be shown that we wander from the truth. If anyone does show this, we shall gladly allow ourselves to be brought back to the right way, and we shall be grateful to the one who brings us back.

units.la: IX. Porro non Veterum tantum, sed ipsorum Aristote-lico. licorum doctrina hac in parte aliquatenus ad nostram accedit. Corrigentes enim Magistri indiligentiam & inconstantiam, qui perpetuo fluctuans nihil certi hic definivit, Principia faciunt alia Externa, alia Interna, quam distinctionem possint videri ab ipso didicisse, qui in primo quinti Metaphysicorum tradit, Τῶν ἀρχῶν τὰς μὲν εἶναι ἐνυπαρχούσας, τὰς δὲ ἐκτός, Principia alia esse inexistentia, alia externa. sed contentus hoc tantum tradidisse, nihil amplius determinat, quænam sint hujus generis, quænam vero illius. ipsi vero hæc ita definiunt, quod Principia externa sint Efficiens, & Finis: Interna, Materia, Forma, & Privatio. quæ Principiorum divisio nonnullam habet cum nostra divisione cognationem; in hoc differens, quod inter Principia externa Finis seorsum collocatur, tanquam diversum ab Efficiente Principij genus: quum revera Fini non aliter locus sit inter Principia, nisi tanquam speciei Efficientis; id quod infra plenius explicabitur. In altero etiam membro peccant, Principijs internis annumerando Privationem; quam in hunc censum nullo modo admittendam esse, à nobis abunde antea est probatum. Hæc duo igitur si excipias, nobiscum consentiunt Peripatetici in generali hac de Principijs doctrina, quod nimirum illa sint duorum generum, Effectiva, & Compositiva. Sed quemadmodum cum hac Principiorum divisione, ita correcta, plane ad sententiam nostram atqVe ad Veritatem accedunt Peripatetici, ita longissime eam relinquunt in explicatione alterius præsertim membri, sive in assignandis Principijs compositivis. Materia enim prima (cui fere servant Principij nomen, Materiâ secundâ eo spoliatâ) & Forma substantialis, nihil sunt nisi commentum merum: sicuti ex primo capite cuivis potest apparere.
units.tr: IX. Moreover, the teaching not only of the ancients but also of the Aristotelians themselves comes somewhat close to ours in this respect. For the Masters, correcting the carelessness and inconsistency of their predecessor, who, fluctuating continually, defined nothing certain here, make some principles external and others internal. They may seem to have learnt this distinction from him, who in the first book of the fifth book of the Metaphysics teaches that "some principles are inherent, others external" [τῶν ἀρχῶν τὰς μὲν εἶναι ἐνυπαρχούσας, τὰς δὲ ἐκτός]. But being content to have handed down only this, he does not determine further which of these things belong to this kind and which to that. The Aristotelians themselves define them thus: the external principles are the efficient and the final cause; the internal are matter, form and privation. This division of principles has some kinship with our division, differing in this, that among the external principles the final cause is placed apart, as a kind of principle different from the efficient. Yet in truth the final cause has no place among the principles except as a species of the efficient cause, as will be explained more fully below. They also err in the second part, by counting privation among the internal principles, which, as we have already sufficiently proved, cannot in any way be admitted into this class. Apart from these two points, then, the Peripatetics agree with us in this general doctrine of principles, namely that they are of two kinds, efficient and compositive. But just as the Peripatetics approach our view and the truth quite closely with this division of principles so corrected, so they stand very far from it in the explanation of the other part, especially in assigning the compositive principles. For prime matter (to which they mostly keep the name of principle, once secondary matter has been stripped of it) and substantial form are nothing but pure invention, as anyone can see from the first chapter.

units.la: X. Et si vel maxime vera essent, quæ de ijs tradunt, sic quoq; manca foret Principiorum Compositivorum, sive Elementorum, quam ipsi tradunt, assignatio. Etenim Aristoteles, cum suis, teneretur, eo crimine, quod Veteribus ipse objicit alicubi, dicens eos plurimum peccare, quia
units.tr: X. And even if what they teach about them were entirely true, the assignment of the compositive principles, or elements, which they give would still be defective. For Aristotle, together with his followers, would be bound by the charge which he himself brings against the ancients somewhere, saying that they greatly erred because
Chapter II.

units.la: τῶν σωμάτων τὰ σαρκεῖα ὑπάρχει μόνον, τῶν δὲ ἀσωμάτων δ', ὄντων καὶ ἀσωμάτων. corporum dantaxat Elementa ponunt, non item incorporeorum, quum sint & incorporea. Culpat hic Veteres, quod solorum corporum Elementa tradiderint, incorporeis omissis; quum tamen tradita ab ipso Elementa, sive Principia constitutiva, neq; ipsa quadrent nisi in res corporeas. Materia enim & Forma ne analogice quidem (uti ex superiori Sectione patet) accommodari possunt Accidentibus compositis. Sola autem Accidentia composita sunt illa Incorporea, de quibus intelligi potest illa Veterum reprehensio, quod Incorporeorum Principia non attigerint. quippe Accidentia simplicia non est verisimile Aristotelem in animo habuisse cum ista scriberet, nisi si fovit deliram istam opinionem, quae Accidentia quaevis constare vult ex Materia & Forma, sive ex duabus partibus, quarum altera sit instar Materiae, & altera instar Formae, quod somnium multis impugnat Suarez disputatione decima quarta. & affine est, aut idem, cum Scaligeri commento, omnia Accidentia ex Esse & Essentia, sive è Potentia & Actu componentis: de quo nos praecedenti sectione multa diximus. Aristotelem autem ita sensisse, nusquam in ipsius scriptis apparet. Sed neq; de Intelligentijs & Mentibus accipi possunt ista Aristotelis verba. quanquam enim illas habet pro incorporeis, simplices tamen illas esse existimat simplicitate essentiali: rebus autem ita simplicibus Principia interna sive componentia non competunt. Quare omnino Accidentia composita sunt illa ἀσώματα, quae intelligi necesario debent, quando Veteres arguit, quod τῶν ἀσωμάτων Elementa praetermiserint. Sed & ipse ea omisit; neq; sectatores ejus illa attigerunt: unde efficitur (sicuti dicebamus prius) vitiosam esse Principiorum componentium assignationem à Peripateticis factam, etiamsi vera essent, quaecunq; de Materia & Forma somniant:
units.tr: Of bodies there are elements only, but of incorporeal things, though they exist, there are none [τῶν σωμάτων τὰ σαρκεῖα ὑπάρχει μόνον, τῶν δὲ ἀσωμάτων δ', ὄντων καὶ ἀσωμάτων]. They posit elements of bodies only, not of incorporeal things, although these are incorporeal. Here he blames the ancients for handing down the elements of bodies alone and leaving out incorporeal things. Yet the elements, or constitutive principles, which he himself hands down do not fit anything except corporeal things. For matter and form cannot even be applied by analogy (as is clear from the previous section) to composite accidents. Composite accidents alone are those incorporeal things, and it is of these that the ancients' reproach can be understood, that they did not touch on the principles of incorporeal things. For it is not likely that Aristotle, when he wrote these words, had simple accidents in mind, unless he cherished that mad opinion which wants every accident to consist of matter and form, or of two parts, one of which is like matter and the other like form. Suarez attacks this fancy at length in his fourteenth disputation. It is akin to, or the same as, Scaliger's notion that all accidents are composed of essence and existence, or of potency and act; on this we said much in the previous section. But that Aristotle held this nowhere appears in his writings. Nor can these words of Aristotle be taken of intelligences and minds. For although he counts them as incorporeal, he thinks they are simple with an essential simplicity, and internal or constitutive principles do not belong to things so simple. Therefore the incorporeal things in question are entirely composite accidents, which must be understood when he argues that the ancients passed over the elements of incorporeal things. But he himself omitted them too, and his followers did not touch them. Whence it follows (as we said before) that the assignment of composing principles made by the Peripatetics is faulty, even if everything they dream about matter and form were true.

units.la: XI. Sed & Prisci, ac Plato Stoicique, sicuti hoc quoq; vitio laborant, quod de Incorporeorum Elementis nihil dixe-
units.tr: XI. But the ancients, Plato and the Stoics too, as they suffer from this fault, that they said nothing about the elements of incorporeal things,

units.la: Sect. I. §. 3. & 4. dixerunt, ita in eo prætereà peccant, quod solam Materiam putaverunt esse Corporum Principium internum. Namq; ut nihil dicamus de corporibus animatis (quorum proxima Elementa sunt Anima & Corpus, neutri ipsorum competente Materiæ appellatione, nedum ut utrumq; pro Materia haberi possit) in reliquis quoq; corporibus verum non est, ea componi ex solâ Materia. Ut enim daretur tale corpus, deberent portiones Materiæ nequaquam alteratæ concurrere; ac proinde illæ concursus nihil esset, nisi acervus iterus. non datur autem ullum corpus Naturale, quod sit tantum acervus. Materia enim corporum e variis corporibus simplicibus conflatorum, non est corpus per se, sed corporis pars duntaxat.
units.tr: (Sect. I. §. 3. & 4.) they also err in this, that they thought matter alone to be the internal principle of bodies. For, not to speak of animate bodies (whose proximate elements are soul and body, neither of which fits the name of matter, much less can both be held as matter), in the remaining bodies too it is not true that they are composed of matter alone. For for such a body to exist, portions of matter would have to come together without being altered; and so that coming together would be nothing but a heap. But no natural body is merely a heap. For the matter of bodies made up of various simple bodies is not a body in itself, but only a part of a body.

units.la: Erraverunt igitur Veteres, solam Materiam facientes Corporum Principium internum.
units.tr: The ancients therefore erred in making matter alone the internal principle of bodies.

units.la: Quanquam sane dubitare licet, an non alterum quoq; Principium compositivum, nimirum concursum Accidentium, Materiæ per ipsam generationem impositorum, agnoverint. Sanè quotquot unicam atq; uniformem statuebant omnium rerum Materiam (ut Thales Aquam, Anaximenes Aërem) non poterant alia corpora simplicia, multoq; minus composita, ex ea fabricari, nisi interventu variarum affectionum; idq; eos fecisse, Aristoteles testatur tum alibi pluries, tum primo Metaphysicor. 4. Οἱ ἐν ποιὰ ὕλης τὴν ὑποκειμένην οὐσίαν, τὰ ἄλλα τοῖς πάθεσιν αὐτῆς γεννᾶσι. Qui unum faciunt subjectam substantiam, reliqua affectionibus ipsius generant. Quod vero illas affectiones habuerint etiam pro Principio, diserte testatur Aristoteles primi Physicorum sexto, ubi tamen non de omnibus Qualitatibus aut Accidentibus loquitur, sed de densitate tantum atq; raritate, quas alio nomine ὑπεροχὴν καὶ ἔλλειψιν, excessum atq; defectum, appellat, ita tamen ut sub hac appellatione etiam comprehendat Platonis τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ τὸ ἧττον, magis ac minus, mira sane, sed ipsi sueta, turbandi libidine, cum Plato per Majus & Minus nihil aliud nisi ipsam Materiam intellexerit, sicuti ipse confitetur tum hoc in loco, tum clarius etiam 1. Metaph. 6. Raritas autem & Densitas non Materia ipsa erat veteribus, sed Materiæ affectiones, & Compositorum Principia, quod sic testatur ipse, Καὶ ἔοικε παλαιὰ εἶν καὶ αὐτη ἡ λόξα, ὅἶ τ᾽ ἓν. καὶ ὑπερoχὴ καὶ ἔλλειψις, ἀρχαὶ τῶν ὄντων εἰσί. Videtur autem prisca esse & hac opinio, quòd Unum, & Excessus atq; Defectus, principia rerum sint. & similiter initio capitis quinti, Παρμενίδης ψυχρὸν καὶ θερμὸν ἀρχὰς ποιεῖ, οἱ δὲ μανὸν καὶ πυκνόν; Parmenides frigidum & calidum facit Principia: alij autem Densum & Rarum: ubi tamen per Calidum, Frigidum, Densum, Rarum, fortasse non ipsæ affectiones, sed corpora istis affectionibus insignita sunt intelligenda.
units.tr: Yet one may doubt whether they also recognised another composing principle, namely the concurrence of accidents imposed on matter by generation itself. Certainly all who posited one and uniform matter of all things (as Thales water, Anaximenes air) could not fashion other simple bodies, much less composite ones, out of it except through the intervention of various affections. That they did this Aristotle testifies, both elsewhere many times and in Metaphysics I, ch. 4: Those who make one underlying substance generate the rest from its affections [Οἱ ἐν ποιὰ ὕλης τὴν ὑποκειμένην οὐσίαν, τὰ ἄλλα τοῖς πάθεσιν αὐτῆς γεννῶσι]. That they also held these affections to be principles, Aristotle clearly states in Physics I, ch. 6. There, however, he speaks not of all qualities or accidents, but only of density and rarity, which he calls by another name excess and defect [ὑπεροχὴν καὶ ἔλλειψιν], excess and defect, yet in such a way that under this name he also includes Plato's "more and less" [τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ τὸ ἧττον], more and less. This is a strange thing, but customary for him from a love of confusion, since Plato by "greater and less" meant nothing other than matter itself, as Aristotle himself admits both here and more clearly in Metaphysics I, ch. 6. But rarity and density were for the ancients not matter itself, but affections of matter and principles of compounds, as he himself testifies: And this opinion seems to be ancient too, that the One, and excess and defect, are the principles of things [Καὶ ἔοικε παλαιὰ εἶναι καὶ αὕτη ἡ δόξα, ὅτι τὸ ἕν καὶ ὑπεροχὴ καὶ ἔλλειψις, ἀρχαὶ τῶν ὄντων εἰσί]. Similarly at the beginning of chapter five: Parmenides makes cold and hot the principles, but others make dense and rare [Παρμενίδης ψυχρὸν καὶ θερμὸν ἀρχὰς ποιεῖ, οἱ δὲ μανὸν καὶ πυκνόν]. Yet by hot, cold, dense and rare perhaps not the affections themselves, but bodies marked by these affections, are to be understood.

units.la: XII. Quanquam si credere Aristoteli libet, non pro Principio Compositivo, sed pro Effectivo Raritatem ac Densitatem Prisci habuerunt.
units.tr: XII. Yet if we are willing to believe Aristotle, the ancients held rarity and density not as compositive but as effective principles.

units.la: etenim antedicto capite sexto ait eos ita sensisse de hisce tribus, ut πάσχειν, τὸ δὲ ἓν δύο ποιεῖν: Unum, pati: duo autem, agere. sed hoc fidem nullam meretur, neq; credendum est, Veteres illos ita desipuisse, ut affectiones, quæ in Materiam introducerentur, cum Efficiente confunderent. Quanquam enim probe scimus, quantum jam olim ante Platonem non pauci, & postea etiam Peripateticorum ac Medicorum pleriq;, & ante omnes Galenus noster, drasticis (ut vocant) Elementorum qualitatibus tribuerint: longe tamen diversissima res est. frigus enim & calor magnas saltem efficiendi vires habent, quæ res bonis istis viris imposuit, ut instrumenta in ipsam primarij Efficientis dignitatem subveherent. alt densitatis & raritatis longe alia est ratio, quippe quæ omni agendi facultate destitutæ, non potuerunt viris sapientibus fraudi esse, ut ab iis pro Principio Effectivo prædicarentur.
units.tr: For in the sixth chapter cited above he says that they thought of these three things in such a way that "to be one is to suffer, but to be two is to act" [τὸ μὲν ἓν πάσχειν, τὸ δὲ ἓν δύο ποιεῖν]: One suffers; two act. But this deserves no credence, nor should we believe that those ancients were so foolish as to confuse the affections introduced into matter with the efficient cause. For although we know well how much, even long before Plato, not a few, and afterwards many of the Peripatetics and physicians, and above all our Galen, ascribed to the so-called drastic qualities of the elements, the matter is far different. Cold and heat, at least, have a real power of acting, and this led those good men to raise these instruments to the rank of primary efficient causes. But the case of density and rarity is quite different, since they lack every power of acting and so could not have deceived wise men into being declared by them to be effective principles.

units.la: Et obiter notetur hic fatalis Aristotelis inconstantia, qui cum in primi Metaphysic.
units.tr: And here, in passing, let Aristotle's fatal inconsistency be noted, who, in the first book of the Metaphysics, [3.]

units.la: 3. Veteres omnes, qui unam modo generalem Materiam ponebant, exagitet, ac si unum modo Principium poneret, nimirum Materiale, non item Effectivum; hic aperte contrarium profiteatur. Non enim Anaxagoræ, Empedoclis, Democriti, Leucippi, aut Platonis est hoc dogma. Densitatem ac Raritatem esse Principia rerum; sed eorum, qui unicam duntaxat uniformem omnium rerum Materiam statuebant. Illi enim, utcunq; de corpore illo primo inter se dissentirent, in hoc omnes conveniebant, ope raritatis ac densitatis alia omnia ex primo illo corpore fieri. Quare qui diceret, nullum istos Philosophos Principium Effectivum agnovisse; non poterat, sine levitatis ac contradictionis nota, ijsdem ascribere quod Raritatem ac Densitatem pro Efficiente habuerint.
units.tr: 3. attacks all the ancients who posited only one general matter, as if they posited only one principle, namely the material and not also the effective, while here he openly professes the contrary. For this doctrine, that density and rarity are the principles of things, is not that of Anaxagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Leucippus, or Plato, but of those who held that there is only one uniform matter of all things. For those men, however much they disagreed among themselves about that first body, all agreed in this: that by means of rarity and density all other things are made from that first body. Therefore, one who said that those philosophers did not recognise any effective principle could not, without the mark of levity and contradiction, ascribe to them the view that they held rarity and density as efficient causes.

units.la: XIII. Et sane alibi in hoc ipso primo Physicorum libro veriora de eadem hac re loquitur, aiens, eos hoc con- trariorum par non loco Efficientis, sed pro Materiae Affectionibus habuisse,
units.tr: XIII. And indeed, elsewhere in this same first book of the Physics, he speaks more truly about this same matter, saying that they held this pair of contraries not in the place of the efficient cause but as affections of matter,

units.la: Οἱ ἐν πυκνῷ καὶ μανῷ τὸ ὂν σῶμα τ' ὑποκείμενον, ἢ τῶν τριῶν ἕν, ἢ ἄλλο, ὃ δὴ πυρὶ μὲν πυκνότερον, ἀέρι δὲ λεπτότερον, τἆλλα γεννῶσι πυκνότητι καὶ μανότητι, πολλὰ ποιοῦντες. ταῦτα δ' ἐναντία, καθόλου δ' ὑστερόχρη καὶ ἔλλειψις, ὥσπερ τὸ μέγα φησί γ' ὁ Πλάτων καὶ τὸ μικρόν. ὥστε ὁ μὲν ταῦτα ποιεῖ ὕλην, τὸ δὲ ἓν, τὸ εἶδος. οἱ δέ, τὸ μὲν ἓν τὸ ὑποκείμενον ὕλην, τὰ δὲ ἐναντία, διαφορὰς καὶ εἴδη.
units.tr: Οἱ ἐν πυκνῷ καὶ μανῷ τὸ ὂν σῶμα τ' ὑποκείμενον, ἢ τῶν τριῶν ἕν, ἢ ἄλλο, ὃ δὴ πυρὶ μὲν πυκνότερον, ἀέρι δὲ λεπτότερον, τἆλλα γεννῶσι πυκνότητι καὶ μανότητι, πολλὰ ποιοῦντες. ταῦτα δ' ἐναντία, καθόλου δ' ὑστερόχρη καὶ ἔλλειψις, ὥσπερ τὸ μέγα φησί γ' ὁ Πλάτων καὶ τὸ μικρόν. ὥστε ὁ μὲν ταῦτα ποιεῖ ὕλην, τὸ δὲ ἓν, τὸ εἶδος. οἱ δέ, τὸ μὲν ἓν τὸ ὑποκείμενον ὕλην, τὰ δὲ ἐναντία, διαφορὰς καὶ εἴδη. [Those who make the underlying body, which is, either one of the three or something else, which is denser than fire and thinner than air, generate the rest by density and rarity, making many things. These are contraries, and in general excess and defect, as Plato says of the great and the small. So the one makes these matter, and the one makes the form. But the others make the one underlying thing matter, and the contraries differences and forms.]

units.la: Qui corpus subjectum fecerunt unum, aut aliquod trium, aut aliud quoddam, igne quidem densius, aere autem tenuius, reliqua gignunt densitate & raritate, multa facientes. hac autem sunt contraria, in universum vero excessus & defectus, sicuti magnum & parvum dicit Plato: nisi quod hic quidem ista facit Materiam; Unum autem, Formam. illi autem, Unum subjectum faciebant Materiam; contraria autem, differentias & Formas. Dicens Veteres Raritatem & Densitatem fecisse Materiae διαφορὰς καὶ εἴδη, satis indicat, quod eas pro Efficiente non habuerint. quippe διαφοραὶ τῶν στοιχείων, differentiae Elementorum nihil aliud sunt Aristoteli, quam ipsa eorum πάθη, affectiones, quorum introductione aut abolitione fit alteratio, sicuti è primo de Ortu & Interitu liquet. Et ut adhuc certius constet, quod Raritatem ac Densitatem nihil aliud fecerint Veteres quam Materiae medium affectiaffectiones, alterum apponimus ex Aristotele locum, superiore clariorem, qui sic habet: Οἱ ἐν ποιότησις τὴν ὑγρὸν μένην ὁσίαν, τὰ ἄλλα τοῖς πάθεσιν αὐτῆς γεννᾶσι, τὸ μανὸν καὶ τὸ πυκνὸν ἀρχὰς τιθέμενοι τῶν παθημάτων. Qui subjectam substantiam faciunt unam, reliqua ipsius affectionibus gignunt, raritatem ac densitatem ponentes. Principia affectionum. è quo loco hoc amplius discimus, quod non ipsarum tantum rerum sive corporum, quæ ex primo illo corpore generantur, sed & aliarum affectionum, quæ ad talium corporum generationem requiruntur, Principia fecerint Prisci illi, unius Materiæ autores, Raritatem ac Densitatem: Hujus autem rei causam discere licet ex octavo Physicorum, ubi Aristoteles ex propria quidem persona, sed ex aliorum dogmatis loquens, (quod illi perquam familiare, haud secus quam si propriæ Philosophiæ dissideret) sic inquit: Πάντων τῶν παθημάτων ἀρχὴ, πύκνωσις καὶ μάνωσις, καὶ γὰρ βαρὺ, καὶ κοῦφον, καὶ μαλακὸν, καὶ σκληρὸν, καὶ θερμὸν, καὶ ψυχρὸν, πονο-τῆτες ἀραιότης καὶ ἀραιότητες εἶναι. Omnium affectionum principium sunt condensatio & rarefactio. namq; gravitas, levitas, mollities, duritics, calor, & frigus, videntur quædam raritates ac densitates esse. Ex his autem apparet, quod non modo Veteres hi aliud Corporum Principium Compositivum, quam solam Materiam, agnoverint, sed quod & τῶν ἀσωμάτων, incorporeorum (contra quam ijs objiciebat Aristoteles) Elemena quodammodo attigerint.
units.tr: They who made the underlying body one, either one of the three or some other, denser than fire and thinner than air, generate the rest by density and rarity, making many things. These are contraries; in general they are excess and defect, just as Plato says of the great and the small. Except that the one makes these matter, and the one makes form. The others made the one underlying thing matter, and the contraries differences and forms. That the ancients made rarity and density into "differences and forms" of matter sufficiently shows that they did not hold them as efficient causes. For the differences of the elements are, for Aristotle, nothing other than their own affections, by whose introduction or removal alteration takes place, as is clear from the first book of On Generation and Corruption. And so that it may be more certain that the ancients made rarity and density nothing other than affections of matter, we add another passage from Aristotle, clearer than the above, which runs thus: those who make the underlying substance one, generate the rest by its affections, positing rarity and density as the principles of the affections [Οἱ ἐν ποιότησις τὴν ὑγρὸν μένην ὁσίαν, τὰ ἄλλα τοῖς πάθεσιν αὐτῆς γεννᾶσι, τὸ μανὸν καὶ τὸ πυκνὸν ἀρχὰς τιθέμενοι τῶν παθημάτων]: Those who make the underlying substance one, generate the rest by its affections, positing rarity and density as the principles of the affections. From this passage we learn further that those ancient authors, who held that matter is one, made rarity and density the principles not only of the things and bodies generated from that first body, but also of the other affections required for the generation of such bodies. The reason for this may be learned from the eighth book of the Physics, where Aristotle, speaking in his own person but on the doctrine of others (a habit very familiar to him, as if he were disagreeing with his own philosophy), says: The principle of all affections is condensation and rarefaction; for heaviness, lightness, softness, hardness, heat, and cold seem to be certain rarities and densities. [Πάντων τῶν παθημάτων ἀρχὴ, πύκνωσις καὶ μάνωσις, καὶ γὰρ βαρὺ, καὶ κοῦφον, καὶ μαλακὸν, καὶ σκληρὸν, καὶ θερμὸν, καὶ ψυχρὸν, πονο-τῆτες ἀραιότης καὶ ἀραιότητες εἶναι.] From these things it appears that these ancients not only recognised no compositive principle of bodies other than matter alone, but also in some way touched upon the elements of incorporeal things (contrary to what Aristotle objected to them).

units.la: XIV. Quanquam sane tum in hoc, quod Corporum
units.tr: XIV. Although indeed, both in this respect, that they made Densities and Rarities the Principles of bodies,

units.la: tum in eo, quod aliarum Affectionum Principia faciebant duas illas qualitates, Densitatem ac Raritatem, locuti sunt parum consentanea Veritati, quam viderunt veluti per nubem; sicuti in eadem hac re fecerunt reliqui quoq; Veteres, qui non unum aliquod corpus, sed multa diversiformia pro Principio Materiali posuerunt; Anaxagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Leucippus. Quod enim prioribus illis Densitas ac Raritas, idem fere Anaxagoræ & Empedoclis, ...
units.tr: and in that they made those two qualities, Density and Rarity, the Principles of the other Affections, they spoke in a way little in agreement with the truth, which they saw as if through a cloud. The other ancient writers also went astray in this same matter, since they laid down as the material Principle not one single body but many diverse things: Anaxagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Leucippus. For what the earlier ones called Density and Rarity, Anaxagoras and Empedocles called nearly the same thing, ...

units.la: Empedocli συγκρίσις και διάκρισις, congregatio & secretio, Democrito autem & Leucippo ρυσμός, τροπή, διαθιγὴ, sive σχῆμα, θέσις, τάξις, figura, situs, ordo, fuerunt in rerum generationibus. Et de duobus quidem posterioribus expresse testatur Aristoteles, quod hasce tres Materiæ διαφορᾶς differentias dixerint esse τῶν ἄλλων αἰτίας, reliquorum causas, id est, Principia. notum enim est, Aristotelem solere ista duo promiscue usurpare. De syncrisi autem & diacrisi non ita aperte testatur, an illa quoq; pro Principio ab Anaxagora (cujus ἕνωσις nihil est aliud quam quædam διάκρισις & σύγκρισις) & Empedocle habitæ suerint. Et potius credimus, non habitas esse; quandoquidem neq; Stoici qualitates, quarum in Materiam primam introductione omnia generabant, Principiorum nomine afficiebant, neq; Plato τὰ εἴδη. Quanquam enim verum est, quod tradit Aristoteles, Platonem ita philosophatum fuisse, ὅτι ἕκαστον τῶν γινομένων λέγεται τῷ εἴδος, γίνεται δὲ κατὰ τὴν μέθεξιν, καὶ φθείρεται κατὰ τὴν ἀποβολήν, quod unumquodq; eorum, quae sunt, dicitur (esse id quod est) ratione Speciei seu Idea; fit autem per participationem [Idea,] ac interit per amissionem [ejusdem] unde Aristoteles dicit sequi, ὅτι τὰ εἴδη οἴεται αἴτια εἶναι καὶ γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς, quod Ideas opinatur esse causas ortus & interitus. nusquam tamen comperietur Plato τὰ εἴδη, Ideas, Causæ aut Principij appellatione donasse, si per εἴδη intelligas illa Idearum simulacra, quorum in Materiam impositione illæ omnia gignebat. si vero per εἴδη intelligas ipsas Ideas, tunc verum est, quod ea inter Causas ac Principia collocaverit Plato, sed diversissima ratione, atque à præsenti disquitione, ubi de Principijs componentibus agimus, aliena: qua de re in ultima hujus capitis sectione plura dicentur.
units.tr: For Empedocles, the Principles in the generation of things were congregation and separation [συγκρίσις καὶ διάκρισις]; for Democritus and Leucippus they were shape, turning, and contact [ρυσμός, τροπή, διαθιγή], or figure, position, arrangement [σχῆμα, θέσις, τάξις], namely figure, situation, and order. Aristotle explicitly testifies about the last two that they said these three differences of matter [διαφοραί] were the causes of the rest, that is, the Principles. For it is well known that Aristotle was accustomed to use these two terms interchangeably. But concerning congregation and separation he does not testify so openly whether those were held by Anaxagoras (whose union [ἕνωσις] is nothing other than a certain separation and congregation) and by Empedocles as Principles. And we rather believe they were not so held, since neither the Stoics, who generated all things by introducing qualities into primary matter, assigned these to the name of Principles, nor did Plato assign the forms [τὰ εἴδη]. For although it is true, as Aristotle relates, that Plato philosophized in such a way that [each of the things that come to be is called by its form, and comes to be by participation, and perishes by loss of it], that each one of the things that are is called (to be what it is) by reason of its Species or Idea; it comes to be through participation [in the Idea], and perishes through loss [of the same], from which Aristotle says it follows [that he thinks the forms are the causes of both coming-to-be and perishing], that he holds the Ideas to be causes of birth and death. Yet nowhere will it be found that Plato gave the forms, the Ideas, the name of Causes or Principles, if by forms you understand those images of the Ideas by whose imposition upon matter he produced all things. But if by forms you understand the Ideas themselves, then it is true that Plato placed them among the Causes and Principles, but in a very different manner, and foreign to the present inquiry, where we treat of the component Principles. On this matter more will be said in the last section of this chapter.

units.la: Et fortasse Democritus quoq; illa tria modo memorata non fecit Causas vel Principia; quum fieri possit, ut ille duntaxat docuerit, ope istorum omnia fieri è Materia, aut in Materia. Aristoteles vero ipsius opinionem recitans
units.tr: And perhaps Democritus also did not make those three things just mentioned Causes or Principles, since it may be that he taught only that all things are made by means of them, out of matter or in matter. But Aristotle, reciting his opinion
r Metaph. 4.

units.la: r. de Ortu & Interitu. citans, de suo ijs Causæ appellationem tribuerit: quod cum facere solere in hisce, & similibus, sciunt quotquot ejus scripta legerunt, & nos jam antea monuimus. Utrovis modo se res habeat, parum nostrâ refert, quibus propositum non est, Veteres vel hic, vel alibi uspiam, in nostram pertrahere sententiam, aut ipsorum placita per calliditatem ita interpretari, ut nobis favere videantur; sed solummodo in medium proferre, si quando inveninus eas ad sententiam nostram ac veritatem aliquatenus appropinquasse, omissa patrocinatione errorum, quos Veritati immiscuerunt. sicuti hoc in negotio deprehendimus eos illatenus recte sensisse, quod utrumq; Principij genus, Effectivum, & Compositivum, agnoverunt, quodque divisionem Compositivi Principii in Materiale & Naturale, plerique ipsorum non omnino ignoraverunt. Si vero ab his generalibus ad particularem cujusq; Principij explicationem descendatur, plurima, ac fere omnia (æque ac ipsum Aristotelem) eos erasse, ultro ipsi fatemur. namq; & de Efficientibus proximis multa nescierunt, & de Efficiente Universali paucissimi ipsorum, & forte nulli, recte senserunt; & de Materia omnes maximopere (quanquam alius alio magis) decepti fuerunt; & de Natura parum omnino viderunt: sicuti apparebit, si quis ipsorum dogmata cum nostris, quæ in processu hujus operis suo quodq; in loco proponentur, comparaverit. nos jam ad alia pergamus.
units.tr: r. de Ortu & Interitu, citing it, attributed to them the name of Causes on his own account. That he is accustomed to do this in these and similar matters, all who have read his writings know, and we have already warned of it before. However the matter stands, it matters little to us, since it is not our purpose to draw the ancients, here or anywhere else, over to our opinion, or to interpret their views so cleverly that they seem to favour us. Rather we only bring them forward, when we find that they have in some measure come near to our opinion and to the truth, leaving aside the defence of the errors they mingled with the truth. Thus in this matter we find that they were right to a degree, in that they acknowledged both kinds of Principle, the Efficient and the Component, and that most of them were not wholly ignorant of the division of the Component Principle into Material and Natural. But if we descend from these general matters to the particular explanation of each Principle, we ourselves freely confess that they missed very many, indeed almost all, points (just as Aristotle himself did). For they knew little about the proximate Efficients, very few of them, and perhaps none, judged rightly about the Universal Efficient; they were all greatly deceived about Matter (though one more than another); and they saw very little at all about Nature. This will be evident if anyone compares their doctrines with ours, which will be set out in their proper places in the course of this work. Let us now proceed to other matters.
Section Four. Of the Conditions of Principles.

units.la: Principia esse, priora eo, cujus sunt Principia, non est Physice verum de omnibus. II. Neq; verum, Principia esse ἀγένητα καὶ ἄφθαρτα. III. Ne Aristotelicis quidem Principijs hæc conditio quadrat: unde eam hauserit Aristoteles. IV. Plato quoq; particularibus Principijs cipiys eam accommodavit, sed Effectivè, sola Anima, Efficiens Platoni. V. Magnus hic in Platone error, omni Efficienti tribuere has proprietates. VI. Animas esse corporibus priores, non probant Platonis argumenta. VII. Non cum Veritate tantum, sed & secum ipse pugnat Plato, faciendo animas ἀγέννητος. VIII. Conditio contrarietatis, ab Aristotele posita, non competit nostris Principijs. IX. Et neque Aristotelicis competit. Veterum suffragium non rite advocat Aristoteles ad confirmationem istius propositionis.
units.tr: (I) That principles are prior to that of which they are principles is not physically true of all of them. (II) Nor is it true that principles are ἀγένητα καὶ ἄφθαρτα [ungenerated and incorruptible]. (III) This condition does not even fit the Aristotelian principles: whence Aristotle drew it. (IV) Plato also applied this condition to particular principles, but only as efficient cause, namely the soul, which is the efficient cause for Plato. (V) Plato's great error lies in ascribing these properties to every efficient cause. (VI) Plato's arguments do not prove that souls are prior to bodies. (VII) Plato contradicts not only the truth but also himself, in making souls ἀγέννητος [unbegotten]. (VIII) The condition of contrariety, laid down by Aristotle, does not suit our principles. (IX) Nor does it suit the Aristotelian principles either. Aristotle does not properly call upon the testimony of the ancients to confirm this proposition.

units.la: Quot ac quænam sint Principia, antea declaravimus; nunc quid in universum prædicari de ijs possit, quaeq; sibi in communi conditiones vendicent, discipien- dum est, antequam ad particularem singulorum pertracta- tionem progrediamur.
units.tr: We have already set out how many principles there are and what they are. Now we must consider what can be predicated of them in general, and what conditions they share in common, before we proceed to the particular treatment of each one.

units.la: Videtur autem de ijs in universum dici non plus posse, quam quod jam in definitione dictum est, nimirum, Esse ea, per quæ, sive à quibus, res aliqua ortum accipit, & sine quibus oriri non potest. Nam quantum ad eas proprietates attinet, quas Aristoteles ac Aristotelici ascribere Principijs solent; nulla earum Principijs, quæ à nobis constituta sunt, accommodari universim potest, ne illa quidem, de qua minime omnium quispiam dubitaverit, qua nimirum dicitur, Principia esse priora eo, cujus sunt Principia. hanc conditionem & Suarez tradit, & Fonseca, & alij plurimi; & ipse eam indicavit Aristoteles his verbis, Πασῶν κοινὸν ἔστιν ἀρχῶν, τὸ πρῶτον εἶν ὅθεν ἢ ἔστιν, ἢ γίνεται, ἢ γινώσκεται. Omnibus Principijs commune est, esse primum, unde aliquid est, aut fit, aut cognoscitur. quod ille non de Philosophicis tantum, sive Physicis, sed de vulgaribus, itemq; Logicis Principijs protulit; ad quæ omnia etiam Suarez, Fonseca, reliquiq; Peripatetici hanc conditionem extendunt. sed nostra nunc non interest, de duobus istis Principiorum generibus, utpote à proposito nostro alienis, quærere. De philosophicis autem dicimus, quod in ijs veritatem non habeat hoc scitum. Namq; & Efficientes aliqui possunt suis effectis non priores
units.tr: It seems that nothing more can be said of them in general than what has already been said in the definition, namely that they are those things through which, or from which, something comes into being, and without which it cannot come into being. For as far as those properties are concerned that Aristotle and the Aristotelians are accustomed to ascribe to principles, none of them can be applied universally to the principles that we have established. Not even that one, about which hardly anyone has doubted, namely that principles are prior to that of which they are principles, can be applied to all of them. Suarez teaches this condition, and so does Fonseca, and many others. Aristotle himself indicated it in these words: Πασῶν κοινὸν ἔστιν ἀρχῶν, τὸ πρῶτον εἶν ὅθεν ἢ ἔστιν, ἢ γίνεται, ἢ γινώσκεται. Omnibus Principijs commune est, esse primum, unde aliquid est, aut fit, aut cognoscitur. [It is common to all principles to be first, whence something is, or comes to be, or is known.] He put this forward not only of philosophical or physical principles but also of common and logical principles, and Suarez, Fonseca and the other Peripatetics extend this condition to all of them. But it is not our present concern to inquire into these two kinds of principles, since they are foreign to our purpose. As for philosophical principles, however, we say that this dictum does not hold true of them, since some efficient causes may not be prior to their effects.

units.tr: a Disp. 12. sect. 1. §. 8. in fine. b §. Metaph. c. 1. q. 3. sect. 2. c 5. Metaph. t.
Chapter II.

units.la: priores esse; & Elementa, alia possunt non ante compositum existere, alia ne possunt quidem existere ante ipsum. Namq; & Materia potest non praexistere (sicuti non praextitit in prima Creatione) & Natura nunquam potest praexistere, quippe Accidens est: Accidens autem existere prius, quam in suum subjectum introducatur, non potest: ac proinde praexistere composito nequit. Et sane pari ratione falsum etiam deprehenditur hoc axioma, si Aristotelicis Principijs aptetur.
