Formam enim existere prius, quam in suum subjectum introducatur, omnes uno ore negant Peripatetici, sed eodem momento, & fieri Formam volunt, & subjecto uniri: unde omnino sequitur, quod Forma dici prior ipso composito non possit. Nam quod Fonseca ait, Ubicunq; datur ordo, dari prioritatem unius, respectu alterius; imò nihil aliud esse, duo qualibet esse ordinata inter se, quam unum esse prius altero: unde porro infert, Principium esse prius principiato, quum clarum sit, & dari ordinem inter principium & principiatum, & principiatum non esse prius principio: facili negotio hoc solvitur. Etiamsi enim concederemus, dari prioritatem, ubicunq; datur ordo, (id quod multi inter ipsos Peripateticos negant) inde tamen non sequeretur, Principia esse priora principiato per realem prioritatem; de qua nos sola quaerimus. Quod si vero illud placitum, quo omne Principium dicitur esse prius eo, cujus est Principium; ita explicetur, ut non realem tantum, sed & intentionalem prioritatem comprehendat; tunc illud verum esse, libenter concedimus. Namq; hoc pacto & Materia in prima Creatione, & Natura in quavis generatione est prior composito: quomodo nimirum omnes partes sunt priores suis totis. possumus enim nobis imaginari partes per se existentes, quae deinde conjunctae, compositum constituant; quod de composito facere nequaquam possumus, ut illud consideremus sine partibus, e quibus constat; quippe quod non aliud est, quam partes ipsae inter se junctae. Hac igitur ratione, & apud intellectum, Principium est prius eo, cujus est Principium. sed cum haec prioritas Logica magis sit, quam Physica; non est
units.tr: be prior [to the composite]. Some elements cannot exist before the compound, and others cannot even exist before it at all. For matter may not pre-exist (as it did not pre-exist at the first Creation), and nature can never pre-exist, since it is an accident. An accident cannot exist before it is introduced into its subject, and so it cannot pre-exist the composite. By the same reasoning, this axiom is also shown to be false if it is applied to Aristotelian principles. For all the Peripatetics with one voice deny that a form exists before it is introduced into its subject. They hold instead that it is made and united to the subject in the same moment, and so it altogether follows that the form cannot be called prior to the composite itself. As for what Fonseca says: wherever there is order, there is priority of one thing with respect to another; indeed, two things ordered among themselves are nothing other than one being prior to the other; whence he further infers that a principle is prior to what it principles, since it is clear both that there is an order between principle and principled, and that the principled is not prior to the principle: this is easily resolved. For even if we grant that there is priority wherever there is order (which many of the Peripatetics themselves deny), it would not follow that principles are prior to what they principle by real priority, which is the only kind we are asking about. But if that proposition, by which every principle is said to be prior to that of which it is the principle, is explained so as to include not only real but also intentional priority, then we gladly concede it is true. In this way, both matter in the first Creation and nature in any generation are prior to the composite, just as all parts are prior to their wholes. For we can imagine parts existing by themselves, which then joined together constitute the composite. But we can in no way do this with the composite, that is, consider it without the parts of which it consists, since it is nothing other than the parts themselves joined together. In this way, then, and in the understanding, a principle is prior to that of which it is the principle. But since this priority is more logical than physical, it is not

units.la: {§} Metaph. cap. 1. quaest. 2. sect. 1. eur huic scito, quod omnè Principium dicit prius esse eo, cuius est Principium, locus in Physica hac de Principijs tractatione dari debeat; quum physice priora sint illa duntaxat, ὅσα ἐνδέχεται εἶν ἄνευ ἄλλων, ἐκεῖνα δὲ ἄνευ ἐκείνων μή, quae possunt esse absque aliis; illa autem alia non absque illis. sicuti ex Platono ipse Aristoteles narrat ac probat.
units.tr: Why, you should know, the statement that every principle is prior to that of which it is the principle should have a place in this treatment of principles in Physics: physically, those things are prior which can be without others, while the others cannot be without them [ὅσα ἐνδέχεται εἶναι ἄνευ ἄλλων, ἐκεῖνα δὲ ἄνευ ἐκείνων μή], just as Aristotle himself narrates and proves, following Plato. (Metaph. ch. 1, q. 2, sect. 1.)

units.la: II. Sicuti autem hanc Principiorum conditionem rejicimus, ita multo vehementius repudiamus alteram illam, quae Principia facit æterna, utroq; genere æternitatis; ita uti & fuerint semper, neq; unquam desitura sint: cui conditioni connexa est hæc, quae neq; ex se mutuo fieri dicit Principia, neq; ab alio superiore; quia utrovis istorum admisso, desinerent fuisse ab æterno. Loci, in quibus hæc tradit, pauci ex pluribus hi sunt; Τῶν ἀρχῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἑτέρων αἴτιον ἢ ἀλλῶν ὄσων, Principiorum non est alia causa, quum sint æterna, octavo Physicorum capite primo in fine, & 3. Physicor. 4. requirit in Principio, ut sit ἀγένητον καὶ ἄφθαρτον, non genitum, neq; interiturum. & 1. Physicorum quinto; Τὰς ἀρχὰς μήτ' ἐξ ἀλλήλων εἶναι δεῖ, μήτ' ἐξ ἄλλων. Principia neq; ex se invicem esse oportet, neque ex aliis. additq; capite sexto, Τὰς ἀρχὰς ἀεὶ δεῖ μένειν, Principia semper manere oportet. Item quinto de Generat. Animalium. 7. dicit, Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι τὸ ἀρχὴν εἶναι, τὴν αὐτὴν μὲν αἰτίαν εἶν πολλῶν, ταύτης δ' ἄλλο ἀνωθεν μηδέν. Hoc est Principium esse, ipsum quidem esse causam multorum, ipsius autem nullam superius esse causam. hæc apertissime falsa esse, si nostris Principijs applicentur, non est ut multis demonstremus, quum id per se appareat. Nam de Principijs compositivis nonnulla adeo non fuerunt ab æterno, ut quædam ipsorum species ne per minimum quidem temporis momentum præexistere composito possit, sicuti paulo ante diximus. Materia verò licet à principio Mundi fuerit, nequaquam tamen æterna dici potest, quum initium habuerit; quod habuerunt etiam omnes Efficientes, solo Deo excepto. Quantum vero ad æternam durationem; ne illa quidem est universaliter vera. namq; & Efficientium maxima pars perit quotidie; × Incorruptibilia quotidie; & Principium compositivum alterum ne momento quidem temporis composito suo superstes manere potest. Quod autem dicitur, Principia non agnoscere ullum superius Principium, aut ullam superiorem causam; & illud falsissimum est de omnibus Principiorum speciebus, praeterquam de solo Deo. namq; & Elementorum quaedam semper, quoties compositum aliquod generatur, & ipsa tum demum fiunt, quum antea non essent, videlicet Natura; & Materia omnis aliquando facta est: & nullum est Efficiens infra Deum, quod non factum sit vel ab alio Efficiente creato, vel immediate ab ipso Deo. Multa etiam Principia ex aliis Principiis fiunt, ut apparet in animalibus, quorum Principia compositiva cum sint Anima & Corpus, quodq; ipsorum rursus ex suis Principiis, nimirum Materia & Natura, & haec rursus ex aliis Principiis constant. Natura etiam semper fit ab Efficiente; quare Principium Totius, est etiam Naturae Principium. sive igitur illa verba, Quod Principia non fiant ex se mutuo, ita interpreteris, ut fieri ex significet fieri tanquam ex Elementis, sive ut sumatur pro eo, quod est Effici ab alio; veritatem de nostris Principiis non habent.
units.tr: II. Just as we reject this condition of principles, so much more vehemently do we repudiate that other condition, which makes principles eternal, with both kinds of eternity, so that they have always existed and will never cease to be. Connected with this condition is the claim that principles are made neither from each other nor from any higher thing, since if either were admitted, they would cease to have been from eternity. Of the many passages where he teaches this, these are a few. Principles have no other cause, since they are eternal [Τῶν ἀρχῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἑτέρων αἴτιον ἢ ἀλλῶν ὄσων], in the first chapter at the end of the eighth book of the Physics; and in the third book of the Physics, chapter 4, he requires that a principle be ungenerated and imperishable [ἀγένητον καὶ ἄφθαρτον], neither begotten nor destined to perish. And in the first book of the Physics, chapter 5: principles must be neither from each other nor from others [Τὰς ἀρχὰς μήτ' ἐξ ἀλλήλων εἶναι δεῖ, μήτ' ἐξ ἄλλων]. He adds in chapter 6 that principles must always remain [Τὰς ἀρχὰς ἀεὶ δεῖ μένειν]. Likewise, in the fifth book of the Generation of Animals, chapter 7, he says: "For this is what it is to be a principle: to be the cause of many things, and to have no cause above it" [Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι τὸ ἀρχὴν εἶναι, τὴν αὐτὴν μὲν αἰτίαν εἶναι πολλῶν, ταύτης δ' ἄλλο ἄνωθεν μηδέν]. That these statements are most clearly false if applied to our principles does not need to be demonstrated at length, since it is evident in itself. For some of the compositive principles were by no means from eternity, and some of their kinds cannot pre-exist the composite even for the least moment of time, as we said a little before. Matter, indeed, although it has existed from the beginning of the world, can by no means be called eternal, since it had a beginning; and all efficient causes had a beginning too, except God alone. As for eternal duration, that is not universally true either. For the greater part of efficient causes perishes every day, and the incorruptibles too are daily changed, and the other compositive principle cannot remain even for a moment beyond its composite. And what is said, that principles recognise no higher principle or cause, is most false of all kinds of principles except God alone. For some elements are always made whenever some composite is generated, and they themselves then first come to be, when they did not exist before, namely nature; and all matter at some time was made; and there is no efficient cause below God that was not made either by another created efficient cause or immediately by God himself. Many principles also come from other principles, as appears in animals, whose compositive principles are soul and body, and of these each in turn comes from its own principles, namely matter and nature, and these in turn consist of other principles. Nature too is always produced by an efficient cause; hence the principle of the whole is also the principle of nature. Therefore, whether you interpret those words, that principles are not made from each other, so that made from means made as from elements, or take them to mean being made by another, they do not hold true of our principles.

units.la: III. Et sanè mirum non est, axiomata haec de nostris Principiis vera non esse, quandoquidem falsa sunt de Prin- cipiis ipsius Aristotelis, qui illa fabricavit.
units.tr: III. And indeed it is no wonder that these axioms are not true of our principles, since they are false of the principles of Aristotle himself, who devised them.

units.la: Et ut de externis Principiis nihil dicamus, atq; has propositiones in componentibus sive internis (de quibus ille eas praecipuè protulit) examinemus: etiamsi cummaxime vera forent, quae de Materia prima, Forma, & Privatione, ab ipso traduntur; non nisi falso tamen dici posset ista Principia ab aeterno fuisse, atq; in aeternum mansura, neq; aliquam superiorem causam agnoscere. ista enim caderent in Materiam duntaxat, quam ille ἀγένητον cum multis aliis somniavit: non in Formam, multoq; minus in Privationem. namq; hanc ne existere quidem, nisi in instanti; eodemq; momento, quo existere incipit, rursus interire, fatentur Peripateticorum acutissimi, sicuti antea audivimus. Formam vero aut existere ante compositi ortum, aut eo destructo manere, nequaquam ipsi volunt, nisi de sola Anima humana; quam tamen esse hominis Formam, non omnes inter se consentiunt. Non de nostris igitur magis, quam de Aristotelis Principijs salsum est hoc dogma, quod Principia absolute facit æterna; quod ipsi quoq; viderunt Peripatetici: qui propterea ad illud aliquo modo defendendum ridiculas, ut solent, & cum verbis Aristotelis planissime pugnantes opiniones commenti sunt. Namq; Ammonius, Simplicius, Philoponus, Toletus, alteram istius sciti partem, Quod Principia semper debeant manere, ita intelligendam dixerunt, Quod in omni generatione adinveniantur, ita illa dictio, semper, non temporis æternitatem, sed transmutationis universalitatem significat. Archangelus autem Mercenarius hanc expositionem rejiciens, ipse ait, Germanum hujus propositionis intellectum esse; oportere Principia semper manere in ratione Principij, ita ut ex aliys minime fiant. Sed falluntur utriq; haud dubie, neq; aliud cum hoc Axiomate sibi voluit Aristoteles, quam quod ipsa verba sonant, nimirum Principia in æternum manere, atq; fine carere, ita ut illa dictio, semper, temporis æternitatem significet. De hac expositione, quæ & Alexandri est, & è verbis necessario sequitur, dubitare non sinunt testimonia paralella, hic ex alijs Aristotelis locis à nobis adducta, in quibus non tantum ἀγέννητα, ortus expertia, Principia esse vult, sed & ἀφθαρτα, ab interitu immunia. Sed Aristoteli evenit hic, quod alibi sæpissimè, ut in condendis hisce axiomatis magis aliorum placita, quam sui ipsius, ab oculos habuerit: aut potius ne condiderit quidem ipse hæc axiomata, sed ea transcripserit ab alijs, non observato, quod sicuti cum ipsorum placitis plane concordabant, ita à suis plurimum dissentiebant. Etenim Prisci illi quanquam omnem Effectorem omnemque Materiam Principiorum nomine appellabant, præcipuè tamen hoc vocabulum attribuebant Generali Effectori, ac Materiæ; nimirum Deo, ac Corpori illi, vel illis corporibus, è quo vel quibus totum Mundum primitus factum dicebant. Materiam autem illam faciebant Deo coæternam, quippe qui crederent (in quo sane errabant quam crassissime) nullam substantiam, ne Divina quidem virtute, posse è nihilo gigni; sicuti itidem persuasum illis erat, nullum corpus posse in nihilum redigi. hinc igitur nata sunt apud illos haec pronunciata, Quod Principia (videlicet illa prima, Deus, & Materia communis) sint aeterna, ita ut ab aeterno fuerint, atq; in aeternum mansura sint; quodq; nec à se, vel ex se invicem, neq; ab aliis vel ex aliis orta sint, nullamq; superiorem causam, ac nullum prius Principium agnoscant. Quae omnia sicuti verissima forent, si vera esset hypothesis cui superstructa sunt, nimirum somnium illud de Materiae aeternitate; ita necesse est omnino falsa deprehendantur in tribus illis Principiis internis, Materia, Forma, & Privatione (quibus solis Aristoteles ea accommodavit, sicuti è primo Physicorum liquet) etiamsi vera essent, quaecunq; bonus vir de ijs somniavit. quare nimis imprudenter Axiomata, quae de suis Principijs, neq; ijs omnibus, sed universalibus duntaxat, Veteres protulerant, ad sua Principia particularia interna accomodavit.
units.tr: Let us say nothing of external principles, and examine these propositions in the components or internal principles, the ones Aristotle chiefly had in mind. Even if everything he teaches about primary matter, form and privation were entirely true, it could still only falsely be said that these principles have existed from eternity, will remain forever, and acknowledge no superior cause. For that would apply only to matter, which he, with many others, imagined to be ungenerated [ἀγένητον]. It would not apply to form, and much less to privation. The most acute Peripatetics admit that privation does not exist even for an instant, and at the very moment it begins to exist it perishes again, as we heard before. As for form, they do not at all want it to exist before the compound arises or to remain after its destruction, except in the case of the human soul alone; and they do not all agree that this soul is the form of man. Therefore this dogma, that principles are absolutely eternal, is no less false of Aristotle's principles than of ours. The Peripatetics themselves saw this, and so to defend it in some way they devised, as they usually do, opinions that are ridiculous and flatly contrary to Aristotle's own words. Ammonius, Simplicius, Philoponus and Toletus said that the other half of this saying, "that principles must always remain", should be understood to mean "that they are found in every generation": the word "always" signifies not the eternity of time but the universality of change. Archangelus Mercenarius rejected this explanation and said that the true sense of the proposition is that principles must always remain in the character of principles, so that they are in no way made from others. Both are doubtless mistaken. Aristotle meant nothing by this axiom except what the words plainly say: that principles remain forever and have no end, so that the word "always" signifies eternity of time. Parallel passages from other places in Aristotle, which we have cited, leave no room for doubt about this interpretation. It is also Alexander's, and it follows necessarily from the words. In those places he wants principles to be not only ἀγέννητα, free from origin, but also ἄφθαρτα, immune from destruction. But here Aristotle did what he very often does elsewhere: in framing these axioms he followed the opinions of others more than his own, or rather he did not frame them at all but copied them from others, without noticing that they agreed closely with those others' views and differed greatly from his own. For those ancients, although they used the word principle for every efficient cause and every matter, attributed it chiefly to the general efficient cause and general matter: namely God, and the body or bodies from which they said the whole world was first made. They held that this matter was coeternal with God, since they believed (and in this they erred most grossly) that no substance can come from nothing, not even by divine power, just as they were persuaded that no body can be reduced to nothing. Hence these pronouncements arose among them: that the first principles, God and common matter, are eternal, so that they have existed from eternity and will remain forever; that they arose neither from themselves nor from each other, nor from others or out of others; and that they acknowledge no superior cause and no prior principle. All of this would be most true if the hypothesis on which it is built were true, namely that dream about the eternity of matter. So it must necessarily be found false of the three internal principles, matter, form and privation (to which alone Aristotle applied these axioms, as is clear from the first book of the Physics), even if everything that good man dreamt about them were true. Therefore he was very imprudent in transferring to his particular internal principles those axioms which the Ancients had stated about their principles, and only the universal ones, not all of them.

units.la: IV. Ducem vero sibi habuit in hoc errore Platonem, qui itidem Veterum haec axiomata à Generalibus Princi- pijs ad Specialia transtulit, sed disparí tamen ratione quam Aristoteles.
units.tr: IV. Plato was the leader of Aristotle in this error. He too transferred these axioms of the Ancients from general principles to particular ones, but in a different way from Aristotle.

units.la: Non enim internis, sicut hic, sed externis sive Effectivis ipse ea applicavit, sicuti docebit insignis hic è Phædro locus, cujus tantum non ipsa verba ijs in locis Aristoteles, ubi Principiorum proprietates recensét, videtur excripsisse. ita autem se habet: Ἀρχὴ δὲ, ἀγέννητον ἐξ ἀρχῆς γὰρ ἀναγκη πᾶν τὸ γιγνόμενον γίγνεσθαι, αὐτὴν δὲ, μήδ' ἐξ ἑνός. εἰ γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ ἀρχὴ γίγνοιτο, ἂν ἀν ἐξ ἀρχῆς γίγνοιτο. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἀγέννητόν ἐστι, καὶ ἀδιάφθορον αὐτὸ ἀνάγκη εἶναι. ἀρχῆς γὰρ δὴ ἀπολομένης, οὔτε αὐτὴ ποτε ἐκ τοῦ, οὔτε ἐξ ἐκείνης ἄλλο γεννήσεται, εἴπερ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἀεὶ τὰ πάντα γίγνεσθαι. Principium autem est ortus expers, quippe omne id, quod fit, è principio fieri necesse est; ipsum autem, è nullo. si enim principium ex aliquo fieret, fieret, ex principio non fieret. Quandoquidem autem ortûs expers est, & ab interitu immune esse necesse est. namq; si principium perÿsset, neq; ipsam unquam ex alio, neq; ex ipso aliud fieret, siquidem omnia è Principio fieri oportet. Non de omni Principio hæc dici à Platone, sed de solo Effectivo, Anima nimirum, patet cuivis inspicienti locum; cujus scopus est, probare Animæ immortalitatem. probationem autem suam inde desumit Plato, quod omnis Anima se ipsam movet. Quidquid enim semper movetur, semper etiam vivere: semper autem moveri Animam, quippe quæ non ab alio moveatur, sed à seipso. & infert. Τὸ αὐτὸ κινοῦν, ἄτε οὖν ἀπολεῖπον ἑαυτὸ, ὅπερ λέγει κινούμενον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις, ὅσα κινεῖται, τοῦτο πηγὴ καὶ ἀρχὴ κινήσεως. Quod seipsum movet, nunquam cessat moveri, quippe non deserens se ipsum. sed & aliis, quæcunq; moventur, hoc motus principium ac fons est. quibus verbis tunc subjungit illa, Ἀρχὴ δὲ ἀγέννητον, & reliqua modo à nobis recitata. ut planissime appareat, eum non omni Principio, sed Effectivo tantum, sive Animæ, vindicare, ut sit ἀγέννητος καὶ ἄφθαρτος, quod etiamnum magis confirmant ista consequenter posita, Ἀθανάτου δὲ πεφασμένης τοῦ ὑφ' ἑαυτοῦ κινουμένης, ψυχῆς ὀσίαν καὶ λόγον τοῦτο αὐτὸ ὡς λέγων, ὃν αἰσχυνεῖται. Quum planum factum sit, id, quod seipsum movet, immortale esse; si quis hoc ipsum dicat esse animæ essentiam ac rationem, non pudefiet [i. e. revinci non poterit.] & mox, εἰ δ' ὅτι τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχον, μὴ ἄλλο ἢ ἐὰν τὸ αὐτὸ ἑαυτὸ κινοῦν, ἡ ψυχὴν, ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἀγένητόν τε καὶ ἀθάνατον ψυχὴ ἂν εἴη. Quodsi autem hoc ita se habet, nihil aliud esse id, quod se ipsum movet, nisi animam, necessario anima erit ortûs atq; interitûs expers. Quod verò soli Efficienti Principij generale vocabulum velut peculiare hic attribuit Plato, id facit non præter morem suum, qui & alijs in locis id facere soleat, & præsertim in decimo de Legibus: è quo libro addiscere etiam est (quod & hic in Phædro non obscure innuitur) Efficiens & Animam apud Platonem reciprocrari, ac plane idem esse: cujus jus rei ratio petenda est ex illis verbis, ubi animam dicit πηγὴν καὶ ἀρχὴν πάσης κινήσεως, omnis motus fontem ac principium. Motus autem dictionem non in angusta illa significatione sumit, qua solum motum localem denotat, sed in lata illa, in qua & Aristoteli est familiaris, quæq; omne mutationis genus comprehendit; sicut apparet ex hisce locis, è decimo Legum desumptis: [ἡ ψυχὴ] πρῶτον γενέσεως καὶ φθορᾶς αἴτιον ἁπάντων. Anima est prima causa ortus & interitus omnium. item, μεταβολῆς σωμάτων καὶ μετοικοσμήσεως ἁπάσης ἄρχει. Omnis corporum mutationis ac in novum statum deductionis auctor est. & postea [ψυχὴ κίνησις] ἑαυτὴν τε ἀεὶ καὶ ἕτερα δυναμένη κινεῖν, κἂν τε συγκρίσεις, ἐν τε διακρίσεσιν, αὐξαις τε καὶ ἐναντίω, καὶ γενέσεσι, καὶ φθοραῖς. Anima est motus [i.e. principium motivum] quae & seipsam semper, & alia movere potest, tum in congregationibus ac secretionibus, tum in incrementis & in contrario, itemq; in ortibus ac interitibus: ac mox, ἡ ἑαυτὴν τε κινοῦσα, καὶ ἕτερα, ἐναρμόττεσθαι πᾶσι μὲν ποιήμασι, πᾶσι δὲ παθήμασι, καλυμένη δὲ ὄντως τῶν ὄντων πάντων μεταβολή τε καὶ κίνησις. Quae seipsam aliaq; movens, & ad omnes concurrens effectus atq; passiones, verè appellatur omnium Entium mutatio atq; motus. (in quibus verbis quod actionum nomina pro ipso Agente ponit, in eo facit rem sibi valde suetam) & rursus, Ἀρα ἓλ πoϑῆμεν, μὴ ἱκανῶς δεδεῖχθαι, ψυχὴν ταυτὸν ἐν, καὶ τὴν πρώτην γένεσιν καὶ κίνησιν τῶν τε ὄντων καὶ γεγονότων καὶ ἐσομένων, καὶ πάντων αὖ τῶν ἐναντίων τούτοις: ἐπειδὴ γε ἀνεφάνη μεταβολῆς τε καὶ κινήσεως ἀσάσης αἰτία ἁπασί. Numquid igitur adhuc desideramus, quominus sufficienter demonstratum sit, quod Anima idem sit cum prima generatione ac motione eorum quae sunt, quaeq; fuerunt ac erunt, omniumq; etiam iis contrariorum: postquam quidem apparuit eam omnibus causam esse omnis mutationis ac motus. Ex hisce locis sicuti evidenter colligitur id, quod demonstrandum suscepimus, Platonem per motum intelligere omne genus mutationis: ita ita ex ijsdem quoq; liquet, quod prius dicebamus, eundem solam Animam habere pro Efficiente, quippe quam omnis mutationis facit autorem; in quam sententiam quoq; dicit eodem libro Τὴν ψυχὴν ἁπάντων τελεόν ἀρίλλων, διοι- κῶν τε καὶ ἐνοικοῦν ἐν ἅπασι τοῖς πάντῃ κινουμένοις· ἄγειν τε πάντα τὰ κατ' ἐρχὴν καὶ γῆν, καὶ θάλαττὰν τοῖς ἑαυτῆς κινήσεσι, εἰς αὔξησιν καὶ φθίσιν, καὶ συγκρισιν καὶ διακρισιν. Anima ponenda est omnium causa, omnia dirigens, ac in omnibus inhabitans, quæ ubicunq; moventur; omniaq; in cælo, in terra, atq; in mari ducens suis ipsius motibus ad incrementum & decrementum, itemq; ad concretionem & secretionem. itidemq; in Phædro (quanquam obscuriuscule) Ἡ ψυχὴ πᾶσα πάντῃ ἐπιμελεῖται τὸ ἄψυχον. Omnis anima curam gerit omnis rei inanimatæ. & in Epinomide, ψυχῆς γένεα προσήκει, πλάττειν καὶ δημιουργεῖν. σώματα δέ, πλάττεσθαι καὶ γίγνεσθαι. Animæ convenit effingere ac fabricari: corpori autem, effingi & fieri. & postea, Τὸ μὲν [ἡ ψυχὴ] ἄρχιον ἁπάντων. Τὸ δὲ [τὸ σῶμα] ἀναίτιον πάσης πάθης. Anima omnium causa est. corpus autem nihil confert ad quamcunq; passionem [efficiendam.] Quanquam autem solam Animam facit Principium Effectivum, non propterea denegat corporibus (tum simplicibus, tum compositis, quatenus ex simplicibus constant) vires effectivas. namq; quatuor illa Terram, Aquam, Aërem, Ignem, aliaq; ex his conflata, agnoscit habere facultates suas, nequaquam ab Anima manantes: quas etiam enumerat, calorem, frigus, gravitatem, levitatem, duritiem, mollitiem, colores, sapores, & si quæ sunt his similia. Iis tamen Principij atq; Efficientis appellationem denegat, quia nullum ipsæ motum incipiunt, sed necesse est prius ab alio, nimirum Anima, moveantur, quàm ipsæ alteram rem moveant; neq; quicquam suâ sponte efficiunt, sed Animæ Efficienti inserviunt: quare corpora, cum illis facultatibus sibi propriis, vocat κινήσεις ἔλεγα μὲν δυναμένας κινεῖν, ἑαυτὰς δὲ ἀδυνατούσας. Motus, qui alia quidem possint movere; se ipsa autem non possint: itemq; ἔλεγον.
units.tr: For he applied them not to internal but to external or efficient principles, as this notable passage from the Phaedrus shows. Aristotle seems to have copied its very words in the places where he lists the properties of principles. It reads: "A principle is ungenerated [Ἀρχὴ δὲ ἀγέννητον]: for everything that comes into being must come from a principle, but the principle itself cannot come from anything else. For if a principle came from something, it would not come from a principle. And since it is ungenerated, it must also be indestructible. For if a principle were destroyed, it could never come from anything, nor could anything else come from it, since all things must come into being from a principle." That this is said of every principle and not only of the efficient one is clear to anyone who looks at the passage, whose aim is to prove the immortality of the soul. Plato draws his proof from the fact that every soul moves itself. Whatever always moves will also always live, and the soul always moves, since it is moved not by another but by itself. He concludes: "That which moves itself, since it never leaves itself, never ceases to move; and it is the source and beginning of motion for all other things that are moved [Τὸ αὐτὸ κινοῦν, ἅτε οὐκ ἀπολεῖπον ἑαυτό, οὔποτε λήγει κινούμενον· ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις, ὅσα κινεῖται, τοῦτο πηγὴ καὶ ἀρχὴ κινήσεως]." After these words he adds the sentence "A principle is ungenerated" and the rest that we have just quoted. So it plainly appears that he claims for the efficient principle alone, namely the soul, that it is ungenerated and indestructible. This is confirmed even more by what follows: "Since it has been made clear that what moves itself is immortal, whoever says that this very thing is the essence and definition of the soul will not be put to shame [i.e. he cannot be refuted]." And soon after: "But if it is so, that nothing other than soul is that which moves itself, then soul must necessarily be ungenerated and immortal [εἰ δ' ὅτι τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχει, μὴ ἄλλο ἢ ἐὰν τὸ αὐτὸ ἑαυτὸ κινοῦν ἡ ψυχή, ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἀγένητόν τε καὶ ἀθάνατον ψυχὴ ἂν εἴη]." That Plato assigns the general word "principle" as if it belonged peculiarly to the efficient cause is not out of keeping with his habit, for he does this in other places too, especially in the tenth book of the Laws. From that book one can also learn (as is obscurely hinted here in the Phaedrus) that for Plato the efficient cause and the soul are interchangeable and are entirely the same. The reason for this is to be sought in those words where he calls the soul "the fountain and principle of all motion". He takes the word motion not in the narrow sense, in which it denotes only local motion, but in the broad sense that is also familiar to Aristotle and that embraces every kind of change. This is clear from these passages in the tenth book of the Laws: "The soul is the first cause of the coming into being and the destruction of all things." Also: "It rules every change and every transformation of bodies." And later: "Soul is motion, able to move both itself and others always, in combinations and separations, in increase and decrease, and in generations and destructions." Soon after: "That which moves itself and others, and joins in all actions and all passions, is truly called the change and motion of all beings." (In these words he puts the names of actions in place of the agent itself, a habit very familiar to him.) And again: "Have we then not yet sufficiently shown that the soul is the same as the first generation and motion of things that are, that have been and that will be, and of all their opposites too, since it has appeared to be the cause of every change and motion?" From these passages it is clearly inferred what we undertook to show: that Plato understands by motion every kind of change. From the same passages it also appears what we said before: that he takes the soul alone as the efficient cause, since he makes it the author of every change. He says the same in the same book: "The soul must be posited as the cause of all things, directing all things and dwelling in all things that move in any way, and leading everything in heaven, on earth and in the sea by its own motions, to growth and decay, to combination and separation." Likewise in the Phaedrus, though rather obscurely: "Every soul takes care of everything that is without soul." And in the Epinomis: "It belongs to soul to shape and to create; bodies are to be shaped and to come into being." And later: "Soul is the cause of all things; body contributes nothing to any passion [to be produced]." Although he makes the soul alone the efficient principle, he does not on that account deny efficient powers to bodies, whether simple or compound insofar as they consist of simple ones. He acknowledges that those four, earth, water, air and fire, and the things compounded from them, have their own faculties, in no way flowing from the soul. He lists them: heat, cold, heaviness, lightness, hardness, softness, colours, tastes, and whatever is similar to these. Yet he denies them the name of principle and efficient cause, because they initiate no motion themselves; they must first be moved by another, namely the soul, before they can move anything else. Nor do they effect anything of their own accord, but serve the efficient soul. So he calls bodies, with their own faculties, "motions which can indeed move other things, but cannot move themselves [κινήσεις, ἃ μὲν δυναμένας κινεῖν, ἑαυτὰς δὲ ἀδυνατούσας]", and so on.
Chapter II.

units.la: ἕτερον ἀεὶ κινοῦσης, καὶ μεταβαλλομένης ὑφ' ἑτέρας. qui alind semper moveant, aut ab alio mutentur. & facultates quoq; illas vocat Ἀκίνητον ... κινήσεις, motus secundario operantes, sicuti eas quæ Animæ propriæ sunt, vocat πρῶτον κινοῦντας, primariò operantes. Principium igitur Effectivum Platoni est sola Anima, quia hæc ex ipsius opinione est in quaq; re primum movens: & Principium movens, ac Primum movens, ab ipso pro eadem re habentur; sicuti declarant hæc verba, ex eodem libro, è quo præcedentia omnia, nimirum Decimo Legum, desumpta: Ὅταν ἕτερον ἄλλο ἡμῖν μεταβάλλῃ, καὶ τοῦτο ἄλλο ἕτερον ἀεὶ, τῶν τοιούτων ἀρχὴ ἔσται τὸ πρῶτον μεταβάλλον; καὶ πῶς, ὅταν ὑπ' ἄλλε κινῆται, ζῷον ἔσται πολὺ τῶν ἀλλοιούντων πρῶτον; ἀλλὰ ἀνάγκη γάρ. ἀλλ' ὅταν ἀρχὴ αὐτὸ αὐτὸ κινῇ, ἕτερον ἄλλο ἀλλοιώσῃ, τὸ δ' ἕτερον ἄλλο, καὶ οὕτω δὴ χίλια ἐπὶ μυρίοις γίγνεται τὰ κινηθέντα, μιᾶς ἀρχὴ ὡς αὐτῶν ἔσται τῆς κινήσεως ἀπάσης ἄλλη, πλὴν ἡ τῆς αὐτῆς αὐτὴν κινησάσης μεταβολή; & mox, Ἀρχὴν ἄρα κινήσεων πασῶν καὶ πρώτην, εἴπερ ἐσῶσι γιγνομένην, καὶ ἐν κινουμένοις οὖσαν, τὴν αὐτὴν κινοῦσαν φήσομεν ἀναγκαίως εἶναι. Quando unum aliud immutat, idq; rursus aliud porrò, horumne aliquod erit primum mutans? & quomodo, quum ab alio moveatur, hoc erit primum alterantium? sane impossibile id est. Sed quum aliquid seipsum movens, aliud alteraverit, idq; rursus aliud, & sic multa millia fiant eorum quæ moventur, num omnis ipsorum motus aliud erit principium, præterquam mutatio ejus motus, qui ipse seipsum movet. Itaq; necessario dicemus principium motuum ac primum movens esse, & in ijs existens quæ stant, & in ijs quæ moventur, id quod seipsum movet.
units.tr: Always moving another, and being changed by another [ἕτερον ἀεὶ κινοῦσης, καὶ μεταβαλλομένης ὑφ' ἑτέρας]. Those which always move another thing, or are changed by another. He also calls those faculties "motions that operate secondarily" [κινήσεις], and calls those that belong to the soul proper "primarily operating" [πρῶτον κινοῦντας], and calls the unmoved [Ἀκίνητον] ... Thus for Plato the only efficient principle is the soul, because according to his opinion it is the first mover in every thing; and the moving principle and the first moving thing are held by him to be the same. The following words, taken from the same book as all the preceding ones, namely the tenth book of the Laws, make this clear: "When one thing changes another, and that again another, will the first thing that changes be the principle of such things? And how, when it is moved by another, will it be the first of the things that alter? That is certainly impossible. But when a thing that moves itself alters another, and that another, and thus thousands and tens of thousands of things come to be moved, will not the principle of all their motion be the change of that which moves itself, and nothing else? Therefore we shall say that the principle of all motions, and the first mover, which is both generated and existent within moving things, must necessarily be that which moves itself." When one thing changes another, and that again another in turn, will any one of these be the first changer? And how, since it is moved by another, will this be the first alterer? Surely that is impossible. But when something moving itself alters another, and that another, and so many thousands of things come to be moved, will not the change of that which moves itself be the one principle of all their motion? Therefore we shall say that the principle of all motions, and the first, which is generated and exists both in things that stand and in things that move, is necessarily that which moves itself.

units.la: V. Quanquam igitur Plato prisciis in eo consenserit, quod Deum ita facit Mundi autorem, ut Materiam ipsi faciat coæternam, quare ijs etiam consentire debuit in eo, ut hæce ἀγεννησίας καὶ ἀφθαρσίας aeternitatis ortu atq; interitu carentis conditiones duobus illis primis Principijs principaliter attribueret: præterea tamen alteri quoq; PrinciPrincipiorum particularium, videlicet omni Efficienti, eas assignavit, ut superiora testimonia docent. In quo sane non minus fallitur, quam Aristoteles, qui eas Principijs suis internis, Materiae, Formae, Privationi, attribuit. Nam quantum ad Immortalitatem, ea falsò omnibus Animis attribuitur, quum solis humanis competat, reliquis omnibus statim in ipsa morte, sive compositi dissolutione, pereuntibus, non quidem in nihilum, sed eo tamen modo, ut Animae esse desinant, amittantq; eas proprietates omnes, per quas fiebat, ut in corpore dum essent, Animarum dignitatem obtinerent.
units.tr: V. Although Plato, in the earlier part, agreed with those who make God the author of the world in such a way that they also make matter coeternal with him, he ought therefore also to agree that the conditions [ἀγεννησίας καὶ ἀφθαρσίας] of being without birth and without decay, of eternity, belong chiefly to those two first principles. Besides this, however, he also assigned these conditions to the other kind of particular principles, namely every efficient cause, as the passages above show. In this he is certainly no less mistaken than Aristotle, who attributes these to his internal principles: matter, form, and privation. For as regards immortality, it is falsely attributed to all souls, since it belongs only to human souls; all the others perish at death itself, that is, at the dissolution of the compound, not indeed into nothing, but in such a way that they cease to be souls and lose all those properties by which, while they were in the body, they possessed the dignity of souls.

units.la: Æque igitur in hoc errat, quod omnem Animam facit immortalem, ac Aristoteles, qui omni Principio hanc praerogativam asserit. magis tamen sibi constat, quam Aristoteles. hic enim falsa loquitur, etiamsi vera esset ipsius de Principijs internis doctrina, quippe solam Materiam manere statuit; Formam autem perire, simul ac compositum perit; & privationem, simul ac compositum generatur. Plato autem vult, omnem Animam esse immortalem, atq; post excessum quoq; è corpore, manere, ac subinde nova corpora induere: ita ut omnium viventium similes sint inter se animae, & quae nunc est Formicae, Ostrei, aut Asini, alias esse possit hominis, & contra. notum enim est, tum ex aliis libris, tum praecipue ex hoc legum decimo, itemq; Phaedone, ac Timaeo, eum amplexum fuisse Pythagoricam Metempsychosin. quae res etiamsi est delirij plenissima, sibi tamen (ut dixemus) in eo constat Plato, quod omne Principium sive Efficiens facit immortale. hoc enim sequitur ex Metempsychosi, praesertim quomodo ipse eam statuit, qui in Phaedone plurima verba facit ut persuadeat, non aliquibus modo corporibus superstitem manere Animam, neq; post detrita aliquot domicilia, ipsam quoq; tandem interire: sed aeternum hunc esse ipsi immigrationis in corporea habitacula atq; emigrationis orbem, ita ut ipsa nihil unquam de suo statu deperdat, eademq; semper maneat quae erat prius. Quantum vero ad argumentum illud, quo Animarum immortalitatem ex eo probat, quod seipsas movent, id nullius planè
units.tr: Plato therefore errs in this just as much as Aristotle, who asserts this prerogative for every principle; yet he is more consistent with himself than Aristotle. For Aristotle speaks falsely even if his doctrine of the internal principles were true: he holds that only matter remains, while form perishes as soon as the compound perishes, and privation is generated as soon as the compound is generated. Plato, however, maintains that every soul is immortal, and remains even after its departure from the body, and then puts on new bodies again; so that the souls of all living things are alike among themselves, and the soul which is now that of an ant, an oyster, or an ass may be that of a man, and conversely. For it is well known, both from other books and especially from this tenth book of the Laws, and likewise from the Phaedo and the Timaeus, that he embraced the Pythagorean metempsychosis. Although this doctrine is full of folly, Plato nevertheless agrees with himself in this, as we have said, that he makes every principle or efficient cause immortal. For this follows from metempsychosis, especially as he himself laid it down; for in the Phaedo he makes many arguments to persuade us that the soul does not remain only through some bodies and then, after some dwellings have been worn out, finally perish too, but that this cycle of migration into bodily habitations and emigration from them is eternal, so that the soul never loses anything of its state, and always remains what it was before. As for that argument by which he proves the immortality of souls from the fact that they move themselves, this is by no means...
They posit / They are ignorant
Chapter II.

units.la: plane est ponderis. cujus enim voluntate factum est, ut seipsas movere possent, ejusdem arbitrio hanc facultatem, quando ipsi visum est, rursus deponunt. Quare ut haec argumentatio valeret, deberent Animae illam sese movendi vim non ab alio accepisse, sed semper habuisse. & hoc quidem dicitur expresse in Phaedro, sed itidem collectum vitiosissimo syllogismo. quomodo enim ex eo, quod Animae seipsas movent, colligit, eas semper mansuras; ita inde etiam concludit, eas semper fuisse. quae sane consequentia nulla est, nisi ut monstretur prius, non posse Deum rebus impertire hanc facultatem, seipsas movendi, quum ea prius carerent: Haec enim potestas Deo si tribuatur, corruit totus ille syllogismus, qui Animarum ἀγεννησίαν, ortus carentiam, ab earundem αὐτοκινησίᾳ, facultate seipsas movendi, deducit. Tribuit autem Deo hanc potestatem non Veritas modo, sed & ipse Plato: qui in Timaeo diserte docet, Deum animas fecisse, non alias modo, sed & illam Mundi, de qua sic loquitur. Τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν ὃν ὡς νῦν ὑστέρων ἐπιχειρεῖσθαι λέγειν, οὕτως ἐμηχανήσατο καὶ ὁ θεὸς νεωτέραν. Non autem quomodo nos nunc ultimo loco de anima dicere aggredimur, ita Deus quoq; eam novissime fabricatus est. paucisq; interjectis, Ὁ δὲ καὶ γενέσει καὶ ἀρετῇ πρότερον καὶ πρεσβύτερον ψυχὴν σώματος, ὡς δεσπότην καὶ ἄρξοντα ἀρξομένου, συνεστάτο. Animam & generatione & praestantia priorem ac antiquiorem corpore, nimirum Dominam & imperaturam parituro, constituit. & de particularibus Animis (sive Animabus quis mavult) itidem testatur Deum illas αὐτίφυ καὶ ὑπάρξαθαι, seminasse atq; existere fecisse. neq; Animas tantum a Deo factas, sed & Deos omnes inferiores ab eodem fabricatos asserit: quae omnia quam longissime absunt ab eo somnio, imo illi ex diametro repugnant, quo res se ipsam movere potis, dicitur debere ab aeterno fuisse. quare id pro futilissimo explodi debet, non modo ab amatoribus Veritatis, sed & a discipulis ipsius Platonis; qui & in Decimo Legum, quanquam ibi verbosissime tractat illam Animarum se ipsas movendi vim, nusquam illam consequentiam, quod
units.tr: This is plainly a matter of weight. For by the will of him who made them able to move themselves, they in turn lay this faculty down again at their own pleasure. Therefore, for this argument to hold, the souls would have to have received that power of self-motion from no other source, but to have always possessed it. This is indeed stated expressly in the Phaedrus, but it is likewise inferred by a most faulty syllogism. For just as he infers from the fact that souls move themselves that they will always remain, so from the same premise he also concludes that they have always existed. This inference is certainly invalid, unless it is first shown that God could not impart to things this faculty of self-motion, since they previously lacked it. For if this power is attributed to God, that whole syllogism collapses, which deduces the unbegottenness of souls [ἀγεννησία], their lack of origin, from their self-motion [αὐτοκινησία], their faculty of moving themselves. Plato himself, however, not only Truth, attributes this power to God, for in the Timaeus he clearly teaches that God made souls, not only other souls but also that soul of the world, of which he speaks thus: "But as we now set about speaking of the soul last, so God too devised it as the younger." [Τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν ... νεωτέραν] That is, "Just as we now undertake to speak of the soul last, so God too fashioned it most recently." And after a few words: "But he who was prior and elder than the body in both generation and excellence, as master and ruler of what is ruled, was constituted." [Ὁ δὲ ... συνεστάτο] That is, he established the soul as prior and older than the body in both birth and dignity, clearly as its mistress and the one who would command what is born. And concerning the particular souls (or souls, as some prefer), he likewise testifies that God caused them to be sown and to exist [αὐτίφυ καὶ ὑπάρξασθαι]. He asserts that not only souls but also all the lesser gods were fashioned by God. All these things are far removed from that dream, indeed they flatly contradict it, that a thing which can move itself must have existed from eternity. Therefore that notion ought to be rejected as most worthless, not only by lovers of truth but also by the disciples of Plato himself. In the Tenth Book of the Laws, although there he treats very wordily that power of self-motion in souls, he nowhere touches on that inference, that they must therefore have existed from eternity. He professes only this there: that the soul is prior to the body and was made before it, [γενέσεως ἐν πρώτοις ἐστιν, σωμάτων ἐμπροσθεν ἁπάντων γενομένη] that is, it was born first, born before all bodies. And again: "The soul was first, not fire, nor air: the soul was born among the first..." [ψυχὴ πρῶτον ... γεγεννημένη, &c.] that is, "The soul came first, not fire nor air. Indeed the soul was born among the first things." And he says more than once: "The soul is older than the body" [Τὴν ψυχὴν πρεσβυτέραν εἶναι τοῦ σώματος]. And he concludes his discussion about the priority of the soul thus: [Οὕτως ... ἀρχούσης ἀρχομένας φύσιν] "Therefore we shall rightly, properly, and most truly and perfectly say that the soul was born prior to the body, while the body was born second and after the soul, since by nature the one rules and the other obeys." In these passages he describes the soul as older than the body in such a way that he says it was not existent before, but was made before; which he says even more clearly at the end of the Twelfth Book of the Laws: "The soul is the most ancient and most divine of all things, which, having received generation from motion [that is, the moving principle or efficient cause], has provided an everlasting essence." [ἡ ψυχὴ πρεσβύτατον τε καὶ θειότατον ... ἀέναον οὐσίαν ἐπόρισεν.] These words, somewhat obscure, he then explains by other clearer ones: "The soul is the most ancient of all things that have received birth, and immortal." [ψυχὴ ἐστι πρεσβύτατον ... ἀθάνατόν τε.] Those passages, however, say the plain opposite of those in the Phaedrus, where souls are declared to be unbegotten [ἀγέννητοι].

units.la: scripsitae alia[?] quod propterea oporteat eas ab æterno fuisse, attingit, sed hoc tantummodo ibi profitetur; quod Anima sit corpore prior, atq; ante ipsum facta, γενέσεως ἐν πρώτοις ἔσιν, σωμάτων ἐμπροσθεν ἁπάντων γενομένη. Generata primò fuit, nata ante omnia corpora. & postea, ψυχὴ πρῶτον, οὔ πῦρ, οὐδὲ ἀὴρ: ψυχὴ δ' ἐν πρώτοις γεγεννημένη, &c. Anima primò fuit, non ignis, nec aer. Sane anima inter prima est genita. & plus semel dicit, Τὴν ψυχὴν πρεσβυτέραν ἔιν τὸ σώματος. Animam corpore vetustiorem esse. & disputationem illam de Animæ prioritate ita concludit. Οξ ὧς ἀρχ νοῦ' νυρίως ἀληθεστάτα τε νοῦ' τελεώταῖσα εἰρηνόμες ἄμεν, ψυχὴν μὲν πρεσβέραν σώματος γεγονέναι ἡμῖν, σῶμα δὲ δεύτερον τε καὶ ὕστερον ψυχῆς, ἀρχούσης ἀρχομένας φύσιν. Recte itaq; ac proprie, & verissime perfectissimeq; dixerimus, animam priorem corpore genitam esse, corpus autem secundo loco ac post animam, quum naturaliter hæc imperet, illud autem pareat. In hisce Animam corpore vetustiorem ita prædicat, ut eam dicat non fuisse prius, sed prius factam esse; quod adhuc expressius dicit in Duodecimo Legum versus finem, ἡ ψυχὴ πρεσβύτατον τε καὶ θειότατον ἔστι πάντων, ὧν κίνησις γένεσιν παραλαβοῦσα ἀέναον οὐσίαν ἐπόρισεν. Anima est antiquissima ac divinissima omnium, quibus motus [id est, principium movens sive Efficiens] assumta generatione, perennem essentiam exhibuit. quæ verba subobscura mox aliis clarioribus ita explicat, ψυχὴ ἐστι πρεσβύταλον ἀπάντων, ὥσε γονῆς μεταλήφεν, ἀδάνατόν τε. Anima est antiquissima omnium, quæ generationem sortita sunt, atq; immortalis. qui loci plane contrarium dicunt illi in Phædro, ubi Animæ statuuntur ἀγέννητοι.
units.tr: ... that for this reason they must have existed from eternity, but he only professes this there: that the soul is prior to the body and was made before it. "It was generated first, born before all bodies." And afterwards: "The soul came first, not fire, nor air; but the soul was born among the first..." "The soul was first, not fire nor air. Indeed the soul was born among the first." And he says more than once: "The soul is older than the body." And he concludes his disputation on the priority of the soul thus: "Therefore we shall rightly, properly, most truly and most perfectly say that the soul was born prior to the body, but the body second and after the soul, since by nature the one rules and the other is ruled." In these places he so describes the soul as older than the body that he says it did not exist before, but was made before. He says this even more expressly near the end of the Twelfth Book of the Laws, and so on as above.

units.la: VI. Et ut hoc in transitu dicamus; ne illud quidem, quod Anima sit corpore prior, evincitur ipsius argumen- to; quod ita se habet.
units.tr: VI. And to say this in passing: the argument does not even prove that the soul is prior to the body, as follows.

units.la: Anima inquit est ἀρχὴ, princeps, & corpus ἀρχόμενον, sub principe positum, duplici respectu. namq; Anima & ἀρχὴ est, quatenus primo movet, & corpus
units.tr: The soul, he says, is a beginning [ἀρχή], a ruler, and the body is what is ruled [ἀρχόμενον], placed under a ruler, in a twofold respect. For the soul is a beginning insofar as it first moves, and the body
Chapter II.

units.la: corpus ἀρχόμενον utpote quod non moveat, nisi acceptô ab Anima movendi initio & praeterea Anima est ἀρχὴ, quia imperat; corpus ἀρχόμενον, quia ipsi imperatur, animaq; imperium in ipsum obtinet. utroq; autem respectu indecorum putat, τὸ ἀρχόμενον ἢ ἀρχῆς ortu prius esse, propterea q; Deum nequaquam voluisse committere ut animam posterius quam corpus fabricaret. hoc indicant postrema verba testimonij ultimo loco à nobis positi, itemq; ista in Timaeo, Οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἀρχεσθαι πρεσβύτερον ὑπὸ νεωτέρας σωτείρας εἴασε. Quippe vetustiore & juniore in unum conclusis, illi ab hoc imperari passus non fuisset. & vehementius adhuc inculcat illud in Epinomide, πρεσβύτερον ψυχὴ σώματος ἄπασα παντός. ὁ γὰρ ἄρχων καὶ παλαιότερον καὶ θειοτέρον, πιθανὸν οὖν τὸ χείρονος καὶ νεωτέρας καὶ ἀμυδρότερον, παντάχῃ τε ἄρχον ἀρχομένης πρεσβύτερον καὶ ἄγον ἀγομένης πάντη. Omnis anima omni corpore antiquior est. quod enim est melius, vetustius & divinius, & omnimodis imperans, ac quoquo ducens, id probabile est antiquius esse pejori, ac juniori, & viliori, eoq; quod paret & ducitur. in quibus verbis hoc mirifici inest, quod τὸ παλαιότερον vetustius colligit esse πρότερον καὶ πρεσβύτερον, quod est plane τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ κείμενον sumere. Sed ut hoc mittamus; quam inanis sit utraq; ista ratio, verbo monstrari potest, nemo enim negaverit fabrum aeque commode posse uti suis instrumentis, si ante ipsum, quàm si post facta sint. & quod natu priora sint etiam praestantiora, fallum scimus ex hominis creatione, qui post omnia factus est, quum dignitate esset ante omnia, saltem ante mundum hunc, omniaq; quae in eo continentur. & non modo ipse factus est posterius iis, quibus usurus & imperaturus erat, sed & in ipso ἡ ἀρχὴ τοῦ ἀρχομένου posteriorem sortita est generationem; si quidem corpori prius efformato, postea Animam Deus inspiravit. Quanquam igitur verum fortassis est in quotidianis atq; ordinarijs generationibus, animam esse corpore priorem, neq; aliter fieri potest, quia ipsa sibi corpus anima architectatur; in illa tamen generatione, ubi non
units.tr: is what is ruled, inasmuch as it does not move unless it has received the beginning of motion from the soul. Moreover, the soul is a ruler because it commands, and the body is ruled because it is commanded, and the soul holds dominion over it. In either respect, however, he thinks it unseemly that what is ruled [τὸ ἀρχόμενον] should be prior in origin to the ruler [ἀρχή]; therefore God would by no means have willed to make the soul later than the body. The final words of the testimony we placed last indicate this, as do those in the Timaeus: "For he would not have allowed the elder to be ruled by the younger and inferior." [Οὐ γὰρ ἂν ... εἴασε.] Indeed, the elder and the younger being joined together, the former would not have allowed himself to be commanded by the latter. And he presses this even more vehemently in the Epinomis: "Every soul is older than every body. For what rules is both older and more divine, while what is worse, younger and feebler is probable, and that which rules everywhere is older than what is ruled, and that which leads in every way is older than what is led." [πρεσβύτερον ψυχὴ σώματος ἄπασα παντός... ἀγομένης πάντη.] Every soul is older than every body; for that which is better, older and more divine, and which commands in all respects and leads in every way, is probably older than what is worse, younger and more base, and what obeys and is led. In these words there is a remarkable feature: he infers that what is "older" [τὸ παλαιότερον] is therefore "prior and elder" [πρότερον καὶ πρεσβύτερον], which is plainly to assume what is the very point at issue [τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ κείμενον]. But leaving this aside, how empty each of these arguments is can be shown in a word. For no one will deny that a craftsman can use his tools equally well whether they were made before him or after. And we know from the creation of man that what is prior in nature is not therefore more excellent. Man was made last of all, though in dignity he was before all things, at least before this world and all that is contained in it. And not only was he made later than those things which he was to use and rule, but in him the ruler [ἡ ἀρχὴ] of the ruled [τοῦ ἀρχομένου] received a later origin as well; for God formed the body first and afterwards breathed in the soul. Although, therefore, it is perhaps true in ordinary and everyday generations that the soul is prior to the body, and it cannot happen otherwise, because the soul itself builds the body for itself; nevertheless in that generation, where not

units.la: Ratio. non anima tantum, sed & corpus ab alio sit Efficiente, minime id necesse est, ut anima corporis ortum tempore praecedat, & nequaquam id efficiunt Platonis rationes; qui eas non ad illum modo, sed & ad hunc ortum extendit, in quo anima non suum ipsa sibi domicilium fabricat, sed formato ab alio Efficiente corpori imponitur.
units.tr: Argument. Not only the soul but also the body is from another efficient cause, and it is by no means necessary that the soul should precede the body in time of origin. Plato's reasons by no means establish this; he extends them not only to that origin, but also to this one, in which the soul does not fabricate its own dwelling for itself, but is placed into a body already formed by another efficient cause.

units.la: VII. Sicuti autem fraudi fuit Aristoteli, conditiones illas, quas duobus Principijs primis attribuerant Antiqui, inconsiderate ad tria illa sua Principia transferre, non perpenso diversam admodum esse utrorumq; rationem; ita & Plato deceptus fuit, easdem Principijs Effectivis quibusvis accommodando. Namq; illa, Principium non debere ex alio fieri, quia sic ipsum non esset Principium. neq; debere perire, quia non esset unde rursus fieret: vera sunt, ad Veterum mentem. qui cum censerent (falso quidem, & impie, sed censerent tamen) Materiam non posse a Deo fieri; convenienter suis hypothesibus dicebant, Principia prima utraq; debere ab aeterno fuisse, & in aeternum manere: quia alterutrum, si sublatum semel foret, revocari aut reparari nullo modo posset. De Principijs autem Effectivis particularibus salsissima haec sunt, in Platonis quoq; schola, ubi cum statuatur Deus omnes animas ab initio creavisse; posset alias, quotiescunq; vellet, de novo creare, etiamsi omnes priores sublatae essent. atq; quam apertissime ista sibi adversantur, tradere Deum omnium animarum Creatorem; & Animas, quia Principia sint, non debere ex alio fieri. nam sive illud ἐξ Materiam denotet, sive Efficiens, sive utrumq;, omnino ἐξ ἄλλων factae sunt animae, secundum ea quae in Timaeo docentur. namq; & Deum ijs dat efficientem, & Materiam ijs non potelt denegare; quum fuerit in eadem cum Veteribus aliis haeresi; quod substantiam nullam ex non substantia creare Deus possit: quod si in corporibus verum est, in animas quoq; tanto nobiliores substantias expetat necesse est. & ipse diserte scribit, ex Materia factas esse illas propria quadam ac peculiari, neq; intelligibili, quales sunt Ideae, neq; corporea, quali constant Elementa (falso
units.tr: VII. Just as Aristotle was led into error by carelessly transferring to his three first principles those conditions which the ancients had attributed to two first principles, without weighing that the reasoning of the two is quite different, so Plato was also deceived, by applying the same conditions to effective principles of any kind. For those propositions, that a principle must not be made from another, because thus it would not be a principle, and that it must not perish, because there would be nothing from which it could be made again, are true according to the mind of the ancients. Since they held (falsely indeed and impiously, but nevertheless held) that matter could not be made by God, they consistently with their hypotheses said that both first principles must have existed from eternity and remain forever, because if either were once removed, it could in no way be recalled or restored. But concerning particular efficient principles, these views are most absurd, also in the school of Plato, where, although it is asserted that God created all souls at the beginning, he could otherwise, whenever he wished, create them anew, even if all the earlier ones had been removed. And how openly these things contradict themselves: to teach that God is the Creator of all souls, and that souls, because they are principles, must not be made from another. For whether that "from" [ἐκ] denotes matter, or efficient cause, or both, souls were indeed made from others, according to what is taught in the Timaeus. For he both gives God as their efficient cause and cannot deny them matter; since he holds the same heresy as the other ancients, that God can create no substance from non-substance. And if this is true of bodies, it must also be sought for souls, which are much nobler substances. And he himself plainly writes that they were made from a certain proper and peculiar matter, neither intelligible, as the Ideas are, nor corporeal, as the Elements consist (falsely...

units.la: Cap. II. ... ita hanc supra dicta "Impietas" a Deo sabus a Deo, sed jurat(?) a Deo.
units.tr: Thus the "impiety" mentioned above is from God, but [text unclear in the scan] is from God.
Chapter 2. On the Soul

units.la: fo enim hoc præceptori imponit Aristoteles quod ἐν ᾿Ιιμαίῳ τὴν ψυχὴν ἐκ τῶν στοιχείων ποιεῖ. in Timæo Animam ex Elementis faciat, sed tertia quadam inter utramq; media : de qua Animæ Materiâ multa nugatur absurda plane ac ridicula, ad ostendendam scilicet intimam quandam Pythagoricæ Mathematicæ scientiam : quæ pro mysterijs, ac immensæ cujusdam sapientiæ involucris, suspiciunt ac venerantur stulti : quum revera nihil sint aliud, nisi inanissima ac nullius frugis commenta. Non enim Aristoteles tantum innumera, sed & Platone permulta in Philosophiam invexit ejusmodi figmenta, quæ si ab aliis profecta essent, pro veteris ægroti somnijs condemnaturi essent etiam illi, qui nunc tantopere ea admirantur, ut maximos humanæ sapientiæ thesauros in ijs latere, sibi persuadeant. quorum nos hominum infœlicissimam fortem & ridemus sæpè, & miseramur : qui ipsi sic affecti simus, ut nemini quidem concedamus in Veteribus candidè tractandis, ubi Veritatem tenuerunt, aut aliquo modo ad eam accesserunt; semper tamen illibatam servemus libertatem ad ea, quæ ipsi falsa aut absurda protulerunt, aperte ac fortiter repudianda, ac quoties res fert etiam confutanda.
units.tr: For Aristotle imputes this to his teacher, that in the Timaeus he makes the soul out of the elements [ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ τὴν ψυχὴν ἐκ τῶν στοιχείων ποιεῖ], but of some third thing intermediate between the two. Concerning the matter of the soul, Plato talks a great deal of plain nonsense and ridiculous stuff, evidently to display a certain hidden Pythagorean mathematical science, which fools admire and venerate as a mystery and as a wrapping of some immense wisdom, when in truth these are nothing but the emptiest and most worthless inventions. For Aristotle has not only introduced countless such fictions into philosophy, but Plato has too. If these had come from others, even those who now admire them so greatly, persuading themselves that the greatest treasures of human wisdom lie hidden in them, would condemn them as the dreams of a sick old man. We often both laugh at and pity the most unhappy lot of these people. We ourselves are so disposed that we grant no one the right to deal fairly with the ancients where they held the truth or came somehow near to it, yet we always keep our freedom intact to reject openly and boldly, and where the matter calls for it to refute, those things they put forward that are false or absurd.

units.la: Sed ut ad rem redeamus; apparet omnino vanam esse illam in Phœdro argumentationem, qua animæ statuuntur immortales, quia sunt Principia; Principijs autem non competat, ut ex alio fiant, sed ut alia fiant ex ipsis. hoc enim non omnibus Principijs proprium est, sed Primis duntaxat, quę & Veteribus plerisque & ipsi, duo erant, revera autem non nisi unum est; nimirum Deus. reliqua autem Principia non eo minus sunt Principia, quia ab alio facta sunt; sed inde id tantum habent, ut non possint Principia prima dici, sed secunda; non vero, ut omnino Principia dici non mereantur. Itaque & ipse tum in Timæo, tum in Decimo Legum, animas vocat ἀρχὰς, Principia, quanquam ijs in libris fateatur, eas factas esse à Deo, ac proinde ἐξ ἄλλο ex alio. Ex alio, dicimus, id est ab alio. ita enim intelligi debere illa in Phœdro, evidenter apparet; quandoquidem illic de Animis sub Principiorum nomine agens, ait, omnia debere fieri ἐν τῶν ἀρχῶν, hoc est, à Principijs. aliter enim hoc exponi non potest, nisi ut
units.tr: But to return to the point: that argument in the Phaedrus is plainly worthless, by which souls are declared immortal because they are principles. A principle, however, is not suited to be made from another, but rather to make other things from itself. For this belongs not to all principles but only to the first ones, which were for most of the ancients, and for Plato himself, two, though in truth there is only one, namely God. The remaining principles are no less principles because they were made by another; they only have this from it, that they cannot be called first principles but second ones, and not that they do not deserve to be called principles at all. Accordingly Plato himself, both in the Timaeus and in the tenth book of the Laws, calls souls principles [ἀρχάς], although in those books he admits that they were made by God, and so are "from another" [ἐξ ἄλλου]. "From another," we say, that is, made by another. That the passage in the Phaedrus must be understood in this way is clear enough, since there, speaking of souls under the name of principles, he says that everything must come to be "from the principles" [ἐν τῶν ἀρχῶν], that is, by principles. For this cannot be explained in any other way, unless his own mind is plainly contradicted, since he nowhere says that anything comes from souls as from matter, but that all things come from them as from an efficient cause. And let this suffice on the conditions of being unbegotten and incorruptible, which Plato and Aristotle, though in different ways, transferred from the first principles, ascribed by the ancients, to the secondary or particular principles.

units.la: Nota marginal annotations not legible in detail. ut ipsius menti manifeste contradicatur, quum nusquam dicat, aliquid fieri ex Animis, tanquam e Materia, sed omnia fieri ab illis, tanquam ab Efficiente. Et tantum quidem dictum sit de conditionibus ἀγεννησίας atque ἀφθαρσίας, quas Principijs Primis à Veteribus attributas, ad Principia secunda sive particularia Plato & Aristoteles, sed diversis modis, transtulerunt.
units.tr: so that his own mind is plainly contradicted, since he nowhere says that anything is made out of Souls as out of matter, but that all things are made by them as by an efficient cause. Let so much be said about the conditions of ungeneratedness [ἀγεννησίας] and incorruptibility [ἀφθαρσίας], which the Ancients attributed to the First Principles and which Plato and Aristotle transferred to the secondary or particular principles, though in different ways.

units.la: VIII. Alia Principiorum conditio ab Aristotele posita, haec est, ut sint invicem contraria. Ἐναντίας ἔν ἀεὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς, Principia oportet esse contraria, inquit primo Physicorum. sed neque haec conditio Principijs nostris competit.
units.tr: VIII. Another condition of Principles laid down by Aristotle is that they be contrary to one another. "Principles ought to be contrary" [Ἐναντίας ἔν ἀεὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς], he says in the first book of the Physics. But this condition does not suit our Principles either.

units.la: Quantum enim ad Principia Compositiva, neq; Anima Corpori, neq; Materia Naturae, neq; partes Naturae inter se sunt contrariae, nisi Contrarij vocabulum latissime sumas ad significandum quicquid quocunq; modo est dissimile. & ita sumi quoq; solet, non ab Aristotele modo, sed & à Platone, Galeno, aliisque. Supervacua tamen, ne dicamus inepta, erit haec Principiorum conditio sub ista Contrarij acceptione; quum nihil amplius inde cognoscatur, quam si omnino non poneretur. & certum est, Aristotelem non hoc voluisse, sicuti vel ista verba è capite sexto evincunt, ubi testatur se de tali agere contrarietate; qualis una est in omni genere; ἀεὶ γὰρ ἐν ἑνὶ γένει μία ἐναντίωσίς ἐστί. Semper in uno genere una est contrarietas. Ista autem contrarietas non potest accipi de illa dissimilium (quippe talia contraria permulta sunt in unoquoque genere) sed de ea, quae est aut inter duos habitus invicem oppositos ac quam plurimum dissidentes, aut inter habitum & privationem. Talis autem Contrarietas in nullo eorum est, quae modo nominavimus. Quanquam enim multa dentur corpora, quae in alia sui parte sunt dulcia, in alia amara; in alia alba, in alia nigra; inde tamen non sequitur, partes Naturae istius corporis esse inter se contrarias. Namq; Natura corporum dissimilarium non constat proxime ex qualitatibus illis, quae sunt in singulis partibus, sed ex integris Naturis partium similarium. & licet darentur corpora similaria, in quorum Natura ista contrarietas inveniretur, hoc tamen non faceret fulciendo isti axiomati, quum multo major Principiorum Componentium pars ab ista contrarietate immunis sit. Sed neq; inter Principia Effectiva & Compositiva invenitur contrarietas, neq; dici potest, cur Efficiens contrarium sit vel Materiae vel Naturę; nisi verum sit illud axioma, quod omnem actionem & passionem vult inter contraria fieri. hoc pacto enim utriq; contrarium esset, & Naturae, utpote quam generat, & Materiae, quam alterat, Naturam ipsi ingenerando. sed nobis veritatem habere non videtur hoc effatum, sicuti in libro quarto, ad quem magis proprie pertinet haec disquisitio, demonstraturi sumus.
units.tr: For as regards the Compositive Principles, neither Soul to Body, nor Matter to Nature, nor the parts of Nature among themselves are contrary, unless you take "contrary" very broadly, to signify whatever is dissimilar in any way at all. And it is commonly taken in that sense, not only by Aristotle but by Plato, Galen and others. Under that sense of "contrary," however, this condition will be superfluous, not to say silly, since nothing more is known from it than if it were not laid down at all. And it is certain that Aristotle did not mean this, as even those words from chapter six prove, where he says that he is treating of such contrariety as there is in every genus: "for always in one genus there is one contrariety" [ἀεὶ γὰρ ἐν ἑνὶ γένει μία ἐναντίωσίς ἐστί]. Such contrariety cannot be understood as the contrariety of dissimilar things, for there are very many such contraries in each genus; it must be that which holds either between two mutually opposed and widely disagreeing habits, or between a habit and its privation. Now such contrariety is found in none of the things we have just named. For although there are many bodies which are sweet in one part of themselves and bitter in another, white in one part and black in another, it does not follow from this that the parts of the nature of that body are contrary to one another. The nature of dissimilar bodies does not consist directly of those qualities which are in the individual parts, but of the whole natures of the similar parts. And even if there were similar bodies in whose nature this contrariety was found, that would not support the axiom, since a much greater part of the Component Principles is free from such contrariety. But neither is contrariety found between Effective and Compositive Principles, nor can it be explained why the Efficient is contrary either to Matter or to Nature, unless that axiom is true which requires every action and passion to take place between contraries. For in that case the Efficient would be contrary to both: to Nature, which it generates, and to Matter, which it alters by generating Nature in it. But this saying does not seem to us to hold true, as we shall demonstrate in the fourth book, to which this inquiry more properly belongs.

units.la: IX. Nostris igitur Principiis non quadrat haec conditio; quod sane mirum non est, quum ne Aristotelicis quidem congruat.
units.tr: IX. Our principles, therefore, do not fit this condition; which is hardly surprising, since it does not even agree with the Aristotelians.

units.la: Etenim neque Materiam & Formam, neq; Privationem & Materiam inter se contraria esse aut ipse dixit, aut quisquam de ipsius sectatoribus. & neq; dicere possunt, cum statuant, unum contrarium non posse esse in altero tanquam in subjecto: ast & Formam & Privationem in Materia inesse dicunt; quare haec non possunt Materiae contraria statuere. Itaq; sola Forma & Privatio relinquuntur, de quibus verum esse queat hoc effatum, Principia debere esse contraria. quod animadvertens Toletus, sic excusare conatur: Propositio illa indefinita est, Principia sunt contraria, id est, aliqua Principia. Quum igitur nequaquam sit generalis haec conditio, nequaquam tot de ipsa verba facere debuerat Aristoteles, etiamsi vera essent, quaecunq; de Forma & Privatione ipse tradit: quum per se apertum esset, illa privative invicem opponi. Tantopere tamen in hac Thesi sibi placuit, ut magnam partem istius primi libri physicorum in ea consumpserit, neq; contentus varia in hanc rem ab Accidentibus exempla adduxisse, Veteres quoq; faciat hujus sententiae suffragatores: quod fecit perquam incommode, & maxima cum confusione. res enim diversissimas (quod jam supra ex parte monuimus) corrasit, atq; in unum acervum conjecit; Parmenidis Frigidum & Calidum, sive Terram & Ignem; Xenophanis Humidum & Siccum, sive Aquam & Terram; Thaletis aliorumq; Densum & Rarum; Demo-
units.tr: For neither Aristotle himself nor any of his followers has said that matter and form, or privation and matter, are contraries to one another. Nor can they say so, since they hold that one contrary cannot be in another as in a subject; yet they also say that both form and privation are in matter. Therefore these cannot be held to be contraries of matter. So only form and privation remain, of which the saying could be true that the principles must be contraries. Toletus, noticing this, tries to excuse it thus: "That proposition is indefinite: the principles are contraries, that is, some principles are." Since this condition is by no means general, Aristotle ought not to have spent so many words on it, even if everything he teaches about form and privation were true, since it would be plain in itself that these are opposed to each other by privation. Yet he took such pleasure in this thesis that he spent a great part of the first book of the Physics on it, and not content with adducing various examples of it from accidents, he also makes the ancients supporters of this opinion. He did this very awkwardly and with the greatest confusion. For (as we have already noted in part above) he has heaped together and thrown into one pile things most widely different: Parmenides' cold and hot, that is, earth and fire; Xenophanes' moist and dry, that is, water and earth; the dense and the rare of Thales and others; Demo-

units.la: Democriti Solidum & Inane, Itemq; ejusdem Positum, Figuram, Ordinem; Pythagoreorum Par & Impar; Empedoclis Amicitiam & Litem; ut mirum sit, qua ratione dicat, Veteres hosce omnes, quatenus T' ἀναλʼσία ποιῆσι τὰς ἀρχὰς, ταυτὸ λέγειν τῶς, ἢ ἀνάλογον, contraria habent pro principiis, idem dicere, saltem analogice. quae enim hic analogia, ubi unus loquitur de Principiis Materialibus, alter de Effectivis, alius de Formalibus (ut ipsius more nunc loquamur.) Sane ad confirmationem ejus thesis, quod omnis Forma substantialis oppositam sibi habeat Privationem, quodq; in omni generatione haec illam praecedere debeat, facere nonnihil fortasse potest, quod Veterum nonnulli Densitatem & Raritatem, alij Par & Impar, alij aliud quoddam par ejusmodi faciebant Principia Generationis. quomodo vero eodem pertineat, quod alij statuebant Materiae diversas species, diversis aut contrariis qualitatibus instructas, alij vero Efficientes primos introducebant duos, invicem adversantes seu contrarios; id vero pervidere non possumus. Sed hoc misso, ad potiora praevertamur.
units.tr: Democritus' solid and void, likewise his position, figure and order; the Pythagoreans' even and odd; Empedocles' friendship and strife. So it is remarkable by what reasoning he says that all these ancients, insofar as they make contraries the principles ["ἀναλογία"? no: "ἀναλογία" as printed], "say the same thing, at least by analogy" [τὰ ἐναντία ἀρχὰς ποιοῦνται, ταὐτὸ λέγειν τοὺς ἢ ἀνάλογον]. For what analogy is there here, where one speaks of material principles, another of efficient ones, another of formal ones (to speak in his own manner now)? Certainly, to confirm his thesis that every substantial form has privation opposed to it, and that in every generation the latter must precede the former, it may perhaps help somewhat that some of the ancients made density and rarity, others even and odd, others some other such pair, the principles of generation. But how this bears on the same point, that others held that matter has diverse species furnished with diverse or contrary qualities, and others introduced two first efficient causes opposing and contrary to each other, we cannot see at all. But setting this aside, let us turn to weightier matters.
SECTION FIVE
ON CAUSES.

units.la: I. Causae nomen soli Efficienti damus. id fecerunt etiam Stoici. II. Veteres quoq; ante Aristotelem idem videntur fecisse. III. Eadem quoq; fuit Platonis sententia, quo respectu ille Elementa sive Materiam concausas vocaverit. IV. Amplius docetur, quid Platoni sint Concausae. Aristoteles quoq; Concausas eodem sensu ac Plato dixit. V. Causa Divina Platoni non est Finis, sed Efficiens. VI. Testimonia, quibus docetur, Platonem soli Efficienti proprium fecisse Causae nomen. Valesij παρόραμα super doctrina Platonis de Causis. VII. Seneca, Toleti, aliorumq; error, Platoni ascribentium, quod quinq; vel sex Causarum genera fecerit. VIII. Aristote
units.tr: I. We give the name cause only to the efficient cause, as the Stoics also did. II. The ancients also seem to have done the same before Aristotle. III. Plato's view was the same, and in that respect he called the elements, or matter, co-causes. IV. It is further explained what Plato means by co-causes. Aristotle too used the term co-causes in the same sense as Plato. V. For Plato the divine cause is not the final cause but the efficient cause. VI. Testimonies showing that Plato reserved the name cause for the efficient cause alone; Valesius's oversight [παρόραμα] concerning Plato's doctrine of causes. VII. The error of Seneca, Toletus, and others, who ascribe to Plato five or six kinds of cause. VIII. Aristotle
Chapter II.

units.la: stotelis in Platonem calumnia, quod solâ Materiali & Formali Causa usus sit. IX. Idea, Platoni Causa Efficiens. X. Ideis nequaquam convenit cum Forma Aristotelica, sed Idearum simulacris: quid illa sint Platoni. XI. Ista simulacra nequaquam pro Causa habuit Plato. XII. Ideas à Platone inter Causas Efficientes haberi; negat Aristoteles; & sic omnem calumniæ suæ (qua Platoni imponit quod Efficientem Causam neglexerit) excusationem sibi præcludit. XIII. In vulgato etiam loquendi usu Causa & Efficiens pro ijsdem habentur.
units.tr: Aristotle's charge against Plato, that he used only the Material and Formal Cause. IX. For Plato the Idea is an Efficient Cause. X. The Ideas by no means agree with the Aristotelian Form, but with the images of the Ideas: what these are for Plato. XI. Plato did not at all regard these images as a Cause. XII. Aristotle denies that Plato counted the Ideas among the Efficient Causes, and so cuts off for himself any excuse for his accusation (that Plato neglected the Efficient Cause). XIII. In common usage too, Cause and Efficient are taken to be the same.

units.la: QUum Principij ac Causæ vocabula tam cognata sint Aristoteli, significationesq; ita affines obtineant, ut sæpè parum aut nihil inter ea distinguat, alterumque pro altero usurpet; & non raro etiam per vices alterum alterius & genus & speciem faciat (sicuti ista superius suis locis demonstravimus) mirum non est, si & tractatio ipsorum apud ipsum est conjuncta, atq; adeo confusa. Nostra vero alia est ratio, atq; in generali de Principijs sermone pauca nobis de Causis dicenda sunt, itidem ac de Elementis & Natura; quandoquidem uti hæc, ita Causæ quoq; una tantum Principiorum species sunt, ac proinde peculiarem sibi atq; accuratam seorsim edissertationem postulant. Quippe quod B. Augustinus quodam in loco dicit, Omnem Causam, Efficientem esse, eadem nostra quoq; est sententia, neque discrimen inter ista ponimus, sed reciproca esse, atq; inter se converti existimamus; idq; inducti tum illustrium pleroruinq; de Veteribus Philosophis exemplo, tum vulgata quoq; loquendi consuetudine: quæ sane in Philosophia quoque magni facienda est ad formandas sermonis leges, præsertim ubi ipsos huius sapientiæ Antistites habet suffragatores; id quod hic evenit. Et verum hoc esse, quod plerique præter Aristotelem Philosophi Causam atq; Efficientem promiscue usurpaverint, tanquam unius ejusdemq; rei duo diversa nomina, inter quæ nihil intersit; haud obscure ostendi potest. Certè Stoici ita senseruut, sicuti vel ex illo Senecæ testimonio, quod huiusdem Capitis Sectione tertia §. 1. aliâ occasione recitavimus, apparet; & non minus clare ex isto (quod in eadem Epistola 65. extat) Stoicis placet unam Causam esse, Id quod facit. idemq; à Laërtio etiam in vita Zenonis confirmatur. Quare sui oblitus, parumq; Stoice locutus alibi est Seneca, quando Elementa, Causas compositi nominavit, Hoc interest (inquiens) inter Decreta Philosophiæ & Præcepta, quod inter Elementa & Membra. hæc ex illis dependent. illa etiam horum Causæ sunt; & omnium.
