units.tr: Since the terms Principle and Cause are so closely related in Aristotle, and carry such akin meanings, that he often makes little or no distinction between them and uses one for the other, and not seldom makes one the genus and the other the species, by turns (as we have shown above in their proper places), it is no wonder that their treatment in him is joined and therefore confused. Our own method, however, is different. In the general discussion of Principles we must say a few things about Causes, just as we did about Elements and Nature, since, as these are, so Causes too are only one kind of Principle, and therefore need their own accurate and separate treatment. Indeed, we hold the same view as Blessed Augustine, who says in a certain place that every cause is efficient. We do not make a distinction between these terms, but think them reciprocal and interchangeable. We are led to this both by the example of many illustrious philosophers among the ancients and by common usage of speech. This certainly deserves great weight in philosophy too, for fixing the rules of discourse, especially when the very leaders of this wisdom are on its side, as happens here. That it is true that most philosophers, apart from Aristotle, have used Cause and Efficient interchangeably, as two different names for one and the same thing with no difference between them, can be clearly shown. Certainly the Stoics thought so, as appears from that testimony of Seneca which we cited on another occasion in section 3, §1 of this same chapter. It is no less clear from that passage in the same Epistle 65: "It pleases the Stoics that there is one cause, namely that which makes." Laertius also confirms this in the life of Zeno. Hence Seneca, forgetting himself and speaking less like a Stoic elsewhere, when he called the Elements causes of the compound, says: "This is the difference (he says) between the decrees of philosophy and its precepts, as between elements and limbs: the latter depend on the former. The former are also causes of the latter, and of everything."
Chapter II.

units.la: II. Prisci quoq; illi ante Aristotelem & Platonem Philosophi, videntur solam Causam agnovisse Efficientem. Namq; quod Formam non habuerint pro Causa, clarum est ex Aristotele, qui toties eos super hoc accusat; quod ne attigerint quidem illam, ut neque Finem, nedum ut illa inter Causas collocaverint. Materiam eos pro Causa agnovisse, videtur indicare lib. 5. de Gener. Anim. in principio, ubi ait eos non vidisse, ἀπλῶς ὅσως τὰς αἰτίας, ἀλλὰ μόνον τὴν τε ὕλης καὶ τὴν τε κινήσεως, reliquas causas, sed duntaxat Materialem ac Moventem. sed revera nihil aliud dicit, quam quod ex illo Causarum numero, quem ipse statuebat, duo tantum fuerint priscis Physiologis cognita; quod autem utrumq; eorum indigitaverit Causæ nomine, id non sequitur ex illis verbis, non magis quam ex illis. 1. Metaph. 7. Ἀναξαγόραν δὲ εἶναι ὑπολάβοι δύο λέγειν στοιχεῖα, μᾶλλον δ' ἂν ὑπολάβοι τὸν λόγον; si quis existimet Anaxagoram duo Elementa ponere, rationi maxime consentanea existimet, sequitur quod Anaxagoras Mentem Divinam, Mundi Opificem, appellaverit Elementum: de quare & in præcedenti capite nonnihil diximus. Et veteres illos contrarium potius fecisse, soliq; Efficienti Causæ nomen tribuisse, ex eo colligas licet, quod ubicunq; de Materia sola loquuntur, eam semper generali Principii vocabulo (nondum inventis; aut potius ad hunc usum nondum translatis ut videtur, στοιχεῖα Elementi & ὕλης Materia vocabulis) appellant, Causæ vero nunquam.
units.tr: II. The early philosophers, before Aristotle and Plato, seem to have recognised only the Efficient as a cause. That they did not regard Form as a cause is clear from Aristotle, who so often accuses them of this, and that they did not even touch on it, let alone place it among the causes. That they recognised Matter as a cause seems to be indicated in the fifth book of On the Generation of Animals, at the beginning, where he says they did not see the causes simply, "but only that of matter and that of motion": that is, the remaining causes, but only the Material and the Moving. But in truth he says nothing more than this: of the number of causes that he himself laid down, only two were known to the early natural philosophers. That each of these two was named a cause does not follow from those words, any more than it follows from those in the first book of the Metaphysics, where he says that if anyone should suppose Anaxagoras posits two elements, one would rather suppose it to be reason. Rather, it follows that Anaxagoras called the Divine Mind, the Maker of the world, an element, about which we said something in the preceding chapter. You may gather that those ancients did the opposite, and assigned the name of cause only to the Efficient, from the fact that wherever they speak of Matter alone, they always call it by the general term Principle (the words element [στοιχεῖον] and matter [ὕλη] not yet having been invented, or rather, as it seems, not yet transferred to this use), and never cause.
III.
Chapter II.

units.la: III. Sed de his quidem in medio relinquatur. De Platone autem, non minus quam de Soicis, clara res est, quod soli Efficienti proprium fecerit Causæ nomen, quicquid dicat Ψευδάρυμος ille Plutarchus, autor nimirum libelli De placitis Philosophorum, qui inter Plutarchi opera circumfertur. ipse enim scribit, Materiam quoq; & Formam à Platone inter Causas fuisse relatas, sic inquiens: Πλάτων τειχῶς τ᾽ αἴτιον φησὶ ὑφ᾽ ὧν, ἐξ οὗ, πρὸς ὅ. Plato triplicem statuit Causam, putà A quo, ex quo, Ad quod. Addit quidem, quod Efficientem habuerit pro principali Causa, κυριώτερον δὲ ἡγεῖται τ᾽ ὑφ᾽ ὧν, sed revera soli Efficienti Plato Causæ nomen concessit, quod vel ex Timæo apparet, ubi τ᾽ ποιοῦν καὶ τ᾽ αἴτιον, Efficiens & Causam, tanquam prorsus synonyma usurpat. Et quanquam eodem in libro Causas ita dividit, ut aliæ sint primariæ, aliæ secundariæ, quarum has appellat ξυναίτια & ξυμπαραίτια, concausas, idq; nomen Elementis attribuit, è quibus corpora componuntur, terræ, aquæ, aëri, & igni: non tamen Elementa facit Concausas, quatenus Materiæ vicem gerunt, sed quatenus & ipsa quoque suam efficiendi vim habent, ac ἀρχηγικὸς efficaces illas qualitates obtinent; quibus nonnullos tantum tribuisse ait, ut superiorem Efficientem nullam agnoscerent, illisq; solis omnem effectum ascriberent. Itaq; Elementa ipse fecit Concausas eodem respectu, quo alij illa faciebant. Causas Principales, quatenus nimium viribus effectivis prædita sunt. Et proinde etiam dicit in eodem libro, Deum, Principalem Efficientem, in operibus suis usum fuisse Elementis, sive potius Elementorum Qualitatibus, tanquam αἰτίας ὑπηρετούσας, causis ministrantibus, eaq; τ᾽ ἀναγκαῖον τῆς αἰτίας εἶδος, necessariam causæ speciem, appellat, opponens nimirum θεῷ θείῳ, divina, hoc est, ipsi Deo, primario effectori.
units.tr: III. But let these matters be left undecided. Concerning Plato, however, it is as clear as it is concerning the Stoics that he made the name of Cause the peculiar property of the Efficient alone, whatever that pseudo-Plutarch says, the author of the little book On the Opinions of the Philosophers, which circulates among the works of Plutarch. For he himself writes that Matter and Form too were reckoned by Plato among the causes, saying: "Plato posits a threefold cause: by which, from which, toward which." He does add that Plato held the Efficient to be the principal cause, "but he considers the by-which more principal," yet in truth Plato granted the name of Cause to the Efficient alone. This appears even from the Timaeus, where he uses "the maker" and "the cause" [τὸ ποιοῦν καὶ τὸ αἴτιον] as entirely synonymous. And although in the same book he divides the causes so that some are primary and others secondary, calling the latter concauses [ξυναίτια] and co-operating causes [ξυμπαραίτια], and attributes this name to the Elements of which bodies are composed, earth, water, air and fire, yet he does not make the Elements concauses insofar as they take the place of Matter. He makes them so insofar as they too have their own power of effecting, and possess those productive [ἀρχηγικός], efficacious qualities. He says that some had attributed these to the Elements so fully that they acknowledged no superior Efficient and ascribed every effect to them alone. Thus he himself made the Elements concauses in the same respect in which others made them principal causes: as having too much effective power. Accordingly he also says in the same book that God, the principal Efficient, used the Elements in his works, or rather the Qualities of the Elements, as causes ministering [αἰτίας ὑπηρετούσας], and calls them the necessary kind of cause [τὸ ἀναγκαῖον τῆς αἰτίας εἶδος], setting them against the divine, that is, God himself, the primary efficient.

units.la: IV. Et non solere Platonem per Concausas intelligere peculiare Causæ genus, ab Efficiente distinctum, sed Efficientis quandam speciem, nimirum Efficiens minus principale; cipale, atq; alteri Efficienti ad productionem sui Effecti ministrans, è Politico quoq; excipere licet, ubi quum dixisset, Δύο τέχνας εἶναι περὶ πάντα τὰ λεγόμενα, τὴν μὲν γενέσεως αἰτίαν, τὴν δὲ αὐτὴν αἰτίαν, duas artes versari circa omnia quae fiunt, quarum altera sit generationis concausa, altera vero ipsa causa. id porro ita explicat, Οἱ μὲν τὸ σχῆμα αὐτοῖ μὴ δημιουργοῦσι, τοῖς δὲ δημιουργοῖς ἔργανα παρεσκευάζουσιν, ὧν μὴ παραγενομένων οὐκ ἂν ποτε ἐνεργαθεῖη τὸ προσεταγμένον ἑκάστῃ τῶν τεχνῶν, ταύτης μὲν ξυναιτίας. Τὰς δὲ, αὐτὸ τὸ σχῆμα ἐργαζομένας αἰτίας. Concausas dicimus, quae rem ipsam non efficiunt, sed efficientibus parant instrumenta, quibus non adhibitis nequeat effici id quod unicuique arti propositum est: Causas vero, quae ipsam rem efficiunt. Atq; huc istius vocis usum, à Praeceptore acceptum, ipse etiam retinuit Aristoteles, uti apparet ex hoc loco, Δοκεῖ δὲ ζῷον ἡ τῶν πυρὸς φύσις ἀπλῶς αἰτία τῆς τροφῆς καὶ τῆς αὐξήσεως. Τὸ δὲ, ξυναίτιον πως μὲν ἐστιν, τὸ μὲν ἁπλῶς γε αἴτιον, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἡ ψυχή. videtur quibusdam ignis simpliciter causa esse nutritionis & incrementi, quum potius concausa sit. non enim ipse simpliciter est causa, sed magis Anima. quanquam autem in verbis proxime sequentibus Ignem Materiae accensET, non tamen eum ξυναίτιον concausam vocat hoc respectu, sed inquantum est Agens Instrumentarium, sicuti claret è 2. de Gener. & Corrup. cap. 9. ubi similiter castigans eos, qui non aliud Efficiens agnoscunt, quam ipsam Materiam, quatenus Qualitatibus activis instructa est; ait eos errare, quod Instrumenta habeant pro principali Agente, similiterq; eos facere, ac si quis serram faceret principalem Causam & Efficiens ejus actionis, ad quam obeundam ipsa pro instrumento adhibetur. & subjungit, ὥσε εἰ ὅτι μάλιστα πυρ ποιεῖ ἡ ἡ κινεῖ τὸ πῦρ, ἀλλὰ πᾶς κινεῖ οὐ προσδιώρισται; quare licet omnino ignis efficiat & moveat, non tamen considerant quomodo moveat. in quibus verbis quum fateatur ignem agere & movere, quanquam non principaliter; apparet quod hoc respectu in 2. de Anima eum appellaverit ξυναίτιον.
units.tr: IV. And that Plato did not usually mean by concauses a peculiar kind of cause, distinct from the Efficient, but a certain species of Efficient, namely one that is less principal and serves another Efficient in producing its effect, may also be gathered from the Politicus. There, after saying that there are two arts concerned with all things that are made, one of which is the concause of generation and the other the cause itself, he explains this: "Those who do not make the form itself, but prepare instruments for the craftsmen, without which what is assigned to each art could never be carried out, these are the concause of that art. But those which work the form itself are the causes." Aristotle too retained this use of the word, which he had received from his teacher, as appears from this passage: "It seems to some that the nature of fire is simply the cause of nutrition and growth. But it is in a way a concause. It is not simply the cause, but rather the soul." Although in the words that immediately follow he says fire is kindled for the matter, he does not call it concause [ξυναίτιον] in this respect, but insofar as it is an instrumental agent. This is clear from On Generation and Corruption 2.9, where, rebuking in a similar way those who recognise no other Efficient than Matter itself, insofar as it is endowed with active qualities, he says they err in taking instruments for principal agents. They do the same as if someone made a saw the principal cause and efficient of the action for which it is used as an instrument. He adds: "So, although fire does make and move most of all, they do not determine how it moves." Since in these words he admits that fire acts and moves, though not principally, it is apparent that in this respect he called it a concause [ξυναίτιον] in the second book of On the Soul.
Cap. II.
by what reason, in what order.
Cap. II.

units.la: συναίτιον, concausam, non inquantum Materia aut Materiæ pars est. prorsus ut hac in re Magistri ductum secutus videatur.
units.tr: A concause [συναίτιον], not insofar as it is the matter or a part of the matter. It seems that in this matter he followed the lead of his teacher.

units.la: V. Falluntur autem in eo plerique, interq; eos Galenus, quod in Timæo per τὸ οἰκεῖον τῆς αἰτίας γένος, divinum causæ genus, non ipsum Deum opificem, sicuti nos modo dicebamus, sed Causam Finalem putant designari; ad quam etiam referunt, quæcunq; in Phædone περὶ τοῦ βελτίστου, de optimo, disputantur: adeo ut Fonseca asseveret, Nemini, qui Phædonem legerit, dubium fore, quin ibi solum finem pro causa habeat Plato: distinctis enim verbis eum hoc dicere; cæteraque quæ videntur causæ esse, non pro causis habere, sed pro iis, sine quibus causa non sit causa. Et in eandem sententiam scribit etiam Suarez; qui hoc ita solvit, ut dicat, Platonem & Socratem illo in loco Moraliter potius quam Physice loqui. In Moralibus enim finem esse quodammodo totam causam actionum seu effectuum. sed neq; res vera est, neque solutio proba. namq; tantum abest, ut Socrates eo in loco Moraliter potius quam Physice loquatur; ut tota illa de causis disputatio, quæ satis est prolixa, sit merè Physica, nihil Moralis admixtum habens, nisi unum alterumq; versiculum de condemnatione Socratis; ipsiusq; proposito, non aufugiendi, neq; pœnæ se subtrahendi. reliqua omnia, quæ ibi dicuntur, Physica sunt ut quicquam aliud, sicuti unusquisq; locum inspiciens statim deprehendet. Quantum vero ad rem ipsam, nihilo verius est quod dicunt, solum finem ibi à Platone aut Socrate causam statui. non modo enim non statuitur sola causa, sed ne causa quidem omnino. etsi enim multa ibi dicuntur περὶ τοῦ βελτίστου, de optimo, & quædam ejusmodi verba jaciuntur, unde aliquis, cui non satis familiare aut perspectum Platonicum dicendi genus, colligere posset, ipsum illud βέλτιστον, optimum statui causam, revera tamen res non ita habet; id quod probatu est facillimum. fatentur enim ipsi, estque per se manifestum, unam tantum causam illic à Platone poni. at manifestissimis verbis declarat, Mentem esse rerum causam, itaq; ait, cum incidisset in librum brum Anaxagoræ, in quo tradebatur, ὡς ἂρα νοῦς ἐστιν ὁ διακοσμῶν τε καὶ πάντων αἴτιος, Quod Mens sit quæ omnia ordinat, omniumq; Causa est, se gavisum fuisse ταύτῃ τῇ αἰτίᾳ, hac causâ, & quod diceretur τὸν νοῦν εἶναι πάντων αἴτιον, Mentem esse omnium Causam posteaq; culpat Anaxagoram, quod causâ hac à se invectâ non sit usus in reddendis rerum rationibus, προοῖόν καὶ ἀναγινώσκων, ὅξω ἀνδρὶ λέγω, ὅς μὲν νῦν ὅλον χρώμενον, ὅδε ἅνας αἰτίας ἐπαιτιώμενον εἰς τὸ διακοσμεῖν τὰ πράγματα, ἀἰθέρας δὲ καὶ ἀέρας καὶ ὕδατα αἰτιώμενον. Pergens in legendo, video virum Mente ad nihil uti, neq; ipsi causas ordinationis rerum acceptas referre, sed æthereas aeresq; & aquas facere causas. Nῦν; Mens igitur est illa Causa, quam tantopere illic deprædicat Socrates: cur autem tam multa adjungat περὶ τῶν βελτίστων, de optimo, ea ratio est, quod Mentis est, facere unumquodq; ita, quomodo optimum factum est: ἔδοξέ μοι ἐν ἔχειν τὸν νοῦν εἶναι πάντων αἴτιον, καὶ ἡγησάμην, εἰ τοῦτο ὅτως ἔχει, τόν γε νοῦν κοσμοῦντα, πάντα κοσμεῖν, ἡμᾶς ἕκαστον ὡδέναι ταύτῃ, ὅπῃ ἂν βέλτιστα ἔχοι. Visum mihi est recte habere, quod Mens sit omnium Causa, atq; existimavi, si id ita habet, Mentem omnino ordinare omnia, & unumquodq; disponere quàm optimè. Et exemplo rem declarat, ἀμελήσας τὰς ὡς ἀληθῶς αἰτίας λέγειν, ὡς ἐπεὶ δὴ Ἀθηναίοις ἔδοξε βέλτιον εἶναι ἐμοῦ καταψηφίσασθαι, δι᾽ ταῦτα ἐμοὶ βέλτιον εἶναι δέδοκται ἐνθάδε καθῆσθαι. Negligens veras Causa afferre, sicuti quod mihi melius visum est hic sedere, quia Atheniensibus melius visum est me condemnare. in quo exemplo evidenter declarat, quid sibi velit in tota illa disputatione, nimirum, non ipsum τὸ βέλτιστον optimum esse causam, sed mentem, cui aliquid βέλτιον videatur, si quidem ὁ νοῦς (ut ibidem subjungit) πράττει τὴν τοῦ βελτίστου αἵρεσιν. Mens agit, eligendo optimum. Et quam malè ejus mentem capiant, qui dicunt eum, ipsum τὸ βέλτιστον inter causas referre, apparet ex Hippia majore, ubi ex professo tractans hanc thesin, conceptis verbis negat, τὸ καλὸν, pulcrum, hoc est finem debere inter causas referri. & negationem suam duplici probat argumento, tum quod solum Efficiens sit Causa; tum quod Finis & τ' καλὸν, pulcrum, est Effectum, non Efficiens, τὸ γιγνόμενον, αἴτιον οὐκ ὄξι. id quod fit, non est Causa. quae à nobis non eo dicuntur, ut Finem è Causarum numero eximamus, (quippe Finem certo modo esse Efficiens, ac proinde Causam, statuimus) sed ut genuinam Platonis super hoc negotio opinionem aperiamus, alioqui tumq; male ipsius dicta capientium errorem detegamus.
units.tr: Most people go wrong here, Galen among them, when they think that in the Timaeus the "kind of cause that is akin" [τὸ οἰκεῖον τῆς αἰτίας γένος], the divine kind of cause, designates not God the Maker himself, as we have just been saying, but the Final Cause. They also refer to it whatever is argued in the Phaedo concerning the best [περὶ τοῦ βελτίστου], concerning the best. So much so that Fonseca asserts that no one who has read the Phaedo will doubt that Plato there holds the end alone to be the cause; for he says this in so many words, and treats the other things which seem to be causes not as causes but as those without which the cause is not a cause. Suarez also writes to the same effect, and he resolves the matter by saying that Plato and Socrates in that passage speak morally rather than physically; for in moral matters the end is in a certain way the whole cause of actions or effects. But neither is the claim true nor the solution sound. For it is so far from being the case that Socrates in that place speaks morally rather than physically, that the whole long discussion of causes is purely physical, containing nothing moral except one or two little verses about Socrates' condemnation and his purpose of not fleeing or evading the penalty. Everything else said there is as physical as anything could be, as anyone who looks at the passage will immediately see. As for the matter itself, it is no more true that Plato or Socrates there sets up the end alone as the cause. Not only is the sole cause not set up, but not even a cause at all. For although many things are said there concerning the best [περὶ τοῦ βελτίστου], concerning the best, and certain such words are thrown in, from which someone who is not sufficiently familiar with or acquainted with the Platonic manner of speaking might gather that the best [βέλτιστον], the best, itself is set up as the cause, yet in truth the matter is not so; and this is very easy to prove. For they themselves admit, and it is obvious in itself, that Plato there posits only one cause. But he declares in the plainest words that Mind is the cause of things; and so he says that when he had come upon a book of Anaxagoras, in which it was taught that Mind [ὡς ἂρα νοῦς ἐστιν ὁ διακοσμῶν τε καὶ πάντων αἴτιος] is what orders all things and is the cause of all, he rejoiced in this cause [ταύτῃ τῇ αἰτίᾳ], and that it was said that Mind [τὸν νοῦν εἶναι πάντων αἴτιον] is the cause of all. Afterwards he blames Anaxagoras because, though he had brought in this cause, he did not use it in giving the reasons of things, but made the causes of the ordering of things to be ether, air and waters. Reading on, I see a man who makes no use of Mind, and does not assign to it the causes of the ordering of things, but makes ethereal things, airs and waters the causes. Now then: Mind, therefore, is that Cause which Socrates there so greatly extols; but why he adds so many things concerning the best, concerning the best, the reason is that it belongs to Mind to make each thing in the way in which it is best made. [ἔδοξέ μοι...] It seemed to me right that Mind is the cause of all; and I thought that if this is so, Mind, ordering all things, arranges each one in the way in which it is best. And he makes the point clear by an example, neglecting to speak of the true causes: since it seemed better to the Athenians to condemn me, for this reason it has seemed better to me to sit here. Neglecting to give the true causes, such as that it seemed better to me to sit here because it seemed better to the Athenians to condemn me. In this example he plainly shows what he means in that whole discussion: namely, that the best [τὸ βέλτιστον] the best itself is not the cause, but the mind to which something seems better, since Mind (as he adds in the same place) acts by choosing the best [ὁ νοῦς πράττει τὴν τοῦ βελτίστου αἵρεσιν]. Mind acts by choosing the best. And how badly those understand his mind who say that he counts the best itself among the causes, appears from the Greater Hippias, where, treating this thesis expressly, he denies in so many words that the beautiful [τὸ καλὸν], the beautiful, that is, the end, ought to be counted among the causes. He proves his denial by a double argument: first, because only the efficient is a cause; second, because the end and the beautiful [τὸ καλὸν], the beautiful, is an effect and not an efficient: [τὸ γιγνόμενον, αἴτιον οὐκ ἔστι] that which comes to be is not a cause. We do not say these things in order to remove the end from the number of causes (for we hold that the end is in a certain way an efficient and therefore a cause), but in order to lay open Plato's genuine opinion on this question, and to expose the error of those who misunderstand his words.

units.la: VI. Solum verò Efficiens esse Causam, hisce in Hippia verbis dicit Plato, τὸ ποιοῦν δὲ γ' ἐστιν ἓν ἄλλο τι ἢ τὸ αἴτιον, Efficiens nihil est aliud quam Causa.
units.tr: VI. That only the efficient is the cause. Plato says so in these words in the Hippias: "the efficient is nothing other than the cause" [τὸ ποιοῦν δὲ γ' ἐστιν ἓν ἄλλο τι ἢ τὸ αἴτιον]: the efficient is nothing other than the cause.

units.la: Excipit quidem Suarez, ex hoc loco non recte tribui Platoni, quod Causam & Efficiens dixerit idem esse; quia illa propositio, Efficiens nihil aliud est quam causa; non posset simpliciter converti, sed fallitur. si enim dixisset Plato, Efficiens est causa. non poterat illa propositio converti, non magis quam illa, Causa est Principium. quippe inde non sequitur, omne principium esse causam. ast si dicamus, Causa nihil est aliud quam Principium: omnino inde recte inferas, solam causam esse Principium: & proinde etiam è verbis Platonis recte concludas, solum efficiens esse causam. reciprocantur enim tales propositiones. & Platonem voluisse ita sua verba intelligi, satis liquet, cum ex ipso disputationis filo, tum ex eo, quod ipse postea dicit, propositionibus illis inter se conversis, Ού δ' αἴτιον ποιοῦν ἔφατη; πάντυγε. Nonne confectum est, Causam esse Efficiens? Omnino. Super omnia autem sunt, quae in Philebo hac de re scribit. ibi enim apertissime declarat, solum Efficientem sibi pro Causa haberi. quippe dicit, Efficiens & Causam solo nomine differre, quum re ipsa unum & idem sint, οὐκοῦν ἡ τοῦ ποιοῦντος φύσις ὀνόματι διαφέρει τῆς αἰτίας. τὸ δὲ ποιοῦν καὶ τὸ αἴτιον ὀρθῶς ἂν εἴη λεγόμενον ἕν. Itaq; Efficiens nihil nisi nomine differt à Causa & recte dicitur, Efficiens atq; Causam idem esse. Itaq; Diogenes etiam Laërtius, Platonis dogmata recensens, observavit, solum Efficiens causæ nomine ab eo donari: Δύο τῶν πάν- των ἀπεφηνεν ἀρχὰς, Θεὸν νοῦν ὓλην, ὃν νοῦν προσαγορεύει, καὶ αἴτιον. Duo tantum omnium declaravit principia, Materiam itemq; Deum, quem & Mentem vocat, & Causam. Et Valesius I. Controv. 4. nimis perfunctorie Timæum percurrit, qui ex eo hanc hauserit sententiam, ac si non finem modo, sed & materiam ibi Plato inter causas retulisset: Omnia (inquit) ex aliquo, & alicujus gratia fiunt. Hæ sunt duæ causarum species, necessario distinguenda, quarum, ut Plato inquit in Dialogo de Natura, altera necessaria est, altera divina. sed plurimum deceptus fuit Vir Doctissimus, quum non modo non utrumq; sed neutrum pro Causa Plato habuerit: sicuti præter illa, quæ antea dicta sunt, ex hisce, quæ nunc diximus, liquido apparet. qui enim solum Efficiens pro Causa habuerit, neque potuit Materiam Causis annumerare, neque Finem ita, ut eum (pro Mente Valesii & Aristotelis) omnino distinctum ab Efficiente Causæ genus faceret.
units.tr: Suarez does object that this passage wrongly attributes to Plato the view that cause and efficient are the same, because the proposition "the efficient is nothing other than the cause" cannot simply be converted. But he is mistaken. If Plato had said only "the efficient is the cause," the proposition could not be converted, any more than "the cause is the principle" can be converted, since it does not follow that every principle is a cause. But if we say "the cause is nothing other than the principle," then it rightly follows that only the cause is the principle, and so from Plato's words one may rightly conclude that only the efficient is the cause. Propositions of this kind are reciprocal. That Plato meant his words to be understood this way is quite clear, both from the thread of the argument itself and from what he says afterwards, when the propositions have been converted: "Has it not been agreed that the cause is the efficient? Entirely so" [Οὐκοῦν ἔφατη; πάντυγε]. Above all, however, is what he writes on this matter in the Philebus. There he declares most plainly that he holds only the efficient to be a cause. He says that the efficient and the cause differ only in name, while in fact they are one and the same: "Then the nature of the agent differs from the cause only in name; and it would be right to call the efficient and the cause one thing" [οὐκοῦν ἡ τοῦ ποιοῦντος φύσις ὀνόματι διαφέρει τῆς αἰτίας. τὸ δὲ ποιοῦν καὶ τὸ αἴτιον ὀρθῶς ἂν εἴη λεγόμενον ἕν]. Therefore the efficient differs from the cause only in name, and it is rightly said that the efficient and the cause are the same. Diogenes Laertius too, when he lists the doctrines of Plato, observed that only the efficient is given the name of cause by him: "He declared that there are only two principles of all things, God, whom he calls Mind, and the cause" [Δύο τῶν πάντων ἀπεφηνεν ἀρχὰς, Θεὸν νοῦν ὓλην, ὃν νοῦν προσαγορεύει, καὶ αἴτιον]. He declared only two principles of all things, matter and God, whom he calls Mind and Cause. Valesius, in his first Controversies, chapter 4, runs through the Timaeus too hastily, and draws from it the opinion that Plato counted not only the end but also matter among the causes: "All things (he says) come into being from something and for the sake of something. These are two kinds of causes, which must be carefully distinguished, of which, as Plato says in his dialogue On Nature, one is necessary and the other divine." But that most learned man was greatly mistaken, since Plato did not regard either of these, nor indeed neither of them, as a cause. This is clear, as well as from what has been said before, from what we have just said. For one who held only the efficient to be the cause could not count matter among the causes, nor could he make the end a kind of cause quite distinct from the efficient, as Valesius and Aristotle would have it.

units.la: VII. Multo autem etiamnum gravius hallucinatus est Toletus, asserens Platonem sex causarum species statuisse, quatuor nimirum Aristotelicas, & præterea exemplarem, ac instrumentalem: cum quo consentit etiam Suarez, dicens certum esse, quod Plato posuerit omnia genera causarum, quæ Aristoteles posuit, & fortasse plura. & trita satis ac vulgo recepta est hæc sententia, ac vetus quoque, quam & Seneca secutus est. sic enim scribit epist. 65. Quinque causæ sunt, ut Plato dicit: id ex quo, id à quo, id quo, id ad quod, id propter quod: novissime, id quod ex his est. Tanquam in statua, id ex quo, æs est: id à quo, artifex est: id quo, forma est, quæ aptatur illi: id ad quod, exemplar est, quod imitatur is qui facit: id propter quod, facientis propositum est: id quod ex istis est, ipsa statua est. Falluntur tamen, quotquot statuunt, Platonem tot Causarum species statuisse, quum ille, si ipsi de se credere æquum est, non nisi unam statuerit, puta Efficientem. Ortus autem ex eo error est, Platoni hæc ascribendi, quia Platonici vulgo tot Causas
units.tr: VII. Toletus has gone much more seriously astray, asserting that Plato laid down six kinds of cause: namely the four Aristotelian ones, and in addition the exemplary and the instrumental. Suarez agrees with him, saying it is certain that Plato posited all the kinds of cause that Aristotle posited, and perhaps more. This opinion is quite common and commonly accepted, and it is old too, and Seneca followed it. For he writes thus in Epistle 65: "There are five causes, as Plato says: that from which, that by which, that in which, that for which, and that for the sake of which; and last, that which comes from these. As in a statue: the bronze is that from which; the sculptor is that by which; the form that is fitted to it is that in which; the model that the maker imitates is that for which; the purpose of the maker is that for the sake of which; and the statue itself is that which comes from these." Yet all who hold that Plato laid down so many kinds of cause are mistaken. If it is fair to believe Plato about himself, he laid down only one, namely the efficient. The error arose because it became customary for Platonists to ascribe all these causes to Plato.
2. Phys. qu. 8.
Metaph. Disp. 12. sect. 3. §. 6.
Chapter II.

units.la: Causarum genera ponunt. Sed illi à magistro suo (utcumque ipsius verba torqueant) aperte desciverunt: cum nos abunde monstraverimus, illum de quatuor illis causis, quas ponit Aristoteles, solum Efficiens pro Causa agnovisse. ad Efficientem autem reducit & Exemplarem causam, & instrumentalem: sicuti de illa quidem non multo post propabimus; de ista vero libro quarto planum faciemus. Quantum vero ab eo abfuerit Plato, ut instrumenta absolutè pro causa habuerit, aut peculiare aliquod causæ genus constituere voluerit, apparet è Phœdone, ubi exemplo à partibus corporis sumto, nullo modo pati vult, ut ipsæ dicantur causa earum actionum, quæ per ipsas eduntur; magnæque socordiæ eos accusat, qui οὐχ οἷοί τε εἰσὶ διελέσθαι, ὅτι ἄλλο μέν τί ἐστι τὸ αἴτιον, ὃ δὴ ἐκεῖνο, ἀνευ ὧν οὐκ ἂν ποτε εἴη αἴτιον. nequeunt distinguere quod aliud sit Causa rei, aliud verò illud, sine quo Causa non posset esse Causa. Et Materiam quoq; quàm non pro Causa habuerit, quum alibi sæpe declarat, tum valde aperte in Epinomide, ubi quum omnia entia divisset in Animam & Corpus (per Animam intelligendo Efficientem, & per Corpus Materiam) sic ait: Τὸ μὲν αἴτιον ἐστὶν ἀντων, τὸ δὲ ἀναίτιον πάσης πάθης: horum alterum [Anima seu Efficiens] omnium rerum causa est; alterum vero [corpus sive Materia] nullius affectionis est causa.
units.tr: They lay down kinds of causes. But these men have openly deserted their master, however much they twist his words. We have amply shown that he recognised only the efficient cause among the four causes that Aristotle posits. He reduces the exemplary cause and the instrumental cause to the efficient cause. We shall prove this a little later for the exemplary cause, and make it plain in the fourth book for the instrumental. How far Plato was from regarding instruments as a cause in their own right, or from wishing to set up some special kind of cause, appears from the Phaedo. There, using the example of the parts of the body, he by no means allows that they should be called the cause of the actions performed through them. He accuses of great foolishness those who cannot distinguish [οὐχ οἷοί τε εἰσὶ διελέσθαι] that one thing is indeed the cause, and another is that without which it could never be a cause. "They cannot distinguish what is the cause of a thing from that without which the cause could not be a cause." That he did not count matter as a cause he declares often elsewhere, and very plainly in the Epinomis. There, having divided all beings into soul and body (understanding by soul the efficient cause, and by body the matter), he says: "The one [soul] is the cause of all things; the other [body] is the cause of no affection" [Τὸ μὲν αἴτιον ἐστὶν ἀντων, τὸ δὲ ἀναίτιον πάσης πάθης]. "Of these two, the one [the soul, or efficient cause] is the cause of all things; the other [the body, or matter] is the cause of no affection."
VIII.

units.la: Ex hisce omnibus apparet, Platonem præter Efficientem, nullam aliam Causam agnovisse. ac propterea judicatu facile est, quid statuendum sit de manifestissima illa Aristotelis in Præceptorem Platonem calumnia, qua negat illum Efficienti locum inter Causas fecisse. hoc enim manifesto sequitur ex eo loco, ubi ausus est scribere, Platonem non nisi Materialem ac Formalem Causam agnovisse. Φανερον δὲ (inquit) ἐκ τῶν ἐιρημένων, ὅτι δύοιν αἰτιῶν μόνον νεχρημένος, τῇ τε τὸ εἶδος καὶ τῇ καταὶ τὴν ὕλην. Ex dictis manifestum fit, quod duabus tantum Causis usus sit, eâ quâ quid est, & materiali, ut jam mirum non fit; si Prisicis quidvis assingere sibi permisit, qui veritus non est, in re tam manifesta, id scribere, quod omnes, talium curiosi, scirent esse salsissimum; nimirum, Causam Efficientem Platoni agnitam non fuisse: qui adeo eam agnovit, ut nullam aliam agnoverit praeter illam. Quare etiam falsum est, quod dicit, Platonem posuisse Causas Materialem & Formalem; nisi haec exponas eo modo, ut Plato dicatur de quatuor illis Aristotelicis Causarum speciebus non nisi duas usurpasse; quibus verbis id modo falsi inest, quod Efficientem Platoni eripiunt: reliqua vero excusari possunt. non enim inferunt necessario, quod Plato Materiam & Formam Causae nomine insigniverit, sed duntaxat, quod illa agnoverit: quale quid & antea, & in hoc ipso etiam capite, de consimilibus Aristotelis locutionibus monuimus. Si vero istorum verborum haec mens est, quod Plato istis duobus tantum Causae nomen tribuerit; illa falsitas, qua Plato accusatur Efficientem non habuisse pro Causa, cumulatur nova falsitate, quod idem Materiam & Formam numeraverit inter Causas. hoc enim a veritate alienum esse, inde apparet, quod supra ostendimus Platonem non aliud, quam Efficientem, pro Causa agnoscere.
units.tr: From all this it is evident that Plato recognised no cause except the efficient cause. Therefore it is easy to judge what must be said of that most manifest calumny of Aristotle against his teacher Plato, by which he denies that Plato gave a place to the efficient cause among the causes. This clearly follows from the passage where he dared to write that Plato recognised only the material and the formal cause. "It is evident (he says) from what has been said that he used only two causes, the formal and the material" [Φανερὸν δὲ ἐκ τῶν εἰρημένων, ὅτι δυοῖν αἰτιῶν μόνον κεχρημένος, τῇ τε τὸ εἶδος καὶ τῇ κατὰ τὴν ὕλην]. So it is no wonder that he allowed himself to add anything he liked for the Pythagoreans, since he did not hesitate in so manifest a matter to write what all who are curious about such things would know to be most false. Namely, that the efficient cause was not known to Plato, when in fact he knew it so well that he recognised no other cause besides it. Hence it is also false that he says Plato posited the material and formal causes, unless you explain these words in such a way that Plato is said to have used only two of Aristotle's four kinds of cause. In those words there is only this falsehood, that they take away the efficient cause from Plato; the rest can be excused. For they do not necessarily imply that Plato gave the names of cause to matter and form, but only that he recognised them. We have pointed out something similar, both earlier and in this very chapter, about similar expressions of Aristotle. But if this is the meaning of those words, that Plato gave the name of cause to only these two, then the falsehood with which Plato is charged, of not regarding the efficient cause as a cause, is compounded by a new falsehood, that he counted matter and form among the causes too. That this is far from the truth is clear from what we showed above, that Plato recognised only the efficient cause as a cause.

units.la: IX. Haud quidem inficiamur, quin Ideas pro Causa habuerit Plato, non modo ob testimonium Laertij, qui sic de ijs scribit, Τὰς Ἰδέας ὑφίσταται αἰτίας ζωὰς καὶ ἀρχὰς, τὸ τοιαῦτ' ἔιν τὰ φύσει συνεστῶτα, ὁ̈ιαπέρ ἔστιν αὐτά, Ideas statuit Causas quasdem & Principia, per quas Composita naturalia sint talia, qualia sunt; sed quia id clarum est ex verbis ipsius Platonis, apud quem in Phaedone de Ideis disturus Socrates, ita praefatur: Ἐρχομαί σοι ἐπιχειρῶν ὀ̈ειξαι τὸ εἶδος τῆς αἰτίας ὃ πεπραγμάτευμαι, Aggredior tibi ostendere Causae genus, in quod inquisivi. & postea rursus sic de ijsdem loquitur, Φαίνεταί μοι, εἴπερ ἔστιν ἄλλο καλὸν, πλὴν αὐτὸ τὸ καλόν, ὅτι δι' ἓν ἄλλο καλὸν εἶναι, ἢ διότι μετέχει ἐκείνου τοῦ καλοῦ. καὶ πάντα λὴ ὅτι λέγω. Τὴν τοιαύτην αἰτίαν συγχωρεῖς; Συγχωρῶ ἔφη; Apparet mihi, si quid aliud est pulcrum, praeter ipsum pulcrum, per nihil aliud esse pulcrum, nisi quia illius pulcri partis
units.tr: IX. We do not indeed deny that Plato regarded ideas as a cause, not only on the testimony of Laertius, who writes of them thus: "He posited ideas as certain causes and principles, through which natural composites are such as they are" [Τὰς Ἰδέας ὑφίστησι αἰτίας ... τὸ τοιαῦτ' εἶναι τὰ φύσει συνεστῶτα, ὅπερ ἐστὶν αὐτά]. It is clear also from Plato's own words, where Socrates, about to discuss the Ideas in the Phaedo, introduces them thus: "I am going to show you the kind of cause that I have investigated" [Ἔρχομαί σοι ἐπιχειρῶν δεῖξαι τὸ εἶδος τῆς αἰτίας ὃ πεπραγμάτευμαι]. And afterwards he speaks of the same things again: "It seems to me that if there is anything beautiful besides the beautiful itself, it is beautiful for no other reason than that it partakes of that beautiful. And I say this of everything. Do you grant such a cause?" "I grant it" [Φαίνεταί μοι, εἴπερ ἔστιν ἄλλο καλὸν πλὴν αὐτὸ τὸ καλόν, ὅτι δι' ἓν ἄλλο καλὸν εἶναι, ἢ διότι μετέχει ἐκείνου τοῦ καλοῦ. καὶ πάντα δὴ ὅτι λέγω. Τὴν τοιαύτην αἰτίαν συγχωρεῖς; Συγχωρῶ].
Chapter II.

units.la: participes est: Nonne huic Causæ assentiris? Assentior, inquit. In hisce verbis Ideæ apertissime causæ nomine insigniuntur. Hoc tamen non juvat Aristotelem, neq; inde sequitur, quod Formalem Causam, ab Efficiente diversam, Plato statuerit. Ideas enim ipse pro Efficiente habet, ut facile pervidebit, quisquis ea perpendet, quæ in Timæo super ijs tradidit. Esse nimirum uniuscujusq; rei species quasdam æternas, intelligibiles, nequaquam mutabiles; quarum simulacris in communem Materiam impressis, unaquæq; res hic apud nos generetur. Quicquid enim sunt nostratia, id esse τῆ τῶν εἰδῶν μεθέξει, Idearum participatione, quam μέθεξιν ipsæ Ideæ efficiant, suam Effigiem materiei communicando; quare etiam patri Ideas assimilat, sicuti Materiam matri. Tria enim dicens consideranda esse in omni generatione, τὸ γιγνόμενον, rem ipsam quæ fit, τὸ ἐν ᾧ γίνεται, id in vel è quo res fit, καὶ τὸ ὅθεν ἀφομοιούμενον φύεται τὸ γιγνόμενον, id ad cujus exemplum conformatur id quod fit, id est, ipsas Ideas, quas & τὰ ἀεὶ ὄντα entia sempiterna appellat, subjungit, Καὶ δὴ καὶ προσεικάζει πρέπει, τὸ μὲν δεχόμενον, μητέρι, τὸ δ' ὅθεν πατρί, τὴν δὲ μεταξύ τούτων φύσιν ἐκγόνῳ. Licet assimilare suscipiens, matri; id verò unde, patri: ast naturam inter hæc mediam, proli. non potuit manifestius Ideas inter Efficientes numerare, quam patri eas assimilando. sic enim & alibi Efficientem Causam solet Patri assimilare, ut in Hippia majore, Εἰ ἀρα τὸ καλὸν ὅτιν ἄλλου ἀγαθοῦ, γίγνοιτ' ἂν ὑπὸ τοῦ καλοῦ τὸ ἀγαθὸν, καὶ διὰ τοῦτ' ὡς ἔοικε, σσασλάζομεν καὶ τὴν Φρόνησιν, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα ὅσα καλὰ, ὅτι τὸ ἔργον αὐτῶν καὶ τὸ ἐκγονον σσασδασὸν ἔστι, τὸ ἀγαθόν. καὶ μυσκωντ-εν, ἐξ ὧν εὑρίσκομεν, παιδὸς ἴν ἰδέα ἐν τὸ καλὸν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ. Si pulcrum est causa boni, sequitur ut bonum fiat à pulcro. ideóq; ut videtur, prudentiam atq; reliqua omnia pulcra exoptamus, quia opus ac proles ipsorum, putà Bonum, est optabile. videturq; ex iis, quæ invenimus, Pulerum se habere ad Bonum in modum patris. Itaq; etiam illa μιμήματα imita-mentę menta seu ἀφομοιώματα assimilamenta, quorum in Materiam ingtessu res generentur, ab ipsis Ideis dicit effingi, ἐμπαθέντα ὑπ' αὐτῶν. Quare hoc quidem recte, non magni alias aeris autor, qui libellum περὶ φιλοσοφίας ἱστορίας, de philosophica historia dictum scripsit (impudentissime enim Galeno attribuitur) observavit, ita scribens de Ideis, ex Platonis sententia, ἰδέα ἐστὶν ἐσίν ἀσώματος, αὐτὴ μὲν ὑφεστῶσα καὶ ᾽ αὐτὴν, κινοῦσα δὲ τὰς ἀμοιρφοῦς ὕλας, καὶ αἰτία γιγνομένη. Idea est substantia incorporea, quae ipsa per se subsistens, informi Materiae imaginem imprimit, atque causae vicem praestat. Neque tamen propterea tollit proprios cujusque rei Efficientes, sed iis Ideas συνεργὸς adjutrices adjungit, quae opus suum faciant miro quodam & inenarrabili modo, τέχνον ἵνα ἀδύνατον καὶ ἀνώφελον.
units.tr: partakes of it: Do you not agree with this account of cause? I agree, he says. In these words the Ideas are most plainly named as causes. This, however, does not help Aristotle, nor does it follow that Plato posited a formal cause distinct from the efficient. For Plato himself regards the Ideas as efficient causes, as anyone will readily see who weighs what he teaches about them in the Timaeus: that there are certain eternal, intelligible species of each thing, by no means changeable, and that when their likenesses are impressed upon a common matter, each thing is generated here among us. For whatever our things are, they are so by participation in the Ideas [τῆ τῶν εἰδῶν μεθέξει], a participation which the Ideas themselves bring about by communicating their own image to matter. Hence he also likens the Ideas to a father, just as he likens matter to a mother. For, saying that three things must be considered in every generation, namely that which comes to be, the thing itself that is made; that in which it comes to be, the matter in or from which it is made; and that from which, by likeness to which, the thing that is made takes its form, that is, the Ideas themselves, which he also calls eternal beings, he adds: "And indeed he compares them: the one receiving to a mother, the one from which to a father, and the nature between these to an offspring." He could not have numbered the Ideas among efficient causes more plainly than by comparing them to a father. He does the same elsewhere, comparing the efficient cause to a father, as in the Greater Hippias: "If the beautiful is the cause of other good things, then the good would come to be from the beautiful; and for this reason, it seems, we also desire wisdom and all other beautiful things, because their work and offspring, namely the good, is desirable. And from what we have found, it appears that the beautiful stands to the good as a father [παιδὸς ἴν ἰδέα ἐν τὸ καλὸν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ]." Thus he says that those imitations [μιμήματα], or likenesses [ἀφομοιώματα], by whose entry into matter things are generated, are fashioned by the Ideas themselves, being impressed by them [ἐμπαθέντα ὑπ' αὐτῶν]. Wherefore the author of the little book On the History of Philosophy (which is shamelessly attributed to Galen), who is not of great account otherwise, rightly observed this, writing of the Ideas according to Plato's opinion: "The Idea is an incorporeal substance, which, subsisting in itself and by itself, moves the formless matters and becomes a cause. The Idea is an incorporeal substance, which, itself subsisting, imprints an image upon formless matter, and takes the place of a cause." Nevertheless, he does not on that account remove the proper efficient causes of each thing, but adds the Ideas as helpers [συνεργὸς] to them, which perform their work in a wonderful and inexplicable manner, a thing which is impossible and useless.

units.la: Haud inficias imus quin hoc, quod in omni generatione duos hos Efficientes concurrere vult, Ideam, & qui proprie Genitor vocetur, delirij plenum fit, sicuti & totum hoc de Ideis negotium (de quibus planiora sunt tot in locis Platonis verba, quam ut credere debeamus hominibus istis, qui persuadere mundo conantur, non res per se, sed in mente Divina existentes, cum Idearum nomine ubiq; intellexisse) non videmus tamen, cur ipsi minus hoc licuerit, quàm Aristoteli Solem ac coelum omni generationi interponere: de qua re alias dicetur.
units.tr: We do not deny that this view, that in every generation these two efficients concur, the Idea and what is properly called the begetter, is full of absurdity; and so is this whole business of the Ideas. (On the Ideas, Plato's words in so many places are too plain for us to believe that those men, who try to persuade the world that the Ideas are not things in themselves but exist in the Divine mind, have understood the name of Ideas in that sense anywhere.) Yet we do not see why it should be less permitted to him than to Aristotle to place the Sun and the heaven among the causes of every generation. That matter will be discussed elsewhere.

units.la: X. Itaque pro Causis quidem habuit Ideas Plato, non ita tamen, ut sejunxerit ab Efficiente, sed ejus speciem fecerit. ac proinde Praeceptoris mentem manifeste pervertit Aristoteles, quando ipsi imponit, quod Ideas (quas haud dubie respexit, quum scripsit quod Plato usus sit τῆ τί ἐστιν εἶδος (Causa qua quid est) fecerit genus Causae ab Efficiente diversum, ac Formali ipsius Causae respondens; eum qua nullam certè ipsae cognationem habent. Formis enim Aristotelicis quodammodo congruunt non ipsae Ideae, sed earum simulacra, quorum in materiam informem receptione (quomodo & Aristoteles Formas suas materiae informi imponit) unaquaeque res fiat. Plurimum autem inter ista interest, sicuti cuivis per se apparet, & clarius etiamnum fiet, ascriptis huc Senecæ verbis ex Epist. 58. ubi Platonis de Ideis Idearumque simulacris sententiam diligenter explicat. Ideas (inquit) vocat, ex quibus omnia, quæ videmus, fiunt, & ad quas cuncta formantur. Hæ immortales, inviolabiles, immutabiles sunt. Idea enim est eorum, quæ naturâ sunt, exemplar æternum. Et adjicit exemplum, quo rem amplius declaret: Volo imaginem tuam facere. exemplar pictura te habeo, ex quo capit aliquem habitum mens, quem operi suo imponat. ita illa, quæ me docet & instruit facies, a qua petitur imitatio, idea est. talia ergo exemplaria infinita habet natura rerum, hominum, piscium, arborum, ad quæ, quodcunque ab illa fieri debet, exprimitur. Hæ igitur sunt Platonis Ideæ: quibus nihil commune esse cum Forma Aristotelica, manifestum est. Magis cum ijs, ut dicebamus, congruunt Idearum imitamenta, ut Plato vocat, qui nullum istis proprium nomen fecit. discipuli ipsius vocaverunt εἶδη, cum alioquin εἶδος & ἰδέα pro eadem plane re promiscue usurpata sint tum ab ipso (cujus rei ex Parmenide, Phædone, ac Timæo, multa afferri possent exempla) tum ab Aristotele, sicuti passim ex ipsius scriptis apparet, ubi multo sæpius εἶδη quam ἰδέαι appellantur: sicuti contra ἰδέας appellat interdum Plato ipsa idearum ἀφομοιώματα, ut hisce in Timæo verbis, Ἀμορφον οὖν ἐκεί-νων ἁπάντων τῶν ἰδεῶν, ὅσας μέλει δέχεσθαι ποδεῖν, Informe atq; expers omnium illarum idearum, quas alicunde acceptturum est. Platonicis tamen placuit, hoc vocum discrimen invehere, ut commodiorem haberent viam ad tradenda magistri sui placita. Quid autem sint illa idearum imitamenta atq; εἶδη, sic explicat Seneca, Pictor cum reddere Virgilium coloribus vellet, ipsum intuebatur: Idea erat Virgilij facies, futuri operis exemplar: ex hac quod artifex trahit, & operi suo imposuit, εἶδος est. Quid interest, quaris? alterum exemplar est, alterum forma ab exemplari sumta, & operi imposita. alteram artifex imitatur, alteram facit. Habet aliquam faciem statua: hæc est Idos. habet aliquam faciem exemplar ipsum, quod intuens opifex, statuam figuravit: hæc Idea est.
units.tr: X. Plato, then, did indeed hold the Ideas as causes, but not in such a way that he separated them from the efficient cause; rather, he made them its species. And so Aristotle clearly perverts his teacher's mind when he imposes upon him that he made the Idea (which he doubtless had in view when he wrote that Plato used the "what it is" [τῆ τί ἐστιν], the "form" [εἶδος], that is, the cause by which a thing is what it is) into a kind of cause distinct from the efficient, corresponding to the formal cause of Aristotle, with which they have no kinship at all. For it is not the Ideas themselves that agree in some way with Aristotelian forms, but their likenesses, by whose reception into formless matter (just as Aristotle also imposes his forms upon matter) each thing is made. And the difference between these is very great, as is plain to anyone, and it will become clearer still if we add the words of Seneca from Epistle 58, where he carefully explains Plato's view of the Ideas and their likenesses. He calls them Ideas, from which all things we see are made, and to which everything is shaped. These are immortal, inviolable, unchangeable; for the Idea is the eternal pattern of those things which exist by nature. And he adds an example to make the matter clearer: I wish to make your image. I have you as a picture to serve as the model, from which the mind takes some form to impose upon its work. So that face which teaches and instructs me, from which the imitation is sought, is the Idea. Therefore nature of things has infinite such patterns, of men, of fishes, of trees, to which whatever is to be made by her is fashioned. These, then, are Plato's Ideas, and it is plain that they have nothing in common with the Aristotelian form. The likenesses of the Ideas, as Plato calls them, agree more closely with them, as we said; to these he gave no proper name. His disciples called them eide [εἶδη], although eidos and idea were used interchangeably for exactly the same thing, both by Plato himself (of which many examples could be cited from the Parmenides, the Phaedo, and the Timaeus) and by Aristotle, as appears everywhere in his writings, where eide is called far more often than ideai. Conversely, Plato sometimes calls the likenesses of the Ideas themselves ideai, as in these words in the Timaeus: "Therefore formless and devoid of all those ideas which it is about to receive" [Ἀμορφον οὖν ἐκεί-νων ἁπάντων τῶν ἰδεῶν]. Nevertheless, the Platonists chose to introduce this distinction of words, so that they would have an easier way of handing down their master's opinions. What those likenesses of the Ideas and the eide are, Seneca explains thus: When a painter wished to render Virgil in colours, he looked at him: the face of Virgil was the Idea, the pattern of the work to come. What the artist draws from this and imposes upon his work is the eidos. Why do you ask what the difference is? One is the pattern, the other is the form taken from the pattern and imposed on the work. The artist imitates the one, he makes the other. A statue has some face: this is the idos. The pattern itself has some face, which the craftsman, looking at it, shaped in the statue: this is the Idea.

units.la: [Catchword "Ifriani" appears lowest at right, partly cut; it is recorded in bottom_margin.] Etiamnum aliam desideras distinctionem? Idos in opere est, Idea extra opus; nec tantum extra opus est, sed ante opus. Quae omnia exacte ad Platonis mentem dicta esse, deprehendet, quisquis Phaedonem, ac Parmenidem, & praecipue Timaeum legerit.
units.tr: [Catchword "Ifriani" appears lowest at right, partly cut; it is recorded in the bottom margin.] Do you still desire another distinction? The idos is in the work, the Idea is outside the work; and not only outside the work, but before the work. You will find that all these things are stated exactly according to Plato's mind, whoever reads the Phaedo, the Parmenides, and especially the Timaeus.
XI.

units.la: Ex praedictis autem satis patet, quod dicebamus, Aristotelem male Ideas Formae suae assimilasse. Quod si quis dicat, eum, quando dicit Platonem agnovisse Τὴν ἀιτίαν ἐξ ... non Ideas in animo habuisse, sed εἰδώλα, ipsa minimum Idearum simulacra, quae in materiam imponuntur; neque sic rem expediverit. Namque fatemur quidem, illa εἴδη magnam in multis habere cum Forma Aristotelica cognationem, ac propterea licuisse Aristoteli dicere, quod Plato Formam ipsius quodammodo agnovisset: vere tamen dicere non potuit, quod Plato εἴδη pro causa habuerit (multo minus, quod illa duntaxat, & Materiam, Causas fecerit) siquidem Plato Idearum imagines, quae Materiae sociantur, nunquam Causas appellavit; ac neque appellare potuit, quippe qui solum Efficientem pro Causa agnoscat: Idos autem (quomodo nunc cum Seneca ac Platonicis hanc dictionem usurpamus) ipsi non est Efficiens, sed Ideae Effectus.
units.tr: From what has been said, it is clear enough that what we said is true: Aristotle wrongly made the Ideas the same as his Form. But suppose someone says that when Aristotle writes that Plato recognised the cause [τὴν αἰτίαν], he meant not the Ideas but the eidola, the mere images of the Ideas that are impressed upon matter. This explanation will not work either. We grant that those eidē have much in common with the Aristotelian Form, and so Aristotle could say that Plato had in some way recognised his Form. Yet he could not truly say that Plato regarded the eidē as a cause, much less that Plato made these alone, together with matter, the causes. Plato never called the images of the Ideas, which are joined to matter, causes, and indeed he could not, since he acknowledges only the efficient cause as a cause. The eidos, as we now use this term with Seneca and the Platonists, is not the efficient cause of the thing but its effect.
XII.

units.la: Verumtamen sive Ideas, sive εἴδη intellexit Aristoteles, quando scripsit Platonem usurpasse Τὴν ἀιτίαν; hoc manifestum est, eum nimis calumniose tractasse praeceptorem, scribendo, quod hac solum & materiali causa usus sit, hoc est, quod aliam Causam non agnoverit, ac propterea ne Efficientem quidem; quum tamen clarum sit ex Platonis scriptis (uti supra monstravimus) quod solum Efficientem Causae appellatione donaverit. Unica restat Aristotelem excusandi ratio, si dicatur ita explicanda esse haec ipsius verba, quomodo ea explicare voluisse videtur Toletus, Comment. ad 2. de Gener. & Corrup. 9. quod nimirum Plato putaverit Causam Formalem esse simul Efficientem illiusmet, cuius est Forma. sed haec explicatio admitti nequaquam potest; tum quia nec hoc quidem verum est, quod hic dicitur; tum quia id ex Aristotele elici non potest. Non esse verum, ex ijs liquet, quæ supra diximus; quod nimirum non Ideæ respondeant Formæ Aristotelicæ, sed Idearum simulacra. efficiendi autem vim non simulacris, sed ipsis Ideis Plato tribuit. quamobrem vere dici non potest, Formam & Efficientem Platoni idem esse. Præterea hæc expositio manifeste pugnat cum verbis Aristotelis, qui cum in illo primo Metaphysicorum examen instituat, quasnam de quatuor ipsius causis agnoverint vetustiores ipso Philosopho; postquam aliorum historiam absolvit, dixitq; quosdam solam Materiam, quosdam Materiam & Efficientem, nonnullos etiam Finem agnovisse; tandem ad Platonem deveniens, ait, eum sola Materiali & Formali causa usum esse, delibata etiam quodammodo Finali; quibus verbis apertius nihil dici potest, ad asserendum, quod Plato Efficientem Causam non posuerit.
units.tr: Yet whether Aristotle meant the Ideas or the eidē when he wrote that Plato had used the cause, it is plain that he dealt with his teacher far too calumniously when he wrote that Plato used only the formal and material cause, that is, that he recognised no other cause and therefore not even the efficient cause. Yet it is clear from Plato's writings (as we have shown above) that he gave the name of cause to the efficient cause alone. There remains one way to excuse Aristotle, if these words of his are to be explained as Toletus wished to explain them in his commentary on the second book of On Generation and Corruption, 9: that Plato, of course, thought the formal cause was at the same time the efficient cause of that very thing of which it is the form. But this explanation can by no means be admitted: first, because what it says is not even true; second, because it cannot be drawn out of Aristotle. That it is not true is clear from what we said above, namely that the Ideas, not the images of the Ideas, correspond to the Aristotelian Form. Plato attributed the power of producing things not to the images but to the Ideas themselves. Therefore it cannot truly be said that for Plato the Form and the efficient cause are the same. Moreover, this exposition plainly contradicts Aristotle's own words. In the first book of the Metaphysics he examines which of the four causes the earlier philosophers recognised. After he has run through the views of others, saying that some recognised only matter, some matter and the efficient cause, and some even the final cause, he at last comes to Plato and says that Plato used only the material and formal causes, touching only lightly on the final cause. Nothing could be said more plainly to affirm that Plato did not posit the efficient cause.

units.la: Confundit ille quidem, & in illo libro, & in aliis, Exemplaria cum simulacris, atque ad eum modum de ijs loquitur, acsi sensisset Plato, ipsas Ideas esse rerum generatarum Essentiam sive Formam; ut propterea, congruenter isti confusioni, potuerit etiam dicere, Causam Efficientem ac Formalem Platoni eandem esse, quum ille Ideas habuerit pro Efficiente; quod & dicit aliquatenus primi Metaphysic. sexto: sed pluribus tamen in locis, & quidem ijs, ubi ex professo hanc rem tractat, omnino negat Ideas esse Efficientes, sed tantum Formam. etenim in ipso capite sexto primi Metaphysicorum, sic scribit: Τὰ δὲ τἀ τὴν εἶναι, καὶ τὰ ἐν τοῖς εἴδεσι λέγουσιν. ὅτε δ' ὡς ὕλην τοῖς ἀϊδίοις τὰ εἴδη, ἡ δὲ τὰ ἐν τοῖς εἴδεσιν, ὡς ἐντεῦθεν τὴν ἀρχὴν ἡ κίνησεως γινομένην ὑπολαμβάνουσιν, &c. Quidditatem & Essentiam diluci de nemo tradidit, & tamen præcipue attingunt, qui ponunt ideas, eaq; quæ ad Ideas attinent. Neq; enim existimant sensibilium Materiam esse Ideas, & quæ ad Ideas spectant, neq; item id, unde motus profisciscitur. Et postea rursus capite septimo, non procul à fine libri, Ὅλως δὲ ἀμφότερον
units.tr: Admittedly, he confuses exemplars with likenesses, both in that book and in others, and speaks of them as if Plato had held that the Ideas themselves are the essence or form of generated things. So, consistently with this confusion, he could also say that for Plato the efficient and the formal cause are the same, since Plato took the Ideas as efficient. He does say something like this in the sixth chapter of the first book of the Metaphysics. But in many other places, and especially where he treats this matter expressly, he flatly denies that the Ideas are efficient and says they are only form. In the sixth chapter of the first book of the Metaphysics he writes as follows: "Those who speak of the what-it-was-to-be and of things in the forms [τὰ δὲ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι καὶ τὰ ἐν τοῖς εἴδεσι λέγουσιν]. They make the forms the cause of eternal things, and they take the forms to be the source from which motion begins [ὡς ἐντεῦθεν τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς κινήσεως γινομένην ὑπολαμβάνουσιν]." Nobody has handed down a clear account of quiddity and essence, yet those who posit Ideas, and what pertains to the Ideas, chiefly touch on them. For they do not think the matter of sensible things is the Ideas, nor the things that pertain to the Ideas, nor again that from which motion proceeds. Then again, in the seventh chapter, not far from the end of the book, he says: "Speaking generally, ..."

units.la: {y} ... Ἀ δὲ Φύσεως περὶ τῶν φυσικῶν ἀλλὰ ἄλλον, τοῦτο μὲν ἐκ ἀρχῆς ... In totum autem quum sapientia quærat causam eorum quæ manifesta sunt, hoc quidem facere omisimus: nihil enim dicimus de causa, unde initium mutationis, putantes autem nos essentiam eorum exponere, alias substantias inducimus. in quo sane loco non modò expressè negat, Ideas Platoni pro Efficientibus haberi, sed & renovat ac confirmat calumniam illam, quod Plato nequaquam agnoverit Causam Efficientem, quodq; nihil de ea dixerit: quo mendacio impudentius nihil fieri potest, quum adeo pro Causa agnoverit Efficientem Plato, ut non aliam agnoverit nisi illam (quod jam sæpius repetere coacti sumus) & plurima dixerit de Efficiente, tum de Universali, ipsius Mundi opifice, ut ex Timæo notum est; tum de particularibus, sicuti vel illa, quæ ex decimo de Legibus allegavimus in Sectione quarta, abundè testantur. Quicquid igitur & alij dicant, & ipse Aristoteles; nobiscum in eo sensit Plato, quod solus Efficiens Causæ nomen meretur, quodq; nulli rei hæc appellatio donanda sit, nisi in quantum vi aliquid faciendi atq; producendi prædita est. quem Platonis, Stoicorum, aliorumq; hac in parte nobiscum facientium consensum, non est cur vereamur opponere & anteferre autoritati Aristotelis, qui alijs quoq; nulla efficiendi vi præditis, aut saltem non eo respectu, Causæ nomen communicandum putavit.
units.tr: {y} ... Concerning the things of nature, [the Ideas do not account for the causes of natural things, and so] the first principle of change is left out [Ἀ δὲ Φύσεως περὶ τῶν φυσικῶν ἀλλὰ ἄλλον, τοῦτο μὲν ἐκ ἀρχῆς ...]. In sum, since wisdom seeks the cause of things that are manifest, we have left this aside: we say nothing about the cause from which change begins, and, thinking we are explaining their essence, we introduce other substances. In this passage he not only expressly denies that the Ideas were held by Plato as efficient causes, but also renews and confirms the charge that Plato never recognised an efficient cause and said nothing about it. No lie could be more shameless than this, since Plato recognised the efficient cause so fully that he acknowledged no other cause (as we have been forced to repeat many times), and he said a great deal about the efficient cause, both of the universal maker of the world itself, as is known from the Timaeus, and of particular things, as the passage we quoted from the tenth book of the Laws in Section four amply attests. Therefore, whatever others, and Aristotle himself, may say, Plato agreed with us in this: that only the efficient cause deserves the name of cause, and that this name should be granted to nothing except insofar as it has some power of doing or producing something. There is no reason for us to hesitate to set this agreement of Plato, of the Stoics, and of others who agree with us on this point against the authority of Aristotle, who thought the name of cause should be extended to things that have no power of efficiency, or at least not in that respect.

units.la: XIII. Sed & vulgatus omnium hominum loquendi usus idem hoc confirmat, atque soli Efficienti Causæ nomen atque dignitatem tribuit.
units.tr: XIII. But the common usage of all men's speech also confirms this, and grants the name and dignity of Cause to the Efficient Cause alone.

units.la: Quum enim omnes τὸ ἀίτιατον sive Effectum pro Causæ correlativo habeant; si quis quærat, hoc aliquid cujus rei Effectum sit (quod plane eundem habet sensum, acsi alijs verbis quæratur, quæ sit Causa hujus alicujus; quomodo eodem redit, dicasne, cujus filius est hic, an verò, quis est hujus pater) nemo, qui Aristotelis doctrinâ non imbutus sit, materiam, nec aliud quid afferet, sed Efficientem. ut siquis quærat, cujus effectum sit ensis vel scamnum, non de ligno aut ferro, sed de fabro (faber autem est Efficiens) respondentes audies. dicere autem quod ensis sit effectum fabri; idem est ac si dicas (sicuti jam nunc ajebamus) Fabrum esse Causam ensis: quum istæ duæ propositiones æquipolleant, eundemq; plane sensum in se contineant. Clarum hoc est, nec ipsi possunt diffiteri Peripatetici; de quibus Zabarella, Efficiens ait absolute effectus Causam dici; & Conimbricenses, Quando causa spectatur ut ordinem habens ad Effectum, solam Agentem Causam complecti. Quod vero ijdem, ad solvendam hanc objectionem, respondent, nimis pressam esse hanc usurpationem, quâ Causa spectatur uti ordinem habens ad effectum, frigidum est, neq; aliter accipiendum, quam si dicerent, displicere sibi hanc loquendi consuetudinem, utpote cum suæ scholæ institutis parum convenientem. quæ responsio nullum pondus habet contra eam argumentandi Formam, quâ nos hic utimur, quamq; in ipsa apud omnes recepta loquendi consuetudine fundamus. Iam sicuti minime nefas est in Philosophia à vulgato loquendi usu discedere, quoties id res exigit; ita non videmus, quare id faciendum sit, quando neq; evidens aliqua ratio urget (qualem hic ab Aristotelicis vix ullam posse afferri putamus, quæ præceptorem eorum permoverit, ut hanc innovationem introduceret) & insignes Philosophi vulgatæ illi sermonis consuetudini subscribunt: quod illustrissimos ante ac post Aristotelem Philosophos hic facere, monstravimus. Et has quidem rationes habuimus, quare soli Efficienti, contra quàm Aristoteles, Causæ nomen proprium faceremus, neq; ulli rei id impertiremur, nisi quatenus ad Efficientem reduci potest, ac quædam Efficientis species constituí. Atq; hinc porrò apparet, quod in hujus sectionis initio diximus, quamobrem generali de Principijs tractationi Causarum tractationem (id quod Aristoteles fecit) non permisceamus. Et hîc quidem primus liber finem nobis habeto.
units.tr: For since everyone regards the effect (τὸ ἀίτιατον) as correlative to cause, if someone asks, "of what thing is this something the effect?" (which has plainly the same sense as if one asked in other words, "what is the cause of this thing?", just as it comes to the same whether you say "whose son is this?" or "who is this one's father?"), no one who has not been steeped in Aristotle's teaching will answer with the matter or anything else, but with the efficient cause. So if someone asks whose effect a sword or a bench is, you will hear the answer: not of wood or iron, but of the smith (and the smith is the efficient cause). To say that the sword is the effect of the smith is the same as saying (as we were just now saying) that the smith is the cause of the sword, since these two propositions are equivalent and contain exactly the same sense. This is clear, and the Peripatetics themselves cannot deny it. Among them Zabarella says that "the efficient is absolutely said to be the cause of the effect," and the Conimbricenses say, "When cause is considered as having an order to the effect, it embraces only the agent cause." As for their answer to this objection, that this usage, by which cause is considered as having an order to the effect, is "too strained," it is feeble, and it can be taken in no other way than as saying that they dislike this manner of speaking as too little in keeping with the principles of their school. That answer has no weight against the form of argument we use here, which we ground in the common manner of speaking accepted by all. Now, just as it is by no means wrong in philosophy to depart from common usage whenever the matter requires it, so we do not see why this should be done when no clear reason urges it (and we think that the Aristotelians can hardly bring forward any such reason as would have moved their master to introduce this innovation), and when outstanding philosophers subscribe to that common manner of speaking, as we have shown that the most illustrious philosophers both before and after Aristotle did. These then are the reasons why we make the name of cause proper to the efficient cause alone, contrary to Aristotle, and do not grant it to any thing except insofar as it can be reduced to the efficient cause and constitutes some species of the efficient. And from this it further appears what we said at the beginning of this section: why we do not mix the treatment of causes into the general discussion of principles, as Aristotle did. And let this be the end of the first book here.
THE END.
ERRATA

units.la: Et alia, praeter haec, circa distinctiones errata saepius occurrunt, sed minoris momenti, quae propterea hic omittenda, ac lectoris correctioni relinquenda duximus: uti & ea, quae passim in vocum Graecarum aspirationes atq; accentus peccata sunt, dum vel omittuntur, vel superflue adduntur, vel transponuntur, vel unum genus pro alio adhibetur: quae omnia sicut sensui nullum damnum adferunt, ita a quovis linguae Graecae vel leviter perito facillime emendari possunt.
units.tr: Other errors besides these concerning the distinctions occur fairly often, but they are of minor importance, and for that reason we have thought fit to omit them here and leave them to the correction of the reader; likewise those faults that are committed throughout in the aspirations and accents of the Greek words, whether they are omitted, added superfluously, transposed, or one kind is used for another. All of these, while they do no harm to the sense, can very easily be corrected by anyone with even a slight knowledge of the Greek language.
TO THE BENEVOLENT READER.

units.la: Nequem turbent contrariae expositiones axiomatis Aristotelici (Principia semper manere oportet) a nobis allatae pag. 201. p. & 335. m. sciat, priore loco nos isti axiomati aptavisse eam expositionem, quae ipsis verbis per se consideratis maxime quadrare, atq; ex omnibus minimum absurditatis aut falsitatis continere videbatur. Posteriore autem loco eum ipsi sensum tribuimus, quem collatio diversorum minimeq; dubiorum locorum postea nos docuerat ab ipso Aristotele ipsi attributum fuisse: quum alioquin id, quod verbis istis sic intellectis dicitur, sit salsissimum (uti ibi monstratur) ob quam causam Alexandri expositionem (quam nunc apparet caeteris omnibus praeferendam ac veram esse, si ipsius Aristotelis mens spectetur) tunc rejiciebamus. Itaq; quae ibi dicta sunt, innixa expositioni isti meliori quidem, sed a mente Aristotelis alienae, pro non dictis habentur: & a nobis ipsis fuissent delata, nisi serius hoc animadvertissemus. Priores
units.tr: Lest the contrary expositions of the Aristotelian axiom (Principles must always remain), which we have brought forward at p. 201 and p. 335, should disturb anyone, let him know that in the first place we fitted to that axiom the exposition which, taken by itself in its own words, seemed best to suit it and to contain the least absurdity or falsity of all. In the latter place, however, we gave it the sense which the comparison of various and less doubtful passages later taught us had been attributed to it by Aristotle himself; otherwise what is said, with the words so understood, is most false (as is shown there). For this reason we then rejected Alexander's exposition, which now appears to be preferable to all the others and true, if the mind of Aristotle himself is considered. Therefore, what was said there rests upon that better exposition, which is nevertheless foreign to the mind of Aristotle, and is to be held as unsaid; and we would have retracted it ourselves had we not noticed this too late. The earlier
