units.la: Priores cifra Caput; posteriores, paragraphos indicant. Numerus Romanus in medio positus, Sectionis index est. Cifrae solitariae, vel quibus p. praemittitur, paginas libri denotant. Post cifras p. principium: m. medium f. finem paragraphi aut pagina, prout alterutrius notis apponuntur, designant: ast t. declarat toto paragrapho, tota-ve pagina, rem eam, de qua agitur, pertractari. Asteriscus prefixus denotat dogmata nostra, hoc primo libro obiter tantum & per occasionem delibata, sed sequentibus libris, suo quodq; loco, plenam probationem acceptura.
units.tr: The first figures denote the chapter, the later ones the paragraphs. The Roman numeral placed in the middle is the index of the Section. Solitary figures, or those preceded by p., denote the pages of the book. After the figures, p. marks the beginning, m. the middle, and f. the end of a paragraph or page, according to which of these signs is attached to them; but t. declares that the matter in question is treated throughout the whole paragraph or the whole page. A prefixed asterisk denotes our doctrines, which are touched on only in passing and by way of occasion in this first book, but which will receive full proof in the following books, each in its proper place.
ACCIDENS. ACCIDENTIA.

units.la: Accidentia alia, vera entia per se: alia, non nisi modi substantiarum, 66. f. Accidentibus nonnullis suimodi essentiales, 305. f. Accidentia sunt non entia Aristoteli, 169. p. Accidentia neque fieri neque interire, sed Composito confieri & cointerire, falsum Aristotelis dogma, confutatur, 1. III. 3. & §. 56. ac 57. Accidentia alia simplicia, alia composita, 2. II. 2. Scaligeri opinio, Accidentia omnia componentis ex Esse & Essentia, 2. II. 26. evertitur, §. 27. Accidentium Principia negletta ab Aristotele & Priscis, 326. Accidentium compositorum duo genera, 264. p. Accidentia quae habeant partes quantitativas, quae non, 280. p. Accidentium compositorum partes sunt Essentiales, 300. p.
units.tr: Some accidents are real beings in themselves, others are only modes of substances, 66. f. Some accidents are essential of their kind, 305. f. Accidents are non-beings for Aristotle, 169. p. The view of Aristotle that accidents neither come into being nor pass away, but come into being and pass away together with the composite, is false and is refuted, 1. III. 3, and §§ 56 and 57. Some accidents are simple, others composite, 2. II. 2. The opinion of Scaliger, that all accidents are composed of Esse and Essence, 2. II. 26, is overthrown, § 27. The principles of accidents are neglected by Aristotle and the ancients, 326. Composite accidents are of two kinds, 264. p. Some accidents have quantitative parts, others do not, 280. p. The parts of composite accidents are essential, 300. p.

units.la: Accidentium arctissimus nexus cum subjecto, 66. f. Accidentia non uniuntur, nisi unione subjecti, 300. f. Suarezij contraria opinio, [Unum Accidens posse esse alterius subjectum] examinatur, 2. II. 25. Subjectum non esse Materiam Accidentium, contra eundem Suar. 2. II. 28. Ex Accidentibus & Subjecto fit Substantia vere & essentialiter una, 66. f. Ex Accidentibus separabilibus & Subjecto posse fieri unam Essentiam per se, contra Fonsecam monstratur, 1. III. 21.
units.tr: The most intimate bond of accidents with their subject, 66. f. Accidents are united only by the union of the subject, 300. f. The contrary opinion of Suárez, [that one accident can be the subject of another], is examined, 2. II. 25. That the subject is not the matter of accidents, against the same Suárez, 2. II. 28. From accidents and a subject there arises a substance truly and essentially one, 66. f. That from separable accidents and a subject one essence per se can be made is shown against Fonseca, 1. III. 21.

units.la: * Accidentium ope diversissimae Substantiae constituuntur ex eadem quoque Materia, 48. * Accidentibus duntaxat inter se Substantiae differunt, ac novorum Accidentium introductione generatio substantiarum pergitur, 53. Accidentaliter, seu per Accidentia, & Essentialiter differre, non repugnant, 48. Accidentia ad Compositorum Essentiam pertinere, vel ipsis Peripateticis velint nolint fatendum est, 67. & 75. f. Ex Elementis, & Accidentibus seu Qualitatibus, omnia fabricabant Stoici, 193. p. Ex Accidentibus tantum & Materia non posse conflari Composita, argumenta Peripateticorum, 1. III. 19. diluuntur, §. seqq.
units.tr: * By means of accidents, substances most widely different are constituted from the same matter, 48. * Substances differ only in their accidents, and by the introduction of new accidents the generation of substances goes on, 53. That things may differ accidentally, or through accidents, and essentially, is not contradictory, 48. Accidents belong to the essence of composites; whether the Peripatetics wish it or not, this must be admitted, 67 and 75. f. The Stoics made everything out of elements and accidents or qualities, 193. p. The arguments of the Peripatetics that composites cannot be compounded from accidents and matter alone are refuted, 1. III. 19, §§ following.

units.la: Unde fiat, ut talia atque talia Accidentia in quaque Specie reperiantur, 1. III. 20. p. Unde fiat, ut alia Accidentia sint separabilia, alia secus, 91.
units.tr: Whence it comes that such and such accidents are found in each species, 1. III. 20. p. Whence it comes that some accidents are separable and others not, 91.
The operation of accidents: see Operation and Quality.
Per ACCIDENS.

units.la: * Quae fiunt per Accidens, non minus verè fiunt, quam quae fiunt primario, 280. f. Res potest aliquid pati per se, & tamen certo respectu dici quod id patiatur per Accidens, 131. m. Frivolum Peripateticorum dictum, Formas, quanquam partes habent, non esse tamen quantas nisi per Accidens, excutitur, 128. m. & 129. Eorundem dictum de Formarum divisione per Accidens, excutitur; monstraturque nullam rem posse pati id, quod non sit nata pati per se, 130. 131. Formam generari per Accidens, Thomae dictum, non placet Suarezio, 176. f. 177. p. Compositum potius dicendum interire per Accidens, quam Formam; contra quam Aristotelici dicunt, 186. m. 187. p. Haud quaquam dicendum fieri per Accidens, quae necessariâ consequentiâ fiunt, 187. m.
units.tr: * Things that come about per accidens come about no less truly than those that come about primarily, 280. f. Something can suffer per se, and yet in a certain respect be said to suffer it per accidens, 131. m. The frivolous saying of the Peripatetics, that forms, although they have parts, are nevertheless not quantitative except per accidens, is examined, 128. m. and 129. Their saying about the division of forms per accidens is examined; and it is shown that no thing can suffer what it is not born to suffer per se, 130, 131. That a form is generated per accidens, the saying of Thomas, does not please Suárez, 176. f. and 177. p. It should rather be said that the composite perishes per accidens than the form, contrary to what the Aristotelians say, 186. m. and 187. p. It is by no means to be said that things which come about by necessary consequence come about per accidens, 187. m.
ACTION. AGENT. TO ACT.

units.la: * Actio non est nisi accidentalis ac temporarius modus Agentis, 279.p. Actionum nomina pro ipso Agente usurpare solet Plato, 340.m. Actio non est scopus, 222. f. Agentium repassio, vi. Repassio. Actiones indissita, 85.p.
units.tr: * Action is nothing but an accidental and temporary mode of the agent, p. 279. Plato is accustomed to use the names of actions for the agent itself, p. 340 m. Action is not the end, p. 222 f. Repetition of agents, vi. Repetition. Actions indistinct, p. 85 p.

units.la: Ob Actionum defectum partes cadaveris Aristoteli non idem, quod erant manente vita, nisi æquivoce, 101. p. refellitur, ibid. f. initio, §. 32.
units.tr: Because of the lack of action, the parts of a corpse are not the same as they were while life remained, except equivocally; Aristotle is refuted on this point, p. 101 p., ibid. f. initio, §. 32.

units.la: Agentium Naturalium vis omnem Artificium industriam longe superat, 105.f. quomodo Agentia naturalia, cum sint cognitionis experientia, agant tamen propter Finem, I.V,5. & seqq.
units.tr: The power of natural agents far surpasses all human industry in art, p. 105 f. How natural agents, although they have no knowledge, nevertheless act for the sake of an end, I.V,5 and following.

units.la: Ad Agendum, aliquid ab altero cieri tribus modis: & in quo Agentis Primarij ac Instrumentarij ratio consistat, 58.f.
units.tr: To act, something must be moved by another in three ways; and in what the account of the primary agent and the instrumental agent consists, p. 58 f.

units.la: Plura, quæ huc referri possunt, vi in Operatio, & in Qualitas.
units.tr: Several further matters that may be referred here are found under Operation and under Quality.
ACTUS.

units.la: Actus Existentiæ, 119. f. Quod ipsum Actu non est, non potest efficere ut alterum Actu existat, 117. m. vide plura in Potentia.
units.tr: Act of existence, 119 f. What is not in act itself cannot bring it about that another act exists, 117 m. See more under Potency.

units.la: ÆQUANIMITATIS non est, sed stoliditatis, velle ea nescire, quæ se nosecenda ultro ingerunt, 114.p.
units.tr: It is not a sign of equanimity but of stupidity to wish not to know those things which thrust themselves upon us to be known, 114 p.
Equivocal things by chance, 258 m.
ETERNITY.

units.la: Mundi Æternitas ab Aristotele primum in Philosophiam inuecta, 314, f. Æterna facit Principia Aristotelis, ortus interitusque experientia, 2, IV,2. cujus dogmatis falsitas ostenditur ibid. & §. seq.. Platoni quoque omne Efficiens æternum, 2, IV,4, qui error coarguitur, §.5. & seqq.
units.tr: The eternity of the world, first introduced into philosophy by Aristotle, 314, f. Aristotle's principles make things eternal, the experience of generation and destruction, 2, IV,2. The falsity of this doctrine is shown ibid. and in the following §. Plato also makes every efficient cause eternal, 2, IV,4; this error is refuted in §.5 and following.

units.la: ALBERTI dictum, Formam omnem esse intelligibilem, & principium intelligendi, excutitur, 47.
units.tr: The saying of Albert, that every form is intelligible and the principle of understanding, is examined, 47.

units.la: ALEXANDRI Aphrod. peculiaris opinio de Formis, 1, III,4, 84.
units.tr: The peculiar opinion of Alexander of Aphrodisias about forms, 1, III,4, 84.

units.la: ALIENA dogmata pro suis usurpare, atqs ita doctrinæ suæ monstrosam confusionem ac falsitatem inducere, Aristoteli solenne, 2,III,4,5,& pag. 59, ac 75, 330, m, 337, f. 338, p.
units.tr: To pass off others' doctrines as one's own, and so to introduce a monstrous confusion and falsity into one's teaching: a habit peculiar to Aristotle, 2,III,4,5, and pp. 59, 75, 330 m, 337 f, 338 p.
ALIMENTA. See CIBUS.
ALLIARIA, grown from the seed of Apium, 138, &c.
ALTERATION.

units.la: Alterationem omnem fieri per poros, ridicula opinio, & ab Aristotele quoq; damnata, Scaligero tamen hæsit, 283, p. ab Alterationibus petitum pro forma argumentum, refellitur, I, III, 28.
units.tr: That all alteration takes place through the pores is a ridiculous opinion, and was also condemned by Aristotle, yet it clung to Scaliger, 283, p. An argument drawn from alterations, taken as a formal argument, is refuted, I, III, 28.
AMBIGUITY, AMPHIBOLY.

units.la: Ambiguitatibus ludere in Philosophia, ineptum, 243, f. Ambiguitate vocum abusus Aristoteles ad nectenda sophismata, I, V, 5, f. & 6, p. & pag. 246, f
units.tr: To play with ambiguities in philosophy is foolish, 243, f. Aristotle abused the ambiguity of words to tie together sophisms, I, V, 5, f. and 6, p. and p. 246, f.

units.la: AMOREM movet species, non ipsum objectum, 233, f.
units.tr: Appearance, not the object itself, moves love, 233, f.
AMYGDALINE plum, 133, f. Almond-peach, 134, p.

units.la: ANALOGIA inter Principium vulgare & philosophicum, 258, f. 259, p.
units.tr: ANALOGY between the common and the philosophical principle, 258, f. 259, p.
ANAXAGORAS' expressions [ἐκφράσεις], 331, p.
ANGELS.

units.la: * Angeli sunt, corpora compósita è Materia & Natura, 1, I, 1. & p. 262, m. etiam Peripatetici in Angelis compositionem agnoscunt, sed longe diversam, minimeq; physicam, 304, f * Angelos movere Orbes, figmentum, 105, p
units.tr: Angels are composite bodies made of Matter and Nature, 1, I, 1. and p. 262, m. The Peripatetics also acknowledge a composition in angels, but a very different one, and by no means physical, 304, f. That angels move the spheres is a fiction, 105, p.
SOUL.

units.la: Animarum plurimæ proprietates multum diversæ ab ijs, quas Formis suis ascribunt Peripatetici: quare perperam Formarum nomen ijs imponitur, atq; ad reliquas quoque Formas probandas adhibentur, 96.
units.tr: Many properties of souls are very different from those which the Peripatetics ascribe to their Forms; hence the name of Form is wrongly imposed on them, and they are also used to prove the remaining Forms, 96.

units.la: Animæ consideratio Aristoteli ad Naturalem Philosophum pertinet, 195, p.
units.tr: The consideration of the soul belongs to the natural philosopher, according to Aristotle, 195, p.

units.la: * Animæ brutorum & stirpium, & existunt antequam in corpora sua ingrediantur, & manent postquam ex ijs excesserunt (sed non sub ratione animarum) 198, p. * Animæ amissis facultatibus desinunt esse Animæ, 92, p. * Anima quæcunq; non Rationalis definit esse Anima, simulatq; corpore excedit, omnibusq; facultatibus suis exuitur, 103, p. 143, p. * Animarum plerarumq; partes, simulac à Toto divisæ sunt, redeunt ad naturam simplicis Elementi, 285, f. * Animæ subsistere non valent, si nimium carpantur, 299, p.
units.tr: Souls of brutes and plants both exist before they enter their bodies and remain after they have left them (but not under the aspect of souls), 198, p. Souls cease to be souls once they have lost their faculties, 92, p. Any soul that is not rational ceases to be a soul as soon as it leaves the body and is stripped of all its faculties, 103, p. 143, p. The parts of most souls, as soon as they are divided from the Whole, return to the nature of a simple element, 285, f. Souls cannot subsist if they are too much pulled apart, 299, p.

units.la: Animæ nonnullorum viventium compositæ, diversis Animis in idem conflatis, 124, f. 125. Animæ Animalium, ex heterogeneis parentibus procreatorum, manifestè compositæ, atqué ab utroqué parente aliquid habentes, 134, m. Animæ cuique, præter Mentem, heterogeneas partes assignant. Peripatetici nonnulli, 135. * Animæ omnes perfectiores sunt Composita Dissimilaria, 286, p. * Animæ nonnullarum stirpium & insectorum constant è partibus quantitativis, non modò inter se, sed & Toti similibus; quod contra se habet in majori Animarum parte, 285, f.
units.tr: The souls of some living things are composite, different souls having been fused together into one, 124, f. 125. The souls of animals produced from heterogeneous parents are clearly composite, and have something from each parent, 134, m. Some Peripatetics assign to each soul, besides Mind, heterogeneous parts, 135. All more perfect souls are Dissimilar Composites, 286, p. The souls of some plants and insects consist of quantitative parts, which are alike not only among themselves but also to the Whole; in the greater part of souls the opposite holds, 285, f.

units.la: Anima humana, vid. Mens. * Duæ distinctæ in homine Animæ, 85, m. 95, p. 290, p. 297, p. In homine animas tres, realiter distinctas, statuerunt Peripatetici nonnulli, 115, m. Animæ Immortalitas, vi. Immortalitas. Animas nostras extrinsecus advenire, alicubi docet Aristoteles, 195, m
units.tr: Human soul, see Mind. Two distinct souls in man, 85, m. 95, p. 290, p. 297, p. Some Peripatetics have held that there are three souls in man, really distinct, 115, m. Immortality of the soul, see Immortality. Aristotle teaches somewhere that our souls come to us from outside, 195, m.

units.la: * Anima nequaquam tota in toto, 271, m
units.tr: The soul is by no means wholly in the whole [body], 271, m.

units.la: * Animæ corporibus ita continentur, ut ijs includantur, 116. & 300, m. * Anima corpus sibi fabricatur, 220, f. 346, f. Animæ substantia Facultatibus suis non cooperatur, neque eas circ ad agendum, 1, III. 26. Animam esse Animalis Formam, Finem, & Efficiens; Aristotelis dictum: examinatur, 1, V. 4.
units.tr: Souls are so contained in bodies that they are enclosed by them, 116. and 300, m. The soul fabricates a body for itself, 220, f. 346, f. The substance of the soul does not cooperate with its faculties, nor does it move them to act, I, III, 26. That the soul is the Form, End and Efficient of the animal: a saying of Aristotle, examined, I, V, 4.

units.la: Animarum Materia Platonica, 347, f. Animas esse corpore priores, Platonis opinio, 344, m 345. argumenta, quibus id probare nititur, coarguuntur, 345, f. 346. Sola Anima, Efficiens Platonis eæque omnes æternæ, 2, IV. 4. Omnes Animæ Platoni immortales, ac inter se similes, 343, m. Anima Mundi Platonica, nulla, 198, m.
units.tr: Platonic matter of souls, 347, f. Plato's opinion that souls are prior to bodies, 344, m. 345. The arguments by which he tries to prove this are refuted, 345, f. 346. For Plato the soul alone is the Efficient, and all souls are eternal, 2, IV, 4. For Plato all souls are immortal and similar to one another, 343, m. Platonic World-Soul: none, 198, m.
ANIMAL.

units.la: * Animalia, uti & alia Animata, composita ex Entibus completis: neque tantum ipsa tota, sed & corpora ipsorum, 66, m. Animalis partes essentiales, Anima & Corpus, 362, p. Animalium heterogeneorum genegatio, 134, m. Animalium cibus, 23.
units.tr: Animals, like other animate things, are composed of complete beings: not only the whole animal but also its bodies, 66, m. The essential parts of an animal, soul and body, 362, p. The generation of heterogeneous animals, 134, m. The food of animals, 23.

units.la: * ANIMI impulsio ab Obiecto, vel Obiecti specie, metaphorica duntaxat; quum Animus seipsum libere ac sponte moveat, 236, p.
units.tr: The impulse of the mind from an object, or from the species of an object, is merely metaphorical, since the mind moves itself freely and spontaneously, 236, p.

units.la: ANNIHILATIO, vide INTERITUS. ANTILOGIA, v. CONTRADICTIO. APII e femine enata Alliaria, 138, f. * ad APPETENDUM movemur non ratione ipsa, sed a specie rei, 233, f. * motus ille est duntaxat metaphoricus, 236, p.
units.tr: ANNIHILATION, see DESTRUCTION. ANTILOGY, or CONTRADICTION. Alliaria, sprung from the seed of the apium, 138, f. We are moved to APPETITE not by reason itself but by the appearance of the thing, 233, f. That motion is merely metaphorical, 236, p.
APPLICATION

units.la: Applicatio, tertius eorum modorum, quibus unum agens ab altero cietur ad agendum, 59, m. duo diversi ejus modi, 61, f. Applicatio Animae ad facultates suas interoperandum, nulla intelligi potest, nec propria, nec metaphorica, 2, III, 26.
units.tr: Application is the third of the ways in which one agent is moved by another to act, 59, m. There are two different kinds of it, 61, f. The application of the soul to its faculties for mutual operation can be understood neither properly nor metaphorically, 2, III, 26.

units.la: APTITUDO Materiae secundae frustra ponitur a Peripateticis, si Elementa non manent in Mixto, 1, II, 6.
units.tr: The aptitude of secondary matter is posited in vain by the Peripatetics, if the elements do not remain in the mixed body, 1, II, 6.

units.la: ARBORUM variae permutationes, 139, p. plura vi in Stirpes.
units.tr: The various changes of trees, 139, p. More under Stirpes.
ARISTOTLE

units.la: Aristotelis pleraque dogmata adeo portentosa, ut ipsa illa monstra, in quae sententias Priscorum passim deformat, aut aequent aut antegrediantur, 194, p 210, f. Ex Aristotelis erroribus, praeter eos quos ipsa institutione necessitate passim producimus, & quos Ramus alijq; ante nos exagitaverunt, ingens volumen conficere possumus, 194, p. Aristotelis non minus vera quam ingenua confessio, vespertilioni se suosq; comparantis, 103, f. 104, p. Primus in Philosophiam invexit salsum ac stultum dogma, de Mundi aeternitate, 314, f.
units.tr: Most of Aristotle's doctrines are so monstrous that they either equal or surpass those very monsters into which he distorts the opinions of the ancients everywhere, 194, p; 210, f. Of Aristotle's errors, besides those which we necessarily point out throughout the teaching itself and which Ramus and others before us have attacked, we could compile a huge volume, 194, p. Aristotle's confession, no less true than ingenuous, comparing himself and his people to bats, 103, f; 104, p. He was the first to introduce into philosophy the foolish and absurd doctrine of the eternity of the world, 314, f.

units.la: Aristoteli non insolens, dvorvalloqui, 25, f. sua de Formis placita ipse alicubi evertit, easque extrinsecus advenire vult, 1, III, 70, magna levitate. Privationem invehit pro Principio, quam ipse fateatur non esse ad generationes necessariam, 1, IV, 9, magna inconstantia sibi ipsi contraria dicit uno eodemque in loco, 278, f. aliud inconstantiae ac antilogiarum exemplum, 328, f. scripta ejus innumeris antilogijs scatent, 253, f.
units.tr: It is not unusual for Aristotle to speak equivocally, 25, f. He himself overturns his own opinions about Forms in places, and wants them to come from outside, 1, III, 70, with great levity. He introduces privation as a principle, though he himself admits it is not necessary for generation, 1, IV, 9. With great inconsistency he says things contrary to himself in one and the same place, 278, f. Another example of inconsistency and contradiction, 328, f. His writings abound in countless contradictions, 253, f.

units.la: Mira turbandi atq; diversissimas res in idem confundendi libido, 327, f. 350, f. confusa tractatio de Principijs & Causis, 1, I, 3, & seqq. Variandi sermonis curam majorem gesit, quàm accuratę rerum traditionis, 1, I, 6, f. & 323, p. Confusè admodū ac perversè passim, ubi de Forma agit substantiali, delabitur in mentionem Formæ accidentalis, 1, III, 2. passim adhibet exempla, quę rem multo magis obscurant quàm illustrant, 225 f. sæpe, loco docendi, sophismata & inanes captiunculas nectit, 1, V, 5, 6. & 246, f. solenne ipsi, ita fluctuare, acsi nescierit quid ac quomodo probandum haberet, thesesq; cum probationibus, ac probationes cum thesibus confundere, 172, p. libri ejus physici & metaphysici scatent non falsis modò, sed amethodis prorsus atq; pugnantibus sermonibus, 254. Inconditissima eius fluctuatione vehementissimè offensus summus ipsius Admirator Scaliger, qui acerrime eam castigat multis in locis, 255.
units.tr: A wondrous lust for confusing things and mixing very different things together, 327, f; 350, f. A confused treatment of principles and causes, 1, I, 3, and following. He took more care to vary his language than to deliver the matter accurately, 1, I, 6, f; and 323, p. Very confusedly and perversely, wherever he treats of substantial Form, he slips into mention of accidental Form, 1, III, 2. Everywhere he uses examples that obscure the matter far more than they illustrate it, 225, f. Often, instead of teaching, he weaves sophisms and empty little quibbles, 1, V, 5, 6; and 246, f. It is characteristic of him to waver as though he did not know what he ought to prove or how, and to confuse theses with proofs and proofs with theses, 172, p. His physical and metaphysical books abound not only in false statements but in methodless and utterly contradictory discourses, 254. Scaliger, his greatest admirer, was greatly offended by his disordered wavering, and rebukes it most sharply in many places, 255.

units.la: Gloriatur Aristoteles Formam à se introductam in philosophiam, & tamen ne unum quidem pro ea argumentum attulit, 1, III, 1, 2, 6. similitudines tantum afferens pro omni argumento ad probandam Formam, eas ipsas adhibet dissimillimas, & ex ijs tamen præcipua sua de Forma axiomata excudit, §. 3. 57, 58. mira ejus in hoc negotio vertigo, §. 58. pro Materia prima nullum unquam argumentum produxit, 1, II, 3. Ridiculum exemplum, serram non posse fieri e ligno aut lana, p. 21, m Mirificum ejus dictum, Formam, Finem, & Efficiens, idem esse in naturalibus: vanitatis coarguitur, 1, V, 4.
units.tr: Aristotle boasts that he introduced Form into philosophy, and yet he did not bring forward even one argument for it, 1, III, 1, 2, 6. Offering only comparisons as his whole argument for proving Form, he uses comparisons that are most unlike, and yet from them he hammers out his principal axioms about Form, 3, 57, 58. His dizziness in this matter is remarkable, 58. He never produced any argument for prime matter, 1, II, 3. A ridiculous example: that a saw cannot be made of wood or wool, p. 21, m. His wondrous saying that Form, End and Efficient are the same in natural things is shown to be vanity, 1, V, 4.

units.la: Tractatio ejus de Causis, secundo physicorum institituta, valde manca ac mutila, 1, V, 3, 10, 12. Ennumeratio significationum vocis Principium, facta 5. Metaphi primo, valde misera & confusa, 2, I, 5. In tractatione de Partibus & Toto, admodum confuse & sine delectu congerit illa, è quibus nemo fiat doctior, 266, p. tractatio ejus de Mutilo, plane Philosopho indigna, 295, f. quæstio valde otiosa, de Unitate partium Definitionis, 1, III, 11.
units.tr: His treatment of causes in the second book of the Physics is very defective and mutilated, 1, V, 3, 10, 12. His enumeration of the meanings of the word Principle, made in the fifth book of the Metaphysics, is very wretched and confused, 2, I, 5. In his treatment of parts and whole he very confusedly and without discrimination heaps together things from which no one becomes wiser, 266, p. His treatment of the mutilated is entirely unworthy of a philosopher, 295, f. A question very idle: on the unity of the parts of a definition, 1, III, 11.

units.la: Aristoteli familiare, aliena dogmata, propriæ philosophiæ haudquaquam congrua usurpare pro suis, ijsq; sermonem accommodare, & demonstrationes superstruere, 1, III,4,5,59. & p.330,m. ac 1,V,9,p. ita conditionem Æternitatis, à Veteribus attributam Principijs primis, per summam impudentiam, ad Principia sua interna transtulit, 337,f, 338,p.
units.tr: It is familiar to Aristotle to appropriate as his own doctrines foreign to his own philosophy by no means agreeing with it, to adapt his discourse to them, and to build demonstrations upon them, 1, III, 4, 5, 59; and p. 330, m; and 1, V, 9, p. Thus, with the greatest impudence, he transferred to his own internal principles the condition of eternity, which the ancients had attributed to first principles, 337, f; 338, p.

units.la: Veterum axioma, Ex nihilo nihil fieri, ac, substantias non generari, maligne in alienum sensum detorquet, 1,II,1.& 1,III,47.itemq; aliud, Agentia naturalia agere necessario, 1, V, 9. calumnia in Veteres, quòd Principium Materiale tantùm posuerint, non Essectivum, 2, III, 2. manifestissima calumnia in Platonem præceptorem, quòd sola Materiali ac Formali Causa usus sit, 2, V, 8, 12. sæpe quæsivit, quomodo à Priscis dissentirét, etiam ubi plane eorum sequebatur opinionem, ideoq; eorum sententias dedita operâ in omnia alia distorsit, 320, f. suetum ipsi, Priscis mera opinionum monstra affingere, & tamen alijs in locis ea prodere, unde calumniæ falsitas liquido dilucescat: quod insigni in Parmenide exemplo docetur, 2,III,5.
units.tr: He maliciously twists the ancient axiom, Nothing comes from nothing, and that substances are not generated, into a foreign sense, 1, II, 1; and 1, III, 47; likewise another, Natural agents act necessarily, 1, V, 9. He slanders the ancients for having posited only a material principle and not an efficient one, 2, III, 2. The most manifest slander against Plato his teacher, that he used only the material and formal cause, 2, V, 8, 12. He often sought how he might differ from the ancients, even where he was plainly following their opinion, and so deliberately distorted their opinions into every other shape, 320, f. He was accustomed to attribute to the ancients sheer monstrosities of opinion, and yet in other places to set forth those same opinions, whereby the falsity of the calumny becomes clear; this is shown by the notable example of Parmenides, 2, III, 5.

units.la: Aristoteles multa mala multis bonis pensavit, & non prava tantum ac damnosa scripta, sed & egregia ac fructuosa nobis reliquit: ideoq; moderatio in ipso reprehendendo servanda, 257,m.
units.tr: Aristotle weighed many evils against many goods, and he left us not only corrupt and harmful writings but also excellent and fruitful ones. Therefore moderation must be observed in reprehending him, 257, m.
ARISTOTELIANS.

units.la: Aristotelici nimium creduli præceptori suo, 1,III,59. Aristotelicis in more, dicta at decreta præceptoris non examinare, sed pro oraculis venerari, 174,f. Dum Aristotelis omnia dicta propugnare volunt, ad plurima summe absurda comminiscenda adigantur, 202,f.210,f.211,p. 337,p. passim nihil pensi habent, quam fatuum sit aut vecors quod dicunt, dum Aristotelem habeant autorem, ejusq; propugnandi aliquam viam ineant, 164,f.165,p: 187,f.188,p. Aristotelicis certum, hypothèses suas defendere, in quæcunq; tandem absurda detrudantur; unde saepe mirificas admodum solutiones comminisci coguntur, 232, f. 233, p. saepe mera monstra proferunt, 235, p. solenne ipsis, ut quidvis sibi dicere permittant, 159, m. 169, p. praeconceptarum opinionum amore adeo seipsos excaecant, ut videre non possint res cuivis etiam idiotae apertissimas, 161, f. Non raro, ad tuendas deliras quasdam naemias, in ipsorum aut Aristotelis cerebro natas, sustinent ea afferre, in quibus certissimo sensuum indicio falsi revincuntur, 103, m. suetum ipsis, contradictionibus involvi, 1, III. 17, f. Mirabilis ipsorum audacia in difficultatibus solvendis, & in quidvis fingendo, 60, m. Familiariter in probationibus suis circulum committunt: quod alicubi ingenue fatetur Suarez, 99, p. omnes loquendi leges quandoq; pervertunt, 151, m. enormia opinionum portenta, ex Aristotelis hypothesibus fluentia, tantum abest ut ipsos de ijs repudiandis cogitare faciant, ut ipsa quoq; pro verissimis axiomatis amplectantur, 254, f. Perpetuum ipsorum fatum, ut dum Praeceptorem ab antilogijs vindicare satagunt, in maximas incidant absurditates, 253, f.
units.tr: The Aristotelians are too credulous toward their master, and they do not examine the sayings and decrees of their teacher but venerate them as oracles, 1, III, 59; 174, f. While they wish to defend all of Aristotle's sayings, they are driven to invent many things that are utterly absurd, 202, f.; 210, f.; 211, p.; 337, p.; and throughout, they take no account of how foolish or senseless what they say is, so long as they have Aristotle as their authority and can find some way of defending him, 164, f.; 165, p.; 187, f.; 188, p. For the Aristotelians it is certain that they must defend their hypotheses, however absurd the things into which these are thrust; hence they are often compelled to devise remarkably contrived solutions, 232, f.; 233, p. They often put forward sheer monsters, 235, p. It is customary for them to allow themselves to say whatever they please, 159, m.; 169, p. Through love of their preconceived opinions they so blind themselves that they cannot see things that are most obvious even to any layman, 161, f. Not infrequently, to defend certain absurd fancies born in their own or Aristotle's brain, they venture to assert things by which they are refuted by the most certain evidence of the senses, 103, m. It is their habit to become entangled in contradictions, 1, III, 17, f. Their boldness in resolving difficulties and in inventing anything is remarkable, 60, m. In their proofs they freely commit circular reasoning, which Suárez frankly admits somewhere, 99, p. At times they pervert all the laws of speech, 151, m. The monstrous opinions that flow from Aristotle's hypotheses are so far from making them think of rejecting them that they embrace them even as most certain axioms, 254, f. It is the constant lot of these men that, while they strive to vindicate their Master from contradictions, they fall into the greatest absurdities, 253, f.

They absurdly prove Form through prime Matter, though they must concede that this cannot be proved except through Form, 1, III, 7. units.la: Unitas Compositi non pendet a Forma, ut Peripatetici somniant, 1,III, 11, uti neq; altera rerum Unitas, ut sint Unum essentialiter, ac non acervu, §. 18. Ens simpliciter Unum potest e pluribus Entibus completis constituri, ibid. Unam per se Essentiam fieri ex Subjecto & Accidentibus separabilibus, contra Fonsecam monstratur, 1,III, 21. Unitatem Veram cum Unitate Simplici, & Unitatem Numeralem cum Naturali perperam confundunt Peripatetici, 67, f. 68. Unitas Compositi ex Partium componentium concursu exurgit, 264, m. Res Unitatem simplicem sorticæ, 68, m. Varij modi Unionis partium Essentialium, seu Principiorum Compositivorum, 300, m. Accidentia non uniuntur, nisi Unione subjecti, 300, f. Diversæ plantæ in unum coalescunt quandoque, 125.
units.tr: The unity of a compound does not depend on form, as the Peripatetics dream, 1, III, 11; nor does the other unity of things, so that things are one essentially and not as a heap, §. 18. A being that is simply one can be constituted from several complete beings, ibid. That one essence is made per se from a subject and separable accidents is shown against Fonseca, 1, III, 21. The Peripatetics wrongly confuse true unity with simple unity, and numerical unity with natural unity, 67, f. 68. The unity of a compound arises from the concurrence of its component parts, 264, m. Things obtain simple unity, 68, m. Various modes of union of the essential parts, or compositive principles, 300, m. Accidents are not united except by the union of their subject, 300, f. Different plants sometimes grow together into one, 125.

units.la: Unitatem Formæ in uno corpore, necessariò ex hypothesibus de Forma fluentem, multa premunt absurda; quibus adacti multi de Peripateticis, plures in uno corpore Formas statuerunt, 1, III, 36. sed eos, qui ita faciunt, nihilo melius sibi consulere, inq; alia haud minora incommoda incidere, monstratur, §. 37. 38. 39.
units.tr: Many absurdities press upon the unity of form in one body, which necessarily flows from hypotheses about form; driven by these, many of the Peripatetics, and more, have posited several forms in one body, 1, III, 36. But it is shown that those who do so do no better for themselves, and fall into other no less serious inconveniences, §. 37, 38, 39.
